->§. 1.<-

Distinctive divine Wisdom has most gloriously and holily represented—through the Israelite Tabernacle and the Temple construction, along with its service—both the outer mortal tabernacle of our body (which is born out as either male or female according to the two natures or <term>tinctures: In the mystical tradition of Jacob Boehme, "tinctures" refer to the essential spiritual qualities or life-forces—often divided into "fire" (masculine) and "light" (feminine)—that animate all of creation.</term>), as well as the inner eternal spirit-tabernacle and temple of our souls after the Holy Rebirth <note>referring to the spiritual transformation or "being born again" described in the New Testament.</note>, wherein we are neither man nor woman, but one in Christ. The Tabernacle with its various coverings (Exodus 26) and the Temple with its holy forecourts are one and the same. The male forecourt of Israel was more inward; the female was more outward, which the Gentile <note>original: "Heidniſche," referring to non-Jewish people.</note> forecourt surrounded, which did not actually belong to the Temple. Those two forecourts indicate the two separate bodily tabernacles of the male and female sex. ->The character and physical appearance of the Virgin Mary are described by Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a bishop and author who wrote about the early history of the Church.</note> in the works of Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos was a 14th-century Byzantine historian who compiled earlier traditions.</note> as follows:<-

She was honorable and serious in all her dealings, spoke little and only what was necessary, but listened gladly; and she was very affectionate toward all, showing the proper respect. In height, she was of average stature, or slightly above. In speech, she possessed a modest frankness toward all people, without laughter or confusion, and was free from all anger. Her complexion tended slightly toward yellowish <note>original: "Gelbliche." This likely refers to a "wheat-colored" or olive complexion common in Mediterranean historical descriptions.</note>, she had brown hair, and sharp eyes that were yellowish-white with brown irises. Her eyebrows were elegantly placed and blackish. Her nose was somewhat elongated, and her lips were red and full of pleasant words. Her face was neither round nor pointed, but somewhat elongated, as were her hands and fingers. One sensed no pride in her, but rather simplicity shone forth from her sincere face; nothing pampered or delicate was seen in her, but rather an exceptional humility. Her clothing was plain and undyed, as her surviving holy head-covering <note>The "holy head-covering" refers to a relic of Mary's veil (maphorion) which was historically claimed to be preserved in Constantinople.</note> still testifies. In short: in all things about her, something divine shone forth. She passed away <note>The text uses the euphemism "entschlief" (fell asleep) to refer to her death or Dormition.</note> in Jerusalem / in the house of John the Evangelist, when she was almost 60 years old, in the fifth year of Emperor Claudius / in the year 45 after the birth of our Lord, and in the 12th year after His Ascension. Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, chapter 23 <note>original: "Niceph. L.2. Hist. Eccl. c. 23."</note>.

<header>II. The Life of St. Syncletica <note>Syncletica of Alexandria (c. 270–350 AD) was a Christian saint and "Desert Mother" of the early church, known for her asceticism and wisdom.</note>.</header>

The worldly <note>original: "fältigen," likely referring to the "many" or the common, worldly people.</note> know little of what is truly useful; this 
befalls them because they have let their minds become
altogether clumsy through negligence. Thus, the most precious
pearls often fall into the hands of poor and lowly people; 
but he who does not know the art of handling them 
regards them then as minor things. In this manner, 
we also did not initially value this present pearl 
when we first obtained it—because our mind was 
still quite childish, unpracticed, and inexperienced; 
hence we looked merely at the outward appearance 
and remained far removed from the knowledge of her 
nature itself. But after we recognized her beauty 
a little from the conclusion <note>likely referring to the conclusion of her life or the summary of her works.</note>, a divine love for her 
was planted in us, because the matters themselves 
awakened the desire within us. But what do we say 
of these present things, or how can we count ourselves 
among those who could know or say anything of the 
excellent Syncletica? For we believe that all men 
are too lowly to recount her good works. But if 
someone takes it upon themselves to speak of them, 
and be they ever so wise and learned, they will 
nevertheless fail in what is required for it; for 
just as those suffer damage to their sight who 
frequently wish to look into the sun; so, he 
who wishes to look most closely at her life 
will get a kind of dizziness from her great deeds, 
so that he will either withdraw or find his 
thoughts confused out of weakness. Nevertheless, 
we wish here to follow her affairs according to our 
strength, and to begin to write what we have learned 
from those who grew up with her regarding her early 
life, and also otherwise, since they are in part 
somewhat enlightened by her works themselves, 
so that we may lay up for ourselves, as it were, 
a holy food as a treasure; for to speak of it 
with proper dignity is not only impossible for 
us, but also difficult for many others.

...having arrived there <note>referring to Alexandria, the great center of learning and faith in Egypt</note>, and finding even more than they had heard, they gladly lived there. However, they had no desire for the multitude of people, nor were they amazed by the great crowd; instead, after having found a simple faith with a pure love, they preferred the state of pilgrimage to their own homeland. The blessed Syncletica was well-provided for, both by her noble lineage and by the other charming things of this life. She had one sister who was of the same mind as her, as well as two brothers who were likewise raised in a well-ordered life; one died in his childhood, and the other was married off by his parents in the twenty-fifth year of his age. But when everything was prepared for the undertaking, and the betrothal had taken place according to custom, this youth flew like a bird from the snares <note>A reference to Psalm 124:7, suggesting he escaped the "trap" of worldly life through a timely death</note>, and exchanged his earthly bride for the blameless and free community of the saints. She herself, however, while she was still being raised by her parents, was well-practiced in the love of God above all things. She did not care so much for her body, but rather kept a close watch over the desires of nature. For she was pure and exceedingly beautiful in body, so that in her youth many courted her—partly out of desire for her wealth, partly because of the noble status of her parents, and especially because of her beauty. Her parents also pressured her greatly to marry in order to preserve their lineage; but she was so wise and magnanimous that she would not give her will over to it at all. Instead, whenever she heard of worldly marriage, she was intent upon a divine life, and thus she rejected many suitors so that she might incline her heart alone to the heavenly bridegroom <note>The "heavenly bridegroom" is a traditional metaphor for Jesus Christ in monastic literature</note>.

## Chapter 3.
### A comparison with Saint Thecla, along with her great earnestness.

One saw in her a true disciple of the blessed Thecla <note>Saint Thecla was a legendary 1st-century follower of the Apostle Paul and a model for female Christian ascetics</note>, because she followed the very same teachings. For they both had one bridegroom, Christ, and one bridal-attendant, Paul; I also believe they shared the same bridal bed, namely the Church. David also sings of this in both glorious and divine psalms; for he gladdens the God-dedicated souls with well-sounding cymbals, and gives them the most perfect song upon the ten-stringed psaltery. Miriam <note>The sister of Moses; in the early church, she was often viewed as a leader of virgins</note> also leads the dancers into this holy wedding, who say: Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously exalted. They also struggled together, for the martyrdom of the blessed Thecla <note>St. Thecla was a legendary early Christian saint and follower of St. Paul, famous for surviving fire and wild beasts in the arena.</note> is unknown to no one—how she had to struggle and fight with fire and wild beasts. And I consider that Thecla labored less, because the enemy in his malice was overcome when he fought her from the outside; but against this woman, he showed a more violent malice, attacking her from within through evil thoughts.

No beautiful dress could deceive her, nor all kinds of beautiful gemstones; no music deceived her ears, nor did any instruments deceive the earnestness of her soul. No tears from her parents could soften her, nor any other admonition from her relatives; rather, she had a mind as firm as adamant <note>original: *Demant*, meaning diamond-hard or unbreakable.</note>, and would not be turned away. She closed all her senses like doors so that she might converse with her Bridegroom alone, and spoke from the Scripture:
> I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine. <note>original: Cant. 2, v. 16; refers to the Canticle of Canticles, or Song of Solomon 2:16.</note>

Whenever they happened upon impure or dark conversations, she would walk away and gather herself in the inner chamber of her soul. But where one heard of wholesome and enlightened admonitions, there she used her whole intellect to grasp what was said.

For when that which rules the body <note>the soul or spirit</note> is troubled, then the body itself is changed. ## II. The Life of St. Syncletica.

[...one who] takes [nourishment] is fresh and healthy of body; whereas another becomes thin and dry, as the weak testify. Since the Blessed One sought to weaken her body, her spirit was all the more cheerful; and it happened as the Apostle says: **The more the outer man perishes, the more the inner man is renewed.** <note>original: 2 Cor. 4, v.16.</note> Thus she practiced herself, so that many did not know of it. After the death of her parents, she was driven even more by the Spirit of God; she took her sister with her, who was blind, left her father’s house, and hid herself in a relative's tomb <note>Living in tombs was a common practice for early Christian ascetics in Egypt, symbolizing a "death to the world."</note> located far from the city. She had sold all her remaining goods and distributed them to the poor; she called one of the elders to her, cut off her hair, and thereby laid aside all her adornment, for women are accustomed to call their hair their adornment. This was only a sign of how her soul would become pure and without any excess; and only then was she worthy of the name of a virgin. 

After she had given all her possessions to the poor, she said: "I have become worthy of a great name, yet I have nothing fitting with which I can repay Him who granted it to me. For if some, in outward things, risk all their goods for the sake of a fleeting honor; how much more must I, alongside these so-called goods, also give up my body. But what can I say of the gifts of goods and of the body, since everything belongs to Him? **For the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.**" <note>original: Ps. 24, v. 1.</note> And through such words she established herself firmly in humility and led a quiet life. She was already well-practiced in labor in her father’s house, and she grew all the more in virtues now that she stood at the head of the battleground <note>original: *Kampf-Platz*, referring to the spiritual arena where the ascetic struggles against temptation.</note>. 

For whoever has committed himself to this divine mystery without practice and caution has not attained his goal, because he has not first considered everything well; for just as one who wishes to travel first concerns himself with travel-money <term>Zehr-Pfennig: literally "consumption penny," referring to the funds or provisions needed to sustain a traveler on a journey.</term>; so, since she had well prepared herself through her previous labor, as if with travel-money, she began her pilgrimage undaunted. She first procured everything that belongs to the building of a house, and then she completed her strong tower. Physical buildings are built outwardly from all kinds of external materials; she, however, did the opposite; for she did not gather external things, but rather emptied her inner self of them. For as she gave what was hers to the poor, and abandoned anger as well as craving <note>original: *Nachgier*, an archaic term for persistent longing, envy, or greed.</note>, she also...

# II. The Life of St. Syncletica.

[...she] drove away envy and ambition; she built her house upon a rock, whose tower was clearly visible, and the structure could be damaged by no storm.

### Chapter 5.
->Her Growth and Vigilance.<-

And what more shall I say? Even in the beginning, she surpassed those who had long practiced the solitary life; for just as well-behaved children, even while learning their ABCs, often outpace others who are older and more experienced, so was she so fervent in spirit that she outstripped the rest. Her labor-blessed and <term>ascetic|a lifestyle of rigorous self-denial and spiritual discipline</term> life is not easily described; for she let no one watch her in it and desired no one to praise her **manly** <note>In early Christian literature, "manly" (männlich) was a common term of praise for women who showed exceptional spiritual strength, endurance, and fortitude.</note> deeds. Indeed, she did not seek so much to do good as to preserve and hide it; and this was not out of envy, but from the instruction of Divine Grace; for she always held the word of the Lord in her heart: **"When your right hand does something, let not your left hand know it"** <note>original: Matth. 6, v. 3.</note>. And thus she performed everything in secret that belonged to her profession of faith. 

From her childhood until old age, she not only fled the company of men but also often turned away women; and this for two reasons: partly so that she would not be praised for her extraordinary, God-blessed practices, and partly so that she would not stray from virtue through physical social interaction. She took great care regarding the first impulses in her soul, not allowing them to be carried away by fleshly desires; just as a tree is pruned because of its barren shoots. She quickly and successfully cleared away all the thorny outbursts of the mind through fasting and prayer. And if anything peeked through in the slightest, she inflicted all kinds of hardships upon it and subdued her body through various labors.

### Chapter 6.
->Her Moderation and Heroic Courage.<-

She was satisfied with little bread, which barely stilled her hunger, and drank water only as much as was strictly necessary. As often as the **enemy** <note>In this context, "the enemy" refers to the devil or personified spiritual temptation.</note> stirred up a struggle against her, she called upon her Lord above all things as her fellow combatant; for it was not enough for her to repel the onslaughts of life through mere practice alone. The Lord was also immediately present at her prayer, and the enemy had to flee; yet He sometimes delayed and did not drive him away instantly, so that...

## II. The Life of St. Syncletica.

...the virtuous soul would become all the stronger in her practice; thus, through the increase of her spiritual gifts, she became ever more powerful for victory over the Enemy <note>In this context, "the Enemy" refers to the devil or demonic temptations common in desert monasticism.</note>. It was also not enough for her to **mortify** <term>mortify|from the Latin 'mortificare', meaning to 'put to death' the desires of the flesh through self-denial</term> herself with meager food; rather, she sought to distance herself from every other delicate way of life. She ate mostly only bran bread and often did not even drink water, sleeping for a time on the bare earth as long as the struggle lasted. She used such weapons as these: she put on prayer as a shield and a bow; her helmet was prepared from faith, hope, and love. Yet faith preceded the others and held all the members of the soul together, as it were. Nor did she lack mercy—though not in deed <note>As a recluse in a tomb, she had no possessions to give away, so her "mercy" was expressed through her intent and her prayers for others.</note>, but certainly in her intent. 

When she had overcome the Enemy through these means, she ceased this strict way of life so that her body would not completely collapse. This was a sign of her humility; for what hope for battle does a soldier have if his weapons fall away? For this reason, some who have consumed themselves through excessive and thoughtless fasting have fatally wounded and ruined themselves, like one who is no longer a match for the enemy. But she did not act in this way; instead, she did everything with **discernment** <term>discernment|the spiritual gift of 'discretio', or knowing the proper measure in all things to avoid the traps of pride or exhaustion</term>. 

Against the Enemy, she fought bravely through prayer and holy practice; but so that her own ship might proceed more calmly, she also provided for the body. For even sailors remain sober during a raging storm and pit all their skill against the obvious danger; but when they are once again safe in their lives, they also care for their own preservation. They do not always face tempests but also enjoy some rest during the calm; yet even then, they are not without worry, because they have learned much from the past and weigh the future carefully. For although the storm has subsided, the sea has not become any smaller because of it; and when the second wave is over, the third is still to come. Indeed, even when the event has passed, its cause remains present. So it is in this matter: even if the spirit of lust is driven out, the one who has power over it is not far away; therefore, one must pray without ceasing because the sea is unstable and the Enemy is violently embittered.

...and 60-fold and 30-fold <note>These figures refer to the Parable of the Sower in Matthew 13, representing different degrees of spiritual fruitfulness.</note>. The hundred-fold is our way of life, the sixty-fold is the company of the continent <term>continent|those practicing 'Enthaltsamkeit' or ascetic self-restraint, particularly celibacy</term>, and the thirty-fold belongs to those who, following wisdom, remain in ordinary life. Now it is good to come from the thirty-fold to the sixty-fold, because it is beautiful to grow from the smaller to the greater. But to go back from the greater to the lesser is not without danger. For whoever once turns toward the worse cannot remain even in the least [state], but is instead dragged away as if into the depths of perdition. 

Therefore, when some have committed themselves to virginity, but are enticed by their own reasoning out of a weakness of the mind, they seek to excuse their sins; for they say to themselves—or rather to the Devil: "If I live temperately (though in truth, foolishly) in ordinary life, I will at least enjoy the thirty-fold harvest"; for, they say, the entire Old Testament remained within the procreation of children. So let it be known to whoever is thus minded that such thoughts come from the Enemy. For whoever comes down from the greater to the smaller without a divine cause is overthrown by the Adversary <note>original: 'Widerwärtigen', meaning the opponent or the Devil</note> and is regarded as a deserting soldier; nor is he spared because he has entered into a lesser service, but rather he is punished because he has thoughtlessly run away from his post. 

Therefore we must, as I have said, go from the smaller to the greater, and indeed as the Apostle teaches: *Forgetting everything that is behind, and reaching out for what is before us.* Philippians 3, v. 13. Thus, those who have the hundred-fold must apply it to themselves and put no end to the number; for He says: *When you have done everything, say: We are useless servants.* Luke 17, v. 10.

## II. The Life of Saint Syncletica.

...[as an] instrument of songs of praise, should bring forth shameful words. Indeed, one should be ashamed not only to speak such things, but also to do them. However, it is impossible for us to maintain this state if we do not go among people with great caution. For thieves enter through our senses even against our will. And how can a house remain unblackened by soot if smoke is made outside and the doors are left open? Therefore, it is highly necessary that we avoid going out to public places as much as possible. For if we recognize it as unseemly to look upon our own brothers or parents while they are naked, how much more harmful will it be for us if we perceive indecent exposures on the streets and are forced to hear unchaste words, from which unseemly and pestilential images arise. 

But even when we hide ourselves at home, we must not be without concern even there, but must remain vigilant; for it is written: *Watch!* <note>original: 'Wachet!'; see Matthew 24:42</note>. The more firmly we establish ourselves in abstinence <term>abstinence|'Enthaltung', refers here to ascetic self-denial and the avoidance of worldly pleasures</term>, the more violent are the thoughts with which we must fight. For it is said: *He who increases knowledge, increases pain.* <note>original: 'Wer Erkänntniß darzu setzet, der wird Schmerzen darzu setzen'; Ecclesiastes 1:18</note>. Likewise, *the flesh lusts against the spirit.* <note>Galatians 5:17</note>. And the more the combatants <note>The 'combatants' are the ascetics or monks who view their spiritual life as a form of holy warfare.</note> grow in strength, the greater are the adversaries they have to deal with. 

See to it, then, what you have already escaped from, and do not think lightly of your present trials. If you have overcome physical and actual fornication <term>fornication|'Hurerey', used here in a broad sense to mean any sexual immorality or lustful act</term>, behold, the enemy then assails you with that which happens through the senses. And even if you abstain from this—because fornication is the foremost evil—the enemy still lies hidden in the camp of your thoughts and stirs up a spiritual (immaterial) war. For he suggests to the one living in solitude all kinds of evil visions, unseemly figures, and their former conversations. But one must not give approval to such fantasies, for it is written: *Abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul.* <note>1 Peter 2:11</note>. 

Therefore, the struggle against fornication is very great, and this is the enemy's primary tool for the destruction of the soul. The blessed Job hints at this when he speaks of the demon of fornication: *His strength is in the navel of his belly.* <note>original: 'Seine Kraft ist im Nabel seines Bauchs'; Job 40:11 (in modern bibles, Job 40:16). Indeed, the villain has even at times perverted brotherly love into his own wickedness. ## Chapter 10.
### Regarding Vigilance against Satan, Evil Thoughts, and Evil Lusts.

What should we do then in this regard? *Let us become wise as serpents and innocent as doves* <note>original: 'klug wie die Schlangen, und ohne Falsch wie die Tauben'</note> Matthew 10:16, so that we may employ all careful precautions against his snares. For the words "be serpents" are said so that the assaults of the devil might not be hidden from us; for a thing can be recognized most quickly by its like. The innocence of the dove, however, signifies the purity of one's works. If all good works consist in the avoidance of evil, how shall we escape that which we do not recognize? Therefore, we must take the cunning of the enemy to heart and guard ourselves against his evil schemes. For it is written: *He goes about and seeks whom he may devour.* 1 Peter 5:8. And his baits are choice.

Therefore, one must always be on watch; for through external things he battles us, and through internal thoughts he conquers us; yes indeed, through the internal ones, because he approaches us in a spiritual manner day and night. What then is necessary for us in such a battle? Nothing but diligent practice and pure prayer. And these indeed are the general means against all destructive thoughts. We must also use specific remedies to drive away the present corruption of the soul: when a shameful thought occurs to us, we must set a good one against it. 

If there were an image of a beautiful face in the mind, it must be rebuked by the Word: Tear out the eyes of the idol, mangle its cheeks, cut off its lips, and see then the hideous bones, and despise that which is common even to the cattle. <note>This "memento mori" style of meditation was common in early monasticism; by mentally visualizing the skull beneath the skin, the monk sought to break the power of physical attraction.</note> For to one whose thoughts are thus redirected, they can be brought back from vain error. In such a way must shameful malice be driven away; and just as one nail drives out another <note>A common proverb of the time meaning that a strong new impression or habit can displace an old one.</note>, so must one drive out the evil spirit. Beyond this, one must discipline the body...

### Chapter 11.
#### Saint Syncletica’s Teaching on Holy Poverty.

This was now a truly divine banquet for the assembled persons, where they were gladdened by the cup of wisdom, and the blessed Syncletica poured out the divine drink for them. Each one accepted what she wished. However, one of them asked this: whether absolute poverty was a perfect good? To which she replied: It is certainly a perfect good for those who are capable of it. For those who endure in it experience indeed tribulation in the flesh, but rest in the soul; for just as sturdy clothes are only truly washed and made white through forceful stomping and rubbing, so also is a soul that is already strong further strengthened through voluntary poverty. 

But those who are of a heavy spirit <note>meaning those who are spiritually weak or still attached to the world</note> experience the opposite. For if they are required to suffer even a little, they perish, being unable to endure the refining torment through virtue. The washing process and the master-craftsman are the same for both, but the outcome is different; for the latter tear and perish, while the former become white and beautiful. 

Thus, one might well call voluntary poverty a magnificent jewel for a courageous <note>original: "Männliche" (masculine). In early ascetic texts, this referred to spiritual fortitude and strength of character, regardless of the person's gender.</note> soul, for it is a bridle against actual sins. Yet one must first practice the initial steps—namely fasting, sleeping on the ground, and similar partial disciplines—before one can attain the rest. Whoever does not do this, but immediately casts away their goods, usually regrets it soon. For wealth is a tool of a pleasure-seeking life; therefore, first abolish your gluttony and lust, and then you will be able to prune your possessions quite easily. For it is a hard thing when the habit of luxury remains, but the tools for it are missing. And if the first is not cast off, how can one be rid of the other? 

Therefore, when the Savior spoke with the rich man, He did not immediately command the casting away of his goods, but first asked whether he had kept the commandments. Matthew 19:16. Thus the Lord proved Himself a righteous master, asking him: have you learned the letters, have you grasped the syllables, and gained a knowledge of words? If so, then proceed afterward to the complete...

Furthermore, the enemy <note>a common term for the devil or spiritual tempter</note> is much more easily overcome by such poor ones, because he has nothing through which he can harm them. For the greatest sorrow and temptation arises over the loss of possessions. But here, the Adversary can do nothing of the sort. Should he set fire to their goods? There are none. Destroy their livestock? They have none. Lay hands on their most beloved things? These too they have long since renounced. Is voluntary poverty then not a great plague to the enemy and a precious treasure of the soul?

It would be a great thing if we could endure as much effort in caring for true goods as the lovers of the vain world endure. They suffer shipwreck, they venture among robbers, they fall among murderers, they endure storm and weather, and when they have taken something, they still pretend to be poor because of those who envy them. We, however, do not take so much danger upon ourselves for the sake of a true conscience. 

And if we ever achieve even a little, we make ourselves great with it and boast before people, and indeed often do not even tell the truth. Thus, through the enemy’s <note>Referring to the Devil.</note> cunning, we lose everything before we have rightly gained even a spark of the good. Those people, the more they have won, the more they desire, holding what they have at present as nothing and seeking what is to come: We, however, though we have nothing visible, yet do not wish to acquire anything heavenly; and while we lie sick in the direst poverty, we still praise ourselves as rich. Therefore, it is good that whoever does something good reveals it to no one. For such people will suffer all the more harm, because even that which they think they have will be taken from them.

## Chapter 16.
->Concerning Vigilance Against Various Enemies.<-

**B**ut the more we strive for spiritual growth <note>original: "Wachstuhm"</note>, the more that one <note>This refers to the Devil or the Adversary.</note> seeks to hinder us through his snares. And is it any wonder that we have adversaries when we strive for the good, since they begrudge us even in minor things? Yes, they do not even allow people to take buried treasures out of the earth: If they are thus opposed to us in earthly, apparent things, how much more will they begrudge us the Kingdom of Heaven. Therefore, one must be armed in every way against them. For they assault us from without as well as from within. And our soul becomes, as it were, like a ship, sometimes overwhelmed by external floods, but sometimes by internal filth <note>The text uses "Wust" (rubbish/mess), likely referring here to the bilge water that accumulates inside a ship.</note>; thus we are sometimes ruined by external forces, and sometimes we are brought to nothing by internal thoughts. Therefore, one must take heed of the external attacks of spirits as well as, so to speak, scoop out the internal impurities of thoughts; especially must one always watch against thoughts, for they are unceasingly present. When sailors cry out during external storms, they are often saved by the nearest ships: But if they have water inside the ship and sleep while doing so, then death overtakes them even in the greatest calm. Thus one must fight more vehemently against thoughts; For the enemy, who wishes to overturn the soul like a house, attempts its fall either from the foundation, or tears it down completely starting from the roof, or creeps in through the window, first binds the Master of the House, and thus overpowers everything. The foundation is good works, the roof is faith, the windows are the senses. Through all these the enemy fights: so that whoever wishes to be saved must have many eyes. For here no carelessness applies, as the Scripture says: *Let him who stands take heed lest he fall.* 1 Cor. 10, v. 12. We sail in uncertainty, and our life is called a sea by the holy singer David. Ps. 104, v. 25. Now in the sea there are rocky cliffs, strange beasts, and also quiet places. ### Chapter 17.

->Warning against Complacency, Pride, and Disobedience.<-

These words serve to prevent one from becoming haughty. He who has fallen will be saved through turning back and sighing. But you, who stand, look to yourself. Two kinds of fear lie before you: either that you fall back into your former ways when the enemy attacks you during your negligence, or that you might be tripped up <note>original: "untertreten," literally to be stepped on or undermined</note> in the middle of your race. For our enemy the devil either pulls one toward himself from behind—when he sees the soul is idle and lazy—or, if the soul seems to be diligent and hardworking in its spiritual practice, he sneaks in secretly through pride <term>Pride (Hochmuht): In this ascetic context, this refers to spiritual arrogance, where a person attributes their progress to their own strength rather than divine grace.</term> and thus ruins the soul. This lure is the last and highest of all evils. Through it, the devil himself fell, and he still overcomes even the bravest spirits with it. For just as the bravest soldiers, when they have shot their small arrows and still see enemies remaining, draw their strongest weapon, namely the sword; so, when the devil has lost his first snares, he uses his final sword: pride. What were his first snares? Certainly intemperance, sensuality, and impurity. For these spirits especially attack young people, followed by greed and the desire to have more. Now, when the wretched soul has overcome all this—when it keeps the belly in check, when it conquers fleshly lusts through modesty, and despises money—then the villain does not know what he should

A soul so deceived is corrupted and brought to nothing because it has received an almost incurable wound. What, then, is to be done when such thoughts manifest themselves? Let them be made to perform all kinds of service, and present to them the most excellent ways of life of the Saints; and the others should strive for several days to carry their spiritual exercises to the highest degree, so that the person may see the height of such virtues and consider themselves lesser. Before this ailment, however, precedes another evil, namely disobedience: which is to be healed through its opposite, namely obedience. For it is said: **Obedience is better than sacrifice. 1 Samuel 15:22.**

For the Devil, who desires to overturn everything, seeks to hide the sins of those who are diligent and practiced, for he loves to see pride grow. He presents to the person a heap of good works and makes them forget all their sins, so that they might exalt themselves over their companions. He removes their misdeeds from their mind, and does this not for their benefit, but only so that they cannot speak these healing words: **Against you alone have I sinned, have mercy on me, O Lord God.** <note>original: "Ps. 51. v. 6." In modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 51:4.</note> He also will not allow them to say: *Lord, I will confess to you with my whole heart.* Instead, just as he said in his own heart, *I will ascend into the heights, and set my throne on high;* <note>Isaiah 14:13</note> so he also suggests to such a person thoughts of dominion, of the seat of honor, of mastery, and of the gift of healing. A soul so deceived is corrupted and destroyed because it has received an almost incurable wound. 

What then is to be done when such thoughts manifest? One must remember the Divine Word without ceasing, as the blessed David cried out, saying: **I am a worm and no man,** <note>Psalm 22:6</note> and elsewhere it is said: **But I am earth and ashes.** <note>Genesis 18:27</note> Likewise, the memorable words of Isaiah read: **All the righteousness of man is like a stained garment.** <note>Isaiah 64:6</note> If such thoughts come to someone who lives in isolation, let them go into a communal monastery <term>communal monastery (gemein Kloster): a "cenobitic" house where monks live and work together, rather than living as solitary hermits</term>. Let them be brought food twice a day, if they have perhaps fallen into this condition through excessive fasting; their companions must scold and rebuke them as if they had done nothing special. Let them be made to perform all kinds of menial service, and present to them the most excellent ways of life of the Saints; the others should strive for a few days to carry their own spiritual exercises to the highest degree, so that the proud person may see the greatness of such virtues and consider themselves insignificant. But before this affliction, another evil often occurs, namely disobedience: which is to be healed through its opposite, namely obedience. For it is written: **Obedience is better than sacrifice.** <note>1 Samuel 15:22</note>

### Chapter 19.

->On Humility.<-

Thus it is now manifest that among all evils, pride is the greatest, and this is shown by its opposite, namely **humility** <term>original: *Demuht*</term>. This, however, is not so easily attained; for whoever is not far removed from all ambition will not come upon this treasure. Humility is so great that the Devil seems to mimic all other virtues, and yet he does not even know what humility is. Therefore, because the Apostle knew its constancy and firmness, he commands us to deeply impress **lowliness** <note>original: *Niederträchtigkeit*; in modern German this means "meanness" or "baseness," but in this historical spiritual context, it refers to the literal state of being "low" or humble before God.</note> upon ourselves, and even when we have done all that is good, nonetheless to put it on.

When the enemy stirs up discord, the *Lord* arms us with moderation; if the former brings forth pride, then lowliness <term>original: *Niederträchtigkeit*; in this historical context, it refers to a state of humble "lowness" or humility rather than the modern German meaning of "baseness" or "malice"</term> is not far off; if the former has planted hatred, then love comes onto the path. Indeed, however many arrows the enemy may shoot, the *Lord* has provided us with even more weapons, both for our salvation and for the defeat of the enemies. Thus, anger is the evil among evils, for it is written: The anger of a man does not work the righteousness of *God*. *James 1, v. 20.* But one must govern it well, for at times it seems to be useful; for to be angry and moved against evil spirits is good; but to be vehemently moved against a person is of no use, even if he has sinned; rather, one should restore him with goodness once the anger has passed.

## The 21st Chapter.
->Of Revengefulness.<-

Indeed, it is a lesser thing to be angry in the heat of bad things, but to keep that evil constantly in memory is the worst of all. For anger soon passes away like smoke once it has disturbed the soul a little; but revengefulness <note>original: *Rachgier*; a persistent, vengeful spirit or the nursing of a grudge</note> is pressed into the mind and makes it more cruel than a beast. A dog soon lets go of its anger if one satisfies it with food; and other animals are tamed and quieted through habit. But whoever is seized by revengefulness can be pacified neither by persuasion nor by food, and time, which otherwise changes everything, cannot lift this sickness. These are the most godless and unjust people, for they do not obey the Savior, who says: Go first and be reconciled with your brother, and then bring your gift here; *Matt. 5, v. 24.* and elsewhere: Let not the sun go down on your bitterness <note>original: *Erbitterung*; often translated as "wrath" in English versions of Ephesians</note>. *Eph. 4, v. 26.*

## Chapter 23.

->Distinction between evil, pious, and holy people.<-

There are three kinds of images of the senses in human life: The first is of the greatest wickedness; the second is of a mediocre kind, which still worries over both sides and partakes of both; the third, when it is led to the heights of contemplation <term>Beschaulichkeit</term> <note>original: *Beschaulichkeit*; this refers to a state of deep prayerful observation or mystical "seeing" of divine truths.</note>, does not only restrain itself but also seeks to lead the other two. The wicked, when they are mixed among those even worse than themselves, increase their wickedness the most. The middle sort seek indeed to avoid the revelers <note>original: *Schwelger*; refers to those living in excess or debauchery.</note> out of concern that they might be led astray by them in turn; for they are still young children in the virtues. The third kind, who have a mature spirit <note>original: *Männlichen Sinn*; literally "masculine mind," used here to denote spiritual strength, courage, and maturity regardless of the person's actual gender.</note> and a practiced understanding, associate with the wicked with the intent to make them blessed, even if they themselves are tormented by them. For the evil spirits often attack them fiercely because they are being robbed of their tools through such people; and for this reason, they are reviled by those on the outside and laughed at by others who see them surrounded by dissolute people, and they are slandered as if they were just like them. They, however, hear the scolding of the people as praise and fulfill the Divine work without fear; for He says: *Rejoice and leap for joy when men speak all kinds of lies against you.* Matt. 5, v. 12. Thus, their deed is truly Divine, for the Lord also ate with tax collectors and sinners. Their mind is aligned more with brotherly love than with self-love; for when they see the sinners as if in a great fire <term>Feurs-Brunst</term>, they put their own concerns aside and strive to rescue the stranger who is about to perish; and even if they are scorched by burning slanders, they endure it nonetheless. The middle sort, however, when they see a brother inflamed in sin, run away for fear that the fire might also seize them. But the third kind are like the evil neighbors who ignite those already burning even more, and provide them with enough wood and material for the blaze—namely, their own wickedness; as if into a ship that is docking and burning with pitch, they throw fiery matter instead of water. The pious <note>In this context, the author uses "pious" to refer to the highest group previously described as "holy."</note>, however, prioritize the salvation of such people over their own; these are the marks of a true love, and such people preserve pure love.

<vocab>St. Syncletica, wickedness, contemplation, revelers, virtues, dissolute people, brotherly love, self-love, great fire, those on fire</vocab>

She emphasizes that true brotherly love imitates Christ by seeking out and rescuing those "on fire" with sin.</summary>

## Chapter 24.
### On Love, Almsgiving, and Mercy.

Just as one vice hangs upon another, and from greed follow envy, cunning, perjury, anger, and spite; so also, conversely, from love come gentleness, long-suffering, the bearing of evil, and that perfect good: **voluntary poverty**. For no one can reach this first virtue except through poverty; and the Lord has not commanded us to love only a single person, but all. Now, whoever possesses something should not pass by anyone in need, for otherwise he is secretly drawn away from love; although it is impossible for one human being to share with everyone, for that is the work of God. Why then do you trouble yourself over almsgiving <note>The text suggests that for those who have taken a vow of poverty, maintaining possessions just to give them away as "alms" can be a trap or an excuse to remain tied to worldly wealth.</note>, and use this as a pretext to possess something? This is commanded to the *worldly people*. For mercy is not imposed so much for the purpose of feeding a poor person, but for the sake of love; for the same God who governs the rich also feeds the poor. Is almsgiving then commanded to excess? Far from it; rather, it becomes a beginning of love among those who do not yet know it. Just as circumcision was a precursor to the circumcision of the heart; so mercy is made to be a teacher of love. And thus, for the one to whom love is given by grace, almsgiving is superfluous. I say this not as if I wished to diminish mercy, but only to indicate the purity of **voluntary poverty**. The small must not become a hindrance to the great. If you have given everything away at once, then you have correctly settled the small matter in your humble state; henceforth you must reach for something greater, namely love; for you are a cross-bearer <term>Creuz-Träger</term> <note>original: *Creuz-Träger*; a term referring to a monastic or ascetic who "takes up their cross" (Matthew 16:24) to follow a life of self-denial.</note>, therefore you must speak out these joyful words:

> Behold, we have left everything and followed you. Matthew 19:27.

You have become worthy to follow the bold tongue of the Apostles; for Peter and John say:

> Silver and gold have we none. Acts 3:4, 6 <note>original: *Actor. 3*; referencing the Acts of the Apostles.</note>.

There were indeed two tongues, but one single faith. Among the *worldly people*, mercy must not be practiced haphazardly and without distinction; for it is written:

> Let the oil of the sinner not make my head fat; Psalm 141:5 <note>The original German uses "fett machen," following a literal translation of the Latin Vulgate (*non impinguet caput meum*). Modern translations often render this as "Let not the oil of the wicked anoint my head."</note>.

Thus, one who shows mercy must use the prudence of Abraham, and act as justly as he did. For when that righteous man was hospitable, he also proved his intention through a meal; for—

# Chapter 25.

->Distinction between the worldly or married and the chaste states.<-

Just as worldly lords have different types of servants; some they send into the field to till the land and sustain the lineage; when they see their children are of good character, they take them into their service. Thus the Lord has placed human beings who stand in the honorable **state of marriage** into the estate of this world; but their children, as many as have formed a right intention, He has presented to Himself for service. These are estranged from all earthly business; for they are deemed worthy of the Lord’s table itself in a special way; they do not worry about clothing, for they have **clothed themselves in Christ**. ...from a single grain of wheat come both the stalk and the fruit; so too do they come from one God—both those who live well in the world and those who have chosen the solitary life. ### Chapter 26.
->Concerning Inexperienced Teachers and Vigilant Care of the Soul.<-

It is dangerous for anyone to presume to teach if they have not been raised through spiritual **practice** <term>original: "Praxin"; refers to the practical application of spiritual discipline and lived experience rather than theoretical study</term> in life. For just as one who leads his guests into a dilapidated house only harms them through the house’s collapse, so too do those people—because they have not first built themselves up firmly—destroy others along with themselves. With words they have invited them to salvation, but through their wicked life they have harmed the listeners more. For the mere interpretation of words is like paintings made of water-colors, which are destroyed in a short time by wind and rain. But a teaching that comes from experience cannot be destroyed even by eternity; for the Word, which carves and shapes the essence of the soul, grants to the faithful the eternal image of Christ. Therefore, we must not care for the soul superficially, nor merely according to appearance, but we must decorate it through and through, and above all, we must not neglect its depths. The life according to the world—honor, fame, wealth, fine clothes, delicate bathing, good food, and the like—we have cast away in appearance when we cut our hair (*); but let us tear out the main faults that destroy the soul, which are these: evil thoughts, backbiting <term>original: "Afterreden"; speaking ill of others behind their backs</term>, swearing, and the love of money. Among such soul-destroying beasts is also this one: when someone lets themselves be persuaded that there is a fate <note>original: "Fatum"</note> or a predetermined fortune, which they also call "the origin" <note>original: "Geneſin" (Greek: Genesis); here used in the sense of one's astrological destiny</note> or birth-charts; and this is a powerful arrow of the devil. # Chapter 29.

->Scholars should not engage in mere speculation, but should become like children.<-

Some he perverts through improper questions, when they wish to dispute concerning **GOD** and His essence, and thereby suffer shipwreck; for since they cannot progress well in the active or practical life, they have fallen into the contemplative life, where they have been seized by spiritual vertigo and have fallen. <note>In the ascetic tradition, "practical life" refers to the struggle against vices, which must precede "contemplation" or the study of God.</note> For because they did not attain that which was first according to the proper order, they also failed at the second. It is just like one who learns the letter A: he first looks at its shape, then names it, then learns its number, and finally its reward. <note>original: "Lohn." Likely referring to the value or ultimate use of the letter in grammar.</note> If so much practice, persistence, and art are necessary for the very first letter, how much more time and labor must precede the study of the Creator, if one wishes to contemplate His unspeakable glory? Therefore, no scholar who is drawn by **GOD** should, as soon as he descends from his worldly wisdom, proudly venture to investigate Divine things through speculation; for such a person deceives himself and is only mocked by Satan. He must first become a child; for it says in the Psalms: *Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained praise;* Psalm 8:2. <note>The German text cites v. 3, following different numbering.</note> And the **Lord** himself said in the Gospel: *Suffer the little children to come unto me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven;* Luke 18:16. And elsewhere he says: *Except ye be converted, and become as little children...* Matthew 18:3. If you have been learned for the sake of the world, then become a fool for the sake of the **Lord**; tear out the old so that you may plant the new; overturn the corrupt foundation so that you may lay the **Lord's** foundation of diamond beneath it, and, like the Apostle, be built upon the firmest of foundations.

Rather, just as common folk or sailors have some obscure knowledge of wind and rain from the appearance of the clouds, so these people have their wretched divination from spirits <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to demons or fallen angels who, according to desert theology, possess a keen but limited natural intelligence about the physical world.</note>; for they also babble things out of conjecture, much like the pagan soothsayers. And this could further refute their wicked opinion: for if such conjectured lies come from the spirits, then their calculations are in vain. But if the Enemy <note>A common name for the Devil.</note> wishes to defend them further, you can convict him of lies by the fact that he assails the soul now with these, and then with those thoughts. Now, that which is irrational is weak, and that which is weak is near to its end; for the Devil does not rest in his initial malice, but he presents the soul with its own movements and the bloom of nature <note>The "bloom of nature" refers to the natural impulses and physical desires of youth which the devil uses as a distraction.</note>, offering our own senses as a guide, so that the soul may perish through negligence. But when such dark phantoms approach, we must not assent to them as if they were true; for they betray their own malice by expressing themselves now one way, then another, and flying away again in an instant. I know a servant of **GOD** <note>Likely referring to a desert monk or ascetic.</note> who lived according to virtue, who, as he sat in his cell, paid close attention to the onslaught of his thoughts. He weighed which was the first and which was the second; how long each one lasted; and whether it had decreased or increased since the previous day. In this way, he recognized the grace of **GOD** precisely, as well as his own strength and power, and the defeat of the Enemy.

What we do or gain here, we must consider of little value in comparison to the goodness to come. If we have tasted worldly foods, let us now desire those that are Divine. If we have enjoyed the present light, let us long for the Sun of Righteousness <term>Sun of Righteousness: A common title for Christ, derived from Malachi 4:2, representing the source of spiritual truth and life.</term>; let us call the upper Jerusalem our city and mother, but **GOD** our Father. Let us live temperately here, so that we may attain eternal life. Just as children in the womb, when they are fully formed, are led from meager food to something greater, so also the righteous pass from this worldly life to heavenly prosperity, as it is written:

But sinners are cast from one darkness into another, like a child who perishes in the womb; for they die on earth, surrounded by many sins, and when they are led out of this life, they are cast into the darkest and most hellish places. We are born unto life three times: First, when we are brought out of the mother's womb and from one earth to another; the other two births bring us from the earth into heaven, of which one is by grace and occurs through the Divine Bath <term>Divine Bath: A poetic name for the Sacrament of Baptism, which was often called the "laver of regeneration."</term> (for this we truly call the bath of rebirth); the third, however, comes to us by grace through repentance <note>original: "Busse," which can mean penance or repentance.</note> and in good works; in this birth we now stand.

But what is this promise? To care little for the body, but to attend to the soul all the more; for this is indeed our covenant with Him. Just as no one can pull two full water-vessels upward at the same time, but as the axle turns, the empty one is brought down and the full one is brought up; so it is with us. <note>Syncletica uses a mechanical metaphor—likely a pulley or water-well system—to show that as we "fill" the soul with spiritual things, the body must "lighten" through fasting so the soul can rise.</note> For when we turn all our cares toward the soul, it is filled with good and brought on high through the longing for what is above; the body, however, having become light through chastening, does not weigh down the governing power of the spirit. And the Apostle testifies to this when he says: The more the outward man perishes, the more the inward man is renewed. *2 Corinthians 4:16.*

### Chapter 34.

->One should follow God with a good conscience in order to overcome the various deceits of the devil.<-

Not everything serves everyone; but let each person be bold in their own conscience. For many it is good to be in a community, but for many to live alone. For just as some plants grow better in damp places, and others in dry ones when they stand alone; so some people find themselves well in high places, while others are preserved in lowly ones. Therefore many have become blessed who imagined a wilderness for themselves while in the city, and many have perished on the mountains because they pursued worldly things; for it is indeed possible for one to be solitary in the *spirit* <term>Gemüht: The inner disposition, encompassing both mind and heart.</term>, though they walk with many, and another may live in their thoughts among the common people while they are alone.

The devil has many assaults; if he could not lead the soul astray through poverty, then he brings wealth as a lure; if he cannot overwhelm through disgrace and shame, then he lays out praise and honor; if he is defeated during days of health, then he makes the body sick; for if he cannot deceive through pleasures, then he seeks to overturn the soul through adverse labor, and to make it unwilling and incautious. For he is permitted to impose the heaviest illnesses, by which he terrifies the faint-hearted and disturbs their love for God; however, whether the body suffers and burns in the hottest fevers, or is tormented beyond this with unquenchable thirst; you must, if you suffer it as a sinner, [think of the]

## Chapter 35.

->The Benefit of Physical Weaknesses.<-

Let us not be distressed if, due to weakness and the plague of the body, we cannot stand during prayer or sing outwardly; all of this serves to clear away our desires. For fasting and lying upon the ground are imposed upon us because of shameful pleasure; when such pleasure is killed, then such labor is of no further use. Why do I say of no use? Because such ruinous occurrences are stilled by a stronger medicine, namely, bodily weakness. <note>Syncletica argues that if the body is too weak to pursue "shameful pleasures," the traditional rigors of asceticism like fasting are no longer necessary, as the illness itself does the work of purification.</note> And this is a great exercise: to restrain oneself even in sickness and to bring songs of thanks to God for it. Is our sight taken from us? Let us not be distressed; for although we have lost the instruments of insatiable desire, we nonetheless behold the glory of the Lord with our internal eyes. Have we become deaf? Let us give thanks to God that we have voluntarily lost the hearing of vanities. Do we become weak? Then let us have our internal hands ready for the struggle against the enemy. Does weakness take over the entire body? Then the health of the inner man grows all the more.

## Chapter 36.

->On Obedience and Strict Exercises of Penance, such as Fasting, Vigil, and the like.<-

When we live in holy community, we must prefer obedience to exercises of penance; for the latter make one proud, but the former teaches humility. Indeed, a strict exercise can even be imposed by the enemy <note>the devil</note>, for his followers do the same. How then shall we distinguish the Divine and Royal exercise from the tyrannical and devilish? Truly, by moderation. Let your entire life be a single rule of fasting, so that you do not fast for perhaps 4 or 5 days and afterwards gorge yourself with even more food; this pleases the enemy well, because immoderation is always destructive. Do not ruin your weapons all at once, lest you be found defenseless in the struggle; our weapons are the body, and our soul is the fighter; if both are to be of use to you, you must take good care of both. Fast while you are still young and healthy, for old age and weakness will surely come; gather food <note>meaning spiritual merit and discipline</note> while you can, so that you may find it in your weakness. Fast with understanding and caution; beware that the devil does not sneak into your fasting. I believe the Savior spoke of this when He said: *Be wise money-changers*; <note>original: "Seyd kluge Wechsler." This is a famous "agraphon" or unwritten saying attributed to Jesus in early Christian tradition, meaning one should be like a skilled banker who can distinguish between genuine and counterfeit coins.</note> that is: recognize the royal stamp well, because there are also counterfeit coins; although the money may have the same nature, they are distinguished by the stamp. The "money" represents fasting, abstinence, and alms; but the Greeks <note>pagans</note> or heathens also strike their image upon it, and all who are in error boast of it; such people must be regarded and avoided as counterfeiters. See to it that you do not carelessly fall among them and suffer harm; take the Cross of the Lord securely upon yourself, which is marked with His virtues—that is, faith together with good works. We must govern our soul with all discernment, and when we are in communal life, we should not seek our own nor follow our own will, but obey the spiritual mother. We have made ourselves exiles <note>original: "Exulanten"</note>; that is, we have gone out from worldly borders. Since we have now been cast out, let us not seek the world again. There we had honor, here shame; there pleasant food, here perhaps even a lack of bread. In the world, evildoers are thrown into prison against their will; here, let us place ourselves in prison for the sake of our sins, so that future punishment may be averted. If you fast,

### Chapter 37.
->She becomes very ill in her old age.<-

But the devil, as an enemy of all good, could not endure so many glorious things, and he reflected within himself how he might prevent the rise of such goodness. Finally, he challenged the magnanimous virgin to a final struggle and displayed such hostility toward her that he did not begin to plague her merely on her external limbs, but touched her innermost being and caused her deep pain, so much so that she was deprived of all comfort from human help. To be sure, he first wounded her lungs, as an organ necessary for life, and gradually inflamed the evil through dangerous illnesses. Now, he could have quickly brought death upon her through God's permission, but like a bloodthirsty executioner, he showed his cruelty through many plagues over a long time; for she lay for a long time with consumption <note>original: *Lungensucht*, a term historically used for tuberculosis or chronic wasting of the lungs</note> and also had a constant fever, which consumed her body.

She was 80 years old when the devil plagued her like *Job*, for he used the very same scourges against her; however, this time he shortened the time and made the pains all the greater. ### Chapter 38.
->Her Magnanimity and Her Teaching Regarding It.<-

But the Blessed Woman endured this plague with great magnanimity and did not lose heart; rather, she armed herself ever more against the Enemy. Indeed, through her good teachings, she also healed those who had been wounded by him, and snatched souls unharmed from the jaws of the bloodthirsty lion <note>A common metaphor for the devil in early Christian writing</note>. She bound up the wounded with the healing medicines of Christ; others, however, she kept unharmed by showing them the cunning snares of the devil, thereby setting them free from sin.

And the wonderful virgin spoke: "Souls dedicated to God must never be careless, because the devil stalks them most of all. For even when they rest in silence, he roars and torments himself when he is overcome; he withdraws for a little while and waits to see if they will fall asleep, and then he attacks them, so that he might suppress them in the very area where they are most careless. For just as it is impossible that even the most godless should not have a small spark of good, which restrains them in their unrighteousness, so too do the pious have something adverse within themselves. For in things that contend with one another, there is always something of the opposite present. Therefore, a person who lives in all manner of sin and shame may nonetheless sometimes be merciful; and a righteous person who walks in abstinence, fasting, and a strict life may well at times be stingy and prone to slander <note>original: *afterredend*, meaning backbiting or gossiping maliciously</note>, if they are not careful. For this reason, one must not set aside small things as if they could not cause harm; for water also softens stone over time. Thus, the very greatest part of what is good in a human being comes from Divine Grace; but that which seems small, we know that it must be driven out by ourselves. ### Chapter 39.
->The Enemy paralyzes her tongue / and rouses a rot in her mouth.<-

Now, when the Enemy of all that is good <note>A common epithet for the Devil</note> saw that she was once again strengthening herself against him, it vexed him, and he devised another ruse, because he saw his tyranny being brought to nothing; therefore, he injured the organs of speech so that he might hinder her teaching, intending that those who came to her should perish from hunger for the Divine Word. But although he deprived his own advantage of hearing her <note>The devil hoped to silence her, but his plan backfired by providing a visual example of endurance</note>, a greater benefit was nonetheless granted to her followers; for when they looked upon the sufferings of the virgin with their own eyes, they were even more firmly established in their purpose. The wounds of her body healed the wounds of their souls. One could see that it was truly wholesome for the onlookers when they witnessed the magnanimity and strength of the blessed virgin.

The Enemy also stirred up this pain in her: from a toothache she eventually developed a rot in the gums, and the bone was finally affected as well; indeed, the ulcer seized the entire jawbone, and furthermore, the connected parts of the body began to rot, and after forty days the jawbone was entirely eaten away, until after two months it developed a large hole. Then everything all around turned black; the bone itself perished little by little, and the decay, together with a terrible stench, took over the entire body; so much so, that those who nursed her suffered more than she did herself, and they stayed away most of the time because they could not endure the horrific smell. However, when necessity demanded it, they lit much incense and thus went inside, but because of the stench, they soon left again.

They even brought a physician to her, who was meant to talk her into a cure; but she would not allow it and said:
> Why do you keep me from this blessed battle? Why do you seek only that which is visible, when you do not know that which is hidden? Why do you trouble yourselves over what is happening, and do not look upon Him who does it?

Then she finally allowed it, solely out of compassion for the others present. Who was not terrified when they saw this cruel plague? Who was not edified by the contemplation of her great patience? Who did not improve themselves when they saw the defeat of the Enemy? For he had struck her in the very place from which a healing and sweet spring of her words had flowed. His excessive cruelty allowed for no comfort; like a bloodthirsty beast, he also hindered all care so that he might carry off this prey. But while he sought food, he himself became food, having been lured by the weakness of her body as if by a fishhook; for he did not know her masculine spirit <note>In early Christian writing, a "masculine spirit" was a technical term for spiritual strength and courage that transcended gender</note>, seeing only her sick limbs, and in his blindness could not recognize her stout-hearted soul. In this manner, she stood in this battle for three months, and yet through Divine power, her whole body was sustained, in that the very thing which was to give her support was never diminished. She could consume nothing, because due to the great rot and stench she could take no food, and sleep also departed from her, as the pains prevented it.

# III. The Life of St. Sarah.
## Described by Pelagius, etc.

### Chapter 1.
### Saint Sarah’s Secluded Life and Proven Humility.

This holy matron lived in such earnest abstinence <note>Original: *Enthaltung*, referring to the ascetic practice of self-denial and sensory fasting</note> that, although she lived for sixty years by the Nile River in the desert, she never once turned her eyes toward it to look upon it with pleasure. <note>Original citation: Pelagius Book 7. n. 19. *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* in Sarah n. 3.</note>

2. Once, two elders who were famous hermits came to her from the region of <term>Pelusium</term> <note>An important city in the eastern extremes of the Nile Delta</note>; as they approached, they conferred with one another and said: "We want to humble the old woman!" Accordingly, they said to her: "Take care that your heart does not become puffed up, and you say to yourself: 'Behold, such great hermits come to visit me, who am only a woman!'" Then the holy Sarah gave them this answer: "I am a woman by gender, but not in spirit." <note>Original citation: Pelagius Book 10 n. 73. *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* n. 4.</note>

### Chapter 2.
### Her Temptations from the Spirit of Lust.

It was told of her that for thirteen whole years she was violently tempted by the demon of lust <note>Original: *Huren-Teufel*, literally "whore-devil," a term used in early modern German to personify the temptation of fornication</note>, and yet she never prayed that the struggle might cease, but rather said: "God, give me strength!" <note>Original citation: Pelagius Book 5. n. 10. *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* n. 1.</note>

2. Once, this impure spirit pressed her very hard and filled her mind with a heap of worldy vanities. But she, by means of the fear of God and a serious way of life, [did not] yield

## Wise Sayings.

Once, brothers from **Scetis** <note>Original: *Scithi*, referring to the Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, a famous center of early Christian monasticism</note> came to this holy **Mother Sarah**, and she set before them a basket of fruit. ## The daughter of the brother of the Desert Father Abraham (*).
### Described by St. Ephrem the Syrian.
#### Chapter 1.

->The Holy Mary’s divine conduct from the seventh year of her age until the twenty-seventh.<-

Father Abraham had a biological brother who, after his passing, left behind an only daughter of seven years. When the deceased man's good friends and acquaintances saw her placed in the state of an orphan, they led her immediately to her uncle, Father Abraham, in the desert. He then received her into the outer room of his cell; for he himself lived in the back section of the same. In the partition wall, however, there was a small window-hole, through which he taught her the Psalter <note>The Book of Psalms</note> and other things from the Scriptures; so that she kept watch with him in the praising of God, and sang Psalms no less than he, and applied herself to imitating her uncle in all abstinence. As she grew joyfully in this life she had begun, she strived to fulfill all virtues of the spirit.

For the holy man prayed unceasingly with tears to the Lord for her, that her mind might not become entangled in earthly things, because her father, after his death, had left her an unspeakable wealth; which the man of God, therefore, immediately after the death of his aforementioned brother, had distributed to the poor and orphans, after this daughter was brought to him. She also later daily asked him to pray to God for her, that she might be saved from shameful thoughts and the many snares of the devil. Thus she practiced with a brave spirit and preserved her holy way of life. The blessed man, however, rejoiced greatly as he saw her grow so swiftly without any stumble in all virtues, namely in tears of repentance, in humility,

## Father Abraham’s vision of her misfortune.

With this he awoke full of great distress and began to weep bitterly, thinking the dream meant that Satan would stir up a persecution by the heathens against the Church and cause many to fall away from the faith; or perhaps that a new sect would arise in the holy community of **Christ**. For this reason, he fell upon his knees and prayed to the Lord, saying:

> O most gracious God, you who know all things beforehand and are a lover of mankind, you also know what this vision signifies.

Thereupon he saw for the second time after two days the same dragon-serpent in the previous manner to his

O, what wondrous and kind condescension, You highest God! Who would have thought the maiden had said in her heart: "How similar is this old man to my uncle <note>original: *Oheim*. This is to be believed for no other reason than that the tears of Your servant, her uncle, have worked this through You—that You have made impossible things possible. 

Thereupon the holy man took out his ducat <note>a gold coin</note> which he had brought with him, gave it to the host, and said to him: "Make us, dear friend, a good evening meal, so that I may show myself truly joyful with this maiden; for out of love for her, I have come a long way." 

O, true wisdom from God! O, true spiritual understanding! O, right and soul-saving discernment <note>original: *Discretion*, referring to the spiritual gift of *discretio spirituum*, or the ability to judge the right course of action in complex moral situations</note>! For fifty years of his mortified life, he had not once eaten bread; and now he had no hesitation in eating roast meat to save a lost soul. The choir of holy angels rejoiced over this discernment of the holy man—that he ate and drank so freely without distinction, so that he might save the soul sunk in the mire <note>original: *Koht*, meaning filth or excrement, used here as a metaphor for sin</note>! O, wisdom of the wise and understanding of the understanding! O, discernment of the discerning! Who will help me wonder at this boldness? From where did this simple and unlearned man receive such perfection, wisdom, testing, and understanding? That he knows how to rescue the swallowed soul so craftily from the jaws of the lion, and to release the bound soul from the bonds and the dark dungeon.

## Chapter 10.
### Her further penance until her end.

### Chapter 2.

->Saint *Marina* travels to the market with a cart.<-

When she entered her seventeenth year, her biological father died, and she remained alone in her father’s chamber, keeping all his wholesome teachings and being obedient to all the brothers; so much so, that she was dearly loved by the holy Old Man and all the brothers. The monastery, however, had a pair of yoked oxen and a cart, because it was not far from the sea, where almost a mile away lay a market town from which the brothers fetched their necessities by means of the said oxen and cart. One day, the Old Man said to her: "Brother *Marine* <note>original: *Marine*, the Latin vocative form of Marinus</note>, why do you not also go for once to the city with the brothers and help them?" She answered: "Do you command it, dear Father?" There was, however, an inn in that same market town. Thus Brother *Marinus* began to travel there frequently with the cart; and if he was ever delayed, he stayed overnight in the aforementioned inn, along with the other brothers.

# V. The Life of Saint Marina the Virgin.
<meta>catchword: then</meta>

## Chapter 3.

->She is falsely accused by a disgraced innkeeper’s daughter and cast out.<-

It happened through the snares of the evil enemy <note>the Devil</note> that the innkeeper had a daughter, a young woman, who allowed herself to be bedded by a certain soldier, by whom she became pregnant. When her parents noticed this, they began to question the girl sharply, saying: "Tell us, by whom did you become pregnant?" She answered them: "By that monk <note>original: *Einsamen*, literally 'the solitary one' or hermit</note> named Marinus, who often stays overnight with us with his cart; he has humbled me so that I have become pregnant." Immediately, the parents went to the monastery and spoke to the Father: "See here, Father, what your disciple Marinus has done, and in what manner he has deceived our daughter!" The Old Man <note>term: *der Alte*, the Abbot</note> answered them, saying: "Wait, we will investigate whether it is as you say." So Marinus was called forward, to whom the Old Man said: "Brother Marinus, have you committed such a shameful act with these people’s daughter?" He <gloss>(She)</gloss> stood for a long time and reflected; finally she said with a sigh: "I have sinned, dear Father, and will gladly do penance for this sin; pray for me." Then the Old Man became very angry and ordered her to be lashed and whipped, saying: "Truly, I tell you, because you have committed such wickedness, you shall not remain in this our community!" and he thrust her out of the gates. But she never revealed her secret to anyone; instead, she lay outside the gates in penance and mortified her flesh <note>original: *castenete sich*, a term for religious self-discipline, often through fasting</note> as if she had committed the sin herself; she also begged the brothers who went in or out for a mouthful of bread. This lasted for three years, and she did not move from there. In the meantime, the innkeeper's daughter had given birth to a son, and after she had weaned him, the girl's mother brought him there, laid him down at the gates of the monastery, and said: "Look, Brother Marinus, raise your son as best you can!" Then she left him there and went home. The holy virgin Marina, however, took the child in as her own son and nourished him with the morsels of bread she received from those entering; this continued for another two years.

There were some young men who had a harlot with them. Now, the old men <note>referring to desert fathers or monks</note> sat alone, and one of them took the New Testament and read from it. ### Chapter 3.

->Antigonus dies / and Euphrasia entrusts her young daughter Euphrasia to God and the Emperor.<-

As Antigonus now led a glorious way of life in this manner and distributed much to the poor, he lived for one more year in all godliness after the renunciation of his wife <note>Meaning the renunciation of marital relations</note>, until he died at the end of that year and was buried in peace. The Emperor and the Empress, however, wept for him as their relative and as a dear, faithful, and godly man. They also had compassion for the widowed Euphrasia left behind, not only as their blood-relative, but because she was still young. For she had had her husband for only two years and three months, of which they had lived together as brother and sister during the final year. After Antigonus had been buried, the Emperor and Empress comforted Euphrasia. She, however, took her young daughter and placed her into the hands of the Emperor and the Empress; she then threw herself down at their feet and spoke with a loud voice amidst many tears: "I now commend this little orphan <term>Wäißlein</term> <note>An archaic German diminutive for an orphan child</note> into God’s and your hands; if the memory of Antigonus, your relative, is dear to you, then receive this child and protect her, and be in the place of father and mother to her." Those present shed many tears over this, so much so that tears even came to the eyes of the princes and the Emperor himself.
