# VII. The Life of St. Euphrasia.

## Chapter 4.
->The young Euphrasia is betrothed; the bridegroom petitions for the mother through the Empress.<-

After a short time had passed and the mourning for the deceased Antigonus was over, the Emperor advised the widow to betroth her daughter Euphrasia to a very wealthy privy councilor <note>The German "geheimten Rahte" refers to a high-ranking advisor or member of the imperial court</note>. It also happened that Euphrasia received the betrothal gift, after which the bridegroom would have to wait several years for his bride; for she was still very young when she received the gift, barely five years old.

Not long afterward, however, the aforementioned councilor and bridegroom of the young Euphrasia took it into his mind to marry the mother and widow of Antigonus herself. Through his pleading and the intercession of the ladies-in-waiting, he persuaded the Empress to send word—without the Emperor’s prior knowledge—and propose the marriage to Euphrasia the Elder. But when she heard this, she wept bitterly and said to the matrons who brought the proposal:

> Woe to you in the world to come, you who advise me thus, and with such a purpose set yourselves against a woman who intends to live according to the zeal of God <note>original: "GOTTES-Eifer"</note>. Depart from me, for you have now performed your meddling errand <note>original: "fremdes Amt," literally "foreign office," implying a task that is none of their business</note>.

So they went away in shame and announced to the Empress what had happened. But when the Emperor learned of this, he became very indignant with the Empress and spoke to her with an earnest manner:

> Truly, My Dear <note>original: "Euer Liebden," a formal and affectionate address used among nobility</note>, you have meddled in foreign matters that are not in accordance with the walk of Christ! Are these the undertakings of an Empress? Have you vowed to rule so godlily with us? Is this the good memory of our late dear faithful cousin Antigonus, who served us honestly at all times? You have begun something unbefitting our reign, in that you wish to drag back into the world a young woman who lived in actual marriage with her husband for barely a year, and who by mutual consent abstained from one another for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; you do not fear God, then, that you have committed such a sin. Who will convince the people that such a thing did not also happen with our will? This thing is not good, and should not have been heard of in our reign, especially for the sake of our well-proven friend Antigonus.

## Chapter 5.
->Euphrasia travels with her daughter to Egypt.<-

Because of this rebuke, the Empress turned red with shame and remained motionless and without a word for nearly two hours.

## Chapter 6.

->Description of a certain female monastery in Egypt.<-

Now, in a certain city, there was a convent <note>The text uses "Weiblich Kloster," specifically referring to a nunnery</note> in which there were one hundred and thirty rooms and as many sisters living together, of whom people told of great and wonderful virtues. For in that monastery, none tasted any wine; none of them ate apples, nor grapes, nor figs, nor any such good fruits which the earth brings forth in abundance. Indeed, some of them, who had renounced the world, would not even consume oil; others fasted daily until sunset, some for two days, and some for three days long. None of them washed their feet, and if any even heard the mention of a "tender bath" <term>zärtliche Bad: a luxurious or comforting bath, which these ascetics viewed as a worldly indulgence</term>, they laughed at it and called it a shame and an abomination that they did not wish to hear of. Each one, however, slept on the bare earth and had a small pillow of coarse cloth, one cubit <note>An "Elle" (cubit) was an old unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm</note> wide and three cubits long, which they rolled up and rested upon for a little while. Their clothes were made of hair-cloth <note>A rough garment, often made of goat hair, worn against the skin as a form of penance</note> and hung down from their heads to their feet. Each worked as much as she was able; and if one of them happened to fall ill, she was given no medicine nor extra care, but they accepted such a visitation as a great grace from God, and bore the weakness until Divine medicine made them well again. ### Das 7. Capitel.

->The monastery will not permit fixed annual revenues.<-

Euphrasia <note>This refers to Euphrasia the Elder, the mother</note> loved the counsel of these holy women because of their virtuous conduct, and thus she visited this monastery frequently, bringing incense and wax candles. One day, however, she petitioned the spiritual mother and the leaders of the monastery, saying: "I wish to bring a small blessing to you without causing you disturbance, and to provide thirty pounds of gold annually from my income, so that you may pray for this your servant, my daughter, and for the late Antigonus, her father." To this, the Abbess, or spiritual mother, gave her this answer: "My honored matron, your handmaidens need no annual income, nor do they have a desire for money; for they have forsaken everything and despise all in this world so that they may become partakers of eternal goods. Thus, they wish to possess nothing certain, lest they be robbed of those eternal treasures. However, so that I do not grieve you and let you depart without a blessing, bring a little oil for the light in our lamps; this shall be for us a reward of righteousness." When Euphrasia had brought this, she again entreated the Abbess that they should pray for her daughter Euphrasia and for Antigonus.

On the following day, the Abbess took Euphrasia and led her into the inner prayer chamber, and prayed over her, and then put the clothing of the solitary virgins <note>The monastic habit or veil worn by nuns</note> upon her; afterwards, she spread out her hands toward heaven, prayed for her, and said: "You King of Eternities, who has begun the good work in her, complete it in peace; grant her that she may walk worthily according to your name, and that this child may always find boldness before your countenance." Furthermore, her mother, Euphrasia, also prayed and then said: "My daughter, do you find pleasure in this clothing?" The young Euphrasia gave her mother the answer and said: "Certainly, dear mother! For, as I have understood from the Lady Abbess, and as the honored sisters have also said, the Lord Jesus Christ gives this clothing as a pledge and a bridegroom’s gift <note>original: "Bräutigams-Gabe"; this refers to the tradition of a nun being "wedded" to Christ</note> to those who love him!" The mother then said: "To him whom you are now betrothed, make yourself worthy of his marriage!" Having said this and prayed for her daughter, she took leave of all the sisters and kissed her daughter for the last time; then, according to her custom, she traveled about and provided the poor with their necessities <note>original: "Nohtdurft"</note>.

### Chapter 11.
->The holy conduct of the elder Euphrasia.<-

Everywhere, however, the holy conduct of the elder Euphrasia became known, and how much love she showed to the solitaries and saints; so much so that even the Emperor <note>original: "Kayser"</note> heard of it, and all the councilors <note>original: "Rähte"</note> loved her dearly and glorified God because of her. For they heard that she even abstained from fish and drank no wine; but besides such rich alms which she gave to everyone, she also fasted daily until evening, when she sometimes ate peas or beans, and sometimes only herbs.

## Chapter 12.

->*The elder Euphrasia is informed of her end; she dies.*<-

After a few days, the aforementioned Abbess called the mother, Euphrasia, and spoke secretly to her: "Honored lady, I have something to tell you; do not let it alarm you!" She answered: "Worthy lady, tell me whatever you wish!" The Abbess then spoke: "I saw your husband Antigonus in a dream in great glory, and he asked the Lord Jesus Christ that you might depart from this earthly tabernacle <note>original: "Leibes-Hütten"; a common metaphor for the physical body in early modern religious texts</note> and henceforth be with him, enjoying the glory that your husband Antigonus possesses." When she heard this, she returned to her house as a godly matron, and was so little troubled by it that she instead rejoiced greatly; for she prayed to God that she might be released from this life to be with Christ. She also soon called her daughter and spoke to her: "My daughter, the worthy Lady Abbess has informed me that the Lord Christ is calling me, and the end of my life is drawing near. Behold, I hand over all my property and your father's into your hands; manage it piously so that you may attain the heavenly inheritance!" When the young Euphrasia heard this from her mother, she began to sigh and weep, saying: "Woe is me, for I am a stranger and an orphan!" Her mother said to her: "Daughter, you have Christ as your father and bridegroom; therefore you are neither a stranger nor an orphan. You also have the Lady Abbess in place of a mother. See then, my daughter, do not delay in fulfilling your promise; fear God and honor all the sisters, and serve them with all humility. Never let the thought enter your heart: 'I am of imperial blood' <note>The family were relatives of the Emperor Theodosius, making their choice of a humble monastic life particularly striking to contemporary readers</note>; and do not say: 'They must serve me!' Be poor on earth so that you may become rich in heaven. Behold, everything is under your hand; use the estates and money for the solitary ones <note>original: "Einsame"; likely referring to the monastic community or those living in religious seclusion</note>, for the blessing of your father and myself, so that we may obtain mercy from God and be delivered from eternal punishment." After she had commanded these things to her daughter, she passed away three days later, and they buried her in a vault in the monastery.

> "Most Serene Emperor! Do Your Imperial Majesty command your handmaid to leave Christ and unite herself with a perishing man, whom the worms shall finally devour; who is here today and gone tomorrow? Far be it from Your Majesty's handmaid that I should commit such wickedness. Therefore, Most Serene Emperor and Lord! May Your Imperial Majesty, together with your consort, also pray for your handmaid, that I may be found worthy to serve Christ, who has graciously chosen me as His handmaid."

After this, she sealed the letter and gave it to the messenger, who hurried on his return journey and handed the letter to the Emperor. He opened it and read it with the Empress in the private chamber <note>original: "Cabinette"; a small, private room used for personal business or study.</note>; at this, tears rose to their eyes, and they offered their prayers for Euphrasia. On the following morning, however, the Emperor called the whole council, as well as the father of Euphrasia’s bridegroom, and commanded the letter to be read aloud.

### Chapter 14.

->The Emperor’s death; the virtuous conduct of Euphrasia.<-

After the Emperor Theodosius had managed everything in a God-fearing manner and had distributed the maiden’s goods, he also fell asleep <note>A common euphemism for death in hagiographic texts.</note> (in Milan, in the year 395) and was buried (in Constantinople) with his fathers. Euphrasia, however, was glorified and walked according to the will of God, living in abstinence beyond her years and growth; for she was twelve years old at the time and trained herself courageously for the struggle <note>This "struggle" refers to the spiritual combat against worldly desires and demonic temptations.</note>. At first, she ate only once a day in the evening; later, however, every other day; and finally, only every third day. No one but she alone cleaned the chambers and made the sisters' beds; she even carried the water into the kitchen herself.

Now, it was the custom in that same monastery: whenever it happened that one of the sisters was tempted by the devil in a dream, she would tell the Abbess; the Abbess would then pray to God with tears that Satan might depart from the tempted sister, and she would command her to carry stones and scatter ash upon her bed, whereupon she would sleep in this manner at night for ten days. One day, Euphrasia was also thus tempted by the devil, so she scattered ash upon her bed. When the Abbess noticed such ash on Euphrasia’s bed, she smiled and said to one of the eldest sisters: "In truth, this young sister is already being tempted!" And the Abbess prayed and said: "O God, who hast created her according to Thy will, strengthen her also in Thy fear!"

And the Abbess called her and said to her: "Why did you not make the temptation of the devil known to me?" But she fell at her feet and said: "Forgive me, Honorable Mother! I was ashamed to tell you." Then the Abbess said to her: "My daughter, behold, you have begun to struggle; hold yourself manfully <note>original: "männlich"; in early Christian ascetic literature, spiritual strength and endurance were often described using "manly" virtues, regardless of the individual's gender.</note>, so that you may overcome and be crowned."

## Chapter 15.
->She confesses her temptations to a sister and the Abbess.<-

After a few days, however, she was once again tempted; she recounted this to a sister named Julia, who loved Euphrasia dearly and also practiced alongside her in the struggle <note>The "struggle" or *Kampf* refers to the ascetic life—the spiritual battle against one's own desires and the temptations of the devil.</note>. Then Julia said to her: "Dearly beloved Euphrasia, do not hide this from the Abbess, but report it to her so that she may pray for you; for we are all tempted by the devil, but we hope in the name of Christ that we shall overcome him. Thus, dear sister, you shall not die; simply tell the Abbess of the matter and do not be ashamed." When Euphrasia heard this, she thanked Julia and said to her: "May GOD be your helper in return, dear sister, for you have built me up and strengthened my soul; I will now go in without hesitation and tell the Lady Abbess everything." Julia said: "Yes, do so, that she may pray for you and assign you a penance <term>Buß-übung: a spiritual exercise or disciplinary task intended to foster repentance</term>." So she went in and told the Abbess of the matter. Then the Abbess said to her: "Fear not, my daughter, all the struggle of the devil with which he opposes us; therefore, fight bravely with an unwavering mind, and he will have no power against you; for you will be tempted by him in many ways. But fight so that you may overcome and obtain the victory and the palms <note>The "palm" is a traditional symbol of victory and martyrdom in Christian iconography.</note> from your bridegroom, Christ, and live as much as you are able in a sober and moderate manner; for whoever struggles the most shall also receive the greatest reward of grace." After a short time, the Abbess questioned her, saying: "How many days do you fast, my daughter?" She answered: "For three days, Honorable Lady." The Abbess then said to her: "Add one more day to that." She then obeyed such a command with great joy and retired to her chamber.

She performed this command joyfully and cheerfully.

## Chapter 19.

### After another temptation in a dream, she fasts for seven days straight.

Once again the Devil tempted her in a dream and set her in a great struggle <note>The "struggle" or "battle" (*Kampf*) refers to spiritual warfare, a central concept in early monastic life where physical hardships were used to defeat demonic influence.</note>. She recounted this temptation to the Abbess, who then prayed for her and said to her: "My daughter Euphrasia, now is the time of the battle; see to it that the Devil does not make your spirit weary, causing you to lose your reward; for when he has fought with you for a little while longer and you have overcome him, then he shall flee from you." Likewise, Julia also spoke to her: "My honored mistress <note>original: *Herrscherin*; Julia uses this title because Euphrasia was of noble imperial lineage before entering the convent.</note> and sister, if we do not resist him now and overcome him in the struggle, what kind of battle shall we wage against him in our old age?" To this, Euphrasia gave her answer: "As surely as the Lord lives, sister Julia! If the Abbess were to command me to fast the entire week, I would taste no bread until I had overcome him with the Lord's help." Julia said to her: "If you can fulfill this on earth, you shall be blessed in heaven; for in this monastery, not a single woman has yet been able to pass an entire week without food, except for our mother the Abbess alone." Then Euphrasia went in and recounted her nightly temptation in the dream to the Abbess, and begged her that she might command her to fast the entire week. She said to her: "Do all that pleases you, my daughter! May God, who created you, strengthen you and grant you victory against the Devil." So Euphrasia began to fast the entire week, and she neglected neither the hours of prayer and song, nor her usual work in service of the sisters, so that all admired her enduring patience, as well as her beauty and young years. Some among the sisters, however, said: "It has already been a year since we have [set eyes] on Euphrasia..."

But there was one among them named Germana, who was born of a slave or a bondwoman; she envied Euphrasia and rebelled against her secretly in the kitchen, saying to her: "Tell me, Euphrasia, see, you eat only once throughout the entire week, by the order of the Abbess, which we cannot do; if the Abbess now wanted to compel us to do so as well, what should we do?" But Euphrasia gave her this answer: "Pull the wood out carefully; my eye is unharmed." So she pulled the wood out of the wound, from which a great deal of blood flowed. The Abbess then brought oil and, after offering a prayer, anointed her with her hand. Thereupon she spoke to her again: "Go and lie down upon your bed and rest; I will assign your service to the venerable sisters." But Euphrasia said: "As truly as my Lord lives, I will not lie down to rest until I have finished my work." And although the sisters pleaded with her greatly that she should rest on account of the wounds she had received, she nevertheless did not grant it; instead, wounded as she was, with blood flowing from both injuries, she stood and served the sisters, nor did she neglect prayer and other duties.

# Chapter 27.

## Euphrasia brings food to the possessed woman and tames her with sternness.

Now when she saw that she had overpowered the possessed woman, the woman became quiet. Whenever she wanted to behave unruly, the sisters said to her: "Be still, sister, and do not be naughty, for if the Venerable Sister Euphrasia hears of it, she will give you the rod"; with that, she quickly became well-behaved.

Thereupon, she began to tell everyone what goodness Euphrasia had to look forward to; furthermore, she begged Euphrasia to pray to the Lord for her, so that she too might share in her salvation; for she prayed that she might walk with her in Christ and obtain the same good things that Euphrasia was to enjoy.

## Chapter 32.

->She falls ill, and after all the sisters have taken their leave of her, she dies.<-

But while Euphrasia was still kissing the Abbess's feet, she began to have chills and shudders, followed by a violent fever. The Abbess said to the sisters: "Take her, and let us go into the prayer hall, for the hour of her departure draws near." So they laid her down in the prayer room and watched over her until evening. When evening had come and the hour for the meal approached, the Abbess commanded them to go out, and kept only Julia <note>Julia was Euphrasia’s close companion in the monastery; in many versions of the story, they were childhood friends</note> with her so that they would not leave Euphrasia alone; and they remained with her behind closed doors the entire night. But Julia begged Euphrasia and said: "Dearest sister, do not forget me; remember that I have been inseparable from you upon this earth; pray to God for me, that He may not separate me from you. Remember that I in many good..."

They buried her in the tomb where her biological mother, the elder Euphrasia, also rested. And they glorified God that they were made worthy to have such a sister with God.

### Chapter 33.

-> *Her teacher, Julia, also dies.* <-

But Julia, her teacher, wept incessantly for three days and would not leave her grave; for she had taught the blessed one how to read and the Psalter <note>a book containing the Psalms, often used as a primary textbook for literacy in monastic settings</note> when she had been her pupil and was of imperial blood <note>original: "Kayserlichem Geblüte"; a reference to Euphrasia's noble lineage as the daughter of Antigonus, a relative of Emperor Theodosius</note>. On the fourth day, however, Julia took heart and went joyfully to the Abbess and said to her: "My honorable mother, pray for me, because the Lord Christ has called me through the intercession of the blessed Euphrasia." When she had said this, she kissed all the sisters. On the fifth day after Euphrasia's passing, her teacher Julia also passed away and was buried in the tomb of the blessed Euphrasia.

### Chapter 34.

->The Abbess also takes her leave and dies, after Theogenia was elected in her place.<-

After thirty days, the Abbess summoned the eldest virgins and said to them: "My daughters, choose for yourselves a mother and set her in my place, so that she may preside over you." But they answered: "Venerable Mother, why do you speak thus? Tell us this; for you have never said such things to us, your handmaidens." The Abbess said to them: "The Lord has called me! For the venerable Euphrasia has prayed to the Lord for me, and earnestly persisted with petitions, so that I shall be worthy of the **Heavenly Wedding Garment** <note>original: "Himmlischen Hochzeit-Kleides"; a common biblical metaphor representing the purity and readiness of the soul to meet Christ</note>; for Julia, too, through Saint Euphrasia, has become a partaker of the same and has entered into the **Palace not made with hands** <note>original: "Pallast, der nicht mit Händen gemachet ist"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 5:1, signifying the eternal home in heaven</note>; and I hasten to be made worthy of it and to find a small place among them." When the sisters heard this of Euphrasia and Julia—that they had been translated into the highest glory—they rejoiced, and prayed together that they too might be made worthy of this wedding garment. In the meantime, they chose one of the sisters named **Theogenia** to preside over them; the Abbess called her to herself and said to her: "See the good testimony which all the sisters have given of you, and have chosen you to be our successor and the guardian of our **Divine Statute** <note>the rule or set of religious laws governing the monastery</note>; I adjure you by the immaculate <term>Triune Essence</term> <note>original: "drey-einige Wesenheit"; the Holy Trinity</note>, that you do not seek the riches and goods of this world, nor entangle the sisters in earthly cares; but rather that they should despise earthly goods and become worthy to attain the eternal ones." Afterward, she spoke once more to the sisters: "Just as you are fully aware of the holy <note>original: "Wandel"; refers to one’s spiritual conduct or way of life</note> and life of Euphrasia, be her followers, so that you may become partakers of her fellowship." When they had all said "Amen" to this, she took her leave of them and went into the oratory, closed the door behind her, and commanded that no one should come in to her until tomorrow morning. When morning came and they went in to her, they found that she had **fallen asleep in the Lord**. And after they had sung a song of praise to the Lord, she was laid in the grave where the blessed Eudoxia lay buried. From that day on, however, they have buried no one else there.

### The 35th Chapter.

->Miracles at Euphrasia’s grave; the moral conclusion of this story.<-

Many signs and wonders occurred at the aforementioned grave, and the cast-out spirits cried and shouted: "Euphrasia overwhelms us even after her death, and she pursues us!" This is, according to the truth, the life of the blessed matron Euphrasia, who was made worthy of the **heavenly choir of the Elders** <note>original: "himmlischen Chors der Aeltesten"; a reference to the twenty-four elders mentioned in the Book of Revelation</note>. Let us then, both brothers and sisters, lead such a holy life and pursue humility, alongside obedience, labor, gentleness, and patience; so that we too may enter into the company of the holy angels and with joy become partakers of our **great Lord and Savior Jesus Christ**; to whom be glory and honor for all eternity. Amen! *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "Vit. PP.", short for *Vitae Patrum*, a classic collection of biographies of early Christian desert monks and saints</note>, Book 1, page 351.

# VIII. The Life of the Virgin St. Euphrosyna.

->Described by Anonymous.<-

## The 1st Chapter.

->Paphnutius and his barren wife pray to God for a blessing of children.<-

There was a man in Alexandria named Paphnutius, who was highly honored by all and walked in the commandments of God. He took a wife suited to his station, who was also full of good virtues, but she was barren and bore no children. The man, however, was very distressed because of this, as he had no one to whom he might leave all his goods and who would properly manage them after his death. Therefore, he did not cease to serve the poor day and night, and was diligent in the assembly of the congregation, and persisted in fasting and prayer, seeking to entreat a son from God. Likewise, his wife was also most sorrowful when she saw how her husband tormented himself; she also gave much money to the poor and to the **hermits** <note>original: "Einsamen", meaning those who live in solitude for religious reasons, such as monks or anchorites</note>, in order to become a partaker of their desire. ### The 3rd Chapter.
->Euphrosyna is well-raised after her mother’s death and receives a bridegroom.<-

But when she was twelve years old, her mother departed from this life. Her father then stayed with her and instructed her in the Scriptures and the various wisdom of this world. The maiden then became so learned that even her father marveled at it. The rumor of her spread through the whole city, as much for her wisdom as for her learning, and because she was very beautiful and of good manners in body and mind. Many, however, took great pains and courted her for their sons, and many sought to move her father, but they could not achieve their goal; yet he said: The Lord's will be done! One, however, who surpassed all others in status and wealth, sent for her father and desired of him that he would give his daughter to his son in marriage; and he promised her to him.

When the father heard this, he summoned *Smaragdus* and spoke to him: "My son, the beauty of your face is burdensome to the weak brothers; therefore, I desire that you remain alone in your hut, and therein sing and eat, and do not go out from there." 

And he commanded *Agapitus* to prepare a chamber alone and let *Smaragdus* dwell therein. Thus *Agapitus* did everything that was commanded of him by the father of the monastery and led *Smaragdus* into a chamber alone; therein she devoted herself to prayer, and was diligent in fasting and vigils day and night, thus serving the LORD in simplicity of heart. So much so, that the aforementioned brother *Agapitus* marveled at it, and reported her <note>Original German: "seine (ihre)" — the text acknowledges both the male persona and the female reality.</note> steadfastness to all the brothers, and all praised GOD, who worked such things in weakness <note>This likely refers to the contemporary view of women as the "weaker vessel," making her spiritual discipline seem even more miraculous to the monks.</note>.

VIII. The Life of St. Euphrosyna.

### Chapter 9.
->She is sought everywhere in vain.<-

After her father came home, he hurried quickly into the bedchamber where his daughter used to stay, and as he did not find her, he became distressed and sad, and began anxiously to ask the servants and maidservants <note>The original German "Dirnen" here refers to young female servants, which was its standard meaning before it acquired a modern negative connotation.</note> how things stood with Euphrosyna. The young men, however, gave report and spoke: "We still saw her late yesterday evening; but early this morning she did not appear, and we are of the mind that the father of that son to whom she had been betrothed has taken her away." Thereupon he sent his servants to that man's house, but they did not find her. But when her bridegroom, along with his father, heard this, it grieved them greatly, and they came to Paphnutius, whom they found extremely distressed and lying upon the earth, to whom they spoke: "Perhaps someone has enticed her and led her away." 

Immediately, servants on horseback were sent throughout all Alexandria; likewise, she was sought in the ships that lay in and before the harbor; also the nunneries, the desolate places, the cellars, and the houses of friends and relatives were visited. And when she was found nowhere, they mourned her as one deceased; the father-in-law lamented his daughter-in-law, and the bridegroom wept for his bride. The father, however, wailed for his daughter and spoke: "Alas! Alas! My lovely daughter! Alas! Comfort of my eyes! Who has stolen my goods? Who has taken away my property? Who has ruined my vineyard? Who has extinguished my lamp? Who has destroyed my hope? Who has shamed the beauty of my daughter? Which wolf has taken my little sheep? What place hides such a face? What sea carries away her royal beauty as a prisoner? The courageous soul <note>original: "Sele"</note>, the comforter in all misery, the rest of the sorrowful; she who was a haven for all the troubled! O earth, earth, hide not my blood <note>A biblical allusion to Job 16:18, expressing a cry for justice and the revealing of a hidden tragedy.</note> until I see what has happened to my daughter." This and the like spoke the deeply distressed father Paphnutius, and all present raised their voices and wept; indeed, the entire city of Alexandria lamented her.

Now when Smaragdus—namely, Euphrosyna—recognized that her end was drawing near, she called Paphnutius and spoke to him: "Almighty God has well preserved my wretched life until now, and fulfilled my desire, which I have manfully <note>original: "männlich". And because I promised the spiritual Father <note>The Abbot of the monastery.</note> that I possessed many goods, and that if I could persevere in this place, I would devote them here—so you must now fulfill such a promise, because this place is honorable, and pray for me." When she had said this, she gave up her spirit on New Year’s Day.

### Chapter 15.

### Chapter 16.

->The whole monastery laments her and buries her with honor.<-

He then came and fell upon her face, wept and said: "Euphrosyna, you bride of Christ and daughter of the saints, do not forget your fellow servants and this monastery, but pray for us to the Lord Jesus Christ, that he may help us to fight manfully and reach the harbor of salvation, and have a share with him and his saints." Thereupon he ordered that all the brothers should assemble and help bury the holy body with due honor. Now as they were gathered and looked upon such a great wonder, they glorified God, who works such miracles even in the weak female sex <note>This reflects a common theme in medieval hagiography where the spiritual strength of a woman is presented as a special sign of divine power</note>. One of the brothers, however, who had only one eye and was blind in the other, kissed her face with tears; as soon as he touched her, he became seeing again in the other eye. When all the other brothers who were present saw this, they praised God and thanked him from whom all good things come. And so they buried her, much edified and strengthened, in the burial place of the fathers of the monastery. Her father, however, distributed everything he had among the poor in the community, as well to the hospital as to the monastery—the largest part of his fortune—and died in that same chamber and on the same mat,

# IX. The Life of St. Thais the Prostitute.

->Written by an Anonymous Author.<-

->Chapter 1.<-

->Father Paphnutius goes to the prostitute Thais and converts her.<-

<note>(*) Cephala, whose life is described in the first part, Num. XXIII. page 359.</note>
There was a certain prostitute named Thais, of such exceptional beauty that many, for her sake, lost all their property and possessions and fell into the most extreme poverty. Likewise, her impure lovers often fell into such bloody quarrels with one another that Thais’s doorstep was splattered with blood. When Father Paphnutius (*) heard of this, he put on worldly clothing and took a ducat <note>A gold coin used as currency in various European countries; here used as a literary device to represent a significant sum of money</note> with him, and traveled to a certain city in Egypt where she resided. When he arrived at her house, he gave her the ducat, as if he were delivering the wages of sin to her. Once she had received the gold, she said: "Let us go into the chamber!" So he went in; and as he sat down upon the costly daybed, he pressed her and said: "If there is yet an inner chamber, let us go in there." She said: "There is indeed another, but if you fear men, you need not worry about any here, for no one is allowed inside; but if you fear God, then no place is hidden from His Divine eyes." When the Elder heard this, he said to her: "Do you know that there is a God?" She gave him the answer: "I know

## Chapter 2.

->She is imprisoned for three years.<-

When everything had been destroyed by the flames, she went to the place where the Elder had directed her; he then took her with him to a place where a company of secluded holy virgins resided, and shut her there in a small hut, the door of which he locked and sealed, leaving only a small window open through which a little food was passed to her; for he commanded that the sisters should give her a little bread and a little water daily. But when he was about to depart from the hut, Thais said to him: "Dear Father, where shall I perform the necessities of nature <note>A period euphemism for using the toilet</note> with the door locked?" He said: "In the hut, as you deserve." She further asked: "How she should pray correctly?" He spoke: "You are not worthy to name **God**, nor to take His most holy name upon your lips, nor are you worthy to lift your hands toward heaven, for your lips are full of malice and your hands full of impurity; but instead, just sit, and turn your face toward the East <note>The traditional direction of prayer in early Christianity, symbolizing the rising sun of Christ</note>, and repeat these words alone many times: 'You who have created me, have mercy on me!'"

### Chapter 3.

->Paphnutius learns that God has forgiven her sins, lets her out, whereupon she dies a blessed death.<-

After she had been thus shut away for three years, Father Paphnutius felt compassion for her and went to Father Anthony <note>St. Anthony the Great, the famous father of Christian monasticism</note> so that he might learn from him whether the Lord had forgiven her sins or not. When he arrived there and told him the whole matter in the finest detail, Father Anthony called his disciples and commanded them to keep watch through the night and to persist together in prayer, each one individually, to see if it might please God to reveal to one of them the answer to Father Paphnutius’s inquiry. When they had all gone to their separate places and persisted earnestly in prayer, Father Paul the Elder (*) <note>Known as Paul the Simple</note>, a disciple of Father Anthony, suddenly saw in heaven a resting bed made of precious fabric, where three virgins with radiant faces were waiting. When Paul saw this, he said: "This is for no one else but my father Anthony!" But a voice answered him: "It is not for your father Anthony, but for Thais, who was once a prostitute." When Father Paul told this publicly, Father Paphnutius recognized the Divine Will and returned to the community of solitary virgins where Thais was imprisoned. He opened her locked door and told her to come out; but she begged that she might remain imprisoned there longer. After the door was opened, however, he said to her: "Come out, for God has forgiven your sins." She answered: "I testify before God that since I came in here, I have made a bundle, as it were, of all my sins and kept it always before my eyes, so that my sins never left my sight, but I have constantly wept over them." Thereupon Father Paphnutius said to her: "God has not forgiven your sins because of your harsh way of life, but because you have always held such thoughts <note>meaning her constant state of repentance and mindfulness of her failings</note>." After he had led her out of the hut, Thais lived for only fourteen days longer and then fell asleep in peace. *Lives of the Fathers*, Book 1, page 374 <note>original: "Vit. PP. L. 1. pag. 374" (Vitae Patrum)</note>.

# X. The Life of St. Pelagia the Prostitute. <note>original: "S. Pelagiæ Meretricis" (Latin: Sanctae Pelagiae Meretricis)</note>
## Described by James the Deacon. <note>James the Deacon was the traditional biographer of Pelagia; he presents himself as an eyewitness to her conversion.</note>
### Author's Preface by JAMES.

We are duty-bound to praise our Lord at all times and to thank Him most highly, who does not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that they all should repent and turn toward life. Hear then the great miracle which has happened in our days. It seemed good to me, poor sinner James, to describe this and to pass it on to you, holy brothers, so that you might come to know it through reading or hearing, and that you might be built up by it for the salvation of your souls. For God is indeed merciful, and so that no one may be lost, He has ordained it so in this life that through repentance, misdeeds are forgiven; for in the world to come, judgment shall be upheld, where each shall receive the reward according to his works. So give me now your ear, and look upon me with all the care of your heart, because our report is full of nourishment for the heart.

## Chapter 1.
->Council at Antioch.<-

The holy Bishop of Antioch called to himself all the bishops living around him because of a certain matter of business; thus, eight bishops came to him, among whom was also the very holy man of God, Nonnus, my bishop of Edessa <note>Edessa was a major center of early Christian learning in Upper Mesopotamia, now modern-day Şanlıurfa, Turkey</note>; a wondrous man and a proven hermit from the brotherhood of the Tabennisiotes <note>The Tabennisiotes were a monastic community in Egypt founded by St. Pachomius, known for their strict communal life</note>; for because of his incomparable life and well-conducted path, he had been called from his solitude to the office of Bishop. When they had now gathered in the aforementioned city, the Bishop of this city of Antioch commanded us that we should go to the church of the holy martyr Julian. So we repaired there, just as the other bishops had also gathered themselves there at the door of this main church.

## Chapter 2.

->The holy Bishop Nonnus gazes upon the beautiful prostitute Pelagia.<-

As they had now sat down together, some of the bishops asked my Lord Nonnus that he would build them up with his teaching and word; immediately the holy bishop, with his anointed mouth, began to speak for the edification and salvation of all the listeners. While we were together admiring his teaching; behold, there suddenly came passing by the most prominent <term>actress</term> <note>original: "Comödiantin"; in the late Roman world, this referred to a public performer or mime, a profession then associated with low social status and often prostitution</note> of Antioch, namely the lead dancer of the great theater; she sat upon a donkey and came along with great splendor, so adorned that one saw nothing on her but gold, pearls, and precious stones; even her bare feet were covered with gold and pearls. She had with her a magnificent troop of boys and girls, decorated with costly garments, and a golden chain upon her neck. Some went before, some followed after her; but among all people in the world, she had no equal in beauty and elegance. As she passed by us, she filled the air with a glorious scent and <term>musk</term> <note>original: "Biesem"; an archaic term for musk or perfume</note>, and other lovely and fragrant things. But when the bishops saw her, that she passed by so shamelessly with an uncovered head and bare breasts, with such a large entourage, having neither head nor breasts covered; they sighed silently to themselves and turned their faces away from such grave sin.

***

## Chapter 3.

->Nonnus admires her beauty and adornment with holy intent.<-

But the most blessed Nonnus looked at her closely, and for a good while at that; so much so that he continued to contemplate her even after she had passed by, and watched her go. Afterwards he turned his face away from her and spoke to the bishops who sat around him: "Did you not take delight in her beauty?" When they did not answer, he bowed his face down to his knees and wetted the holy <term>manual</term> <note>original: "Manual" (Hand-Book); a small, portable prayer book or liturgical volume</note> that he held in his holy hands—indeed, his whole lap—with tears; he sighed deeply and spoke again to the bishops: "Did you then not take delight in such exceptional beauty of hers?" When they still gave no answer, he said: "Truly, it has greatly delighted me, and her beauty has pleased me; God will present her publicly before the throne of His terrible and wonderful seat, when He shall judge us and our <term>bishopric</term> <note>original: "Bischof-Amt"; refers here to the office and responsibility of being a bishop</note>."

Further he spoke to the bishops: "What do you think, my beloved friends, how many hours has this woman spent in her chamber washing and adorning herself? ## Chapter 4.

->Bishop Nonnus laments the carelessness of Christians in comparison to the adorned Pelagia.<-

After he had spoken all this, he took hold of me, a poor sinner (the deacon), and we came to the inn where a room had been assigned to us. There he went into his small bedchamber and threw himself to the floor, lying with his face upon the earth, beating his breast, weeping, and saying:

"Lord Jesus Christ, forgive me, a sinner and unworthy man! For this immoral woman has adorned herself more beautifully for a single day than I have ever adorned my soul. I am completely naked, both in heaven and on earth; I do not fulfill your command and commandment; therefore, I have no hope from good works, but my hope stands upon your mer—"

## Chapter 5.
->A Remarkable Dream of Bishop Nonnus.<-

But when the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note> arrived, and we had finished the night prayers, the holy Bishop Nonnus said to me: "My deacon and dear brother, I must tell you this: I have had a dream and am very troubled, because I do not know what it might mean." And he immediately said further to me: "I saw in a dream how a black dove stood at the corner of the altar; it was very hideous and filthy. It flew around me, and I could not endure its shameful stench and foul impurity. It remained with me until the prayer of the newly-joining Christians <note>catechumens, or those receiving instruction before baptism</note> was over. But after the deacon who teaches the <term>Catechism</term> <note>religious instruction for converts</note> cried out publicly and said: 'Step forward!' <note>The traditional dismissal of those not yet baptized before the start of the Communion service</note> it was suddenly seen nowhere. And when the young believers had gone out and the <term>Lord’s Supper</term> <note>the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> was performed, and when the congregation was dismissed and I was just stepping out of the church, that same unclean dove returned at the church door and flew around me. But I stretched out my hand, seized it, and threw it into the <term>baptismal font</term> <note>original: "Tauf-Stein"</note> which stood in the courtyard of the holy church; there it left all the dung and filth with which it was soiled in the water, came out, and was as white as snow, flew away, and soared into the heights, and thus vanished entirely from my sight." When the holy Bishop and man of God Nonnus had told his dream, he took me with him, and we came with the other bishops to the main church; there we greeted the Bishop of the city.

The holy Bishop Nonnus could hardly persuade her to stand up from his feet again; but when she had stood up, he spoke: The priestly orders <note>These are the established rules of the early church regarding the administration of sacraments</note> dictate that one should not baptize a dissolute woman unless she provides witnesses as guarantors <note>These "guarantors" acted like sponsors or godparents, promising to ensure she would not return to her former life</note> that she will no longer wallow in such sins. ## Chapter 11.
->She hands over all her possessions for the benefit of the poor.<-

Immediately, he summoned the eldest steward <note>original: "Diener," likely referring to a church treasurer or oikonomos.</note> of the church, placed all such goods into his hands, and said: "I adjure you by the indivisible Trinity that you let none of these things enter the bishopric or the congregation, but rather that they be given to the common widows, orphans, and the poor. But if you, despite this solemn oath, should embezzle any of this yourself or through another, then may a curse come upon your house or theirs, and such a person shall have his part with those who cried out: 'Crucify, crucify Him!'" She, however, summoned all her bond-servants and maids and gave them their freedom. She gave them the golden chains from her hands and said: "Hurry and release yourselves from this evil world full of sin, so that just as we have been together in this world, we may also remain together without pain in that life of highly desired blessedness."

## Chapter 12.

-> She flees to the desert on the Mount of Olives with the counsel of Father Nonnus. <-

**O**n the eighth day, however, when the white baptismal robes were laid aside <note>It was tradition for the newly baptized to wear white garments for one week following their initiation into the church.</note>, she rose up during the night without our knowledge, took off her baptismal robe, and put on a hair shirt <note>A garment made of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a form of penance.</note> and an outer garment belonging to the holy Bishop Nonnus. From that day on, she was seen no more in the city of Antioch. The holy Romana wept bitterly for her, but Nonnus comforted her, saying: "Do not weep, my daughter, but rather rejoice greatly; for Pelagia has chosen the better part, like Mary, whom the Lord preferred over Martha in the Gospel" <note>A reference to Luke 10:41–42, where Jesus commends Mary for listening to his teaching while Martha is distracted by chores.</note>. Pelagia, however, traveled toward Jerusalem and built herself a hut there on the Mount of Olives, where the Lord had prayed.

## Chapter 13.

-> James the Deacon travels to Jerusalem and wishes to visit Pelagia without being recognized. <-

**A**fter some time had passed, the Bishop of Antioch summoned the other bishops to him, so that each might return home to his own people. After three or four years had gone by, I, James the Deacon, felt a longing to travel to Jerusalem so that I might worship at the site of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ; I therefore asked my bishop if he would allow me to travel there. He granted me leave and said to me: "Dear brother Deacon, I tell you, when you come to Jerusalem, inquire there for a brother named Pelagius. He is a hermit and a eunuch <note>original: "Verſchnittener." In hagiography, female saints living as monks often passed themselves off as eunuchs to explain their lack of a beard and high voices.</note> who has lived there for many years shut away in the desert. Visit him, for you can certainly be edified by him." He said all this, however, concerning the servant of God, Pelagia, though in a veiled manner.

# Chapter 15.
## Pelagia’s Blessed Death.

Now much was said in the monasteries about Brother Pelagius; therefore, I decided within myself that I would travel there once more and refresh myself with his wholesome teaching. When I came to his hut and knocked boldly, calling him by his name, he answered nothing. Therefore I said to myself: "Either there is no one inside, or the hermit who lived here has wandered away." Nevertheless, **GOD** put it in my mind that I should think further: "I must see whether he has perhaps died"; and I went before the shutter of the little window and peered inside, and I saw that he was dead. Then I closed the little window again, sealed it diligently with clay <note>original: "Laimen." Then the holy fathers came, together with the hermits from various communities; thus the little door of the cell was opened, and his holy body was carried out, which they laid down reverently as if it were gold or precious stones. This is the "pious fraud" trope common in hagiography, where a woman lives undetected as a monk to achieve greater sanctity.</note>. # XI. The Life of St. Melania the Elder.
<note>original: "S. Melania Romana." She is known as "the Elder" to distinguish her from her granddaughter of the same name.</note>

->Described by Palladius and Heraclides.<-
<note>Palladius of Galatia and Heraclides of Cyprus were 4th and 5th-century authors who documented the lives of early Christian desert saints.</note>

### Chapter 1.
->The lineage, marriage, and widowhood of the holy Melania, along with her choice of the spiritual life.<-

The holy and highly blessed Melania was born in the city of Rome and was the daughter of a Roman consul <note>original: "Bürgermeisters." While this literally means "mayor," in the context of ancient Rome, it refers to the high office of consul.</note> named Marcellinus; she was the wife of a very noble man whose name I (Palladius) cannot remember. In the twenty-second year of her age, in the year 368 AD, her husband died, and in that same year, two of her little sons died, leaving behind a single, still-young infant. She remained a widow who, out of divine love, now surrendered herself to the eternal Bridegroom and loved Him until the end of her life. After she had assigned faithful guardians to her little son, she secretly sold all her immovable property <note>In legal terms, "immovable property" refers to land and buildings.</note> (on account of Emperor Valens, who at the beginning of his reign was a zealous persecutor of the Orthodox <note>original: "Recht-gläubigen," literally "right-believers." Emperor Valens favored Arianism and persecuted those who held to the Nicene Creed.</note>). With her movable goods, along with several trusted servants and attendants, she quickly took ship for Alexandria. Once she had also turned all her mobile possessions into money here, while she was with the priest <note>original footnote: "Paulinus Ep. 10. ad Severum." This refers to a letter from Paulinus of Nola to Sulpicius Severus regarding Melania's life.</note>...

## Chapter 2.

->She serves the imprisoned Fathers; she is imprisoned herself for it, and then reveals her identity.<-

However, after this, the Governor, or Imperial Prefect of Alexandria, drove out the holy men—Isidorus, Pissimius, Adelphius, Paphnutius, Pambo, and Ammon Parotes, along with twelve bishops and priests, totaling one hundred and twelve in number—from Egypt, and banished them into misery in Diocaesarea in Palestine. The blessed Melania followed them there and provided for them from her own means, serving them with her own hands. And when the guards who watched over those imprisoned saints tried to prevent her (as the Fathers Pissimius, Isidorus, Paphnutius, and Ammonius later told me themselves), the blessed woman disguised herself in the clothing of a servant and brought them all the necessities of life in the evenings.

When the Governor in Palestine heard of this, he hoped to fill his pockets with her money and to blind her eyes with smoke <note>original: "mit Rauch die Augen zu verblenden." This is an idiom meaning to deceive or intimidate someone through confusion or a show of power.</note>; for he did not actually know who she was. He therefore ordered that she should be seized and thrown into prison. But she sent word to him through messengers, saying: "I am the daughter of the Roman Consul Marcellinus, and I was the wife of a certain nobleman; but now I am a servant of Christ. Do not think, therefore, that you may despise me because of my current humble clothing. For if I wished to exalt myself over you, I could do so; yet I do not fear you, and I will not allow you to take any of my goods for yourself. However, so that you do not fall into trouble on my account, I have [sent] this to you..."

## Chapter 3.
->Saint Melania builds a convent for virgins in or near Jerusalem and serves the strangers alongside Rufinus.<-

After the aforementioned holy fathers, bishops, and priests were released from their imprisonment, the holy Melania traveled to Jerusalem. There, using her own resources, she built a monastery or dwelling for the virgins consecrated to God; she took sixty of them into her care and provided for them for thirty-seven years until her blessed end. There was also a man in her acquaintance named Rufinus (*) <note>original: Ruffinus</note>, born in Aquileia in Italy—a noble-minded, virtuous, and learned man who was later called to the priesthood. Together with her, he was devoted to receiving all the hermits, bishops, virgins, and God-devoted persons who came to Jerusalem. They served these people from their own means, according to the vow they had made to God. They also brought back to the holy community forty people who had separated themselves from the congregation of God because of the erroneous teachings of Paulinus <note>Paulinus of Antioch (died c. 388) was a key figure in the Meletian schism, a complicated theological and jurisdictional dispute in the early Church.</note>, Bishop of Antioch. They also used their love and teaching to convince and help many heretics from the sect of the "Inspirants" <note>This likely refers to the Pneumatomachians, or "Spirit-fighters," who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>—who wage a war against the Holy Spirit of God—back to the right path. Thus, they spent their lives in holy conduct and, as much as was in their power, gave no one the slightest cause for offense; on the contrary, they served and filled almost the whole world with spiritual edification.

XI. The Life of St. Melania of Rome <note>original: "S. Melaniae Rom."</note> 135

For the good deeds and alms of this immortal woman are known not only in the West but also in the East—yes, even toward the South and North. For thirty-seven years she received all strangers and provided them with everything they required; she supported the churches, monasteries, and hospitals, and fed the prisoners. To say it in a single word: no one who visited her was sent away without being refreshed by her. Furthermore, funds were sent to her annually by her blood-relatives, her son, and his guardians. While she practiced such hospitality, she herself possessed not even a hand’s-breadth of earth as her own property; nor could any longing for her only son separate her from the love of Christ. Through her prayers, however, the boy attained great understanding and became a youth of good conduct until he married a noble maiden of his own rank and attained worldly offices of honor, eventually having two sons through the blessing of marriage.

### Chapter 5.

->She travels again to Rome in her old age, winning over her entire family and other nobles to Christ; and she dies.<-

Many years later, however, when she heard of the condition of her sister's daughter <note>While the text says "sister's daughter," historical records identify Melania the Younger as the granddaughter of Melania the Elder.</note>—that she had married and was now minded to renounce the world—she (Melania) became concerned that the woman might be led astray by such emotional stirrings, or be seduced into heresy, or otherwise fall into error. Thus, this holy woman, now a sixty-year-old elder (*in the year 406*), took to the sea, departed from Caesarea, and arrived in Rome within twenty days. There she visited her relatives with a spiritual purpose and taught the foundations of the Christian faith to her sister's husband, Apronianus <note>original: "Aproniano"</note>—who was a wise and highly respected man, but still a pagan—so that he became a Christian. She also moved him to a life of chastity and abstinence, according to the wish of his chaste wife, her own sister, named Avita. She also strengthened their daughter, the younger Melania, in her godly purpose, along with her husband, Pinianus <note>original: "Pinniano"</note>. Furthermore, she instructed Albina, the wife of her son, in the foundations of the Christian faith. She convinced all of them to sell everything and depart from Rome with her, heading toward the secure harbor of a secluded, holy life. Meanwhile, she also fought with the "wild beasts," namely the Great Ones <note>This is a metaphorical reference to the powerful Roman aristocracy who opposed her family's decision to give away their massive wealth.</note>

## Chapter 6.

# XII. The Life of St. Melania the Younger. <note>original: "S. Melaniâ Parvâ," literally Melania the Small or the Younger, to distinguish her from her grandmother.</note>
## Described by Palladius and Heraclides. <note>Palladius and Heraclides were early Christian historians who documented the lives of the Desert Fathers and prominent ascetics.</note>
### Chapter 1.

->Melania is forced into marriage; after she had borne two children, she won her husband for Christ, and they chose the path of chastity.<-

It would be unjust if we were to neglect the holy life of the younger Melania and pass over the exceptional virtuous conduct of the granddaughter or niece <note>The text says "Schwester Tochter" (sister's daughter), though historical records identify her as the granddaughter of Melania the Elder.</note> of the great Melania; which truly far surpasses many wise and diligent elders. Though young in years, but old in godly experience, her parents married her off against her will and joined her with one of the most prominent men of the city of Rome. Because she constantly remembered her grandmother’s teachings on chastity, her conscience was so wounded that she could not reconcile herself to the married state. After she had borne two children and they had died, she felt such a distaste for the state of marriage that she spoke to her husband, Pinianus—who was a son of Severus, one of the provincial governors <term>Land-Verweser: a high-ranking administrative official or governor acting on behalf of the emperor</term>—saying: "If you are willing to live with me in abstinence according to the law of chastity, I will acknowledge you as my dear lord and entrust my life to your power. But if this is too burdensome for you as a young man, then keep all my dowry; only grant me the freedom to satisfy my longing in God, as I desire to become an heir to the divine virtuous conduct of my grandmother, whose name I also bear. For if God had wanted to keep us in this world and desired that we should enjoy the world and the flesh longer, He would not have taken my two sons, whom I bore to you, so prematurely." After they were unable to agree with one another on this matter for a long time, God finally took pity on the young man and awakened in him also a zeal for godliness, so that he too renounced the whole world and all fleshly things; then that which the Apostle had written: <meta>catchword: written:</meta>

# XII. The Life of St. Melania the Younger.
## Described by Palladius and Heraclides. <note>Palladius (c. 363–420 AD) was a monk and bishop who wrote the *Lausiac History*, a primary source for the lives of the Desert Fathers and Mothers.</note>
### Chapter 1.

->Melania is forced into marriage; after she has born two children, she wins her husband for Christ, and they choose chastity.<-

It would be wrong if we were to overlook the holy life of the younger **Melania**, and pass by the exceptional virtuous conduct of the elder **Melania's** granddaughter <note>The text adds "or sister's daughter," reflecting historical uncertainty about the exact lineage, though she is most commonly known as the granddaughter.</note>; who truly far surpasses many wise and diligent elders. This woman, though young in years but old in godly experience, was married by her parents against her will and bound to one of the most noble men in the city of **Rome**. Because she constantly remembered her grandmother’s teachings on chastity, she was so wounded in her conscience that she could not adapt herself to the married state.

After she had now given birth to two children, and they both died, she felt such a loathing for the state of marriage that she spoke to her husband, **Pinianus**—who was a son of **Severus**, one of the provincial governors <term>Land-Verweser: a high-ranking administrative official, likely referring to a Roman prefect</term>—saying: "If you wish to live with me according to the law of chastity in abstinence, I will recognize you as my dear lord and leave my life in your power; but if this is burdensome to you as a young man, then keep all my dowry, only grant me the freedom to satisfy my longing in God. For I desire to become an heir of the divine virtuous life of my grandmother, whose name I also bear. For if God had wished to keep us in this world and intended for us to enjoy the world and the flesh longer, He would not have taken my two sons, whom I bore to you, so prematurely." 

After they both could not agree with one another regarding this for a long time, God finally took pity on the young man and awakened in him also a zeal for godliness, so that he too renounced the whole world and all fleshly things; then that which the Apostle has written was fulfilled:

# XI. The Life of St. Melania of Rome.

...of Rome and their wives, who wished to prevent them from selling their estates; to whom the handmaid of Christ spoke: "My children, it has been nearly four hundred years since it was written: *It is the last hour*; <note>original: *1Joh.2,v.18.*</note> Why then do we still wish so gladly and willfully to persist in the vanity of this life? Let the days of the Antichrist not come and find you no longer able to enjoy your estates and the heritage of your ancestors." When she had convinced them all to love the departed life <note>A life "departed" or "withdrawn" from the world; a monastic or ascetic life.</note> with these and similar persuasive speeches, and had instructed them more deeply, they traveled over to **Sicily**, where they turned their remaining manors and landed estates into money. From there they traveled toward **Jerusalem**. And after she, **Melania**, had completely distributed her entire fortune to the poor, she died after forty days in a good age and the highest gentleness, leaving behind a venerable memory and the monastery at **Jerusalem**, for which she provided sufficiently even after her death.

### Chapter 6.

->The city of Rome is horribly devastated by **Alaric**, the King of the Goths, in the year 410.<-

After all those whom the blessed **Melania** had convinced and instructed had escaped from **Rome**, the barbarians fell upon the city of **Rome** with a storm, conquered and plundered it, and left not even a statue or erected metallic honorary image within it. The fury of the enemy so completely devastated everything that this city of **Rome**—which at that time had flourished and been in good standing for one thousand two hundred years with an innumerable multitude of inhabitants—now became a gruesome wasteland. As the **Sibyl** <note>Referring to the Sibylline Oracles, a collection of ancient prophecies often cited by early Christians.</note> had previously said, it should be called **Rhyme** <note>original: *Rhyme*; a wordplay on the Greek *rhyme* (street/lane/ruin) versus *Roma* (strength/glory).</note>, that is a village, but not **Rome**. When those who had previously escaped on **Melania's** advice heard such news, they praised God, who through such a transformation had overcome their unbelief. And while all others, the noble along with the lowly, were led into slavery and barbaric servitude, they and their families alone were rescued, having sacrificed themselves to the Lord through the blessed work of the holy **Melania**.

# XII. The Life of St. Melania the Younger.
## Described by Palladius and Heraclides.
<note>Palladius (c. 363–420 AD) was a bishop and author of the *Lausiac History*, one of the most important sources for the lives of early Christian desert fathers and mothers.</note>
### Chapter 1.

->Melania is forced into marriage; after she had given birth to two children, she wins her husband over to Christ, and they choose the path of chastity.<-

It would be unjust if we were to neglect the holy life of the younger **Melania**, and pass over the exceptional and virtuous conduct of the elder **Melania's** granddaughter or niece; <note>Historical records confirm she was the granddaughter of Melania the Elder.</note> whose conduct truly far surpasses many wise and diligent elders. Though young in years, she was old in God-fearing experience. Her parents married her off against her will, uniting her with one of the most prominent men of the city of **Rome**. Because she constantly remembered her grandmother’s teachings on chastity, her conscience was so deeply moved that she could not settle herself into the married state. 

After she had given birth to two children and they both died, she developed such a distaste for the married state that she spoke to her husband, **Pinnianus**—who was a son of **Severus**, one of the <term>Governors</term> <note>original: "Land-Verweser"; likely referring to a high-ranking Roman official such as a City Prefect.</note>—saying: "If you will live with me in abstinence according to the law of chastity, I will recognize you as my dear lord and yield my life into your power. But if this is too burdensome for you as a young man, then keep all my dowry; only grant me the freedom to satisfy my longing in **God**, as I desire to become an heir to the divine and virtuous life of my grandmother, whose name I also bear. For if **God** had wanted to keep us in this world to enjoy the world and the flesh longer, He would not have taken my two sons, whom I bore to you, so prematurely." 

After the two of them were unable to agree on this matter for a long time, **God** finally took pity on the young man and awakened in him a zeal for godliness, so that he too renounced the whole world and all fleshly things; thus was fulfilled what the **Apostle** had written: <note>This likely refers to 1 Corinthians 7, where Paul discusses marriage and devotion to God.</note>

## Chapter 2.
->She distributes her wealth to the members of Christ.<-

**S**o it was that at the age of twenty, having been released from the [marital] obligations to her husband, she now renounced this world. She first gave all her silk outer garments to the service of the altar; her remaining silk clothing she unraveled and fashioned into various church vessels. Her silver and gold, however, she entrusted to Paul—a priest of the holy solitaries—and sent it across the sea to the Eastern lands, namely to Egypt and the Promised Land or Palestine. To the solitaries in Egypt and the <term>Thebaid</term> <note>An ancient region in Upper Egypt famous for its many early Christian hermits and monasteries.</note> she bequeathed ten thousand <term>ducats</term> <note>Though the original text uses "ducats" (a later European currency), in the 4th century this would have been a massive sum of Roman gold solidi.</note>; Antioch in Syria and the surrounding regions likewise received ten thousand ducats; and Palestine also ten thousand ducats. Of her own bondservants and maids, she granted freedom to eight thousand; the others, however, did not wish to be free, but preferred to remain with her current spiritual brother and former husband, **Pinianus**. All the estates she owned in Spain, France, and the other cities of Italy, she sold and distributed the money down to the last penny. Those she possessed in Sicily, Campania, and Africa, she retained, in order to gradually do good for the solitaries and the destitute (*). This is the wise steward<meta>ship</meta>

### Chapter 3.

->Pinianus and Melania visit Augustine.<-

During the time that they were liquidating their estates in all places, Melania, along with her "marriage-brother" Pinianus <note>They were legally married but lived in a "spiritual marriage" as celibates, hence "Ehe-Bruder" or marriage-brother.</note>, traveled to their estates in Africa, specifically to Thagaste <note>The birthplace of St. Augustine in modern-day Algeria.</note>. There they visited Saint Augustine, the Bishop of Hippo, whose zealous congregation attempted to seize Pinianus by force to ordain him as a priest. Their motive was to improve the church's revenues through his vast estates; however, Augustine himself prevented this, though he suffered much criticism for it. Pinianus, fearing that the irrational mob might do him violence, fled Hippo by night and returned to Thagaste. There, he and the chaste Melania founded two monasteries or dwellings for those seeking solitude, providing them with sufficient maintenance. In one were eighty brothers, and in the other, one hundred and thirty God-devoted virgins. <note>original: "August. Ep. 224. & 225." These refer to Letters 224 and 225 written by Saint Augustine regarding this specific dispute.</note>

### Chapter 4.

->They travel to Egypt and Jerusalem. The conduct of Pinianus and other saints.<-

After they had settled their affairs in Africa, they finally traveled to Jerusalem. Once they had visited the Desert Fathers in Egypt, they both separated from one another, and each led a particularly holy and secluded life. Saint Pinianus practiced his devotion in the company of thirty solitaries, reading the Divine Scriptures and tending the garden while engaged in God-fearing conversation. They <note>Meaning Melania and Pinianus.</note> showed us (Palladius and his companions) much love and honor and provided for us abundantly when we were being persecuted because of the blessed John Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom was an influential Archbishop of Constantinople who died in exile; the author Palladius was one of his supporters.</note> and met them while they were still in Rome. Thus, they proved their godliness through their deeds and made it sufficiently known that they earnestly strove for the eternal life of our Lord JESUS. It also happened in Jerusalem that a Roman Senator named Pammachius came to him; he too, on the advice of the elder Melania <note>Melania the Younger's grandmother.</note> and the good example of Pinianus, had renounced the world and led an excellent life. He gave his estates, which were of such a [vast size]...

...that not even a Roman army of 72,000 men could have been maintained by their annual rents.

### Chapter 5.
->The holy, solitary lifestyle of Melania and her mother Albina.<-

The holy Melania conducted her life in the following manner: she had built herself a hut on the Mount of Olives and there spent her angelic life <note>The "angelic life" (from the Greek *bios angelikos*) was a common historical term for the monastic life, as monks and nuns were thought to live like angels, neither marrying nor seeking earthly comforts.</note> with great moderation. Initially, she often did not eat for five days; but usually, she ate every other day. She served her own handmaids in all things, for she had awakened them to be holy fellow-combatants <note>A metaphor for those living the disciplined, ascetic life of a nun.</note>—at least those who, as mentioned before, had not desired to be set free. Moreover, she also stirred many of her relatives to divine zeal, so that they served God conscientiously alongside her. This is the life of the younger Melania through our Lord Jesus Christ. However, her mother Albina also visited her; she likewise lived in godly practice and distributed her money specifically among the poor. She lived with her household on her estates, sometimes in Sicily, sometimes in Campania, with fifteen eunuch servants <note>original: "verschnittenen Dienern." These were castrated attendants, common in the households of the late Roman aristocracy.</note> and many virgins and female slaves. <note>original: "Pallad. cap. 119.--124." refers to chapters in Palladius's history.</note>

### Chapter 6.
->Melania travels to her cousin in Constantinople.<-

Melania received letters from her cousin Volusianus, who at that time was appointed Governor of Rome but had been sent on an embassy to Constantinople to the Empress Eudoxia. The content of the letter was that he had long desired to see and speak with her, which could now conveniently happen since she was nearby. She, likewise, had a desire to speak with her cousin and to lead him away from the pagan errors in which he still remained. Because she was in doubt, however, fearing she might act imprudently against God’s counsel and will in this matter, she consulted with experienced solitaries <note>Experienced monks or hermits.</note> who approved of her journey to Constantinople; and so she departed—

Wherever she passed through a city or region, she was shown all honors befitting her rank; for the priests and bishops of the cities showed her no small honor; and the God-devoted holy virgins, along with the famous hermits of all places, received her with humble respect and greeting, looking upon her as one who came to them from heaven. ### Chapter 7.

->Miracles at Chalcedon; Melania arrives at Constantinople and visits Volusianus.<-

She took up lodging at Chalcedon with the clergy at the temple of the most blessed martyr Euphemia <note>St. Euphemia (d. 303 AD) was a celebrated martyr; the Council of Chalcedon was later held in her basilica.</note>; there, at midnight, a very pleasant fragrance arose from the tomb of this most blessed martyr, which filled everything with unspeakable sweet loveliness. Through this she gained good courage, so that early the next morning she boldly sailed across the strait and proceeded all the way to Constantinople. There, a distinguished but devout man named Lausus hosted her; he was a counselor of the Empire and the Grand Chamberlain <note>The *Praepositus Sacri Cubiculi*, one of the highest-ranking officials in the Byzantine court. The "Lausiac History" was dedicated to him.</note> (*). She then also found her cousin Volusianus <note>Gaius Ceionius Rufus Volusianus, a high-ranking Roman official who remained a pagan long after much of his family had converted to Christianity.</note>, who was indeed bedridden with a serious illness; he marveled greatly at her poor clothing, typical of a hermit, and was horrified at her decayed appearance and lowly status (for the spiritual struggle had greatly emaciated her), so that he cried out aloud: "O dearest Melania, how you have changed, in view of your previous state and beauty!" She took the opportunity from these words to represent to him the transience of this life, and replied: "Then learn from me, fortunate cousin, and take into consideration the future goods of heaven. For I would not have set aside and despised worldly glory, along with money and the care of my body, if I had not been convinced that I would receive far more glorious things in exchange." But the blessed Melania exerted herself not only for her own person, but also through the persuasion of many others regarding Volu-

### Chapter 8.

->Melania defeats the erroneous spirit of the Nestorians and is sorely tempted.<-

<note>(*) Nestorius and his followers made two persons out of Christ and taught that the Word in Christ was something distinct, and the man Christ was also something separate; they claimed that Mary had given birth to this man alone, and must not be called the <term>Mother of God</term> <note>original: "GOttes-Gebärerin"; the Greek term is *Theotokos*.</note>, as she had been named by the ancients. They did not recognize the mystery of the Word made visible, or the Son of God’s love, born of the Virgin Mary.</note>

But when Volusianus noticed that Melania also wanted to persuade the Emperor Valentinian <note>Valentinian III, Western Roman Emperor.</note> to contribute something toward his conversion, he feared that people might think he was being baptized more out of fear and political interest than of his own free will, and that he might consequently lose the blessing of baptism. Therefore, he exhorted her to desist from such a plan, as he would afterwards complete the holy work of his own accord; and so he renounced pagan superstition and was brought to Christ. 

She, however, cared not only for him but also for many others. For at that time, the blasphemous teaching of Nestorius (*), the former Bishop of Constantinople, had arisen, and the evil enemy <note>A common reference to the Devil.</note> led many astray, even among those who had understood the truth more deeply. She went boldly to such people and put his rationalistic arguments to shame, giving answers from morning until evening to those who questioned her, so that many of the deceived were convinced and set right again. This greatly vexed the Wicked One <note>The Devil.</note>, that he should be overcome by a woman; he appeared to her in the form of her husband Pinianus in a piteous manner, as if he were coming to her in wretched and torn clothing, and he terrified her with threats, initially saying to her that he intended to bring the Emperor and his counselors to other thoughts...
