## Chapter 9.

->She has herself carried, while ill, to the dying Volusianus; she is healed on the way upon the news of his conversion.<-

When she heard this, although she could hardly move because of the pains in her hip, she nevertheless had herself carried there on a litter and by hand. For she was greatly anxious—not that he might die, but that his soul might remain in death, since he was not yet baptized at that time. But while she was still on the way, another messenger came and announced to her that Volusianus had been baptized; for after he had frequently asked for her and learned that she could not leave the house due to painful physical weakness, he had obtained another leader of salvation and, through him, had become a son of light and had thus been baptized. When this was announced to her, the pains of her body suddenly ceased along with those of her soul; her hip no longer hurt her, and she could move her foot again as before, to the great shame of the common enemy <note>The "common enemy" is a traditional epithet for the Devil.</note>. Thus, she was now able to walk the rest of the way herself, and those who had carried her instead spread their hands toward heaven and praised God. When she then came to her cousin and had strengthened him with edifying words and instructed him regarding the next life, she brought him joy and let him journey on the way to God in good hope, after he had received the magnificent <term>Viaticum</term> <note>original: "Zehrpfennige"; refers to the final Holy Communion given to a person near death to sustain them on their journey to the afterlife.</note> of the precious body and blood of Christ, bidding him depart in consolation.

### Chapter 10.

When she reached **Antioch**, the holy **Melania** went to meet her and was received by the Empress with great reverence, for the Empress regarded her as her mother. As she expressed it, she thanked Divine Providence for two things: first, that she was deemed worthy to see **Jerusalem** and the holy sites, and second, that she had become the spiritual daughter of such a mother. Indeed, it is a sign of the Empress’s great love for **Melania** that she did not hesitate to undertake such an arduous journey for her sake, arriving there to greet and kiss the God-devoted virgins <note>The nuns in Melania’s convent.</note> as sisters.

# XIII. The Life of St. Theodora.
->Described by Palladius, etc.<- <note>Palladius (c. 363–420 AD) was a monk and bishop who wrote the "Lausiac History," a primary source on the lives of early desert fathers and mothers.</note>

## Chapter 1.
->The noble descent, chosen poverty, and patience of Saint Theodora.<-

I also saw the blessed Theodora, the daughter of a guild master <note>A "Zunft-Meister" was a high-ranking official or master of a trade guild, indicating Theodora came from a wealthy, respectable background.</note>, who attained such extreme poverty that she even died while receiving alms. She once asked Bishop Theophilus of Alexandria how the Apostolic saying was to be understood: *Redeem the time* <note>original: "Erkaufet die Zeit." — Colossians 4:5.</note>. He gave her the answer that the saying indicates a gain; for when the time and opportunity for disgrace are present, one should "buy" such a time of contempt with humility and patience, and thus draw the gain to oneself. The time of dishonor is here—endure it, and you shall win. Thus, all contrary things become a gain to us, if only we ourselves are willing. In this enduring patience, the blessed Mother Theodora was well-experienced; therefore, her own admonition was: *Strive to enter through the narrow gate* <note>original: "Trachtet darnach, daß ihr eingehet durch die enge Pforte." — Luke 13:24.</note>. For just as trees cannot bring forth fruit unless they stand in the open air amidst rain, storms, and cold; so too is this world our time of tribulation and winter, and we cannot become heirs of the Kingdom of Heaven except through many tribulations and temptations.

## Chapter 2.
->Her love for silence and vigilance, and her saying regarding it.<-

She conducted her way of life in silence and said: It is good to lead a calm and quiet life; for a wise person loves silence. Truly, it is a great thing for a virgin or a hermit to live quietly and withdrawn, especially when she

Know, however, that as soon as one resolves to live quietly and in seclusion, the evil enemy <note>A common reference to the Devil in ascetic literature.</note> arrives immediately and burdens the soul with boredom and despondency <note>This refers to *accidie*, a state of spiritual listlessness or "the noonday demon" often described by early monks.</note> in one’s thoughts. He also weighs down the body with weaknesses and ailments, and makes one so weary in the knees and all limbs that the legs can no longer carry the person, so that body and soul become powerless. From this comes the common complaint: "I am so weak, and I cannot perform my duties." But when we keep watch, all of this is frustrated. There was a certain solitary <term>solitary: an anchorite or hermit living alone</term> among the brothers who, whenever he was supposed to perform his duties, was always seized by chills and fever and found himself very ill. Finally, he thought to himself: "Behold, I am sick and must now die; I will yet stand up before my end and perform my prayer." With such thoughts, he forced himself <note>literally "did violence to himself," signifying a great act of will</note>, stood up, and prayed. When the prayer was completed, his fever-sickness was also over. The brother did this a second time, and thus overcame this temptation.

### Chapter 3.

->Examples that one should not scold in return, should restrain one's body, and that a teacher should be perfect.<-

Further, this wise Mother Theodora related and said: A holy man was mistreated by someone with insulting words, and he said to them: "I could certainly do the same and insult you, but the command of God holds my mouth shut." Again she said: A certain Christian had to argue with a Manichaean <note>Manichaeism was a dualistic religion that taught the physical world and the human body were inherently evil and created by a dark power.</note> concerning our body (*), and said to him: "Set laws for your body (of moderation, chastity, etc.), and you will see that the body is from God." Again she said: A teacher should be a stranger to the love of power, a stranger to vain glory, far removed from pride; he should not let himself be made a mockery through flattery, nor be blinded by gifts, nor overcome by the belly <note>meaning gluttony</note>, and not let himself be taken captive by wrath; rather, he should be patient, gentle, and humble to the highest degree. He should be faithful and long-suffering, diligent, and a lover of souls.

---

(*) The Manichaeans taught without discretion that the outer body originated from the devil; they thus denied that the Lord Christ had a true body, like ours.

## Chapter 4.

->It is not the humbling and chastising of the body, but of the spirit, that makes a Christian. Likewise, one cannot run away from the Tempter.<-

Her discretion <note>original: "Discretion"; in this context, it refers to the spiritual gift of discernment (*discretio*), or the ability to judge spiritual matters wisely.</note> and gift of discernment is shown in her following wise pronouncement: "Neither the strict way of life in solitude, nor vigils <note>original: "Wachen"; the practice of staying awake for prayer during the night.</note>, nor any other physical labor earns salvation, but rather sincere humility alone. For there was a certain solitary <term>solitary: a monk or hermit living alone in the desert</term> who was able to cast out unclean spirits; he asked them, while they were in a possessed person, saying: 'Which virtue drives you out? Is it perhaps because we fast?' They answered: 'We do not eat or drink at all.' He asked further: 'Is it perhaps because we keep watch?' They answered: 'We also know no sleep.' 'Do you then depart,' he said, 'because we dwell in the desert?' They gave for an answer: 'We also dwell in the desert.' 'What then drives you out?' the brother asked. They replied and said: 'Nothing overcomes us but humility!' There you see that humility even defeats the devils."

Another time, this Mother Theodora related and said: "There was a certain solitary who was completely oppressed by heavy temptations; he said to himself: 'I am leaving this place!' Just as he was about to put on his shoes, he saw a strange figure standing beside him, also putting on his shoes, who began to ask him, saying: 'Are you perhaps leaving because of me? See, wherever you go, I shall be there before you.' Thus the brother remained where he was and overcame the tempter with enduring patience." <note>These stories are cited from Palladius, Chapter 128, and the *Apophthegmata Patrum* (Sayings of the Desert Fathers) under the name Theodora.</note>

# XIV. The Life of St. Asella.
K 3
<meta>catchword: Mar-</meta>

...a virgin daughter was presented. While she had not yet put aside her childhood clothes, and had scarcely reached her tenth year, she already dedicated herself to her future blessedness. But all this we attribute solely to Divine Grace, and not to her own effort and labor; although God, who foreknows the future, sanctified Jeremiah in his mother’s womb (Jeremiah 1:5), let John the Baptist be joyful in the womb (Luke 1:44), and called Paul to the Gospel even before the redemption of the world (Galatians 1:15). I proceed then to that which she acquired, attained, and constantly preserved through her own diligence and sweat (by means of Grace). After she was twelve years old, she truly began to lead a paradisiacal life <note>original: "Paradeisischen Wandel"; a lifestyle reflecting the purity and devotion of the Garden of Eden</note> in her chamber. The earth or the floor of her chamber was her place of prayer, upon which she simply knelt, and upon which she slept without cushions or beds. Fasting was to her but a pastime, and hunger she called her resurrection; but when she had to eat—not out of a desire for food, but out of human necessity—she sustained her hunger with dry bread, salt, and water rather than driving it away, so little did she consume.

# XIV. The Life of St. Asella.

She hurried to the monuments and chapels of the martyrs—which were now almost loathed <note>by the worldly Roman upper class who looked down upon the humble shrines of the dead</note>—to awaken her prayerful devotion there. And because she rejoiced in remaining unhindered in her holy purpose, it was all the more pleasing to her that no one recognized her in her humble appearance and clothing. She fasted throughout the entire year, so that every second or third day she refreshed herself only with a little bread, salt, and water. During the usual Lenten season of the forty days before Easter, however, her earnestness in this was exceptional; for she ate only seven times throughout the seven weeks, and that with a joyful countenance.

### Chapter 4.

->Her constant health, steady prayer upon the hard earth, and the rest of her holy conduct.<-

**W**hat may perhaps seem unbelievable to many is, however, an easy thing for **God**; she has now reached her fiftieth year and has never had stomach pain, nor colic, nor any other bodily affliction from such a strict way of life. The hard floor upon which she sleeps has not made her thin limbs sore; her hardened skin has taken on neither rot nor deformity from the coarse smock <term>smock: a rough garment, often made of goat hair, worn as a sign of penance instead of soft linens</term> which she wears instead of a shirt. Instead, she is of healthy body and even healthier spirit. Solitude is her luxury, and in the restless city of *Rome*, she possesses the desert of the solitary <note>a reference to the "Desert Fathers," suggesting she lived as a hermit despite being in the middle of the capital</note>. Indeed, you (*Marcella*) know this yourself better than I, for I have heard it partly from you, whose eyes have seen that her—Asella’s—knees of her holy body have become as hard as a camel’s skin from constant kneeling in prayer upon the hard earth. We say only what we ourselves can know: nothing is more pleasant than her earnestness, nothing more earnest than her pleasantness; her sweetness has something of tartness in it, and her tartness is mixed with sweetness. Her pale face is so shaped that one can indeed read her great abstinence from it, yet it does not smell of Pharisaical hypocrisy <note>original: "Pharisäischem Schein"; referring to those who made a public show of their fasting to appear holy</note>. Her words are adorned with a quiet nature, and her silence speaks. She does not run when she walks, nor is she a pious creeper; she always maintains the same clothing and appearance. She keeps herself clean, but without making much of it; her humble clothing is without special elegance—she adorns herself without adornment. Through her steadfast <note>original: "gleich-gültige," used here in the archaic sense of being consistently balanced and unchanging in virtue</note> way of life alone, she has achieved that in the magnificent, arrogant, and voluptuous city, wherein humility is considered...

# XVI. The Life of **St. Magna.**
->Described by **Palladius** and **Heraclides**.<-

### Chapter 1.
->The prudent conduct of Saint **Magna** regarding a forced marriage.<-

<margin>(*) Others name **Caesarea** in **Cappadocia**.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'I' featuring scrolling floral motifs.</image-desc>
In the city of **Ancyra** in **Galatia** (*) we found many virgins dedicated to God, numbering up to two thousand and even more, who live in great abstinence and practice every path of virtue; all of them were most exceptional women adorned with good character. Among them, one named **Magna** shines more brightly than all others in the radiance of her virtue. However, we do not know whether it is best to call her a virgin or a widow; for her biological mother had forced her into marriage with great violence. Yet, with an innocent trick, she deceived her bridegroom or forced husband, keeping him away from marital love with all sorts of pretenses, requesting that he have patience with her sickly physical condition. By this means she preserved her virginity and remained unsullied until her husband died shortly thereafter and she became the sole heir to everything. Then, she exchanged her temporal goods for eternal ones and devoted herself entirely to God...

# XVIII. The Life of St. Silvania.

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, referring to a companion of the narrator.</note> is Bishop of Ascalon, a pious and learned man. As a great heat came upon us and we arrived at Pelusium, it happened that the holy Jubinus, exhausted by the heat, took a washbasin and washed his feet and hands with cold water; and having done this, he lay down upon a rough blanket on the ground to rest. When the holy Silvania noticed this, she stepped toward him like a wise mother to her son and rebuked his delicacy <term>delicacy: here meaning "softness" or a lack of ascetic discipline regarding bodily comfort</term> and self-indulgence, saying: "How dare you, in such youthful years when your blood is still so hot, care for your body in this way? Do you not notice what harm arises from this for your soul? Believe my words for certain: although I have now reached sixty years of age, I have washed neither my mouth, nor my feet, nor any limb of my body with water, except for my bare fingers alone. Indeed, I have maintained this even with a constantly sickly body, even when the doctors advised me to make use of the bath; yet I did not wish to accustom my body to it. I have never rested on a soft cushion as you are resting there, nor have I allowed myself to be carried in a litter."

## Chapter 2.
->Concerning her rare learning.<-

This honorable woman was very eloquent and a learned lover of books, so much so that she spent day and night in reading, and the books of all the ancient commentators of the Scripture were very familiar to her. She had read many thousands of sayings. The writings of Gregory Nazianzen, Pierius, Stephanus, Basil the Great, and other learned Christians—some bishops and some notable men—she had read not merely superficially, but each one many times with great care. By means of such God-blessed pens <note>A metaphor for the writings of the Church Fathers</note>, she was able to soar upward and, in good hope, fly like a holy bird to Christ, from whom she received immortality as a reward. Palladius, chapters 142, 143. Heracleides, chapter 42.

# XIX. The Life of St. Candida.

->Described<-
->By Palladius and Heraclides.<-

## Chapter 1.

->The Labor and Vigilance of Saint Candida.<-

There was also a holy worshiper of the name of Christ, *Candida*, the wife of General *Trajan* <note>original: "Trajani." This refers to a high-ranking official under Emperor Theodosius, not the earlier Roman Emperor Trajan.</note>, who honored the servants of Christ through a chaste life devoted to God, and dedicated her only daughter to holy virginity. She sent her daughter ahead to *Christ* as His greatest gift, whom she had carried beneath her heart <note>This implies her daughter died at a young age while maintaining her vow of virginity.</note>. Afterward, when she had completed her own blessed and active life and had distributed all her goods to the poor, she followed her daughter. We ourselves saw this extraordinary matron working all through the night, grinding at a hand-mill <term>hand-mill: a small stone mill used for grinding grain by hand; manual labor was used by early Christians to humble the body and prevent idle thoughts</term> to suppress the strength of her body; as she kneaded the bread for the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Abendmahl," referring here to the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> with her own hands, she said: "Because fasting is not sufficient, industrious vigilance must join it, so that I may tire out my *Esau* <note>Esau: A traditional biblical metaphor for the "fleshly" or "old" nature of man, which must be disciplined to allow the spirit to thrive</note> and weaken the desire for pleasure." For this reason, she also abstained from eating all meat, except that she enjoyed fish, oil, and garden herbs on feast days; at all other times, however, she made do with sour whey <term>Wattig: likely referring to "Molke" or whey, the watery part of milk that remains after curds are formed</term> and dry bread. In such a strict way of life she persevered until the end, when this most blessed woman fell asleep in peace and now enjoys the eternal goods which are prepared for those who do not love their lives for Christ's sake. *Palladius, chapter 145. Heraclides, chapter 44.*

# XX. The Life of St. Gelasia.

->Described<-
->By Palladius and Heraclides.<-

## Chapter 1.

->Of the holy Gelasia’s great gentleness and forgiving spirit.<-

<margin>
Palladius, chapter 146.
Heraclides, chapter 44.
</margin>
Following that holy Candida in her sacred life was the chaste Gelasia, who joyfully bore the gentle yoke of virginity for Christ; she was the daughter of an official. Regarding this precious warrior of the faith, it is particularly recounted that this was her virtue: the sun never saw her angry <note>original: "daß die Sonne sie niemalen zornig gesehen." This is a reference to the biblical command in Ephesians 4:26: "Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry."</note>, neither against her servants, nor her maids, nor anyone else. Thus, this blessed woman had escaped the path of those who harbor grievances—a path that leads to eternal destruction—namely, the stings of the devil, such as hatred and resentment. Because she herself desired an eternal forgiveness of her own sins, she gladly forgave minor offenses so that her own great transgressions against God might be remitted by Him.

## By Palladius and Heraclides.

### Chapter 1.
#### The Labor and Vigilance of the Holy Candida.

There was also a holy worshiper of the name of Christ named Candida, the wife of General Trajan <note>original: "Trajani." She persevered in such a strict way of life until the end, when this most blessed woman fell asleep in peace and now enjoys the eternal goods prepared for those who do not love their lives for Christ's sake. <meta>This page continues the biography of St. Olympias. The catchword "keit" from the previous page likely completed the word "Gottseligkeit" (godliness) or "Ehrbarkeit" (honorability) in the final sentence of page 157.</meta>

...but according to the spirit, a true daughter of God. The Governor Ablavius <note>Ablabius was a high-ranking Roman official; his son Nebridius served as the prefect of Constantinople.</note> was her father-in-law; and she was the betrothed bride of his son, Nebridius, and for twenty months his wedded wife, adorned with wealth, beauty, and all the glories of this life. After her husband passed away prematurely—who is said never to have touched her—she dedicated her virginity to Christ and wedded herself to humility, stooping down to poverty, in whose fellowship she also shared her goods and unspeakable riches. Indeed, the Emperor Theodosius the younger <note>While the text says "the younger" (Theodosius II), historical accounts of Olympias's life usually involve Theodosius the Great (Theodosius I).</note> wanted to marry her off anew to one of her relatives, promising to place him in all the high offices and dignities suited to his rank; she, however, chose chastity and the life of the wisdom of Jesus. Accordingly, she despised all the pleasures of this world and held them to be unseemly for noble, virginal souls. She abstained from all earthly coarseness of nature, by which the soul is clouded and covered, and was very moderate in eating and in sleep for the mortification <term>Kasteyung: the practice of self-denial or physical discipline for spiritual purposes</term> of her body; which she wished to have as an assistant and tool for the soul, but not as a harmful enemy. She was not only content with the chastity of the flesh, but also strived for the clarity and purity of the spirit.

### Chapter 2.
->She is instructed by Chrysostom to distribute her property wisely.<-

AS she was a matron of great means, she initially distributed great sums to whoever came before her eyes and complained. But when that exceptional light of the church, John Chrysostom, Bishop of Constantinople, saw this, he said to her: "I certainly admire, O woman, your resolve and intention to renounce the vain treasures of this world; but whoever strives for the highest step of virtue must know how to use discretion and measure in giving and dispensing. You often give to those who have no need, and pour water into the sea <note>A metaphor for wasting resources on those who already have plenty.</note>, and wishing to lend to it; you must consider that you have voluntarily dedicated your goods to God and bequeathed your property and money to the Lord; know then that they are now God's by right, therefore distribute them with greater fairness <note>original: "Billigkeit," meaning equity or discernment in this context</note>, for you must give an account of them if you go to work unwisely. If you will now take my advice, then consider the necessity of those who ask during your generosity; then many will be truly helped, and you the mercy—

[prudence] and care in the distribution, which is necessary for money consecrated to God, and to obtain the reward through the grace of God. From that time on, she primarily devoted her money to the care of the saints <note>In this context, "saints" likely refers to the poor and the devout members of the church community.</note> and provided for the lovers of virtue with a generous hand, a liberality that was joined with joyfulness. Neither the city, nor the country, nor the desert was excluded from the extraordinary generosity of this maiden; she provided not only for the needs of the teachers <note>The clergy and theologians of the early church.</note>, but also refreshed with her kind gifts those living apart in lonely huts and monasteries, the hospitals and poorhouses, the prisoners in dungeons, and those condemned to the stone quarries and mines. In a word, she scattered the seed of her blessing across the entire world.

### Chapter 3.

->*Her hospitality. The conduct of Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria. Her love for Chrysostom.*<-

With her famous hospitality, she refreshed many; in particular, she showed her magnanimity to Bishop Theophilus of Alexandria when he came to Constantinople, believing him to be a dear friend of God. In return, she received his ill-nature and slanderous tongue as her reward, because she also hosted the servants of God and His favorites, the precious fathers Ammonium and Isidorum, after they, along with other fathers (*) had been driven out of the desert by Theophilus and were forced to go to Constantinople to defend themselves, where she and Chrysostom treated them kindly. She honored all who led a God-fearing and holy life and served them with great zeal and proper care. She was especially devoted to Father Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), the Archbishop of Constantinople known as "Golden-Mouthed" for his eloquence.</note> and was very intimate with him, surrendering herself entirely to his hints and holy will. She made his clothes and prepared suitable meals for him, providing him every assistance, like another Thecla to this Paul <note>A reference to the Acts of Paul and Thecla, an early Christian story of a woman who left her life to follow the Apostle Paul.</note>.

### Chapter 4.

->*Chrysostom's banishment, because of which Olympias must go before the court.*<-

However, at the instigation of adverse-minded bishops and clergy—whose lives and conduct he wished to reform for the sake of his office and conscience, and among whom was also Theophilus of Alexandria—Chrysostom was sent into exile <term>ins Elend: literally "into misery," a common historical term for banishment or forced travel away from home</term> to Cucusus in Armenia by the Emperor Arcadius...

[He] was banished, and during such dealings the common people in Constantinople rose up in riot, during which the main church, Sophia or of Wisdom <note>The Hagia Sophia (Holy Wisdom), the cathedral of Constantinople.</note>, where Chrysostom used to preach, was unexpectedly consumed by fire. <header>XXI. The Life of St. Olympias. 162</header>

...had to take struggles upon herself; she who also lived for a long time in countless tears and subjected herself to all the misery of human nature for the sake of the Lord's will. She was subject to the holy bishops in all godliness; she honored godly priests and all clergy; she held the practice of godliness in the highest esteem. She received the holy virgins, helped the widows, cared for the orphans, protected the elderly, visited the sick, had mercy on sinners, and helped the erring onto the right path. She was compassionate toward all, but overflowing in her generosity toward the poor. She instructed many wives of the unbelievers in the foundations of Christianity, for whom she also provided the necessities of life; thus, throughout her entire life, she earned a lasting reputation for kindness. 

She helped a great multitude of prisoners from servitude to freedom and made them equal to her own rank—or rather, to say it better, she clothed them even better than her own holy garments were. For nothing could be poorer than her clothing; indeed, even to those who went about in ragged clothes, the clothes of this saint were too meager. Her gentleness was so great that she even far surpassed the simplicity of children. She, who had Christ in her heart, never slandered her neighbors; instead, she led her mortified life in contrition of heart and frequent shedding of tears. One might sooner see a spring dry up in summer than see her humble eyes, which always looked upon Christ, without tears. 

But why do I trouble myself to compose a eulogy for this virtuous <term>matron</term> <note>original: "Matronen"; a title of respect for a high-ranking or dignified woman, often a widow, in the early church.</note>, since my words cannot truly depict her holy works? Let no one think that I am collecting grand or merely magnificent words about this woman who was dead to her own worldly inclinations; I am naming only a small part of the whole Olympias, who was a precious vessel of the Holy Spirit. I have reported what I (Palladius) <note>Palladius of Galatia (c. 363–420 AD) was a bishop and author of the 'Lausiac History,' which records the lives of early Christian saints.</note> have seen with these eyes of mine—namely, the holy life and <term>angelic conduct</term> <note>original: "Englischen Wandel"; 'Englisch' here is an archaic German form of 'Engelisch' (angelic), referring to a life of purity and devotion like that of the angels.</note> of this blessed woman—as I was a trusted friend of this spiritual mother and had close contact with her relatives, so much so that I had to distribute large sums of her money according to her will.

...life is numbered among the **Confessors** (*) <note>original: "Bekenner"</note>, by all the godly in Constantinople, she who as a mother contended for God’s honor even in court. She is subject to no decay but possesses the eternal dwellings with the saints, whom she resembles, and receives with good confidence the reward of her good works from Christ her Lord.

The convent of virgins, which she founded in Constantinople, she entrusted to **Marina**, her relative, and commanded her to sacredly preserve its rules. This was located near the Temple of Holy Peace and the Word of God <note>These refer to the Hagia Irene and Hagia Sophia churches</note>, the old churches of **Sophia**, and stood until the time of the uprising that is still known by the watchword of the common people, **Nika**, which is to say, *Overcome* <note>The Nika Riots of 532 AD, which devastated much of Constantinople</note>. When the Church of **Sophia** burned at that time, the aforementioned monastery of **Olympias** was also consumed by the flames. However, after the glorious temple was rebuilt, this former house of God-consecrated virgins also regained its old ornament and dignity, and now the venerable matron **Sergia** is the Superior there, who also described the life of the blessed **Olympias**. *Pallad. c. 144. ...born of noble parents; she was famous for her chosen, lifelong virginity and her excellent conduct. Among the praiseworthy women of her gender, I (**Sozomen**) <note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church</note> have seen none more modest; for she was consistent in her character, words, and behavior, entirely without pride, and exceptional in her humility among all who lived a holy life. Until her death, she prioritized divine matters over human and earthly ones. She was strengthened with courage and wisdom to endure all adverse circumstances; so much so, that she did not even look back when all her many goods were unjustly seized. And with the little that remained to her, and with which she had to depart from **Constantinople** (at the time when **Olympias** <note>St. Olympias, a wealthy widow and deaconess who was a close ally of John Chrysostom</note> also fled), she managed her household so wisely in her old age that not only she and her close friends, but others as well, were supported by it.

### Chapter 2.

->She prepares medicines, lives in seclusion, and refuses to become a deaconess or abbess.<-

And because she was diligent in her service with joy, she prepared all kinds of **medicinal remedies** for the service of the poor and sick; with these, she helped many of her good acquaintances and friends—those poor sick people whom the common physicians could not help; for through Divine blessing, everything she undertook met with success. In short, she was a paragon of all holy matrons of our time, who, as far as we know, was without comparison in her steady, honorable, and virtuous life. Nevertheless, she remained hidden from the common man; for because of her modest spirit and love for **wisdom** <note>original: "Weisheit," often used in this context to refer to "philosophy" or the pursuit of a contemplative, godly life</note>, she diligently sought to remain always in seclusion. Thus, she would not even accept the ecclesiastical office of a **deaconess** <term>Diaconissa: an official position in the early Church held by women who assisted in baptisms, visited the sick, and managed charity</term>, nor would she, despite **Chrysostom’s** <note>St. John Chrysostom, the Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquence</note> frequent requests, become the **abbess** or mother of the spiritual virgins. This is the faint likeness of the life of the holy, virginal matron Nicareta.
*Sozomen, Book 8, Ch. 23. Nicephorus, Book 13, Ch. 25.*

# XXIII. The Life of Saint *Juliana*.

## Described by *Heraclides* and *Palladius* <note>Palladius (c. 363–420) was the author of the *Lausiac History*, a primary source for the lives of early desert monks and holy women.</note>.

### Chapter 1.

->Of Saint *Juliana*, who sheltered the martyr *Origen* <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) was one of the most influential and prolific early Christian theologians.</note>.<-

In Caesarea in Cappadocia <note>A city in modern-day Turkey, a major center of early Christianity</note>, there lived around the year 230 and the years following a God-fearing and wealthy matron named *Juliana* <gloss>(*) Although she lived a hundred or more years before the flourishing era of the solitary fathers and matrons in the deserts—whose lives are actually our purpose—she is nonetheless worthy of being counted among them.</gloss>; she sheltered the famous church teacher and witness of *Christ*, *Origen*, secretly in her house for two years during the time of the persecution under the tyrannical Emperor *Maximinus the Thracian*, from the year 237 onward. From her own means, she provided this heavily persecuted teacher with all necessities and refreshed him with her assistance. We found this described in a very old book, written by *Origen’s* own hand; his words read as follows: "This book," he writes, "I found at the home of a certain virgin named *Juliana* in the city of Caesarea, when I was forced to stay with her in hiding; and she told me that she had received this book from *Symmachus* <note>Symmachus the Ebionite, a translator who produced one of the Greek versions of the Old Testament used by Origen in his scholarly work.</note> himself, a translator for the Jews."
*Palladius, chapter 147. Heraclides, chapter 52.*

# XXIV. The Life of *Saint Fabiola*.
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

...tore the marriage bond with foreign desires and walked in darkness on unchaste paths; because of this, *Fabiola* was also moved, according to the freedom of *Christ*, to leave this impure man and to vacate the defiled marriage bed. Because she was still young at that time, however, and not yet a match for the tempter of flesh and blood himself, she proceeded—contrary to the mind of *Christ* in *Matthew 5:32* and *1 Corinthians 7:11* (*)—to a second marriage while the adulterous husband she had left was still living. She did this through a poor application of the saying: *It is better to marry than to burn,* *1 Corinthians 7:9.* In this, according to the decline of the times, she may have been encouraged by the inexperienced. 

But the divine voice of repentance was so active in her heart that, after the death of this second husband, she broke out in great sorrow and repentant tears. She recognized her fall and, on Good Friday <note>original: "stillen Freytage." In the German tradition, the Friday before Easter is called "Silent Friday."</note> before Easter, she publicly performed penance for the offense she had given in the congregation of the church of the holy martyr *Lateranus* <note>The Basilica of St. John Lateran in Rome, the oldest of the four papal major basilicas.</note> in *Rome*. There she presented herself as a mourner, with bare, unbraided hair and a bowed head, so that even the Bishop—who had previously excommunicated her—as well as the elders and all the people wept with her. Thus, she revealed her wounds to everyone, and all of *Rome* saw her injury with tears; she also displayed this outwardly to everyone's eyes with torn clothes, a bared face, and bare feet. Thereupon she was again absolved from the excommunication of the church, and as a proof of the forgiveness of her sins, she received the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Abendmahl," literally "Evening Meal," the standard German term for the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> (**) with the congregation as a *Communion* or fellowship with them.

---

(*) The Apostle speaks here of the divorce that occurred because of the great tyranny of a pagan husband; where a weak woman was permitted to escape the unbearable evil for a time until she found an opportunity to reconcile with the man. The reason, however, why those divorced for adultery or other reasons were not allowed to marry elsewhere was the hope of repentance; for when the adulterous party performed penance, the healthy party had to allow themselves to be reconciled; yet the intimacy of the marriage bed remained a matter of their own free choice. *See The Shepherd of Hermas, 4th Commandment, page 243.* <note>The *Shepherd of Hermas* is an early Christian literary work from the 2nd century, considered highly influential in the early Church for its teachings on repentance and morality.</note>

(**) In such a sense, in the early church, the Lord's Supper was a sign and proof of the forgiveness of sins for those who had fallen or were converted from the pagans, so that they were recognized by the holy congregation as fellow members and were absolved by the same through the ministry of the teacher <note>In this context, "teacher" (Lehrer) likely refers to the pastor or presiding elder.</note> in the name of *Christ*.

It highlights the early Christian practices regarding divorce, excommunication, and the restorative power of the Eucharist.</summary>

<header>XXIV. The Life of St. Fabiola.</header>

## Chapter 2.

->*Her Zeal and Earnestness in Penance, Self-Denial, and Works of Love.*<-

After she returned home comforted once more, she did not forget her dark days during her good ones; she removed every opportunity for new sin and veiled her face, with which she had once pleased her second husband. Her precious gemstones, fine linens, and all her feminine finery, which she had already set aside at the beginning of her penance, she gave to the poor; likewise, she sold her estates and distributed all the income from them for the benefit of the needy. First of all, she founded a hospital <note>original: "Kranken-Haus." Fabiola is historically credited with establishing the first public hospital in Western Christendom.</note>, where she took in the sick and infirm from the streets and refreshed them; she did not merely care for them through appointed nurses, but took charge of them personally. She carried them in and out of bed, washed away their wounds and pus, and reached out with her own hands to give them food and drink.

## Chapter 3.

->*Of Her Great Charity and Love for Her Neighbor.*<-

She was no less loving and generous toward the clergy, the holy hermits <note>original: "Einsamen," referring to the desert fathers or anchorites living in solitude.</note>, and virgins devoted to God. Which community of hermits or which convent of virgins was not refreshed and supported by her wealth? For which naked or bedridden person did Fabiola not sew the clothes herself? Which person in distress did she not rush to aid? Rome was too small for her mercy; therefore, she searched the islands and sailed across the Tyrrhenian Sea <note>original: "Hetruscische Meer," the sea bordering the western coast of Italy.</note>. Wherever she knew that hermits were to be found, she either went there herself or sent her bounty to them through holy and faithful men.

## Chapter 4.

->*She Sails to Jerusalem, Visits Jerome, and Is Edified by the Scriptures.*<-

Thus she sailed quickly, and contrary to all expectations, toward Jerusalem, where she was received with joy by many; and when she came to Bethlehem, she stayed a short while with us <note>The narrator is St. Jerome (Hieronymus), who lived in Bethlehem and was a close advisor to Fabiola.</note> as a guest. When I still think of it, it seems to me I see her, leafing through the Divine Books with burning zeal, seeking to satisfy her hunger now in the Prophets, now in the Evangelists, and then in the Psalms. She raised many questions and carefully pondered the explanations <note>original: "Ausschliessung," referring to the interpretation or "unlocking" of difficult biblical passages.</note> given to her in her heart. One day I had the fourth book

## Chapter 6.
->On her love for the solitary life.<-

We must therefore lament that the holy places [of Palestine] are robbed of this treasure, but Rome has received its lost jewel back. Others may praise her mercy, humility, and faith in the Invisible; I would rather praise her earnestness and zeal. The book with which I formerly praised the solitary life in the desert to the young man <term>Heliodorus</term><note>original: "Heliodoro." St. Jerome’s Letter 14, written to his friend Heliodorus, was a famous and influential defense of the ascetic, desert-dwelling life.</note>, she knew by heart, and she only lamented that she had to live so confined within the Roman walls. She forgot her gender and did not think of her weakness, living in her thoughts in the desert where her heart was directed. Her blood relatives were scarcely able to restrain her from actually departing there; for the remaining goods she still possessed by the compulsion of her friends were unbearable to her; she called such slow distribution and use of the income for the poor a "cautious lack of faith"; her wish was no longer to distribute her own goods to others, but to receive alms in the holy poverty of Christ.

## Chapter 7.
->On her blessed death and burial.<-

In such watchfulness of heart, death did not find her unprepared; it freed her from all holy cares and brought her to the eternal enjoyment of heavenly treasures of love. Shortly before, however, she had written to the solitaries in the desert, asking that they might come to her aid and help rid her of the burden of her remaining temporal goods, so that with such <term>unrighteous mammon</term><note>A biblical term from the New Testament referring to worldly wealth or ill-gotten gains used for spiritual benefit.</note> she might make friends who could receive her into their eternal dwellings. Luke 16, v. 9. Thereupon, having laid down her burden, she flew all the more lightly toward heaven. All of Rome lamented her loss and followed her body with songs of praise for her blessed release, so that even the golden roofs of the churches and palaces let the <term>Hallelujah</term><note>Jerome famously described Fabiola's funeral as a public triumph, where the Roman people's chanting of "Hallelujah" shook the gilded ceilings of the temples.</note> be heard in echoing resonance. # XXV. The Life of St. Paula of Rome and Eustochium.

->Written<-
->By Jerome (*).<-

### Chapter 1.

->The noble lineage, marriage, and children of the holy Paula.<-

<image-desc>decorative woodcut initial D featuring scrolling foliage and floral patterns</image-desc>
This holy Paula was, according to the flesh, from the oldest families of the Roman nobility; her father was named Rogatus, of the blood of the <term>Scipiones</term><note>A prestigious family of ancient Rome, famous for military leaders like Scipio Africanus.</note>; her mother was Blesilla, a worthy daughter of the <term>Gracchi</term><note>A noble family famous for the Gracchi brothers, who were populist reformers in the Roman Republic.</note>. After she reached her marriageable years, she was wed to a man named Toxotius, of the house of Aeneas and the <term>Julians</term><note>The family of Julius Caesar, who claimed descent from the Trojan hero Aeneas.</note>. To him, who desired a male heir, she first bore four daughters, then a son, who was also named Toxotius after his father. 

The daughters were: the eldest, Blesilla, who became a widow at only twenty years of age after having lived in marriage with her husband for seven months; afterward, she mourned her lost virginity <note>In the ascetic tradition, Blesilla mourned that she had given up her "virginal state" for a brief marriage before fully committing to a religious life.</note> more than her husband, whom she soon followed in death. The second was named Paulina, who left her excellent husband <term>Pammachius</term><note>A Roman senator and friend of Jerome who became a prominent Christian monk and philanthropist after his wife's death.</note> as the heir to her way of life and her goods. The third daughter was Eustochium, who consecrated her virginity to Christ and went to the monastery in Bethlehem. The fourth daughter, Ruffina, married the famous Aletius and soon departed this temporal life.

(*) This has been condensed from his lengthy eulogy <note>Jerome's "Epitaph of Saint Paula" (Letter 108), written as a biography and tribute to her life.</note>.

# Chapter 2.

->After the death of her husband, she renounces the world and hosts several bishops.<-

After her husband's death, Paula mourned him so deeply that she found therein an opportunity to die to the inconstant world. Thus, she first made friends in heaven with her significant wealth and was generous toward all the needy, sharing everything with them. She saw to the burials of the poor, whom she clothed; to the sick, she gave their livelihood; she sought out all the destitute in the whole city and felt sorry if they had already been provided for by others. She was indeed reminded by her friends of this generosity; however, Christ's grace said that it was for her a sufficient reward and inheritance. She did away with the unrest of formal visits and social calls, and withdrew from polite flatteries. But when a council of the clergy—both Eastern and Western bishops—was held in Rome (in the year 382) <note>This was the Council of Rome called by Pope Damasus I to address various theological disputes.</note>, she not only welcomed them around her but also hosted the Cypriot Bishop Epiphanius in her own home; and for Paulinus, Bishop of Antioch, she assigned one of her other houses with hospitable entertainment. Through the virtue of these men, she was further inflamed to leave her homeland and forgot her house, children, family, possessions, and all that was hers; she even ventured to travel all alone through the deserts of Egypt, where Antony and Paul <note>St. Antony the Great and St. Paul the Hermit, known as the "Desert Fathers" and pioneers of Christian monasticism.</note> had lived.

# Chapter 3.

->She travels from Rome by ship toward Antioch.<-

When at last the bishops traveled home again the following spring, she sailed with them. As she prepared to board the ship along with her daughter Eustochium <note>original: "Eustochii"</note> (who shared her blessed purpose), her closest relatives and her other children accompanied her to the harbor. And although everyone wept, and her young son Toxotius pleaded pitifully with raised hands, she did not let herself be held back—neither by the children's sorrowful pleas to stay with them, nor by their painful tears—from setting sail immovably, because her love for God overcame this natural love, and she wished rather to be a servant of Christ than a mother of earthly children. After they landed at the island of Ponza <note>original: "Pontiam"</note>, she viewed there the cell of the martyr Flavia Domitilla <note>A Roman noblewoman exiled for her faith during the reign of Domitian.</note>, who had been sent there by the Emperor Do-

### Chapter 4.

-> From Antioch she journeys toward Jerusalem and Bethlehem and views everything. <-

From Antioch, she traveled further toward Jerusalem and passed many famous places along the way that are mentioned in Holy Scripture. When she arrived at Jerusalem, the Governor sent his servants to meet her and had a magnificent palace prepared and furnished for her sake; she, however, chose a lowly dwelling instead and visited all the holy sites and places that were a monument to the Divine Incarnation. She performed her devotions at the Cross of Christ, which the Empress Helena had found again in the earth at Golgotha and had ordered to be erected; she went into the Holy Sepulchre and kissed the stone that had lain before it and had been rolled away by the angel; Matthew 28, verse 2. She ascended Mount Zion in Jerusalem, where David formerly had his palace and dwelt; 2 Samuel 5, verse 7. Here she also saw the pillar, which now supports a church, where the Lord was bound and scourged, and which is still splattered with His blood; they also showed her the place where the Holy Spirit fell upon the one hundred and twenty believers; Acts 2, verse 1, etc. When she had viewed everything in Jerusalem and distributed what she could to the poor members of the faith according to her means, she journeyed toward Bethlehem and viewed there the holy cave of the Virgin in which she gave birth to the Savior, as well as the stable and the manger; whereby the word of the Prophet was fulfilled: *The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib!* Isaiah 1, verse 3. Here she began to weep and said: "See, I, a miserable sinner, have been deemed worthy to kiss the manger in which the Lord wept as a little child, and to pray in that very cave in which the Virgin gave birth to the Lord! Here shall be my rest, because it is the birthplace of the Lord; here will I dwell, because they..."

whom the Savior has chosen. I have prepared a lamp for my Lord Christ; my soul shall live for him, and my seed shall serve him. <note>original: "Ps. 132, v. 22." In modern English Bibles, the "lamp" reference is usually found in Psalm 132:17.</note>

## Chapter 5.
->She visits the holy fathers in Egypt and Nitria.<-

As she further inspected the remaining holy memorial sites everywhere in Palestine, both throughout the land and by the Jordan and the borders; she then traveled with her virgins <note>The "virgins" refers to her community of female followers and fellow ascetics.</note> also to Egypt and came to Nitria <note>Nitria was one of the earliest and most important Christian monastic settlements in the Egyptian desert.</note>, where she was able to see the holy fathers Isidore, the two Macariuses, Arsisius, Serapion, and the other pillars of the community of Christ, and she kissed their feet; for through her faith, she saw Christ within each one of them. She traversed all the huts of the solitaries <note>hermits</note> on foot and honored all the brothers by prostrating herself before them, for she recognized the Lord in them. She would have remained there with her virgins, had her longing to live near the holy sites and the caves of the virgins <note>likely referring to the site of the Nativity</note> not been so great. Thus, she returned again to Bethlehem and lived for three years in a small hut; in the meantime, she built monasteries for virgins and hostels for travelers on that very road where Mary and Joseph once found no room.

## Chapter 6.
->Her great humility and tears of repentance.<-

Concerning her virtues, and specifically the foundation of all virtues, humility: she had so greatly humbled herself that anyone who had not seen her before and judged her by her noble lineage would not have recognized her, but rather would have taken her for the lowliest maid. For among the many virgins with whom she was surrounded, she appeared to be the least of all due to her plain clothing, humble words, and lowly appearance. From the death of her husband until her own end, she never dined with a man, however holy he might be; she made use of no bath except in the most extreme necessity. She refused to lie upon a soft bed even during a severe fever; instead, she rested on a hard hair-cloth <note>A rough fabric made of goat's hair, used by ascetics to encourage physical discipline.</note> for as much time as her incessant prayers allowed her to rest. She wept over her slightest sins as if she were the greatest of sinners; and when we admonished her to spare her eyes and preserve them for reading the Gospels, she said: "That face must be made unsightly which was formerly adorned and dressed up against God’s command."

the body must be afflicted, which formerly enjoyed so much pleasure; former laughter must be mourned with constant tears; soft linen clothes and precious silk sashes shall be exchanged for a rough sack <note>original: *Sack*; referring to sackcloth, a coarse fabric worn as a sign of mourning or penitence</note>; I have pleased man and the world, now I desire to please Christ.

### Chapter 7.
->Her Chastity, Discretion, and Great Love of Poverty.<-

Even in her blooming married and worldly state, she was a chaste model for all Roman matrons <note>In Roman society, a *matrona* was a woman of high social standing recognized for her dignity and virtue</note>, and conducted herself so honorably in her way of life that even the resentful eye of slanderous tongues found nothing to reproach in her. Toward those of lower station, she was kind and friendly; she did not seek out the noble, yet she did not even despise the ambitious. Wherever she saw a poor person, she supported them; and the rich she exhorted to do good works. In her generosity she went so far that, if her income was not sufficient, she took out money on credit <note>original: *Geld auf Renten*; likely referring to loans or drawing against future annuities</note> and gave it away, so that she might refuse no one.

I must confess my own weakness, writes Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the influential theologian who translated the Bible into Latin and served as Paula's spiritual guide</note> / I rebuked her for this and held before her the words of the Apostle: "You should not refresh others and suffer want yourselves, but let your abundance serve their lack"; 2 Cor. 8, v. 15. <note>Jerome is quoting St. Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians</note> Also because the Lord says in the Gospel: "He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none"; Luke 3, v. 11. I argued that she must be mindful so that she would have something to give for a long duration, and I presented other similar arguments to her.

To this she replied with modest humility and called God to witness that she did everything for the sake of His name, and had vowed to Him to die as a beggar. She also intended to leave not a single penny <note>original: *Heller*; a small German copper coin used here to represent a tiny amount of money</note> to her daughter, and wished to be buried in a donated shift <note>original: *Hemde*; a simple linen tunic or undergarment</note>. Finally, she added: "If I must indeed beg, I shall find enough people who will give to me; but if I do not help these poor, forsaken ones now, even with borrowed money, and they should die, from whom will their souls be demanded?"

I wished, said Jerome / that she would manage her household more prudently! But she burned with faith and was entirely devoted to the Savior, and wished to follow her poor Lord, poor in both spirit and body. She indeed achieved her goal, though within the bounds of human weakness; in that she left her daughter burdened with the great debts of the borrowed money, which she has not yet paid off to this day,

## Chapter 8.

->Regarding her abstinence, fasting, vigils, and her composure in the face of contempt.<-

She lived in such strict abstinence that she almost exceeded all measure in this regard, and weakened her body too much with excessively severe fasting and vigils; only on feast days did she enjoy a little oil in her food. What she thought of wine, fish, milk, honey, and eggs can be inferred from this: some consider it a marvel how moderate they are, even when they merely fill their bellies with such things (*). Whenever someone mocked and scorned her, she remained silent and well-content, mindful of the words of the Psalmist: *When the sinner rises against me, I become dumb and remain silent.* Psalm 39:2. When a flatterer said to her that because of her great virtue, some held her to be insane and out of her mind, she gave him this answer: *We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.* 1 Corinthians 4:9. Thus she endured the foolishness of wicked hearts; in such patience she remained until her end.

## Chapter 9.

->Regarding the monasteries and convents she established, and the order she maintained within them.<-

Regarding the monasteries she built, the first was for men; afterwards, she established three for the female sex, gathering women from various lands—those of noble as well as middle and low social standing. These she divided into three groups <note>original: *Haufen*; referring to the different monastic communities or classes of sisters</note> and distinguished them in their work and food; however, for prayer and singing, they came together. Once the *Hallelujah* had been sung, no one was allowed to remain in her cell, but she was the first to arrive, calling the others to the holy work and assembly by her own example. Early in the morning at the break of day, then at 9 o'clock <note>the hour of Terce</note>, again at midday <note>Sext</note>, then at 3 o'clock in the afternoon <note>None</note>, further in the evening at 6 o'clock <note>Vespers</note>, and finally at midnight, psalms were sung; all the sisters were required to know these by heart and to learn something from the Scriptures daily. On the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note>, they went only to the church near which they lived; each monastery and group had its own spiritual...

# Chapter 11.
->Her compassion toward others who were sick, and her severity toward herself.<-

Toward the sick, she showed herself to be exceptionally kind and diligent, serving them with admirable obedience. She gave them everything that might serve for their refreshment, including strong soups and meat; <note>In many early monastic rules, meat was strictly forbidden for healthy monastics but permitted as a medicine for the infirm.</note> yet if she herself ever became ill, she allowed her body no such care. For as compassionate as she was toward others, she was just as unmerciful toward herself. None of the young daughters, who were of healthy and strong body, lived as temperately as she did in her weak, old, and fragile frame. I must confess, in this regard she was somewhat stubborn, for she did not spare herself and would give no ear to anyone who advised her otherwise. This I experienced myself. In July, during the greatest heat, she fell into a violent fever. When she had recovered by God's grace from this life-threatening danger, the doctors advised her that it was necessary to take a little wine to refresh her exhausted body, so that she would not become <term>dropsical</term><note>original: "Wassersüchtig." Dropsy, or edema, is a swelling caused by excess fluid; the doctors feared her heavy water consumption and weakened state would cause her body to retain fluid.</note> from drinking too much water. So that she might be persuaded to do this, I secretly asked the blessed father and Bishop Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a close friend of Jerome and a major figure in the early church.</note> to admonish her and induce her to drink wine. Because she was sharp-sighted and clever, she noticed the ruse immediately and kindly gave him to understand that this was my doing. When the blessed bishop returned from her after a long time of vain effort, and I asked him what good he had accomplished, he said: "I have achieved only this much: she almost persuaded an old man like me to stop drinking wine as well." I tell this only to demonstrate her zeal and earnestness in <term>abstinence</term>.

# Chapter 12.
->The excesses of her nature.<-

Moderation is considered a virtue, and excess is rightly considered a vice, according to the judgment of all sensible people. According to this, one must confess that she had her weaknesses; and just as she exceeded the capacity of human nature in her asceticism, she was likewise extremely tender-hearted and dejected in times of grief for her loved ones. ## Chapter 13.
### Concerning her learning, and her daughter Eustochium.

She possessed a very keen intellect and knew the Holy Scriptures by heart. Although she also took great pleasure in the literal history <note>original: "äussern Historie"; referring to the plain, factual reading of the biblical text.</note> and called it the foundation of truth, she followed the spiritual, hidden meaning even more and was edified by it. She urged me to explain the entire Old and New Testaments to her and her daughter. Though I initially refused out of modesty, I was forced to do so by her frequent insistence; in this, she practiced me well with her many questions, so that I often had to confess my ignorance to her. She mastered the Hebrew language—which I had learned from my youth with great effort—so well that she sang the Psalms of David in Hebrew and spoke the language without difficulty. We see this same quality in her daughter Eustochium, who never left her mother’s side and desired not a single penny for her own power, but rather rejoiced when she saw her mother distributing her entire inheritance to the poor.

## Chapter 14.
### Her final illness; the filial loyalty of Eustochium, and the mother’s blessed death.

Finally, the blessed Paula fell into a terminal illness, for which she had long yearned so that she might be with the Lord. It was here that Eustochium’s godliness was truly revealed; she sat incessantly by the bed, fanning the air to cool it, holding her mother’s head, adjusting the pillows, rubbing her feet, warming her stomach with her hand, making the bed, cooling the drinking water, and spreading the tablecloth before her to refresh her with a little something—performing all the duties of a servant-maid. How often during this illness did she run to the Grotto of the Lord <note>original: "Höhlen des HErrn"; the Cave of the Nativity in Bethlehem, located near their monastery.</note> where He was born, to offer her prayers there and beg the Lord that she might be allowed to die at the same time as her mother? The needy lamented the loss of their mother and nurse. It was a marvel to behold; the pallor of death had not changed her countenance at all, but she lay there with such solemnity that one would have thought she was merely sleeping. Thus, the holy bishops took hold of her coffin, together with the funeral bier, with their own hands and carried her upon their shoulders; while other bishops went before them with torches and wax candles, and still others sang psalms, until they laid her to rest in the middle of the church, above the Grotto of our Savior in Bethlehem. One could hear psalms being sung by the various nations in the Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and Syriac languages; <note>This highlights the international nature of the monastic community Paula and Jerome founded in Bethlehem.</note> not only for the three days until she was buried, but throughout the entire week, as each group held its own solemn funeral rites.

## Chapter 16.

->Concerning the Virgin **Eustochium**; the younger **Paula**; and the time of the elder's passing.<-

Her venerable daughter, **Eustochium**, was like one who had only just been weaned from the breast, and she would not allow herself to be pulled away from her mother’s body. She kissed it with many tears and embraced it for a long time, wishing to be buried with her. She was not the heir to even a single penny <term>Heller: a small copper coin used here to denote total poverty</term>, but rather an heir to great debts, as was mentioned before. What was most burdensome was that the great number of brothers and sisters in the established monasteries weighed upon her spirit; to support them was difficult, and to abandon them would be ungodly. Yet she remains calm and content, knowing her inheritance in secret; for the Lord is her portion. The younger **Paula**, daughter of the son **Toxotius** and of **Laeta**, was also an heir to her grandmother’s godly spirit; she had been dedicated to God by her parents while still in her mother’s womb, and when she could scarcely walk or speak, she was already stammering out the Hallelujah <note>original: "Hallelujah stamlend anstimmte"; showing her early devotion.</note>. The blessed elder **Paula of Rome** fell asleep in Bethlehem on the 26th of **January**, on the Sabbath day or Saturday after sunset, in the year of Christ 404; and she was buried on the 28th of **January**, during the sixth consulship of **Honorius Augustus** and the consulship of **Aristaenetus**. She lived in Rome for five years in her holy purpose after her husband’s death, and twenty years in Bethlehem; so that her entire age reached fifty-six years, eight months, and twenty-one days. **Jerome, Epistle 27 to Eustochium.** <note>This letter, often numbered as Letter 108 in modern collections, is the primary historical source for Paula's life.</note>

## Chapter 17.
->Palladius’s brief report concerning Jerome and Paula.<-

This is the life of the blessed matron Paula, drawn together in the best possible order from the rambling narrative of Jerome, while omitting many of the questionable emotional outbursts of this man. His excessive devotion to literal-minded piety and scholarship proved a hindrance to much of the good these matrons might have achieved at that time. Palladius laments this in few words when he writes the following concerning this holy Paula and her daughter Eustochium: Among the holy matrons in Palestine was also the Roman Paula, mother of the younger Toxotius and wife of the elder Toxotius. She was very well-suited and capable in the spiritual life; but one named Jerome, a native of Dalmatia, hindered her spiritual growth. Although she might have surpassed many—indeed all others—in total sanctification, possessing as she did the noblest disposition for a virtuous life, this man prevented her breakthrough and kept her to himself. Her daughter Eustochium still lives in Bethlehem, whom I (Palladius) have not seen myself; however, it is said that she lives very temperately and has a congregation of fifty virgins with her. <note>Palladius of Galatia, author of the 'Lausiac History', was often critical of Jerome, reflecting the historical tensions between different factions of early Christian monasticism.</note> Palladius, chapters 125 and 126.

## Chapter 17.
->Palladius’s brief account of Jerome and Paula.<-

This is the life of the blessed matron Paula, drawn together in the best possible order from the lengthy narrative of Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymi." Jerome was Paula's spiritual mentor and biographer, though his intense personality often colored his writing.</note>, while omitting many of the questionable passions of this man. His excessive love for literal piety and scholarship was, at that time, a hindrance to much of the good these matrons might have achieved. Palladius <note>Palladius of Galatia (c. 363–420 AD) was a bishop and historian of early Christian monasticism; he was often a critic of Jerome’s temperament.</note> laments this in few words when he writes of this holy Paula and her daughter Eustochium: "Among the holy matrons in Palestine was also the Roman Paula, a mother of the younger Toxotius and wife of the elder Toxotius <note>Toxotius was the name of both Paula’s husband and her only son.</note>. She was very capable and fit for the spiritual life; but one named Jerome, a native of Dalmatia, held her back in her spiritual growth. Though she might have surpassed many—indeed all others—in complete holiness, possessing the noblest disposition for a virtuous life, this man hindered her breakthrough and kept her tied to himself. Her daughter Eustochium still lives in Bethlehem, whom I (Palladius) have not seen myself; but it is said that she lives very temperately and has a gathering of fifty virgins with her." Palladius, chapters 125 & 126.

# XXVI. The Life of St. Marcella and St. Principia.
->Described by Jerome.<-

## Chapter 1.
->Saint Marcella becomes a widow early, rejects further marriage, and dedicates herself to chastity.<-

This God-fearing matron was also of ancient Roman nobility, whose ancestors had been mayors <term>Bürgermeister: likely referring to the Roman office of Consul</term> and governors. After she became an orphan through the death of her father, she also became a widow in the seventh month of her marriage through the passing of her husband. Because she was still young <note>original: "Diese ist die erste heilige Matrona in Rom der Zeit gewesen / und lebte zur Zeit Antonii und der ersten Väter." This Marcella was the first holy matron in Rome of that era, living during the time of Anthony the Great and the first Desert Fathers.</note>

and beautiful, moreover of good character, and from an ancient noble lineage, the Consul <note>original: "Bürgermeister," likely referring to the Roman office of consul.</note> Cerealis—whose family was no less famous—courted her and desired her for marriage. He even promised to bequeath all his great estates to her, not as a wife, but as a daughter. Her mother Albina welcomed this, seeing him as a pillar of her house; but Marcella answered: "If I indeed had to marry, and did not wish to dedicate myself from now on to eternal chastity, I would seek a husband, not a father or an inheritance." Thus, he had to serve as an example to others, so that no one else would tempt her further.

### Chapter 2.

->*The Nature of Pagan Widows and the Exemplary Conduct of Saint Marcella.*<-

This woman, now devoted to God, first silenced the mouths of the slanderers in her chaste state of widowhood. She provided the pagan widows an example of honor and showed them what a Christian widow should be like, which she demonstrated both in her conscience and her clothing. Those other widows paint their faces, dress shamelessly in thin, transparent silk, sparkle with gemstones, and wear golden chains around their necks; they pierce their ears and hang from them the most precious pearls of the Red Sea. While weeping for their husbands' deaths, they are surrounded by the sweet scent of musk <note>original: "Bisem," a common perfume ingredient in the early modern period.</note>, so that one can tell the loss of such mastery is pleasant to them in their newfound freedom. They do this so they may now take other husbands of lower status, whom they do not wish to submit to according to the will of God, but rather wish to command; 1 Peter 3, v. 5. For this reason, many widows choose poor men, so that they may cover their licentiousness with a husband's name, while the poor man dare not look sourly upon them, or else he is cast out and disinherited. 

Our Christian widow, however, made use of such clothing that was not burdensome in the heat, and yet completely covered her body. No gold touched her, except for the signet ring <note>original: "Siegel-Ring."</note> alone; everything else she preferred to keep with the poor rather than in purses. She was never without her mother; nor did she ever wish to see or speak with a clergyman or a monk <note>original: "Einsamen," literally "lonely ones," referring to ascetics or hermits.</note> (who might call upon her on account of her extensive household) without others being present. In her company were always virgins and honorable widows, well-knowing that one is judged by the company one keeps.

## Chapter 3.
### *Her moderate, chaste way of life and obedience toward her mother.*

Her love for the Holy Scriptures was incredible, and she was always singing psalms. She practiced moderate fasting but abstained entirely from eating meat; she would merely catch the scent of wine rather than drink it, on account of her weak stomach and frequent illnesses. She rarely appeared in public and particularly avoided the company of the nobility, so that she was not forced to look upon the very things she had renounced. In the churches of the holy apostles and martyrs, she offered her prayers in quiet corners so that she might avoid the crowds; she was so obedient to her mother that she even did things that did not please her. For while her mother loved her own kin <note>original: "Blut," literally "blood," referring here to the family lineage.</note> and, having no children or grandchildren of her own, intended to leave everything to her brother’s children, Marcella had chosen poverty and wished to give her wealth to the needy. Nevertheless, she deferred to her mother in obedience and left her jewelry and furnishings to the wealthy relatives, preferring to lose her money and property rather than distress her mother’s heart.

## Chapter 4.
### *Marcella learns from Athanasius and other bishops and teachers from Egypt about the life of the solitaries.*

At that time, the life of the secluded solitaries <note>original: "Einsamen," referring to the early monastic or ascetic movement of monks and nuns.</note> was not yet known among the noblewomen of Rome, and none dared to take upon themselves the new and despised name of "the solitary." But this Marcella was the first who was instructed by the teachers from Alexandria and by Bishop Athanasius—and later by his successor, Peter—who had fled to Rome during the persecution by the Arians <note>A 4th-century theological group that disagreed with the orthodox view of the Trinity, leading to the exile of many bishops like Athanasius.</note>. From them, she learned of the life of the great Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great, considered the father of Christian monasticism.</note>—who was still living at that time—and of the solitary community of Father Pachomius in the Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt that became a famous center for early communal monasticism.</note>, as well as the God-consecrated virgins and widows in Egypt. As soon as she heard of these things, she was not ashamed of them and confessed that she had now learned how to truly please Christ. After many years, she was followed by Sophronia and others. The venerable Paula sought her friendship, and her daughter Eustochium was mostly raised in this holy Marcella’s chamber; from this, one can easily see what a mother such disciples found in her. Thus, she spent many years of her life in God-consecrated stillness, so that she grew old before she even realized it; for she lived already as one dead to the world. Her

# XXVI. The Life of Saint Marcella

Her clothing was her grave, and she presented herself as a **living sacrifice pleasing to God.** *Romans 12:1.*

## Chapter 5.
->She becomes acquainted with *Jerome*, who admires her wisdom.<-

Finally, when I (*Jerome*) arrived in *Rome* around the year 382, in the company of the holy bishops *Paulinus* of *Antioch* and *Epiphanius* of *Cyprus*, although I sought to avoid the company of Rome’s noble matrons, I could not escape her close observation. For because I had a reputation for being well-versed in the Scriptures, she always took the opportunity to discuss them with me. I am ashamed to say how much virtue, intellect, holiness, and purity of spirit I found in her, for people might not believe me. This alone I must confess: what we scholars gather with great effort, she knew as a triviality. It reached such a point that the final decision rested on her judgment if the meaning of a passage seemed doubtful during our discussion. And because she was very wise and possessed that quality of mind which scholars call *prepon* <note>original: "Præpon," a Greek term (πρέπον) referring to what is "fitting," "proper," or "decorous."</note>, or the skill of prudence, she knew how to answer questions in such a way that she presented her own wisdom as if it came from someone else. And although she taught others, she still wished to be seen as one who was learning from them; for she knew the Apostolic saying: I do not permit a woman to teach; *1 Timothy 2:12.* She did this so that she would not shame the male sex, nor at times the priests, who often brought obscure questions to her for their own instruction.

## Chapter 6.
->On the virgin *Principia's* intimate companionship with her.<-

The virgin *Principia* (to whom *Jerome* wrote this) sought the close fellowship of this wise matron and never strayed from her side by so much as a hair's breadth. She lived with her in one house and slept in her bedchamber, so that it became known to everyone in the city that this girl had found a mother, and *Marcella* had found a daughter. A country estate <note>original: "Meyer-Hof," a manor or farmstead.</note> outside the city was their convent, and the fields served them in place of the desert. Thus they lived for a long time and gained so many followers of their godly way of life that *Rome* at that time became a *Jerusalem*. This good beginning ensured that, eventually, the multitude of virgins consecrated to God and the countless throngs of secluded men who served God—
