## Chapter 7.
### Regarding the Captivity of Saint Marcella and Principia during the Conquest of the City of Rome, and the Subsequent Death of Marcella.

At this time, in the year 410, **Alaric**, King of the **Goths**, besieged the city of **Rome**. The city fell into such a dire famine that even mothers did not spare their own children, and so many people were carried away by hunger that, following the nighttime conquest of the city, only a few captives remained. Among these were Saint **Marcella** and the virgin **Principia**, who received the enemy into their house with fearless countenances. When the soldiers demanded gold from them, the women used their lowly clothing to demonstrate that they had none left; however, the soldiers would not believe in their voluntary poverty and instead beat them with sticks and whips. Marcella did not even feel this torture, but only fell at their feet and pleaded with tears that they should not be separated, so that the young virgin might not fall into that danger <note>A reference to the threat of sexual violence, which Marcella, as an elderly woman, felt she was less likely to suffer.</note> which the old woman had no cause to fear. The Lord Christ softened the hard hearts of the soldiers, and the fear of God found a place even among bloody swords. Both women were then led to the **Church of the Apostle Paul** <note>During the Sack of Rome, Alaric declared the great basilicas of St. Peter and St. Paul as places of sanctuary.</note>. For this, Saint Marcella especially thanked God with joy: that she could keep Principia with her, her honor unblemished, and that captivity could not make her any poorer than she already was. Although they now lacked bread, they sated themselves on Christ and felt no hunger. The blessed Marcella then spoke in words and in deed:

> Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked must I depart; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord! Job 1:21-22.

After a few days, she fell asleep in the Lord while in a healthy, uninjured, and fresh state of body. She left the virgin Principia as her heir—or rather, through her, she made the poor her heirs. After Principia had closed Marcella's eyes and Marcella had joyfully surrendered her spirit while the girl kissed her with tears, she died with a good conscience...

# XXVII. The Life of Saint Piamun.

->Described by Palladius and Heraclides.<-

## Chapter 1.

->The virgin Piamun possesses the gift of prophecy and prevents bloodshed.<-

There was a certain virgin named **Piamun**, who spent her entire life with her mother, diligently spinning and sewing; she ate only a little every other evening. She was so pleasing to God that she received from Him the gift of <term>prophecy</term> <note>The original German uses "Weissagung," referring to the divine ability to foresee future events.</note> concerning things to come. Now it happened once, during the annual flooding of the **Nile River**, that one village community rose up against another. (For they usually cannot agree on the water that floods their fields and <term>fertilizes</term> them, <note>The text notes that the Nile water "makes the fields fat," a reference to the nutrient-rich silt left by the annual flood.</note> so that they even come to bloodshed and murder against one another).

As the stronger village was preparing itself against the weaker inhabitants of the Lower Village, where the holy Piamun lived, and relied on their greater numbers—armed with spears and swords, and some with large clubs—they marched forth to pierce the dikes of the Lower Village and to destroy the inhabitants along with their houses. Behold, the Angel of the Lord stood by her and announced to her the arrival of the enemies, which no one else suspected. The virgin then went to the priests of the village and said to them: "Go out to meet the neighbors who are already on their way to your total destruction; and so that you and your houses might not be destroyed, plead with them to abandon their warlike intent and return again in peace."

## Chapter 2.

->She prays and causes the hostile peasants to be unable to advance.<-

But because the priests were very much terrified by this news and were afraid, they fell before the virgin

Therefore, they sent several of their own men unarmed into the village and asked for peace, delivering these words:

> Give thanks to God, who has rescued you from your destruction through the prayer of Piamun!

Palladius, chapter 37. Heraclides, chapter 37.

(*) Standing prayer is most appropriate against the powers of darkness, where the spirit of faith must be lifted up with raised hands. Kneeling prayer awakens the humility of the spirit in its holy temple, where the soul sees itself in lowliness but sees God in the heights. The former—standing—was customary in the early Church on the <term>Lord’s Day</term> <note>The "Day of the Lord" refers to Sunday.</note> as a memorial of the victory of Christ's resurrection from hell, in which He crushed the head of the serpent.

# XXVIII. The Life of St. Poemenia.

->Described<-
->By Palladius and Heraclides.<-

## Chapter 1.

### The Mortal Danger of Poemenia, Foretold to Her by John.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial D featuring foliage patterns.</image-desc>
This holy matron, devoted to Christ, once visited Saint John in Lyco <note>original: "Johannes in Lyco," known to history as John of Lycopolis, a famous 4th-century desert hermit and seer in Egypt.</note> and wished to see him; however, he did not allow her to come before him, but instead revealed several mysteries to her through his disciple; among other things, he gave her the following instruction: "When you travel home again from <term>Thebaid</term> <note>Thebaid was a region in Upper Egypt, a major center for early Christian monasticism.</note>, do not go toward Alexandria; for you will fall into temptation <note>In this context, "temptation" (Versuchung) refers to a dangerous trial or physical peril.</note> on such a journey." She, however, perhaps did not hold the prophecy of the great John in high regard, or had forgotten it, and turned toward Alexandria to see the city and also to visit the saints of that place. On the journey, however, near the city of Nicia, where they arrived via the Nile River, the ships dropped anchor to rest from the long journey. When the servants went ashore for a while, they began a willful quarrel with the inhabitants of that place; who were senseless, wicked people, and took the matter poorly, and cut off the finger of one of her eunuchs <note>original: "Verschnittenen"</note>; and even killed another. The holy Bishop Dionysius, who was also on the ship, they threw into the water without knowing who he was, so that he nearly drowned; they scolded Poemenia herself and cursed her, wounding all her servants as well. Only then did she remember the word of Saint John in Lyco, and thanked God, who had preserved her herself unharmed. Palladius, chapter 47. Heraclides, chapter 22.

But the old woman turned him away and said: "You people consumed her wealth from the beginning; now she is poor." Father **John** said: "Just tell her; I bring her a beneficial message." Then the maidservants laughed and asked him: "What could you possibly have to give her that makes you want to speak with her?" He answered: "How can you know what I have to give?" So the old woman went up and announced Father **John’s** arrival to the lady, who said: "These hermits often go walking by the Red Sea and find pearls." <note>A reference to the spiritual "pearls of great price" or wisdom gathered by the monastics living in the Egyptian wilderness near the Red Sea.</note>

When she had adorned herself, she said: "Let the man come up to me." After she caught sight of him, she first sat down on the couch; Father **John**, however, sat down beside her, looked at her intently, and said: "What has the **Lord JESUS** done to offend you, that you have fallen into this sinful state?" When she heard this, she was struck numb. Father **John**, with his head bowed, began to weep bitterly. She finally asked him, saying: "Father, why do you weep?" He looked upward, bowed down again, wept once more, and said: "I see Satan sporting before your eyes, and should I not weep?" When she heard this, she said: "Is there not still time for repentance, dear Father?" He answered: "Yes, certainly!" She said to him: "Lead me wherever you will." The old man said: "Come, let us go!" So she stood up and followed him.

# XXXII. The Life of St. Marana and St. Cyra.

->Written by Theodoret.<- <note>Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c. 393 – c. 458 AD) was a bishop and influential theologian who wrote the *Historia Religiosa*, documenting the lives of early Christian hermits in Syria.</note>

## Chapter 1.

->Saint Marana and Cyra betake themselves to live under the open sky in a strict way of life.<-

This example of Saint Marana and her sister Cyra surpasses all others in patient endurance. They were natives of Beroea in Syria <note>Modern-day Aleppo, Syria.</note>, of noble lineage and an upbringing appropriate to their status. They renounced all of this, however, and went outside the city to live in a small space, surrounded by an old wall, in which they enclosed themselves, sealing the entrance with stones and clay. Their maidservants, however, who also wished to partake in their holy way of life, had to build a hut outside such a place and live therein. The two sisters, however, watch everything they do through a tiny window, often exhorting them to prayer and kindling them toward Divine love. They themselves have neither house nor hut but live under the open sky; instead of a door, there is a small window-hole in the perimeter of the walls through which they receive necessary sustenance and speak with the women who [come] to them

to come to them. They have, however, set a specific time for such conversation, namely at Pentecost; all other times they live in silence. The holy *Marana* alone speaks with those who address them; the other [Cyra] no one has ever heard speak. They also wear iron around their necks and feet, and such a heavy burden that even *Cyra*, who is of a weaker body, walks bent down toward the earth and cannot straighten her body. They have very large veils or coverings that hang down over their feet in the back and reach to the belt in the front, beneath which their faces, necks, chests, and hands are entirely covered.

### Chapter 2.
->Bishop *Theodoret* visits them; they go about in heavy irons to practice patience.<-

I (*Theodoret*) <note>Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c. 393 – c. 458 AD) was a bishop and historian who personally knew many of the desert fathers and mothers he wrote about.</note> have seen them often, as I was permitted to enter to see them out of the reverence they held for my office as bishop. I then saw the heavy iron, which even a large, strong man would have had enough to carry; since I pleaded with them, they allowed me to take it off them. But after I departed from them, they put it back on: the collar around the neck, a heavy iron belt around the loins, and the irons used for the hands and feet. In this manner they have lived not only for five or ten years, but already for nearly forty-two years; and although they have struggled so long, it is as if they had only just begun, so joyful are they in it. For they have beheld the beauty of the Bridegroom <note>A mystical reference to Jesus Christ, often used in early Christian writing to describe the spiritual focus of consecrated women.</note> in the spirit, and now gladly endure the burden of their course, hastening to reach the desired end where they see the Beloved standing and reaching out the crown of victory to them. Therefore they regard neither downpours, snow, nor hot sunshine, and feel no cross <note>In this context, "cross" refers to physical suffering or hardships endured for faith.</note> nor pain, but rather find their heart's joy in this difficult way of life. They follow the example of the man of **God**, *Moses*, and have fasted three times for forty days, during which they took only a little food; they also lived in temperance like *Daniel* and fasted for three weeks before refreshing their bodies.

->They visit the holy places in Jerusalem and the tomb of *Thecla* without eating for forty days.<-

# XXXIII. The Life of Saint Domnina.
## Described by Theodoret.
### Chapter 1.

->The holy Domnina lived in a straw hut in the garden, in constant penance and mortification.<-

This God-devoted matron *Domnina* built a small hut, covered with straw, in her mother’s garden. There she sat, and with constant tears of penance, she moistened not only her cheeks but also her clothes of camel hair <note>A traditional ascetic garment echoing the biblical description of John the Baptist.</note>; for with such she covered her body. At midnight (*), however, she went into the temple <note>meaning the church</note>, which was not far from her, with other women and men, and offered her sacrifice of praise to the Lord. This she did not only early in the morning, but also in the evening. Her nourishment, however, was peas soaked in water. She was entirely wasted away and thin in body, yet she lived so moderately. Her skin was very delicate and thin, and her bones so small that one could see neither fat nor flesh, so much did she fast. She allowed herself to be seen by all who came to her, whether they were men or women; yet her face was not seen, as it was covered, and she also [did not look]...

<note>(*) Nighttime church devotion was mostly customary in the hot Eastern and Southern lands because of the great heat of the day, both in the early and subsequent periods of the Church; this was also beneficial to them during times of persecution.</note>

# The Life of Anonyma I.
## Chapter 1.

->A remarkable example of hidden holiness in the convent of virgins at Tabenna.<-

In a certain society of the oldest solitary matrons and virgins, who had their dwelling on an island of the Nile River up in Tabenna <note>Tabenna, or Tabennisi, was the site of the first monastery founded by Saint Pachomius in the 4th century, marking the birth of communal monasticism.</note>, there was a certain virgin who, for Christ’s sake, let herself be considered foolish, and as if she possessed an unclean spirit. She was held in such great contempt by everyone that they would not even dine with her, a fact in which she rejoiced. Thus, she never left the kitchen and performed all the lowliest services there; for she was, according to the common proverb, the sponge and foot-cloth <note>original: "Schwamm und Fuß-Hader," an idiom meaning she was treated as the lowest servant, literally a rag used to wipe floors.</note> for them all, fulfilling in deed what is written: *Whoever desires to be great among you, let him be the servant of all;* Mark 10, v. 43. Likewise: *If any among you thinks he is wise according to the world, let him become a fool, that he may become wise.* 1 Cor. 3, v. 18. She went barefoot and had an old rag wrapped around her head, in which manner she served everyone. The other virgins, however, had their head-hair shorn off as a sign of renounced finery, and covered their heads with proper caps. Not one

## Chapter 6.
->The Nature of this Convent for Virgins.<-

The aforementioned community of virgins lived on the other side of the water, while the community of the brotherhood, which Father *Pachomius* had gathered, remained on this side of the river. Whenever a virgin died, the other virgins sang the customary songs of praise and victory over the body, then carried the coffin with the body out to the bank of the river. Then the brothers came over from the other side, holding palms and olive branches in their hands, as they also sang songs of victory to the honor of God and the blessed one; and so they brought the body across, which they buried in the grave <term>Begräbniß: a prepared tomb or burial place</term> prepared for it. For official duties, no one crosses over to this female community except the Elder, or Priest and *Deacon*, and indeed this only happens on Sundays. These secluded female solitaries have the same rule and arrangement as the aforementioned brothers of *Pachomius*, who was the founder of both; more about this in the life of this holy father. See in the first part *Number VI, page 135. Palladius, chapter 39.*

# The Life of Anonyma II.
## Chapter 1.
->A holy virgin relates the life of her pious father and godless mother.<-

A holy Desert Father <term>Alt-Vatter: literally "Old Father," referring to the Desert Fathers, the early Christian hermits of the Egyptian desert</term> related a story and said: There was a certain virgin who had reached a great age in the fear of God; I asked her how she had come to such a holy way of life <term>Wandel: conduct or spiritual path</term>? He worked daily in his courtyard and spent his life in that way. When he was a little strong and healthy..."

She gave her body up so shamefully that no one in the village had peace because of her. ## Chapter 2.

->She further recounts how the father and the mother met such contrasting ends.<-

Meanwhile, it happened that my father died after a long confinement to bed, just as a wicked weather set in, with tempests, thunder, and lightning, and the heavy downpour lasted for three days and three nights, so that we had to let our father lie unburied for three days against the custom of the land. At this, the village people shook their heads and marveled, for they did not know how to interpret such a tempest, and said: "It seems the man must have been a great enemy of God, that he cannot even come to the earth in peace." But so that the corpse, which in the heat already began to smell badly, might be removed from the house, we finally had to bury it with great difficulty during the continuing stormy and rainy weather. My mother, however, lived thereafter even more freely and unrestrainedly than before, and misused her body for the greatest lewdness and impurity; she turned our home into a house of ill-repute <term>Hur-Haus: literally a "whore-house" or brothel</term>, and maintained a daily life of luxury in all the lusts of the flesh. I was still small, and our fortune was consumed, when finally her death occurred, with great anxiety, as it seemed to me; yet the sky was bright and clear, and the funeral procession <term>Leich-Begängniß: a formal funeral ceremony or walk to the grave</term> was held with all desirable and convenient circumstances.

<header>The Life of Anonyma <note>Latin: "Anonymæ," the feminine form of Anonymous</note> II.</header>

->She, as a daughter, ponders whether she wishes to follow her father or her mother in her way of life.<-

## Chapter 3.

When, after her death <note>referring to the mother's death</note>, I had outgrown my childhood years and my fleshly desires began to stir, I sat one evening and reflected upon whose life I wished to follow. Perhaps my father’s, who had lived honorably, gently, and soberly? Yet it also occurred to me that he never had a good hour, and spent his whole life in sickness "under the Cross" <note>a historical metaphor for enduring suffering and trials as a test of Christian faith</note>, and even met such a poor end that he could hardly be buried with honor. If such a way of life were pleasing to God, I thought, why then did my father suffer so much misery, having chosen such a life? Therefore, my thoughts said, it is better to live like my mother, in pleasure, gluttony, and impurity; she neglected no wicked deed, yet in her drunkenness she was always hale and healthy, and even ended her life in that state. What then is to be done, I asked? I will live as my mother did, for it is most certain to believe what one sees before one's eyes, and to let no pleasure pass by.

## Chapter 4.
->She recounts the beginning of her vision <note>original: "Gesichts"</note>.<-

While I, wretched as I am, had resolved this within myself, night fell and sleep overcame me. There appeared to me in a dream a tall man of dreadful appearance, who terrified me with his angry gaze, and asked me with a harsh voice, saying: "Tell me, what are you thinking in your heart?" I trembled, however, and dared not look at him because of his fearsome form. Then he asked once more with a harsher voice what I had thought. But I was quite beside myself with fear and had forgotten all my thoughts; so I said I could remember nothing. When I denied it, he brought back to my mind everything I had thought and resolved. By this I was convicted and shamed, and I begged for forgiveness, explaining the reasons for such thoughts. He then spoke to me: "Follow me, and see the condition of both your father and your mother; afterwards, choose which life you want." With that, he took my hand and led me away.

## Chapter 2.

->She further recounts how the father and the mother had such dissimilar ends.<-

Meanwhile, it happened that my father died after a long period of being bedridden, just as a wicked weather set in, with tempests, thunder, and lightning; and the heavy downpour lasted for three days and three nights, so that we had to leave our father lying unburied for three days, contrary to the custom of the land. At this, the villagers shook their heads and wondered, because they did not know how to interpret such a tempest, and they said: "It appears the man must have been a great enemy of God, since he cannot even come to the earth in peace." However, so that the corpse, which began to smell poorly in the heat, might be removed from the house, we finally had to bury it with great difficulty while the stormy, rainy weather still persisted. After this, my mother lived even more freely and unrestrained than before, and misused her body for the greatest lewdness and impurity; she turned our home into a house of ill repute <note>original: "Hur-Haus," literally a brothel or house of harlotry</note> and maintained a daily life of luxury in all the lusts of the flesh. I was still small, and our fortune was consumed, when finally her death followed—with great anguish, as it seemed to me—at which time the sky was bright and clear, and the funeral rites <note>original: "Leich-Begängniß"</note> were held with all desirable and convenient circumstances.

# The Life of Anonyma III.
## Chapter 1.
->Two elders find an old female warrior in a cave shortly before her end, and bury her.<-

Two famous elders <note>The "elders" (Alte) refer to the Desert Fathers, early Christian hermits noted for their wisdom.</note> wandered through the desert that borders Scetis <note>original: "Scithi," referring to the Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, a famous center of early monasticism.</note>. As they heard the sound of a human voice echoing from somewhere out of the earth, they searched and found a cave into which they entered. There they found an old, holy maiden <note>original: "Jungfrau," often used for a woman who has taken a vow of celibacy.</note> lying quite weak, to whom they spoke: "When did you come here, blessed mother? And who assists you?" For they found nothing else in the cave but the sick woman alone; she said: "I have already been here in this cave in the desert for thirty-eight years and have served the **Lord** Christ with all contentment; since that time, I have seen no human being until today. But God has sent you here so that you may bury my body." When she had said this, she fell asleep in peace. The two fathers praised God, and after they had buried her corpse, they returned to their place. <note>Joh. L. 3. n. 9.</note>

He left again that time, however, and waited two or three days before visiting her, at which time he spoke to her: "How is it that you sit here thus?" She gave him the answer: "I do not sit; rather, I walk!" He spoke: "Where are you walking to, then?" She answered: "To GOD!" He spoke further: "Are you then living or dead?" She gave the answer: "I trust in my GOD that I am <term>dead to the world</term> <note>original: "abgestorben," a Pietist and mystical term for being spiritually deceased to worldly desires.</note>; for whoever lives according to the flesh does not walk so." Then Father Serapion spoke to her: "So that you may convince me of this—that you are dead—do what I do." She answered: "Command; everything that is possible for me, I will do!" But he spoke to her: "To one who is dead, nothing is impossible to do, except only that he cannot be ungodly; therefore, come out and follow me." Afterwards, when Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius the Great (c. 296–373 AD), the Bishop of Alexandria and a staunch defender of Orthodoxy against Arianism.</note>—then Bishop of Alexandria—was summoned to court around the year 354 by Eusebius, the Governor of Egypt under Emperor Constantius, upon the accusation of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius who disagreed with Athanasius on the nature of Christ's divinity; the Emperor Constantius II favored their faction.</note>, he did not wish to submit himself to a biased judge. Instead, when the court officials came to seize him, he took pen and paper and went secretly at midnight to this virgin. When this virgin was greatly terrified by such an unexpected occurrence, the Bishop spoke to her: "The Arians seek to take me prisoner and have accused me of hideous, wicked deeds. Now, so that I do not fall under suspicion through an unjust trial as if I were such a person, and also so that I do not give cause for sin to those who persecute me, I have decided to flee; for God has revealed to me this night that I shall be safe nowhere else but with you alone." When she heard this, she cast aside all doubt and sheltered the holy Bishop with great joy for six years (*) until Emperor Constantius died in the year 360. She washed his feet, even cleaned his <term>commode</term> <note>original: "s. v. Nacht-Stul." The "s.v." stands for the Latin *salva venia*, meaning "with your permission" or "saving your reverence," a polite way to mention a "night-stool" or toilet chair.</note> herself, and assisted him in everything, providing him with books and whatever he required. No one in all of Alexandria discovered during those six years where the blessed Athanasius was staying. However, after news arrived of Emperor Constantius’s death and he heard of it, he put on his episcopal robes and allowed himself to be found in the church during the night, appearing before everyone. They were all greatly amazed and rejoiced, for they received him back as one living from the dead. When his friends asked him where he had kept himself so hidden, he said: "I did not wish to hide among you for this reason: so that you could take an oath with a good conscience that you did not know where I was. On the other hand, I stayed with this virgin, for no one could have imagined that I would be with her, since she is beautiful and young; but I have served her soul, as she has served my honor and safety."

(*) During which time he also visited the fathers in Nitria and the Thebaid <note>Famous monastic regions in the Egyptian desert.</note> in an unrecognized manner and wrote various works; for he then took his secret lodging with this virgin in Alexandria, where no one could have suspected him.

# The Life of Anonymous Woman <note>original: "Anonymæ," the Latin genitive form meaning "of the Anonymous woman."</note> VIII.
## Chapter 1.
->Concerning a virgin to whom the Martyr Colluthus appeared.<-

There lived near the city of Antinoopolis <note>original: "Antinoum," an ancient Egyptian city founded by Emperor Hadrian.</note> a virgin whose face I (Palladius) never saw; for they said that from the moment she began to renounce the world, she never emerged from her hut. After she had practiced her devotions for sixty years alongside her biological mother, her end drew near. Then the holy martyr Colluthus <note>Saint Colluthus (or Koluthos) was a physician-martyr from Antinoopolis, highly venerated in the Coptic tradition.</note>, whose church stood in her neighborhood, appeared to her and said: "Today you shall journey to the Lord and shall see all the saints; come then, and dine with us for your farewell!" <note>original: "zum Valet," derived from the Latin *valete*, a formal leave-taking or "farewell."</note> After she arose early in the morning, she took a basket of bread, olives, and garden herbs, and for the first time in so many years, she went out from her hut, went to the church of Saint Colluthus, and prayed there. Once everyone else had left and she remained alone, she called upon Saint Colluthus and said: "Holy Colluthus, come and bless my food, and let me journey from here in your company!" Thus she ate, and after eating she prayed, and toward sunset returned to her hut. There, she gave her mother a book by Clement of Alexandria <note>A prominent Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 150–215 AD).</note> concerning the prophet Amos, titled *Stromateus* <note>Usually referring to the *Stromata* or "Miscellanies," Clement's famous work on Christian life and philosophy.</note>, and said to her: "Give this to the exiled bishop, and tell him to pray for me; for I journey this night to my Lord." She died that same night without any physical illness, having dressed herself in the clothes she was to be buried in and laid herself down, commending her spirit into the hands of God.
Palladius, chapter 139. Heraclides, chapter 48.

<margin>Palladius, chapter 140. Heraclides, chapter 56. <note>These refer to the *Lausiac History* by Palladius and the *Paradise of the Fathers* attributed to Heraclides, which are major 4th- and 5th-century collections of stories about desert monastics.</note></margin>
When she saw herself forsaken by all people, she entered into such a deep repentance <note>original: "Busse," a term implying both internal remorse and outward acts of penance.</note> for her sins that she went too far in it and wrestled with despair, in which she wished to starve herself to death. She pleaded with God with constant tears, saying:
> O You great God, who are accustomed to bearing the sins of us all—yea, of the entire world—and who do not desire the death of the sinner, nor take pleasure in the destruction of the wrongdoer, but show Yourself merciful to all creatures because it is Your holy will to preserve us all; show also this grace to me, a lost woman, and take the child of sin [born] of my wickedness from this life, so that I do not kill myself out of despair!

The outcome showed that God heard her prayer, for the child died not long thereafter. From that day on, she saw the impure violator of her honor no more, but instead surrendered herself entirely to chaste abstinence and served the sick, the lame, and the infirm for thirty years. Thus she reconciled herself with God in such a manner that it was revealed by God to a holy Elder on her account that she now pleased God much more in her repentance than previously in her virginal exercises. This serves to remind us that we should not despise those who fall and repent from the heart; just like this blessed woman, who spent her life after her fall steadfastly until the end in a contrite heart and the deepest humility, and was not rejected by the Lord.

# The Life of Anonymous Woman XI.
## Chapter 1.

->Concerning a harlot who gave her wages of harlotry as alms and was converted.<-

Father and Priest Timothy <note>Timothy was a common name among the early Egyptian desert monastics.</note> asked Father Poemen <note>original: "Pastorem." "Poemen" is Greek for "Shepherd" or "Pastor," and refers to one of the most famous of the Desert Fathers.</note> and said: "In Egypt, there is a certain well-known harlot who gives her wages of harlotry to the poor; what do you think of this?" Father Poemen said: "She will not remain a harlot, for the fruit of faith is showing itself in her." 

It happened, however, that the mother of the priest Timothy came to this her son; he questioned her and said: "Is that woman still a harlot?" She answered: "Alas, yes; she has even more lovers <note>original: "Buhler," meaning paramours or illicit lovers.</note> than before, but she still gives her unclean money as alms!" Father Timothy told this to Father Poemen. The latter maintained his position that she would not persist in harlotry. 

Again, Father Timothy's mother came and said to him: "What do you think? The harlot in our place now wishes to travel here with me and seek your intercession." When Timothy heard this, he reported it to Father Poemen, who said: "Go to her now and visit her." Father Timothy then traveled to the woman. When she saw him and heard the Word of God from him, she was moved in her heart and began to shed tears of repentance; she wept and said: "From this day on, I will cling to God and be a harlot no more." Thereupon she went immediately into a convent for virgins and led a holy life well-pleasing to God. *Sayings of the Fathers in the Life of Timothy, page 700.*

## Chapter 2.

->Concerning a virgin who did not wish to see her brother.<-

Another brother wished to visit his sick sister in the cloister; she was, however, a famous servant of GOD and led a very holy life. Therefore, she did not wish to be seen by any man, nor even to speak to her own brother, so that he would not take the opportunity to enter a virgin’s cloister. Instead, she sent word to him at the door, saying: "Go home, dear brother, and pray for me; for through the grace of GOD our Savior, I shall see you in the eternal life, in the kingdom of our Lord JESUS Christ." *Rufinus, Book 3, number 33. Pelagius, Book 4, number 61.* <note>Rufinus of Aquileia was a monk and historian who translated many Greek monastic texts into Latin.</note>

## Chapter 3.

->Concerning a brother who carried his old mother.<-

A certain brother was traveling with his old mother; when they came to a river, the old woman could not wade through it. Then the son took his cloak and wrapped it around his hand, so that he would in no way touch his mother’s bare body, and thus he carried her across the river. But his mother said to him: "My son, why have you thus wrapped your hand?" He answered: "Because the body of a woman is fire; if I had touched you directly, the memory of other women might have come to my mind, leading to defilement." <note>This story illustrates the extreme caution (and psychological struggle) early monks practiced regarding physical contact with women, even family members.</note> *Pelagius, Book 4, number 68.*

## Chapter 2.

->She is found by an elder after seventeen years.<-

After a long time, however, it happened by the providence of GOD—so that her exceptional conduct might become known—that a certain hermit by the Jordan saw her in the desert and said to her: "What are you doing here in this desert, dear mother?" She, however, wished to remain hidden from the hermit and answered: "Forgive me, dear father, I have lost my way; but I pray you, do me the kindness and show me the way again." But he had already received a sign from GOD concerning her and said to her: "Believe me, dear mother, you have not strayed from the way, nor are you seeking any way; since you know that lies are of the devil, tell me the truth: what are you doing here, and how did you come here?" Then the virgin said to him: "Forgive me, dear father, a certain youth was scandalized <note>The German *geärgert* implies the youth was led into the sin of lust or spiritual stumbling by her presence.</note> by me; therefore I went into this desert, because I held it better to die here than to cause someone an offense; according to the Apostolic teaching of 2 Corinthians 6, verse 6. <note>While the text cites verse 6, the Apostolic teaching regarding "giving no offense" is typically found in 2 Corinthians 6:3.</note> The elder asked her further, how long she had already been there? She gave the answer: "Through the grace of Christ, I have been here for seventeen years." Again the elder asked her and said: "With what have you then nourished yourself?" She said: "See, this hair-cloth garment I took with me from the city, and these few soaked peas and beans. But GOD has so graciously preserved me, a miserable woman, with them, that I have eaten of them all this time, and yet they have not decreased; know also, dear father, that His mercy has so shielded me that I have been seen by no one in all those seventeen years, though I have seen others traveling past; you alone see me today." When the elder heard this, he glorified GOD. *John Moschus in the Spiritual Meadow, chapter 179.* <note>John Moschus (c. 550–619) was a monk who traveled the Mediterranean collecting stories of desert monastics for his book, the *Pratum Spirituale* or "Spiritual Meadow."</note>

### Chapter 2.

->She has the youth summoned and gouges out her own eyes.<-

One day, then, she sent her maid to him and had him told that he should come, as the virgin wished to speak with him. He went there in haste, full of joy, intending to satisfy his lust. The holy virgin, however, went to sit upon her bed, and when the youth was let in, she said to him: "Sit down beside me!" When he had seated himself, she spoke further: "I ask you, my brother, tell me, why are you so troublesome to me, and do not let me go out of my house?" The youth said: "Truly, beautiful virgin, I love you very much, and when I look at you, I am entirely inflamed with love for you." She spoke again to him: "What beautiful thing do you see in me, for which you love me so?" The youth said: "Your eyes, they seduce me." When the virgin heard that her eyes had seduced him, she quickly took a little knife and gouged out both of her eyes. When the youth saw that she had gouged out her eyes for his sake, he was greatly dismayed and so stirred in his heart that he went into the deserts of Scetis <note>Scetis, or Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, was one of the most famous centers of early Christian monasticism and the home of the Desert Fathers.</note> and renounced the world, thus becoming a holy and famous hermit. <note>original: "Joh. Mosch. in Prato Spirit. cap. 60." refers to John Moschus, a 7th-century monk and author of the famous hagiographic work *The Spiritual Meadow* (Latin: *Pratum Spirituale*).</note>

# The Life of Anonymous Woman XV.
## Chapter 1.
-> Of a merchant in Ascalon who lost everything and was thrown into the debtors' prison. <-

Father Eusebius in the monastery at Ascalon told Moschos <note>John Moschos (c. 550–619 AD) was a Byzantine monk and author of the *Pratum Spirituale* (The Spiritual Meadow), a famous collection of stories about holy people.</note> and his traveling companions the following occurrence, and said: A certain merchant lived here who lost his ship and all his goods—both his own and those he owed to others—in a storm at sea, and barely escaped with his life. # The Life of Anonymous Woman XVI.

## Chapter 1.

->Concerning a pagan man who, upon the advice of his Christian wife, lends his money to the **Lord Christ** at interest.<-

When we (**Moschus** and **Sophronius**) were on the island of **Samos**, the venerable lover of the poor, **Maria**, the mother of Lord **Paulus**, told us a story, saying: When I was in the city of **Nisibis** <note>An ancient city in upper Mesopotamia, modern-day Nusaybin</note>, there lived a Christian woman who had a pagan husband. They were poor, and their entire liquid assets consisted of one hundred **Imperial Thalers** <term>Reichs-Thaler: large silver coins used throughout the Holy Roman Empire; here used to represent ancient currency</term>. One day, the husband said to his wife: "Let us put this money out at interest so that we might gain something from it; otherwise, we will consume it bit by bit until nothing is left." The faithful woman then said to her husband: "If it pleases you to seek a profit with it, come, and let us lend it at interest to the **God** of the **Christians**." The husband answered: "Where then is the **God of the Christians**, that we may give it to Him?" She said: "I will show Him to you; for if you give it to Him, you need not worry that you will lose it. He will correctly pay you both the interest and return the capital to you twofold." He then said: "Come, let us go to Him; show Him to me, and we will give it to Him." She went with her husband to the assembly of the holy congregation. The church had five large doors, two on each side and one in front. They went inside to where the poor were standing. She pointed these out to her husband and said: "If you distribute it to these people, the **God of the Christians** receives it, for they are His servants." Thereupon, he immediately and joyfully distributed the money to the poor, and so they both returned home.

# The Life of Anonymous Woman XX.
## Chapter 1.
->Of a merciful girl who saves a life with her money and property.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>
Father Theonas and Father Theodorus told us that in Alexandria, during the time of Archbishop Paul, a certain girl was left as an orphan after her wealthy parents died; however, she was not yet baptized. One day, it happened that this daughter went into the orchard she had inherited from her parents, which lay among other gardens in the middle of the city; there she saw someone who was preparing a rope and intended to hang himself. But she ran quickly to him and spoke to him: "What are you doing, man?" He gave her the answer: "Leave me be, woman, for I have fallen into despair." She spoke: "Tell me the reason; perhaps I can help you." He spoke to her: "I am very heavily oppressed by a burden of debt, and my creditors almost want to strangle me; therefore I would rather die once than daily." She then spoke to him: "Just take everything that is mine and pay the debts; only do not kill yourself." He accepted this offer and paid everything.

## Chapter 2.

It is indeed possible for someone, out of spiritual impulse and divine longing, to come to the aid of their relatives if they fall into need and suffer want, provided they do not neglect their own soul. But if someone gives themselves over so completely, body and soul, that the soul is neglected and stifled by outward care for friends, they fall under the law of regarding their soul as nothing; of which David, the composer of the Psalms, sings: *Who shall ascend the holy hill? and who shall stand in the holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who does not neglect his soul, and does not swear falsely!* Ps. 15, v. 3. 4. <note>In modern Bibles, this text is found in Psalm 24:3-4. The author's numbering follows a different tradition, likely the Vulgate.</note> These, however, are the ones who regard their soul as nothing: those who live as if there were no other life after death, and who do not seek spiritual strength.

### Chapter 4.

When the holy *Macarius* <note>Saint Macarius of Alexandria (d. 395 AD), a famous desert hermit known for his austerities and service to the poor.</note> had received the money, he gave it to the hospital for the service of the infirm. After a considerable amount of time had passed—as the old man was known throughout all *Alexandria* as a very godly and merciful man, and was nearly 100 years old (whom we, *Palladius* <note>Palladius of Galatia (c. 363–420 AD), the author of the *Lausiac History*, which recorded the lives of the Desert Fathers.</note> and others, have also seen)—she was nevertheless hesitant to remind him of the matter. Finally, she encountered him one day in the church and said to him: "I beg you, tell me, what do you command that we should do with the gemstones for which I paid the thousand Imperial Thalers?" He gave her an answer and said: "As soon as you gave me the money, I applied it to the gemstones. If you wish to see them, come to me at the hospital; for I have kept them there. Look at them; and if they do not please you, you can still get your money back." So she went very gladly. In the hospital, the infirm women were kept upstairs and the men downstairs. When she arrived, he led her into the vestibule from which one could also go upstairs; there the holy *Macarius* said to her: "What do you want to see first, the *hyacinths* or the *emeralds*?" She answered: "Whatever seems best to you." Then he led her upstairs and showed her the lame, blind, and infirm women, and said: "See, these are the *hyacinths*." Afterward, he led her downstairs to the men and said: "Behold there the *emeralds*! I believe they are precious and worth the money; if they please..."

## 2. The Puffed-up Woman who Fell into Fornication.
### Chapter 1.

I (*Palladius*) also know a certain virgin in *Jerusalem* who for six years had worn a sackcloth or a simple, coarse sleeveless shirt and had shut herself in a hut; she enjoyed nothing that served her pleasure, but lived in the highest degree of abstinence. Afterward, however, she was deprived of Divine assistance because of her vain imagination—as though she were something special—so that she opened the door of her hut to the man who used to bring her food and committed unchastity with him. This happened because she did not practice her devotion out of Divine zeal and love for Christ, but only to be seen as a holy and special sister; for the sake of which vain honor many torment themselves and endure much. For her mind was occupied only with condemning and judging others; because of this, she fell into the hands of the spirit of pride <note>original: "Hochmuht". In this context, it refers to the "demon of pride" who targets those successful in asceticism.</note>, taking such pleasure in herself that the guardian angel of her chastity departed from her. *Palladius* chapter 34. *Heraclides* chapter 16.

### 3. A Double Fall due to Slander.
<note>This sentence begins mid-thought from the previous page.</note> [A man] had traveled across the water by mistake to these secluded women and was seeking work. Now it happened that a younger sister had just gone outside, perhaps for natural necessities <note>A common euphemism in monastic texts for using the latrine</note>—for it is a lonely, desolate place—and she met him against her will. Upon his questioning whether they had any shoes there to be made or mended, she gave him the answer: "We have our own shoemakers." Another sister, however, who had observed their conversation, made use of this when a disagreement arose between the two of them after some time had passed. Out of the instigation of the devil and the extreme malice of an inflamed spirit, she slandered the other woman to the sisters and brothers because of that conversation. Some gave credit to this slanderer, though not necessarily out of such a malicious intent. But this went so deeply to the heart of the accused woman—that she had fallen under such slanders which had never even entered her thoughts—that she could not endure this temptation; instead, she secretly threw herself into the River Nile and thus died. When the slanderer learned of this, and well knew that she had maliciously plunged the woman into such misery and caused such suffering to the entire brotherhood, she likewise drowned herself in despair. When the priest arrived, the other virgins recounted to him everything that had happened, with all the circumstances. Then the priest forbade that anyone should give alms or pray for either of the two, as was otherwise customary for deceased good acquaintances for the refreshment of their souls. Those, however, who had not sought peace and had believed the slander, he separated from the fellowship of Holy Communion for seven years. *Palladius* <note>original: "Pallad." Referring to Palladius of Galatia's Lausiac History.</note> chapter 40. *Heraclides* <note>original: "Heraclid."</note> chapter 20.

## 4. Case of a Chaste Female Suicide.

<margin>Palladius, Chapter 150.</margin> [The story concerns] a noble matron (*) whose husband, out of fear of the tyrant, said to him: "Send for her and have her brought to you." When the soldiers came to the woman, she said to them: "Wait a little while until I have adorned myself." However, she went into her bedchamber, took a dagger, and plunged it into her own heart. Although this was a spiritually dubious act of suicide—as she could have allowed the LORD Christ to save her chastity—nevertheless, those who call themselves the brides of Christ should see themselves reflected in this and be ashamed; those who prefer to associate with men rather than their own gender, and who deny Christ through secret unchastity. But may God grant us all the strength to preserve our virginity and to sing along with the Psalmist with a joyful spirit: "Crucify the lusts of my flesh in your fear, for I dread your judgment." <note>original: "Creuzige in deiner Furcht meines Fleisches Lüste, denn ich fürchte dein Gerichte." This is a variation of Psalm 119:120, using the ascetic language of "crucifying the flesh."</note> Psalm 119, verse 120. Thus we can also say with the Apostle: "I no longer live according to the flesh, but Christ is my life." <note>original: "Ich lebe nicht mehr nach dem Fleische, sondern Christus ist mein Leben." # 5. The Fallen Daughter of a Priest.
### Chapter 1.

The daughter of a certain priest in Caesarea, Palestine, had been seduced by a rogue who persuaded her that she should name a certain lector and **Deacon** <term>Deacon: A high-ranking lay official or subordinate minister in the early church</term> named **Eustathius** as if he were the culprit. When she became pregnant and her father questioned her sharply, she named the aforementioned Deacon. When this reached the ears of the Bishop, he summoned the **consistory** <term>Consistory: A formal council or administrative court of the clergy</term> and gathered all the clergy, before whom the Deacon had to appear to defend himself. When the Bishop asked him if he had committed such a disgrace, he denied it, as he had indeed not done it. But the Bishop took this very poorly and said to him with a stern voice: "Will you not confess your fall and do penance, O wretched one, full of impurity?" The Deacon spoke: "I beg you, most honorable Bishop, I have told the truth; how shall I confess what does not concern me? For I am innocent, as one who has not even thought of such things. But if you truly wish to hear what is not true..."

## Chapter 2.

Once the man had received her from the hand of the Bishop and from her father, and had spoken to her kindly, he led her to a convent for women with a request to the Mother Superior that they might house her until she had given birth.

## Chapter 3.

After this was done, Eustathius went away to live in a wretched hut and led a very strict life; in his contrite heart, he drew near to Christ with sighs and tears, prayed, and said to him: "You, O Lord, know my conduct—you who know all, see all, and judge all; you know that I have been slandered, and you are my judge, to whom I hold fast!" In such prayer, he persisted with constant fasting until the time of her birth-pangs arrived, and with them, God’s righteous judgment. For she suffered such great and unbearable pains that she had to howl and shriek violently, and in her fainting spells, she saw the souls of the damned in torment. This lasted for several days with indescribable pain; for not only was she in distress on the first and second day, but it continued through the third and fourth, and even on the fifth, sixth, and seventh day she lay in such terrifying darkness and could not give birth. During these seven days, she neither partook of food nor did sleep come to her eyes, until finally, Divine Omnipotence overcame her hardened heart, so that in her unbearable pain she finally had to cry out: "Woe is me, wretched woman! I am at death’s door, and fallen into double sin: into **fornication** <note>original: "Hurerey"</note> and **slander** <note>original: "Verleumdung"</note>; for the Deacon is innocent—another is the culprit!"

5. The Fallen Priest's Daughter. 237

## Chapter 4.

When the virgins of the convent <note>German: *Jungfrauen des Kloſters*; referring to the nuns in the house where Eustathius had placed her</note> learned of this, they announced everything to her father. The father, however, out of fear that he might be viewed as a slanderer, concealed it for two more days. In the meantime, the wretched woman could not come to the birth, but had to lie in such agony even through the eighth and ninth day, surrounded by constant **hellish visions**. Because the company of the virgins could no longer bear to hear the great and constant screaming, they went to the Bishop and reported the whole matter to him: that she could not give birth and had confessed that the **Deacon** <term>Deacon: A rank of ordained ministry below that of a priest</term> had been falsely accused by her. As soon as the Bishop heard this, he sent two deacons to the innocent man to tell him everything and to beg him to pray for the wretched woman so that she might be released. But the excellent man gave them no answer, nor would he open the door; for from the day he had entered there, he had not come out, but persisted with constant fasting and prayer. The father, however, took pity on his daughter and came to the Bishop with a most earnest plea that prayer might be offered for her in the congregation. Yet, although this was done by everyone, the wretched woman was still not released from her distress; for the prayer of the slandered man held back the prayers of all the others, so that they did not penetrate through to the Lord.

## Chapter 5.

So the Bishop himself stood up and went to the Deacon's hut and knocked; but he would not open. When the Bishop had stood outside for a long time, he finally commanded that the door be opened by force. There they found the Deacon lying in prayer on his knees, to whom the Bishop said: "My son **Eustathius** <note>original: *Euſtathi*; the Latin vocative form of the name</note>, you worthy Deacon, your innocence has become manifest through **Divine Providence** <term>Divine Providence: The protective care of God as a spiritual power</term>, and your prayer is heard; so now have mercy on her who sinned against you and has been tormented for it for so long! Have mercy on the wretched woman and **loose what you have bound** <note>A reference to the biblical power of "binding and loosing" (Matthew 16:19); the text implies Eustathius's own spiritual state was preventing her delivery</note>, for she suffers this because of your prayer; tell the Lord that He should release her from the birth-pains." When the chosen Deacon, together with the Bishop, prayed earnestly, the wretched woman was immediately freed from her distress and gave birth to a child; she thereafter begged everyone that her wickedness might be forgiven her, through the intercession of the righteous man.

## 6. The Fallen Five Refugees.
### Chapter 1.

When we (Moschus <note>John Moschus, a 7th-century monk and travel writer.</note> and others) came to the Monastery of the Eunuchs by the Jordan, Father Nicholas, who was the priest of the monastery, told us a story and said: In my homeland of Lycia <note>An ancient region in what is now southern Turkey.</note>, there is a convent of virgins where nearly forty live together. Among these were five who had conspired with one another; they intended to flee at night and take husbands. Now, on a certain night when all the other sisters were asleep, they packed their clothes together and intended to leave at that moment; but in that same hour, all five were possessed by an evil spirit and could not escape. After they were eventually delivered from this possession, they no longer desired to renounce their holy way of life, but recognized their sin, thanked God, and said:
> We thank you, O God, you great Rewarder, that you have so chastened us, so that our souls were not lost. 
John Moschus in the *Spiritual Meadow* <note>Original Latin title: *Pratum Spirituale*</note>, Chapter 135.

# 7. Maria, the Drowned Sinner.

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

...had men on board. When he reached the high seas and saw all the other ships sailing away with a good wind—some toward Constantinople <note>The capital of the Byzantine Empire, modern-day Istanbul.</note>, some toward Alexandria, and some elsewhere—he alone could not move from the spot with his ship. So we lay there, he reported, for nearly fourteen days in silence, remaining motionless in the place where we were; because of this, we fell into great worry and distress, not knowing what had befallen us. But I, as the captain <note>The original German uses "Schiffer," meaning the master or owner of the vessel.</note>, who was responsible for the entire ship and everything within it, prayed to God for enlightenment in this matter; until finally one day, an unknown voice said to me: "Throw Maria overboard, and you shall sail happily." I then began to ponder what this word meant and which one was Maria. While I stood in doubt regarding this, the voice spoke a second time and said: "I have told you: throw Maria overboard, and you shall all be saved." Then I thought once more about what that could be, and called out loudly: "O Maria!" for I did not know who was named Maria. She, however, was in her place, and when she heard her name called, she answered and said: "What do you command, my lord?" Then I said to her: "Do me a kindness and come here to me." So she rose quickly and approached.

### Chapter 2.

When she had come to me, I went with her alone and said to her: "You see, dear sister Maria, that because of my sins, you are all about to perish!" <note>The original idiom "um den Hals kommen" literally means "to come around the neck," signifying a violent or untimely death.</note> But she sighed deeply and said: "Truly, my lord captain, I am the sinner." Then I said to her: "What sins have you committed then, O woman?" She said: "Woe is me, there is no sin that I have not committed, and it is because of my sins that you have all come into this distress!" Thereupon the woman began to tell me what evil she had done, and said: "Truly, my lord captain, I had a husband and bore him two sons. When one was nine years old and the other was five years old, my husband died, and I remained a widow. A certain soldier, however, lived not far from me, and I would have liked to have him as a husband; I sent word to him through several women. But he did not want me, saying: 'I do not care for a woman who has children.' When I saw that he would not take me because of the sons, I killed both my children out of love for him, and had him told afterward,"

**n.** refers to the entry numbers, followed by the chapter number. **Anon.** refers to the number of Anonymous or unnamed individuals. **Fallen** <note>original: "Gefall."</note> refers to the number of the fallen women listed at the end.

### A.

**The Lord's Supper** <note>original: "Abendmahl"; refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> / was given to the baptized immediately after their baptism, n. 10: 8. n 12: 9. Those who had been excommunicated received it after absolution as a sign of fellowship with the community, n. 24: 1.

**Abraham** <note>original: "Abrahamus"</note> / Desert Father, uncle of Mary the Harlot <note>original: "Mariæ Meretricis"</note>, n. 4: 1. c. has a vision of her, c. 3. disguises himself in soldiers' clothing and goes to her in the brothel, c. 4. 5. 6. 7. and rescues her from an impure life, c. 8. 9.

**Absolution**, see **Forgiveness of Sins**.

**Adelphius** / Desert Father, is sent into exile, n. 11: 2.

**Abbess** <note>original: "Aebtissin"</note> / see **Spiritual Mother**.

**Egypt** / societies of hermits <note>original: "Einsamen," literally "solitary ones"</note> of both sexes there, n. 7: 5. 6.

**Backbiting** <note>original: "Afterreden"</note> / see **Slander**.

**Agapitus** / a brother of the monastery of Saint Euphrosyne, n. 8: 8.

**Alexius** / a son-in-law of Paula of Rome, n. 25: 1.

**Alexandra** / a holy virgin, her life, n. 30. she dwells in a tomb-cave, lives in it for twelve years and dies, c. 1. fled there because of a persistent suitor, c. 2. how she spent her time therein, c. 3. see a nearly identical story, Anon. n 13.

**Alexandria** / a city, the birthplace of Saint Euphrasia, n. 8: 1.

**Almsgiving** <note>original: "Almosen-Geben"</note> / kindles love further in the heart, n. 2: 24. when everything has been given away, then love for God truly begins, in the same place <note>original: "ibid."</note>. It serves as a spiritual exercise for those living in the world, in the same place.

# Introduction.

## JESUS our High Priest!

->§ 1.<-

It is the inner court of the priests / where on the holy altar sacrifices were brought to the Lord and the animals were slaughtered; at the time of such slaughtering, it looked very bloody and unclean here / to that end, however, both the water of the bronze sea <note>The "bronze sea" was a large basin in the courtyard of Solomon's Temple used by priests for ritual washing (1 Kings 7:23).</note> and a living spring-fountain were led there close at hand / to wash away all animal filth / which had not been consumed by the holy fire. This holy fire was initially lit by the Lord himself / and had to be constantly maintained by the steady adding of wood / which the citizens of Gibeon, who had crept in among Israel / brought there / after they had been appointed by Joshua as wood-cutters and water-carriers of the House of God <note>This refers to the story in Joshua 9, where the Gibeonites deceived the Israelites into a treaty and were subsequently assigned to perform menial labor for the Tabernacle.</note>. On this inner court, all sacrifices were slaughtered through priestly service and offered to the Lord; but during the slaughter of the Passover Lamb, every individual from Israel performed the priestly office themselves.

§ 2. # Introduction.

The persecutions of the orthodox <term>orthodox: "Recht-Gläubigen," meaning those holding the established, correct faith</term> by the Arians <note>Arians: followers of Arius who denied the full divinity of Christ, a major theological conflict in the early church</note>—who denied the true foundation of salvation, the Divine Revelation in the flesh—under Emperor Valens, as well as the Goths in Hungary and the Vandals in Africa during the 4th and 5th centuries, clearly bear witness to this. However, the very decayed state of the church itself was to blame for this, since the teachers, acting as heads of the congregations, themselves handled the fire wrongly <note>original: "im Feur misgriffen," an idiom suggesting they mishandled a dangerous situation or acted out of misguided zeal</note> and abused the secular power under Emperor Constantine the Great and his sons against others, though they should have only cut off the wicked from the Spirit. Therefore, those who took up or approved of the sword were also bound to perish by the sword of the aforementioned persecution; yet those who suffered for the sake of the pure confession of Christ are rightly to be counted among the martyrs, as the 100th story in this volume testifies at greater length.

§ 8. We have thus intended to depict the history of the holy martyrs and confessors of the Early Church—who suffered under the pagans and the Antichrist from the time of the Apostles until the year 500—as simply, as authentically, and as fully as they remain available, here in this Priestly part of the Temple <note>The author likely uses the "Priestly part of the Temple" as a metaphor for this specific section of his historical work, treating history as a sacred space</note>. This is not painted with new colors, but rather presented as it was described by the ancients themselves, word for word, either from judicial records <term>judicial records: "Gerichtlichen Acten," official Roman trial transcripts</term>, by the shorthand notaries, or even by faithful eye- and ear-witnesses. In this, we have passed over everything regarding the suffering of our Lord Jesus Christ and the persecution of the holy Apostles that is already sufficiently known from the four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles. We have also deliberately omitted forged documents and the mere listing of names of many martyrs, for a disciplined reader will find sufficiency in the hundred stories provided here.

<summary>This page discusses the shift from pagan persecution to internal Christian conflict involving the Arians and the misuse of state power by church leaders. The author explains his methodology, focusing on authentic historical records for 100 selected martyr stories while omitting biblical accounts and forged documents.</summary>
<keywords>Arianism, Emperor Valens, Constantine the Great, Vandal persecution, ecclesiastical history, martyrdom methodology, judicial acts</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction’s overview of ecclesiastical history. # Introduction.
<meta>catchword: reign/</meta>

§ 9. It is customary to divide the history of the holy martyrs into ten major persecutions, drawing a comparison to the ten Egyptian plagues <note>A reference to the biblical plagues sent upon Egypt in the Book of Exodus</note>; however, not to mention that the church was persecuted much more than ten times, even those who initially favored this number—such as *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the first great historian of the Christian Church</note>, *Augustine* <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian</note>, and *Sulpicius Severus* <note>A chronicler (c. 363–425 AD) who wrote a history of the world from a Christian perspective</note>—differed entirely in their ordering of them. Moreover, it is also inappropriate to compare the holy sufferings of Christ within the holy martyrs to the plagues of *Egypt*, etc., from which the children of Israel were delivered. Nevertheless, so that one may have some knowledge of them, the martyr-histories of the first three hundred years are commonly distributed among ten emperors as the primary persecutors in the following manner:

§ 10. The 1st persecution was under *Nero* <note>original: "Nerone"</note> from the year 65 to 69; to this belong numbers 1 and 2 of our history. The 2nd was under *Domitian* <note>original: "Domitiano"</note> in the year 96; of this, no credible full accounts are available. The 3rd was under *Trajan* <note>original: "Trajano"</note> from the year 104 to 120; to this belong numbers 3 and 4. The 4th was under *Hadrian* <note>original: "Hadriano"</note> from the year 126 to 139; there belongs number 5. The 5th was under *Antoninus Pius* and the *Philosopher* <note>original: "Antonino Pio und Philosopho"; the "Philosopher" refers to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, known for his Stoic writings</note> from the year 141 to 180; there belong numbers 6 to 12. The 6th was under *Severus*, etc., from the year 200 to 222; there belong numbers 13 to 16. The 7th was under *Maximinus the Thracian* <note>original: "Maximino Thrace"</note> from the year 236 to 238; of this, no records exist. The 8th was under *Decius* <note>original: "Decio"</note> from the year 250 to 254; there belong numbers 17 to 26; in this persecution, the martyrs were hunted into the deserts, from which the life of the hermits <note>original: "Einsamen," referring to the early Christian anchorites or desert fathers who sought spiritual solitude</note> arose. The 9th was under *Valerian* and *Gallienus* <note>original: "Valeriano und Gallieno"</note> from the year 254 to 262; there belong numbers 26 to 36. The 10th was under *Diocletian*, *Galerius Maximianus*, *Maximian Herculius* <note>The co-emperor Maximian, who took the title "Herculius" to associate himself with the hero Hercules</note>, *Maxentius*, and *Licinius* from the year 285 to 325; there belong numbers 37 to 84. Thus far go the histories of the so-called ten persecutions, up until the peaceful reign <note>original: "fried samen Re- gierung"</note> of Emperor *Constantine the Great*...

(***) Although this holy James was an apostle and bishop of the Christians (mostly those of Jewish origin), he, along with other Jewish believers, remained devoted to the Temple until it was destroyed <note>The writer refers to the Destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note>, at which time the service of the Mosaic Law completely ceased.
(†) The ancients were accustomed to interpret the sayings that point to Christ as also referring to His exceptional witnesses, as has happened here.

# 3. St. Simeon.
## The 1st Chapter.

->The holy Simeon, second Bishop of Jerusalem, is betrayed for being of the Royal Line of David.<-

Following the general persecutions of **Nero** and **Domitian**, the Church of **Christ** had to endure much in various cities due to the particular uprisings of the pagan rabble under the Emperor **Trajan**. Among others, this affected the holy **Simeon**, the son of **Cleopas** (*), who was chosen by the **Apostles** as the second bishop or overseer <note>original: "Aufseher" — a literal translation of the Greek 'episkopos,' from which the word 'bishop' is derived.</note> of the congregation at **Jerusalem** after the death of **James**; who, as stated, became a martyr under the Emperor **Trajan**. **Hegesippus** <note>A 2nd-century Christian chronicler whose works are mostly lost, though fragments survive in the writings of later historians like Eusebius.</note> is his witness, writing as follows: 

> Several of the Jewish sectarians denounced one named **Simeon**, son of **Cleopas**, charging that he was of **David’s** lineage and a Christian (**). 

Thus this holy **Simeon**, an old man of one hundred and twenty years, became a martyr at the beginning of the reign of Emperor **Trajan**, when **Atticus** was governor <note>original: "Landpfleger" — a term for a Roman provincial governor or prefect.</note> in **Syria**, in the year of **Christ** 104. However, the very accusers of **Simeon** were themselves convicted of being from the Royal Line of the tribe of **Judah**, which at that time was being investigated very strictly. So far **Hegesippus**.

## The 2nd Chapter.

->Regarding other relatives of the Lord who were still alive in the year 104; also regarding Simeon’s slow martyrdom and death on the cross.<-

**Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History."</note>, who cites the preceding account, writes further: It is therefore not unreasonable to assume that this holy **Simeon** was an eyewitness and listener of the **Lord**; this is made credible by both his great age and the testimony of the **Gospels**, in which **Mary**, the daughter of **Cleopas**, is mentioned, whose son he was. But **Cleopas** was the brother of **Joseph** <note>Joseph, the foster-father of Jesus.</note>, according to the testimony of **Hegesippus** (***). The same also testifies that there were others still, namely

---

(*) The brother of **Salome** and **Mary Cleophas**.
(**) For Emperor **Trajan** ordered a search for all those among the Jews who were of the family of **David**, some of whom he had killed out of fear that they might cause an uprising and strive for the crown.
(***) **Eusebius** Book 3, Chapter 11.

namely, the grandchildren of Jude, the **LORD's** brother (*Joseph’s* son from his first marriage), had lived until the reign of *Trajan*; who, during the persecution of *Domitian* earlier in the year *92 AD*, had steadfastly confessed their faith in *Christ*, though they nevertheless escaped with their lives. They remained until that time, writes *Hegesippus* <note>A chronicler of the early Church whose works are preserved primarily through the historian Eusebius.</note>, and were, as martyrs and relatives of *Christ*, pillars of the whole Church. And because the congregations achieved great peace after the death of *Domitian*, they were still alive until the time of Emperor *Trajan*; until the aforementioned *Simeon* (son of *Cleopas*, who was the brother of *Joseph*, the **LORD's** foster-father) was denounced by the sectarian spirits <note>original: "Rotten-Geistern" — referring to schismatic or heretical groups seeking to cause division.</note> along with them, and was accused before the governor *Atticus*. When he had endured torture for many days and had steadfastly confessed the faith of *Christ*, even the governor himself and all those present were greatly astonished that it was possible for a man of one hundred and twenty years of age to endure so much torture. Finally, by the judge's sentence, he was nailed to the cross.

## Chapter 3.

->The Decline of the Church of Christ after the first hundred years.<-

Until this time, *Hegesippus* further reports, the Church of *Christ* was still a chaste virgin, which until then (namely, for seventy years from *Christ’s* Ascension) had remained pure and undefiled; for those who sought to corrupt the true teaching of the Gospel had to remain hidden in their corners because of the presence of the Apostolic men. But after the holy company of the Apostolic congregation had been executed through various martyr-deaths, and all those were dead who had heard Divine Wisdom itself with their own ears; then finally the bond of godless error arose through the deceit and malice of false teachers. These men, as no Apostle was left, went against the proclamation of the truth with a "bold, bare forehead" <note>original: "verwegener blossen Stirn" — a German idiom for acting with shameless audacity.</note> (to speak proverbially) and introduced their falsified, adulterous doctrine (*). So far *Hegesippus* in *Eusebius, Book 3, chapter 32.*

---

(*) Thus the righteous already lamented in those early times; what might they not have done later, when the most wicked church teachers became almost the most famous men?

<header>History of the Martyrs / Year 104.</header>

# 4. St. Ignatius.

## Chapter 1.

->The condition of Saint Ignatius before his martyrdom.<-

When Trajan had only recently taken over the Roman Empire, Ignatius—the disciple of the Apostle John—was a man apostolic in every way, and he carefully governed the congregation at Antioch. This man had barely survived the storms of the previous persecutions under Domitian <note>Domitian was the Roman Emperor from 81 to 96 AD, known in Christian tradition for a harsh persecution of the Church toward the end of his reign.</note>. As a good helmsman, using the rudder of prayer and fasting, along with persistence in teaching and struggling in the spirit, he had withstood the oncoming storm; for he feared that someone among the faint-hearted and simple might fall away. Therefore, while he was in good spirits regarding the peaceful state of the congregation, as the persecution had subsided for a little while, he was nonetheless distressed within himself that he had not yet attained a true, essential love for Christ, nor the perfect rank of a disciple. For he considered within himself that the confession made through the glory of martyrdom could bring him closer to the Lord. Therefore, after he remained with the congregation for a few more years, illuminating the mind of everyone like a divine light through the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, he attained his wish.

## Chapter 2.

->How the holy man defended himself before Emperor Trajan.<-

For after Trajan, in the ninth year of his reign, became proud over his victory against the Scythians <note>A group of nomadic tribes living in the regions north of the Black Sea.</note>, the Dacians <note>People from the region of modern-day Romania and Moldova.</note>, and other nations, he believed that the pious assembly of Christians remained for him to subdue. Moreover, he threatened with persecution those whom he could not force to submit to the service of idols like all other heathens; the fear of this forced all who lived piously either to offer sacrifices or to die. At that time, the courageous warrior of Christ, who was so solicitous for the Antiochian congregation, was voluntarily brought before Trajan, who was staying at Antioch at the time while preparing for war against the Armenians and Persians. When he now stood before the face of Emperor Trajan, the Emperor said: "Who are you, you evil spirit, that you take such pains to transgress our commands? Indeed, you even persuade others to do so, only so they may perish miserably?"

Ignatius said: "Let no one call a <term>God-bearer <note>translated from the Greek *Theophoros*, a title Ignatius used for himself to signify one who carries God within.</note></term> an evil spirit; for the spirits have departed from the servants of God. If, however, you call me evil toward the unclean spirits because I am troublesome to them, then I confess this with you; for because I have Christ, the heavenly King, I shatter their cunning schemes." Trajan said: "Who then is a God-bearer?" Ignatius answered: "He who has Christ in his heart." Trajan said: "So you think that we do not have the gods in our minds, whom we also employ as defenders against our enemies?" Ignatius said: "You err when you call the unclean spirits of the nations 'gods.' For there is One God, who made the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and everything that is in them; and One Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God; and oh, that I might receive His kingdom!" Trajan said: "Are you speaking of the one crucified under Pontius Pilate?" Ignatius said: "The one who crucified my sin along with its author, and who has banished all devilish error and malice under the feet of those who carry Him in their heart." Trajan said: "So you then carry the Crucified one himself within you?" Ignatius answered: "Yes, for it is written: *I will dwell in them and walk within them.* (2 Cor. 6:16)." Trajan spoke the judgment: "We command that Ignatius, who claims he carries the Crucified one within himself, be led by soldiers bound to the great city of Rome, to become food for wild beasts for the entertainment of the people." When the holy martyr heard this judgment, he cried out with joy: "O Lord, I thank You that You have deemed me worthy to honor You with perfect love, as I, like Your apostle Paul, am bound with chains." When he had said this and accepted the bonds with joy, having first prayed for the congregation and recommended them to the Lord with tears, he was—as a distinguished ram and leader of the excellent flock—torn away by the fierce and insolent soldiers, and led away to Rome to be food for the bloodthirsty beasts.
