<header>Martyrology / Year 107.</header>
<sig>(B)</sig>
<meta>catchword: us</meta>

...sat around, with heated spirits and longing eyes that looked upon the murder with pleasure, since the rumor had already spread everywhere that the Bishop from Syria would fight with the wild beasts. Then he turned to the people with a brave and steadfast spirit, as one who boasted and rejoiced in the shame he suffered for Christ's sake: "Men of Rome," he spoke, "and spectators here present of this struggle, this does not happen to me because of evil deeds for which I might be punished; (for the heathens called the Christians evildoers, and said that they must be condemned as evildoers and authors of all misfortune,) but rather so that I may come to God, for whom I long and whom I desire insatiably. For I am His grain of wheat, and must be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, so that I may become His pure bread." <note>This famous metaphor appears in Ignatius’s *Letter to the Romans*. He views his body as a sacrifice, paralleling the Eucharistic bread.</note> When he had said this, the lions were released, which suddenly tore him apart and devoured him; only the large, hardest bones they left lying. Thus his wish was fulfilled, (Ignatius to the Romans, Chapter 4) that the beasts might become his grave. Thus was he thrown to those cruel beasts by the temple, so that the holy martyr Ignatius's wish was immediately fulfilled, as it is written: *The desire of the righteous is acceptable.* <note>original: *Pfal. 10, v. 17*; likely a reference to the sentiment found in Proverbs 10:24 or Psalm 10:17 regarding God hearing the desire of the humble/righteous.</note> This was so that he would not be a burden to any brother in the collection of his relics (or the remains of his body), just as he had previously wished for his own completion in his writing; for only the hard parts of his holy body remained, which were brought to Antioch and wrapped in a linen cloth as a precious treasure, left to the holy congregation by the grace that was in the martyr.

### Chapter 6.
#### Visionary Appearance of Ignatius after his Martyrdom.

This, however, occurred on the twentieth of December (in the year of salvation 107), when Sura and Senecius were mayors <note>original: *Bürgermeister*; referring to the Roman Consuls, who were the chief magistrates of the year.</note> for the second time. We (*) saw it all ourselves, and stayed awake at home with many tears through the whole night, praying fervently to the Lord on bended knees that He would give us weak ones full certainty (through a vision) of what had happened. Now, when we had fallen asleep for a little while, some suddenly saw him standing by them in a vision and embracing us; others again saw the blessed Ignatius for...

# St. Ignatius’s Letter to the Romans (*).
## Chapter 1.

->Greeting and praise of the congregation in Rome.<-

Ignatius, also named Theophorus <note>The name Theophorus literally means "God-bearer" in Greek.</note>, to the congregation <note>The original German uses *Gemeinde*, meaning the local church body or community.</note> that has obtained mercy in the majesty of the most high Father and JESUS Christ, His only Son; to the beloved and enlightened congregation, according to the will of Him who wills all things that exist according to the love of JESUS Christ our God; which also presides in the capital city of the Roman territory; to the God-worthy, honorable, blessed, and praiseworthy congregation, which is worthy to obtain its desire; to the very chaste and loving [church], named after the name of Christ and the Father; which I kiss in the name of JESUS Christ, the Son of God the Father; which is united both according to the flesh and the spirit according to all His will; filled unbreakably with divine grace and free from all hypocrisy. Much irreproachable joy in JESUS Christ our God beforehand. Since God has granted my prayer that I might see your honorable faces; and having obtained even more than I asked, I hope, bound in Christ JESUS, to kiss you; 1 Cor. 16, v. 20 <note>original: "1 Cor. 16, v. 20"; refers to the "holy kiss" greeting mentioned in the New Testament.</note> if it is otherwise God's will that I be found worthy to reach the end. For the beginning starts well, if I am graced to receive my lot without hindrance; but I fear your love, that it may be harmful to me—

<header>Martyrdom History / Year 107</header>

...might be harmful (*); for it is a small thing for you to do as you wish: but for me, it is difficult to reach God if you should spare me.

## Chapter 2.

->An exhortation that they should not rob him of the martyr’s crown through untimely love.<-

For I do not want you to seek the favor of men, but to please God, just as you already please Him. For I shall never again experience such a time to attain God; nor will you ever subscribe to a better work than if you remain silent. For if you remain silent concerning me, I shall come to God; but if you love me according to the flesh <note>In this context, "loving according to the flesh" means wishing to save his physical life rather than supporting his spiritual desire for martyrdom.</note>, I must begin my race all over again. You can do nothing better for me than to allow me to be sacrificed to God while the altar is still prepared; so that you may harmonize together in love and sing praises to God in Christ Jesus (**), because God has deemed the Overseer <note>original: "Aufseher" — a German translation of the Greek *episkopos*, from which we get the word "Bishop."</note> of Syria worthy to be called from the rising of the sun to its setting. It is good to go down from the world to God, so that I may rise in Him.

## Chapter 3.

->Intercession; the difference between the visible and the invisible.<-

You have never envied anyone; you have instructed others; but I desire that what you have commanded in your teaching may be proven true. Only pray that I may obtain strength both inwardly and outwardly; so that I may not only say it, but also do it; so that I may not merely be called a Christian, but also be found to be one. For if I am found to be one, I can also truly be called one. And then I am able to be faithful, when I am no longer seen by the world. Nothing visible is eternal! For what can be seen is temporal; but what is invisible is eternal. 2 Cor. 4, v. 18. For even our God, Jesus Christ, appears more glorious in the Father. Christianity is not merely a work of silence, but also of glorification <note>original: "Herrlichung." Ignatius suggests that faith is not just a private, quiet matter, but a public testimony that brings glory to God.</note>.

<header>4 St. Ignatius</header>

### Chapter 4.
->Ignatius’s desire to reach Christ through martyrdom.<-

I am writing to the churches and declaring to everyone that I die willingly for God’s sake, if only you do not hinder it. I warn you: do not show me an untimely favor. Allow me to be the food of wild beasts, through which I can reach God. I am the grain of God, and I am ground by the teeth of beasts so that I may be found to be pure bread of Christ. <note>Ignatius uses the imagery of wheat being milled into bread to describe his body being prepared as a holy offering to God.</note> Rather, provoke the wild beasts so that they may become my grave and leave nothing of my body behind, so that I do not become a burden to anyone when I have fallen asleep. (*) Only then will I be a true disciple of Christ, when the world no longer sees my body. Pray to Christ for me, that I may become a sacrifice through these instruments. I do not command you as the Apostles Peter and Paul did; they are Apostles, I am a condemned man; they are free, but I am still a servant. But if I suffer, I shall become a freedman of Christ and shall rise free in Him. Now, in my bonds, I am learning to desire nothing worldly or vain.

### Chapter 5.
->Concerning the martyrdom he endures on the way, and his further longing for it.<-

From Syria all the way to Rome, I fight with wild beasts by land and sea, by night and day. I am bound to ten leopards—that is, to a company of soldiers (**); who only become worse even after receiving kindness. But through their cruelty, I learn all the more; yet I am not justified by this. (1 Corinthians 4:4). Oh, that I might reach the beasts that wait for me! I wish that they would set upon me freshly! Indeed, I will provoke them so that they devour me quickly—not as they have shied away from some and not touched them. But if they are unwilling, I will force myself upon them. Forgive me,

(*) These true Christians held relics in such low regard that they would rather see their "maggot-sack" <note>A humble, earthy term used by the author to describe the mortal human body.</note> entirely in the bellies of wild beasts than be a burden or a cause of stumbling to others. For they foresaw—and partially experienced—that the graves of saints would be decorated. First, it was Christian love, then holy simplicity, and finally, it became outright idolatry.

(**) The holy martyr had to lie, stand, and walk with a chain on his right hand, fastened to the left hand of whichever soldier was on watch, one after another—as was the Roman custom. (See Justus Lipsius <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish philologist and humanist.</note> in his notes on Tacitus). Peter was likewise bound to two soldiers with two chains. Acts 12:6.

<summary>Ignatius describes his journey to Rome under guard, comparing his captors to leopards and expressing his intense desire to be martyred by wild animals. The text also includes a polemic against the later veneration of relics, arguing that Ignatius preferred his body to be entirely consumed.</summary>

<header>History of the Martyrs / Year 107</header>

I know best what is useful for me. Now I begin to be a disciple <note>original: "Lehr-Jünger," literally a "teaching-disciple."</note>, Luke 14:27. Nothing, whether visible or invisible, shall prevent me from attaining Christ. Fire and the cross, whole packs of wild animals, the tearing apart of limbs, torture, breaking on the wheel, the mutilation of members, the crushing of the entire body, and the devil’s cruel torments may all come upon me, if only I may become a partaker of Jesus Christ.

### Chapter 6.

**Contempt for the world, and the insight and love of Christ drives him to martyrdom.**

The pleasures of the world can help me nothing, nor can the kingdoms of this age. It is better for me to die in Christ Jesus than to rule over the whole circle of the earth. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers damage to his soul? Matthew 16:26. I seek Him who died for us. I desire Him who rose for our sake; this birth is now before me. Forgive me, dear brothers; do not hinder me from living; do not desire that I should die. I, who wish to belong to God, have no joy in the world. Allow me to enjoy the clear light. When I have arrived there, I shall be a divine man. Permit me to be a follower of the suffering of my God. If anyone has Him within himself, let him consider what I desire, and have compassion for me, because he knows what oppresses me. <note>From the Martyrdom of Ignatius, Chapter 2.</note>

### Chapter 7.

**How the Word calls within him and bids him come to the Father.**

The Prince of this world <note>A traditional title for Satan.</note> wishes to rob me and disturb my mind, which is directed toward God; therefore, let none of you who are present help him. Rather, take my side, which is the side of God. Do not speak of Jesus Christ while you long for the world. Let no envy dwell within you. Do not believe me even if I, being present with you, should beg for my release; rather, believe what I am writing to you now. I write to you while still alive, yet I fervently desire to die. My earthly passion is crucified, and within me there is no longer any fire of natural love (*). Instead, there is a living and speaking water (John 4:14) within me, which says to me from inside: "Come to the Father!" I have no more desire for perishable food, nor for the pleasures of this life.

(*) *Philoylon* <note>original Greek: "φιλόϋλον"</note>, natural love, or the love of material things; thus Ignatius speaks of fleshly love (*Eros*) being crucified within him. This saying has been misunderstood by some to refer to Christ being crucified. Galatians 5:24, 6:14.

### Chapter 8.
->A request that they should not hinder him.<-

I no longer wish to live according to the way of men, which will happen if you only will it. Allow this to please you, so that you may also be pleasing. I ask this of you through a short letter; believe me; Jesus Christ will reveal to you that I speak the truth. He is an unerring mouth, through which the Father has spoken truly. Pray for me, that I may attain it. I have written to you not according to the flesh, but according to the will of God. If I suffer, you have shown me favor; but if I am rejected, then you hate me. <note>Ignatius fears that the influential Christians in Rome might use their legal or social standing to stop his execution, which he views as a rejection of his spiritual destiny.</note>

### Chapter 9.
->Intercession for the congregation at Antioch, and greetings.<-

Remember in your prayers the congregation in Syria, which has God as its shepherd in my place. May Jesus Christ alone be its overseer <note>original: "Aufseher," likely a translation of the Greek *episkopos* or bishop.</note>, and your love. But I am ashamed to say that I am one of them. For I am not worthy, being the least among them and an untimely birth <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul’s description of himself in 1 Corinthians 15:8.</note>. But mercy has been shown to me, so that I shall be one of them when I have come to God. My spirit greets you, as does the love of the congregations that have received me in the name of Jesus Christ, not merely as a traveler passing through. For even those who did not know me in the flesh accompanied me through the cities along my journey.

### Chapter 10.
->Conclusion and greeting to his disciples who traveled ahead.<-

I write these things to you from Smyrna, by way of the praiseworthy Ephesians. For among many others, Crocus is with me—a name so dear to me. Regarding those who have gone before me from Syria to Rome for the glory of God, I believe you will have knowledge of them. Tell them that I am coming soon. For they are all worthy of God and of you, and it is fitting for you to refresh them in all things. I have written this to you in the night before the twenty-fourth of August <insert>[in the year 107 after the incarnation of Christ.]</insert> Fare you well until the end, in the patience of Jesus Christ. Amen.

<header>History of the Martyrs / Anno 107.</header>

After the martyrdom of Saint Ignatius, the entire Christian Church enjoyed a brief period of peace. God used two imperial governors as His instruments for this: namely, Tiberianus, the governor in Palestine, and Pliny the Younger, who was the governor in Bithynia and Pontus. Like other governors, both of these men had imperial orders to either persuade the Christians to commit apostasy <note>The act of renouncing one's religious faith, often under pressure from Roman authorities.</note> or to put them to death. However, they found that there were so many Christians that their destruction would result in great harm to the Roman Empire and the loss of many thousands of subjects. Consequently, they wrote to the Emperor to seek further counsel from the court on such a weighty matter. These letters provide a clear light regarding the state of the Church and the martyrs, which is why we include them here:

### The Letter of Tiberianus (*), Governor in Palestine, to the Emperor Trajan.

->To the invincible monarch and deified Emperor Trajan, greetings.<-

I am weary of punishing and killing the Galileans <note>original: "Galiläer." A common Roman name for Christians, often used dismissively to emphasize their provincial origins.</note> (who are known among us by the name of Christians), according to Your Imperial Majesty’s orders. For they do not cease to offer themselves up to death. And although I have used every effort, through both warnings and threats, to ensure they would not dare to profess this teaching, they have nonetheless endured every torture and yet do not desist. Your Majesty may deign to inform me what will further benefit your Empire.

### The Report of Pliny (**), the Younger, from Asia Minor to the Emperor Trajan, concerning the Christians.

It is my custom, my Lord, to refer all matters about which I am in doubt to you. For who can better correct my errors or instruct my ignorance? I have never before been present at the trials <note>original: "Untersuchung," referring here to the formal legal proceedings and interrogations of Christians.</note> of Christians; therefore, I do not know how or in what manner they ought to be punished and examined. And I have been in no small doubt whether one should not...

<note>(*) see Cotelier, *Monuments of the Apostolic Fathers*, Volume 2, page 179.</note>
<note>(**) Book 10, Letter 97.</note>

### 4. Saint Ignatius

whether a distinction of age should be made, or whether the tender children should not be distinguished from the adults? Whether a period for repentance should be granted? Or whether one who was truly a Christian should be shown no mercy for their apostasy <note>The act of renouncing one's faith.</note>? Should the mere **name** <note>The legal question of whether being called a "Christian" was a crime in itself (*nomen Christianum*), or if specific crimes had to be proven.</note> be punished, even if it were not criminal, or the vices that may be linked with it? 

In the meantime, I have followed this method with those who have been brought before me as Christians: I asked them if they were Christians? When they said Yes, I questioned them a second and third time, threatening them with death; those who persisted, I ordered to be executed. For I believed without a doubt that, whatever it might be they confessed, their **stubbornness** and **invincible obstinacy** <note>original: "Steifsinnigkeit und unbezwingliche Hartnäckigkeit." In Roman law, this defiance of a magistrate (contumacia) was often the technical reason for execution rather than the religious belief itself.</note> must be punished. There were others possessed by similar folly who were Roman citizens; I have had them recorded so that they might be sent to the City (Rome) (*). 

Next, in the same region (as usually happens) where this vice has spread, I encountered many different types of it. A document was presented (without the author's name) containing many names, who however denied that they were Christians or had ever been so; who, following my example, invoked the gods and offered incense and wine to your image (which I had brought for that purpose along with the images of the gods), and moreover cursed Christ; none of which things, as I have been told, those who are truly Christians can be forced to do. Therefore, I released them. 

Others named on the said register confessed they were Christians but soon denied it; they said they had been, but had ceased to be; some three years ago, others more years ago, and one even 20 years ago. All of these honored both your image and the likenesses of the gods, and they also cursed Christ. They affirmed, however, that this was the extent of their crime or error: that they were accustomed to gather on a certain day before sunrise and sing a hymn together to Christ as to a God; then to bind themselves **sacramentally** <term>Sacramentally: Referring to the Latin *sacramentum*, which was originally a Roman military oath of loyalty. Here, Pliny describes it as a moral pledge rather than a conspiracy.</term>, not for any wickedness, but that they would not steal, nor murder, nor commit adultery, nor act deceitfully, nor deny goods entrusted to them. From this, it is easy to see what a great number of people could still be saved if they were given time for reconsideration. Thus far Pliny, the pagan judge.

### Emperor Trajan's Response (*) to This.

For in a general matter, no certain rule can be given that one must be bound to; if they are accused and convicted, they must be punished; yet with the distinction that whoever denies being a Christian and proves it by action—that is, by kneeling before our gods—even if they were otherwise suspected, shall nonetheless obtain mercy because of their repentance. Without knowing who the author of the mentioned document is, however, no accusation shall be accepted; for it is a shameful example and unsuitable for our times.

5. St. Symphorosa and her 7 Sons

...come to a constant counsel, so that finally the Emperor allowed his decree for persecution to be publicly revoked, of which the church histories report more (*).

---

# 5. St. Symphorosa / with her seven sons.

## Chapter 1.

->Emperor Hadrian, on the advice of the idol-priests, has the holy Symphorosa summoned before him; her husband and his brother had also been martyrs.<-

When Emperor Hadrian, in the year 138, had built a palace or pleasure-house in the Tiburtine garden <note>This refers to the famous Villa Adriana (Hadrian’s Villa) at Tivoli, near Rome.</note>, and wished to consecrate it according to his superstition, he sacrificed to his idols and the evil spirits who lived within the idols, so that they might make their will known to him by means of an answer. They then gave him an answer through the service of the deceitful idol-priests, who said: "The Christian widow **Symphorosa**, with her seven sons, torments us with her daily prayer to her **God**; if these will now sacrifice, the gods promise to do everything for which you will ask!" Then Emperor Hadrian commanded that she and her sons should be brought there; and when they had come, he exhorted them with friendly words that they should throw incense onto the brazier <note>German: *Feuer-Faß*. A ritual vessel used for burning incense in Roman religious ceremonies.</note> in honor of the idols, and thus sacrifice to them! But the blessed matron **Symphorosa** answered the Emperor: "When my husband **Getulius** and his brother **Amatius** were your officers <term>Amte-Leute</term> <note>These were high-ranking administrative or military officials in the Roman service.</note>, they endured many kinds of martyrdom for the sake of the name of Christ, and would not consent to sacrifice to your idols, but as good soldiers overcame your evil spirits in death; for they would rather be beheaded than allow themselves to be conquered, and for the sake of the name of Christ would rather suffer a death that, among earthly-minded men, brought them a temporary shame, but honor and eternal glory among the angels and the chosen; among whom they now walk, and shine with signs of victory for their suffering, as they share in the kingdom with the eternal King of eternal life in heaven."

History of the Martyrs / Year 138.

## Chapter 2.
### The Faithful Confession of the Holy Symphorosa.

Emperor **Hadrian** then said to Saint **Symphorosa**: "Either you and your sons must sacrifice to the almighty gods, or I will make you and your sons into a burnt offering!" The blessed **Symphorosa** answered: "How have I received such great blessing, that I should be deemed worthy to be a sacrifice to **God** along with my sons?" **Hadrian**, the Emperor, spoke: "I intend to sacrifice you to my gods!" The blessed **Symphorosa** gave this answer: "Your gods cannot receive me as an offering; however, if I am burned for the sake of the name of **Christ**, my **God**, such a scent will instead drive away your gods, and I shall burn them." The Emperor spoke: "Choose one of the two: either sacrifice to my gods, or die a wretched death." The blessed **Symphorosa** answered him: "You perhaps think that my mind will change through some terror; yet I longingly desire to be in the place of rest where my husband **Getulius** is now, whom you killed for the sake of **Christ's** name!" Thereupon, Emperor **Hadrian** commanded that she be led to the idol-temple of **Hercules**, and there first be given shameful blows to the cheeks <note>German: *Backen-Streiche*. In the Roman context, this was a form of legal and social humiliation as much as physical punishment.</note>, and further be hung up by her hair. But when she could in no way be turned from her good purpose, nor by any fear of death, he finally commanded that she be taken down, an enormous stone tied to her neck, and cast into the river. After this was done, her brother **Eugenius**, who was the High Official <term>Ober-Amtmann</term> <note>A senior administrative or judicial officer.</note> at the Tiburtine court, had her body pulled out and buried before the city of **Tibur** <note>The ancient name for modern-day Tivoli, Italy.</note>.

## Chapter 3.
### The Emperor Commands that Her Seven Sons Also Be Executed.

On the following day, Emperor **Hadrian** commanded that all seven of her sons be brought before him at once. When he exhorted them to offer incense to the idols and saw that they were by no means terrified by his threatening words, he ordered that seven stakes be erected near the temple of **Hercules**, and that they be stretched out and tortured upon them by means of a pulley. Then, the throat of **Crescentius**, the first, was slit; the chest of **Julianus**, the second, was pierced; **Nemesius**, the third, received a stab through the heart; **Primitivus**, the fourth, was mortally wounded through the navel;

## Chapter 4.

->The bodies of the martyrs are buried. Divine judgment upon Emperor Hadrian.<-

When Emperor **Hadrian** came to the Temple of **Hercules** the following day, he commanded that all their bodies be taken away and thrown into a deep pit. The idolatrous priests gave that place the name: "To the Seven Who Died by Violence" <note>original Latin: *Ad septem Biothanatos*. The term was often used disparagingly for those who were executed or committed suicide.</note> (**). After this, the persecution ceased for a year and six months; within this period, the bodies of all the other martyrs—whose names are recorded in the Book of Life—were honorably buried. The "Birthday" (***) of the holy martyrs of **Christ**, namely the blessed **Symphorosa** and her seven sons, is celebrated on the 18th of July. Their bodies rest on the Tiburtine Way, about eight thousand paces (or 2 miles) from the city of **Rome**; as our Lord **Jesus Christ** reigns, to whom belongs the honor and glory from eternity to eternity. Amen. (See Ruinart's *Acts of the Martyrs*, page 23).

We have written to you, dear brothers, regarding the martyrs and the blessed **Polycarp**, who, through his martyrdom, brought the persecution to a close, as if sealing it with a signet. For nearly all that preceded it happened so that the **Lord** might show us the ancient, Gospel-standard of martyrdom <note>The text uses "Evangelischen Marter-Stand" to refer to a way of dying for the faith that mirrors the calm, non-provocative example set by Jesus in the Gospels.</note>; For he waited (*), until he was betrayed, just as the **Lord** did; so that we too might become his followers, looking not only to our own concerns, but also to the concerns of our neighbor. For true and righteous love desires not only to ensure one's own salvation, but also the salvation of all the brothers.

### Chapter 2.

->Concerning the martyrs who were executed shortly before Polycarp.<-

While every martyrdom that occurs according to **God’s** will is blessed and noble; we must also be cautious and entrust the power over all things to **God**. Yet, who could not highly admire the nobility, patience, and love for the **Lord** shown by these martyrs? They were so torn apart by scourges <term>Geißeln: whips often tipped with metal or bone used by Roman executioners</term> that the internal veins and tendons of their physical frames were visible; nevertheless, they endured it, so much so that even the bystanders felt pity and wept. But they themselves showed such nobility that not one of them complained or sighed; thus they proved to us all that at the time of their torture, the martyrs of **Christ** were traveling outside of the flesh <note>This suggests a mystical state where the soul is so focused on God that it becomes detached from physical pain.</note>, or rather, that the **Lord** stood by them and spoke with them. And because they focused on the grace of **Christ**, they despised worldly torment. Thus, with one hour of suffering, they ransomed themselves from eternal torment, and the fire of the cruel executioners felt cool to them; for they kept before their eyes the goal of avoiding the eternal and unquenchable fire, and with the eyes of the spirit, they looked upon those good things reserved for those who endure; which...

(*) Among many martyrs, an abuse had crept in where they gave themselves up before they were caught; partly out of a simple-minded belief that to die for **Christ's** sake was "the sooner, the better"; partly out of impure motives, resentment, or even ambition—of which there are sorrowful examples in the histories of the martyrs. The text here refers to this, noting that **Polycarp** did not run to his death himself, but rather followed **Christ's** example by holding back as long as it was beneficial for the flock; see Chapter 4.

### Chapter 3.

For the devil tried many things against them, but thanks be to GOD that he prevailed against none of them. Therefore, dear brothers, we do not praise those who give themselves up; since the Gospel does not teach such things.

### Chapter 6.
->Polycarp is betrayed.<-

And when they did not find him, they seized two young men, one of whom, forced by torture, betrayed his location. Thus it was impossible for him to remain hidden any longer, because his betrayers were of his own household. The city magistrate, who is also called *Cleronomus* <term>Cleronomus: a title for a magistrate or "administrator of the heritage"</term>, named **Herod**, hastened to lead him to the arena. ### Chapter 7.
->He is found / treats his pursuers well / and prays.<-

Having the young man with them, they set out at the time of the evening meal on foot and on horseback, with their usual weapons, as if pursuing a murderer. And when they came upon him in the evening, they found him sitting in an upper bed-chamber on a resting bench; from there he certainly could have escaped to another place, but he would not, saying: "The Lord’s will be done!" When he heard them arriving, he went down and spoke with them; and they marveled at his age and his steadfastness. Some said: "Was so much effort required to capture such an old man?" He immediately commanded, however, that they be given as much food and drink as they desired at that very hour; he then requested of them that they might allow him one hour to pray freely. When they permitted this, he began to pray while standing, filled with Divine grace; he continued for two hours, so that those listening were astonished, and many of them regretted that they had allowed themselves to be used against such a godly old man.

## Chapter 8.

->*Polycarp is brought into the city; along the way, Herod seeks to persuade him.*<-

**A**fter he had finished his prayer—in which he remembered all who had ever crossed his path, both the small and the great, the known and the unknown, and the universal Church everywhere—the hour of departure arrived. They set him upon a donkey and brought him into the city [the next morning], exactly on the Great Sabbath <note>The "Great Sabbath" usually refers to the Saturday before Easter in the Christian calendar, or a high Sabbath in the Jewish calendar.</note>. But the city judge **Herod** and his father **Nicetes** came to meet him; having taken him into their carriage, they pressed him with many words, saying: "What harm is there, after all, in saying: My **Lord** <note>original: *Kyrios*</note> (*), the **Emperor**? and in offering incense and saving one's life through such obedience?" At first, however, he gave them no answer. But when they persisted urgently, he said: "I shall by no means do what you advise me!" They, then, finding themselves disappointed in their hope of persuading him, addressed him with harsh words and thrust him violently down from the carriage, so that he injured his shins. Regardless of this, as if no harm had come to him, he walked briskly on as they led him to the stadium <term>Schau-Platz: an arena or amphitheater used for public spectacles and trials</term>. There was, however, such a tumult in the stadium that one’s own words could not be heard.

## Chapter 9.

->*He is led into the stadium before the court.*<-

**A**s Polycarp was now entering the stadium, a voice came from heaven:
> Be brave / and quit thyself like a man / Polycarp!

No one, indeed, saw the one who spoke; but the voice was heard by our people—

---

(*) Because the heathens understood the word **Lord** <note>original: *HErr* / *Kyrios*</note> when applied to the **Emperor** in a divine sense, the Christians—who nevertheless prayed for the **Emperor**—did not call him **Lord** or *Kyrios*, by which they understood **Christ** alone. Especially on the occasion of a public confession of faith, they did not do so, although otherwise in common life it was quite common among them. *Ephesians 6:5, Colossians 4:1.* So it was also with the offering of incense; the heathens cunningly demanded of the **martyrs** that they should only publicly throw incense powder onto the fire, and could do so in honor of whomever they wished. But because the Christians understood that **Satan** intended to lead them into hypocrisy by this, and that they had to confess **Christ** not only in thought but also in deed, so as not to cause the weak to stumble; they would not offer incense in any way, as the heathens did to honor their gods. At home, however, for common use, it was not forbidden.

As he was led forward, the Proconsul <term>Präsident: the Roman governor or official presiding over the trial</term> asked him: "Are you Polycarp?" ### Chapter 10.
#### Polycarp Confesses Christ.

When the official urged him once more, saying: "Swear by the fortune of the Emperor!", he answered: "Since you vainly persist that I should swear by the fortune of the Emperor, as you say, and you pretend as if you do not know who I am, listen plainly: I am a Christian (**)! If you wish to know the foundation of Christian teaching, then appoint a day and hear it." 

The Proconsul said: "Persuade the people." 

Polycarp answered: "I consider you worthy of a defense; for we are taught (Romans 13:1; Titus 3:1) that we should give to the princes and authorities ordained by God their due honor, so long as it does not harm us. But as for those people, I do not judge them worthy that I should defend myself before them."

---

(*) "Away with the atheists!" This was the slogan of the heathens (see Chapter 3), with which they separated the Christians from themselves as "atheists," or people who did not believe in the gods. These were regarded by the heathen mob as godless people who had neither God nor conscience; other slanders contributed to this view. Thus, the Proconsul intended for Polycarp to join the party of the heathens by using these slogan-words.

(**) "I am a Christian!" This was the slogan of the Christians; the name of Christ was enough for a confession of faith in those times; see the example of the Martyr Sanctus.

## Chapter 11.
->The Governor's Threat and Polycarp's Steadfastness.<-

The governor <term>Präsident: here referring to the Roman Proconsul presiding over the trial</term> then said to him: "I have wild beasts; I will throw you to them if you do not change your mind." To this he replied: "Call them, for we do not change our minds in such a way that we would turn from what is good to what is evil; rather, it is right that I turn from evil to good." Again the governor spoke to him: "I will have you burned with fire, since you despise the wild beasts, unless you change your mind." Polycarp answered: "You threaten me with fire that burns for only one hour and is extinguished after a short while; but you are ignorant of the fire of the coming judgment and eternal damnation, which is prepared for the ungodly. But why do you delay? Bring forth what you please."

## Chapter 12.
->Polycarp is Sentenced to the Fire.<-

He said these things, and much more, full of confidence and joy, and his face was completely radiant; so much so that he was not even terrified by what was being said to him; instead, it was the governor who was astonished. He sent his herald to step into the middle of the stadium <term>Schau-Platz: an arena or amphitheater used for public spectacles</term> and proclaim three times: "Polycarp has confessed himself to be a Christian!" When the herald announced this, the whole multitude of heathens and Jews living in Smyrna cried out with uncontrollable zeal and a great voice: "This is the teacher of Asia, a father of the Christians, a destroyer of our gods, who has taught many neither to offer incense nor to worship the gods!" ## The 13th Chapter.
->The pyre is prepared and the holy martyr is placed within it.<-

Scarcely had they spoken these words before they began to carry them out: everyone quickly gathered wood and brushwood from the workshops and bathhouses; the Jews, especially, helped with this joyfully, as was their custom <note>This reflects the historical tension and polemic between early Christian and Jewish communities in Smyrna during the 2nd century</note>. When the pyre <term>Scheiter-Haufen: a large pile of wood for burning a body as a sacrifice or execution</term> was prepared, he began to lay aside his clothes, loosen his belt, and take off his shoes; which he was not usually accustomed to doing, because the believers always vied with one another to see who might be the first to serve him. For because of his good conduct, he was shown all honor even before his martyrdom. Immediately, they applied the instruments of burning to him. But when they also wished to nail him down, he said: "Leave me as I am; for He who gives me strength to endure the fire will also give me the ability to stand still in the fire without your nails."

## The 14th Chapter.
->Polycarp’s Prayer.<-

They did not nail him, then, but rather bound him. But he, having his hands behind his back and being bound from behind, was like a distinguished ram taken from a great flock as a gift, prepared as an acceptable sacrifice to God. Then he lifted his eyes toward heaven and said:

> Lord, Almighty God, who art the Father of Thy beloved and highly praised Son Jesus Christ, through whom we have received the knowledge of Thee! O God of the angels and powers, and of all creation, as well as the entire race of the righteous who live before Thy face! I thank Thee that Thou hast deemed me worthy of this day and this hour, that I should have a share in the number of the martyrs, and in the cup of Thy Anointed <term>Gesalbten: a translation of 'Christ' or 'Messiah'</term>, unto the resurrection of eternal life, according to soul and body, in the incorruptibility of the Holy Spirit; let me come before Thy face today among them as a fat and pleasing sacrifice, just as Thou hast previously prepared, previously shown, and now fulfilled, Thou unfailing and true God. Therefore, for all things I praise, honor, and glorify Thee, together with the eternal and heavenly Jesus Christ, Thy beloved Son, with whom to Thee and the Holy Spirit be honor, now and into the eternity to come, Amen.

<header>6. Saint Polycarp</header>

...finished his prayer, the executioners lit the fire. But when the flame rose up, we saw a great miracle, those of us who were permitted to see it. We have been preserved so that we might announce to others what took place; for the flame appeared like an arched oven, much like a ship's sail distended by the wind, and it surrounded the body of the martyr like a wall. His body, however, did not look like roasted flesh in the center, but rather like white-baked bread, or like gold and silver glowing in a crucible <note>This description emphasizes the purity of the martyr, comparing his death to a refining process rather than a common execution.</note>. We also perceived such a fragrant scent, as if incense or some other precious spice had been set internal fire.

### The 16th Chapter.
->The holy martyr is stabbed to death in the fire.<-

Finally, when the ungodly saw that his body could not be consumed by the fire, they commanded the executioner to go to him and stab him with a spear. When this was done, such a great quantity of blood flowed out that it extinguished the fire. At this, all the people wondered that there was such a great difference between the unbelievers and the chosen. One of these chosen was the admirable martyr Polycarp, who in our times was an Apostolic and Prophetic teacher, and the overseer <term>Aufseher: a translation of the Greek 'episkopos' or Bishop, the lead official of the local church</term> of the orthodox church in Smyrna. For every word that came from his mouth has either already been fulfilled or will yet be fulfilled.

### The 17th Chapter.
->The zeal of the believers to bury his remains, and how highly they valued them.<-

But when the jealous, envious, and evil adversary of the generation of the righteous saw his glorious martyrdom—and knowing also his blameless life from his youth up, and knowing that he had carried away the crown of immortality as a certain reward—he used all diligence so that his remaining bones might not be gathered by us; even though many desired to do so and wished to have a part in his holy body <note>This marks an early historical record of the veneration of relics, where the physical remains of saints were treated with deep reverence.</note>. He therefore advised Nicetes, the father of Herod and brother of Alce, to petition the Governor so that he would not release the body for burial. This was done lest they, as he said, "abandon the Crucified One and begin to worship this man." And this was said at the suggestion and urging of the Jews, who also kept watch as we intended to pull his body out of the fire. ### The 19th Chapter.

This is the story of the holy **Polycarp**, who, along with twelve others from **Philadelphia**, was martyred in **Smyrna**. ## The 21st Chapter.

->Determination of the Martyrdom Date / Wishes for the Philadelphians / and Praise to God.<-

**P**olycarp suffered martyrdom on March 26, in the year 147 <note>original: "Ao. 147"</note>, on the Great Sabbath day <note>The "Great Sabbath" usually refers to the Saturday before Easter or a high Jewish festival occurring on a Sabbath; it remains a point of chronological debate among historians.</note>, at two o'clock in the afternoon. And Jesus Christ reigned for all eternity; to Whom be glory, honor, majesty, and the eternal throne, from generation to generation, Amen. We wish you, dear brothers, to be healthy and to walk according to the Gospel word of Christ; with Whom be glory to God the Father and the Holy Spirit, for the salvation of the chosen saints; just as the blessed Polycarp has testified; in whose footsteps we wish to be found in the kingdom of Jesus Christ.

## The 22nd Chapter.

->Naming of the Copyists.<-

**G**aius transcribed this from the book of Irenaeus <note>Saint Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD), a prominent early church father and theologian.</note>, the disciple of Polycarp, who also lived in close confidence with Irenaeus. I, Socrates, transcribed it in Corinth from the manuscript of Gaius. Grace be with everyone. After this, I, Pionius (*), transcribed it from the aforementioned manuscripts; after I sought them out with diligence, following the direction of the blessed Polycarp through a vision, as I shall indicate in what follows. There I gathered the papers, which were almost ruined by the length of time; so that the Lord Jesus Christ may also gather me with His chosen ones; to Whom be the glory, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for all eternity. Amen.

<header>Martyrdom History / In the year 147 <note>original: "Ao. 147"</note>.</header>

# 7. Saint Felicitas / with her seven sons; namely:
## Januarius / Felix / Philip / Silvanus / Alexander / Vitalis / Martial.

->The 1st Chapter.<-

<margin>
Saint Felicitas, a chaste widow, is brought before the court on the report of the priests, where she gives an account of her faith.
</margin>

In the times of Emperor Antoninus Pius (around the year 150), the idol-priests in Rome incited a persecution; there too Felicitas, a noble matron, was seized along with her seven Christian sons. She was, however, a widow, and had resolved to serve GOD in chastity; she thus applied herself to prayer day and night, and was an exceptional example to all chaste hearts. Now, when the priests saw that the Christian name was being spread through her holy conduct, they slandered her to Emperor Antoninus and said: "This woman and widow, with her seven sons, despises our gods to the ruin of Your Imperial Majesty; if she will not honor the gods, then we must make Your Piety <note>A formal honorific for the Emperor: "Eurer Gottseligkeit"</note> understand that our gods will be so angered that they cannot be reconciled again by any sacrifices." Then Emperor Antoninus commanded the City Judge Publius <note>Historically identified as the Prefect of Rome.</note> that he should force her and her sons to appease the wrath of their gods with sacrifices. Therefore Publius, the City Judge, commanded that she should be brought before him alone; and after he had unsuccessfully tried to persuade her to sacrifice with flattering words, he then threatened to kill her with various tortures. Felicitas, however, gave him this answer: "Your flatteries shall not persuade me, nor shall your threats change me; for I have the Holy Spirit, who will not permit that I be overcome by the devil; therefore I am confident that I shall overcome you while living, and when I have been killed, I will defeat you all the better as one who has died." Publius said: "If you, miserable woman, have such a desire to die, then..."

<header>7. Saint Felicitas with her seven sons</header>

...keep your sons alive. Felicitas gave the answer: "My sons will remain alive, so long as they do not sacrifice to the idols; but if they commit this base act, they will go into eternal perdition."

## The 2nd Chapter.
->She must answer before the court for a second time, / together with her sons.<-

On the following day, Publius held public court on the Field of Mars <note>original: "Martis-Platze", the Campus Martius in Rome</note>, and commanded that Felicitas be brought forward with her sons; there he spoke to her: "Have mercy upon your sons, who are such good-natured youths and still in the best bloom of their youth." Felicitas answered: "Your mercy, as you intend it, is godlessness, and your admonition is cruelty." With this, she turned to her sons and spoke: "Look, dear children, toward heaven, and gaze on high; there the Lord Christ awaits you with his saints; fight for your souls, and show yourselves faithful in the love of Christ." When Publius heard this, he commanded that she should be struck across the face <note>original: "Ohrfeigen geben", literally to give ear-slaps</note>, and spoke: "Do you dare, in my presence, to give such warnings, that they should despise the command of our most gracious Emperor?"

## The 3rd Chapter.
->The confession of faith of the seven sons before the court.<-

Then he called her first son, named Januarius, and promised him an indescribable wealth of worldly goods; at the same time, he also threatened him with beatings if he should refuse to sacrifice to the idols. But Januarius answered: "You give foolish counsel; for know that the wisdom of my Lord strengthens me, which will help me to overcome everything with which you threaten me." Immediately, the judge commanded that he should be whipped with rods <term>Spieß-Ruten: a form of corporal punishment where a victim is beaten with flexible rods or switches</term> and placed back into prison.

Afterward, he commanded that her second son, named Felix, be brought forward. When the judge Publius exhorted him to sacrifice to the idols, he spoke steadfastly: "We worship only one single God, to whom we bring the sacrifice of holy devotion. Do not think that I, or any one of my brothers, will depart from the love of the Lord Jesus Christ; you may threaten us with blows and carry out your bloody decrees, yet our faith can neither be overcome nor changed."

### Chapter 4
->They are executed by various judges, along with their mother.<-

Emperor **Antoninus** sent them to various judges so they might be executed in different ways. One judge had the eldest brother killed with scourges <note>whips used for corporal punishment</note> that had lead balls attached. The second judge had the second and third brothers beaten to death with clubs. Yet another judge had the fourth thrown down from a great height. Still another killed the fifth, sixth, and seventh with the sword. Likewise, soon after them, the mother was also beheaded. Thus they were executed with various death penalties and are now all victors and martyrs of Christ, triumphing together with their mother, and have ascended to heaven to receive their reward. For because they, out of love for **God**, disregarded the threats of men and the punishments and beatings, they have now become friends of Christ in the Kingdom of Heaven; who lives and reigns with the Father and Holy Spirit for ages of ages <note>original Latin: "in die Ewigkeiten der Ewigkeiten," a liturgical phrasing meaning forever and ever</note>. ...compels me (writes *Justin* the Martyr, in his Defense <note>original: "Schutz-Schrift," referring to Justin's *Second Apology*</note> addressed to the Roman Senate) that I must write this to you for the benefit of our own people, we who are subject to the same human nature and properties as you, and who are nonetheless your brothers (although you do not know it, nor wish to be so because of your prestigious status). Such things are driven by our worst enemies, the malicious and unclean spirits, who have such judges under their authority who serve them under the cover of religion. Even our rulers (the Emperors *Marcus Aurelius* and *Lucius Verus*) have, upon the prompting of such evil spirits, decreed that we should be killed. However, so that the entire unclean business may be more clearly seen, I must mention a judicial record that recently occurred under the Chief Judge of this city, *Rome*, *Urbicus*.

## Chapter 2.

->Regarding a godless woman who became a Christian, and separated<-
->herself from her adulterous husband.<-

A certain woman had a lustful husband, and she herself had previously behaved unchastely. However, after she accepted the healing teaching of Christ, she immediately became modest and also endeavored to persuade her husband to a chaste way of life, seeking to teach him Christian principles and reminding him how the punishment of eternal fire is prepared for those who live in a loathsome and irrational manner. But he remained in his lustful ways and behaved in such a manner that the woman’s heart became completely estranged from him. For the virtuous woman considered it a sin to continue living united in the chaste marriage bed with a man who, against the laws and rights of nature, visited his brothels <note>original: "Huren-Winkel," literally "whore-corners" or dens of vice</note> everywhere; she therefore decided she would leave him. # 9. St. Justin the Philosopher / Chariton / &c.

...who maintained faith and conscience, they caused it to be proclaimed that all those who were Christians should be forced to sacrifice to the idols; then **Justin**, and those who were just then with him, were taken prisoner and led to the Roman city judge, **Rusticus** by name. When they stood before the judgment seat, President Rusticus spoke to **Justin**: "Well then, be obedient to the gods themselves, and to the Emperor’s commands!" But **Justin** answered him and said: "Never has anyone been justly blamed or condemned who has been obedient to the commands of our Savior **Jesus Christ**!" Then the judge Rusticus spoke: "What learned sciences have you studied, and to which philosophical party are you devoted?" **Justin** gave as an answer: "I have endeavored to know the opinions of all the learned, and to become acquainted with all parties (*), until I finally surrendered myself to the **Christian doctrine**, although it does not please those who go blindly in false opinions." Then Rusticus spoke: "Do you, most wretched man, find pleasure in such teaching?" "Certainly," spoke **Justin**, "I follow the Christians in the right doctrine." The President then asked: "What kind of doctrine is it then?" **Justin** answered: "The right doctrine, which we Christians preserve in the fear of **God**, is this: that we hold there is one single **God**, who made and created everything, both what can be seen and what cannot be seen with physical eyes; and we recognize the **Lord Jesus Christ** as God’s Son, who was proclaimed of old by the prophets, and will come again as a judge of the human race; He is the messenger of salvation, and the teacher of those who are well instructed by Him. I, indeed, as a weak human being, am far too insignificant to be able to say anything worthy of His infinite divinity (**), and I confess that such is the office of the prophets; For..."

(*) <note>original: "Gespräch mit dem Juden Tryphon" — Dialogue with Trypho the Jew</note> This **Justin** wrote a book called: *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*; therein he shows at the very beginning how he, as a heathen, sought wisdom in vain among all their sects, first holding to the sect of the **Stoics** <note>A school of philosophy emphasizing duty and endurance</note>, then becoming a **Peripatetic** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note>, then a **Pythagorean**, and finally a **Platonist**; until the way to true wisdom was prepared for him by an understanding Christian.

(**) **Justin** was indeed, as a philosopher, a rational and clever man, but in the mysteries of **Christian doctrine** he was not yet very deeply experienced, as he confesses in humility, and as his writings also testify; although the converted philosophers at that time soon became teachers, from which the decay <note>The author suggests that the influx of secular philosophy into the early church led to a spiritual decline or corruption of simple faith</note> arose.

## Chapter 2.
->Further Examination: Where the Christians held their assembly.<-

The President asked him further: at what place the Christians held their assembly. Justin answered him: everyone went wherever he wished and was able. "Do you think," the President said, "that we all come together in one place? Not at all; for the God of the Christians cannot be enclosed in any one place, but he is invisible and fills heaven and earth, and is worshipped everywhere by the faithful, and his praise is proclaimed." Thereupon the judge spoke: "Well then, tell me, where have you gathered, and where are you accustomed to assemble your followers?" Justin answered: "I have had my lodgings until now near the house of a man named Martinus, by the Timothy Baths <note>original: "Badstuben Timotinum"</note>; and this is now the second time I have come to Rome (*), but I know no other place than the one mentioned, because the first time I also stayed there at the inn. If anyone has visited me there, I have shared the doctrine of truth with them." "So then you are truly a Christian," said Rusticus. Justin answered: "Certainly, I am a Christian."

->They receive the judgment, and are scourged and beheaded.<-

When the President heard this, he pronounced the following sentence: These men, who will not sacrifice to the gods nor obey the Emperor’s command, shall be beaten with the scourge and then beheaded, according to the law. ...and glory from GOD the Father and Christ JESUS our LORD. We can neither express in words nor sufficiently describe with the pen the heavy sufferings, the heathen madness, and the folly directed against the Saints, nor how much the blessed martyrs of our region have endured; for right at the beginning, the enemy <note>The author identifies the source of the persecution as Satan or the Devil.</note> set upon us with all his might and raged quite without restraint, though he only showed the first-fruits and the beginning of the persecution. Inasmuch as Satan left nothing untried, training his servants and, as it were, instructing and exercising them against the servants of God. We were not only barred from houses, public baths, and marketplaces, but it was also commanded that we should no longer let ourselves be seen anywhere.

## The 2nd Chapter.

->How the raging mob vented its fury against them.<-

But the grace of GOD fought for us against the Devil, protecting the weak while setting the strong and the men in Christ as firm and steadfast pillars against the enemy; through their bravery, they were able to take upon themselves every assault of the evil spirit. Now when the enemy engaged with these, they endured every kind of insult and mockery; what others considered tedious and burdensome was light to them as they hastened toward Christ. They proved by their example that the sufferings of this world are not worthy of the glory that shall be revealed in us. <note>original: Rom. 8, v. 18. "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us."</note> At the beginning, they steadfastly withstood the fury of the mob, who exercised their wantonness upon them in crowds—namely, by shouting, beating, robbing, plundering their goods, throwing stones, imprisonment, and everything else that a raging and rioting mob is accustomed to devise against its imagined enemies. Afterward, they were publicly brought before the court in the marketplace by a captain <note>The German "Hauptmann" here refers to a chiliarch or military tribune.</note> and the city authorities, and questioned before all the people. When they confessed their Christian faith, they were led to prison until the arrival of the President or Governor.

[Vet]tius Epagathus <note>Vettius Epagathus was a noble young man and one of the first to be martyred in Lyon.</note>, who was a brother and stood in extraordinary love toward God and his neighbors, led such a strict and earnest life that, even though he was a youth, he was compared to the priest Zacharias; for he walked blamelessly in all the commandments and righteous ways of the Lord, Luke 1, v. 6. He was willing to perform all services of love for his neighbor, full of Divine zeal and fervor of the spirit. Being such a man, he could no longer bear to watch the utterly unjust judgment; rather, moved by zeal, he requested that he also be permitted to speak for the brothers, as he wished to prove publicly that nothing godless or unjust was occurring among us. But as the spectators standing around him raised a shout against him (for he was from a prominent family), and the President <note>The Roman Governor or presiding magistrate.</note> was also annoyed by this otherwise lawful request, he merely asked him whether he too was a Christian. This he affirmed with a clear voice and confessed himself to be a Christian. Thus he had to help increase the number of the martyrs; yet he had the special honor that the judge himself mocked him as the "Advocate of the Christians." ->The Constancy of Sanctus the Deacon under Torture.<-

## Chapter 8.
->The Boldness of the Martyrs in Prison.<-

When all the painful inventions of the tyrants had been overcome and made blunt through the steadfastness of the martyrs for Christ, the Devil devised another trick; namely, that they were placed in a very dark, oppressive prison, and their feet were locked in the block <note>A wooden instrument of torture (stocks) used to restrain and stretch the limbs of prisoners.</note>, stretched very far apart; and the guards, who were hateful toward us and incited by the Devil, inflicted more such torments upon them in the prison; so much so, that very many of them died in the dungeon—those, namely, whom God, who demonstrates His honor in all things, intended to glorify with such a manner of death. Others, who had been very heavily tortured, so much so that it was thought they could not live much longer, even though they were refreshed in every way with medicine <note>This likely refers to basic care or metaphorical spiritual healing, as physical medicine was rarely available in Roman dungeons.</note>, remained in the prison. Although abandoned by human help, they were strengthened by God in both spirit and body; these set the others on fire with spiritual joy and comforted them. Others, however, who had only recently come to the faith and—like those before them—had already suffered many tortures <note>original: "Marter"</note>, had only just been imprisoned; their bodies were not yet accustomed to such hardship, and as they could not endure the harsh treatment in the dungeon, they gave up their spirits within.

He possessed a very weak body, so that he could hardly draw breath due to his great frailty, yet he was strengthened with a wonderful joy of mind by his extraordinary desire for martyrdom. This man was also dragged to the judgment seat; his body, wasted away partly by old age and partly by illness, was entirely frail, but in his soul he was healthy and strong, so that Christ might triumph through him. After he was brought before the court by the soldiers, and the city magistrates met him harshly, while all the people raised their murderous cries against him as if they thought he were Christ Himself, he gave an excellent testimony. For when the President <note>Referring to the Roman provincial governor.</note> asked him what kind of being the God of the Christians actually was, he gave as an answer: "If you are worthy, you shall learn to know Him!" ...was watered and strengthened by the heavenly wellspring of living water that flows from the body of Christ. Furthermore, his entire body bore clear witness to what he had endured, as nothing but wounds and welts could be seen upon him; he was so utterly disjointed and twisted that he no longer even looked like a human being. Within him, Christ Himself suffered and performed great wonders, uprooting the Adversary <note>A common historical title for the Devil.</note> and showing the others through his exceptional example that one must fear nothing where the Father’s love supports them, and that nothing is painful which serves the glory of Christ. 

For when the godless ones brought the martyr forth a second time after several days, they were under the delusion that if they repeated the previous torture while his limbs were still swollen and his wounds inflamed, the pain would be even greater than before, since he could not even bear the touch of a hand without agony. At the very least, they thought this would ensure that if he died under the pain, the others would be terrified by it. However, not only did neither of these things happen, but contrary to their expectations, his disjointed limbs were set right again during the second round of torture, so that he regained his proper form and the use of his limbs. It even reached the point that, through the cooperation of Divine Grace, this second labor of the executioners served more as a medicine than a punishment.

## Chapter 7.

->*Biblias, who had fallen away, strengthens herself again in faith.*<-

One woman, however, named Biblias—who was among those who had renounced the faith in Christ out of fear—the Devil thought he had already swallowed up. He intended to heap even more onto her damnation through blasphemies and lies, and so led her to the torture rack <note>original: "Peinige-Bank"</note>, wishing to force her, as one perceived to be weak and lazy, to confess something godless against us. But she recovered herself in the midst of the pain, and like one waking from a sleep, the present punishment made her think of the eternal punishment of Hell. She therefore resisted the godless ones and said: "How could it be possible that those people would eat the flesh of children and humans, who are not even permitted to eat the blood of animals?" <note>This refers to a common Roman slander that Christians practiced cannibalism during their "love feasts" or the Eucharist.</note> Thereupon, she further confessed herself to be a Christian and was counted among the company of the martyrs.

## Chapter 8.
->The Joy of the Martyrs in Prison.<-

When all the painful inventions of the tyrants had been overcome and rendered blunt by the steadfastness of the martyrs for Christ, the Devil devised another trick: namely, that they were placed in a very dark and oppressive prison, and their feet were locked in the stocks <note>A wooden frame used for punishment, where the legs were often spread to a painful degree.</note>, stretched very far apart. The henchmen, who were hateful toward us and incited by the Devil, inflicted even more of such torment upon them in the prison; so much so, that very many of them died in the dungeon—those, specifically, whom God, who demonstrates His glory in all things, intended to glorify with such a manner of death. Others, who had been so severely tortured that it was believed they could not live much longer, remained in the prison. Although they were refreshed with medicines in every possible way, they were indeed forsaken by human help, but strengthened by God in both spirit and body. These individuals ignited the others with their spiritual joy and comforted them. However, others who had only recently come to the faith and were imprisoned for the first time—whose bodies were not yet accustomed to such hardship—could not endure the harsh treatment in the dungeon and gave up the ghost therein.

## Chapter 9.
->The Martyrdom of Saint Pothinus, Bishop of the Congregation of Lyon.<-

Now the most blessed Pothinus <note>Original: "Photinus." Historically, he was the first Bishop of Lyon and the predecessor to Irenaeus.</note>, who held the oversight or the office of Bishop of the congregation of Lyon, was over ninety years old. He was of a very weak body, so that he could hardly draw breath due to his great frailty, yet he was strengthened with a wonderful joy of mind by his extraordinary desire for martyrdom. He was also dragged to the judgment seat; though his body was entirely exhausted, partly by old age and partly by illness, his soul was healthy and strong, so that Christ might triumph through him. After he had been brought before the court by the soldiers, and the city magistrates treated him harshly, and all the people raised their murderous cries against him as if they believed he were Christ himself, he gave an excellent testimony. For when the President <note>The Roman Governor of the province.</note> asked him what kind of being the God of the Christians truly was, he replied: "If you are worthy, you shall come to know Him!" ->The Wretched State of the Apostates.<-

The believers, indeed, who confessed to being what they truly were, were placed in bonds as Christians without proof of any other vice; but these apostates <note>People who have renounced their religious faith.</note> were kept prisoner as suspected murderers and wicked people, and they endured twice as much as the others. ## Chapter 11.
### The Final Combat of the Holy Martyrs Maturus, Sanctus, Blandina, and Attalus.

In the meantime, the most blessed martyrs received various sentences of death; for they offered to God the Father a single wreath and crown, woven from many kinds of flowers of various types and colors. It was indeed fitting that the brave-hearted warriors, who had fought in so many ways and triumphed so exceptionally, should also receive a magnificent crown of immortality. Maturus, then, and Sanctus, along with Blandina and Attalus, were led into the arena <note>The German "Schau-Platz" refers here to the Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls in Lyon.</note> to the wild beasts, to be a public spectacle of pagan inhumanity; for this purpose, an extraordinary day of games was set aside for the sake of our people.

Maturus and Sanctus, however, had to endure every kind of torture once more in the arena, as if they had suffered nothing before; or rather, like fighters who had already overcome their adversary many times and were now fighting for the crown itself at the very end. They were again scourged with straps in the usual manner and suffered the dragging and biting of wild animals, and everything that the raging mob demanded according to their pleasure. Finally, they were placed on an iron chair <note>The "iron chair" was a notorious Roman torture device used to slow-roast victims over coals.</note> over glowing coals, upon which the martyrs' limbs began to roast, the offensive smell of which filled the nostrils of the spectators. Nevertheless, their frenzy had not yet ended; rather, their rage became all the more intense as they sought to overcome the martyrs' steadfastness by force. But they could not bring any other word out of Sanctus than that which he had spoken from the beginning as his entire confession of faith, namely: "I am a Christian!" <note>original: "Ich bin ein Christ!" This echoes the Latin "Christianus sum."</note> When these had fought to the utmost and held the breath of life long enough, their throats were finally cut; after they had been a spectacle for the world on that day, in place of the many changing events that gladiators <note>original: "Kampf-Fechter," literally combat-fencers, referring to the various types of gladiatorial entertainment.</note> usually present.

Blandina, however, was bound crosswise to a wooden stake and thus thrown to the wild beasts; yet in such a crucified posture, while she fervently called upon God, she gave great courage to her fellow combatants; for they saw in the midst of their struggle, in the form of their sister,

-> Those who had fallen away recover their faith. Other martyrs are <-

This delay and period of time was by no means useless or fruitless for them; for Christ's immeasurable mercy revealed itself in the meantime through their enduring patience. The dead members of the community were renewed to life again through the help and assistance of the living; for the martyrs came to the aid of those who had fallen away from the faith. The Mother and Virgin Church <note>A common early Christian metaphor for the collective body of believers.</note> was filled with uncommon joy as she now received back alive those whom she had previously cast away as an untimely stillbirth. For through these most holy martyrs, those who had denied the faith were once again conceived in the spiritual womb.

10. Saint Pothinus etc. in Vienne and Lyon
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

Those remains which the wild beasts or the fire had left of the other martyrs—half-torn and half-burnt—were put on public display. Likewise, the heads and bodies of all the others remained unburied for many days, over which a guard of soldiers was placed to keep watch. Some heathens were still enraged against the dead, gnashing their teeth at them and demanding an even harsher judge who might subject them to painful questioning once more. Others, however, mocked and jeered, praising their idols and attributing the vengeance visited upon the martyrs to them. Some were slightly more reasonable and seemed to have some pity for our misery; these were saddened by our fate and said: "Where is their God now? What has this faith helped them, for which they have even given up their lives?" In such various ways, the heathens held their reflections upon us. We, however, were meanwhile very distressed that we were not allowed to bury the bodies. For neither the darkness of the night could help us, nor the power of gold bend the guards, nor any pleas move their hearts; instead, they guarded the bodies with such diligence and earnestness, as if they would gain a great profit if the bodies remained unburied.

## Chapter 16.

->The remains of the martyrs are burned by the heathens to prevent the resurrection, according to their foolish delusion.<-

After the bodies of the martyrs had finally been insulted in every way, and had lain on display under the open sky for six days, they were at last burned to ashes. These were scattered by the ungodly into the passing river, called the **Rhone** <note>original: "Rohne"</note> (*), so that no remnant of them could ever be found on earth again. And they did this with the intention of thwarting our belief in the **resurrection** <term>resurrection: the Christian belief that the dead will rise again in physical form at the end of time</term>, as if such a thing were now impossible for God; indeed, as they themselves said, we should have no hope of rising again. "For this reason," they said, "this people brings forward their new and foreign teaching, despising all torture and going so quickly and willingly to death; let us see now if they will rise again, and if their God can help them and deliver them from our hands!"

<note>(*) Rhodanus, the Rhone, is a notable river in France, along which these two cities, Lyon and Vienne, lie close together.</note>

History of the Martyrs / Year 177.

## Chapter 17.

->The humility of the holy martyrs, who did not wish to be called<-
->martyrs during their earthly lives, as well as their love and gentleness.<-

We cannot, however, overlook the great humility of these martyrs, who sought to follow and resemble Christ in all things. For Christ, though He existed in divine equality and did not consider it a robbery of God’s honor to testify that He was equal to God, nevertheless humbled Himself <note>Philippians 2:6</note>. For although these believers had reached such a high level of honor—having been tortured not just once or twice, but many times, and returned to prison from the wild beasts—and though they bore the marks of fire as well as welts and wounds over their entire bodies, they still did not wish to call themselves "martyrs," nor be called such by us. Instead, if one of us wrote to them secretly in prison, or addressed them respectfully as martyrs in conversation, they would earnestly rebuke us. For they said that Christ was the "True Martyr" <note>The word "Martyr" comes from the Greek *martys*, meaning "witness." Here the author emphasizes Christ as the ultimate witness of God’s truth.</note> or "Blood-Witness," as the faithful and true witness and the firstborn from the dead, as well as the source and author of heavenly life. Likewise, they referred to those martyrs who had already departed from this life, saying: "These are the true martyrs, whom the Lord Christ has deemed worthy to take to Himself in their confession, choosing to seal their testimony with their death as if with a ring; we, however, are but lowly and miserable confessors <term>Bekenner: those who admit their faith publicly but have not yet faced death</term>." With many tears, they begged the brothers to pray to God for them, so that they might finally be found worthy to reach a perfect end. In their actions, however, they demonstrated the virtues of martyrs, answering the heathens with great boldness and confidence. Their excellent disposition was made clearly evident through their patient endurance and their lack of fear or terror. Yet they fled from the name of "martyr" itself when it was bestowed upon them by the brothers, who felt bound to use it out of the fear of God. They humbled themselves under the hand of the Almighty, which has now exalted them. At that time, they made excuses for everyone and accused no one; they released all and bound none; so much so that, following the example of the most perfect martyr, Stephen, they even prayed for their...

For in this consisted their greatest struggle against the Devil: namely, for righteous and sincere love. They asked for their own lives, and God granted it to them, which they then shared with their neighbors; thus, they went to God as perfect victors. Since they loved peace and commanded us to keep peace, they themselves traveled to God with peace. Because of this, neither their Mother (the Church) was grieved, nor did the brothers argue over their inheritance; rather, they left behind joy, peace, harmony, and love for all.

### Chapter 18.

->Of Alcibiades, whose self-chosen austere life was set aside by God<-
->through the agency of Attalus.<-

<margin>(*) See above, Chapter 11.</margin>
One among these martyrs, named Alcibiades, led a hard and rough life, and ate no food other than bread and water alone. When he was placed in prison, he wished to maintain his accustomed way of living. However, after Attalus had fought for the first time in the arena (*), it was revealed to him that Alcibiades was not doing right or well by not making use of God’s creatures <note>This refers to 1 Timothy 4:4, emphasizing that all food created by God is good and should not be rejected through extreme asceticism.</note> and thereby giving an offensive example to others. When Alcibiades heard this from Attalus, he obeyed the reminder and began to eat all kinds of food without distinction, with thanksgiving to God. For Divine Grace had not departed from them; rather, they had the Counselor, the Holy Spirit. <note>original: "Euseb. Histor. Eccles. Lib. 5. cap. 1. &c. Ruinart. L. c. p. 62." refers to Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 5, Chapter 1, and Thierry Ruinart’s *Acta Martyrum* (Acts of the Martyrs).</note>
