# II. St. Epiphodius and Alexander.

## Chapter 1.

->Introduction and Praise of the State of Martyrdom.<-

If the glorious deeds of brave men are recorded in annals for the encouragement of posterity—men who gave their lives either for earthly freedom or in the vain service of their fatherland, so that they might leave behind a faint monument of virtues of the flesh <note>The author contrasts "virtues of the flesh" (earthly courage) with spiritual virtues.</note> after their death; with what descriptions of praise should one then celebrate the death of the martyrs? In a wonderfully magnificent brevity, as they stretch out their hands toward heaven, they leave behind an image of their faith and devotion on earth and propagate the life of humanity even through their death. For they do not shed their blood in the service of an earthly Emperor, but for the Heavenly King; not for a fatherland that gives and takes away, nor for a fatherland that one possesses one moment and loses the next, but for the Heavenly Jerusalem and the eternal fatherland. This eternal home is built here through the merit of the Saints, and its highest point reaches into the heavens; its inhabitants cannot die, its freedom is released from the hellish yoke, and it endures with imperishable glory and blessedness. 

Truly, one can only express or suggest the smallest part of the martyrs' eternal reward, since the sufferings of this time are in no way to be compared with the greatness of the heavenly glory, which lasts continually and eternally. <note>This is a paraphrase of Romans 8:18: "For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us."</note> Nevertheless, the victory of the Saints shall be preserved among us forever as a monument. It is right that we pass this down to our descendants through writings, so that even if they have no opportunity for martyrdom itself, they may still be ignited to eager imitation and attain a spotless life through the mortification of the flesh <term>mortification of the flesh: the spiritual practice of self-discipline and the "crushing" (contrition) of worldly desires</term> and the imitation of the martyr's state. Therefore, we wish to report the struggle and victory of the most blessed martyrs Epiphodius and Alexander, and how Christ triumphed in them; so that the faith of the believers may be awakened to imitation by their example.

## The 2nd Chapter.
->Concerning the Great Persecution at Vienne and Lyon.<-

In the seventeenth year of the Imperial reign of Antoninus Verus <note>This refers to Emperor Marcus Aurelius, who reigned from 161–180 AD; "Verus" was part of his family name.</note>, around the Year of Salvation 178, the pagan rage stormed through all lands. It was particularly desolate in the city of Lyon in France <note>Original: "Lion in Frankreich." This refers to Lugdunum in Roman Gaul.</note>; for the more people who resided there because of its great size, the more the pagans' madness burned. Both judges and servants, officers and common soldiers, along with the common rabble of both sexes, raged against the Christians with various cruelties. Though the specific sufferings and names of many were indeed recorded as a memorial for posterity, countless others—who were killed without distinction or died in dungeons and bonds—are written only in the heavenly Book of Life. Following this greatest execution of the martyrs and the cruelty of the raging torturers—of which the servants of Christ, who resided at that time in the two famous cities of Vienne and Lyon, sent a written account to the congregations in Asia and Phrygia (*)—and now that the pagans believed they had almost entirely rooted out the name of Christ; finally, through betrayal within their own household, Epiphodius and Alexander were reported to the Governor as being devoted to the Christian faith. The Governor then gave the order to seek them out with diligent care, so as to completely eradicate the hated religion in them.

## The 3rd Chapter.
->The Origin, Life, Conduct, Flight, and Imprisonment of Epiphodius and Alexander.<-

In the meantime, we wish to interrupt the order somewhat and briefly report what sort of men these two were. Alexander was a Greek by birth, but Epiphodius was a native of the city of Lyon. Both had been schoolmates from their youth, and a manly love <note>In this historical context, "manly love" refers to a deep, virtuous, and platonic bond of spiritual brotherhood.</note> had already bound them together in their youth. Thus, they grew up together in learning and harmony; and because they were Christians, well-instructed by their excellent parents, they had encouraged and spurred one another on in the religion. For in sobriety, temperance, chastity, faith, and works of mercy, they had in such a manner [prepared] themselves to be worthy ...

During the persecution, however, since they could not flee to another or a third city according to the Gospel’s instruction, they kept themselves secretly hidden in their own region. They both gave their names and clearly testified that they were Christians. At this, the judge’s anger was kindled, the murderous cry of the people rose up, and all manner of rage and fury revolted against the innocent men. ## Chapter 6.

->The cruelty of the judge and the people demands that Epiphodius be executed by the sword.<-

The judge was completely stunned with annoyance and amazement at this answer; finally, he broke out in grim anger and ordered that the house of <term>eloquence: "Beredsamkeit", here a poetic reference to the mouth as the source of persuasive speech</term>—namely, the martyr's mouth—be struck with fists. But the holy Epiphodius was only strengthened after receiving these painful blows and spoke through bloody teeth and mouth: "I confess Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as my God; it is only right that I surrender my soul to Him who is my Creator and Redeemer. For in this way I do not lose my life, but rather it is transformed into a better one. It also does not matter what kind of end this weak body meets, so long as the soul reaches its origin in heaven!" 

When the blessed Epiphodius had said this with great boldness, the cruel judge ordered him to be brought to the <term>rack: "Peinige-Bank", a torture device used to stretch the limbs</term>, where he was stretched out and surrounded by executioner’s assistants, who tore his entire body with sharp instruments and hooks. But the people suddenly raised a murderous cry and demanded that they be allowed to stone him or tear him limb from limb in their raving madness! So slow did the judge's cruelty seem to their collective rage. But because the governor had to fear that the people might act violently and dishonor the judicial power and authority through a riot, he ordered Epiphodius to be led away from the <term>judgment seat: "Richt-Stule", the tribunal or official seat of authority</term> and executed with the sword, in order to dampen the sudden and insane folly of the swarming crowd and to eradicate the cause of this unrest.

# Chapter 7.

### Chapter 9.

->Alexander is severely tortured.<-

Thereupon, the enraged and shamed President <note>The presiding Roman magistrate or governor</note> commanded that the holy Alexander be torn and shredded about the body with three-pronged instruments; despite this, Alexander did not let a single faint-hearted word be heard, but instead called upon God for help. The judge then spoke: "The Christians are so foolish that they make an honor of their prolonged suffering, thinking they have overcome their persecutors by it; therefore, one should help them out of it quite quickly. Since he should no longer be heard nor seen in his stubbornness, Alexander shall be nailed to the cross and surrender his spirit as he deserves." When the cruel executioners and their servants heard the sentence, they seized the blessed Alexander and fixed him with outstretched arms and hands to the salutary sign of the cross. The suffering of the blessed martyr did not last much longer; for his body had been so mangled by the cruelty of the torturers that his ribs were stripped of flesh, and one could see his entrails lying within his body. Having now become entirely like Christ, and having called upon Him in his final confession, he gave up his blessed spirit as it departed his body.

## Chapter 12.
### Their Miraculous Works after their Death.

For when the inhabitants of Lyon <note>original: "Lion"</note> were dying in great numbers from the plague, a certain noble youth, who was greatly inflamed by the disease, was reminded through a vision that he should seek help from that woman who had one of the martyr's shoes (*) in her keeping. When he then sought counsel from this woman, she excused herself, saying she understood no medical remedies; yet she did not deny that, by means of the martyr's left-behind shoe which she had kept, she had made many healthy. Thereupon Lucia <note>The woman mentioned in the vision</note> set food before him and offered him a cup to drink; as soon as he had quenched his thirst from it, his burning heat vanished from that hour, so that he had no need to be carried away, but was able to walk home again himself. Such power of faith and of the saints spread immediately throughout the entire city; as a countless multitude regained their health, and through this the number of believers grew again; thus it served as medicine for both body and soul, for time and eternity. Furthermore, many miraculous works were later performed at that place, such as the casting out of evil spirits, the recovery of the weak, and the healing of the sick, which increased daily more and more, despite all secret envy and rage. Thus, faith and words and works must be together; because the kind power, virtue, and effect of God loves the believers, but leaves the unbelievers. # 12. Saint Symphorianus.

## Chapter 1.

->Symphorianus’s Noble Lineage, Christian Upbringing, and Virtuous<-
->Conduct.<-

When a harsh storm-wind rose against the Christian name under Emperor Aurelius <note>Emperor Marcus Aurelius, who reigned 161–180 AD</note> (in the year 180), and Imperial decrees were issued for the eradication of the common faith, there was in the city of Autun <note>original: "Othün"</note> in the Duchy of Burgundy, a son of the noble Lord Faustus named Symphorianus. He was of Christian descent, well-learned, and of good upbringing; so much so that his young, blossoming years reached the wisdom of the elderly and surpassed them with stainless sincerity of mind. After he had passed through childhood and his youth and successfully reached manhood, he gave everyone such hope of his virtues that all righteous people believed he had already attained the company of the higher powers <note>The heavenly or angelic host</note> through his good conduct. For heavenly wisdom and a simplicity adorned with spiritual jewels enlightened him; and because he followed the path of the righteous and did not let go of the rudder of vigilance, he successfully escaped the shipwreck of the vain life of this world.

## Chapter 2.

->Concerning Idolatry in Autun, France; Why Symphorianus was<-
->Captured, Dragged to Court, and Examined.<-

At that time, Autun was a city famous from antiquity, noble, and filled with the manifold ceremonies of a damned religion. ## Chapter 4.

->He is scourged, imprisoned, and soon examined again<-

When the judge now saw that the holy *Symphorianus* would not obey his command, he ordered the executioners to scourge him and then bring him back into the prison! After several days, he ordered him to be brought before the court once again; then they fetched the son of light out of the dark dungeon, he who after such hard bonds was to live eternally with the eternal King. He had been shackled so tightly that the skin was cut through, and the blood ran down, although his spirit stood elevated toward heavenly joys. The judge, however, spoke to him: Would it not be much better, *Symphorian*, if you served the immortal gods and were endowed from the public treasury, for the glorification of your noble rank? But if today you will not honor the venerable image of the Mother and Goddess <note>Referring to the goddess Cybele, often called the "Great Mother"</note> with bowing of the knee, and show yourself a devout servant of the high deity of *Apollo* and *Diana*, you will without all doubt perish.

### Chapter 18.

They brought the martyr to the spring that lay outside the city territory, where he was buried in a small cave; yet he revealed himself at all times through miraculous powers. ### Chapter 1.

->*Preface concerning Divine Grace, which is poured out today just as it was yesterday.*<-

If the ancient examples of faith—which not only bear witness to the grace of God but also contribute to the edification of mankind—were written down so that through their reading and contemplation God might be honored and man strengthened; why should one not also likewise preserve the instructional histories of today, being of the same kind as those? For these too shall in time be called "ancient history" and be useful to posterity, even if in the present time, while they are still new, they are little esteemed due to a perceived high regard for antiquity. However, those people might do well to consider that they judge the singular power of the singular Holy Spirit according to the age of the times; whereas, in truth, the newer grace is to be considered all the greater for the very reason that it is the latest, since the greatest promise was given concerning the abundance of <meta>catchword: Grace</meta>

...grace has been reserved for the final times; *For in the very last days, says the Lord, I will pour out my Spirit upon all people, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy, and upon my servants and my handmaidens I will pour out my Spirit; then shall the young men see visions, and the old men dream dreams.* <note>original: "Joel.2, v.28. Act. 2, v. 17." This refers to the Old Testament prophet Joel and the New Testament book of Acts, emphasizing that spiritual gifts are not limited to the past.</note> Therefore, we too, who accept and hold in honor such promised new prophecies and visions, wish to recognize all other workings of grace of the Holy Spirit as tools of the Church, for whose sake He was sent, and who invariably shares all His gifts among all people. We wish to compose this in writing and offer it to the reader for contemplation to the glory of God, so that the weakness or despair of faith might not perhaps think that in the ancient Apostolic times, God’s grace ruled only among the martyrs and in the gift of revelation (*); Whereas God fulfills His promises at all times, as a testimony to the unbelievers, but as a blessing to the believers. We wish then, dear brothers and sons, to proclaim to you what we have heard and touched, so that you who were present yourselves may be reminded of the goodness of the Lord; and those who now come to hear of it may have fellowship with the holy martyrs, and through them with the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belongs the glory and the honor for all eternity. Amen!

### Chapter 2.
->The Arrest of Revocatus, Felicitas, Saturninus, and Vivia Perpetua.<-

The persecutors have seized the <term>new converts: also known as catechumens, those who were receiving instruction in the Christian faith but had not yet been baptized</term>, Revocatus and Felicitas, his companion; likewise Saturninus and Secundulus, along with Vivia Perpetua, who was of noble descent, well-educated, and married according to her station. Her father and mother were still living, and she had two brothers, one of whom was also a new convert; additionally, she bore a nursing child at her breast; she herself was twenty-two years of age.

### Chapter 1.

->A report on Divine Grace, which is poured out today just as it was yesterday.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'W' featuring scrolling acanthus leaves and floral motifs.</image-desc>

**W**hy were the ancient examples of faith—which not only bear witness to the grace of God but also contribute to the edification of mankind—written down? It was so that through the reading and contemplation of these things, both God might be honored and man might be strengthened. Why then should we not also preserve today's instructional histories of the same kind? For these too will be called "ancient history" in time and will be useful to posterity, even if they are held in low regard at the present time while they are still new, due to a perceived reverence for antiquity. However, let those people reflect well who measure the unique power of the one Holy Spirit according to the age of the times; for indeed, new grace should be considered all the greater for the very reason that it is the last, since the greatest promise [of the Spirit] follows the abundance of the

### Chapter 3.
->Perpetua recounts the beginning of her imprisonment.<-

As we were still, she writes, walking freely among the persecutors, and my father sought to turn me away—striving to persuade me according to his natural affection that I should not call myself a Christian—I said to him: "Dear father, do you see that vessel standing there?" He said: "I see it!" I replied: "Can it be called anything other than what it is?" He said: "No!" "In the same way," I answered him, "I cannot call myself anything other than what I am, namely a Christian." At this, my father was incensed by such a word and lunged at me as if he wanted to tear out my eyes; but he only struck me, and truly he was overcome by all the devil's schemes. After that, my father left me in peace for several days, for which I thanked God, and I was refreshed by his absence. During the span of those few days we were baptized; but the Spirit revealed to me that after such a baptism I must prepare myself for nothing but suffering. A few days later, we were led into the prison, where I was at first terrified because I had never experienced such darkness. O, what a hard day! What heat there was in the crowded space! And how the soldiers pushed us about! Most of all, I was tormented by the care of my child. <note>Perpetua was a nursing mother at the time of her arrest.</note> However, the blessed deacons, Tertius and Pomponius, who assisted us, arranged through bribes for us to refresh ourselves for a few hours in a better part of the prison; there we all went out and drew breath. I gave my breast to my child, who was almost famished; and out of concern for him, I spoke with my mother and comforted her; I entrusted my son to my brother. It grieved me to see them so sorrowful on my account; such anxiety lasted for a long time; but I obtained permission for the child to stay with me in the dungeon. Immediately I became of good cheer, and the worry over the child vanished; then the dungeon suddenly became a palace to me, so that I preferred to be there than anywhere else.

On the sides of this ladder, however, were all kinds of sharp instruments, such as swords, lances, hooks, knives, and the like; so that if anyone was careless, or did not look upward while climbing, he would be wounded and his flesh mangled. Then the dragon hid his head under the ladder, as if he were afraid. When I then stood upon the first rung, I stepped upon his head <note>This imagery reflects the biblical promise in Genesis 3:15 regarding the crushing of the serpent's head.</note> and then climbed up. There I saw above an immeasurably large garden, and in the middle of the garden sat a gray-haired man in the form of a great shepherd, who was milking his sheep; many thousands clothed in white stood around him. He lifted up his head, looked at me, and said to me: "Welcome, dear child!" And he called me to himself and gave me a little of the curdled milk from his sheep. I received it with my hands and ate it; and all those who stood around said: "Amen!" At the sound of this word I awoke, and still I knew not what sweetness I had eaten in my mouth. Then I told it immediately to my brother, and from this we understood that we would have to suffer; therefore, we gave up all hope for this life.

When on another day we were sitting and having our midday meal, we were suddenly taken for interrogation and arrived at the marketplace. ## The 7th Chapter.

*Perpetua has a vision of her deceased brother Dinocrates.*

After several days, while we were all praying, I suddenly had to speak a word during the prayer and said: Dinocrates <gloss>original: "Dinocrates (*)"; see note below</gloss>! I was startled by this myself, because he had never come into my mind until that moment, and I was saddened by this occurrence. But I soon recognized that I was deemed worthy to pray for him. So I began to offer my prayer fervently for him and to implore the Lord; and immediately afterward, during that same night, the following was shown to me in a vision: I saw Dinocrates coming out of a dark place where many others were also; he was very hot and thirsty, looked ugly and pale in the face, and still had the wound on his face from which he had died. This Dinocrates had been my natural brother, seven years old, who had died miserably of cancer <note>The German "Krebs" here likely refers to "noma," a gangrenous infection of the face common in malnourished children in antiquity.</note>; so that his death had been loathsome to all people. For him, then, I had prayed. But there was a great chasm between him and me, so that we both could not come to one another <gloss>original: "(**)"; see note below</gloss>. Furthermore, in the place where Dinocrates stayed, there was a water-basin full of water; but its rim was higher than the boy's height, and Dinocrates exerted himself in vain to stretch out far enough to be able to drink. Then I was moved to pity that the water-trough was indeed full of water, but nevertheless the boy could not drink because of the high rim. At this I awoke and recognized that my brother

# The 8th Chapter.

->Another vision of Perpetua regarding her brother, who is<-
->delivered from eternal distress through her prayer.<-

One day now, while we were still imprisoned in the stocks <note>The "Block" refers to the wooden frame used to restrain prisoners by their feet.</note>, I saw the following: I beheld the previously dark place, which I had seen before, entirely illuminated, and Dinocrates there, clean in body, well-clothed, and refreshed; where the wound had previously been, I saw only a scar; the water basin, however, which I had also seen before, reached the boy up to his waist, and water flowed from it unceasingly; and a golden bowl full of water stood on its rim; Dinocrates approached and began to drink from it, yet the bowl remained always full of water. And after he was satisfied, he went away from there and began to play and rejoice in the manner of boys; at which I awoke and recognized that the boy had been moved out of his distress (*).

***

(*) This story is certainly a sufficient testimony of the incomplete purification of souls after death, mediated by the anointed intercession of the saints on earth or in heaven, wherever the connection between them is opened through Divine providence. To the early Christians, this was not at all foreign, so that one finds no handling of their corpses where they did not testify to such with prayer and alms; like here the blessed Perpetua, who, though she had a nursing child at her breasts, nevertheless had enough courage in Christ to help redeem her brother with holy intercession, as it was revealed to her in a mirror <note>A metaphorical "mirror" of spiritual vision or revelation.</note>; whereas of those who are outside, it is written: *Truly no man can redeem the brother.* Ps. 49, v. 8. The Roman Church indeed still has a glimmer of knowledge regarding this, but reason has entirely transformed and desecrated the truth <note>The author, likely writing from a later Protestant or Pietist perspective, critiques the Catholic doctrine of Purgatory while defending the early Christian practice of praying for the dead.</note>. It mattered not at all whether such a deceased person had not yet been incorporated into the community of Christ through baptism during their physical life; like this Dinocrates, the brother of Saint Perpetua, who as well as her father and another living brother

### The 9th Chapter.

->*Pudens, the jailer, allows the prisoners to be visited; there once again Perpetua’s father comes.*<-

After a few days (*), Pudens, the official and jailer <note>original: "Gewaltiger und Kerker-meister"</note>, who was beginning to hold us in high regard and recognized the great power of God within us, allowed many of the brothers to come to us, so that we and they might refresh one another. But as the day of our sacrifice <note>A reference to their upcoming execution in the arena.</note> drew near, my father came in to see me, completely wasted away with worry and grief; he began to tear out his beard, to throw himself upon the earth, to lie upon his face, and to curse his years with such piteous words that they might have moved even a stone to pity. However, his unhappy old age moved me only to compassion.

### The 10th Chapter.

->*Perpetua fights in a vision with an Egyptian and triumphs.*<-

The day before we entered the struggle, I saw in a vision as if Pomponius the Deacon <note>A deacon of the church in Carthage who assisted the martyrs.</note> came to us at the door of the prison; I went out to him and opened the door for him. He was wearing a long, white, tucked-up tunic <note>original: "Thalar"</note> with many buttons. And he said to me: "Perpetua, come, we are waiting for you!" ->Saturus’s Vision of the Heavenly Forecourts of Paradise and the Temple.<-

### The Personal Appearance of the Lord Jesus in His Glory.

## Chapter 16.

At this, the captain was struck with awe and wondered; he ordered that they should be treated better, and allowed their brothers and others to visit them and enjoy their company; for even Pudens, the officer and jailer, had become a believer. ### Chapter 18.
->They are led to the arena and scourged.<-

The day of their victory dawned, and they walked in line from the prison to the arena <note>original: Schauplatz, referring to the amphitheater</note> as if to heaven, joyful and with bright countenances; and though they trembled, it was for joy and not from fear. Perpetua followed with a calm face and steady steps, as a beloved matron of Christ, our God; she whose gaze <note>literally: the rays of her eyes</note> shamed all the onlookers. Likewise, Felicitas rejoiced that she had safely given birth to her child and was now able to struggle with the wild beasts—going from the blood of the midwife to the net <note>Refers to the transition from the blood of childbirth to the net used to trap victims in the arena</note>, and after the birth, being washed by the second baptism of her martyr-blood. When they had been led in through the usual Gate of Death into the arena, and an attempt was made to force them to put on the customary clothing—namely, the men in the red robes <term>Talahr; a long, flowing priestly garment</term> of the priests of Saturn, and the women in the white caps of the priestesses of Ceres—they resisted it earnestly with heroic steadfastness. For they said: "We have come here voluntarily for this very reason, that we might preserve our freedom of conscience; we have risked our lives so that we would do nothing of the sort: we have made this agreement with you!" Injustice recognized the fairness of this request; therefore, the captain permitted them to be led in just as they were. Perpetua then began to sing, and was already treading upon the head of the Egyptian <note>original: Egyptiers Haupt; this refers to a vision Perpetua had in prison where she fought an Egyptian, representing the Devil, and defeated him</note>. Revocatus, Saturnius, and Saturus signaled to the spectators with threats; and when they caught sight of the judge Hilarianus, they spoke to him: "You judge us, but God will judge you!" ### Chapter 19.
->Each obtains the manner of death he desired.<-

But He who said: *Ask, and you shall receive* (John 16:24), granted those who prayed such an outcome as each had wished. For when they had once spoken of it together earlier in the prison, Saturnius desired to be thrown to all the wild beasts, for the greater glory of his crown <note>The "martyr's crown," a common early Christian metaphor for the reward of eternal life following a death for the faith.</note>. When they had now come into the arena <note>original: Schauplatz</note>, he and Revocatus were tormented by a leopard and a bear. Saturus, however, who did not wish to be killed by a bear, desired to end his life by the bite of a leopard. When a wild boar was to be let loose upon him, the hunter who had the wild boar under his supervision was instead gored by the same beast, so that he died of it after the games were ended; Saturus, meanwhile, was only dragged along by the sow. Afterwards, they tried to set a bear upon him, but the bear would not come out of its cage. Therefore, Saturus was called back a second time.

### Chapter 20.
->How Perpetua and Felicitas are handled by a wild cow.<-

For the women, the devil had prepared a wild cow—an unusual choice made for the shameful mockery of their gender <note>The use of a cow was intended as a cruel irony against Perpetua, a nursing mother, and Felicitas, who had just given birth.</note>. Thus they were stripped, wrapped in nets, and brought out into the arena. The crowd itself was horrified by this, as they saw that one (namely Perpetua) was so delicate, while the other (Felicitas) was fresh from childbirth with breasts still dripping with milk. Consequently, they were called back and dressed in loose robes. Perpetua was then led in first; she was tossed into the air by the cow and fell upon her hips. When she saw that her clothing was torn at the hip, she pulled it over herself, thinking more of her modesty than of her pain. She was then called back, where she first modestly pinned up her scattered hair; for it would not befit a victorious martyr to suffer with disheveled hair like one in mourning, lest she should seem to weep in the moment of her glorification. Thus she stood up, and seeing the other woman (Felicitas) likewise thrown down by the wild cow...

### Chapter 21.

->Saturus’s edifying end, and the final execution of all with<-
->the sword.<-

In the same manner, **Saturus** exhorted the official **Pudens** at the other gate, when he was called back from the arena unharmed by the wild boar and the bear, and said: "Here I am again, as I promised and foretold; I have yet suffered nothing from the beasts. Soon thereafter, at the end of the spectacles, he was thrown to a leopard, which gave him a bite from which he bled so much that the people, as he turned around, gave him the testimony of the baptism of blood <note>In the early church, martyrdom was often called a "second baptism" or "baptism of blood," believed to cleanse the soul of those who died for their faith.</note> and shouted: "He is well washed!" <note>original: "Er ist wohl gewaschen!" A mocking cry from the crowd, ironically referencing the cleansing water of Christian baptism.</note> Truly, he was well off who became such a spectacle. At the same time, he asked for his ring to be handed to him from his finger, which he dipped into the bloody wound and gave back to **Pudens** as a hereditary pledge and a memorial of his blood. Thereupon they brought him, half-dead, to the place where those who had not been completely killed by the beasts were to be finally executed. # 16. St. Leonides, Father of Origen;
# Plutarchus, Serenus I, Heraclides, Heron, Serenus II, Hera, Basilides, Potamiana and Marcella — at Alexandria in Egypt. AD 210 & following.

## Chapter 1.

->On the Persecution under Severus, Anno 210, and the Martyrdom of Leonides, the Father of Origen.<-

When the Emperor Severus, writes <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the early church historian whose *Ecclesiastical History* is the primary source for this account</note>, stirred up a persecution against the congregations of Christ in the year 210, splendid monuments were indeed raised everywhere in all congregations by the holy champions of faith and godliness; but Alexandria became particularly renowned for this, since from all of Thebaid <note>the region of Upper Egypt, centered around ancient Thebes</note> and Egypt the most elect fighters of the faith were led there as to the greatest arena, and endured every manner of torture and death-sentence with unconquerable spirit, receiving the immortal crowns. Among these was also Leonides, who is said to have been the father of the famous Origen — he was beheaded, and left behind the aforementioned son, who was still very young. It is not out of place to record here the fervent longing for the faith that burned in that son, especially since his praiseworthy memory is preserved on the lips of many people.

<header>History of Martyrs / Year 210 AD, etc.</header>

The Prefect <note>The Roman official in charge of the province, likely referring to the period under Aquila or Scapula during the reign of Septimius Severus.</note> stirred up a severe persecution a second time. During this period, Origen visited not only the martyrs in the prisons and those who faced the final sentence of death, but also those who were being led away to their executions after the verdict had been delivered. He spoke with them so boldly, kissed them publicly, and greeted them with such reverence that he would have often been pelted with stones by the raging pagan mob had Divine Goodness not protected him and provided him with the opportunity to escape. Out of the fierce envy of the pagans, they stationed a guard of soldiers at his door because of the many people coming and going who were being instructed by him in the faith. For this reason, he was safe almost nowhere in Alexandria and was forced to change his residence several times. During the day he occupied himself with his spiritual exercises, and for most of the night, he read the Holy Scriptures. He practiced fasting, slept very little, and did so without a bed, lying on the bare earth. Most of all, he took to heart the Savior’s word in the Gospel, where He admonishes that one should not provide for "two tunics nor shoes" <note>A reference to Matthew 10:10; Origen interpreted this literally as a call to extreme apostolic poverty.</note>; that is, not to lose time with worry over future abundance. Therefore, he was so very poor that his close friends marveled at it, and he met many who were willing to support him from their own wealth because of the great effort he applied to teaching the things of the Spirit. But he loved this rigorous poverty; for many years he wore no shoes at all, but went about barefoot. Moreover, he abstained from wine and similar strong drinks, as well as from necessary refreshment and nourishment, to such an extent that it was feared he might shorten his life thereby.

# History of Martyrdom / Year 210, etc.

When the Governor <note>likely referring to the Roman Prefect of Egypt</note> provoked another severe persecution, he [Origen] not only visited the martyrs in the prisons and those facing the final death sentence, but also those who were being led to their deaths after receiving their judgment. He spoke with them so boldly, kissed them publicly, and greeted them with such reverence that he would often have been showered with stones by the raging pagan mob, had Divine goodness not protected him and granted him the opportunity to escape. For this reason, he was no longer safe almost anywhere in Alexandria and had to change his residence several times. During the day, he was occupied with his spiritual exercises, and most of the night he read the Holy Scriptures. He practiced fasting, slept very little, and then without a bed, upon the bare earth. Most of all, he took to heart the Savior’s word from the Gospel, where He admonishes that one should not worry about having two coats or shoes; <note>A reference to Matthew 10:10, where Jesus instructs his disciples on a life of simplicity.</note> that is, not to lose time worrying about future abundance. Therefore, he was so utterly poor that his close friends marveled at it. He met many who were willing to support him from their own wealth because of the great effort he applied to the teaching of the Spirit; but he loved his arduous poverty and for many years wore no shoes at all, but went about barefoot. Furthermore, he abstained from wine and similar strong drinks, as well as from necessary refreshment and nourishment, so that it was feared he might even shorten his life thereby.

# 16. Section on St. *Leonides* and *Potamiana*, etc.

They considered the death of *Plutarch* <note>original: "Plutarchi", the Latin genitive form</note> to be the instrument of his conversion; yet Divine Providence preserved him even then. But from the female sex as well, *Hera*, before she was baptized, departed from this world as a martyr after receiving the baptism of fire (*). The fame of this woman still blooms (*Eusebius writes* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History," who recorded these events in the early 4th century</note> nearly two hundred years later) in those parts of *Egypt*; for she endured countless persecutions from her suitors to preserve her physical chastity and virginity (for besides the beauty of her spirit, she also bloomed with physical beauty), and suffered much for the sake of faith in Christ; until finally, after a nearly cruel and, it must be said, horrific martyrdom, she was consumed by fire along with her mother, *Marcella*. For when *Aquila*, the President <note>The Roman Prefect or Governor of Egypt</note> in *Egypt*, had her most cruelly tortured over her entire body, he finally threatened that he would hand her over to the gladiators to be violated; but when she had reflected for a moment and was asked what she had decided, it is said she gave such an answer that even the heathens were horrified.

### The 8th Chapter.

->How the holy Potamiäna was accused by her unchaste master,<-
->and put to death in a cauldron full of hot pitch.<-

This remarkable story of the most blessed Potamiäna is also described by Palladius <note>Palladius (c. 363–420 AD) was a bishop and historian of early Christian monasticism.</note>, from the report of the priest Isidore, who heard it from the mouth of the great Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great, the famous desert hermit.</note>, with somewhat broader circumstances, as follows: Potamiäna, a certain well-formed daughter <note>Likely meaning a young woman of status or beauty.</note> at the time of the Emperor Maximinus (*) the persecutor, was a servant-girl of a voluptuous, unchaste man, who sought in vain to persuade and defile her with many pleas and promises. Because of this, he finally became enraged and denounced her as a Christian to the President <note>The Roman governor or prefect of the province.</note> at Alexandria, claiming she had cursed the time of the current Emperors because of the persecutions; at the same time, he promised the President a large sum of money to her misfortune, saying: "If you can persuade her to my will, then spare her and do her no harm; but if she remains in her old stubbornness, then kill her, so that she does not bring the lust I revealed to her into public view to my shame!" When the brave virgin was brought before the judgment seat, various painful instruments <note>original: "peinliche Instrumenta," referring to tools used for judicial torture.</note> lay ready, with which her body was to be tortured; but she overcame both these and many clever temptations from the judge, remaining in her spirit as firm and immovable as a tower. However, the judge had devised a particularly cruel kind of torment above all other tools of pain; for he commanded that a large cauldron full of pitch should be set over the fire and made boiling hot. When the pitch was bubbling and very hot, the cruel President turned to the blessed woman and spoke: "Go there, and obey the will of your master; if not, know that I will have you thrown into this cauldron!" She, however, answered and said: "Far be it that a judge should be so very unjust,

### The 2nd Chapter.

First, they seized an elder named Metranus and tried to force him to blaspheme Christ. Following this, they brought a believing woman named Quinta to the Temple of Serapis <note>Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity; his temple in Alexandria, the Serapeum, was one of the most magnificent in the ancient world.</note> and tried to force her to worship the idol. However, as she showed her abhorrence for it and cursed it, they tied her feet together and dragged her by her feet through the entire city over the sharp stones of the alleys; they struck her head against a millstone and scourged her; finally, they brought her out through the gate and stoned her to death. Then they all stormed the houses of the Christians with one mind, and wherever they knew of any nearby, they rushed there, plundered, and robbed whatever they found. What was precious they kept for themselves, but common furniture and wooden items they smashed and burned in the streets. Thus, the city looked no different than if it had been conquered and plundered by enemies. But the brothers <note>A common term for fellow members of the Christian faith.</note> stayed out of their way and saved themselves by flight; they suffered the plundering of their goods with joy, just as the Apostle Paul testifies of the same in Hebrews 10, verse 34. <note>The biblical passage refers to early Christians who accepted the confiscation of their property because they believed they had better and lasting possessions in heaven.</note> Not one of them, as far as I am aware at this time, who fell into their hands—

## The 3rd Chapter.

Such pressure lasted for a long time. This was followed by an uprising and civil war, in which they were made to feel for themselves the same cruelty with which they had raged against us; because of this, we received a little breathing room as their fury turned away from us.

## Chapter 5.

### Chapter 7.

->The Martyrdom of<-
->Heron, Ater, Isidorus, Dioscorus (a boy), and Nemesius<-

Likewise, **Heron**, **Ater**, and **Isidorus**—all three being Egyptians—and with them **Dioscorus**, a boy of fifteen years, were brought before the judge. When the judge first dealt with this youth, Dioscorus, before the others, he hoped to break him—sometimes with words, as one whom he thought could be easily persuaded, and sometimes with torture, hoping to compel a delicate, soft boy. However, the youth yielded neither to persuasion nor to pain. The others were cruelly beaten, and after they had bravely endured their torments, they were surrendered to the fire. But Dioscorus, who had become glorious in the eyes of all the spectators and had answered all questions wisely, was set free by the astonished judge; the judge testified that, because of the boy's youth, he wished to grant him a reprieve for repentance. "This divine Dioscorus still lives among us," Bishop Dionysius writes further, "having been preserved for a greater and more enduring struggle" (*). Furthermore, **Nemesius**, an Egyptian, was initially maliciously accused of being a companion and accomplice to robbers. When he cleared himself of this before the captain, as it was a matter foreign to him, he was denounced as a Christian and led before the governor. This most unjust judge had him tortured and beaten twice as severely as the actual robbers, and afterward, along with the robbers...

(*) This chapter shows the beginning and origin of the lives of the Fathers and Brothers in the desert, which arose through this persecution under the Emperor Decius, as clearly appears from the *Life of Paul of Thebes*; see page 1126 in the first part. ### Chapter 12.

->Of the fallen *Serapion*, his penance, and his death.<-

In the same letter to the aforementioned *Fabian*, Bishop Dionysius mentions another remarkable story concerning one who had fallen away, as follows: Among us there was also a faithful old man named *Serapion*, who for a long time had walked blamelessly but had fallen during the persecution. To this trailing end of the rope they tied the feet of the holy man, and then goaded the ox with sharp spikes, so that it ran from the highest point of the temple <note>This refers to the Capitolium of Toulouse, which sat on a height</note> down the stairs into the street. It was soon over, for on the first steps of the stairs, the blessed martyr struck his head against the stones with such force that his brains spilled out, and all the limbs of his body were shattered; then the Lord Christ received his holy soul, which had fought faithfully for His name’s sake, just as pagan fury <note>original: "Heydnische Raserey"</note> released it to the place where it was crowned after the victory. 

The lifeless body, however, which felt no more violence, was dragged by the raging bull until the rope broke. At that place, he was then buried in haste; for at that time there were few Christians there, who moreover feared pagan rage in burying the holy man’s body. Thus, two women <note>original: "zwey Weiblein"; the text uses a diminutive common in hagiographic descriptions of the "weaker" sex showing "strong" faith</note>, who overcame the weakness of their gender with brave faith and were stronger than all men—having also been encouraged to patience in suffering, I believe, by their bishop's example—took the blessed man's corpse, placed it in a wooden coffin, and buried it in the nearest spot. They leveled the earth again so skillfully as to be unnoticed, so that the holy and venerable remains might be hidden rather than merely buried. This was done to prevent malicious people, should they see any honor paid to the body in its burial, from immediately digging it up and tearing it to pieces, which would have robbed him even of that humble burial. Praise be to Almighty **God**, who has crowned His martyr in peace; to Him belongs the honor and the glory for all eternity. Amen.

# 19. St. Pionius, Lemnus, Sabina, Asclepiades, and Macedonia. Year 250.

## Chapter 1.

->The memory of the Saints should be held in honor.<-

It is the Apostolic command that one must recount the merits of the Saints and keep them in memory, because he <note>Likely referring to the Apostle Paul or the collective apostolic tradition</note> knew that through the remembrance of their conduct, the fire of love grows in the breasts of the Saints—especially in those who strive to faithfully follow their example and struggle to do as they did. Therefore, it would not be proper to remain silent about the suffering of the holy martyr Pionius; for while he was still alive, he showed many erring brothers the right path, and after he later became a martyr, he confirmed his teaching in an exemplary way through his suffering.

## Chapter 2.

->Pionius and his fellow combatants are informed of their imprisonment through a vision; they thus bind themselves with a rope and await its fulfillment.<-

It happened on the twenty-third of February (Year 250), just as there was a great festival day in Smyrna in Asia <note>Smyrna is modern-day Izmir, Turkey</note>, namely the memorial day of the blessed martyr Polycarp <note>Polycarp was a famous early bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of the Apostle John</note>, during the time of the persecution under Emperor Decius, that Pionius, Asclepiades, Lemnus (a priest of the faithful <note>original: "Rechtgläubigen"</note>), as well as Sabina and Macedonia, were seized in the persecution. Because the Lord reveals everything to those who trust Him, Pionius also saw the impending sufferings, which he did not fear. Thus it happened the day before, when they were to celebrate the aforementioned feast of the holy martyr Polycarp, that he, along with Sabina and Asclepiades, was devoutly occupied with fasting and prayer; there he saw in a vision that he would be taken prisoner the following day. As he recognized this clearly and certainly, because it had been shown so brightly to him in the vision, he took a rope and tied his own, Sabina’s, and Asclepiades’ necks together, so that when those came who were to put them in bonds, they [the martyrs]...

...found bound, so that the authorities might recognize that they were doing nothing new to them. They also wished it to be noted that they would not be led away in the same manner as other apostates <note>People who had renounced their Christian faith to escape persecution</note>, because they had already presented themselves even before it was commanded of them, as a testimony of their faith and as proof of their free will.

### Chapter 3.
->Polemon the Chamberlain takes them captive and leads them before the court in the public marketplace.<-

After they had now performed their prayer and partaken of bread and water on the holy feast day, Polemon the Chamberlain entered to them, surrounded by a mob which the High Court had assigned to Polemon to seek out the Christians. When he saw Pionius, he spoke these words to him with his impure mouth: "You know well enough the Emperor’s command, that he has ordered you to sacrifice!" Pionius said: "We indeed know of commands, but only those which bid us to worship God." The Chamberlain said: "Come with me to the marketplace, so that you may learn that I have spoken the truth." Sabina and Asclepiades, however, spoke with a clear voice: "We obey the true God." As they were led to the marketplace and placed before the court, the common people saw the rope around their necks and crowded in out of a curious desire. Thus the entire marketplace was filled with an innumerable multitude, so much so that even the roofs of the houses were full of spectators; an innumerable number of women also arrived because of the festival day; and the Jewish women also left their work and watched, because it was the Sabbath or Saturday. Old and young, great and small were present; the short and small people carried chairs and benches with them so that they would certainly not miss out on the miracle <note>The "miracle" (original: *Mirakel*) refers here to the public spectacle or the extraordinary sight of the Christians' steadfastness</note>.

### Chapter 4.

### Chapter 6.
#### *Saint Pionius* disputes with *Alexander*.

Thereupon, an idle and harmful, evil man among the people named *Alexander* spoke to *Pionius*: Listen now to our arguments <note>original: "Beweis-Reden"</note> concerning our religion! He answered: It is much more fitting for you to listen to me; for what you know is already known to me, but you do not know what I know. Then the former looked scornfully at the martyr’s bonds and spoke mockingly: What are these fetters supposed to mean? He gave him this answer: They signify, when we are led through the streets of the city, that we are not idol-worshippers <note>original: "Götzen-Diener"</note>, and that we do not belong to your idol-temples; moreover, that you may know there is no need for a judicial interrogation, since we have voluntarily given ourselves up as prisoners. When he now fell silent, and the people continued to persist with pleas and persuasion that they should surely comply and sacrifice to the idols, the martyr repeated his previous answer and spoke: We remain firm and immovable in our once-established resolution! Afterward, he began to earnestly rebuke and exhort those standing around, and showed them the past and future judgments of GOD. But *Alexander* spoke: What use is your chattering? Since you have no freedom to live, follow us, for you must necessarily perish.

### Chapter 8.

->The further examination and confession of faith of **Saint Pionius**.<-

Again **Polemon** spoke to **Pionius**: Obey us! **Pionius** answered him: If you have the command either to persuade or to punish us, then you will necessarily have to begin with punishing, since you cannot persuade us after all. He answered: I sacrifice to please no man.

### Chapter 9.

->After Pionius, Sabina—who is called Theodata—is interrogated, and likewise Asclepiades.<-

After this, Polemon (who had a notary <term>notarium: a court reporter or legal secretary who recorded the official proceedings</term> or court clerk as an assistant to write down the answers) spoke to Pionius: "What is your name?" Pionius said: "A Christian!" Polemon asked: "What kind of Christian?" Pionius answered: "Of the orthodox <note>original: "Rechtgläubigen"</note> universal <note>original: "allgemeinen"; referring to the Catholic or universal church as opposed to sectarian groups</note> church." With that, Polemon left Pionius be and turned to Sabina. Now, Pionius had previously advised her that she should call herself Theodata, so that she might not be recognized by her true name and fall back into the hands of her ungodly mistress. This woman, in the time of Emperor Gordian <note>Emperor Gordian III, reigned 238–244 AD</note>, had wanted to force Sabina, as her maidservant, to renounce her faith; she had her imprisoned and banished into the wretchedness of the mountains, where the brothers <note>fellow members of the Christian community</note> secretly provided her with the necessities of life. Afterward, through the care and diligence of the brothers, it came to pass that she was delivered from the woman’s bondage and from her chains by means of flight. However, she stayed close to Pionius, which led to her being captured along with him. When Polemon now asked what her name was, she said: "Theodata, and a Christian." Polemon asked further: "Since you are a Christian woman, from what community of Christians do you come?" She answered: "Of the orthodox universal church." Polemon asked her: "What kind of God do you serve?" She answered: "The Almighty God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and everything that is within them, whom we know through His Word, Jesus Christ." Furthermore, he also asked Asclepiades, who stood nearby, what his name was. Asclepiades gave the answer: "A Christian." Polemon asked: "From which community?" Asclepiades answered: "From the orthodox universal church." Polemon asked: "What kind of God do you honor?" He answered: "Christ." Polemon spoke: "How so? That is surely another one!" <note>The Roman official likely perceived "the Almighty God" and "Christ" as two different deities, highlighting the pagan misunderstanding of Christian monotheism</note> Asclepiades replied: "Not at all; He is the very same one whom they have just now confessed."

Then one answered him and said: "You yourself experienced the famine with us!" He replied: "I had my hope in the Lord through it."

When they were thus gathered together, devout servants of God came to visit them and wished to share alms with them. Pionius and his companions, however, steadfastly refused the charity of these believers, saying: That he had lived in great poverty before, and yet had been a burden to no one; why then should he now be forced to receive alms? This annoyed the jailers <note>In historical prisons, jailers often kept a portion of the food and money brought to prisoners as "fees," so refusing alms cost the guards their profit.</note>, who derived their profit from such alms, and they locked them in the innermost and darkest holes of the dungeon. There, they were deprived of all refreshment and light, and were forced to endure indescribable agony in the darkness and stench. But when they were alone there, they thanked God and sang many songs of praise in His honor; and after they had persevered in this for a long time, they fell silent for a while and performed their remaining devotions. In the hearts of the guards, however, the resulting remorse drove away their anger; for they came and wanted to return the prisoners to a better and previous situation. But they preferred to stay where they were and said with a loud voice: Praise be to You, O Lord, without ceasing, that You turn everything for the best!

### Chapter 12.

->*Pionius delivers a lamentation for those who have fallen and admonishes them.*<-

Nevertheless, they eventually obtained the freedom to do as they wished. Thus, they spent day and night in teaching and prayer; where the stubborn had the opportunity to debate religion with them, for instruction in the faith and as medicine against death. Consequently, during such freedom as they had in the prison, many heathens and idol-worshipers came in to them and wanted to persuade Pionius. But when they heard him speak, they wondered greatly and found themselves rebuked in their consciences for having come to him with evil intent. There also entered those who had allowed themselves to be forced to sacrifice <note>These are the *lapsi* (the fallen), Christians who had yielded to Roman pressure to perform pagan sacrifices to avoid execution.</note>, and they acted most piteously with many tears, whimpering, and lamentations; especially those who had always enjoyed a good reputation for their virtuous conduct. When Pionius saw these people sighing and weeping so piteously without ceasing, he spoke the following words with mingled tears: I am martyred anew, and tormented as if I were being torn limb from limb; for I see the pearls of the church thus lying under the feet of swine, and the stars of heaven pulled down to the earth by the dragon's tail; <note>A reference to Revelation 12:4.</note>. The vineyard, which God’s right hand had planted, is rooted up by a single sow, and is by every

We have cast **God** out from the eyes of our minds; some have become coarse despisers, others have sinned lightheadedly with pleasure, and one has accused and badly wounded another; though it would have been proper for our righteousness to have been better than that of the Scribes and *Pharisees*.

## Chapter 13.
->Speech of Rebuke against the *Jews* / and Proof of *Christ's* Constant Disciples.<-

I also hear, alas, that some of you are going with the *Jews* into their assemblies <note>In the 3rd century, some Christians still maintained ties to Jewish communities or sought refuge in synagogues to avoid Roman persecution, a practice Pionius here strictly forbids.</note>. Do not be with them as "princes of *Gomorrah*" and "judges in *Sodom*," whose hands have washed themselves in the blood of the innocent and in the wounds of the Saints; for we have neither killed the prophets nor betrayed the Savior. I must not linger long with mere words; remember what you have heard. I have found it to be true myself, how they, with their shameful mouths, have spoken wicked words and boasted everywhere that the Lord Jesus Christ was killed by them as a mere man. Tell me then: what man’s disciple, having been cruelly killed, has for so many years in succession driven out evil spirits—and continues to drive them out? For which master’s name, who was crucified, have so many disciples and followers allowed themselves to be so cruelly tortured? Why should I mention the other miracles that have occurred in the universal Church <note>The "universal Church" (German: *allgemeinen Kirchen*) refers here to the collective body of Christian believers throughout the Roman world.</note>, since those people do not want to know that only he dies in an evil and violent manner who, out of a weariness of living, murders himself with his own hands and his own will (such as Judas). But for those wicked souls, it is not enough to blaspheme Him; rather, because they do not know the mystery of His death—how He gave up His life voluntarily—they say that the Lord Christ was a sorcerer, and that He rose after the crucifixion through such arts, but vanished like a shadow. Thus, whatever the Scripture says of the Lord Christ, they transform into blasphemies with their shameful, lying speeches. Are those who say such things not sinners? Are they not slanderers? Are they not godless?

### Chapter 14.

->Proof against the Jews, that the Lord Jesus was not raised from the dead through sorcery like Samuel.<-

I will repeat what I often heard the Jews themselves say in my youth, and I will immediately refute their lies; for it is written: Saul questioned the sorceress and said to her: "Raise up for me the prophet Samuel." Then the woman saw a man ascending with a long robe. Saul believed that it was the true Samuel, and asked him what he wished to know. *1 Samuel 28.* Now then: could the sorceress raise Samuel? If those people say she could do it, then they confess that unrighteousness is more powerful than righteousness. If they deny that the woman truly accomplished this, then they must admit that our Lord Jesus Christ did not rise in such a way, but truly (*), and be condemned, or [the truth]—

...yield approval to the truth. We offer the following proof:
How could the evil spirit of the sorceress <note>This refers to the "Witch of Endor" from 1 Samuel 28, whom King Saul consulted to summon the spirit of the dead Prophet Samuel.</note> bring forth the soul of the holy Prophet from Abraham’s bosom <note>Abraham’s Bosom: A biblical term for the place of comfort in the afterlife where the righteous dead awaited the Messiah.</note>, where it had already been for a long time and rested in Paradise; since the weaker power is always overcome by the greater? They maintain, however, that Samuel was called forth into the light. Not at all! What is the truth of the matter? Just as the angels are at the command of all those who serve God with a pure heart; so too do the evil spirits obey those sorcerers, and soothsayers, and lottery-peddlers, and all those who swarm about in a frantic manner on the wrong paths and sell their mad fortunetelling (*). For the Apostle says: If Satan can transform himself into an angel of light, what wonder is it then that his servants can transform themselves? 2 Cor. 11:13–14. Therefore, the Antichrist looks like Christ. Thus, Samuel was not brought forth, but rather the evil spirits presented themselves to the woman and the transgressor Saul in his form, which the Scripture sufficiently indicates in what follows; for Samuel says to Saul: "Today you shall be with me!" <note>1 Samuel 28:19.</note> How could Samuel and the idolatrous King dwell together? To whom is it not known that Samuel could not be in the place of the unrighteous? Accordingly, since it was not possible for anyone to awaken the soul of a prophet; how then can one believe that a man, through sorcery, has awakened the Lord Christ, whom the disciples saw ascend into heaven and made this known through their own deaths? So then, do not listen to such people who have practiced voluntary harlotry and idolatry, for we Christians are better than they; give them no approval nor promise, but rather become sober and do penance; be converted to Christ, who is kind and will receive you again (**).

## Chapter 15.

->They are tempted by the judge in the dungeon.<-

After he had delivered a long speech to them in this manner, he ordered them to leave the dungeon. Meanwhile, Polemon the Chamberlain <term>Cammer-Herr: A high-ranking court official or chamberlain.</term> and Theophilus the Master of the Horse <term>Stallmeister: Historically, the official in charge of the stables, often a position of significant military or administrative rank.</term> arrived, surrounded by guards and a great crowd, who cried out with a terrifying voice: "Look now, Eudämon your predecessor has sacrificed! <note>Eudämon was the Bishop of Smyrna who reportedly lapsed—committed apostasy—by performing pagan sacrifices to avoid execution.</note> You must obey now as well; come to the Temple of the Magistrate, for Eudämon and Lepidus wish to speak with you themselves." But Pionius answered and said: "It is indeed the custom that prisoners must wait until a Roman Consul or Chief Judge arrives; why do you so boldly interfere in another’s office?" After such a rebuke they left, but soon returned with an even larger crowd. Then the Chief Captain spoke deceitfully and in a feigned manner to Pionius: "The Chief Judge has assigned your case to us, whom you have just seen entering, and has commanded that we should send you to Ephesus <note>A major Roman city in Asia Minor, acting as a regional capital.</note>." Pionius said: "Let whoever was sent for that purpose come; we are ready to go with him." The Chief Captain, who was a man of imposing stature, spoke then: "If you do not obey our command in everything, you shall learn what power I have." As he said this, he seized Pionius by the throat in such a way that he could barely draw breath, and handed him over to the guards so that they might drag him away; they tightened his throat so much that he could neither breathe in nor out. The others were also led to the market, along with Sabina, all of whom cried out: "We are Christians!" (*) And as is customary with unwilling prisoners, they let themselves be dragged along the ground so that they might proceed more slowly and only reach the temple with great effort; thus six guards led Pionius, half carrying and half dragging him. And because they grew weary of pulling, they kicked him in the sides with their feet so that he might lighten their load and, moved by the pain, follow

## Chapter 16.
->They are dragged before the court.<-

In such a manner, they carried him on their shoulders with a jubilant shouting toward the sacrificial altar like a sacrificial offering, and placed him there, where *Eudämon* <note>Eudämon was the Bishop of Smyrna who had famously renounced his faith (apostatized) shortly before this event.</note> also was, who had already sacrificed to the idols. Then *Lepidus* spoke with a solemn voice: "Why will you not sacrifice?" They answered: "Because we are Christians!" The judge spoke again: "What kind of a God do you honor?" *Pionius* answered: "The one who made the heavens and adorned them with stars; who founded the earth and decorated it with flowers and trees; who arranged the rivers and seas around the world and set their boundaries and shores!" Then the other spoke: "Do you mean the one who was crucified?" *Pionius* spoke: "I mean Him whom the Father sent for the salvation of the world!" Then all the court officials began to laugh loudly, and *Lepidus* mocked him as well. But *Pionius* spoke: "Shame on you, you idol-worshipers, and do not disgrace the office of justice; yet if your laws so please, why do you break your own laws and not perform what is commanded of you? For you have orders not to encounter those who contradict you in this way, but to put them to death." <note>Pionius is pointing out the legal hypocrisy: Roman law required the execution of those who refused to sacrifice, not their public mockery or forced participation.</note>

# Chapter 18.

->Further events at the marketplace / and on the way back to the prison.<-

One of the most prominent men, however, said: "Do not speak so loudly, Pionius!" Hereupon came the idol-priest, who was accustomed to performing the sacrifices publicly, and brought the entrails from the slaughtered sacrificial animal as he had roasted them on a spit, intending to bring them to Pionius; however, out of sudden terror, he did not dare to offer it to anyone, but instead gorged the unholy, shameful food into his own idolatrous breast alone before all the people. But they said with a clear voice: "We are Christians!" When these court officials did not know what else to do with them, they led them back to the prison; on the way through the streets, they received many blows to the cheek from the people, who inflicted all kinds of disgrace upon them. When Pionius was about to enter the prison, one of the guards struck him on the head with great force; but that same guard's hand and side swelled to such an extent that he could barely live. ->Quintilianus, the Roman Proconsul, interrogates Pionius and the others in court.<-

After a few days, Quintilianus, the Roman Proconsul and High Judge, came to Smyrna to hold court. When Pionius was brought forward, he asked him: "What is your name?" He answered: "Pionius!" The judge spoke: "Sacrifice!" <note>The Roman authorities demanded that Christians perform a public sacrifice to the Roman gods or the Emperor as a test of loyalty to the state.</note> He gave for an answer: "I will by no means do such a thing." Quintilianus spoke: "Of what sect are you?" Pionius answered: "Of the universal Christian one!" <note>original: "allgemeinen Christlichen." This likely refers to the "catholic" or mainstream church as opposed to various Gnostic groups.</note> The judge asked further: "What are you then?" He replied: "I am a priest or elder of the church." Again the Proconsul spoke: "So, you were their teacher?" Pionius gave for an answer: "Yes, I taught." The judge continued: "Then you were a teacher of folly!" He answered: "Of godliness!" The judge countered again: "What godliness?" The martyr answered: "The godliness with which we serve God, who created heaven, earth, and sea." Quintilianus spoke: "Just sacrifice!" Pionius gave for an answer: "I have learned to worship the living God!" Then the Proconsul spoke: "We honor all gods, including heaven and those within it; why do you look into the air? Sacrifice!" He answered: "I do not look into the air, but at Him who made the air." Again the judge spoke: "Tell me, who made it?" He answered: "I am not permitted; hear me separately." <note>Pionius suggests that the nature of the Creator is a profound topic requiring a more serious, private hearing than a public trial.</note> Again the judge spoke: "You must necessarily confess that it is Jupiter who is in heaven, with whom all gods and goddesses are gathered; so sacrifice to him then, as he is the ruler of all gods and of heaven."

# Chapter 21.
## The Execution of **Pionius** and **Metrodorus**, along with the others.

Thus this extraordinary man went to the place of execution as an example to the Christians, but as a joy to the godless; not as usually happens to those being led to their death, whose feet wobble, whose knees sink, and whose limbs all grow stiff, but rather he was cheerful and of good courage. His mind was conscious of no evil that might have caused him to doubt, nor did any other circumstances hinder his joyful steps; thus he was swift of foot, lively of body, secure in spirit, and with a perfect soul he went to his death. ### Chapter 23.

### Chapter 1.
->Achatius is judicially interrogated by the Governor Martianus.<-

Whenever we contemplate the magnificent deeds of the servants of God, we thank Him who protects the suffering in their pain and crowns the victor with glory. Now Martianus—who was appointed by Emperor Decius as the Provincial Governor in Syria and was an enemy of the Christian faith—ordered Achatius to be summoned before him, having heard that he was a shield and refuge for the Christians in Antioch. When Achatius had been led in to him, Martianus spoke to him: "You ought to love our Emperor and his kin, as you enjoy the benefit of Roman protection as his subject." Achatius answered: "To whom does the Emperor's welfare go more to heart, and who loves him as much as we Christians do? For we pray constantly and without ceasing for him, that God

# 20. St. Achatius

...of which he knew nothing beforehand, he imprudently killed the one he desired to see with a plate <note>original: "Teller"; this refers to the myth of the god Apollo accidentally killing his companion Hyacinthus with a discus, which early modern writers often described as a round "plate"</note>. "Should I sacrifice to the one who once served Neptune and guarded the cattle of Laomedon? <note>Referring to the myth where Apollo and Neptune were forced to labor for King Laomedon of Troy</note> Should I offer a sacrifice to Aesculapius, who was struck down by Jupiter with his lightning, or to the adulterous Venus and the remaining absurd deities? Should I sacrifice to them because of their shameful lives and deaths—they whom I do not consider worthy of imitation, whom I despise, condemn, and abhor? If someone today committed their deeds, could he rightly escape your laws unpunished? And yet, you honor in them that which you rightly punish in other wrongdoers." (*) Martianus spoke: "It is the habit of Christians to invent a heap of blasphemies against our gods; therefore, I command you to go with me to Jove <note>Jupiter</note> and Juno, so that we may hold a joyful feast together and show the gods their due honor." Achatius answered: "How should I be able to sacrifice here to one who lies buried in Crete? <note>Achatius is using a common early Christian argument that Zeus/Jupiter was merely a mortal king, citing the "Tomb of Zeus" in Crete as evidence of his mortality</note> Has he perhaps risen from the dead?"

## Chapter 3.
-> Achatius’s Earnest Defense Against the Judge Martianus. <-

Martianus spoke: "Either sacrifice or die!" Achatius answered: "The Dalmatians <note>A people from the Roman province of Dalmatia, often characterized in ancient texts as unruly or prone to banditry</note> do the same, who are robbers and murderers; for when they hide themselves maliciously in the bushes and narrow paths, they rob all who pass by. If a traveling wanderer comes that way, they force him either to lose his money or his life; thus, no one there asks who is right, but rather who is the strongest. It is just the same with your sentence: you want one to either do what is wrong or you threaten death. But I am terrified of nothing; I fear nothing. Public law punishes a fornicator, adulterer, thief, sodomite, sorcerer, or murderer. If I am guilty of any of these, I would condemn myself even before you do; but if I am to be punished for honoring the true God, then I am condemned not according to the laws, but according to the judge’s will." The Prophet speaks with a threat: "There is no one who does good, they have all gone astray..." <note>A reference to Psalm 14:3 or Romans 3:12</note>

...then, and have all together become corrupt. Psalm 14, verses 3-4. You cannot cleanse yourself in that. Furthermore, it is written: As one judges, so shall they be judged; and as you do, so shall it be done to you, Matthew 7:2, Luke 6:31. **Martianus** spoke: I have not been ordered to judge, but to compel; therefore, if you despise my counsel, be certain of punishment. **Achatius** answered: And I am commanded that I should not deny my **GOD**; so if you serve a mortal and perishable man <note>Referring to the Roman Emperor</note> obediently—one who shall soon be devoured by worms—how much more should I be obedient to the almighty **GOD**, whose power exists eternally, and who has said: Whoever denies me before men, him I will also deny before my Heavenly Father, when I shall judge the living and the dead in glory and power. Matthew 10:33.

## Chapter 4.
->Achatius’s Confession of Christ.<-

Martianus spoke: That which I have always wished to learn, you have just now revealed—namely, the greatest error of your superstition and law; Does **GOD**, as you say, have a son? **Achatius** answered: Yes, He has one! **Martianus** spoke: What is His name? Saint **Achatius** gave the answer: His name is **JESUS** Christ! **Martianus** spoke: Tell me, with which woman did He beget Him? Saint **Achatius** answered: **GOD** did not beget His Son in a human manner or from a woman; rather, He first formed **Adam** with His right hand. Far be it from you to ascribe carnal love of women to the Divine Majesty. He made the body of the first man from clay, and when His entire image was finished, He gave him the soul and the spirit. Thus also the Son of **GOD**, as the Word of Truth, has come forth from the heart of **GOD**; therefore it is written: Out of my heart wells forth the good word, Psalm 45:2. (*) **Martianus** spoke: Is **GOD**, then, corporeal? <note>Meaning, does He have a physical body?</note> **Achatius** answered: He alone knows best how He is, but we do not recognize His invisible essence; rather, we worship His virtue and omnipotence.

The ancients, however, who always placed **Christ** as the foundation of scriptural understanding, always understood this as referring to **Christ**, the eternal **WORD**, which ever wells up from the mouths of **GOD** and the saints; just as it did for **Adam** before the Fall.</note>

**Martianus** spoke: Since He has no body, He can have no heart, for the mind cannot exist without limbs. **Achatius** answered: Wisdom does not testify in these limbs, but is given by **GOD**; does the mind therefore depend on the body? **Martianus** spoke: Look at the Cataphrygians <note>A Christian sect from Phrygia, also known as Montanists, known for their prophetic rigor</note>, people of an ancient religion; they have converted to my mysteries <note>The state-sanctioned Roman religious rites</note>, abandoned their faith, and now they sacrifice along with us to the gods. Do not hesitate to do the same; I shall gather all your fellow believers, the Christians, and they shall follow our Emperor’s religion. Let all the people, who act according to your command, come with you. **Achatius** answered: All these are not ruled by my command, but by **GOD’S** command. Therefore, they may listen to me if I persuade them toward something good; but if I give them perverse and harmful advice, they are free to despise me.

### Chapter 5.
->Achatius refuses to be a traitor to his brothers / despises the gods / and goes free.<-

**Martianus** spoke: Show me all their names! **Achatius** answered: Their names are recorded in the Heavenly Book and upon the Divine Leaves; how should mortal eyes be able to behold what the immortal and invisible power of **GOD** has written down? **Martianus** spoke: Where are the sorcerers and companions of your craft, or the teachers of such artful deception? **Achatius** answered: We have obtained everything from **GOD** and continue to obtain it, but we loathe the company of the craft of sorcery. **Martianus** spoke: You are sorcerers for this reason—because you introduce I-know-not-what new kind of religion. **Achatius** answered: We bring to naught those [gods] whom you first created; and although you created them, you still fear them. For you would lack gods if the artist had no stone, or if the stone had no artist and sculptor. But we fear Him—not the one whom we made, but the one by whom we were made; who created us as our **LORD**, loved us as our Father, and as our Good Shepherd has snatched us from eternal death. **Martianus** spoke: Give me the names, or you shall perish under torture. **Achatius** spoke: I stand here myself before your judgment seat, and you ask for a mere name? Do you expect to be able to overcome many, when I alone overcome you? If you must be served with a name,
