# 21. St. Maximus in Asia.
## Year 250.
### Chapter 1.

->Maximus gives himself up voluntarily and confesses undaunted.<-

When Emperor Decius intended to suppress and defeat the law of the Christians, he issued bloody orders throughout the whole world, that all Christians should fall away from the true living **GOD** and sacrifice to the evil spirits; but those who would not, should be tortured and killed! At that same time, the servant of **GOD**, Maximus, a holy man, made himself known voluntarily; he was an ordinary man <note>original: *gemeiner Mann*, indicating he was a layman rather than a member of the clergy</note> who was occupied with his business affairs. When he was captured, he was brought before the Asian Governor, Optimum. Then the Governor spoke: "What is your status?" Maximus replied: "I am a free-born man, but a servant of Christ, and my name is Maximus." The Governor spoke: "What is your occupation?" Maximus answered: "I am an ordinary man and carry out my business affairs." The Governor asked further: "Are you a Christian?" Maximus replied:

"Although I am a sinner, I am nonetheless a Christian!" The Governor <note>original: *Landpfleger*, a term used here for a Roman proconsul or regional administrator</note> spoke: "Are you not aware of the commands that the invincible Emperors have issued, which have recently arrived?" Maximus asked: "Which ones?" The Governor spoke: "That all Christians should abandon their unnecessary superstition and recognize the true Emperor, to whom all are subject; and worship his gods." Maximus answered: "I have already heard this unjust command of the Emperor of this world, which is why I have voluntarily confessed and presented myself as a Christian." The Governor spoke: "Sacrifice to the gods!" Maximus answered: "I sacrifice to no other than **GOD** alone, to whom I have sacrificed from my youth, praise be to **GOD**!" The Governor spoke: "Sacrifice, so that you may remain among the living; but if you will not, I will weary you with manifold tortures." Maximus spoke: "That is exactly what I have always desired; for to that end have I given myself up, so that I might be taken from this miserable temporal life into the eternal one."

## Chapter 2.

->He is tortured in various ways and finally stoned.<-

Then the Governor commanded that he should be beaten with clubs! And as he was being beaten, he spoke to him: "Sacrifice, Maximus, so that you may be freed from such pain." Maximus answered: "These are not sufferings that are inflicted on me for the name of our **Lord JESUS Christ**, but are purely ointments <note>Maximus suggests that the physical pain of martyrdom is like a soothing balm compared to the spiritual healing it brings</note>; but if I deviate from the commands of my **Lord**, which I have learned from the Gospel <note>original: *Evangelio*</note>, then I would become a partaker of the true eternal sufferings." Thereupon the Governor commanded that he should be stretched upon the rack <note>original: *Peinige-Block*, a torture device used to stretch the limbs</note>. As he was now being stretched upon it, he spoke to him: "Become sober now from your folly, you miserable man, and sacrifice, so that you may preserve your life." Maximus answered: "I shall preserve my life if I do not sacrifice; but if I sacrifice, I lose it; for neither the clubs, nor iron hooks, nor glowing tongs cause me pain, because the grace of Christ is within me, which will preserve me eternally. The prayers of all the Saints who have fought this battle have overcome your rage and left behind for us examples of their virtues." Then the Governor pronounced the judgment against him and said: "He who has been disobedient to the holy laws, and would not sacrifice to the great goddess Diana <note>The Roman name for Artemis, whose temple in Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>, shall, as a terror to the remaining Christians, with

# 22. St. Peter, Andrew, Paul, and Dionysia at Lampsacus in Lesser Moesia on the Hellespont. 250 AD.

## Chapter 1.

->Peter is judicially interrogated at Lampsacus, tortured, and killed with the sword.<-

In the time of injustice, when the servants of **GOD** were warred against, and the earth everywhere bloomed, as it were, with the most blessed blood of the martyrs, there was seized at Lampsacus <note>An ancient Greek city in Asia Minor, on the eastern side of the Hellespont.</note> a youth named Peter, who possessed a heroic faith, beautiful in spirit and well-formed in body. He was presented to Governor Optimus. The Governor said to him: "What is your name?" He answered: "Peter!" The Governor asked him: "Are you a Christian?" Peter answered: "Yes, I am a Christian!" The Governor said: "You have the commands of the invincible Emperors before your eyes, therefore sacrifice to the great goddess Venus <note>original: *Veneri*, the Roman goddess of love and beauty.</note>." Peter answered: "I am amazed, dear Governor Optimus, that you wish to persuade me to sacrifice to an unchaste, shameful woman, who performed such deeds that it is a disgrace to relate them, since your own histories are full of her unchastity; indeed, you yourselves punish her shameful deeds in other unchaste people."

<header>22. St. Peter, Andrew, Paul, and Dionysia</header>

...harlot. <note>The text likely refers to Venus here, continuing from the previous page's discussion of the goddess's perceived immorality.</note> Since you yourselves call her a godless and public [shame], how can you urge me to worship such a disgusting creature and sacrifice to her? Therefore, it is far more fitting that I bring my holy offerings of prayer, supplication, atonement, and thanksgiving with praise to the living, true **GOD**, to the King of Eternities, **Christ**. When the Governor <note>original: *Landpfleger*, referring to the Roman official Optimus.</note> heard this, he commanded that he—even though he was still young in years—be stretched upon the torture-wheel and fastened to it with iron chains; whereby all his bones were broken and crushed into small pieces. But the more the servant of **GOD** was broken on the wheel, the more courageous he became. He remained constant in his vision and laughed at their folly, looked up toward heaven, and spoke: "I thank you, my Lord **JESUS Christ**, that you have willed to grant me this grace of enduring patience to overcome the most wicked enemy!" Now, when the Governor saw his constancy, and [seeing that] he had not become faint-hearted through such martyrdom, he commanded that he be fully executed with the sword.

### Chapter 2.
->Andrew, Paul, and Nicomachus are interrogated; Nicomachus<-
->falls away during torture and dies miserably.<-

At that same time, after the Governor had traveled with great pomp toward Troas <note>original: *Troaden*, an ancient region and city in northwest Asia Minor.</note> (and returned), they presented three others to him, namely **Andrew**, **Paul**, and **Nicomachus**. When he asked them where they were from and what religion they practiced, **Nicomachus** answered with a loud voice out of impatience: "I am a Christian!" The Governor also spoke to **Andrew** and **Paul**: "What do you say then?" They answered him: "We are Christians." Thereupon the Governor said to **Nicomachus**: "Sacrifice to the gods, as has been commanded." **Nicomachus** answered: "As you know, a Christian must not sacrifice to devils." So the Governor commanded that he be stretched upon the torture-scaffold and martyred. As he was being severely tortured and was now at the point of giving up the ghost <note>An archaic expression meaning to die.</note>, he cried out with a great voice: "I have never been a Christian, but am ready to sacrifice to the gods!" Immediately, the Governor had him taken down. But as soon as he had sacrificed, he was in that hour seized by an evil spirit, so that he fell to the ground foaming and bit off his own tongue with his teeth, whereupon his breath departed from him.

### Chapter 3.

->The virgin Dionysia boldly confesses Christ; she is handed over to two scoundrels to be violated, and is protected by Christ.<-

While the mob waited to see what would happen next, a young daughter and virgin named Dionysia, sixteen years of age, cried out and said: "O you miserable and most unfortunate man! Why have you plunged yourself into eternal and unspeakable pain for the sake of a single hour?" <note>Dionysia addresses Nicomachus, who had just renounced his faith to escape torture, only to die shortly thereafter in despair.</note> When the Governor <note>original: *Landpfleger*, referring to the Roman proconsul Optimus.</note> heard this, he ordered that she be brought before him, and he asked her if she were a Christian. She answered: "Of course I am a Christian; for this reason, I also mourn for this unfortunate man, because he did not endure the brief pain so that he might attain eternal rest." The Governor said: "This man has now found rest, since he sacrificed to the gods and the invincible emperors (*) and satisfied them; so that he would experience no further vexation on account of your vain religion, the great goddesses Diana and Venus have deigned to receive him. Therefore, you also sacrifice, so that I do not have you shamefully burned!" Dionysia said: "My **GOD** is greater than you are; therefore, I do not fear your threats. He can give me enough patience in all the suffering you wish to inflict upon me." Then the Governor handed her over to two robust scoundrels <note>original: *Kerlen*, referring here to base or lewd men.</note> to violate her; but he ordered Andrew and Paul to be taken back to prison. These two scoundrels then took God’s most chaste virgin into their house. When they had struggled in vain until midnight to weaken her by force, the desire of their lust vanished. At midnight, however, a bright-shining youth appeared to them, illuminating the whole house. Paralysed with fear, they fell at the chaste virgin's feet; she raised the terrified men up and said: "Do not be afraid, for this is my protector and guardian, since I was handed over to you by the most unjust judge." They begged her, however, to pray for them, so that no evil would befall them.

### Chapter 4.

->Andrew and Paul are stoned.<-

When morning came, all the people came to the Governor with a great outcry, demanding that he deliver Andrew and Paul to them. However, Onesicrates <note>The text cuts off here; Onesicrates is likely an official or a leader of the mob.</note>

<header>22. Saints Peter, Andrew, Paul, and Dionysia</header>

Iphicrates and Macedon, <note>original: "ficrates und Macedon." These were pagan priests who incited the crowd.</note> the priests of Diana, incited such a riot among the people. When the Governor <note>original: *Landpfleger*, a term for the Roman proconsul.</note> ordered the two martyrs to be brought before him, he said to them: "Andrew and Paul, offer sacrifice to the wondrous Diana." Andrew and Paul answered: "We recognize neither Diana nor any other impure spirits, whom you honor, as gods; and we have never shown divine honor to anyone else but **GOD** alone." When the mob heard this, they begged the Governor to hand these men over to them to be killed. When the Governor saw that he could not overcome their steadfastness, he had them severely scourged and handed them over to the people to be stoned. They took them and dragged them by their feet outside the city to be stoned.

## Chapter 5.

->The Virgin Dionysia escapes her guards and desires to die with the two martyrs; she is beheaded.<-

When the virgin of **GOD**, Dionysia, heard this, she cried and lamented, and escaped from the hands of her guards until she came to the place where the martyrs were being stoned. She threw herself upon them and said: "So that I may live with you in heaven, I wish to die with you on earth." It was reported to the Governor that Dionysia—who had been handed over to those two young scoundrels to be violated, but had been preserved by a brightly shining youth <note>A common hagiographical reference to an angel.</note>—had now escaped her watch and thrown herself upon the bodies of Andrew and Paul to be stoned along with them. Then the Governor commanded that she be dragged away and beheaded with the sword. Which was done immediately.

## Chapter 6.

->The victory of these holy martyrs.<-

In this manner, these honorable martyrs, who fought together as one, defeated the world, the devil, and the Governor Optimus through the assistance of Christ. Thus Peter was executed with various tortures, Andrew and Paul with stones, and Dionysia with the sword. This occurred in Lampsacus <note>An ancient Greek city in Asia Minor.</note> on the 15th of May, while Decius was Emperor and Optimus was Governor; there reigned our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belongs glory, honor, and power forever. Amen. <note>original: "Ruinart. Act. Mart. p. 158." Referring to Thierry Ruinart’s *Acta Martyrum* (Acts of the Martyrs), a famous collection of early Christian hagiography.</note>

# 23. Saints Tryphon and Respicius / at Nicaea. In the year 251.

## Chapter 1.

->Saints Tryphon and Respicius are brought as prisoners from Phrygia to Nicaea.<-

After the death of Emperor Gordian <note>original: "Gordiani," referring to Gordian III.</note> and his successor Philip <note>original: "Philippi," Philip the Arab.</note>, while Decius was reigning, it came to the ears of the Governor <note>original: "Landpfleger," a Roman administrative official.</note> Aquilinus in Phrygia and Bithynia that the holy men, Tryphon and Respicius, were highly esteemed by the Christians because of their divine wisdom. He then sent servants to the Magistrate <note>original: "Friede-Richter," a local judicial official.</note> Fronto at Apamea, who pursued the saints with bailiffs and took them both prisoner, according to the Governor's command. After he had found them, he handed them over to the soldiers, who bound them and led them to Nicaea, where they were placed in prison by the Governor Aquilinus because he had other public official business to attend to. Among the Christians, however, they were praised for being worthy of the Christians' **GOD**, namely Christ, and for being complete and perfect in all virtues.

## Chapter 2.

->They are interrogated by the Governor Aquilinus at Nicaea.<-

After a few days, he ordered them to be brought forward. When they entered, they were violently ignited by the fire of the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of the **Lord** with all boldness, fearlessly entering the ultimate struggle of confessing the **Lord**. Pompejanus, however, the Chief Secretary, addressed the Council and Governor thus: "Governor, the Christians from the small town of Sansoro near Apamea are present to be questioned before your illustrious and magnificent judgment seat!" Tiberius Gracchus Claudius Aquilinus spoke: "What is your name?" The saints answered: "One of us is named Tryphon, the other Respicius." Tiberius Aquilinus spoke: "In what station has fortune placed you in this world?" Saint Tryphon spoke: "Christians know of no fortune; rather, everything happens through divine providence, though men have called it fortune. Yet, if you wish to know our lineage, we are free-"

### Chapter 3.

->Their painful interrogation and great steadfastness.<-

Here, Aquilinus commanded that they be tortured if they would not give their consent. But they took off their own clothes and voluntarily surrendered themselves to the executioners' assistants for torture. While they were being very severely tortured, they spoke not a word; instead, they endured patiently, for they had the fear of the **Lord** in their hearts. And although they were martyred in various ways for nearly three hours, they did not yield to the torturers, but finally began to speak courageously to the Governor about the omnipotence of **God** and the torment awaiting the idolaters. When Aquilinus heard this, he commanded that they be taken into the woods and dragged along barefoot in the snow during the frozen wintertime, whereby the soles of their feet were completely split and wounded. When they returned to the palace from such a hunt <note>original: "Jägerey"; used here to describe the cruel "sport" of dragging them through the woods.</note>, the Governor ordered the saints to be brought before him and said to them: "Can you not yet purify yourselves <note>Likely referring to a ritual cleansing or the "purging" of their stubborn refusal to sacrifice.</note>?" Tryphon answered: "We purify ourselves always before the **Lord**, whom we serve without ceasing." Aquilinus said: "Take them back to the prison so that they have time to reconsider and exhort one another to obey the Emperor's command after setting aside their folly; for I swear by our gods, if you do not sacrifice to them, you shall be destroyed with cruel pain and torment."

## Chapter 4.
### Another Painful Examination <note>The term "Peinliches Examen" refers to a formal judicial interrogation conducted under torture.</note>.

During those same days, the Governor <note>Original: "Land-Pfleger," referring to the Proconsul Aquilinus.</note> traveled to other cities. When he returned to Nicaea after several days, where he had his seat of government, he commanded the holy ones of God to be brought before him and said to them: "Have you, in such a long time, reconsidered how you might escape these cruel blows? Listen, my sons, and sacrifice to the gods!" The holy Tryphon answered: "GOD has purified us, He who is the Judge of all and the Creator of the entire world." And again they said: "Ask us nothing new, ask us nothing old; you shall learn nothing other than what you first heard from us, for no one can destroy our faith. Inasmuch as our **Lord** Jesus Christ said: *Whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my heavenly Father.* Matthew 10, v. 33." Aquilinus said: "Have mercy upon yourselves and sacrifice to the great gods, for I perceive in you discipline and wisdom." The holy Respicius said: "We cannot have better mercy upon ourselves than to constantly confess our **Lord** Jesus Christ, the true Judge, who will strictly examine the works of every man." Aquilinus said: "Bring nails here and drive them into the soles of their feet." When this was done, they were led through the middle of the city in the harsh winter during stormy weather. But the devil could do nothing to them; rather, they were strengthened in the **Lord** more and more. Aquilinus said: "How is this! Do you not feel the pain?" The Saints gave him this answer: "No, for the nails are not driven into our feet, but only into our shoes." <note>original: "Sie achteten das Fleisch / an stat des Geistes Schuhe." This marginal note explains the martyrs' riddle: they viewed their physical bodies merely as "shoes" or outer coverings for their eternal spirits.</note>

# 24. St. Lucian and Marcian of Nicomedia.
### Year 251.
### Chapter 1.

->Lucian and Marcian were once sorcerers.<-

I wish to tell you, dear brothers, the story of the martyrdom of Lucian and Marcian, so that you may be built up by hearing it. For while they were still stuck in pagan error, they were so utterly devoted to the service of unclean spirits that they led almost all souls to their damned devil-worship; for with their magical arts and adulteries caused by sorcery, they defiled everyone. They were the leaders of seduction and magical corrupters, such that all who wished to carry out their unclean, evil will or do harm to someone sought counsel from them. But God, who shows Himself kind to the unkind, and through grace helps those who do not know Him toward the knowledge of His name, granted them conversion in the following manner.

->recognizing from this the devil's powerlessness.<-

She prayed, however, without anyone’s persuasion, out of constant resolve, that she might be worthy to preserve her chastity. Toward her, Lucian and Marcian conceived an...

---

(*) This story has a very close relationship with that of the sorcerer *Cyprian of Antioch*, whose conversion was described in the first part, Number *CXXXIII. p. 796.* <note>Referencing an earlier section of this collection of martyr acts.</note> where we reminded the reader that the truth of it is not to be doubted; although he afterward attained the martyr's crown, the records of it are somewhat questionable. The entire error seems to lie in the name and place; it may be that *Cyprian* has been confused with *Lucian* or *Marcian*. *Cyprian* is said to have lived in *Antioch* and been martyred in *Nicomedia*; now these men were also executed in *Nicomedia*, and not far from there lie various cities named *Antioch* in *Phrygia* and elsewhere, where these men, along with the Christian virgin, perhaps lived, and then received the martyr's crown in *Nicomedia*. Thus, one can well reconcile that conversion of *Cyprian* and this conversion of theirs as one and the same story, which does not need to be investigated more deeply here.

## Chapter 7.
->They are sentenced to the fire and burned.<-

Now when the Governor saw their steadfastness, he pronounced judgment against them and spoke: Since Lucianus and Marcianus, as transgressors of our Divine laws who have turned to the vain law of the Christians, have been sufficiently exhorted and warned by us to fulfill the commands of the invincible <note>Refers to the Roman Emperors.</note>Princes and sacrifice, that they might then live; but they have despised such counsel and would not obey, I therefore command that they be burned with fire! As they were then led to the place of judgment, they thanked **God** with one voice and spoke:

> To you, O Lord Jesus, we offer infinite praise and thanks, that you have snatched us, wretched and unworthy, out of heathen error and have allowed us to attain these highest and most glorious sufferings for your name's sake, and have deigned to make us worthy of the fellowship of all your saints. To you be praise, to you be honor; to you we also wish to commend our soul and spirit!

After they had finished their prayer, the <term>bailiffs<note>Original: *Büttel*, minor officials or executioners' assistants responsible for carrying out sentences.</note></term> lit the fire. Thus the venerable martyrs completed their struggle and were deemed worthy of the fellowship of the sufferings of the Lord.

# 25. Saint Hippolytus of Porto.
->Year 254.<-

**Note:** The following history of the martyr and bishop **Hippolytus**, who suffered under the Emperors **Gallus** and **Volusianus** at Porto—the harbor of the city of Rome, situated by the sea—and was torn apart by wild horses, was delightfully described in Latin verses around the year 400 by the Christian poet **Prudentius**, according to his custom. For the innocent diversion of the reader, we wish to translate this into verse and share as much of it as is necessary for the history of the martyrdom.

->§ I.<-

<margin>Prudentius tells Bishop **Valerianus** how he inspected the graves of the holy martyrs in Rome; he then comes to Hippolytus, who advised unity.</margin>

> Countless is the dust of the Saints in Rome,
> Which we, anointed man **Valerian**, have seen;
> You seek the inscriptions of the graves, and ask me of them!
> It is far too difficult for me to go through them all;
> So many righteous ones has the grim enemy consumed,
> While Trojan Rome (*) still honored its old gods.
> Many graves still speak of those to whom they belong,
> Whereon the names of witnesses are yet un-weathered by time.
> Yet the marbles are mostly stripped of such decoration,
> And only show by number how many were there;
> A whole multitude often lies here together,
> Of whom neither rank, nor name, nor anything can be read.
> There, one monument shows a good sixty in number,
> Of whose sanctuary news was given to me;

But Christ alone knows every name together,

As I now let my eyes cast their gaze precisely,

I found Hippolytus, who was previously called a <term>heretic<note>The text refers to the Novatian schism, a 3rd-century division in the Church over how to treat those who had renounced their faith under persecution.</note></term>;

The wavering crowd surrounded him out of love

Reunite yourselves according to the teaching of the Apostles.
If I have not taught it enough, I teach it to you late,
Now as a martyr, now while I am imprisoned;
Leave the left path, choose the right way,
If you wish to reach the true rest of the faithful."

(*) Since in the year 252, the Roman congregation split and elected two bishops; one party took **Cornelius**, who perhaps too thoughtlessly received those who had light-headedly fallen away in the previous persecution of **Decius** and now wished to be readmitted without sufficient evidence of repentance; against this, **Novatus** showed more earnestness and was thus elected bishop by the other party. This man was heavily branded as a heretic; his congregational elder was **Hippolytus**, the martyr mentioned here, who later became Bishop of Porto; whom **Prudentius** introduces as a repentant heretic, but only according to the prevailing view of his time, to which everything that had reached the martyr’s crown had to conform.

(**) In the years 253 and 254, there was a terrible plague in Rome, causing many of the great nobles to go to Porto for the sake of the healthy air.

### 25. Saint Hippolytus

Fear and death abound: this was caused by Abel’s blood <note>A reference to the first murder in the Bible (Genesis 4); the poet suggests the blood of the righteous has been crying out since the beginning of time.</note>, which rose like mist upon the market of Janus <note>original: *Jani Markt*. Likely referring to the Roman Forum or the area near the Temple of Janus, a center of public life in Rome.</note>; the blood of the martyrs, which flowed through markets and alleys like a flood, and left the <margin>Suburra (*) was a suburb near Rome.</margin> Suburra behind, until it increased here and there into a full river, where the fury of the Tyrrhenian (**) caused streams of blood to flow, and where the judge’s grimness exhausted the cities, which had long sat like desolate nests along the wild sea. Just as the tyrant sat on the exalted throne, surrounded by them like a <term>bailiff's diamond<note>original: *Büttel Diamant*. This likely refers to the cold, unyielding hardness of the executioners or the judge himself.</note></term>, and the crowd of servants stood thick upon the stage, to kill those who did not wish to live through dying <note>A common Christian paradox: dying to the world to gain eternal life.</note>.

Here faith was truly tested and proven; the disciples were sought out as harmful rebels against the gods, whom mad cruelty intended to strike down only through fire, cross, and sword. The crowd of desolate henchmen stood like a prison wall around the witnesses to carry out the grim work; the chains rattled, and it became wearying for the executioner, so that he could no longer move his hand or the scourge. Then the rod was of no help, even though it was woven of metal and wire; the hooks in the sides bared the bones and ribs everywhere. One saw the liver and lungs sliding from their place: yet not the brave heart, full of faith, spirit, and courage, which triumphantly overcame its tormentors; because of this, the judge first burst into a rage, as no executioner could be found to secure his victory.

"Cease the tormenting! Stop!" cried the tyrant to the <term>bailiff<note>original: *Büttel*, a minor court official or executioner's assistant.</note></term>, "your art cannot break this mind! A bitter death, which can conquer all, shall avenge the Emperor, ourselves, and even the gods themselves! Take the head from that one; and crucify the other—the birds shall yet devour him alive; roast that one on the grate; cast those from the height; let these others, in the fire of vengeance, honor the one who died on the cross and is unknown to us." Where is the false boat, deceitfully prepared? Place those people inside and push them from the land, until the vessel destroys itself in the middle of the flood.

### § 3.

->*St. Hippolytus is brought before the court; the judgment of the mob; thereafter he is condemned by the judge to wild horses, which drag him to death.*<-

Thereupon, as planned, the old man was presented
Before the elevated seat, his hands tightly bound;
And because the mob loves to pass judgment first,
A wild cry arose: The head of the Christians is found!
Once this is finished, then everyone
Who calls themselves after Christ will bring sacrifices to the gods;
They cried out with great joy, that the executioners should
Exert themselves well this time, for they would succeed!
The judge sat leaning with a puffed-up chest,
And spoke: What is your name? He said his name
Hippolytus (*)! Very well, said the former, for you must
Yet be a plaything for the horses; Harness a pair together
That are wild and untamed, and tear him in two!
Hardly was this word spoken, when one already heard the snorting
Of the wild stallions, who, constantly free from the bridle,
Were accustomed to stripping the bushes in the woods,
Now rearing up high, soon galloping away,
Because their free necks would not let themselves be groomed;
Until finally human wit holds the strength of the horses,
And the foaming mouth must grasp the bit and bridle.
Then they were paired; the drawbar was the rope
Which, between them both, had to follow the dust;
They bound the martyr with ropes, as thick
As an anchor’s cable, his feet to the frame
Of the aforementioned rope. With that, a cry went up!
The whips cracked to frighten the horses;
There the witness <note>The poet uses the word "Zeuge," which is the literal translation of the Greek *martys* (martyr).</note> flew, so that dust and blood were a mush,
And the intestines remained stuck to the stakes.
Yet one still heard the old man's last words:
> They take my body; O Christ, you take the soul!

The monument to this deed shows the spattered wall,

I myself have contemplated the image, from that artist’s hand,
Which one sees standing by the grave,
And tells everything in such a way, as this pen
Cannot vividly express the work of mourning;
For what the brush says there with the colors of life,
Depicts the history even in its smallest pieces.

And buried Hippolytus in the consecrated place,
Whose name flourishes constantly; And the power of his faith
Has exalted him eternally before the throne of the Lamb.

# 26. St. Dionysius / Bishop of Alexandria. Anno 250–264.

**Note:** We made mention above in the 17th martyrdom history of this Bishop **Dionysius**, who was a witness to those holy martyrs **St. Metranus** and the others, and who himself became a martyr-witness for Christ at that time and in the subsequent persecutions; in which he did not lose his life, but suffered all the more and longer in various ways, for which reason the Greek Church has deemed him worthy of the title of a holy martyr. We wish then to cite his sufferings from his own letters in this place, as they have been preserved by **Eusebius**. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, an early Christian historian whose "Ecclesiastical History" is a primary source for this era.</note>

### Chapter 1.

->The Descent, Professorship, and Divine Reminders Experienced by St. Dionysius to Test All Things.<-

and had been a professor of the Gymnasium <note>In this context, a "Gymnasium" refers to a high-level academy of learning, specifically the famous Catechetical School of Alexandria.</note>. As a great lover of scholarship, he read through all kinds of writings, especially those dealing with the errors and schisms of the churches; concerning which he relates the following notable incident in a letter about baptism to Philemon, an elder <note>original: "Aeltesten" – a presbyter or church official.</note> in Rome: "I have devoted much effort to reading the books and doctrines of heretics, and for a short time I defiled my mind with their impure thoughts; yet I gained the benefit of refuting them within myself, and thereafter loathed them all the more. And when a certain brother, who was an elder, warned me against it out of concern that I might stain myself with their filth and lose my soul—in which he spoke the truth, as it seemed to me—I was strengthened in my reading by a divine vision; for I heard a voice clearly saying to me: 'Read everything that comes into your hands; for you are capable of testing and investigating everything, and through this you even initially attained the foundation of faith in Christ!'" I accepted this vision as an apostolic word, as it was said to the elders: *Be wise stewards of the manifold grace of God.* 1 Peter 4, v. 10. <note>original: "Euseb. L. 7. c. 6." Referring to the *Ecclesiastical History* by Eusebius of Caesarea, Book 7, Chapter 6.</note>

## The 2nd Chapter.

->How he was blindly sought by the persecutors and not found.<-

Now after Dionysius was chosen as Bishop of the believers in Alexandria in place of the late Bishop **Heraclas**, and the severe persecution under the Emperor **Decius** began in the year 250, this holy man also had to help bear the heaviest part of the wrath; of which his own words in a letter of defense <note>Dionysius wrote this "Apology" to a fellow bishop named Germanus who had accused him of cowardice for fleeing.</note> to **Germanus** read as follows: "I speak before the face of God, who knows that I do not lie; I have never taken flight by my own will without a sign from God; rather, even before the command for persecution had been issued by Decius, **Sabinus** <note>The Roman Prefect of Egypt.</note> sent a commissioner to seek me out at that very moment. When I heard of this, I remained at home for four days and awaited the arrival of this servant. He, however, went about everywhere and searched for me on the roads, by the rivers, and in the countryside, wherever he thought I might have hidden myself or might have to pass by. But a fog had blinded his sight, so that he did not search for me at home; for he did not suspect that I would remain at home while [the command] against me..."

### The 3rd Chapter.

->Saint Dionysius reports how he was captured during his flight and miraculously delivered.<-

Thereupon he further reports what happened to him after such a flight, and writes: I, indeed, was captured by the soldiers around sunset along with my companions and led to Taposiris <note>Taposiris Magna was an ancient city on the Egyptian coast, west of Alexandria.</note>. Meanwhile, we were brought into servitude. How remarkably, however, did God arrange it? I testify to the truth: As the aforementioned Timotheus ran from the house, fleeing and terrified, he met a peasant <note>original: "Baur" – a farmer or country person.</note> who asked him why he hurried so. He told him what had occurred. When the peasant heard this, he went on his way to a wedding, where they were accustomed to making merry all night. When he arrived, he told the guests of the situation and how we had been led away as prisoners. At this, they gave one another a signal and rose up in a rush, overtaking us with a great shout, which terrified our guard and caused them to flee. They found us just as we were, lying naked <note>In the ancient context, "naked" often meant being in one's undergarments or light sleeping tunic rather than fully unclothed.</note> on the straw bedding. At first sight—God is my witness—I thought they were robbers who had come to plunder and steal; I remained lying in my place naked, covered only by a smock <note>original: "Kittel" – a simple, loose-fitting garment.</note>, and handed them my remaining clothes which lay beside me. But they told me to stand up and commanded that I should get away from there quickly. Only then did I understand for what purpose they had come, and I began to rebuke them, begging and testifying that they should go away and leave us there. And if they truly wished to show us a favor, I begged that they should call back the soldiers who had led us away captive, so that they might strike off my head. While I was [imploring] this...

## The 4th Chapter.

->How it fared in Alexandria during the persecution after the escape of<-
->Dionysius.<-

How it meanwhile fared in Alexandria, the holy Dionysius reports in a letter to Domitius and Didymus with the following circumstances: It is superfluous, he writes, to mention all the martyrs by name, since there are so many and some are unknown to you. Generally, it serves you to know that men and women, young and old, virgins and matrons, noble and lowly—in short, people of every age and kind—some were scourged, others fought with the point of the sword, others with fire, and have attained the crown of victory. Many, however, in a long time of suffering, have not yet been able to become an acceptable sacrifice to God, just as I have not, up to this very day; yet I hope the Lord has chosen a convenient time for me, which is best known to Him, who says: *I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I helped thee.* Isaiah 49, v. 8. In the city (Alexandria), however, several elders, namely Maximus, Dioscorus, Demetrius, and Lucius, have kept themselves hidden to visit the brothers in secret. Faustinus, however, and Aquila, because they were more conspicuous to the people, wander about in Egypt. # 26. St. Dionysius

...testified that he faithfully served the confessors <term>confessors: Christians who maintained their faith under torture or imprisonment but were not executed</term> in prison, and buried the bodies of the completed, blessed martyrs <note>The "completed" martyrs refers to those who had finished their "race" or trial through death.</note> at the risk of his own life. For even to this day, the governor does not cease from treating our people—who are captured and brought before him—partly by killing them in the most cruel manner, partly by mangling them with instruments of torture, and partly by agonizing them in foul prisons. He also forbids anyone to visit them, ensuring a sharp watch is kept. Nevertheless, God provides constant refreshment to the afflicted through the joy and kindness of the brothers. It is also important to know (reports the historian Eusebius) that this deacon, Eusebius, soon after became the Bishop of Laodicea in Syria. The priest or elder Maximus, however, was appointed to rule the Alexandrian congregation as bishop or overseer after the passing of Saint Dionysius. Finally, Faustus, who at that time had earned the honorable name of a confessor along with Dionysius, was preserved until the persecution of our own time—namely until the year 303—and at a great age, full of years, he finally attained the crown of martyrdom, being beheaded for the sake of the testimony of Jesus under Diocletian and Maximian. ### The 5th Chapter.

->How after the deaths of Decius, Gallus, and Volusian, Valerian and<-

After the death of the tyrant Decius, Gallus and his son Volusian ruled for barely two years before they were also executed in the year 254. The holy confessor Dionysius, in a letter to Hermammon, describes how this Valerian changed from a kind master—who was initially well-disposed toward the Christians—into a cruel persecutor, in the following manner: "To the Evangelist John," writes Dionysius, "this time was likewise revealed; for to the beast was given a mouth to speak great things and blasphemies, and power was given to him for forty and two months." <note>original: "Apoc. 13, v. 5." ...been Christians (*), and had shown himself as favorable and well-disposed toward our people as this Valerian did at the beginning of his reign. His entire royal household was filled with godly people and was to be regarded as a congregation of God. However, the teacher and <term>superintendent: a high-ranking official or leader</term> of the Egyptian sorcerer-priests <note>This refers to Macrianus, an influential advisor to Valerian who practiced magic and supposedly turned the emperor against the Christians.</note> finally persuaded him to abandon this path. He then persecuted and killed those upright, holy men as adversaries and enemies of the most impure and cursed sorceries. (For the godly were and are still so powerful that by their mere presence and appearance—even if they only resist with a breath or a single word—they can thwart the deceptions of evil spirits.) Thus, he took up once more those impure ceremonies, damnable incantations, and abominable sacrifices: slaughtering wretched boys, sacrificing the children of unfortunate parents, inspecting the entrails of newborn infants, and tearing apart and cutting up the creatures of God, as if he would be made prosperous by such acts. Thus far Dionysius writes concerning Valerian’s apostasy and his change from Christ to the idols.

Eusebius, Book 7, Chapter 10.

## Chapter 6.

->**St. Dionysius and his fellow confessors are brought before the governor Aemilianus.**<-

Regarding the persecution under Valerian, the holy Bishop Dionysius felt it most severely and, along with others, endured a great deal for the sake of his love for the universal God. This is clearly shown by his words to Germanus, a bishop of that time who had slandered him: "I fear," he writes, "that I shall be considered foolish and simple-minded if I am forced by necessity to recount the wonderful providence and oversight of God regarding us. Yet, because it is indeed laudable—according to the testimony of Scripture—to keep the secrets of the king hidden, but to proclaim the works of God is praiseworthy (Tobit 12:8), I must meet the attack of Germanus more directly. I came before the governor Aemilianus, not alone, but in the company of my fellow elder Maximus and the deacons Faustus, Eusebius, and Chaeremon; and..."

# 26. St. Dionysius

...one of the Roman brothers, who was present at the time, went in with us. Furthermore, Aemilianus did not say to me at the very beginning: "You shall hold no assemblies"; for such a thing was far from his intention and the last thing he sought, as he looked for something much closer to us <note>The governor was more interested in their total apostasy—renouncing their faith—than merely stopping their meetings.</note>. He was not concerned that I should hold no assemblies, but rather his will was that we should not be Christians at all; and he commanded me to desist from my service, believing that if I fell away, the others would follow my example. 

But I answered him briefly and well: **"We must obey God more than men!"** <note>A famous citation from the Bible, Acts 5:29, commonly used by early Christians to justify their refusal to obey Roman laws that contradicted their faith.</note> I testified there openly and publicly that I would worship only Him who alone is the true God, and no other beside Him; from this purpose, I will not be turned away, and I shall never cease to be a Christian! Thereupon he commanded us to depart from Alexandria and go to Cephro, a village located near the desert. But hear the words themselves which were spoken between us, as they are found in the public records in the following manner:

## Chapter 7.

->**Court Records and Confessions of Faith of Dionysius and the others before the Governor Aemilianus.**<-

After Dionysius, Faustus, Maximus, Marcellus, and Chäremon appeared before the court, the governor Aemilianus spoke: "I have dealt with you not only in writing but also orally regarding the clemency of our princes <note>Refers to the joint Emperors Valerian and his son Gallienus.</note>, which they use toward you; for they have placed the preservation of your welfare in your own power, if you will only follow what is according to nature, worship the gods as protectors of their empire, and forget that which strives against nature itself <note>The Roman authorities viewed the exclusive worship of one God as "unnatural" because it rejected the traditional gods believed to protect the Roman State.</note>. What do you say to this? I should hope you will not oppose their clemency with ungrateful hearts, since they advise you for your own good!" 

Dionysius answered: "Not all nations worship all and the same gods, but each one honors those whom he considers to be gods. We honor and worship the one God and Creator of all things, from whom the divinely favored Emperors Valerian and Gallienus have received the empire; to Him, we offer our constant prayers for the welfare of their empire, that it may remain stable and without disruption." 

The prefect Aemilianus spoke once more: "Who then forbids you that you should not also worship this one—if indeed he is a god—along with those who are gods by nature?"

Depart then from here, to where you have been commanded!"

## Chapter 8.

->**How they fared during their misery at Cephro.**<-

Although I was then weak and sick, he nevertheless urged me to travel immediately <note>original: "stehendes Fußes," literally "on standing foot."</note>, and did not grant me even a single day’s delay. How then could I have still held assemblies, or have been able to ordain that they be held? But we were certainly not removed from the physical gathering through the Lord's assistance; rather, I gathered those who remained in the city into the congregation with even greater earnestness, as if I were there myself; though, as said, absent in body, yet present in spirit. At Cephro, a great multitude of the faithful were with us, partly those who had followed us there from Alexandria, and partly those who had gathered there from other parts of Egypt; God also opened a door for us there to proclaim His word. At the beginning, we were indeed persecuted even here by the heathens and pelted with stones; but afterwards, not a few of them abandoned their idols and converted to the living God. For at that time, the seed of the Divine Word was first sown in those places, which they had not known before. It also seemed as if God had led us there for that purpose alone, for after we had performed such office among them, we were banished elsewhere.

## Chapter 9.
->They must leave Cephro and move toward Colluthum.<-

<margin>Eusebius Book 7, Chapter 11.</margin>
Since Aemilianus sent us to harsher places, which he believed were located deeper in the Libyan wilderness, he had ordered all the exiles to gather in the Mareotic district (*), where he assigned to each one the villages and towns that lie scattered around that place. However, he stationed us near the main road, so that we could be recaptured first whenever it pleased him; for his primary intention was that he could have us all back without any effort whenever he wished. 

But when I first received the command to go to Cephro, not knowing where that place was located—indeed, having never even heard the name before—I nevertheless traveled there with a joyful and confident heart. However, after it was announced to me that I should move to the region of Colluthum, those who were present know how I felt, for here I must confess my own weakness <note>original: "mich selbst anklagen," literally "accuse myself," suggesting a lack of faith or patience.</note>. 

At first, I was very dissatisfied with it; for although this region was more familiar and better known to us than Cephro, we were told that there were neither brothers nor honorable people there, and that it was a place troubled by many travelers and robbers. Yet it gave me great comfort that the brothers reminded me the place was not so far from the city (Alexandria). Therefore, although a great many brothers from Egypt gathered at Cephro, such that we could already hold large assemblies there, they said that in Colluthum—because of its proximity to the city—one would be able to see and speak with the dearest and most intimate friends more often; for they would visit us and stay with us, and we would be able to hold assemblies as if in the outlying suburbs. And so it came to pass.

[The previous situation changed] when Emperor Valerian was captured by Shapur in the war against the Persians. Shapur used that persecutor as a footstool whenever he wished to mount his horse, until finally, Shapur, King of the Persians, had him flayed <note>To have one's skin removed.</note> and his skin stuffed as a spectacle. Such events may have caused his son, Gallienus, to reflect; he already had his hands full with the "Thirty Tyrants" <note>A group of thirty usurpers who attempted to seize the Roman throne during this period of instability.</note> who were striving for his crown, among whom was Aemilianus, the Governor of Egypt. Therefore, Gallienus issued orders that the Christians should return from the places to which they had previously been banished and go back to their own people, and that they might freely serve Christ as the true God according to their conscience. Of these orders, the one he sent to Bishop Dionysius and the other banished bishops in Egypt is still extant, and it reads as follows:

The Pious, fortunate, and most illustrious Enlarger of the Empire, Emperor Publius Licinius Gallienus, sends greetings to Dionysius, Pinna, Demetrius, and the other bishops:
We have caused our grace and goodness to be proclaimed to the whole world, so that [the Christians] may depart from those places to which they have been banished; therefore, you also may make use of this our command, and no one shall hinder you. This has already been granted by us for some time, and Aurelius Cyrenius, our Grand Chancellor <note>original: "Groß-Canzler," likely referring to the *procurator summarum rationum*, the high imperial financial official.</note>, holds the original of our command! <margin>(*) Eusebius, Book 7, Chapter 13.</margin>

Following this command, Dionysius and all the confessors <note>Those who maintained their faith under torture or threat but were not killed.</note> finally found peace; they returned to their congregation in Alexandria. However, everything there was in upheaval, as the Governor Aemilianus was rebelling against the Emperor in the manner mentioned above. Consequently, there was such a desolate state of mutual murder and robbery that no peace-loving person dared to step out onto the street. After this internal war, a terrible plague followed, in which the cruelty of the pagans and the loving conduct of the Christians were edifyingly revealed, as the martyr Dionysius relates for a further report of his endured sufferings in a special letter, which we wish to include here:

For now everything is full of weeping and wailing; everyone mourns, and because of the many deceased and the crowd still dying daily, the whole city is filled with sighing. Just as it is written in the holy books regarding the slaying of the firstborn of the Egyptians <note>A reference to the tenth plague of Egypt in the Book of Exodus.</note>, so too is there a great whimpering and lamenting this time; for there is no house in which a corpse is not found—and oh, if only there were but one in each house!

Very many and bitter tribulations have indeed met us before this; for first they drove us out of the city; and although we alone of all people were hunted and oppressed, we nevertheless celebrated the feast days at that time. Every place in which we endured various tribulations particularly—I mean the open field, the desert, the ship, the stable, and the prison—served us in stead of a temple to hold our holy assembly. But the most joyful feast days of all are celebrated by the holy, perfected martyrs, who hold the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Abendmahl"</note> in heaven.

Afterward, war and hunger followed, which we had to endure just as much as the heathens <term>Heyden (Heathens): a term used by early Christians to describe the non-Christian, polytheistic Roman population</term>, though with this difference: that while we alone bore the plagues they inflicted upon us, we also had to suffer the consequences of what they inflicted upon one another. Yet peace gladdened us again, which Christ alone has granted us.

But hardly had we recovered for a short time when the harmful plague <note>Historical records identify this as the Plague of Cyprian (c. 250–266 AD), which severely depopulated the Roman Empire.</note> crept in, which they consider the most horrific and wretched of all—the thing which alone, as one of their own writers says, overcomes all their hope and courage. For this plague visited us as well as them, although the heathens suffered the most from it.

Many of our brothers, out of great love, neglected their own well-being and clung faithfully to one another; they visited the sick freely and boldly, served them constantly, and cared for them in Christ, and because of this, they lost their lives along with them. They willingly took the illness of their neighbors upon themselves and bore it, relieving the pains of others. Many helped their sick fellow members <note>original: "Mit-Glieder"</note> back to their former health and afterwards died of it themselves, having taken death upon themselves for the sake of others. Thus they fulfilled in deed the common proverb, which had been considered merely a word of politeness, and gave up their lives as a sacrifice for their brothers. In such a manner, the best among...

## Chapter 12.

-> St. Dionysius refutes the erroneous opinion of the Thousand-Year Kingdom of Christ in this world. <-

After such a time of plague, which raged around the year 261 in Alexandria and Egypt, the holy Bishop Dionysius lived there for three more years and had to encounter various errors for the general service of the church, both in writing and in speech. Among these was the opinion of the Egyptian Bishop Nepos regarding the Thousand-Year Kingdom of Christ <term>Millenarianism or Chiliasm: a belief based on Revelation 20 that Christ would establish a physical, 1,000-year kingdom on Earth</term>, which he wanted understood in a literal sense according to the secret Revelation of Saint John. To that end, he wrote a book titled: *Refutation of the Allegorists* <note>original: "Widerlegung der Allegoristen"</note>, or of those who interpret the literal words of Scripture in a mystical way. Against this, the holy Dionysius wrote two other books titled *On the Promises* <note>original: "von den Verheissungen"</note>—namely, of God to His church—explaining how these should be understood spiritually and not carnally. Of this affair, an edifying monument remains, showing how modest teachers at that time dealt with conflicting doctrines among one another, according to Dionysius's own account from his aforementioned book against Nepos: "When I," he writes, "was in the Arsinoite district <term>Arsinoitische Vogtey: a region in Egypt now known as Fayyum</term>, where, as you know, this opinion had recently spread so widely that entire congregations had separated themselves..."

Questions, objections, and agreements took place among us with the highest modesty and order; in particular, we prevented with all diligence that we did not stubbornly defend that which we had once approved if we found it to be erroneous, nor did we overlook the objections of others; but as much as was possible, we endeavored to fully resolve the matters under discussion. When we were convinced by reasons, we were not ashamed to change our opinion and agree with one another. Indeed, we rather accepted with a good conscience and without any hypocrisy—our hearts being spread out before God—everything that was confirmed with the best reasons and proof from Holy Scripture. Finally, **Coracio**—who was the head and leader of this teaching (following the passing of **Nepos**) —promised and testified to us in the presence of all the brothers who heard it, that he would henceforth abandon this opinion, nor speak of it further, nor teach it to the people; as one who had been sufficiently and redundantly convinced by counter-arguments. But for the brothers who were present, this disputation and the resulting unification of all minds caused no small joy. <margin>Eusebius, Book 7, Chapter 24.</margin>

# 27. St. Sixtus II, Bishop, and St. Lawrence, Archdeacon, at Rome. Year 258.

### Chapter 1.

->Upon Emperor Valerian's second decree against the Christians, Sixtus is executed along with other clergy.<-

Emperor **Valerian** had, in the year 258, issued for the second time a decree against the Christians to the Council at Rome, as well as to all governors of the provinces. In this decree, it was specifically commanded of them to keep a sharp eye on all bishops, priests, and deacons, and to execute them without delay. However, if anyone from the Council or the nobility and <term>knightly class</term> <note>Referring to the "Ritterstand" or *Equites*, the second tier of the Roman aristocracy.</note> was found to be a Christian, they were to be stripped of their honors and property; and if they nevertheless persisted in the Christian religion, they were to be beheaded. Their wives and the honorable matrons who worshiped Christ were to be banished into exile after the confiscation of their goods. All imperial servants who had previously confessed Christ or still confessed Him were to be dismissed, bound in chains, and banished to the imperial estates for labor. 

Following this harsh ordinance, **Sixtus**, the second of this name, as the then-Bishop of Rome, was first taken prisoner together with **Quartus**, a priest or elder, and the <term>deacons</term> <note>Deacons were ministers responsible for the charitable works and administrative tasks of the early church.</note> **Felicissimus** and **Agapitus**, as well as the <term>sub-deacons</term> <note>The sub-diaconate was a minor order of clergy who assisted the deacons in their duties.</note> **Januarius**, **Magnus**, **Innocentius**, and **Stephanus**...

<summary>This page records the peaceful death of Dionysius of Alexandria in 264 and describes the brutal decree of Emperor Valerian in 258 targeting all levels of the Christian clergy and nobility.</summary>

## Chapter 2.

->*St. Lawrence* desires to die with the holy *Sixtus*; the Governor wants to have the Church treasures from him.<-

Now, when the aforementioned Bishop **Sixtus** was being led away to his death, his <term>Archdeacon</term> <note>A high-ranking deacon responsible for church administration and the distribution of alms to the poor.</note> **Lawrence** followed him, weeping bitterly that he was not to die at the same time, and cried out to him pitifully: "Where are you going, my father, without your son? Where do you hasten, holy priest, without your deacon? Have you found anything displeasing in me, dear father, that you do not deem me worthy of your company in this struggle? Test me, and see if you have chosen a fit servant for the mystery of the chalice?" To this, the holy **Sixtus** replied: "Be content, my brother; I go before you, and after three days you shall follow me! In the meantime, let the treasures of the church (the poor) be recommended to your care." These prophetic words of the dying Bishop reached their complete fulfillment; for it soon reached the ears of the Roman <term>Governor</term> <note>Original: "Stadthalter." ->St. Lawrence promises to hand over the church treasure and assembles<-

The holy **Lawrence** was neither moved nor led astray by such demands, but as if he were ready to obey, he gave a modest answer and said: "I cannot deny it; our church is indeed rich and possesses much money and property, more than anyone in the entire world, so that even the Emperor—to whom all money belongs—does not have so much money in his palace. The Governor was filled with joy at this and was already feasting on the hope of the gold as if he already had it in his house. The granted period of three days seemed almost too long to him, yet because of the great promise given, he let him go home with all courtesy. ### Chapter 5.

->The enraged Governor sentences Saint Lawrence to be roasted on a gridiron.<-

Extreme wrath had paralyzed the Governor's tongue until now, such that he listened to the martyr with silent grinding of teeth; finally, he broke out in full rage and cried: We are being mocked and wonderfully scorned with various spectacles, and the nonsensical head still lives? You thief’s companion, you shall not have played these comedies for me unpunished <note>original: *ungedroschen*—literally "unthreshed," an idiom meaning to escape without a beating or without paying the price</note>; I will teach you, you vagabond, to tell fables. Do you dare to joke with us, and should I be your little story? Does the judicial office no longer command respect, and is there no fear of the sword of justice? You wish for death, indeed, and long to be a martyr; I know such vain imagination, but you shall get a taste of what you will not like; do not even think of a quick death. I will delay your life and prolong your pain; an unending death shall make you properly taste the tedious torment. Quickly prepare glowing coals, but let the heat be moderate, so that it does not suffocate him too soon and reach the heart; blow the fire slowly, so that the pains penetrate the half-roasted body. This very dealer-in-mysteries <term>Geheimniß-Krämer</term> <note>A dismissive term used by the Governor for a Christian who speaks of divine "mysteries" or secrets.</note> has fallen into my hands at the right time; he shall serve as an example to everyone, for which they shall tremble. Now you can climb onto this gridiron and try out the worthy bed; then argue to your heart's content that my Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire; the Governor is sarcastically suggesting his fire is more powerful than Lawrence's God.</note> is powerless.

This section describes the transition from scourging to the famous ordeal on the gridiron, drawing parallels between Lawrence’s radiant face and biblical figures like Moses and Stephen.</meta>

History of Martyrdom / Year 258. 183

While the sentence was being delivered, the cruel executioners were already carrying it out; they began to strip the martyr of his clothes. Thereafter, they bound him fast to the torture block and scourged him first with sharp rods woven from copper wire, tearing his flesh with sharp iron two-pronged hooks; then, they laid him, entirely bloody and wounded, upon the glowing iron gridiron. He, the holy martyr, appeared so joyful and spirited during this that his face seemed to shine, just as that of the lawgiver Moses did when he came down from the mountain, which the defiled worshipers of the golden calf were unable to look upon. Indeed, he looked like the holy Stephen when he saw the heavens open amidst the shower of stones. The newly converted brothers, who had been baptized shortly before, noticed such a glow upon the most blessed martyr; but the blind crowd of the godless did not see the bright light through the dark veil of their own shroud. Just as those Egyptians were condemned to darkness while the Hebrews perceived the bright light of the sun. Exodus 10, v. 21–23. Even the nature of the scent of the burnt skin was perceived differently by them: the heathens smelled a foul stench, but the Christians smelled it as a lovely balsam. Such is the nature of the fire of the eternal Godhead, of Christ, the true fire; He fills the righteous with His light and burns the godless.

## Chapter 7.
### The Holy Martyr’s Boldness, Prayer, and Blessed Death.

Now, after the heat had roasted one side of the martyr long enough, he unexpectedly addressed the judge from the gridiron and said:

> Turn me over now; that side is roasted enough. Try and see what your burning Vulcan <note>original: *Vulcanus*—the Roman god of fire; here used as a metaphor for the flames of the gridiron</note> has accomplished.

The Governor then ordered that he should be turned over and laid on the other side. When this had been done, the martyr spoke once more:

> If the meat is done, then eat, and see whether it be half or fully roasted.

He said this to mock the unclean spirits, and thereafter he looked toward heaven, sighed, and prayed compassionately for the city of Rome, saying:

> O Lord Christ, you sole Godhead, you radiance and power of the Father, you creator of the world and of all mankind, and the author of this city! You who have handed the scepter of the changeable government of this world to Rome, and ordained that all should be subject to its purple <note>The "purple" refers to the imperial authority and robes of the Roman Emperors</note> and yield to its weapons, so that under one law you might bring together the customs, habits, and languages of different peoples

# 27. St. Sixtus II and Lawrence

...and united their heads together <note>This continues Lawrence’s prayer from the previous page, where he speaks of God uniting the disparate nations under Roman rule to prepare the way for the Gospel</note>. Behold, the mortal race is indeed subject to the regime of Remus <note>A poetic reference to Rome, named for its co-founder Remus</note>, and they speak the same language despite their various customs and manners. This was foreseen by You for this purpose: so that the laws of the Christian name might all the more easily unite everyone across the entire earth. Raise up someone who will close the idol-temples and clean their marble of blood—one who will sanctify the bronze gates where the statues now stand! With such a prayer, the holy martyr gave up his spirit. But the holy fathers Justin and Hippolytus, who had become believers through his bold confession, took his holy body and buried him. From that time on, the shameful worship of idols grew colder and colder, and the people bowed before the throne of Christ; for the death of this martyr was the death and downfall of the idol-temples. Vesta <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth and home</note> was abandoned, and the Palladian household gods <note>The Palladium was a sacred image of Pallas Athena believed to protect the safety of Rome</note> were despised; men ceased to offer bowls filled with blood to the gods; even the Senate and the government in Rome, along with all the great nobles, kissed the footprints of the holy martyrs. Yes, even the Heathen Pope (*) began to submit himself to the Crucified One, and the Imperial family has since visited the church established in honor of Saint Lawrence and surrendered themselves to Christ. <note>Citations: Prudentius, *On the Crowns of the Martyrs*, Hymn 2. Leo the Great, *Sermon on Lawrence*. Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book 1, Chapter 41 and Book 2, Chapter 28. See also Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs*, page 187.</note>

# 28. St. Cyprian / Bishop of Carthage. Year 258.

## Chapter 1.

->Pontius, the deacon of Saint Cyprian, describes his life.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring elaborate scrollwork and leafy vine motifs.</image-desc>
Cyprian, the God-blessed leader and victorious <term>witness</term> <note>The word used is "Zeuge," the literal translation of the Greek "martys," from which we get "martyr."</note> of God, wrote much during his life, through which the memory of his worthy name still flourishes. The abundance of his great eloquence, granted by the grace of God, will perhaps not be silent until the end of the world. Nonetheless, we owe this love to his conduct and merit: to compose and briefly describe the course of his life. We do this not as if this great man’s conduct were hidden even from the <term>pagans</term> <note>original: "Heyden," referring to those practicing the traditional Roman religion rather than Christianity.</note>, but so that such an incomparably great and edifying monument might reach our descendants for eternal memory. 

It would certainly be a harsh thing if—given that our ancestors showed such honor and high esteem for the <term>martyrdom</term> <note>original: "Marter-Stand," literally "martyr-state" or the status achieved through suffering for the faith.</note> of common and newly converted martyrs that they wrote down nearly everything about them so that it might reach the knowledge of those of us who were not yet born—we should then pass over the sufferings of Cyprian. He was such a great priest and martyr, who even without his martyrdom would have been a model of doctrine <note>Cyprian was one of the most important early Christian theologians; his writings on the unity of the Church remained influential for centuries.</note>, though his works were not fully appreciated during his lifetime. These works are so many, so great, and so wonderful that I am terrified by them and deem myself unworthy to speak of them according to their merit, for I do not trust myself to describe them in a way that his holy life might be clearly enough recognized. This is to say nothing of the fact that, because of its excellence, his life requires no one to speak its praises. 

However, the burden of my concern increases because you desire with burning longing to know his holy deeds from me in writing—not just in part, but in their entirety—since you lack a verbal account. If I say here that I lack sufficient eloquence, I say too little; for eloquence itself is not capable of satisfying your hungry longing with its full spirit. Thus, we are beset on both sides: he overwhelms us with his virtues, and you weary us with your requests.

28. St. Cyprian / The 2nd Chapter.
<meta>catchword: conversion</meta>

### On the Beginning of Cyprian’s Conversion and His Earnest Self-Denial.

Where should I then begin? Where should I start to describe his virtues, other than at the beginning of his faith and his heavenly rebirth? For one should not begin to tell the deeds of a man of God anywhere else than from the moment he was born of God. Although he was learned, and his devout heart had absorbed the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>original: "freyen Künste"; the classical curriculum including grammar, rhetoric, and logic, which Cyprian mastered as a teacher of rhetoric before his conversion.</note>, I will pass over such things, because they previously had no use other than in this world. I would rather report what I have seen as a close eyewitness, and learned of his very first virtuous conduct, since the time he studied the Holy Scriptures—when the cloud of this world hid itself from him and the light of spiritual wisdom rose within him. However, I stipulate beforehand—should I say too little, as I must necessarily do—that you attribute it to my ignorance rather than to any lack in his virtues. 

Among the first God-consecrated fruits of his faith was abstinence. For he believed that his heart and spirit would then be fit to fully recognize the truth once he had placed the lusts of the flesh under his feet by means of earnest and true sanctification. Who has ever heard of such a wonder? The <term>second birth</term> <note>Referring to the Christian rite of baptism.</note> had scarcely opened the eyes of the <term>new man</term> <note>original: "neuen Menschen"; a biblical reference to the spiritually renewed self after conversion.</note> with the full radiance of divine light, yet in his first knowledge, he already overcame the dark, old lusts of the flesh. 

Furthermore—which is even more to be admired—as soon as he had learned anything from reading the Divine Scriptures (not out of curious desire, but for the service of faith), he demonstrated in deeds how he applied it to godliness. His property had to serve immediately for the support of the poor, as he distributed the price of entire <term>estates</term> <note>original: "Meyerhöfe"; these were large agricultural properties or manorial farms, indicating Cyprian's significant wealth before his conversion.</note>. He combined two good qualities together: he despised the honor of this world, which is a most harmful thing, and he fulfilled the mercy which God has elevated above sacrifice <note>original: "Esa. 1, v. 17"; referring to Isaiah 1:17: "Learn to do right; seek justice. Defend the oppressed. Take up the cause of the fatherless; plead the case of the widow."</note>, which that man who boasted of the whole law had not kept <note>original: "Matth. 19, v. 21"; referring to the story of the Rich Young Ruler who could not bring himself to sell his possessions.</note>. Through rapid growth in godliness, he reached perfection almost before he understood it. Who among the ancients, I ask, has done such a thing? Who among the elders established in the faith, who for many years took the Divine Word into their ears and hearts, has worked such things as this newcomer?

## Chapter 3.
->He is soon called to the office of teacher.<-

The letters of the Apostles do indeed testify that one should bypass new converts for the <term>office of teacher</term> <note>original: "Lehr-Amte"; referring here to the clerical office of a bishop or priest responsible for instruction.</note>, so that any remaining pagan habits in untrained minds might not provide an occasion for sin. *1 Timothy 3, v. 6.* But he was the first (*), and in my opinion, the only one who showed by his example that more is achieved through faith than through the passage of time. Even though it is said in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the <term>eunuch</term> <note>referring to the Ethiopian official converted by Philip the Evangelist.</note> that he believed with all his heart and was therefore immediately baptized by Philip; *Acts 8, v. 37.* yet there is no comparison. For that man was a Jew and came from the Temple of the Lord; he was reading the prophet Isaiah and hoping for Christ, though he did not yet know that He had come. This man [Cyprian], however, was born of unbelieving pagans and possessed from the very beginning such a mature faith as many do not reach even in the end. The grace of God allowed for no delay or postponement in him. I have said almost too little: he received the office of an elder or priest immediately. For who would not entrust everything to such a faithful spirit? Much did he do as a listener, still
<meta>catchword: more</meta>

<note>(*) It would have been better had the Apostles’ spiritual ordinance been maintained, and no new convert called to the office of teacher. This practice began shortly after the time of the Apostles, where converted <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophos"; early Christian intellectuals who often retained their distinctive philosopher's cloaks.</note>—with their impressive, long black robes—were chosen as teachers because of their eloquence and prestige among the people. And so it happened here to Cyprian, as a wealthy and learned man, whose first good spiritual fruits were hardly allowed to ripen; his own writings bear witness to this, suggesting he spoke out too soon and weakened the spirit. However, his deacon <term>Pontius</term> <note>Cyprian's biographer, whose text this translation is based upon.</note>, acting as a skilled orator out of love, describes his virtues, which were also sanctified by his martyr’s crown.</note>

# 28. St. Cyprian

done more than a teacher, and what did he not accomplish—following the examples of the ancients to make himself worthy to the Lord—with complete obedience of faith? For his usual way of speaking was this: whenever he read of someone whom God Himself had praised, he advised that one should investigate by which works that person had pleased God. When of Job, whom God’s testimony glorified, it is said that he was a true servant of God who had no equal on earth (*Job 1:8*), he taught that one should do what Job had done before, so that by doing the same, we might also obtain God’s testimony. Job had despised temporal goods and had progressed so far in the practice of virtues that he did not even feel the temporal loss through the practice of <term>godly works</term> <note>original: "Gottseliger Werke"; refers to charitable and pious actions performed out of devotion to God.</note>. Neither poverty nor the pain of illness broke his grasp of faith in God, nor did his wife’s persuasion <note>referring to the biblical account where Job's wife encourages him to "curse God and die."</note> turn him away, nor the cruel pains of his own body shatter him. Virtue remained with him (Job) in its immovable seat, and his devotion was very deeply rooted; he did not yield to any temptations of the devil, but in all adversities, he blessed his God with grateful faith; his house stood open to all strangers; no widow turned back from him with an empty hand; he left no blind person unguided, no lame person uncarried, no abandoned person without protection and help. In these virtues of Job, he said, those who wish to please God should follow him. In this manner, he ran through all the good examples of the past, and by always following the best, he made himself into a good example for others.

### Chapter 4.
->His reverence toward Caecilius, his spiritual father.<-

He had with us as a housemate the righteous and praiseworthy Caecilius, who was an <term>Elder</term> <note>original: "Aeltester"; used here to denote the ecclesiastical office of a priest or presbyter.</note> in both age and honorary office, and who had led him from worldly error to the knowledge of Divine truth. Him he loved with complete reverence and high esteem, not merely as an ordinary friend of his soul, but as the father of his new life. He won Caecilius's heart through his obedience to such an extent that when the old man was about to die, he called Cyprian before him and entrusted to him his wife (*) and his children, so that he [Cyprian], whom...
