## Chapter 5.
### He is elected Bishop.

It would take too long to go through everything; and it is too burdensome to recount all his works. To testify to his good conduct, I consider it enough alone that he was chosen for the office of Bishop through divine choice and the people’s favor while still a <term>novice</term> <note>original: "Neuling"; refers to a person newly converted to the faith, known in the early church as a neophyte.</note>. Although he was still in the first days of his faith and the beginning of his reborn life, his excellent nature shone forth to such an extent that even before he attained the office, he glowed with promise, and gave every hope of his forthcoming priestly ministry. I also cannot pass over the exceptional example: when the whole people, out of love and high esteem and through divine inspiration, agreed upon his election, he hid himself out of humility and wished to give way to the <term>elders</term> <note>original: "Aeltesten"; referring to the established presbyters or senior church leaders.</note>, considering himself unworthy of such honors, so that someone more worthy might receive it. But he is the most worthy who does not recognize his own worthiness. How did the impassioned people not burn with desire then? Who, with spiritual longing—as the outcome has taught—sought not only a Bishop (for whom they then so zealously longed while he hid himself out of secret divine conjecture) and not only a priest, but also a future martyr. The multitude of the brothers occupied his house, and diligent love kept watch over all the doors. One might have applied the Apostle’s experience to him, that he wished to be let down from the window <note>A reference to St. Paul escaping from Damascus (Acts 9:25), suggesting Cyprian’s desire to escape the burden of office.</note>, if one wished to compare him with the Apostolic honor in the ministry. One saw with pleasure all the others waiting anxiously for him, and when he came, they received him with great joy. I say it reluctantly, but I must say it: some opposed his election (*), so that he might overcome them; for how gently, patiently, and with what affection did he not forgive them? How kindly did he pardon them? And he thereafter held them as his best and most intimate friends, to the great wonder of many.

### Chapter 6.
->Concerning Cyprian’s Good Nature and Mercy.<-

Who is able to recount how exemplary his conduct was? What godliness did he not possess? What earnestness? What mercy? What honor? Such holiness and grace shone from his mouth that one could not look upon him without a sense of humble awe <note>original: "Schaamhaftigkeit"; here implying a respectful bashfulness or modesty in the presence of greatness.</note>. His countenance was earnest and yet friendly; his earnestness was not too gloomy, and his friendliness not too cheerful, but both were so tempered that one knew not whether he should be feared or loved more; his whole demeanor was likewise balanced and wise. Worldly pride had not puffed him up, nor did a forced poverty make him appear ragged; because such a beggarly appearance is no less a form of pride than ambitious splendor (*). How overflowing he was as Bishop toward the poor, whom he had already zealously cared for as a beginning student of love and faith (**), this the overseers of mercy (the <term>Deacons</term> <note>original: "Diaconi"; church officers traditionally responsible for charitable works.</note>) and those whom he appointed to the service of good works, or whom he exhorted thereto according to the general ground of faith, may help to witness more closely. Thus, the Episcopal see received such a perfect Cyprian, and did not first create him.

Who would have raised up so many martyrs with divine exhortations? Do you also wish to know if he stepped out of the way back then out of fear? I need no other defense for him than the fact that he did indeed suffer later; a suffering he could have likewise escaped if he had previously fled out of fear. It was indeed fear, but a righteous one; a fear that was concerned with offending the Lord; a fear that preferred to obey the commands of the Lord rather than be crowned without obedience. For that—

# Chapter 8.
->How useful he was to the shattered congregation.<-

I do not consider it unhelpful to mention a little more about the benefit of his delay <note>Referring to the postponement of his eventual martyrdom.</note>, although we have just mentioned something of it; for when we consider the consequences, we must necessarily approve of his escape and attribute it not to human fear, but to Divine guidance. Not only had the unusual and bitter persecution devastated the people of God, but because the artful enemy <note>A common reference to the Devil.</note> could not deceive everyone with a single ruse, he also mortally wounded each warrior individually with different kinds of injuries wherever he found their breast and heart exposed (*). There simply had to be someone there who could either cut away the diseased flesh or bind up the wounds of the injured people—whom the warlike enemy had shot with many kinds of skill—using heavenly medicinal remedies according to the nature of the wounds. For such a purpose, then, was this man, gifted with wisdom as well as virtues, preserved: so that he might govern the Church, which was hovering in the midst of the waves of various divisions, with the rudder. I ask you, tell me, are these not Divine decrees? Could such a thing have happened without God? Those who believe such things could happen by chance should be careful what they do. The Church answers them with a clear voice and says: I do not believe, nor do I admit, that my most necessary members could be preserved without God’s nod.

# History of the Martyrdom / In the Year 258.

For Christians, this entire world is one single house. Therefore, although he was banished to a remote and desolate place, he knows nothing of misery while occupied with the affairs of his God. Indeed, he is already a stranger in his own city, where he serves God with all his heart; for as the purity <note>original: "Keuschheit," literally chastity or purity</note> of the Holy Spirit abstains from fleshly lusts and abandons the way of the "old man," <note>A reference to the Pauline concept of the "old self" (Ephesians 4:22) which must be cast off to live a Christian life.</note> he is a stranger among his own fellow citizens, and even among his natural parents and relatives. Moreover, what might otherwise be considered a punishment is, in such cases where our virtue is being tested, not a punishment at all, but our glory. Although we do not consider this banishment into exile to be a punishment, it is nonetheless the highest shame and greatest injustice for the persecutors—as their own consciences bear witness—that they inflict upon the innocent what they themselves regard as a penalty. I do not wish to describe the charms of that place now, and I will skip over the preparations for a comfortable life there. Let us suppose the place were a wasteland, miserable to look upon, with no healthy drinking water, no green fields, nor pleasant banks and rivers; but rather monstrous rocks and woods among desolate cliffs, and entirely secluded from all human society. Even if such a place bore the name of "Exile" <note>original: "Elendes," which in archaic German refers both to misery and to the state of being in a foreign land/exile.</note> where Cyprian, the priest of God, arrived—where, in the absence of human assistance, the birds would have to serve him like Elijah, or the angels like Daniel—yet far be it, indeed, far be it from us to believe that the least of those who came there for the sake of confessing the name of Christ should lack for anything. Much less did the priest of God, who was always devoted to works of mercy, suffer any lack of the necessities of life there.

As soon as he saw me, he began to write the sentence on a tablet, though I did not know what it was, for he had not questioned me in the usual manner. However, a youth stood behind him who was very curious and read what was written on the tablet. Because he was not permitted to speak it aloud, he indicated with clear gestures what was recorded there: he spread his hand out and held it flat like a sword of justice, making a cutting motion as executioners do when they behead someone; thus he made it clear enough what he meant to say. 

I understood then the sentence of my future suffering. Immediately within the vision, I began to pray and plead that I might be granted at least one day’s delay until I could put my affairs in order. As I repeated this request several times, the judge began to write again on the tablet—I know not what. But I perceived from the judge’s cleared expression that he was moved by my reasonable plea. Furthermore, that youth, who had recently revealed the manner of my suffering through gestures rather than words, indicated the granted delay until tomorrow with a secret glance, showing it clearly to me with the pressed-together fingers of his hand. Although the sentence had not been read aloud, and my heart rejoiced greatly over the permitted delay, I nevertheless trembled so much because of the uncertain explanation that my heart, filled half with joy and half with fear, beat with a heavy throb (*)."

## Chapter 13.

->Explanation of This Vision<-

What could be clearer than this revelation? What could be more blessed than this mark of honor? Everything that followed was told to him beforehand. Nothing of God’s words was lost; nothing of such a holy promise was diminished. Hear how everything shown to him occurred precisely to the last detail. In the vision, he begged for a one-day delay when his sentence was written, wishing to put his affairs in order during that period of leave. This "one day" signified one year, which is how much longer he lived in the world after the vision. To put it more clearly: exactly one year to the day from when this was shown to him, he was crowned as a martyr. Although we do not read explicitly in the Scripture that "one day of the Lord" signifies one year, we nonetheless find such an interpretation in the prophetic sense. <note>The author likely refers to the "year-day principle" found in biblical prophecy, such as in Ezekiel 4:6 or Numbers 14:34, where a day symbolizes a year.</note> Therefore, it is of no consequence that a year was indicated here under the interpretation of one day, for the greater period is to be regarded as the more perfect fulfillment. 

The fact that it was indicated to him in the vision through gestures rather than through words represented that the clear words were reserved for the "fulfillment of time"; for it is customary for everything to be explained clearly with words only when everything is fulfilled in deed. No one truly recognized why this had been shown to him until he was crowned a year later on the very same day he had the vision. During that intervening time, all the brothers knew for certain of his approaching suffering, but the actual day of that suffering was unknown to them all. 

I find almost an identical example in the Scripture: because the priest Zacharias <note>Original: *Zacharias*. Referring to the father of John the Baptist.</note> did not believe the angel who promised him a son, he became mute, so that he had to request a small tablet with gestures to write the son’s name, because he could not yet speak it. Luke 1, v. 59. <note>In modern Bibles, the naming of John occurs in Luke 1:63; verse 59 describes the circumcision ceremony.</note> It is right that it happened similarly here—that the messenger of God had to indicate the threatening sufferings of the leader <term>Vorsteher: a term for a bishop or presiding officer of the church</term> with gestures, to encourage the faith and strengthen the priest. The request of the leader, however, was grounded in the circumstances of his affairs and the nature of his will. What other matters or what other will should he have had, than those regarding the affairs of the—

---

The debate regarding whether credit should be given to dreams is not to be settled in this place; the learned are referred to the work of the equally learned Dodwell, *Dissertation 4 on Cyprian*, appended to the *Works of Cyprian*, Bremen Edition. <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711) was a prominent scholar whose "Cyprianic Dissertations" analyzed the life and times of the saint.</note>

28. St. Cyprian

...congregation? His highest concern during the remaining time granted to him was the utmost care to provide for the poor members of the church. I believe for no other reason—indeed, for this alone—was he granted such time by those who had banished him to misery and subsequently killed him: so that he, while still present in the body, might refresh those living in physical poverty one last time with his final assistance, or better said, with his entire fortune. When he had thus piously arranged his affairs and made his last will, the following day approached.

### Chapter 14.
-> The martyrdom of the Roman Bishop *Sixtus* is announced. *Cyprian's* preparation. <-

By now, news had resounded from Rome of *Sixtus* <note>original footnote: "Whose martyrdom was previously described in No. 27, chapter 1."</note>, the good and peace-loving priest and therefore most blessed martyr. Daily, the arrival of the executioner was expected, who was to strike through the neck of the most holy sacrifice <note>A poetic reference to Cyprian himself as a "sacrifice" for his faith</note> while he was in prayer. Thus, he died every day in the daily expectation of death, so that every single day could be called a "coronation day" <term>coronation day: a common early Christian term for the day of a martyr's death, viewed as the day they receive their crown in heaven</term>. Meanwhile, many excellent and illustrious persons of high rank visited him, as well as some of the noblest men of this world, who, out of old friendship, advised him to withdraw and hide for a while. To show they were not offering empty advice, they even offered him their own country estates as places of refuge. But he had already forgotten the world in his heart, which was directed toward heaven, and he did not follow those flattering counsels. He might perhaps have done so then, because many believers begged him to, if he had only received a command from God to do so. But for this man’s glorification, it should not be overlooked that the more the world became puffed up and, relying on its rulers, prepared for the persecution of the name of Christ, the more diligently he exhorted the servants of God in the Lord on every occasion. He encouraged them to trample the sufferings of this time underfoot in consideration of the future glory. *Romans 8:18.* Indeed, he spoke of this with such fervor that he even wished to be killed in the midst of such divine discourse.

-> He is captured on his country estates and brought to the governor in the countryside. <-

# History of Martyrdom / Year 258.

...of the priest who was determined as a well-pleasing sacrifice. Behold, by the order of the governor, there came to his **estates** <note>original: "Meyer-Höfe," referring to farmsteads or country villas</note> (I mean those estates which he had sold in the first fire of his faith, and had received back through Divine providence (*), and which he undoubtedly would have sold again for the benefit of the poor had he not feared to incite envy during the persecution) a captain with his soldiers in unexpected haste—or to speak more correctly, he intended to come unexpectedly; for how could a heart that is always prepared be overtaken unexpectedly? Thus he went along to the judge, certain of the victory that had been delayed for so long. He went with a cheerful and exalted spirit, with a joyful countenance, and in his heart he possessed the power of virtue. Yet his judgment was postponed until tomorrow, and he left the courthouse in the custody of the captain. Suddenly, the rumor resounded through all of *Carthage* that *Thascius* <note>Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, the saint’s full name</note> had been brought as a prisoner to the president at *Saturn’s Village* <note>original: "Saturni Dorf," likely referring to the Sexti, a suburban area of Carthage where the proconsul had a villa</note>, whom everyone knew well both for his famous name and his excellent works. From all corners and ends they ran there to see the sight, which was glorious to us for the sake of the confession of faith, but vexing to the heathens. While he was being guarded, however, and staying the one night in the captain’s house, he had sufficient permission from the guards so that we, his usual intimate friends and table-companions, were with him. But all the people, fearing that something might be undertaken at night without their knowledge, kept watch before the captain's door. Likewise, Divine goodness granted to him, the truly worthy one, that the people of God might solemnly observe their priest’s state of martyrdom with a nightly vigil of devotion. But perhaps someone asks for what reasons he had to go home from the judge's house with the captain and receive a delay? Some believe that the governor chose this for his own pleasure. But far be it from me to complain of the judge's laziness in Divine matters! Far be it from me to allow such evil thoughts into my conscience, as if a man's self-will could judge such a most blessed martyr; rather, the...

# Chapter 16.
## His Public Appearance Before the Court.

The following day dawned—the indicated, the promised, the Divine day; which the tyrant, even if he had wished, could not have postponed. It was a joyful day in the conscience of the future martyr, a clear day, free from any clouds across the whole sky, and illuminated by the bright sun. He then went out from the house of the captain—who was himself a captain of Christ and God—and crowds of a mixed multitude surrounded him on all sides. Such a great throng and endless army followed him as if he were about to contest death with an armed hand. On the way to the courthouse, they had to pass by the arena. <note>original: "Schau-Platz," referring to the stadium or theater where public spectacles and executions often occurred.</note> It was quite fitting, and as if done with intent, that he should pass the place of struggle, he who was running toward the crown of righteousness after a completed fight. When he arrived at the courthouse <term>Richt-Haus: the praetorium or official residence of the Roman governor</term> and the governor <note>The Roman Proconsul Galerius Maximus</note> was not yet there, he was taken to a private place. As he sat down there out of weariness from the long walk (the place, however, happened to be covered with a canopy of linen, so that even in his final hour of death he might enjoy episcopal honor [*]), one of the guards came forward. This man had previously become a Christian and offered him his clothes, wanting to exchange the martyr’s sweat-dampened garments for dry ones; perhaps he desired nothing else from all his teacher's possessions than the bloody sweat of the martyr journeying toward God. But Cyprian gave him answer and said: "Why should one seek to delay the discomfort which is likely to end today?" It is no wonder that he who utterly despised death also despised the burdens of the body. In short, his presence was quickly announced to the governor. He was brought forth and presented; asked if he was such-and-such a man, he answered that he was! And thus far, the matter consisted only of words.

sentence, which is spiritual and not to be repeated lightly; a judgment fitting for a bishop and worthy of such a martyr <term>Blut-Zeuge: literally "blood-witness," the early Christian term for one who dies for their faith</term>; a glorious judgment in which he was named the standard-bearer <note>original: "Fahnen-Führer," implying a leader who carries the flag into battle</note> of his sect (*), an enemy of the gods, who should henceforth serve as an example to his followers, and who was to consecrate his teaching with his own blood. Yet this is no wonder, since high priests are accustomed to prophesy when delivering bloody judgments. John 11, v. 51. He was indeed a standard-bearer who had taught others to carry the banner of Christ’s cross; an enemy of the gods who had commanded that the idols be destroyed. Thus he also became an exemplary model, dedicating the firstfruits of his sufferings in that same region to the many martyrs who followed (**). Likewise, he consecrated the teaching with his blood—namely, the teaching of the martyrs who followed this teacher of theirs in equal honor, and through their own example and blood, became a living testament to the doctrine.

### Chapter 18.
->Cyprian is Beheaded.<-

As he now came out through the door of the courthouse <term>Richt-Haus: the praetorium or official seat of judgment</term>, a skilled troop of soldiers accompanied him. And so that nothing should be lacking in his suffering, the captains and officers walked by his side. The place of execution was level and planted with trees, which provided a beautiful sight. Because the area was quite large, however, and the view was obstructed for those far off—especially amidst the confused throng of spectators—some devotees and supporters had climbed up into the trees; so that this, too, was not denied him: that he, after the example of Zacchaeus, was seen from the trees, (†) Luke 19, v. 2. He had already bound his eyes with his own hands and waited longingly for the hesitant executioner, whose gift is the sword. 28. St. Cyprian
<meta>catchword: brought</meta>

was brought. O blessed people of the churches, who mourns such a Bishop with their eyes, thoughts, and public, expressive words, and who—following the Divine judgment and according to the teaching they heard—has awarded him the Crown of Victory (*). For although that which everyone wished for could not happen—that the entire people might share in the same honor—nonetheless, every individual, before the eyes of Christ and the ears of their dying priest, wished from the heart to suffer; and through a capable witness of their desire, they sent, as it were, letters of announcement to God in advance.

### Chapter 19.
->He was the first Episcopal Martyr in Carthage.<-

In such a manner, through these completed sufferings, it was also fulfilled that Cyprian, as an example to all good people, should be the first to receive the Bishop’s Crown of Martyrdom in Africa (at Carthage), for he was also the first worthy man since the time of the Apostles to do so. For although the episcopal office <term>Bischöfliche Stand: the office or station of a bishop</term> has existed in Carthage since then, it is not known that any person there, though there were many good men and bishops, had ever become a martyr. Although God-fearing devotion is always counted as martyrdom for holy people, the Lord’s assistance nevertheless helped Cyprian toward the perfect Crown of Martyrdom (**) by ensuring that in the very same city where he had lived so exemplarily and previously performed so many great works, he should also be the very first to adorn his heavenly priestly office with victorious blood. 

What should I now undertake here? My divided mind, placed by his suffering half in joy and half in sorrow, finds my too-narrow breast burdened all too much with this twofold emotion. Do I regret that I was not his companion in death? Yet because of his victory, I must triumph. I wish to triumph because of his victory! And yet, for the pain of it, I cannot bear that I am not his companion. But I will confess to you simply, so that you may know it: let this be my heart's opinion. I rejoice, yes, I greatly rejoice, because of his glorification; but it saddens me much more that I have not yet finished my own race!

(**) Every earnest warrior of Christ is a martyr when he becomes a public "blood-witness" <term>Blut-Zeuge: a martyr who seals their faith with their life</term>; the ancients called this the "perfect state of martyrdom."

Court Records, Year 257.

# Court Records
## of the Holy Martyr and Bishop Cyprian.
### Chapter 1.

->St. Cyprian’s first interrogation by the Governor Paternus,<-
->In the year 257.<-

When the Emperor Valerian for the fourth time and Gallienus for the third time were Roman Consuls <term>Bürgermeister: literally "mayors," used here to denote the Roman Consuls who served as year-defining magistrates</term>, it happened on the thirtieth day of August (in the year 257) that in the courtroom at Carthage, the Governor <term>Landpfleger: a regional governor or proconsul</term> Paternus spoke to Bishop Cyprian: "The most serene Emperors Valerian and Gallienus have most graciously sent letters to me, in which they have commanded that all those who do not adhere to the Roman religion must adopt the Roman church ceremonies; therefore, I ask after the name of your religion—what do you answer me?"

Bishop Cyprian said: "I am a Christian and a bishop! I know of no other gods but the one true God, who made the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything that is within these three; this is the God we Christians serve; to Him we pray day and night, for ourselves and for all people, and for the well-being of the Emperors themselves!" 

The Governor Paternus said: "So, do you then remain of this mind?" 

Bishop Cyprian answered: "A good mind that knows God cannot be changed!" 

The Governor Paternus said: "Can you then, according to the command of Valerian and Gallienus, travel into exile <term>ins Elend wandern: literally "to wander into misery," a contemporary idiom for being sent into banishment</term> to Curubis <note>original: "Curubin"; a coastal town in Tunisia used as a place of exile</note>?" 

Cyprian the Bishop answered: "I am ready to do so." 

Paternus the Governor said: "They have issued orders to me not only regarding the bishops, but also concerning the priests and elders among you; therefore, I wish to know from you what manner of priests are in this city?" 

Bishop Cyprian gave this answer: "You have very rightly and usefully forbidden in your laws that there should be any informers among the people; therefore, I cannot discover nor betray them; however, they shall be found in their parishes (*)." 

The Governor Paternus said: "I am asking now—"

Early the next morning, on September 14th, a large crowd gathered in that same district at the sixth milestone, according to the command of the Governor **Galerius Maximus**; who on that day sat in judgment at the place where bloody sentences were passed, called **Sauciolum** (**), and ordered **Cyprian** to be brought forward. The Governor **Galerius Maximus** spoke: "Have you allowed yourself to be used as a father to these heretical spirits and banished men?" <note>The Governor is accusing Cyprian of being a ringleader of a forbidden sect.</note> Bishop **Cyprian** answered: "Yes!" Bishop **Cyprian** replied: "Do what you are commanded; in so righteous a cause, there is no need for further consideration."

Early on the following day, which was the 14th of September, a great multitude of people gathered in the same village located at the sixth stone, according to the command of Governor Galerius Maximus; who sat in judgment on that day at the place where the bloody sentences were given, called Sauciolum (**) <note>The name is derived from the Latin "sauciare," meaning to wound or hurt</note>, and ordered Cyprian to be brought forward. ...made holy laws, yet the pious and consecrated princes Valerian and Gallienus, as enlargers of the Empire, and especially the Most Serene Emperor Valerian, have not been able to move you to observe their devout ceremonies. ### Chapter 5.
->His Execution.<-

When this sentence was spoken, the entire multitude of the brethren cried out: "We wish to be beheaded with him also!" Because of this, a great commotion arose among the brethren, and a large crowd followed him to the place of execution. Thus, Cyprian was led out to the field of that same plot of land; there he took off his outer garments, knelt down, and offered his prayer to the Lord. Afterward, he also took off his breast-cloth <note>original: "Brust-Latz," likely referring to a dalmatic or a specific liturgical garment</note> and gave it to the deacons, standing there in his under-tunic <gloss>original: "Hemde"</gloss> to await the executioner’s stroke. When the executioner stepped forward, Cyprian commanded his followers to give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces <note>original: "Gülden" — referring to the Latin *aurei*; it was a custom for the condemned to pay their executioner to show they held no malice and to ensure a swift death</note>. The brethren, however, offered him bandages and cloths, and the holy Cyprian finally bound his own eyes; but because he could not tie the sleeves and collar of his tunic himself, Julian the Elder and Julian the Deacon performed this task for him. Thus the blessed Cyprian suffered, and his body was placed on public display to satisfy the curiosity of the heathens <note>original: "Heyden"</note>; but at night, the brethren took him from there and carried him with wax candles and torches in great triumph and pageantry to the tomb of the procurator Macrobius Candidianus, located on the Mappalian Way near the fishponds. A few days later, the Governor <term>Landpfleger: a high-ranking provincial administrator</term> Galerius Maximus, who had pronounced the sentence upon him, died.

### Chapter 6.
->On the Time of his Martyr-Death.<-

The most blessed martyr Cyprian suffered on the 14th day of September, under the Emperors Valerian and Gallienus; our Lord Jesus Christ reigning, to whom belongs honor and glory through all eternity. Amen.

# 29. St. Fructuosus, Bishop; Eulogius and Augurius, both Deacons at Tarragona (*).

<note>original footnote: "Is a Spanish episcopal city in Catalonia located by the sea, not far from Barcelona." Known today as Tarragona, it was an important Roman administrative center.</note>

## In the Year 259.

### Chapter 1.

->Bishop Fructuosus of Tarragona is taken prisoner.<-

During the time of the Emperors Valerian and Gallienus, when Aemilianus and Bassus were the Roman consuls <note>original: "Bürgermeister" — meaning the annual chief magistrates of Rome</note>, it happened on the 16th of January, on the Day of the Lord <note>Sunday</note>, that Bishop Fructuosus of Tarragona and the deacons <note>church officers who assisted the bishop</note> Augurius and Eulogius were taken prisoner. Bishop Fructuosus was still in his bedchamber when the soldiers on special duty <note>original: "gefreite Soldaten" — likely referring to *beneficiarii*, soldiers exempt from menial tasks to serve as guards or messengers</note> Aurelius, Festucius, Aelius, Pollentius, Donatus, and Maximus arrived at his house. When he noticed their arrival, he rose quickly and went out to them barefoot. The soldiers spoke to him: "Come with us; the President <note>original: "Präsident" — referring to the Roman provincial governor, Aemilianus</note> has summoned you and your deacons to appear before him." Bishop Fructuosus answered them, saying: "Let us go! But if it pleases you, I will put on my shoes." The soldiers replied to him: "Put them on as you wish." After they went with them, they were placed in prison. Fructuosus, however, full of certainty and joy over the expected crown from the Lord to which he had been called, prayed without ceasing. The entire brotherhood visited him, refreshing him and asking that he might be mindful of them.

### Chapter 2.

->He baptizes someone in prison; he is judicially interrogated along with Augurius and Eulogius, and sentenced to fire.<-

The next day, he baptized our brother Rogatianus in the prison. They remained in the dungeon for six days until they were interrogated at noon on the 21st of January, when the Governor <note>original: "Präsident"</note> Aemilianus gave the command and said:

"Bring Bishop Fructuosus, and likewise Augurius and Eulogius, in to me!" The court officials brought them in and said, "They are here!" The Governor <note>original: "Præsident" — referring to the Roman provincial governor Aemilianus</note> Aemilianus then spoke to Bishop Fructuosus: "Have you heard what the Emperors have commanded?" Bishop Fructuosus replied: "I know nothing of their commands, for I am a Christian!" Governor Aemilianus said: "They have commanded that the gods be honored." Fructuosus the Bishop said: "I honor the only God, who created the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything that is within them." Aemilianus said: "Do you not also know that there are gods?" Bishop Fructuosus answered: "That I do not know." Aemilianus said: "You shall find out soon enough." Then Bishop Fructuosus sighed to the Lord and began to pray secretly. Governor Aemilianus spoke: "Who then would hear us, who would be feared, and whom else would we worship if we did not serve the gods and did not adore the image <note>original: "Antlitz" — literally "countenance" or "face," referring to the cult of the Emperor where his statue was treated as a divine presence</note> of the Emperor?" Furthermore, the Governor said to the Deacon Augurius: "Do not pay attention to Fructuosus's nonsense." Augurius the Deacon answered: "I honor the Almighty God." Governor Aemilianus then said to the Deacon Eulogius: "Do you not also worship Fructuosus?" The Deacon Eulogius answered: "I do not worship Fructuosus, but I worship the one whom Fructuosus also worships." Governor Aemilianus spoke to Bishop Fructuosus: "Are you a Bishop?" Fructuosus gave the answer: "I am!" Aemilianus said: "You *were* one." <note>This was a legal formula used to strip a condemned man of his titles and status before execution.</note> Thereupon he pronounced the sentence: that they should be burned alive.

### Chapter 3.
->His journey to the place of execution.<-

When Bishop Fructuosus was led to the amphitheater <note>original: "Schau-Platz" — the Roman arena used for public executions</note> six days later, on the Sabbath <note>referring here to Saturday</note>, along with his deacons, the people felt great pity for him, because not only the Christian brothers but also the heathens <note>non-Christians or pagans</note> loved him. For he was such a man as the Holy Spirit desired him to be through the blessed Apostle Paul—the "chosen vessel" <note>A title given to St. Paul in the Bible (Acts 9:15)</note> and teacher of the heathens. Because of this, the brothers, knowing that he was going toward such glory, rejoiced more than they mourned. When many of them, out of brotherly love, offered them a cup of spiced wine, he said: "The hour has not yet arrived that we may break our fast!" For it was the fourth hour of the day <note>Approximately 10:00 AM; the Bishop refused to break his ritual fast even on the way to his death.</note>;

## Chapter 4.

->He comforts the brothers, and all three are burned.<-

As he now stood at the gate of the arena, and was about to enter—to an incorruptible crown rather than to punishment—notwithstanding that the aforementioned exempt soldiers stood by and heard it, the holy Bishop Fructuosus spoke, prompted by the address of our brother Martialis and moved by the Holy Spirit: 

> "You shall not lack a shepherd now, and the love and promise of the Lord shall not cease, neither here nor in the future; for this which you see is only to be regarded as an hour's weakness." 

After he had comforted the brotherhood, they went in to blessedness, worthy and fortunate in their state of martyrdom, so that they received the fruit promised in Holy Scripture. Since they became like Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael <note>original: "Anania, Asaria, and Misaeli" — the three Hebrew youths cast into the fiery furnace in the Book of Daniel</note>, for in them one also saw the Divine Trinity in the fire; for each of these three was seen standing in the fire, in the form of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (*). Now when the ropes with which their hands were bound had burned away, they performed with per-

### Chapter 5.
#### They appear in a miracle during their ascension.

After this, the glory of the Lord was revealed; for heaven opened so that Babylas and Mygdonius—our brothers and members of the household of the Governor <term>President Aemilianus; "President" here refers to the Roman provincial governor</term>—saw it. They also showed to the daughter of this Aemilianus (their earthly mistress), the holy Bishop Fructuosus along with his deacons, as they ascended toward heaven with the stakes to which they had been bound, wearing crowns upon their heads. They even called out to Governor Aemilianus himself and spoke: "Come and see those whom you have condemned, how they are in heaven and have become partakers of their hope!" But when Aemilianus came and wished to see it as well, he was not worthy to see them.

### Chapter 6.
#### The brothers collect their relics and are warned in a vision to bury them.

The brothers <note>Refers to the local Christian community</note>, however, were troubled because they were deprived of their shepherd; not that they mourned for Fructuosus, but rather they felt a longing for him, mindful of the faith and struggle of each man. When night fell, they hurried to the arena <note>original: "Schau-Platz"</note> and had brought wine (*) with them to sprinkle upon the ashes and bones of the half-burnt bodies, and to extinguish the glowing coals. When this was done, each collected the ashes of these martyrs as best he could and preserved them. But even in this, our Lord and Savior was glorified, so that the faith of the believers might be increased and an example given to the "little ones" <note>A biblical term for new or humble believers</note>; for it was fitting for the martyr Fructuosus that what he had taught in this world through the mercy of God, and had promised in our Lord and Savior, should also afterward in his suffering and resurrection...

---

(*) This was the custom among the Romans during the usual cremation of their corpses: to extinguish the hot ashes with wine, or milk, and collected tears, in order to more easily collect the remains (regarding this, one may read Kirchmannus, Book 3, Chapter 6, *On Roman Funerals* <note>original Latin title: "de Funeribus Romanor."</note>). The Christians also maintained this practice with the burned martyrs.

## Chapter 7.

->The three martyrs appear to Governor Aemilianus; Their bones are buried.<-

In the same way, Fructuosus also appeared with his <term>Deacons; clergy assistants to the bishop</term> in long white robes of promise to the Governor <term>Aemilianus; the Roman provincial official who presided over the trial</term> who had condemned them. He rebuked him and triumphed over him; for it had helped the Governor nothing to believe that he had robbed them of body and life on earth in vain, for he now saw them glorified. When morning came, all the Christians who had collected the <term>Relics; the physical remains or ashes of a saint</term> of the saints gathered together. With great fear and highest joy, they told one another of the identical visions they had seen during the night, and they buried the ashes they had brought with all honor in the church under the holy altar. O blessed martyrs, who were found proven in the fire like precious gold, clothed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation; who are crowned with the unfading crown and scepter because they have crushed the devil's head! O blessed martyrs, who possess a worthy dwelling in heaven, stand at the right hand of Christ, and praise God the Almighty Father, together with our Lord Jesus Christ, His Son. The Lord has received His martyrs in peace through their good confession; to Him belongs honor and glory for all eternity. Amen. <note>original: "Ruinart. Act. MM. pag. 219." This refers to Thierry Ruinart’s "Acta Martyrum" (Acts of the Martyrs), a famous 17th-century scholarly collection of early Christian records.</note>

# 30. St. James, Marianus, Agapius, Secundinus, Aemilianus, Tertulla, and Antonia, etc. at Lambaesis in Numidia(*). In the year 259.

## Chapter 1.

->The author of this history, acting as an eyewitness, reports the circumstances of the martyrs at their own request.<-

Whenever the most blessed witnesses of Almighty **GOD** and His Christ, as they hasten toward the promised kingdom of the heavens, modestly entrust a task to their most intimate companions, they do so mindful of the humility which always makes them glorious in faith. The more humbly they have petitioned, the more effectively they have obtained their request, leaving to us the task of proclaiming their glory as the noble witnesses of **GOD**. I speak of Marianus, one of our dearest brothers, and James, who, as you know, were not only joined with me in the fellowship of a holy faith and life but were also my own house-mates. These men charged us to make known to the brotherhood their difficult struggle, which they maintained with brave spirits at the prompting of the Holy Spirit against the raging oppressions of this world and heathen attacks. They did this not because they desired to desecrate the crown of their glorification with worldly ambition, but so that the community and the people of **GOD** might be strengthened by their prior experience and the example of their faith. It was not without reason that our shared intimacy laid this task upon me; for who could doubt that we, who were found together in united love when the time of persecution arrived, should have lived together in peace?

## Chapter 2.

->The author travels with the martyrs in Numidia, where a great persecution was then occurring.<-

Since we were traveling together in Numidia at the same <margin>(*) This is a Moorish kingdom in Africa, located behind those nests of pirates <note>original: "Raub-Nestern," referring to the Barbary Coast</note> Tunis and Tripoli.</margin>

<summary>This page introduces the account of several North African martyrs, including James and Marianus, written by a companion who lived with them. It establishes the author's purpose: to provide an eyewitness account of their faith during the Roman persecutions in Numidia to encourage the Christian community.</summary>

traveled, and, as always before, were companions and travel-associates on a path which led us to the desired obedience of faith and religion, but led them to heaven. We arrived at the place called Muguas, situated near the city of Cirta; in that city, the blind rage of the heathens and the persecution by the soldiers was like a roaring flood of water, and the madness of the raging devil sought with a famished throat to swallow the faith of the righteous during this trial. Therefore, the most blessed martyrs Marianus and James recognized in themselves the surest and most desired signs of Divine grace: that they had been led at the right time into the land where the tempest of persecution roared violently. They noted that, through Christ's guidance, their path had fallen toward the place of their crowning. For the madness of the bloodthirsty and blind Governor <note>original: "Præsidenten," referring to the Roman *praeses* or provincial governor</note> sought all the beloved of Christ with an armed hand of soldiers, acting eagerly and with hateful intentions. This senseless cruelty raged not only against those who had remained unharmed in previous persecutions to live devoted to **GOD** in freedom; the devil also reached out with his insatiable hands for those who had long ago been banished into misery. These men had already become martyrs, not yet with their blood, but in their spirit, and were now to be crowned by the madness of the cruel Governor.

# Chapter 3.

->Agapius and Secundinus / two bishops / are captured / and<-
->meet the others at an inn along the way.<-

Among these, the bishops Agapius and Secundinus were fetched from their place of exile and led to the Governor. Both were praiseworthy men in spiritual love, especially the latter in his holiness of bodily abstinence <note>Refers to the practice of celibacy or asceticism</note>. They were led, I say, not from one punishment to another, as it seemed to the heathens, but rather from one glory to another, and from one victorious struggle to another. They had already brought the vanity of this world under the yoke by demonstrating the name of Christ, and now they also wished to trample the sting of death underfoot through the power of a perfect faith. For it was not fitting to delay the victory in the struggle on earth, since the **LORD** called them to Himself in haste. It happened, however, dear brothers, that Agapius and Secundinus, the praiseworthy martyrs of the venerable priesthood <note>original: "Priestertuhme," here meaning the high clergy or office of bishop</note>, were traveling according to the temporal command of the Governor—

but according to the gracious election of Christ, they were on the path of their struggle of suffering <note>The "struggle of suffering" refers to the *agon*, the spiritual and physical contest of martyrdom</note> and deemed us worthy to take up lodging with us. They possessed such a spirit of life-giving power and grace that for such holy and excellent witnesses of **GOD**, it was too little to offer up their precious blood through the state of martyrdom itself; rather, they also awakened other martyrs through the inspiration of their faith. These possessed such love and favor toward the brothers that although they could have built up the faith of the brothers silently through their devout and steadfast example of virtue, they nevertheless showered our hearts with wholesome admonitions toward persistent patience; for those who heard **GOD** speaking within them could not remain silent. This was no wonder, since their admonitions so abundantly encouraged all our spirits in so few days, as Christ was already shining forth from them with His radiant grace in view of their imminent sufferings.

### Chapter 4.

->**James** and **Marian** are also taken prisoner / and led toward **Cirta**.<-

Finally they had to depart, and left **Marian** and **James** among us, prepared by their example and service, who soon followed their fresh and glorious footsteps. For hardly had two days passed, behold, the destined palms of victory <note>The palm branch is a traditional symbol of victory in martyrdom</note> already sought our dearest brothers **Marian** and **James**—not, as is customary in other places, perhaps a **corporal** <term>Corporal: here referring to a lower-ranking officer, often a *beneficiarius* in the original Latin</term> with a small group of men, but a captain <note>original: "Hauptmann," referring to a Roman centurion</note> with his entire troop of a hundred men; and the godless crowd came flying with armed hands into the village where we were, as if to a notorious dwelling-place of faith. O desired ambush! O happy terror worthy of jumping for joy! For they came to us for this end alone, so that the righteous blood of **Marian** and **James** might obtain **GOD’S** grace. We can hardly, dearest brothers, restrain our overflowing joy; we who two days ago had bid farewell to those with our **parting**-kiss <note>original: "Valet-Kusse," the *osculum pacis* or kiss of peace shared by the faithful</note>, and now already had two other martyrs in their place. As such a ripe and divine hour of grace occurred, we became partakers in part of the brotherly glorification, because we had just previously set out on the way from **Muzguis** <note>Muzguis, also known as Muguas, was a locality near Cirta in modern-day Algeria</note> toward **Cirta**. We went ahead, and they, Dearest ones, followed us, who were chosen for the palms of martyrdom, whom love for

## Chapter 5.

->**James** and **Marian** are tortured.<-

Thereupon they were attacked with many and harsh tortures by the executioner, the bailiff of the righteous and the pious, at which the authorities of both cities, <term>Centuria</term> <note>A town in the Roman province of Numidia, in modern-day Algeria</note> and <term>Cirta</term> <note>Modern-day Constantine, Algeria; the capital of Numidia</note> / were present as priests of the devil at this sacrifice; just as if the faith, which nonetheless regards the body but little, could be extinguished through the destruction of the limbs. <term>James</term> <note>original: "Jacobus"</note> indeed, who was always very earnest in the power of faith and had already been victorious in the <term>Decian persecution</term> <note>A widespread Roman persecution of Christians (250–251 AD) under Emperor Decius</note>, did not only confess that he was a Christian but also pretended to be a <term>Deacon</term> <note>original: "Diaconus"; a minister in the early church hierarchy</note>. <term>Marian</term> <note>original: "Marianus"</note>, however, allowed himself to be moved by the pains to confess only what he was, namely a Christian and a <term>Reader</term> <note>original: "Vorleser"; an official, also called a Lector, responsible for reading the scriptures during liturgy</note> (*). What horrifying tortures of new invention were these! What punishments, devised according to the poisonous mind of the devil and suited to provoke apostasy <note>Renouncing one's faith</note>, were they not! **Marian** hung there wounded, and—something pleasant for a martyr in the midst of being torn apart—he was tortured to such a degree that the pain elevated him even above his status. He did not hang in the usual manner by the hands, but by the outermost joint of the thumbs, so that the pain in the small joint was sharpened by the heavy body hanging down; in addition, he had excessively heavy weights hanging from his feet, so that the uneven pain from above and below, and the tearing of the internal organs, along with the stretched body hanging only by the tendons, might defeat the spirit. # Chapter 6.
->Marian relates his vision.<-

What do you heathens <note>original: "Heijden"</note> think of this? Do you still believe that Christians fear the punishments of the dungeon and are terrified by the darkness of this world, they for whom the joy of eternal light is prepared? Even though you seek out the most secret and hidden place for punishment, and the heavy darkness of the darkest abyss—yes, the house of darkness itself—yet for those who trust God, no place is inconvenient, no time is sorrowful. The brotherly Christ refreshes these witnesses, devoted to God the Father, day and night. 

Meanwhile, a divine and gracious revelation <note>original: "Offenbarung"</note> for a healthy confidence of faith occurred to Marian <note>original: "Mariano"</note> after he had fallen into a deep sleep following the torture, which he himself told us after he awoke in the following manner: "To me, dear brothers," he said, "a highly exalted, shining judgment seat <note>original: "Gerichts-Stul"</note> was shown, upon which one sat like a judge. There was also a stage for the accused, not low, nor of a single elevation, but raised with many steps; and various parties of <term>Confessors</term> <note>In the early church, those who bravely admitted their faith under torture but had not yet been executed</note> were brought forward, whom the judge condemned to the sword. Thereupon I heard a clear and very strong voice say: 'Bring Marian here!' Then I climbed up onto that same stage; and behold, unexpectedly, **Cyprian** (*) appeared to me on the right of that same judge, and he reached out his hand to me and lifted me to the highest position on the stage, saying to me with friendly gestures: 'Come and sit next to me!' It also happened that other parties were heard, where I also sat as an <term>assessor</term> <note>A legal assistant or advisor who sits beside a judge</note>."

### Chapter 8.

->The Vision of Aemilianus.<-

This grace, however, did not happen only to one or another, but also to Aemilianus, who, although he was a knight <note>original: *Ritter*; here referring to the *Equites*, the Roman social class below senators</note> according to his heathen status, was thrown into prison with our brothers. ## Chapter 11.

->The martyr *Agapius* appears to *James* in the dungeon / and they are all sentenced.<-

**C**oncerning *Agapius* (*), who long ago had confirmed his faith with a martyr's death, he had often repeated his prayer for the two young daughters, *Tertulla* and *Antonia*, whose souls were entrusted to him, that they might also become martyrs with him through *God's* grace. Because of his merits, the following word of revelation came to him: "Why do you ask unceasingly for that which you have already obtained with a single prayer?" This *Agapius* now appeared to *James* <note>original: *Jacobo*; the Latinized dative form of James</note> in his sleep while in the dungeon; for at the hour of his suffering, as he waited for the executioner <note>original: *Nachrichters*; the official who carries out the death sentence</note>, *James* said: "I go joyfully to the banquet of *Agapius* and the other martyrs; since I saw our *Agapius* in a vision last night, most exceedingly joyful among all those who lay imprisoned with us in the *Cirta* <note>original: *Cirtensisch*; referring to the Roman city of Cirta in modern-day Algeria</note> dungeon. He held a heavenly, public feast of joy, to which I and *Marianus* were led, as if to a *love-feast* <term>love-feast (agape); a communal meal shared by early Christians expressing brotherly love</term>, in the spirit of love and goodwill. However, we encountered a boy whom we recognized as one of the two who had suffered together with their mother three days ago; he had a crown of roses upon his head and carried a green palm branch in his right hand, and spoke to us: 'Why do you hurry so? Rejoice and leap for joy, for tomorrow you shall eat with us!' O great and glorious grace of *God* toward His own! O true fatherly love in *Christ Jesus* our *Lord*, who shows His beloved such great benefits and lets them know beforehand what gifts of His goodness He intends to bestow. The first day after this vision dawned, and the judge's sentence served to fulfill the divine promises; for according to it, *Marianus* and *James*, along with the rest of their fellow-officials..."

History of Martyrdom / Year 259.

...brought with honor to the Forefathers <note>original: *Erz-Vätern*; referring to the biblical Patriarchs</note>, and snatched from the oppressions of this world through the death penalty. They were thus led to the place of crowning <note>A common early Christian metaphor for martyrdom</note>, which was by the river, where the high banks on both sides served as seating for the spectators. The river itself received the blessed blood like a brook, and one saw a twofold baptism of the saints with blood and with water.

## Chapter 12.
->Dreadful execution of the martyrs.<-

There one beheld a wondrous and ingenious brevity of cruelty. For because the numerous multitude of the condemned righteous ones waited with longing for the beadle's <note>original: *Büttels*; an official or assistant to the executioner</note> hand and sword, the master of cruelty placed them in order, rank by rank, so that the wasteful blows of the executioner could strike down the holy necks as if in a single fury; he devised such a swift execution of malice so that this bloody and barbaric service did not become too tedious. For had he repeated the blows in one place, an uncommon mountain of corpses would have arisen, nor would there have been enough space in that narrow place by the river. Their eyes were indeed bound according to custom, yet no darkness enclosed the free spirit; instead, a great and priceless radiance of immeasurable light shone upon them. Most of them testified this to the brothers standing near them: that although they no longer saw the physical light, they said they saw wondrous things, and white horses appeared to them, fairer than snow, upon which sat youths shining in white. Other martyrs confirmed their fellow brothers' statements and testified that they heard the rattling of the horses with their own ears. Marianus, however, filled with the Prophetic Spirit, boldly proclaimed the approaching vengeance for the righteous blood, and various plagues of this world: pestilence, imprisonment, hunger, earthquakes, and blood-sucking vermin (*). With which proclamation not only did the faith of the martyrs overcome the heathens... <note>The word *bestie-* is a fragment, likely from *bestieg* or *bestürzte*, meaning "overcame" or "astonished."</note>

---

(*) Such proclamation of the judgments of GOD happened not in wrath, but as a powerful testimony to the heathens, just as the Lord himself foretold the downfall of Jerusalem, etc. Here, everything was fulfilled shortly thereafter, when with the wretched Persian captivity of Emperor Valerian, the "Thirty Tyrants" <note>A group of pretenders who rose to power during the chaotic reign of Gallienus</note> arose and threw everything into turmoil, in addition to which pestilence and hunger came, of which mention has already been made in Saint Dionysius's History of Martyrdom, chapters 10 and 11, page 172.

### Chapter 13.

->*Marianus's mother, named Mary, praises God along with the author.*<-

When this had occurred, Marianus’s mother, Mary, leaped with Maccabean joy <note>A reference to the biblical mother in 2 Maccabees 7, who encouraged her seven sons to undergo martyrdom rather than betray their faith</note>, who, after the completed suffering of her son, congratulated not only him but also herself for having given birth to such a pledge. She embraced her own glorification in her son and kissed the bloody wound of his neck with holy devotion. O blessed Mary! O worthy mother of such a son and such a name! Who would believe this high name was given to her unjustly, which the fruit of her womb has so adorned? Inestimable, however, is the mercy of Almighty God and His Christ toward His own, who not only strengthens those who believe in His name with His grace but also makes them alive through the redemption of His blood. Who can worthily measure His benefits? He who works always with fatherly patience so that He may prove in us that which we believe we shall obtain through the blood of our God: To Him be the honor and dominion for ages of ages. History of Martyrdom / Year 260.

...look upon you as well, and the servants of God and His Christ find nothing more to do than to remember the multitude of the brothers; therefore love has compelled us, and imposed this task upon us to write to you, so that we might leave behind for future brothers both a sincere testimony of the glory of God, as well as a memorial of our blessed labor and enduring patience in the Lord.

## Chapter 2.
->They are taken captive; the early death of Donatianus and Primolus.<-

After the general uprising which the wild Governor <note>The German "Präsident" here refers to the Roman *praeses* or provincial governor.</note> had stirred up for our destruction, and upon which a violent persecution of the Christians arose the following day, we were seized, namely: Lucius, Montanus, Flavianus, Julianus, Victoricus, Primolus, Renus, and Donatianus. Donatianus was still being instructed <note>This refers to a "catechumen," a person receiving basic Christian instruction before baptism.</note>; and when he was baptized in the prison, he immediately gave up his spirit, and thus attained the martyr’s crown unstained, passing from the water-baptism to glory. A similar completion and end was also shared by Primolus, who had been baptized only a few days prior.

## Chapter 3.
->Their arrest in the main guardhouse; they turn away the Governor's wrath through their prayer.<-

When we had been captured and placed in the main guardhouse, the soldiers informed us that the Governor had threatened yesterday to burn us. For, as we truly recognized afterwards, he intended to burn us alive. But the Lord, who alone can rescue His servants from the fire, and in whose hands are the word and heart of the king, turned the fury of the raging Governor away from us, and immediately gave us that for which we had asked, as we devoted ourselves unceasingly to prayer with total confidence. The fire ignited for our destruction was extinguished, and the flame of the burning furnaces was dampened with the dew of the Lord <note>A biblical allusion to the "Song of the Three Holy Children" in the fiery furnace, where God sent a cooling dew to protect the faithful.</note>. For it did not seem impossible to the believers that new histories should match the old ones, which the Lord has promised through His Spirit; for He who worked His glorification in those three youths in the fiery furnace of Babylon was also able to triumph in us.

## Chapter 4.
->They are brought into a dark dungeon.<-

Thereupon the Governor <note>original: "Präfidente", referring to the Roman *praeses* or provincial governor</note>, who had changed his intention through Divine governance, gave the order that we should be led into the dungeon; this was immediately done by the soldiers, though we were not terrified by the foul darkness of that place. For the dark dungeon gave back a reflection of the bright-shining Spirit, and amidst the gloomy horror of the everlasting night, the bright light of faith gave us the light of day. We ascended to the highest place of punishment as if we were intended to go into heaven. What kind of days we had there, and how we spent the nights, cannot be expressed by any tongue. The torments of the prison are incomprehensible; yet we do not shy away from describing the cruelty of the place as it is. For the greater the temptation is, the greater is He who overcomes it within us; the struggle is not ours, but rather the Lord obtains the victory. For it is a small thing to the servants of God to be killed, since death is nothing, its sting and bitterness having been abolished by the Lord, who triumphed over it through the victory-sign of the Cross. No weapons are necessary, except as a soldier should be armed; and he is not armed unless he is to struggle with the enemy. The reward, however, does not follow until one has struggled, and the palm branch is not distributed until after a complete victory. After a few days, we were refreshed by a visit from the brothers, so that all the burden of the preceding night was taken away by the comfort and joy of this day.

## Chapter 5.
->Renus has a vision.<-

Thereupon it was shown to Renus <note>One of the fellow prisoners mentioned on the previous page.</note> in a vision in his sleep that each of us was being led out, and each person's lamp went before him; but he whose lamp did not go before him did not follow. As we were going out together with our lamps, he awoke. When he told us this, we rejoiced in the faithful confidence that we should walk with Christ, who is the lamp unto our feet and the Word of God <note>A reference to Psalm 119:105.</note>.

After that same night, we had a joyful day; for on that day, we were suddenly taken to the City Administrator <note>German: "Stadt-Verweser," likely referring to a magistrate or deputy acting in the governor's stead.</note>

## Chapter 7.
### Victor’s Vision.

But this labor, most beloved brothers, this lack, and this time of need was ordained by God; and just as He allowed us to be tempted, so He also comforted us in the midst of the temptation through a vision. For to Victor—a priest and martyr alongside us, who suffered shortly thereafter—the following was shown: "I saw," he said, "a boy coming into this dungeon whose face shone with an inexpressible radiance. Furthermore, he said: 'Tell them they shall be more gloriously crowned; the spirit is already hurrying to its Lord, and the soul which is very near to suffering seeks its eternal dwellings.'" Victor then asked this Lord about Paradise, and where that might be. He answered: "Outside the world!" The former replied and said: "Show it to me!" Then the angelic youth <note>original: "Englische Jüngling", likely a play on "Engel" (angel)</note> spoke to him again: "Where then would faith remain?" <note>Meaning that if the afterlife were seen clearly, faith would no longer be necessary</note> When Victor, out of human weakness, said: "What you command me, I cannot retain; give me a sign that I may report it to them!" ### Chapter 8.
->Quartillosia’s Vision.<-

**F**or He showed this in a vision to our sister Quartillosia, who lay imprisoned with us; this woman’s husband and son had died as martyrs three days earlier, and she soon followed her kin in death among us. And from the bowls he carried, he gave everyone to drink; yet the milk in the bowls did not decrease. Suddenly, the stone covering the window in the roof (the gap) was removed, and the bright light of heaven shone through the window-hole. The youth then took the bowls he held and set one down on the right and the other on the left, saying: See, you are satisfied, and there is still an abundance; the third bowl shall also be yours! With that, he departed."

## Chapter 10.
->Exhortation to Love and Harmony.<-

Now, most beloved brothers, something must also be said concerning the love we have for one another. We do not wish to teach you with this, but only to remind you; for just as we have been of one mind, so we also live together in the Lord and pray for one another. The unity of love must be kept firm, and the bond of affection must not be broken; then the devil will be brought underfoot, and one will obtain from the Lord whatever they ask for, according to His promise, where He says: *If two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven.* Matthew 18, v. 19. We also cannot obtain eternal life and reign with Christ in any other way unless we do what He, who promised the life and the kingdom, commanded us to do. But the Lord Himself testified that those who preserve brotherly peace obtain the inheritance of **GOD**, when He says: *Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God!* Matthew 5, v. 9. This the Apostle explains, saying: *Let us be children of God; and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.* Romans 8, v. 17. Since no one can be an heir except a son, and no one is a son except a peacemaker, then no one can obtain the inheritance of **GOD** who breaks the peace of **GOD**. And we say these things only as we were exhorted by the Lord Himself, and we testify to it not without a divine sign.

### The 12th Chapter.

->Continuation of the description of their suffering. Flavianus is prevented.<-

All of them wrote this together from the prison. But since it is necessary to perfectly compose the whole account of the blessed martyrs—because out of humble modesty they said too little about themselves, and also because Flavianus entrusted us with such a duty, that we should add what was lacking in their writing—we have had to add the remainder. After they had endured the agony of the dungeon for many months, and had long been tormented by hunger and thirst, they finally received the command to appear before the judgment seat of the Governor. When all had confessed Christ with a victorious voice, the friends of Flavianus, out of a misguided love, tried to pull him away from it, testifying that he was not a Deacon <term>Deacon: A high-ranking officer in the early church; at this time, imperial edicts specifically targeted clergy for execution</term>, as he had claimed to be (*). # History of Martyrdom / Year 260.

...sentence was pronounced upon Julianus and Victoricus; but Flavianus was brought back into the prison. Although he had every reason to be distressed, namely because he was separated from such good company <note>That is, his fellow martyrs who were being led to their deaths while he remained behind.</note>, he nevertheless believed with holy confidence and composure that God's will was being done in him. He tempered his mourning over his solitude with holy wisdom; for he said: "Since the king's heart is in the hand of God <note>original: "Da des Königs Herz in der Hand GOttes ist"</note>, Proverbs 21:1, why should I be troubled or angry at a man who speaks what has been commanded of him?" ## Chapter 13.

->Lucius, Montanus, Julianus, and Victoricus are led to the<-
->place of execution.<-

Meanwhile, the others were brought to the place of their sacrifice. The pagans ran together from everywhere, as did all the brothers <note>The local Christian community in Carthage.</note>, who, although they stood at the service of all the other remaining witnesses of God in faith and love—as they had been taught by Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian, the influential Bishop of Carthage who was martyred two years prior.</note>—nevertheless came at that time in greater numbers and with a complete sense of duty. One could see the martyrs of Christ testifying to their blessed glory with joyful faces, so much so that they encouraged others to follow their virtues even though they remained silent. Yet they did not lack words either, for each one strengthened the people of God with his exhortations. Lucius, indeed, was worn out—not only by his innate gentleness and modest shame, but also by the great weakness and hardship of the dungeon; for this reason, he walked ahead alone with few companions, so that the pressure of the overly large crowd would not completely suffocate him and prevent the shedding of his blood <note>Martyrs often feared dying of exhaustion or disease in prison, as they viewed the public shedding of blood as the ultimate testimony of faith.</note>. Nevertheless, he was not mute, but exhorted those who accompanied him as best as he could. When the brothers said to him, "Remember us!" he spoke in return: "You remember me!" What humility in a martyr, who in the midst of his victorious suffering did not wish to pride himself on the honor! Likewise, Julianus and Victoricus long exhorted the brothers toward peace and commended their teachers to them—especially those who suffered hunger in the dungeon. Thereafter, they reached the place of suffering with glory and joy, without fear.

# Chapter 14.

->*Montanus publicly exhorts the spectators.*<-

**M**ontanus, who was strong in both body and soul, bore himself bravely before his <term>ordeal of martyrdom<note>The original German "Marter-Stand" refers to the specific state or trial of suffering for one's faith.</note></term>. He always confessed the truth with constancy and courage without regard for personhood; indeed, he seemed to grow even stronger during his final trial. He cried out with a prophetic voice: "Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be destroyed, unless he serves the Lord alone!" <note>original: "Wer denen Göttern opfert sol ausgerottet werden, woferne er nicht den HErrn allein dienen wird!" This is a reference to Exodus 22:20.</note> He repeated this frequently and diligently emphasized that one must never abandon the One God, nor turn to idols and the fictitious works of human hands. He also refuted the pride and stubbornness of the heretics, testifying to them that they should recognize the true Church by the great number of its martyrs (*), and that they should return to her. Furthermore, he entrusted the readmission of the <term>fallen<note>Known as the 'lapsi,' these were Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under the pressure of Roman persecution.</note></term> to the judgment of Christ until they had performed full penance. He exhorted those who remained standing in their faith to be vigilant, saying: "Stand firm, dear brothers, and struggle constantly; you have our examples before you. Do not let the unfaithfulness of the fallen overthrow you, but rather let our enduring patience strengthen your crown." Likewise, he exhorted all virgins to preserve their holiness. Generally, he taught everyone to show respect toward their superiors, and he advised these <term>elders<note>Refers to the clergy and leaders of the local church.</note></term> themselves to maintain peaceful unity. He said nothing was better than the united will of the elders; for only then could the people be exhorted to holy obedience and encouraged toward the bond of love—when the rulers of the people preserved the peace. This is what it means to suffer for Christ's sake: to follow Christ even in exhortation and teaching, and to demonstrate faith to the highest degree. O, what a great example of faith!

# Chapter 17.

O, what great confidence! O, true faith! When he subsequently arrived at the courthouse, he stood by the guard to the astonishment of all, waiting until he should be called before the judge.

Thereupon he came forth joyfully again, because through the pronounced sentence of his death he was now certain of his crown; and he still spoke with us very lovingly, commanding us also to write this down and add it to the letter in his own words (*). Oh, precious words of a martyr who encourages another martyr! He denied that the death-stroke hurt, so that he who was also to be killed might be all the more encouraged toward steadfastness, knowing that he would not feel even the slightest pain from the sword. Afterward," he further said, "when my colleagues suffered and I was distressed that I was separated from them, a man appeared to me and said: 'Why are you distressed?' When I told him the reason for my sadness, he said: 'Are you distressed over that? You are now a twofold <term>confessor</term> <note>A "confessor" was a Christian who had publicly acknowledged their faith under interrogation but had not yet been executed</note>, and shall for the third time become a martyr by the sword!' Thus it was also fulfilled. For after he had twice confessed Christ—first in the secret council chamber; afterward publicly, when the people called him back from the others and it was ordered to take him back to the dungeon, as he remained behind his colleagues according to the vision—after such a twofold confession, he received the death sentence for the third time.

## Chapter 23.

### Flavian's Final Speech to the Brothers and his Martyrdom.

<margin>(*) A stable or public inn where they had sought shelter from the rain.</margin>
When he had thus strengthened all the brothers and made full peace with them, he went out from the stable (*) which stands near the estate of Fuscianus <note>Fuscianus was a wealthy landowner in Carthage whose estate was used as a landmark in early Christian accounts</note>. When he had climbed to an elevated spot there, suitable for speaking, he gave a sign for silence with his hand and gave the following speech: "You are at peace with us, most beloved brothers, if you live in peace with the Church and preserve the unity of love. Do not think that I say too little in this, for our Lord Jesus Christ spoke the very same thing shortly before His suffering, when He said: *This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.* John 13:34 <note>The original text cites John 13:14, but the quote corresponds to verse 34</note>." At the very end, he added further and made known his last will as a testament, testifying that the priest Lucianus was, in his opinion, worthy of the office of Bishop. And this was not without reason. For how could it be difficult for one to see such things, who was so near to Heaven and to Christ? After finishing his speech, he went up to the place of his sacrifice, where he bound his eyes with the part of the cloth which Montanus had commanded to be set aside two days earlier; then he knelt down as if for prayer and ended his sufferings in prayer. O excellent monuments of the martyrs! O glorious experience of the witnesses of God! These things are rightly recorded for the memory of descendants, so that we may not only take examples from the ancient scriptures but also learn something from the newer ones.

# 32. Saint Nicephorus and Sapricius the Priest, at Antioch, Year 260.

## Chapter 1.
->The great friendship between Sapricius and Nicephorus falls apart.<-

There was a certain <term>Presbyter</term> <note>A term for a priest or elder in the early Christian Church.</note> and elder named Sapricius; likewise, there was another named Nicephorus, a common man <note>Meaning a layman, someone not ordained as clergy.</note> and a very faithful friend of that priest. These two loved one another to such an extent that people took them for biological brothers born of the same mother; so great was their love for one another in their human nature. They both lived for a very long time in such mutual goodwill, until the evil enemy of the human race <note>A traditional reference to the Devil.</note> envied them and stirred up such hostility between them that they would not even meet one another on the streets, out of the devilish hatred which they bore toward each other.

## Chapter 2.
->The unforgiving nature of Sapricius.<-

After they had been so adversely minded for a long time, Nicephorus came to his senses and recognized that this hatred was of the Devil. He asked several friends to go to the priest Sapricius and, in his name, Nicephorus, beg for his pardon—asking that Sapricius might forgive the debt and receive him back as a penitent. However, the priest would not be reconciled with him. Nicephorus then sent other friends to him again to make peace; but Sapricius would not even listen to their plea. The holy Nicephorus continued and sent good friends to him a third time, with the plea that he might forgive his fault, so that *by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might be established* (Deuteronomy 19:15). But he, being hard-hearted and unforgiving, disregarded the word of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said: *Forgive, and you will be forgiven!* (Luke 6:37); likewise: *If you do not forgive men their trespasses, then...*

# Chapter 3.
->Sapricius is captured as a martyr and confesses Christ.<-

While this was happening, a persecution and great unrest suddenly arose in the same city where they both resided. Sapricius was taken prisoner and handed over to the judge. When he appeared before him, the judge said to him: "What is your name?" He answered: "My name is Sapricius!" The judge said: "What is your faith?" Sapricius gave as an answer: "I am a Christian!" The judge said: "Are you a cleric or an <term>Elder</term>?" <note>The term "Elder" here refers to a priest or presbyter.</note> Sapricius answered: "I am a priest or Elder!" The judge said: "The most illustrious rulers of the Empire and Lords of this land and the Roman borders, Valerian and Gallienus, <note>Valerian and his son Gallienus co-ruled the Roman Empire from 253 to 260 AD; this period saw intense persecution of Christian leadership.</note> have commanded that all who call themselves Christians shall sacrifice to the immortal and eternal gods. If anyone should despise such a command, let him know that he shall be tormented with various tortures and suffer the most bitter death." Sapricius then gave the judge a courageous answer: "We Christians hold Christ for our King, because He is the true God, and the Creator of Heaven and Earth, and of the sea and everything that dwells in or on those three; but all the gods of the heathens are devils; they must all be rooted out from the face of the earth, because they are of no use to anyone, nor can they offend or help anyone, as they are merely the work of men's hands."
