## Chapter 5.
->Saint *Nicephorus* repeatedly begs *Sapricius* in vain for reconciliation.<-

> O you martyr of Christ, forgive me for what I have done against you!

# Chapter 6.
->Sapricius denies Christ.<-

Therefore the Lord also confirmed his word when he says: "If you do not forgive, the Lord will not forgive you"; Matthew 18, v. 34. <note>This refers to the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant. The original text cites the verse as 34, though in modern Bibles the specific sentiment is echoed in Matthew 6:15 and 18:35.</note> For when He saw that he would not be moved, nor have mercy and compassion for his neighbor, but remained unforgiving, He deprived him of Divine Grace; or better to say, he deprived himself of Heavenly Grace, because he had been cruel, unmerciful, and unforgiving toward his brother and trusted old friend. The executioners <note>original: "Schergen" — these were the low-level officials or guards tasked with carrying out corporal punishment.</note> then said to Sapricius: "Kneel down, so that your head may be struck off!" Sapricius asked: "For what reason?" They answered him: "Because you would not sacrifice, but have despised the Imperial command for the sake of a man called Christ." When the miserable Sapricius heard this, he gave answer to the executioners and said: "Do not kill me, for I will do what our Emperors have commanded, and I will sacrifice to the gods." To such an extent had his lack of forgiveness blinded him and taken grace away from him. For he who could not be brought to the conversion of our Lord Jesus Christ through so many various tortures—who had now come to the very end of death and should have received the prize of victory and the crown of glory—he denied it all and became an <term>apostate</term> <note>One who renounces their religious faith or principles.</note>.

# Chapter 7.
->Saint Nicephorus seeks still to win over Sapricius.<-

When the holy Nicephorus heard this, he pleaded with Sapricius and said: "Not so, dear brother, do not fall away in this manner, and do not deny our Ruler Christ! I beg you, do not become an apostate from him; do not lose the Heavenly crown which you have earned through so many endured tortures." But he would not listen to him, but instead hurried toward the ruin of the final death; he who lost such glory in the single moment of a sword-stroke. Such a one has truly become miserable and blinded through lack of forgiveness; since he would not listen to our Lord Jesus Christ, who cries out in the Gospel and says: "When you bring your gift to the altar, and remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there by the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother." Matthew 5, v. 23.

# 33. St. Priscus / Malchus and Alexander /
## at Caesarea in Palestine.
### Year 260.

#### Chapter 1.

->These three present themselves and are thrown to the wild beasts.<-

During the time of the persecution under the Emperor Valerian, there lived in the countryside near **Caesarea** <note>A major Roman port city in Judea (modern-day Israel).</note> three faithful men, one of whom was named Priscus, the second Malchus, and the third Alexander. When these three heard of the persecution, struggle, and victory of their fellow brethren in the cities, they began to reproach themselves as lazy, idle people who were missing the beautiful opportunity in which eternal rewards were distributed to those burning with Heavenly love, and were failing to obtain the **Crown of Martyrdom**. Thereupon, they took counsel together and went to Caesarea, presented themselves to the judge, and confessed that they were Christians! The judge then sentenced them to the wild beasts! This sentence was also immediately carried out upon them; thus they obtained the Divine Crown of Martyrdom. Eusebius Book 7, Chapter 12. Nicephorus <note>The writer refers here to the historian Nicephorus Callistus, not the martyr mentioned earlier on the page.</note> Book 6, Chapter 11. Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs* page 245.

# 34. St. Cyril /
## A Boy at Caesarea. Year 260.

### Chapter 1.

->The boy Cyril is cast out and disinherited by his father.<-

It would be unjust, most beloved brothers, to keep the martyrdom story <note>original: "Marter-Geschichte"</note> of the holy Cyril hidden from you; rather, we wish to share it with you. For it was not without the prompting of a Divine Spirit—or to speak truly and certainly, the LORD fought with and for him—that his faith pleaded on his behalf before the unjust judges at Caesarea <note>A significant Roman port and administrative capital in Palestine.</note>. The youth of the most blessed Cyril filled the spectators with great wonder, while the steadfastness of his faith awakened high praise for Christ; for he always had the name of Christ upon his lips, and confessed that he was driven to do so by his heart. He paid no heed to the blows or threats of his pagan parents, nor to any insults; instead, he endured it all quite willingly—indeed, he even looked forward to further suffering. But as the joy of the spirit grew within him alongside his faith, and he gained many young followers of his own age, his father disinherited him, cast him out of the house, and denied him everything that was in the home. Some praised the father for this; others marveled at the boy, seeing how calm he remained, testifying that for the little that had been taken from him, his faith in the Lord would provide something greater and more salvific.

### Chapter 2.

->His boldness before the judge.<-

Because of this, the judge at Caesarea also became indignant toward him; he had him brought by the soldier guard, intending to terrify him with judicial power. However, he saw from the very beginning that the boy was not afraid, but appeared instantly without any concern, regarding everything as insignificant compared to his faith. "I forgive you your mistakes, O boy," spoke the judge, "and your father also forgives your faults and wishes to take you back into the house; you may enjoy your father's property, if you [turn] from the err-

### Chapter 3.

->He is executed for the crown of martyrdom after testifying to his great longing.<-

It was reported back to the judge, however, that the boy neither wept nor feared the fire, but rather went willingly toward his death. Then the judge had him brought before him again and sought, in the usual way, to persuade him with smooth words: "You have seen the fire, O boy," he said; "you have beheld the sword, O youth; now be sensible, so that you may regain your father’s house and possessions." But he answered: "O tyrant, you have done me harm by calling me back! You have insulted me and treated me poorly! You have lit the fire in vain and sharpened the sword without cause! The house to which I hasten is far greater, and the treasures of heaven far more glorious. I hasten to receive these from the Lord; finish me quickly, so that I may soon enjoy them!" Those standing around who heard this began to weep; but the boy rebuked their tears and said: "You should laugh; you should rejoice; you should accompany me joyfully to my death. You do not know what kind of city I shall inhabit; you do not know what confidence I have. Allow me, then, to end my life in this way!" When he had said this, he was led away to his death. He was a glorious sight to behold, not only to Him who received his soul, but also to all the inhabitants of Caesarea, through the assistance of Him who rules over eternity. # 35. St. Felix,
# Priest at Nola in Campania.

## Year 260, etc.

### Chapter 1.

->St. Felix leaves his paternal inheritance to his brother and becomes a priest.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' featuring intricate foliate scrolls and vine-like patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
There lived in the Carian city of Syrum in Anatolia <note>Modern-day Turkey; the original text uses "Natolien."</note> a man named Hermias, who had two sons; one was also named Hermias, and the other Felix. After their father’s death, these two brothers divided his estate between them in such a way that Hermias kept all the worldly goods, while Felix chose the eternal and spiritual goods for himself. Hermias entered into the Emperor's military service; but Felix practiced in the wars of the Lord Christ, our King. From his youth, he turned his mind toward heavenly things and how he might best serve God, whose grace did not fail him, but rather his spirit was abundantly filled with it. Initially, he served in the congregation of Christ at Nola <note>A city in southern Italy, near Naples.</note>, where he had traveled, in the office of Reader <note>original: "Lector"; a minor order in the early church responsible for reading the Scriptures during services.</note>; later he became an <term>Exorcist<note>original: "Exorcista"; in the early church, this was a specific ministry focused on healing and the casting out of unclean spirits.</note></term> or an expeller of unclean spirits (*). Because he performed this office with great blessing, they chose him to be a Priest and Elder.

### Chapter 2.

->In the persecution at Nola, Bishop Maximus escapes and Felix is captured.<-

At that same time, a heavy persecution arose against the Church, especially against the bishops, priests, and servants of the congregations; therefore Maximus, the Bishop of Nola, who was devoted to the holy Felix with fatherly love, was forced to hide in the wilderness upon the advice of the elders and brothers. In the meantime, he had given the oversight to Felix—

---

> (*) The office of an Exorcist or an expeller of evil spirits has been in the congregation since the time of the Apostles, and was given to the young, spirited fighters of Christ to demonstrate the first lessons of the Spirit against Satan; of which John writes in 1 John 2:13–14, regarding the young men of the Spirit who have overcome the Wicked One; such men could also banish him from others, as their will was sanctified.

# 35. St. Felix

was especially recommended <note>The text continues from the previous page, where Felix was likely entrusted with the care of the church during the persecution.</note>, as he now had to stand against the head of the poisonous dragon <note>A common metaphor in early Christian writing for the Roman Empire or pagan authorities.</note>; for his presence could not long remain hidden, because the radiance of his spirit shone out above all others. The raging pagan mob at Nola, instead of the bishop who had escaped, now sought him out, who as a faithful shepherd after the example of Christ was willing to give his life for the flock. He stood there with his gray hair, entirely enraptured in spirit, full of faith and with God in his heart, mindful of Christ who had completely filled his breast. He appeared holy and heavenly, and his face was full of glory; then behold, he was seized—though to his own joy—and led away with a violent hand. They brought him first into a dark dungeon and placed iron fetters on his hands and feet, which were locked far apart in the stocks <note>original: "Block"; a wooden frame used to restrain prisoners by their limbs, often in agonizing positions.</note>. So that he might neither sleep nor rest, broken, sharp shards were placed beneath him to serve as his bed. Nevertheless, the confessor <note>original: "Bekenner"; a title for one who suffered for the faith but was not (yet) executed.</note> did not lack light and rest, as he was united with Christ, and his crown became only more glorious through his double suffering. His free spirit already wandered in heaven and penetrated into the innermost mysteries of Christ, where his soul refreshed itself in its future eternal reward. The heavy bonds and the dark dungeon caused him blessed suffering; but as much as he suffered as a man according to the flesh, so many palms of victory did his patience obtain from Christ.

## Chapter 3.

->The miserable state of the fugitive Bishop Maximus.<-

Meanwhile, the fugitive Bishop Maximus was in misery alone upon the mountains, content that he had escaped the desolate hands and beastly jaws of the catchpolls <note>original: "Büttel"; minor officials or officers who carried out arrests.</note>; for this he now had to endure various and no less difficult martyries than if he had submitted to the fetters and allowed himself to be tortured or burned. For the concern for his flock pained him far more severely. He was plagued by the biting cold and the frozen frost of the night; he suffered a lack of bread and had to spend day and night watchful in prayer without shelter. The earth, full of thistles and thorns, was his bed; his mind was full of worry, and while he was inwardly troubled, externally he was full of conflict. The thorns pricked his body, and grief tormented his sorrowful soul. ## Chapter 4.

->St. Felix is rescued from prison by an angel.<-

Now, when the merciful Father beheld the priest and confessor <note>term: "Confessor" (German: Bekenner); a title for a Christian who suffered for their faith but was not killed.</note> of Christ in His bright light, and saw him languishing in the hidden forests, He did not let this happen; instead, so that one worthy man might serve another, He chose Felix from among all the prisoners. He entrusted Felix with the merit of reviving the holy old man and comfortingly restoring their shepherd to his frightened flock. Thus, in the stillness of the night, a radiant angel appeared and spoke to the blessed Felix alone among all the prisoners. The terror of the dark dungeon vanished in the glow; nevertheless, Felix trembled before the holy word and light, listening to the angelic voice with watchful ears. Initially, he thought it was a dream-image or a deceptive vision, which caused his fear; he therefore excused himself, saying he could not follow because his shackles prevented it, and moreover, the prison was locked and guarded by sentries. But the divine voice rebuked the hesitant man and commanded him to simply cast off the shackles, which then suddenly fell quite gently from his hands, feet, and neck. O, wonderful faith! The doors of the prison opened without the lock being turned, and the guards had fallen into a deep sleep as the holy Felix walked out undaunted, passing right through those who were supposed to guard the way. # 35. St. Felix <note>original: "S. Felicis"</note>

Is it not the same Christ in all the saints? Just as one single Spirit rules in all who are reborn, so too is grace harmonious in all the pious. It seems to me that I see the history of the ancients returning, when Peter—one among the twelve—received the command in prison to go out, at which point his chains fell away, and he likewise escaped from the locked prison as the angel guided him and delivered him from the hand of Herod. ## Chapter 5.

-> He finds the half-dead old man and revives him miraculously. <-

After he had been led by the angel through the fields into the most hidden thickets of the forest, he finally found the spot where the exhausted old man <note>Bishop Maximus of Nola.</note> lay. He found him with great sorrow, for the man was drawing his final breaths. Scarcely had he caught sight of him when he fell upon him with embraces and kisses, trying to warm the limbs that were stiff with cold, and attempting to revive his faded senses by breathing into his mouth. He could rouse him neither by shouting nor by shaking him; instead, the motionless body lay as insensible as a corpse. However, a gentle breath and a soft movement of the pulse still gave some hope of life. 

The anxious Felix was nearly overwhelmed by such a sight; he felt the unresponsive limbs and looked sadly at the pale mouth, which was sunken from hunger. Nothing was at hand with which he could come to his aid in such deprivation—neither fire to warm him, nor food to refresh him. He searched everywhere in the bushes and called upon the **Lord** Christ in prayer for help, asking Him to bless his service of love in some way. Behold! The Almighty suddenly caused a cluster of grapes to hang down from a thorn bush, so that Felix struck his head against it, allowing him to more easily pluck this fruit of blessing with his hand. 

Saint Felix was divinely encouraged by this and rejoiced with a holy heart over such a gift. He plucked it and held it to the mouth of the dying man. Because the old man had his lips and teeth tightly shut and could not consume the sweet, pleasant food, Felix pressed the full berries with his fingers and smeared the dry lips with them. He continued until, through Divine blessing and much effort, the mouth opened slightly so that he could pour in the sweet juice. Thereupon the vital spirits returned, the warmth made the limbs moveable, and the eyes opened with a renewal of his whole life, along with the return of his speech.

## Chapter 6.
->The conversation between the two.<-

When he had been revived in this manner and saw the face of his acquaintance Felix before him, who was embracing and kissing him, he began to speak with a low voice, saying: "The Lord promised me that you, my heart’s Felix, my most precious pledge <note>The bishop refers to Felix as a "pledge" or "token" of God’s grace.</note>, would come to me; tell me, I pray, where have you been for so long? Although I was dead in body for a short time, my heart remained constant and true. This place and the state in which I currently find myself are sufficient proof that I did not flee out of any fear of death, and that I esteemed Christ more highly than my own life. I did indeed flee, but not out of love for this light <note>Meaning the light of the living world or mortal life.</note>, nor out of fear of losing this weak body, nor to live quietly under a roof; otherwise, I certainly could have remained in the city, had my faith been small and this life dear to me. I sought the unknown mountains and the desolate wilderness, and laid down my head in the bosom of my dear Lord, so that He might be a witness to my death or my life. And such hope of mine has not been in vain, as you see before your eyes; the Almighty has come to my aid and has sent you here to share His goodness with me. Now, my son, perform this service of love for me once more, and carry me upon your shoulders back to the general sheepfold of Christ <note>A metaphor for the Christian community or the church in Nola.</note>."

## Chapter 7.
->Holy Felix carries Maximus home.<-

The blessed Felix immediately and with joy took up this burden of love and this light yoke of Christ <note>A reference to Matthew 11:30, "For my yoke is easy and my burden is light."</note> upon his shoulders, and hurried away with such speed that he seemed more to be carried himself than to be carrying someone else. And truly, the Lord Christ carried the carrier, and God gave wings to his hallowed feet. Felix accomplished everything in a single night; after his own bonds had been broken, he refreshed his bishop and brought him back to his house, which was still being watched over by an elderly woman. She was awakened by the knocking and was initially terrified, but finally, with great difficulty, she recognized the voice. Thereupon, with fear and trembling, she opened the door and let in the master of the house, whom Felix presented to her with the following words: "Receive this pledge, which I, under the guidance of the Lord Christ and by the instruction of the angels and stars, have this night [brought] back—"

## Chapter 8.

->Felix is persecuted another time / escapes miraculously.<-

After this, the holy Felix went to his house and hid himself there until the persecution ceased for a time, during which the congregation of Christ rejoiced greatly over their restored Bishop and Priest—namely, Maximus and Felix. However, the Enemy <note>A reference to the Devil or the spiritual force behind the Roman persecutors.</note> could not grant the children of God their peace, but instead stirred up the serpent’s venom of envy and wrath in the hearts of the evil heathen men. The "serpent" was most enraged against the holy Felix, and the raging mob stormed his house while he stood in an open square in the middle of the city among his people, to whom he was sweetly proclaiming the Words of Life <note>That is, the Gospel or Holy Scripture.</note>. When they did not find him at home, they went to the place where the crowd of believers stood together, feeling quite secure because of the perceived peace. Felix was in their midst, but the pursuers did not recognize him, for they were miraculously struck with blindness so that they sought him there in vain, no matter how close they came to him.

When he recognized the sign from Christ that He wished to save him, he himself answered their inquiry—as they asked who among the crowd was named Felix—with smiling words: "I do not know which Felix you are looking for!" With that, they left him, and he immediately departed from there. He had not gone far when the others searched further, and someone betrayed the matter to them, indicating that the man they had just questioned was the very one they sought. At this, they heatedly rushed after him through the commotion, and he barely escaped their hands in a miraculous way. ## Chapter 9.

->Felix hides himself in a water-cistern / and is fed by a poor woman.<-

After the riot had subsided a little, and everyone had returned home due to the falling night, the blessed Felix crawled out of his corner again and sang a song of praise to the Lord from the 23rd Psalm in the secrecy of his heart:

> The Lord is my shepherd! I do not fear,
> Even though I walk through the dark valley;
> I fear no death nor terrifying fall,
> For you, Lord, are with me! my staff, my light,
> My comfort in abandonment,
> My eternal grasp;
> The Lord is my shepherd, I do not fear!

Amid such triumphant awakenings, he went far away to a place where there was a water-cistern <note>The original term "Wasser-Kasten" refers to an underground reservoir or cistern.</note> in the earth, and there he hid himself. However, a holy, God-devoted poor woman lived there in a miserable hut, who, in an unknown manner, was compelled to miraculously feed the holy priest Felix. It seems perhaps doubtful, yet not impossible, what occurred there: this poor woman cooked a few gathered herbs for him daily, and whatever her poverty allowed, and brought it to him along with bread, as if in a trance <note>original: "Verzuckung"—meaning a state of spiritual ecstasy or divine compulsion where she was unaware of her specific actions.</note>, for she did not know what she was doing or whom she was feeding. This lasted for six whole months, during which time the witness of Christ remained in the aforementioned water-cistern, which was dry during that period of drought; therefore, he also had to refresh his thirst from the dew of heaven.

### Chapter 10.
-> When this persecution subsided, Felix returned home; Maximus died; Quintus became Bishop. <-

After the passing of the aforementioned six months, this persecution had also entirely subsided; therefore, he was divinely reminded to return to the city to the flock of Christ. Everyone was terrified by his unexpected presence and doubted whether it was truly him, until he recounted his wonderful rescue to the praise of God and Christ. In the meantime, Maximus, the holy Bishop, had passed <note>original: "gewandert," literally "wandered" or "journeyed."</note> into blessed eternity; therefore, the entire congregation desired Felix to be their Bishop. He refused, however, and objected that such honor and high office belonged to his fellow elder <term>Quintus</term> <note>A "fellow elder" or "presbyter" refers to a priest of equal rank; Felix argues for seniority based on the date of ordination.</note>, as he had attained the priesthood before him, though only by seven days. Thus, they elected Quintus as Bishop, and Felix faithfully administered the priestly office of elder under him; the former tended his congregation as a shepherd, while the latter served as their mouth and teacher.

### Chapter 11.
-> Felix’s spiritual virtues and love for the poverty of Christ. <-

The grace of Christ, however, had adorned the holy Felix <note>original: "Felicem," the Latin accusative form of Felix.</note> with many other virtues, and in times of peace, he was no lesser a warrior than during the time of persecution. Back then, he had set aside his physical welfare; now, in a time of rest, he did not fix his eyes upon it, but only upon how he might carefully preserve the hard-won treasures of eternal life. That he had completely overcome greed is evidenced by his renunciation of all his goods, which he had received back from his paternal and fraternal inheritance. Though these had been stripped from him during the persecution, they were now legally restored to him; yet he did not even wish to take possession of them, remembering the word:

> All things are lawful for us, but not all things are helpful;

Thus, he preferred what was helpful over what was lawful and fled from the possession of many country estates. Many people called him to account for this and sought to mislead him with plausible words—above all, a certain Christian noblewoman named Archelais, who was as holy as she was noble. She was a very wealthy widow who loved Felix in a Christian manner and frequently urged him to take up his rightful inheritance, under the pretense...

### Chapter 12.
-> He embraces poverty and dies in peace. <-

In such a spirit, all he possessed of his own were three meager fields, which he tilled with his own hands without a servant, as the owner of a humble garden. Yet, even from his poverty, he shared with the Lord, giving half of his few herbs to the poor. He hardly had a single garment for himself, and if he received a better one, he dressed the naked with the best he had. Very often he provided the wretched with new clothes, while he himself was recognized by his old rags; but in secret, his soul was magnificently clothed. In such a godly way of life, he finally concluded his days, full of life <note>original: "Lebens satt," meaning he died at an advanced age, satisfied with his life's work.</note>; he did not merely end the time of his holy life, but transformed it into the unending, blessed eternities. Paulinus of Nola <note>original: "Paulinus Nolan."</note> in *The Life of Saint Felix* (*). Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs* <note>original: "Act. MM."</note>, p. 249.

### Chapter 4.
->Asturius stops the satanic deception at Caesarea Philippi.<-

**M**any magnificent things are told of this man by those who were his close companions and who, as Eusebius writes, are still alive in our own time. Of these, we wish to mention only one: Near the city of Caesarea Philippi, which the Phoenicians call Paneas, they say that on the annual feast day, the inhabitants of that city used to throw a certain sacrifice into the springs found at the foot of Mount Paneion (from which the Jordan takes its source). Through devilish magical arts, this sacrifice would instantly disappear, so that all those present were greatly amazed. Once, however, Asturius was there as a spectator, and when he saw that the crowd was terrified by this supposed miracle, he took pity on those who were being led astray. He lifted his eyes to heaven and prayed to God above all things, through Christ, that the seductive evil spirit might be revealed and kept from misleading mortals! As he was praying, the disappeared sacrifice immediately floated to the top of the water; because of this, the great wonder of the bystanders ceased, and from that time on, nothing strange ever occurred at that place again.

# 37. St. Claudius / Asterius / Neon / Domnina and Theonilla / at Aegea in Cilicia / In the Year 285.

## Chapter 1.

-> A stepmother denounces her stepchildren; Claudius is judicially interrogated and tortured. <-

In Aegea <note>A coastal city in the Roman province of Cilicia, modern-day Turkey</note>, Claudius, Asterius, and Neon were denounced to the judge by their stepmother on the grounds that they were Christians and despisers of the gods; likewise, Domnina and Theonilla were also betrayed. They were all shackled and cast into the dungeon until the arrival of the governor <note>original: *Landpfleger*</note> *Lysias*. # 38. Saint Genesius the Mime / or the Comedian;

->At Rome. In the year 286.<-

## Chapter 1.

->Genesius, a comedian, wishes to be baptized on the stage during a play.<-

The blessed martyr Genesius was, before his conversion in Rome, a master of comedians or performers <term>German: *Operisten*; in this era, it referred generally to stage actors or entertainers</term>, and presented human affairs in song upon the public stage. One day it happened that he wished to portray the mysteries of the Christians for laughter before the Emperor *Diocletian*; since the Emperor, as a fierce tyrant who hated Christians, appeared along with all the people, Genesius lay down in the middle of the *theater* in feigned illness and desired to be baptized, using these common words of penitent believers: "Ah, dear brothers, I find myself burdened, and wish to be lightened (*)<note>Original Latin: *Eia nostri, gravem me sentio, levem me fieri volo!* ("Come, my friends, I feel heavy, I wish to become light!")</note>!" His companions then asked him and spoke: "How shall we lighten you, if you are heavy? Are we perhaps carpenters, and should we plane you with a coarse plane?" At this, the people began to laugh. Genesius spoke once more: "You fools, I desire to die as a Christian!" They asked him: "Why?" Genesius answered: "So that on that day I may be found in God as one who has fled [from sin]!" Thereupon, in the supposed play, they called forth a priest and an exorcist <term>German: *Beschwörer*; one who performs rites to cast out spirits</term>; meanwhile, his heart was suddenly touched by the Spirit of God, and he became a believer.

### Chapter 1.

<margin>The uncertainty of this history concerning the Theban Legion.</margin>
Because this famous story regarding the martyrdom of the Theban Legion—a Roman regiment of soldiers who were all said to have been Christians—does not entirely correspond with the historical truth of that time; since no historians, neither pagan nor Christian, from the time when it was supposed to have occurred until two hundred and fifty years <note>The German "drittehalb hundert" literally means two and a half hundred, or 250 years.</note> afterward make mention of it, but was first dubiously described in the sixth century by Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon in France; we have chosen to draw the narrative together only briefly, and at the same time to append a more magnificent monument to the name of Christ regarding the so-called Thundering Legion.

The history of the martyrdom of the Theban Legion is thus told:

# Chapter 2.
-> A short narrative of the execution of the Theban Legion. <-

**W**hen, under Emperor Maximianus, the believers were being executed with great torture, and the tyrant began to lack enough executioners <note>The original German "Bütteln" refers to low-level officials or beadles who carried out arrests and executions.</note>, the Theban Legion of Roman soldiers received an Imperial command that they, along with other regiments, should be employed in the execution of Christians. Because they all—or perhaps only the leader Maurice along with many other officers and commoners—had themselves become Christians and believers, they refused to help persecute their fellow brothers and sent a proper petition <note>original: "Memorial"</note> to Emperor Maximianus. In response, however, he gave the order to kill every tenth man <note>This practice is known as decimation, a form of military discipline where every tenth soldier in a rebellious unit was executed.</note>. When the rest continued to withdraw from the tyrannical command, they were all executed in the Agaunian Mountains in France <note>Now Saint-Maurice in the Valais region of Switzerland, which was then part of the Roman province of Gallia.</note> near the Swiss borders. While the murderous soldiers were making merry with the loot and feasting joyfully, it happened that Victor, a retired soldier and a Christian, passed by that way. They invited him to eat with them, but he turned them down once he understood the reason for their luxury. They then asked him whether he was perhaps also a Christian; he gave them the answer: "Yes, I am a Christian, and I intend to remain one forever." Immediately they fell upon him and killed him; he is thus counted among the previous ones. Furthermore, Ursus and Victor—fellow brothers of the said Theban Legion—are said to have received the crown of martyrdom at Solothurn in Switzerland.
<margin>Ruinart. *Acts*. page 274.</margin>

# Chapter 3.
-> Concerning the Thundering Legion of Roman soldiers, and to what extent Christians served as soldiers. <-

**T**his history of the martyrdom of the Theban Legion also gives occasion to mention here the true history of the so-called Thundering Legion <note>original: "blitzenden Legion." This refers to the *Legio XII Fulminata*, famous for a miracle where a storm allegedly saved the army in response to the prayers of Christian soldiers.</note>; although this occurred a hundred years earlier, namely in the year 174 under Emperor Marcus Aurelius, and strictly speaking does not belong among the histories of martyrdom, even though the entire Church of Christ was thereby freed from a severe persecution. A "Legion" <note>original: "Legio"</note> refers to a large regiment of Roman soldiers consisting of six thousand common soldiers.

It was, however, so far from the case that the first anointed Christians, after their call in Christ, should have entered external military service <note>original: "Krieges-Diensten"</note>, if they were free, that they much rather wanted to die as martyrs than allow themselves to be recruited, of which testimonies will follow later. **Tertullian** / in whose time all ranks, even the military camps, honored Christ's name, nevertheless testifies that Christ's teaching requires that one rather let oneself be killed than kill others. (Apology cap. 37.) Frequently, however, the first Christians are called *Milites* or soldiers <note>Latin: "milites"</note>, not in the outward physical sense, but in the spiritual understanding, as warriors of Christ <note>original: "Streiter Christi"</note>, who have to lead a far heavier battle in the spirit with Satan and their own evil will, than in physical, bloody wars. This nonetheless gave occasion for great misunderstanding afterward, so that those were often held to be outward soldiers who had never girded on the external sword, but had only been spiritual soldiers; of which kind also were those poor Christians who, in a figurative sense, were named **Legio Fulminatrix**, or the Thundering Band, by Emperor **Marcus Aurelius** himself, in the name-identity with that pagan actual regiment which was so called. The event of this is clear from the Imperial letter of grace <note>original: "Gnaden-Briefe"</note>, which he sent on this account to the Council at Rome, to make such publicly known in all cities of the Roman Empire; therefore this worthy old monument to the glorification of Christ’s name [continues] up to our

Since we had only the First, Tenth, Gemina, and Fretensis Legions (together four to twenty-six thousand men) with us, but the enemies had gathered up to seventy-seven thousand, against which great multitude of barbarian enemies our small crowd was hardly to be compared; I then began to call upon the ancestral gods for help; but because they provided me no help, and the enemies pressed us, considering the small number of our soldiers, we had all the so-called **Christians** summoned before us, of whom we found a great multitude in the camp (**). <header>History of Martyrs / Year 286.</header>

# 40. St. Rogatianus and Donatianus / in Nantes in Brittany / in France.

->Year 286.<-

## Chapter 1.

->Tyranny and Deceit against the Christians in France.<-

It is beneficial for Christian readers to recount the glorious deeds of the victorious struggle of the martyrs, and to offer the thirsty people a drink from the cup of their holily-shed blood; whereby some may learn the venerable mysteries therefrom, and others may be stirred to die blessedly for Christ’s sake. When, therefore, Diocletian and Maximian <note>Roman Co-Emperors known for the most severe persecution of Christians.</note> sat at the helm of the Roman state, and bestial cruelty raged at their command against the Christian name, so that they might trample the holy teaching of Christ underfoot through pagan laws, they sent letters to the Governor in France <note>original: "Frankreich," referring to Gaul.</note>, and gave orders that the images of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> or Apollo / which are not gods, but devils, should be divinely worshipped by everyone; with the added promise that those who performed such idolatry and offered sacrifices devoutly should be publicly rewarded! This was done so that the snare of desire might the more easily catch the human soul, and that gifts might deceive those who could not be overcome by reason. But those, the command further stated, who persisted in the confession of the Christian name, should first be tortured, then killed! This was intended so that the believers might stray from the right path out of fear.

In such a flourishing spiritual state, the lovely fragrance of his sweet mouth filled the heart of his biological brother Rogatianus, who still remained in the service of idols. Rogatianus now hurried to his younger brother—who, according to faith, was the elder—and begged him that he might be gifted with Christian baptism before the storm of the impending persecution broke out. He did this so that the blessed struggle would not overtake him as a heathen or as an unbaptized <term>catechumen; a student of the faith who has not yet received the sacrament</term>, and so that he might share no less in the victory than in the struggle alongside his brother. <header>41. St. Sebastian, etc.</header>

# 41. St. Sebastianus / Nicostatus / Claudius / Victorinus / Symphorianus / Caius / Tiburtius <note>original: "Tibtius"</note> / Castulus / Marcellinus / Marcus and Zoe.

->in Rome / In the year 286.<-

## Chapter 1.

->Cruel persecution under Diocletian and Maximian. Chromatius departs to his country estates with many Christians upon the advice of Bishop Caius.<-

After the Emperor Carinus was killed at Margum <note>original: "Murgum," referring to the Battle of the Margus in modern-day Serbia</note> in Hungary in the battle against Diocletian, at the time when Maximian and Aquilinus were Consuls <note>original: "Bürgermeister," literally 'mayors,' but here referring to the Roman Consuls whose names marked the calendar year</note>, such an appalling persecution arose that no one was permitted to buy or sell anything unless they first burned incense before certain small idols that were placed at the locations where trade was conducted. Furthermore, sentries stood by the islands in the Tiber, in the alleys, and by the wells, who gave no one permission to mill grain <note>original: "mahlen"</note> or draw water, unless they offered incense to the idols. 

Then, upon the advice of the holy Bishop Caius, Chromatius—a man of great power—sheltered all those Christians who were under suspicion in his house, and provided for them in such a way that no one was forced to sacrifice to idols out of necessity <note>meaning they did not need to visit the markets where sacrifice was mandatory to obtain food</note>. However, as the persecution became so great that his own Christianity could no longer remain hidden, Chromatius received a holy command that, for the sake of safety, he should go to his country estates in Campania. He then gave all Christians who wished to travel with him to escape the persecution the freedom to choose as they pleased. Because of this, a pious disagreement arose between Saint Polycarp and Sebastian as to which of the two should remain in the city, and which should go with Chromatius, who [sheltered] so many Chri—

### Father Caius’s Exhortation. Tiburtius’s Fiery Faith. The
### Naming of the Believers before Caius.

The Day of the Lord arrived, on which the Bishop (*) Caius performed the divine duties of his office, and in the house of Chromatius, where they were all assembled (**), he addressed them, saying: "Our Lord Jesus Christ, who well foresaw our human frailty, has ordained two ranks for his believers, namely the <term>Confessors</term> <note>Those who suffered for the faith but were not killed.</note> and the <term>Martyrs</term>; so that those who cannot bear the burden of martyrdom may hold fast to the grace of confession, and by yielding the priority to those warriors of Christ who suffer for His name's sake, they may diligently care for them. Therefore, whoever wishes, let him depart with our sons Chromatius and Tiburtius; and whoever wishes, let him remain with me in this city. For earthly distance does not separate those whom the grace of Christ has joined; thus our eyes do not notice your absence, for we look upon you with the eyes of the inner man." Originally, *Pontifices* <note>original: "Pontifices"</note> were "bridge-builders"; because the priests of the idols taught that souls must cross a dangerous water of death after passing, they were also called spiritual bridge-builders or *Pontifices*. This practice passed from paganism into a corrupted Christianity, so that the Bishops of Rome were called *Pontifices Maximi* <note>original: "Pontifices Maximi"; the author is expressing a typical Protestant critique of the era regarding the origins of the Papal title.</note>.

The <term>Pantheon</term> in Rome, or the Temple of All Gods, is a witness to this even now; it was consecrated to all the saints and is now called *Maria Rotunda* <note>original: "Maria rotunda," referring to the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres.</note>.

## Chapter 3.

->The Believers Hide with Castulus in the Imperial Palace.<-

But because there was no safe place to be found where they might hide themselves, they all stayed with a certain gentleman named Castulus, who was a Christian and a Chamberlain <note>German: *Cammer-Herr*. A high-ranking court official who managed the private living quarters of the Emperor.</note> in the Imperial Palace, where he lived on the top floor. This residence was convenient for them because Castulus and everyone in his household were secret Christians; furthermore, the strict decree regarding sacrifices to idols, which raged everywhere with the utmost severity, was in no way enforced upon those living in the Emperor's palace, as no suspicion could fall upon them. Therefore, as mentioned, they all stayed with Castulus along with the holy Father Caius; day and night they were occupied with sighing, weeping, fasting, and praying, asking the Lord that they might be found worthy of patient endurance in the confession of His name and be included in the number of the holy martyrs. However, devout men and women secretly climbed up to them, receiving various gifts of health from the holy ones; for the eyes of the blind were opened through their prayers, the sick recovered, and unclean spirits were driven out of those who were possessed.

## Chapter 4.

->Tiburtius Heals a Man Nearly Fallen to Death and Converts Him and His Parents.<-

While these things were taking place, it happened that the blessed Tiburtius the younger, while walking through the streets, encountered some people carrying a man who had fallen from a great height. His head and all his limbs were so shattered that his parents were already thinking of his burial. To these people, who were walking along weeping, the blessed Tiburtius spoke: "Allow me to say a word to him; perhaps he will regain his health!" When they all made room for him, he stepped toward the man; and after he had spoken the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed <note>German: *Apostolische Glaubens-Bekentniß*. One of the oldest statements of Christian belief.</note> over him, while touching his wounds, his bones were so strengthened, and likewise his head and all his internal organs became so healthy, as if nothing bad had happened to him. After this had occurred, Tiburtius went away from there; but the parents of the man who had been made healthy held him fast and said: "Come and take

## The 6th Chapter.
->She appears to Sebastian; Tranquillinus is stoned.<-

After attaining such a state of martyrdom, she appeared to the blessed Sebastian in a dream and announced to him in what manner she had become a martyr for Christ's sake. When Sebastian related this to the others, Tranquillinus—the father of Marcellianus and Marcus—broke out and said: "The women precede us in receiving the crown; why should we live any longer?" Eight days later, as he was praying at the tomb of the holy Apostle <note>Likely referring to the tomb of St. Peter.</note>, the treacherous heathens seized him, and the mob stoned him until he died; then his body was likewise thrown into the Tiber. Afterward, when Nicostratus, along with Claudius, Victorinus, and Symphorian, sought the bodies of the saints along the banks of the River Tiber, they were also seized and led to the City Prefect <term>Fabiano</term> <note>Fabianus, the Prefect of Rome</note>; he exhorted them to offer sacrifices [to the Roman gods]. Although he tested them for ten days, sometimes with threats and sometimes with flattery, he could not turn them away in any manner. Therefore, he reported it to the Emperors, who gave the command that they should be tortured to the third and highest degree. When they could not be moved even by such martyrdom, the sentence was passed that they should be sunk into the middle of the sea! Thus, an immense weight of stones was hung upon them, and they were buried in the waves of the sea, so that they might attain the Crown of Martyrdom in a pure place within the water. In such a way, the unbelievers laid snares for the believers and persecuted them with a godless madness, so much so that they could not look upon them with a quiet heart, nor even tolerate their name.

History of Martyrs / Year 286. 285
42. S.

...[that we] were adversaries, when instead everything improves and prospers through their prayer; for they do not cease to pray for your empire and for the welfare of the Roman camps! When he had said this and more of the same, Emperor Diocletian said to him: "Are you not Sebastian, whom we long ago ordered to be killed with arrows?" Sebastian answered: "My Lord Jesus Christ willed to preserve me for this purpose, that I might testify before you in the presence of all the people that your persecution of the servants of God is unjustly founded." Then he ordered him to be led to the hippodrome <note>original: "Roß-Platz"; a stadium or arena for horses within the palace grounds, likely the Stadium of Domitian or the Palatine Hippodrome.</note> of the palace, and to be beaten with clubs until he had given up the ghost. Afterward, they took his body and threw it during the night into the largest sewer <note>original: "Canal"; likely referring to the *Cloaca Maxima*, the main sewage system of ancient Rome.</note> through which the filth of the city is directed, and said: "So that the Christians do not find him again and make a martyr of him."

## Chapter 13.

->Lucina finds Sebastian’s body and buries him.<-

Holy Sebastian, however, appeared at night to a devout matron named Lucina and said to her: "Search in the sewer near the racetrack; there you will find my body hanging on a hook. Wash it, and bury me in the tombs of the Apostles (*)." Thus Lucina went there with her servants at midnight, and when she had found the body, she placed it with her in her litter and brought it to the place where he had commanded; there she carefully buried him, and did not leave the holy place for thirty days. After several years, however, when the persecution had ceased, she allowed the congregation to hold their meetings in her house and bequeathed all her goods to the Christians for their refreshment; after she had thus appointed the congregation of Christ as her heir, she rested in Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever <note>original: "in die Ewigkeiten der Ewigkeiten"; translating the Latin liturgical phrase *in saecula saeculorum*.</note>. Amen.

# 42. St. Boniface /
# at Tarsus. Year 290.

## Chapter 1.

->The wealthy Aglaes’s wicked lifestyle with the lustful Boniface;<-
->also, concerning his good qualities <note>original: "Funken," literally "sparks," referring to the remaining light of goodness or potential for virtue in his soul.</note>.<-

When Domitian <note>The text likely means Diocletian, who reigned during this period with Maximian, or is referencing a specific consular year</note> entered his fourth consulship and Maximian his third, a very great upheaval arose during the time of the persecution against the Christians; for the servants of God were being driven to bow down before shameful idols. The tyrants, along with their extensive orders, also sent the fierce and cunning judge named Simplicius into the Eastern lands to Tarsus—which is the capital city of Cilicia—so that he might publicly and judicially examine all Christians there, of whatever rank, sex, or age they might be, and bring them by various tortures to share in his madness. At that time, there was a noblewoman in the city of Rome named Aglaes, a daughter of Acacius, of consular rank <note>original: "Bürgermeisterlichem Stande," referring to the Roman office of Consul.</note>. She lived very magnificently in the city of Rome like a princess and had seventy-three bailiffs who managed her estates, and a chief bailiff who had authority over all the others named Boniface. As humans are, alas, prone to vice, he was involved with her in a sinful relationship. He was a drunkard and an adulterer, and a friend of everything that the Lord God hates. However, he possessed three kinds of good works: namely, hospitality, generosity, and mercy. Whenever he saw a foreign traveler arrive, he joyfully compelled them into his house for lodging and had them served. At night, he would often go through the alleys and markets of the city and give to the poor lying here and there everything they required.

# History of the Martyrs / Year 290.

...into what sins we are entangled, and we do not think about the fact that we must appear before God and give Him an account of all the evil works we have done in this world. But now I have heard several Christians say that if someone serves the saints who suffer for the name of Jesus Christ and must fight for His sake, they will become their fellow-companions on the day of God's terrible judgment. Since I have understood from some that the servants of Christ in the Eastern lands <note>original: "Morgen-Länder," referring to the eastern provinces of the Roman Empire, such as Cilicia.</note> have to strive against the devil and must hand over their bodies to the executioners <note>original: "Bütteln," the officials or guards tasked with carrying out arrests and punishments.</note> so that they do not deny Christ, go there and fetch the bodies of the holy martyrs for us from there; so that perhaps, if we establish houses of prayer over their graves, we might be saved through their holy prayer, along with many others besides us.

### Chapter 3.

->Boniface's Preparation for the Journey / and Farewell from his Mistress.<-

Thus the steward <term>Hofmeister|The chief administrator or majordomo of a noble household.</term> Boniface received much gold to purchase the bodies of the holy martyrs from the soldiers and to provide for the poor; in addition, he took twelve mounted servants with him along with three supply wagons, as well as all sorts of spices and ointments to honor the holy martyrs. As he was about to begin his journey, he spoke to his mistress upon parting: "Mistress, if I encounter the corpses of the holy martyrs, I will bring them with me; but if my own dead body comes back to you, receive it in place of a martyr." At this, his mistress gave him her answer and said: "Leave off your drunkenness and joking, and behave yourself so that you may be worthy to carry the bodies of the holy martyrs with you; but I, a sinner, although I am unworthy, will soon await your return. May the Lord and God over all, who for the sake of our salvation <term>Seligkeit|The state of eternal happiness or spiritual grace.</term> took on the form of a servant and shed His blood for the sake of the human race, send His angel before your face and direct your path according to His goodness; may He fulfill my desire for the best and not remember my sins."

### Chapter 5.
->His Arrival in Tarsus.<-

Then, after several days, he came to Tarsus <note>A major city in Cilicia, southern Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), and the birthplace of the Apostle Paul.</note> and learned that the holy fighters of Christ were even then being martyred and killed; then he spoke to his servants: "Men and brothers, go and seek out a lodging for us; and let the beasts rest there; I will meanwhile [go] and see those whom I have greatly longed to see."

### Chapter 6.
->The Circumstances of the Martyrs in Tarsus.<-

Now, when he came to the place of execution <note>original: "Schau-Platze," literally 'show-place' or theater, where public executions and spectacles occurred.</note> where the holy martyrs were fighting, he saw how they were being martyred; one was hung up with his head toward the earth, with fire beneath him; another was stretched out <note>original: "ausge-[span]net," meaning racked or tensioned.</note> on four stakes and was being slowly quartered; another's entire face was desecrated, his lips, nose, and ears cut off, and his eyes gouged out; another was torn with sharp hooks; another had his hands chopped off; another they had impaled through the neck into the ground; another had his hands and feet tied together behind his back, and so he was beaten to death by the henchmen <term>Schergen|The low-level officials or executioner's assistants responsible for carrying out corporal punishment.</term> with clubs. All who watched such a spectacle, however, were greatly terrified; yet it was seen with joy how the devil was overcome and the servants of Christ fought against him with brave spirits.

Boniface gave as answer: "I have already told you, I am a Christian; but if you wish to know my common name, I am called Boniface." Boniface spoke: "I have told you several times already that I am a Christian and do not sacrifice to demons; whatever you wish to do, do it; see, here is my body before you."

### Chapter 9.

The blessed Boniface was martyred on the 14th of May in Tarsus, the capital of Cilicia, and was buried near Rome on the 5th of June.

## Chapter 17.
->She renounces the world and lives holily until her end.<-

The blessed Aglaes, however, renounced the world and its splendor, and distributed all her goods to the poor. She also gave complete freedom to all her bondservants <term>Leib-eigenen Knechten und Mägden</term> <note>referring to domestic slaves or serfs bound to her service</note> and kept only a few virgins with her, who together with her renounced the world and devoted themselves to Christ. She became so magnificent that she obtained grace from God and was able to cast out demons and heal many kinds of diseases. Thus, the blessed Aglaes lived in such a spiritual state for thirteen years, until she fell asleep in the Lord and was buried in peace near the aforementioned martyr. In this manner, the glorious martyr Boniface fought his struggle and carried away the crown of victory to the honor and praise of God the Father, and His only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, now and forever and into the ages of ages. Amen! Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs* <note>original Latin: "Act. MM." for Acta Martyrum</note> page 284.

43. St. Victor / etc.

# 43. St. Victor, Alexander, Felicianus, and Longinus at Marseille in France. In the year 290.

## Chapter 1.

->A description of the city of Marseille as it was in the third century.<-

Marseille <note>original: "Marsilien"</note> in Provence, by the sea in France, has been a great city since antiquity, well-built and one of the most beautiful, situated on fertile soil in France toward Italy. Its commerce, by both water and land, was convenient for all nations, resulting in an unspeakable wealth within it; it has always been famous for its inhabitants and its fortifications. For these reasons, it was deemed worthy to be the seat of Roman power in the West <note>original: "Abend-Ländern," literally 'evening lands,' a term for the Occident</note>; just as it was a diligent worshiper of the Roman gods—or rather, of the Roman evil spirits—and was considered an insane defender of accursed superstition. Because of these things, it also became very proud and malicious, and went to work so fiercely in martyring Christians and killing the saints as if it had forgotten all humanity. Like wolves, they dragged the flocks of Christ, gathered here and there, before the court, especially when the emperors arrived. They did not even spare their own fellow citizens; if they found anyone who confessed the name of Christ, they were mocked in many ways for the triumph of their evil spirits, without any mercy and without regard for age or gender. They were tormented with countless types of torture and finally slaughtered like cattle.

## Chapter 2.

->The tyranny of Emperor Maximian against the Christians in Marseille.<-

Among such jewels of the holy martyrs, Saint Victor shines forth magnificently like a bright star above the others; partly because he was more noble, and partly because he was more grounded in our religion, more fervent, and more called than others.

Here he intended to fill the measure of his vices with a shameful life; and so that he might lack no evil, he declared war in full madness against godliness <term>Gottseligkeit</term> <note>a state of living in holy devotion to God</note> like an insatiable tormentor, as if he had done too little until now. He commanded that the worshipers of Christ, if they did not sacrifice to the idols, should be executed with the most terrible kinds of death. Now, when our people saw such dark clouds hovering over their heads and their spirits were very dismayed, the invincible Victor stood in their midst and went out every night to visit the brothers, whose hearts he encouraged and strengthened toward the love of eternal life and the contempt of temporal death.

# Chapter 3.
## Victor is captured / and brought before the lower judges.

Amid such efforts, he was seized as a blessed sacrifice and placed before the judgment seat <note>original: "Richt-Stul," the seat of authority where a judge or magistrate presided</note>. At first, the judges sought to persuade him leniently so that he would not despise the service of the gods, nor neglect the usual military pay <note>Victor was a Roman officer, and "Krieges-Besoldung" refers to his rank and financial stipend</note> and the Emperor's friendship, for the sake of an unknown man who had long since been crucified. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, replied that their supposed gods were unclean spirits, and that from now on, as a soldier of Christ, he would never again seek military pay or the Emperor’s friendship to the shame of this, his King. For the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Son of the highest God, had indeed been a mortal man out of love for the restoration of the human race and had allowed Himself to be killed by the ungodly; but through the omnipotence of His divine power, He rose again on the third day and finally ascended to heaven...

...ascended to heaven, where He has received the imperishable kingdom from God His Father! This he testified with an unchanging countenance and a bold voice, full of earnestness. Thereupon, a cry suddenly arose from those standing around that reached even to the heavens, and the godly Confessor <term>Bekenner</term> <note>A "Confessor" is a title for a saint who suffered for the faith but was not necessarily killed at that moment.</note> of the Lord had to endure being slandered by everyone; but because he was a man of high standing, the judges decided that his case must be brought before the Emperor. ## Chapter 4.
->His Defense before the Emperor.<-

Thus was the most blessed Victor presented before the judgment seat of the raging Emperor, and was besieged from all sides with many accusations, and forced with all manner of cunning and the greatest terrors to offer sacrifices to devils <note>referring to pagan Roman gods</note>. The martyr, however, became only the stronger through the terror, as one who conquered hell with little effort; he did not consider the things offered to him worthy of mention, as one who had already experienced heavenly citizenship. Therefore, refreshed by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, he refuted the grim Emperor and all his princes with admirable wisdom and boldness, overthrew their idolatry, and demonstrated with irrefutable reasons that Jesus Christ is the true God.

## Chapter 5.
->At the Emperor’s command, he is dragged by ropes through all the streets<-
->of the city.<-

Then the most godless Emperor, who was more grim than a beast and more malicious than a dragon, became insane with devilish fire and commanded that the holy martyr be dragged by ropes through the entire city. He intended to use this shameful punishment to avenge the perceived injustice done to his gods and to further terrify our spirits. After the sentence was given, the host of the senseless mob cried out, and crowds ran from all sides to the spectacle. While the warrior of Christ was being dragged through the entire city, bound fast by his hands and feet, godless hands and insulting, blasphemous mouths increased his sufferings however they best could; so much so, that it was considered no small crime if someone did not help in despising him.

## Chapter 6.
### His Repeated Interrogation Before the Associate Judges.

After such mockery, once he had sufficiently and abundantly satisfied the eyes of the malicious mob, the most holy Victor was brought again before the judges, torn and wounded. They dealt with him even more sharply concerning the denial of Christ and the worship of the gods; for they supposed that his spirit had become despondent through punishment, disgrace, and the raving of the people, and that he would no longer use so many words, having been made wise through his own hard experience to look after his own best interests. They complained greatly that he had insulted the Emperor himself and the commonwealth <term>gemeine Weſen</term> <note>The "commonwealth" or "public weal" refers to the Roman state (Res publica), which viewed the refusal to worship the state gods as a form of treason.</note>; they said it was indeed the highest insanity, and nothing was more wretched than to disregard the friendship of all the gods and the most invincible Emperors, and to deny all the pleasure, magnificence, and honor of the world—even to let go of the sweet delight of one's own body for that which one has never seen—and for that reason to bring upon oneself the hatred of all gods and men, and with the greatest sorrow of all good friends, to hasten toward destruction through the greatest tortures. 

Therefore, as one who had now tasted something of misery, he should adopt better thoughts and not despise the gods, whose manifest majesty shone gloriously in the temples, and whose benefits were felt by all those who worshiped the venerable antiquity <term>Ehr-würdige Altertuhm</term> and honored the Emperors; when they were well-disposed, all things rejoiced; on the other hand, if they were angry, even the world could not stand. He should deny the one who during his own life had been the poorest, and who had testified by his death how powerless he was. If he, Victor, would do this, he could still escape the impending torture; and they would take care that they had reason to congratulate him on account of the most intimate friendship with the Emperor and the good fortune of the highest honorary offices. But if he despised this advice for the honor of his Christ—whom no one had ever seen—then no other means remained but to proceed quickly to his shame and contempt before the people, using all torture and insult as an example to others.

## Chapter 6.
->His repeated interrogation before the sub-judges.<-

After such mockery, once the eyes of the malicious mob had been more than sufficiently satisfied, the most holy Victor was once again brought before the judges. Although he was torn and wounded, they dealt with him even more sharply regarding his renunciation of Christ and the worship of the gods. For they suspected that his spirit had been discouraged by the punishment, the shame, and the clamor <note>original: "Geras"; likely referring to the jeering or noisy commotion of the crowd</note> of the people, and that he would no longer use so many words, having been "wised up" through his own harsh experience to look after his own best interests. They complained bitterly that he had insulted the Emperor himself and the commonwealth; they argued it was the height of insanity, and nothing was more unfortunate than to disregard the friendship of all the gods and the most invincible Emperors. They asked why he would deny all the pleasure, glory, and honor of the world—even forsaking the sweet delights of his own body—for something he had never seen, only to load the hatred of all gods and men upon his neck and hurry toward his own destruction through the greatest tortures, to the profound grief of all his good friends. Therefore, as one who had now tasted something of misery, he should adopt better thoughts and not despise the gods, whose manifest majesty shone so gloriously in the temples, and whose benefits were felt by all who worshipped according to venerable antiquity and honored the Emperors. When the gods were well-disposed, all things rejoiced; conversely, if they were angry, even the world could not stand. He should instead deny the one who had been the poorest of men during his own life and had proven by his death how powerless he was. If Victor would do this, he could still escape the impending torture; and they would take care to ensure they had reason to congratulate him on his intimate friendship with the Emperor and his attainment of the highest honorable offices. But if he despised this advice of theirs for the sake of the honor of his Christ—whom no one had ever seen—then no other means remained but to proceed quickly with every torture and insult to his shame and contempt before the people, as an example to others.

### 48. St. Victor / etc.

...began to speak in the following manner, saying: "I am accused of having offended the Emperor and the commonwealth; against this, I solemnly testify that I have never done harm either to the Emperor or to the Republic <note>The German text uses 'Republic' to refer to the Roman state or 'res publica.'</note>. I have not diminished the honor of the Empire, nor have I withdrawn from its defense. Daily I offer diligently for the welfare of the Emperor and the entire Empire; daily I sacrifice my spiritual offerings to my GOD for the well-being of the land. 

But I consider that man to be truly held as the most foolish of all who loves a single thing so much that he will not let it go for that which is a hundred times better. Indeed, if one cannot have that single thing according to one's desire—and even if one has it, cannot rejoice in it without fear, nor can one keep it forever even if one cares for it—whereas this hundredfold good is at hand according to desire, and once possessed, one can delight in it securely because it is infinite and imperishable, and cannot be taken away by violence. 

Who does not know, according to sound reason and the judgment of all the wise, that the intimate friendship of princes, the pleasures of the world and its glory, honor, bodily health, dear relatives and the like—and finally even temporal life itself—cannot be attained according to one's full wish? And even if one had it all, it could not be securely possessed or long retained. Therefore, these are to be followed by the inexpressible, constant joy of eternal life and the possession of the supreme Creator <term>Urheber; literally 'author' or 'originator,' referring here to God as the source of all existence</term> of all things. 

For if one loves Him, one has Him; and when one has Him, one possesses everything with Him. And one does not regret having left the short-lived joy, because in exchange for that small thing, one has received something priceless and eternal. These things cannot be called tortures, but rather rightly called refreshments, through which eternal pain is driven away; and this is not to be called death, but a healing cup <note>A reference to the 'cup of salvation' or the 'cup of suffering' (Calix) often cited in martyr narratives</note>, through which one attains such eternal life. 

That man is truly most senseless, and according to the testimony of every conscience, a faint-hearted fool <note>original: "verzagter Tropf"; a disparaging term for someone weak or pitiable</note>, who sets aside such a supreme good without any cause, and worships the manifest enemy of his life as GOD. Therefore, after this life, such a person has nothing else to expect but the punishment of eternal death and infinite pain. Who indeed is a more cruel enemy of the human race than he who teaches such things and proves by his example what the most [great...]"

Therefore, the same prophet also testifies: Blessed are all those who fear the Lord, who walk in His ways (Psalm 128, v. 1). For the faithful warriors will share in their King’s glory; therefore, we confidently take death upon ourselves for the sake of His testimony, and we prove how certain our hope is by our <term>example of suffering<note>German: *Leidens-Exempel*; a common term in martyr literature referring to the martyr's death as a public testimony or "pattern" for others to follow.</note></term>.

## Chapter 10.

->Victor is tortured; during his martyrdom,<-
->the Lord Jesus appears to him.<-

After the martyr had finished his speech in such a manner, the most godless judges, overwhelmed by his strong arguments, began and said: "Will you not even once stop philosophizing, O Victor? Choose one of two: either reconcile the gods <note>That is, offer a sacrifice to the Roman gods to appease them.</note>, or expect the most miserable end!" He gave them answer to this and said: "If you wish it so, then we must prove our words with works: I despise your gods, and confess that I am a Christian! Inflict upon me now all the torture that you can; increase the torments!" At such an answer of his, the shameful judges became so enraged that they fell into one another's hair <note>German: *in die Haare geriehten*; a vivid idiom meaning they began to argue or fight amongst themselves.</note> while deliberating on the type of torture, as each wanted to surpass the other in cruelty. While he was then being tormented to the extreme for a long time, he lifted his eyes toward heaven and prayed to God the merciful Father, whose gift it is, for holy patience. And the most kind Jesus could no longer hide Himself, but appeared to His soldier with the sign of the struggle and the victory—namely, the cross in His hands—in the form of a comforter, and spoke to him: "Peace be with you, our Victor! I am Jesus, who endures the injustice and the martyrdom in my saints; hold yourself manly and be strong; for I am a strong helper to you in the struggle, and your faithful rewarder after the victory in my kingdom!" At such a word from the Savior, all pain vanished from that hour, and all torture was in vain. He, however, began with a joyful heart and countenance to praise Him, and to thank his visitor and comforter with all his soul.

## Chapter 11.

->He is taken into prison / Angelic appearance therein /
and the conversion of three soldiers.<-

When the cruel henchmen, utterly exhausted, saw that their efforts against the rejoicing martyr were in vain, they took him down from the rack of torture by order of the most wicked President <term>President<note>German: *Präsident*; here referring to the Roman provincial governor or high-ranking official presiding over the trial.</note> and brought him under a guard of soldiers into the darkest dungeon. Behold, the most kind Jesus, mindful of His promise, sent him an Angelic visitation <note>German: *Englische Besuchung*; in archaic German, "English" (*Englisch*) was the adjective form of "Angel" (*Engel*).</note>; immediately the locks and fetters of the dungeon opened, the night vanished, and the Heavenly light illuminated the entire prison brighter than the day. The joyful martyr sang songs of praise to the Lord with the angels, who gently stroked him; but the soldiers, when they beheld such clarity of the lightning-flash, fell at the feet of the Saint, begged him for forgiveness, and desired baptism. After he had diligently instructed them as time permitted, he led them that same night to the sea and took the priests with him; when they were baptized, he lifted them out of the water with his own hands. When morning came, the rumor of the conversion of the holy soldiers **Alexander**, **Longinus**, and **Felicianus** (for so they were named) rang out; at this the great dragon, the Emperor **Maximian**, flew into a rage and issued frantic orders that all of this should be most harshly avenged upon **Victor** as the instigator; the soldiers, however, were either to turn back to the gods or pay with their lives!

## Chapter 12.

The enemy intends to ambush you unexpectedly as beginners, so that if he did not find you on your guard, he could claim the palms of victory for himself. ...of the eternal King Christ! He also threw away his <term>vine-staff<note>original: "Trauben-Stab" — the *vitis*, a staff made of grapevine wood carried by Roman centurions as a symbol of their rank and authority.</note></term> (as the centurion’s sign) and his weapons, and spoke: "From now on I cease to fight for your emperors, and I cannot worship your wooden and stone gods, which are deaf and dumb idols. If one must be a soldier on the condition that one must sacrifice to your gods and the emperors; see, then I throw away the vine-staff and the belt, and I resign my commission, and refuse to fight."

## Chapter 2.
->He is taken into custody and interrogated.<-

At this, the soldiers who heard it were terrified; they took him into custody and led him to Anastasius Fortunatus, the commander of that legion, who gave the order to put him in prison. After the banquets <note>The festivities for the Emperor's coronation day.</note> were over, however, he held a court martial and ordered the centurion Marcellus to be brought forward. The Anastasian captains then led Marcellus into the military council. Anastasius Fortunatus the commander then spoke to him: "What moved you to publicly cast off your belt against military custom, and throw away your weapons along with the centurion’s staff?" Marcellus answered: "I have already testified recently on the 21st of July, in the presence of all the officers of this legion, when you celebrated the coronation day of the Emperor, with a public voice that I am a Christian, and that I cannot fight under any <term>oath<note>original: "Sacramente" — referring to the *sacramentum militare*, the Roman military oath of allegiance.</note></term> other than that of my Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God the Almighty Father." Anastasius Fortunatus spoke: "I must not hide your boldness, therefore I shall let this reach the governors and the Emperor; you shall be sent unharmed to my lord Aurelius Agricolanus, the Governor, and the Chief Auditor Caecilius shall present your case."

Agricolanus spoke: "Let it be read to us!" Thus it was read with the following content:

# Chapter 4.
->Marcellus is heard by Agricolanus.<-

When this letter had been read, Agricolanus spoke: "Did you say these things in the military council?" Marcellus answered: "I did say them." Agricolanus spoke: "Did you hold the <term>rank of centurion<note>original: "Hauptmanns-Platz" — the position of a centurion, an officer in the Roman army who commanded roughly 100 men.</note>?" Marcellus answered: "I did!" Agricolanus spoke: "What madness came over you, that you rejected your <term>military oaths<note>original: "Sacramenta" — referring to the *sacramentum militare*, the sacred oath of allegiance sworn by Roman soldiers to the gods and the Emperor.</note> and spoke such words?" Marcellus answered: "Those who fear the Lord are not mad." Agricolanus spoke: "Did you say everything that is contained in the military record?" Marcellus answered: "I said it." Agricolanus spoke: "Did you throw your weapons away?" Marcellus answered: "I threw them from me; for it is not fitting for a Christian, who is a soldier of his Lord Christ, to wage worldly wars."

# Chapter 5.
->Agricolanus sentences Marcellus to death.<-

Agricolanus spoke: "Marcellus’s crimes are so great that they must be sternly avenged!" Thus he passed the sentence: "Marcellus the centurion, who publicly abandoned his <term>military oath<note>original: "Sacramentum"</note> and said he was defiled by it, and furthermore spoke other insane words before the military council, shall be executed with the sword!" As they were leading him away to his death, he said to Agricolanus: "May God grant that it goes well for you!" In this way, it was fitting for a martyr to depart from this world. After these words, he was beheaded, and suffered for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is glorious for ages of ages. Amen! <note>Ruinart, p. 302 — This refers to Thierry Ruinart’s "Acta Martyrum," a famous 17th-century collection of historical documents concerning early Christian martyrs.</note>
