Now, when Aurelius Agricolanus <note>The Roman Deputy Prefect of the province of Mauretania Tingitana.</note> sought to deter Marcellus—the <term>centurion<note>original: "Hauptmann" — a professional officer of the Roman army.</note></term> of Anastasius—from his confession at Tangier on the 30th of October with many harsh words and through his judicial authority; Marcellus, that most blessed martyr, confessed himself to be a soldier for Christ. With great boldness, he testified that he could no longer be a worldly soldier, a fact which Marcellus magnanimously proved by acting as a "judge of the judge" <note>This suggests that Marcellus, though the accused, held the higher moral and spiritual authority over his own executioner.</note>. In response, Aurelius Agricolanus spat out words full of fury against him, which Cassianus—along with the rest of the pronouncements—was required to record officially in the trial transcripts. He was further forced to listen as the defeated governor, Aurelius Agricolanus, condemned the godly martyr to death. At this, Cassianus testified to his own disgust with a loud voice and threw the written protocol and court ledger to the ground. The entire council was horrified by this; Marcellus, however, smiled. The trembling Aurelius Agricolanus sprang up from his chair and cried out: "Why did you throw the judicial records to the ground with such resentment?" The most blessed Cassianus answered him: "Because you have passed an unjust judgment." Thereupon, the governor commanded that he be taken away immediately and cast into the dungeon, so that he would no longer be rebuked by him.

### Chapter 7.
->The Condemnation of Cassianus.<-

The blessed martyr Marcellus laughed because he rejoiced and, through the Holy Spirit, foresaw that Cassianus would become his companion in martyrdom. He himself went that very day, accompanied by the great longing of the people, to his desired death as a martyr. Not long thereafter, namely on the 3rd of December, the praiseworthy Cassianus was also led to the same place where Marcellus had previously stood and been judicially interrogated. By giving nearly the same answers and receiving the same judgment through which the holy Marcellus had triumphed, he attained the victor’s crown of martyrdom; through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belongs honor and glory, power and might, for ever and ever. Amen. <note>original: "Ruinart. l.c.p.304." — A reference to Thierry Ruinart's "Acta Sincera," a 17th-century collection of authentic martyr records, in the place cited, page 304.</note>

<header>46. The Last General Persecution</header>

# 46. Concerning the Holy Martyrs in the Tenth General Persecution under Diocletian and Maximian in the Year 303, etc. (*)

## Chapter 1.
->The Imperial General Decrees against the Christians.<-

In the nineteenth year of the reign of Emperor Diocletian, in the month of Dystros <note>original: "Dystro" — a month in the Macedonian calendar.</note>, which the Romans call March, it happened during the season of Lent, shortly before Good Friday <note>original: "Stillen-Freytage" — literally "Silent Friday," the traditional German name for the Friday before Easter.</note>, the day of the Lord’s Passion, that imperial mandates were posted everywhere. The content of these decrees specified that the houses in which the Christians gathered were to be razed to the ground and their holy books burned. Those of high rank were to be stripped of their honors and offices, while the common people were to lose their freedom if they persisted in the Christian faith. This was roughly the content of the first <term>edict<note>An official public decree or law issued by the Roman Emperor.</note></term> against us. Not long thereafter, however, additional orders were issued which stated: All leaders of the congregations <note>This refers to the clergy, such as bishops, priests, and deacons.</note> in all places were first to be thrown into prison and then forced, by every means and method, to offer sacrifices <note>To "sacrifice" in this context meant performing a public act of worship to the Roman gods or the Emperor, which Christians considered idolatry.</note>.

## Chapter 2.
->Concerning the Martyrs of that Time in General.<-

At that time, very many leaders and governors of the congregations endured the most severe tortures with a joyful spirit, appearing as exceptional champions upon the judicial stage. Not a few others, being of a faint-hearted and discouraged spirit, fell away at the very first sign of trouble out of fear; the rest were forced to experience all manner of martyrdom.

> (*) Although these two tyrannical emperors had already raged enough against the Christians previously—as the examples already cited testify—they specifically pursued this last and most violent persecution from the year 303 until 312, of which the writer Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian who lived through these events and recorded them in his "Church History."</note> was an eyewitness.

...endured. One was flogged, another unbearably tortured and torn with hooks; under which martyrdom several died a cruel death. Others maintained their struggle in other ways. These were dragged away half-alive, and carried off on the shoulders of the bearers as if dead; those others lay upon the earth and were dragged by their feet for a great distance, and counted among those who had sacrificed. One cried out and testified unceasingly that he despised their sacrifices; another shouted that he was a Christian, and preserved the saving confession of this name. So greatly did the enemies of godliness <note>original: "GOttseligkeit" — a term often used for piety or the Christian life.</note> imagine themselves to have gained a great victory, if they could but obtain the appearance of their evil will. But this plot against the holy martyrs succeeded with little satisfaction; if we were to tell the history of all of them in detail, where would we find the end of our speech?

under Decius and Valerian; <note>original: "Decio und Valeriano" — Roman Emperors who preceded Diocletian and conducted earlier persecutions in the mid-3rd century.</note> at that time he <note>Referring to the devil or the spirit of persecution.</note> pursued the Church of God only secretly and in hiding, and did not declare war upon us all at once and collectively. At that time, I say, many were seen who preferred to leave their military profession and lead a quiet, secluded life rather than deny the service of the Highest Creator. For after a certain Roman General—I do not know exactly who it was—began to persecute the Christian soldiers and for that purpose inspected the camps, he gave those who were Christians the free choice: would they either obey the Emperor’s command and keep their positions of honor, or otherwise be dismissed from service? Then many warriors of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ gave up their rank for the sake of his name without delay; among whom some, though only very few, lost their lives along with their military office in the defense of their faith. Because the one who deceitfully plotted against our religion did not dare to shed more than the blood of a few; he was deterred, as it seems, by the great number of the faithful, which made him shy away from declaring war on everyone at once. But after he prepared himself more publicly for war this final time, it is impossible to say how many and which martyrs of Christ were seen here and there in all places and in all cities.

# Chapter 5.
## The Martyrdom of the Imperial Chamber Pages, Dorotheus, Peter, and Gorgonius.

Among all those, whether Greeks or Barbarians <note>In the classical sense, "Barbarians" referred to anyone not part of the Greco-Roman world.</note>, who have ever been admired and famous for their courage, are the glorious and magnificent martyrs of God who suffered in those times of unrest—namely, Dorotheus and the other chamber boys (pages). Although they were held in high honor by the Emperors and loved as sons, they nevertheless endured every disgrace for the sake of their godliness. They considered the tribulations and the various methods of death devised against them to be much more honorable and worthy than the status and prosperity of this world. I will recount the end of only one of these, so that the readers may recognize from it what happened to the others. He was brought forward in the aforementioned city of Nicomedia in the presence of the said Emperors; he was commanded to offer sacrifices to the gods! When he steadfastly refused to do so, he was hoisted up naked on a stake and beaten until he would finally obey, even against his will. Although he was completely mangled by such torture, he remained constant in his resolve. Therefore, they poured salt and vinegar into his wounds, which reached down to the bare bone. And as he endured even these pains, they brought out fire and a grill and roasted his flesh as if it were being prepared for food; this did not happen quickly all at once, but gradually, so that he would not die too soon. The executioners <term>Büttel</term> <note>A term for a low-ranking officer or bailiff, often tasked with carrying out punishments.</note> were ordered not to leave him until, after so much pain, he obeyed the command to sacrifice. But he remained steadfast in his holy conviction and, like a victor, gave up his spirit in the midst of the torture. Such a state of martyrdom was achieved by one of the Emperor's chamber pages, who was worthy of his name, for he was called Peter <note>The name Peter comes from the Greek 'Petros,' meaning 'rock,' symbolizing his steadfastness.</note>.

(*) Lactantius <note>A prominent Early Christian author and advisor to Constantine the Great.</note> writes in the 13th chapter of *On the Death of the Persecutors* <note>original: "vom Untergange der Verfolger" — referring to the Latin work *De Mortibus Persecutorum*.</note> that this blood-witness tore down the edict—which was against the law—yet with great courage. While doing so, he said mockingly that the victory of the Goths and Sarmatians <note>Tribal groups who were frequent enemies of the Roman Empire; the martyr was suggesting the Emperor was more focused on fighting peaceful Christians than his actual enemies.</note> was proclaimed in it. After this, he was tortured, slowly roasted over a fire, and finally completely burned with admirable patience.

The bloody sufferings of the others, which were no less severe, we shall pass over for the sake of brevity. It shall suffice only to mention that Dorotheus and Gorgonius, along with many other court servants <note>These were high-ranking officials within the imperial household.</note>, were strangled with a rope after various struggles and have attained the reward of the Divine Victory <note>original: "Göttlichen Sieges," a reference to the crown of martyrdom.</note>.

## Chapter 6.

->The martyrdom of Anthimus, Bishop of Nicomedia; an unexpected fire in the palace increases the persecutors' rage.<-

At that time, Anthimus, bishop of the congregation at Nicomedia, was also beheaded in the same city for his confession of Christ. To him was added a very great multitude of martyrs; for in those days it happened—no one knows how or in what manner—that a fire broke out in the imperial palace. Out of false suspicion, this was blamed on our people. Because of this, by imperial command, the worshipers of the true God were executed in heaps along with their entire families, some with the sword and others by fire. At that time, with a divine and inexpressible joy, the condemned men and women leaped into the burning pyres. Countless others were bound, placed in boats, and thrown into the sea by the executioners' henchmen. Furthermore, the bodies of the imperial chamberlains, which had been properly buried after their martyrdom, were exhumed on the orders of their own masters and thrown into the sea, so that no one—according to their delusion—might take them for gods and worship them later. This occurred at the very beginning of the persecution in Nicomedia.

## Chapter 7.

->The new edicts against the teachers of the congregations are strictly executed.<-

What business then transpired is impossible to express in words; for an innumerable multitude of people were thrown into the dungeon everywhere, and the prisons, in which one formerly used to place murderers and grave-robbers, were at that time filled with bishops, elders, deacons, readers, and exorcists <term>exorcists: members of the lower clergy responsible for healing and casting out demons</term>, so much so, that those who were...

# Chapter 8.

->Concerning the martyrs in Palestine and at Tyre; concerning a joyful youth and four others.<-

Of such people, we know that some suffered in Palestine, and some also at Tyre in Phoenicia. Should anyone have seen those countless strokes [of the whip], who would not marvel at them? Especially at the patient endurance of such victorious champions of godliness; for after the scourging, the struggle with wild beasts began—animals accustomed to licking human blood—namely, the combat with fierce panthers, cruel bears, wild boars, and bulls, which were provoked against them with fire and glowing irons.

In this, we ourselves were eyewitnesses when it happened, where we also saw the Divine Power of our Savior *Jesus Christ*, whose witnesses the martyrs then were, prove itself present to the martyrs. For the ravenous beasts for a long time would neither touch the bodies of the saints nor dare to approach them; instead, they rushed at the others who, as outsiders to our faith, provoked them from nearby. Only the holy champions, who stood there naked and with bare bodies, and who incited the beasts toward themselves by moving their hands (as they had been commanded to do), were not even touched. Indeed, at times the beasts would make a leap toward them but suddenly retreat, as if a Divine Power terrified them. At this, the spectators were greatly amazed, as it lasted a long time; especially since not only one beast, when it would not bite, but also a second and third were let loose upon one and the same martyr. Here one had to marvel at the undaunted courage of the saints against these trials, and at the constant and...

# 46. The Final General Persecution

...firm and brave courage in their tender bodies. For one saw there a youth, who might have been barely twenty years old, standing unbound and naked, with his hands spread out in the shape of a cross, praying devoutly to God with a steady and undaunted spirit; during which he did not leave the place where he stood nor yield in the slightest, even though the fury of bears and leopards <note>original: "Parder," an archaic term for panthers or leopards.</note> blew death from their maws and came so close to him that they were about to bite; but I know not how their maws were held shut by a hidden Divine Power, and they quickly retreated. This happened in the manner described. Again, others were seen (as there were five martyrs in total) who were thrown before an enraged bull, which tossed others from the number of the unbelievers <note>Likely referring to the beast-handlers or non-Christian prisoners used to goad the animals.</note> high into the air with its horns and tore them apart, so that they had to be carried from the arena half dead; yet toward those blessed holy martyrs, although it charged at them raging and threatening, it could not approach, but instead it stomped its feet against the earth, goring here and there with its horns, and raged and fumed because of the glowing iron with which it was provoked; nonetheless, Divine Providence drove it back again. When they were in no way harmed by it, they released other beasts upon them again. Finally, after so many and such horrific attacks by wild animals, they were all pierced with the sword and, in place of a grave, were sunk into the depths of the sea.

## Chapter 9.

->Egyptian Martyrs.<-

These are the struggles of those Egyptians who fought victoriously for the sake of godliness in the city of Tyre. But one must also rightly admire those Egyptians who became martyrs in their own fatherland; for there, countless men, together with women and children, despised this temporal life <note>A common theological term for earthly life, which is fleeting compared to the eternal life promised in heaven.</note> for the teachings of our Savior and suffered many kinds of death; some, after being tortured with hooks and ropes until they received cruel blows and endured manifold and even unspeakably horrific torments, were at last consumed by flames; others drowned in the sea; others offered their heads to the executioners to be struck off with a joyful heart. Some died under torture, others were wasted by hunger, still others crucified...

## Chapter 10.
### Martyrs of the Thebaid.

But unspeakable are the types of torture and pain suffered by the martyrs in the Thebaid <note>The region of Upper Egypt centered around the ancient city of Thebes.</note>, who were rolled around naked on sharp shards instead of sharp hooks; women were tied by one foot and hoisted up, hanging head downward; thus they were pulled high with ropes and pulleys, hanging there with entirely naked and exposed bodies as an inhuman spectacle for all. Others were torn apart by the branches and limbs of trees; for they used certain machines to force the thick branches of trees growing near each other together, and tied the martyr’s legs to both sides, then let the branches spring back to their natural position, so that they tore the limbs of those destined for such martyrdom apart with a single pull. And all this occurred not within a few days, nor in a short span of time, but over many (namely, ten) years; when ten, then twenty or more, sometimes thirty and sixty, even as many as a hundred men together with women and children were killed in one day, having been sentenced to various types of death.
We ourselves <note>The author, likely Eusebius of Caesarea, writing as an eyewitness.</note>, while we were staying in those places, saw many groups on a single day, some beheaded, some burned; so many that the swords themselves became blunt and, because they were no longer useful, snapped in two; indeed, the weary executioners had to take turns. At such a time, we saw with our own eyes a wonderful zeal of spirit, and a true Divine power and joy in those who believed in the Anointed of God <note>original: "Gesalbten GOTTES," a reference to Jesus Christ.</note>; for hardly had the death sentence been passed upon the first, when others jumped forward here and there to the judgment seat and confessed that they were Christians, caring little for the danger and various types of torture; they testified to the service of the Highest Divine Being publicly without the slightest fear, and received the death sentence joyfully and cheerfully with laughing gestures; so much so that they struck up songs of praise and thanks to the Creator of all, and until their last breath...

# Chapter 11.
->Concerning Philoromus and Phileas<-

But most worthy of praise and wonder were those who were wealthy, of noble birth and rank, and who had attained great honor due to their eloquence and learning, yet nonetheless preferred true godliness and faith in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ above all such things. One such man was Philoromus, who held a prominent official position as a Justice Counselor <note>German: *Justiz-Raht*. This refers to a high-ranking judicial official in the Roman administration of Egypt.</note> in Alexandria; in accordance with the dignity of his office and his Roman rank, he held court daily, surrounded by attendants and a bodyguard. Likewise, there was Phileas <note>original: "Phileas(*)"</note>, Bishop of the congregation in Thmuis <note>An ancient city in the Nile Delta; the text uses the Latinized "Thmuita".</note>; a man who had previously administered all civil offices of honor in his fatherland with great credit and was very famous for his learning. 

These two, although they had many relatives and good friends who, along with others from the council and the noble class, pleaded with them—and even the judge himself exhorted them to have compassion for themselves and to look out for the welfare of their wives and children—could not be persuaded by any of these to set aside the divine laws concerning the confession or denial of the name of Christ for the sake of preserving their lives. Instead, with a valiant and philosophical mind <term>philosophical mind</term> <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to the steadfast, disciplined endurance and spiritual wisdom shown by martyrs under pressure.</note>, or rather with a conscientious and God-consecrated spirit, they remained constant against all the threats and insults of the judge and were beheaded with the axe.

Because the examples, signs, and glorious teachings from Holy Scripture were well known to these most blessed martyrs who lived among us, they directed the eyes of their minds faithfully to the highest God above all else without any delay. For the sake of godliness, they accepted death with a willing spirit, thus taking serious heed of their calling. Since they well knew that our Lord Jesus Christ became a man for our sake, so that he might both eradicate sin and provide us, who strive for eternal life, with sufficient means for the journey <note>German: *Reise-Mittel*. This likely refers to the concept of spiritual "viaticum"—the provisions or grace needed for the soul's journey from this life to the next.</note>; for Christ, who appeared in the image of God, did not consider it a thing to be grasped to be equal with God, but he humbled himself and took the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a man, and humbled himself even unto death, namely, the death of the cross; Philippians 2:6–7. Following this, the martyrs, who carried Christ in their hearts, also strove for the best gifts of grace and endured all misery and all kinds of torture <term>Marter</term> <note>The German *Marter* refers specifically to agonizing physical torture or martyrdom.</note> that could be imagined, not only once, but several times over. But where can one find words enough to describe their strength of spirit and brave courage in all their torture? For since everyone was free to abuse them, some struck them with sticks, others with rods, and still others with whips; some had leather thongs, others ropes, with which they lashed out at them. It was a manifold spectacle <note>original: "Spectakel"</note> of their torture, full of malice; for some of them, whose hands were tied together behind their backs, were pulled up by them onto posts, and then all their limbs were stretched apart with certain instruments. Thereupon the tormentors, by the judge's command, had to mangle them over their whole body with curved iron hooks—not just on the ribs alone, as is customary for murderers, but also over the belly, legs, arms, and on the cheeks. Others were hung up by one hand, to whom the stretching of all their limbs caused more pain than any other torture. Others were thrown onto the floor; these remained lying there due to excessive pain and offered the onlookers a far more agonizing spectacle than when they were actually being tortured, as they displayed the various devised types of torture upon their bodies. While this was happening, some gave up the spirit in the midst of the torture and, with their steadfastness, forced a blush of shame upon the adversary; others were brought back to the prison half-dead and gave up the spirit after a few days from the endured pain; the rest, who were refreshed again through means of recovery, became only more courageous over time and through the long imprisonment. Therefore, when they were later given the free choice: whether they would rather defile themselves with shameful sacrifices and be freed from all hardship through their [the heathens'] abominable absolution and release, or if they wanted to pay with their lives in case of refused sacrifice? Then they were all ready and went with a willing spirit to their deaths, since they well knew what Holy Scripture says: *He who sacrifices to foreign gods shall be rooted out* <note>original: "Wer fremden Göttern opfert, sol ausgerottet werden"; Exodus 22:20.</note>; and again: *You shall have no other gods besides me alone.*

## Chapter 14.

->A Christian City in Phrygia is Besieged and Burned.<-
->Of Adauctus.<-

For indeed, they besieged a Christian city in Phrygia in an orderly fashion with armed troops, and by throwing in fire, they burned the entire city along with the men, women, and children who called upon Christ, the universal God. This was done for the sole reason that all the inhabitants of this city, as well as the Chief Treasurer <term>Ober-Rente-Meister</term> <note>A high-ranking financial official in the Roman provincial administration.</note> and the entire magistracy, along with all those of high and low rank, confessed they were Christians and would by no means obey the command to offer sacrifices. Likewise, one named Adauctus—of noble Italian descent, who held distinguished Roman offices of honor and had risen through all the ranks of honor in the Emperor’s palace (inasmuch as he faithfully administered the offices of High Chancellor and Chief Judge, and was moreover famous among the believers and confessors of the name of Christ for his many excellent acts of charity)—while he was still Chief Magistrate, was adorned with the crown of martyrdom.

### Chapter 16.
#### Concerning the Martyrs in Antioch.

Should we also bring forth the events at Antioch? There, some were placed upon iron grates and roasted, not until death, but for a long-lasting torture. Others preferred, by judicial order, to hold their right hand into the fire rather than touch the ungodly sacrifices with it. Some of these, fearing the danger before they were captured—and so that they might escape the hands of those lying in wait—threw themselves down from high rooftops (admittedly, an impulsive act), regarding death as a gain because of the wickedness of the ungodly. 

Thus did a holy woman named Domnina, who was admirable for her outspokenness and famous in Antioch for her great wealth, noble status, and virtuous conduct. She had two daughters, Prosdoce and Berenice, who were still virgins of beautiful physical form and in the flower of their youth, well-instructed in the doctrines of the Christian religion. For when many, driven by envy, scouted out their hiding places and learned that they had hidden themselves among strangers outside the city, she <note>Domnina</note> was brought back toward Antioch. 

Now, as the woman <note>original: "We-" for "Weib," meaning woman or wife</note> found herself with her daughters in the net of the soldiers, she became desperate as to what she should do; she therefore spoke to her two daughters and explained to them what evil they would have to endure from the soldiers. The greatest and most unbearable evil, however, would be the violation of their honor <note>A historical euphemism for sexual assault</note>, which would be a shame even to hear about. Furthermore, they would have to surrender their souls to the obedience and servitude of unclean spirits <note>referring to being forced to participate in pagan rituals or demonic worship</note>, which would be worse than any death or destruction. 

After she had testified these things to her daughters, she said the only remedy remaining was to take refuge in Christ. Thereupon all three agreed, once they had traveled half the way back, that they would ask the soldiers for permission to step aside from the path alone for a moment. When they had received this, they tucked their clothes gracefully and modestly around their feet and threw themselves into the passing river; in such a manner they drowned themselves (*). Two other—

## Chapter 17.
->Concerning the Martyrs in Pontus.<-

However, what took place in Pontus <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea</note> is terrifying even to hear told. Some had the fingers of their hands pierced with sharp reeds from above, between the nails; others had hot molten lead poured over their bare backs, thereby burning the most vital parts of the body. Some suffered shameful and unspeakable tortures in their bowels and secret parts of the body without any mercy, as the high-minded and unjust judges demonstrated their diligence by competing with one another daily in the invention of new tortures—as if they were practicing in a race-track for a reward—to see who could be the most wicked inventor. Furthermore, these tribulations did not come to an end until the judges despaired of thinking up more afflictions and grew weary of the slaughter, having drunk themselves to the point of nausea on the blood of the saints. Whereupon they turned toward a feigned, supposed goodness and clemency <note>original: "Leutseligkeit," meaning affability or a pretense of being approachable and kind</note>, so that it appeared they would henceforth practice no more cruelty against us. For they said it was unjust that the cities should be defiled with the blood of citizens, and that the Emperors themselves—who were otherwise so kind and gentle toward all—should be regarded as cruel; rather, it was fitting that the Imperial goodness and benevolence be poured out over everyone, and after this, our people should no longer be punished by death: for we were to be freed from such punishment through the Imperial grace.

<header>46. The Final General Persecution</header>
<meta>catchword: her</meta>

...Christians did not [flee], who trampled the fear of death underfoot and despised such violent tyranny of a man. For the men endured fire and sword, being nailed to crosses, wild beasts, the depths of the sea, the cutting off and burning of limbs, the gouging and digging out of eyes, and finally the mutilation of the entire body. Furthermore, they suffered hunger, exile to the mines <term>Berg-Werke; penal labor in state-run mines was often a slow death sentence</term>, and chains. In all of this, they preferred to prove their endurance for the sake of godliness rather than abandon the service of God to worship idols. Likewise, women were strengthened by the teaching of the true faith no less than the men; some of them fought the same battles as the men and attained equal rewards for their virtues. Others, who were dragged away to be violated, preferred to lose their lives rather than their honor.

At the very least, one Alexandrian Christian matron named **Dorothea**, who was of noble birth and wealthy, overcame with a manly spirit the unrestrained will of the Emperor **Maximinus** <note>original: "Maximini"; likely referring to Maximinus Daia, who ruled the Eastern Roman Empire and was notorious for his lust and cruelty</note>, who had tyrannically violated other pagan women. This woman was prominent because of her noble ancestry and great estates, but even more so, her extraordinary wisdom made her exceptional. Above all these gifts of nature and mind, however, she valued chastity. Therefore, when the tyrant frequently made dishonorable demands of her and could achieve nothing, he hesitated to have her beheaded—even though she preferred to die—because his desire overcame his cruelty. Instead, he had all her property seized and banished her into misery. A thousand other examples exist where the governors <term>Landpfleger; provincial Roman officials</term> demanded shameful things from our people, which they would not even listen to, but rather endured all pain, torture, and capital punishments.

<header>47. Palestinian</header>

# 47. Of the Martyrs in Palestine /
## during the time of the Emperors Diocletian / Maximian / Maximinus and Maxentius / from the year 303 to 311.

### Chapter 1.

->The Imperial Edicts against the Christians are also proclaimed in Palestine.<-

In the nineteenth year of the Emperor Diocletian, in the month of Xanticus <note>A Macedonian month roughly corresponding to April</note> / which the Romans call April, while Flavianus was governor <term>landpfleger: a high-ranking administrative official or proconsul</term> in Palestine, shortly before Good Friday (*) the orders were quickly proclaimed, in which it was commanded to tear down the meeting houses of the Christians and to burn the holy books; those of high rank were to be stripped of their honors, and the commoners and servants were to be made into serfs, so long as they persisted in the Christian faith. This was the content of the first edict. But not long afterward another order was issued, by means of which all leaders of the churches were first to be taken prisoner, and then forced by all possible means to offer sacrifices.

### Chapter 2.

->Procopius is taken prisoner before the gate / examined / and beheaded.<-

Accordingly, the first of the martyrs in Palestine was Procopius / a reader and interpreter <note>original: "Dolmetscher." Likely referring to his role in translating the scriptures into the local vernacular during liturgy</note> for the congregation at Scythopolis <note>Modern-day Beit She'an</note> / who was captured at the gate of Caesarea upon entering, and not first brought to the dungeon, but immediately <note>original: "stehendes Fusses," meaning "on the spot" or "without delay"</note> led to the judgment seat of the president; when the latter commanded him to sacrifice to the gods of the heathens, he gave the answer that he knew of only one God, to whom one must sacrifice in such a manner as He Himself had commanded. When, upon this, it was de-

(*) In the previous description in Chapter 1 it is stated / that such an edict was published at the end of March in Nicomedia; thus it took several more days until the beginning of April, when it became known in Palestine.

commanded that he should then sacrifice in honor of the four Emperors; he recited a verse from Homer, which did not please them:

> Many masters must not be in the government;
> One ruler is enough; let one King reign alone!
<note>original: "Viel Herren müssen nicht am Regimente seyn; Ein Herrscher ist genug; Ein König herrsch allein!" This is a quote from Homer's Iliad (Book 2), which Procopius used to argue that there is only one true King (God), directly insulting the Roman Tetrarchy—the rule of four Emperors.</note>

After that, he was beheaded on the eighth day of the month of Desius <note>A Macedonian month roughly corresponding to June</note>; that is, according to the Roman calendar, the 8th of June, on a Wednesday; this was the first history of martyrdom at that time in Caesarea in Palestine.

## Chapter 3.
### The diverse conditions of the martyrs at Caesarea.

After this, in the same city, very many leaders of the congregations of that land endured the most severe martyrdom with joyful courage, and presented a spectacle of glorious struggles. Not a few others, however, became faint-hearted and weak out of laziness, and were overthrown at the very first assault. The others suffered various kinds of torment; one was beaten with scourges <term>Geiffeln: whips used for judicial punishment</term>, another was tormented with unbearable torture and hooks, and almost strangled with bonds; so much so that some people's hands, after the bonds were loosened, were paralyzed and cut through. But each one endured everything that the secret judgments of God ordained for him with brave spirit; for one man was seized by the hand and dragged to the altar, and then the shameful and loathsome incense for sacrifice was thrown into his right hand, so that he was forced to let it fall into the sacrificial fire; afterwards, he was cunningly released, as if he had sacrificed. Another, who had not touched the incense with his fingers, had to go away in silence (*) based on the false pretense of witnesses that he had burned incense. One they tortured half to death and pulled him up high, then threw him down as if dead; they then released him, and he was counted among those who had sacrificed. Another cried out and testified that he did not agree to what was demanded of him by force; whereupon his mouth was smashed, and silence was imposed upon him by many appointed for that purpose, and then he was pushed away with violence, although he had in no way sacrificed; so greatly did they value it if those people only appeared to have done what they wanted.

(*) Such silence rightly made them suspect of hypocrisy; among them the author Eusebius himself was accused, as has already been noted in the previous history Num. 46, chap. 2. <note>The author is referring to the historical controversy where Eusebius of Caesarea was accused by his contemporaries of having given in to the Roman authorities or at least appearing to do so to survive the persecution.</note>

<header>47. Palestinian Martyrs</header>

## Chapter 4.
### The Martyrdom of Alphaeus and Zacchaeus.

Out of such a great number, only Alphaeus and Zacchaeus, Deacons of Gaddi <note>original: "Gaddi," likely referring to Gadara, a city of the Decapolis</note>, attained the crown of martyrdom. After being scourged <term>Geisselung: ritualized whipping used as a Roman judicial punishment</term> and imprisoned, after enduring the harshest bonds and the most extreme pains thereof, and after many kinds of torture—during which they were kept for twenty-four hours with their feet in the stocks stretched four holes apart <note>The "block" or stocks had holes for the legs; being forced into the fourth hole meant their legs were stretched to a painful, unnatural width</note>—they were executed because they confessed one single God and one King and Lord, Jesus Christ. They were treated as if they had spoken something godless and were executed in the same manner as the first martyr, Procopius; they were beheaded. This occurred on the seventh day of the month of Dius <note>A Macedonian month</note>, which according to the Roman calendar is the 17th of November.

## Chapter 5.
### The Martyrdom of the holy Romanus, a Deacon of Caesarea, in Antioch.

What occurred with the martyr Romanus (*) on that same day in Antioch is also noteworthy. This man was a native of Palestine and served as a Deacon and Exorcist <term>Exorciste: a minor clerical office in the early church responsible for preparing converts and praying over the possessed</term> for the congregation at Caesarea. He arrived in Antioch at the very time when the houses of assembly <note>churches</note> were being torn down. When he saw countless men, women, and children running to the temples of the idols to offer sacrifices, he found it unbearable to watch. Stirred by zeal for the true service of God, he stepped closer and began to rebuke them with a loud voice. Because of this bold act, he was immediately seized and adorned with a martyr's crown as magnificent as any that has ever been. For when the judge condemned him to the fire, he accepted the sentence with a cheerful countenance and a very joyful spirit, and was led away to his death. Then, having been tied to the stake and surrounded with brushwood and timber (which, however, would not burn because of a sudden heavy rain), the court officials appointed to light the fire waited for further orders from the Emperor (Galerius), who was then present in the city. Meanwhile, the martyr spoke to them: "Where then is your fire?" Upon this, he was brought before the Emperor and sentenced to a new kind of torture: the cutting out of his tongue. He bravely endured this punishment and showed everyone through his deed that divine power always comes to the aid of those who suffer all manner of pain for the sake of godliness, soothing their sorrows.

---

(*) The history of his martyrdom follows separately hereafter.

### Chapter 6.
->Of Timothy, Agapius, and Thecla.<-

In the second year thereafter, when the rage of persecution burned more fiercely against us and Urbanus was Governor <term>Landpfleger: a regional administrator or prefect representing Roman authority</term> in Palestine, imperial written orders were sent at the beginning of the year. By these, it was generally commanded that everyone in all places and corners should publicly sacrifice and offer incense to the gods. At that time, Timothy endured countless tortures in the city of Gaza in Palestine, and was finally consumed by a gentle, slow fire; having given a sufficient testimony of his godliness with constant patience in all suffering, he carried away the crown of martyrdom. Likewise, Agapius and Thecla (the namesake of the first ancient martyr <note>Referring to Saint Thecla, a famous 1st-century martyr and follower of the Apostle Paul</note>), having shown an uncommon steadfastness of spirit alongside the aforementioned Timothy, were condemned to the wild beasts <note>original footnote (**): Regarding Agapius, he had to remain in prison for two more years before this sentence was carried out on him, as follows further in Chapters 15 and 16.</note>.

->Of six young men who turned themselves in, bound.<-

For when the pagans were celebrating their public festival days and customary spectacles, a great rumor arose among all that, in addition to those they were persecuting with all zeal, those Christians who had recently been sentenced were also to fight with wild beasts. After such a report became known everywhere, six young men came forward. One of them, a Pontic by birth <term>Pontiker: a person from Pontus, a region on the southern coast of the Black Sea</term>, was named Timolaus; the second was a Phoenician from Tripoli named Dionysius; the third was a Subdeacon <term>Subdiaconus: an assistant to the deacon in the early church hierarchy</term> of the congregation at Diospolis named Romulus; along with these were two Egyptians, Paesis and Alexander; and finally another of the previous name, Alexander, a native of Gaza. However, after both the Governor and those standing around had wondered at them not a little, they were immediately taken to prison. But after a few days, when a couple of others had been joined with them—one of whom was named Agapius, who had already suffered martyrdom long before and was famous for many confessions; the other, named Dionysius, had provided them with the necessities for their bodies—these eight were all beheaded on one day in the city of Caesarea. This occurred on the 24th day of the month of Dystrus <note>original: "Distri"; Dystrus was a month in the Macedonian calendar corresponding to March</note> or the 25th of March.

### Chapter 9.

->Galerius Maximianus gives new Edicts against the Christians. The Martyrdom Story of **Apphianus**, /<-
->a student.<-

From that time on, **Maximinus** (by **Galerius Maximianus**) was raised to the imperial throne; to prove his hatred against **God** and his innate godlessness, he persecuted our people <note>the Christians</note> even more violently than the previous Emperors. Now, as everyone was in the highest confusion, fleeing here or there and striving to escape the danger—since all lands stood in movement and unrest on that account—with what words shall I worthily explain the Divine fervor of love and the entirely confident confession of faith of the blessed and truly innocent sheep, **Apphianus**, the martyr? Before the gate of the city of **Caesarea**, he set before the eyes of all its inhabitants a wonderful example of pure love for the true **God**, and that while he was not yet twenty years old. Already before, while he was staying for a considerable time at the university in **Berytus** <note>modern-day Beirut, which was a famous center for legal studies in the Roman Empire</note> for the sake of his **studies** (seeing as he was born of very wealthy parents), it is impossible to say how he trampled the desires of youth underfoot in that city. He allowed himself to be led astray neither by the fiery drive of nature nor by dissolute company, but rather surrendered himself to discipline and walked honorably, soberly, and godly according to Christian teaching, conducting himself modestly. Shall I also mention the praiseworthy fame of his fatherland and the city in which such a courageous champion of our religion was born? I shall do so gladly. Does anyone know the notable city of **Patara** in **Lycia**? From there our noble youth was born. ## Chapter 10.

->**Apphianus** arrives in **Caesarea** and approaches the Governor himself.<-

Furthermore, the captains <note>original: "Haupt-Leute," referring to military officers or centurions</note> fetched everyone according to the name-register, causing the Christians in all places to be very distressed. Then the aforementioned scholar <note>term: "Studiosus" (originally Latin) refers to a student or dedicated scholar of the faith</note> **Apphianus**, without having consulted with anyone, and even without the knowledge of us who lived together in one house, and before the bodyguard surrounding the Governor even noticed, went fearlessly up to the Governor himself. The Governor was just then standing and about to sacrifice as an example to others; **Apphianus** faithfully grasped his right hand, thereby preventing him from sacrificing. He immediately began, like a wise counselor, to remind him with Divine earnestness to desist from this error—

# History of the Martyrs / Years 303–311.

## Chapter 11.
### Apphianus’s Horrific Martyrdom.

Thereupon, the soldiers standing around the Governor <note>German: *Präsidenten*, referring to the Roman official Urbanus</note> attacked the aforementioned youth like wild beasts, threw him down, and after giving him countless blows over his entire body, they led him to the dungeon. When he had sat therein for a day and a night with his feet in the stocks <note>German: *im Block*; a wooden frame used to restrain prisoners by the ankles</note>, he was dragged before the court the following day. When the judge then exhorted him to sacrifice to the gods, he showed an invincible constancy of mind against all tribulation and the cruelest pains, although his chest was torn with hooks not once but several times down to the ribs, and his face was beaten with straps from which lead balls hung <note>a type of scourge known as a *plumbata*</note> in such a way that even his best acquaintances did not recognize him because of the wounds and swellings. 

But as he paid no heed to all such pains, the torturers, at the order of the Governor, took flax soaked in oil and wrapped it around his feet, then set it on fire, from which the most blessed martyr suffered unspeakable pains; for after the flesh was consumed, the fire penetrated to the bones, so much so that his fat and blood dripped down like melted wax. Nonetheless, such torture did not overcome him, although his defeated and—due to his horrific courage—dispirited adversaries brought him once again into the dungeon. Thereupon, three days later, he was carried once more before the judge, and after he persisted in his constancy of faith and confession, the Governor had him thrown half-dead into the sea,

47. Palestinian [Martyrs]

## Chapter 12.

->The submerged body of Apphianus returns to the shore by means of an earthquake.<-

That which occurred immediately thereafter will perhaps seem unbelievable to those who did not see it with their own eyes when I tell it to them. Yet, although I am certainly aware of this, I cannot hide a real event from posterity, especially since nearly all the inhabitants of Caesarea are witnesses to this miracle, as both young and old were present at this terrifying spectacle. After they had thrown that most holy and blessed youth into the middle of the sea, into the deepest abyss as they thought, there suddenly arose such a movement and crashing, not only in the sea but also in the air, that even the earth and the city of Caesarea trembled because of it. And in that same moment, as the sudden and wonderful earthquake occurred, the body of the divine martyr—which the sea waves could not keep—was thrown by them before the gates of the city. This was the end of the wonderful Apphianus, on the second day of the month of Xanthicus <note>original: *Xanthici*; a month in the Macedonian calendar, corresponding to the Roman month of April</note>, which is the third of April, on a Friday in the year 306.

## Chapter 13.

->The Martyrdom of Ulpianus.<-

At the same time, in nearly those same days, another young man named Ulpianus, after cruel torture and harsh scourging, was sewn into a sack made of raw ox-leather together with a dog and snakes <note>This specific form of execution, the *poena cullei* or "penalty of the sack," was traditionally a Roman punishment for parricide (killing a parent)</note>, and thrown into the sea; therefore, we rightly remember him alongside the martyrdom of Apphianus.

## Chapter 14.

->The Martyrdom of Aedesius, Brother of Apphianus.<-

Shortly thereafter, Aedesius, the spiritual and biological brother of Apphianus, suffered exactly what the former had endured. Accordingly, after such varied confessions, after long imprisonment and burdensome chains, and after the sentencing by the Governor <note>German: *Präsidenten*</note> who had condemned him to the mines in Palestine, and after his entirely philosophical life, which he always led while wearing the philosopher's cloak <note>German: *Philosophischen Mantel*; the *pallium*, a garment worn by scholars and teachers which many early Christians adopted to signify their dedication to the "true philosophy" of the Gospel</note> (for he had advanced further in his studies than his brother, having applied himself properly to philosophy), he ventured to perform the same deed that his brother had committed. ## Chapter 15.

->The Emperor’s Coronation Day is celebrated.<-

In the fourth year of the persecution stirred up against us, on the twentieth day of the month of Dius <note>original: *Dii*; a month in the Macedonian calendar</note>, or the 21st of November, on a Friday in the year 306, a very significant martyrdom occurred in that same city of Caesarea. This was in the presence of the tyrant Maximinus <note>original: *Maximini*; refers to Maximinus Daza</note>, who was staging spectacles for the joy of the people on the occasion of his birthday. Since it was an old custom that such spectacles had to be even more magnificent in the presence of the Emperors to provide greater pleasure to the spectators, new and exotic wild animals were procured from all corners—both from India and Ethiopia or elsewhere—and led into the arena. Meanwhile, the gladiators, who had trained well beforehand, gave incredible displays of their skill and experience, bringing the spectators to wonder. Furthermore, because the Emperor himself was present and hosting these spectacles, there had to be even more extraordinary things to see. What was this? A martyr of our faith was brought forward to fight for true and unique godliness, named Agapius; of whom we already made mention in the second year of the persecution, above in the 6th Chapter, stating that he along with Thecla had been condemned to the wild animals.

# Chapter 22.
->The Tyranny of the New Judge Firmilianus.<-

When the storm-wind of persecution had raged against us for six years without ceasing, a group of confessors <note>In the early church, a "confessor" was someone who suffered for their faith but was not executed</note> of the Divine Religion—of whom an innumerable multitude had long since been held in the Thebaid <note>The region around Thebes in Egypt</note>, at the place called Porphyrites (named after the porphyry marble that is quarried there)—were sent to the Governor in Palestine. There were nearly a hundred men, specifically ninety-seven, along with their wives and very small children. When they all confessed God, the Creator of all things, and Christ, the Governor Firmilianus (who had succeeded Urbanus in office) ordered the tendons of their left feet to be seared with a glowing iron. He also ordered their right eyes to be first gouged out with a point through the membrane into the eyeball, and then bored through with a branding iron until all the nerves were destroyed, as if the Emperor had commanded it. Then, he sent them to the mines of Palestine so that they might ultimately perish through labor and misery. 

But it was not these alone whom we saw condemned and enduring martyrdom in this manner, but also the three Palestinians of whom we spoke shortly before (in Chapter 20), whom the judge Urbanus had condemned to gladiatorial combat <note>original: *Kampf-Fechten*; forced participation in lethal public games</note>. These men, however, would neither accept the usual pay from the Emperor’s treasury nor practice daily as fighters; consequently, they were brought not only before the imperial officials but before Maximinus <note>The Roman Emperor Maximinus Daza</note> himself. Having proven their invincible constancy in the confession of Christ through the hunger and floggings they endured, they suffered the same punishment as the others, alongside several more confessors in the city of Caesarea.

# 47. Palestinian [History]

[The] consequences gained force, and once again—I know not how—the fire was kindled against the Christians. Forasmuch as the sudden orders of Maximinus <note>original: *Maximini*; refers to Emperor Maximinus II, who reigned during the Great Persecution</note> against the Christians were sent into all the provinces, and the governors together with the Grand Chancellor promoted the edicts, letters, and commands, charging the judges, magistrates, and heralds in the cities with the execution of the Imperial decree. It was commanded that the idol-temples <term>Götzen-Tempel: temples dedicated to polytheistic Roman gods, viewed as "idols" by the chronicler</term> which had fallen into ruin through age should be repaired with all diligence, and that all men and women, together with their servants and children, should sacrifice to the immortal gods and eat of the sacrificial meat. Likewise, all meat in the market was to be sprinkled with the water of idol-offerings <note>original: *Götzen-Weih-Wasser*; water used in pagan rituals, intended here to make it impossible for Christians to buy food that hadn't been "defiled" by pagan practice</note>; similarly, guards were to be secretly stationed before the public bathhouses to defile all those who wished to bathe there for the sake of cleanliness with the cursed objects of idolatry. When this occurred, our people found themselves—as can easily be imagined—in the utmost distress and embarrassment; so much so that even the heathens themselves, who were strangers to our faith, disapproved of such heavy and excessive fury. For it seemed to them to be nothing but sheer arrogance and wantonness, as enough unrest and tribulation already threatened everyone everywhere. Yet the Divine power and omnipotence of our Savior gave His combatants such courage that although no one drove or pulled them, they nevertheless voluntarily trod the threats of the adversaries underfoot.

## Chapter 27.

->The Martyrdom History of *Antoninus*, *Zebina*, and *Germanus*.<-

Accordingly, three of their number from the circle of the believers, acting as a united little band, confronted the Governor while he was just then sacrificing to the idols, and cried out that he should desist from his error, for there was no other God but the Master and Creator of all things. When they were thereupon asked what kind of people they were, they boldly gave the answer that they were Christians! At this, Firmilianus became so incensed that in his haste he had them beheaded without the usual preceding torture. The first of these was a priest and elder named *Antoninus*; the second, *Zebina*, was a native of *Eleutheropolis* <note>an important Roman city in Palestine, located between Jerusalem and Gaza</note>; the third was named *Germanus*. This occurred on the thirteenth day of the month of Dius <note>original: *Dii*; a month in the Macedonian calendar</note>, that is, the 13th of November in the year 308.

[To these was] added a certain virgin from Scythopolis <note>modern-day Beit She'an in Israel</note> named Ennathas, who was also adorned with the virgin’s cap (*). She had not acted in the same manner as the three previously named <note>referring to Antoninus, Zebina, and Germanus, who had voluntarily confronted the governor</note>, but had been dragged by force before the sub-judge. There, she suffered scourging and grievous insults, which were inflicted upon her without the command of the Governor <term>Präsident: the Roman provincial governor, likely Firmilianus</term> by her neighbor and Quartermaster named Marys (called "the Snorer"). This was a man far worse than his name implied—strong and possessing great physical power, yet malicious and of a wicked character and mind, for which he was hated by all who knew him. This man had ordered the blessed virgin to be stripped completely naked, so that she was covered from the loins to the feet, but her upper body was entirely exposed. In this condition, he had her led throughout all of Caesarea and scourged with leather straps in all the marketplaces of the city; in this consisted his "heroic deed." After such scourging, she was also led before the Governor’s tribunal; and as she likewise proved her great steadfastness there, the judge commanded that she be burned alive.

## Chapter 29.
->Cruelty committed against the dead corpses of the martyrs.<-

**B**ecause he wished to truly demonstrate his cruelty and madness against the worshippers of God, he even transgressed the laws of nature itself; forasmuch as he did not shrink from refusing burial to the corpses of the saints. Therefore, he left the bodies of the last-mentioned martyrs lying under the open sky for the wild animals and ordered guards to keep diligent watch over them day and night. Indeed, for many days, a considerable number of men were seen obeying this inhuman and bestial counsel, keeping watch just like the appointed guards to ensure the corpses were not stolen, as if this were a matter of great importance. Prostitutes, however—who were also privileged to a certain degree among the heathens—were recognized by their bare breasts and decorated hair. <note>original: *Historici & Critici passim*; Latin for "historians and critics everywhere [mention this]"</note>

# 47. Palestinian [History]

Animals, and likewise birds of prey (such as eagles, ravens, and vultures), scattered the human limbs here and there, so that the countryside all around the city lay strewn with entrails and bones. This spectacle was so cruel and horrific that even those who had lived through previous persecutions testified to never having seen its like; for everyone lamented not only the misery of those upon whom this was inflicted, but also the shame brought upon their own nature and common humanity. This spectacle was visible almost to the very gates of the city, surpassing all murders and all tragedies; for the human flesh was not consumed in a single place, but lay dragged here and there by dogs. Some testified that they had seen limbs, pieces of flesh, and entrails lying even within the city gates.

## Chapter 30.
->A Wonder that occurred in Caesarea.<-

While this was occurring for many days in succession, the following wonder took place: The air was serene and clear, and the whole sky was bright and without clouds, when unexpectedly a great many of the pigeons <note>original: "Tauben." While the text reads "pigeons," historical accounts of this event by the chronicler Eusebius typically describe the "columns" or "porticoes" of the city weeping. It is possible "Tauben" is a transcription error for "Säulen" (columns), or a specific local legend.</note> which the inhabitants of the city kept let fall what seemed like teardrops; the marketplaces and alleys were also completely soaked with water, even though it was not raining at all, from an unknown source. It became a common saying that the earth had wept in a wondrous and incomprehensible way because she could no longer endure these abominations; and to convict the merciless and barbaric human minds, even the stones and lifeless things showed their sorrow over what was happening. I do not doubt that posterity will consider what I have said to be dubious and hold it for fables; yet those who witnessed the truth of the matter in the present time are sufficiently assured of it (*).

(*) Eusebius, being an eyewitness himself, would not have been permitted to write such things if it had not been an undeniable matter. # Chapter 31.
->History of the Martyrdom of several Egyptians,<-
->among them Ares, Probus, and Elias.<-

On the fourteenth day of the following month, which we call Appelläus <note>original: "Appelläum," a month in the Macedonian calendar</note>, which is the 15th of December, several Egyptians were again taken prisoner. They had traveled from their fatherland to perform acts of charity for the confessors <note>Christians who had "confessed" their faith despite the threat of torture</note> in Cilicia. They were captured by those who examined travelers at the city gates. Some of them suffered the same punishment as those they had come to serve, being deprived of the use of their right eye and left foot <note>This was a common Roman judicial mutilation, often preceding a sentence to the mines</note>. Three of them, however, suffered various martyr-deaths in the city of Ascalon where they had been captured, after demonstrating wonderful courage of spirit; for one, named Ares, was consumed by flames, while the other two, one named Probus and the other Elias, were beheaded.

---

# Chapter 32.
->History of the Martyrdom of Peter the Ascetic and Asclepius.<-

On the eleventh day of the month Audynäus <note>original: "Audynäi," roughly corresponding to January</note>, that is, the 12th of January (Year 309), Peter the <term>Ascetic</term> (*), also called Abselamus, hailing from the village of Anea in the territory of Eleutheropolis, gave an extraordinary testimony of his faith in Christ in the city of Caesarea. He was proven like pure gold refined in the fire; for although the judge himself and all who encountered him exhorted him to spare himself and take pity on his youth and prime of life, he courageously despised their advice. He preferred his hope in God his Creator above all things, even his own life. Along with him, a man named Asclepius—a bishop of the Marcionite sect <note>The Marcionites were an early Christian group often viewed as heretical by the mainstream church because they rejected the Old Testament and the physical nature of Christ</note>—was burned on one and the same pyre and departed this life. He acted, in his own view, out of godly zeal, though [according to the author] not according to true conscience. In this manner, these martyrdoms took place.

---

...those who were martyred with Pamphilus, whose name and memory I hold very dear, have left a legacy behind. There were twelve of them in all, gifted with a prophetic or rather an Apostolic grace, equal in number <note>A reference to the twelve Apostles</note>; among whom Pamphilus shone most brightly, he being the only one among them honored with the priestly dignity at Caesarea. He was a man who conducted himself virtuously throughout his entire life, whether one looks at his flight from and contempt for this world, or his generous distribution of alms to the poor, or his setting aside of the worldly high offices he could have attained, and especially his practice of a secluded, <term>philosophical life</term> (*). But above all other men of our time, there shone forth in this man a burning desire for the Holy Scriptures, and an untiring diligence and labor in those things he had undertaken; alongside this, he possessed a particular kindness toward his neighbors and all who came to him. However, those who desire to know more extensively of this man's remaining life and glorious works, we refer to the specific work in which we have described him more fully, which is contained in three books (**). For now, we wish to complete the story we have begun regarding our martyrs.

# Chapter 34.
## The Martyr-History of Valens and Paul.

The second combatant after Pamphilus was Valens, a deacon at Jerusalem (otherwise called Aelia, after the Emperor Aelius Trajan <note>original: "Aelia Trajano," referring to Aelia Capitolina, the name given to Jerusalem by Emperor Hadrian</note>). He was an imposing gray-haired man of venerable age, who was more experienced in the Holy Scriptures than others; for he knew them so well by heart that it was all the same whether he read from the book or recited entire pages of the book from memory. The third among them was named Paul, a native of Jamnia <note>original: "Jameien"</note>, a small town belonging to the territory of Caesarea, a fiery man, full of a fervent spirit, who...

## Chapter 35.

->The Martyr History of Elijah, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Samuel, and Daniel.<-

When the three aforementioned men had lain in prison for two years, the arrival of several Egyptian brothers—who were also martyred with them—gave occasion for such a crown of victory. These Egyptians, out of honor, had visited the confessors banished to the Cilician mines. As they were returning to their fatherland, they were questioned at the gate of the city of Caesarea by the guards (who were rough fellows) just as those we mentioned above in Chapter 31. They were asked who they were and where they were from; since they confessed their way and life simply and without any evasion, they were immediately taken prisoner as evildoers and bound. There were five of them, who also spoke boldly before the tyrant and had to go straight to prison. On the following day, which was the sixteenth of the month <term>Peritii</term> <note>A month in the Macedonian calendar used in the Roman East</note>—that is, according to the Roman naming, the 17th day of February—they, along with Pamphilus and his previously mentioned companions, were presented to the judge by command. The judge first wished to test the established constancy of the Egyptians through all kinds of torture and various inventions; and after he had severely tormented the most prominent among them in such a manner, he first asked him who he was. In response, he heard his prophetic name; for they had changed their original Egyptian names (because they perhaps sounded like idolatry) and called themselves: the first, **Elijah**; the others, **Jeremiah**, **Isaiah**, **Samuel**, and **Daniel**, as the true and right Israel, which are the hidden <term>Jews of the heart</term> <note>original: "Herzens-Juden"; a reference to Romans 2:29, implying those who are spiritually, rather than just ethnically, God's people</note>, as which they rightfully presented themselves not only through their works but also through their names.

But the martyr, whose hands were bound behind his back and whose feet were stretched in a certain manner, testified that he had spoken the truth. When he was asked again and again to confess what kind of city it was and in which land it was located, he answered: It is the fatherland of the worshippers of the true God alone; and no one has <term>citizenship</term> <note>The German "Bürger-Recht" implies the rights and status of a citizen in a specific community</note> within it but them; it is situated in the East, exactly at the place where the morning dawn of the sun breaks forth. The martyr philosophized in such a manner, thinking not of the pains in which he lay, but appearing as if he had no flesh or body and was incapable of feeling. The judge, however, raged with worry and anxiety, imagining that the Christians had built a city somewhere for the downfall and destruction of the city of Rome. When he saw that the brave man remained constant and immovable in his words after all the scourging that had mangled him, and after every pain and torture, he sentenced him to death by beheading. Thus, the event with this martyr was like a tragedy. After it had gone almost the same way with the others, they suffered the same <term>martyr-death</term>.

## Chapter 37.

->The death sentence of Pamphilus to be beheaded.<-

Thereupon the weary judge, who now saw that all his torments were in vain and had seen enough of them, turned again to Pamphilus and his companions. And because he had sufficiently learned that the bold freedom of their faith could be conquered by no torture, he asked them only once more whether they would finally be obedient to the Imperial commands? But when he could get no other word out of them except that single last one which is the hallmark of all martyrs (namely: I am a Christian!), he sentenced them, like the previous ones, to be beheaded.

## Chapter 38.

->The Story of Porphyry’s Martyrdom.<-

When this occurred, a certain youth from the household of Pamphilus—who had been well-raised by this man and had eaten with him at his table—was among the crowd of spectators. As he heard the judgment pronounced against his master, he cried out with a clear voice and demanded that the bodies of the slain should at least be buried! The judge, however, who was unworthy of the name of human and should rather have been called a beast or something even worse, showed no regard for his youth. Instead, when he learned upon questioning the youth that he was a Christian, he grew pale, as if an arrow had wounded his heart, and commanded the tormentors to rage against the youth with all their might. Afterward, he commanded him to sacrifice, and when he refused, he ordered the youth's chest and ribs to be torn with iron hooks down to the bone and the inward parts, behaving no differently than if he had stone or wood, or some other lifeless thing, and not a human being before him. When this had gone on long enough, and the judge saw that the youth’s entire body was torn apart, yet he did not utter a sound nor seem to feel any pain, standing there like a dead man, he realized that his labor was in vain. Nevertheless, he remained fixed in his old cruelty and rage, and commanded that, wretchedly mangled as he was, he should be burned upon a great pyre. Although this youth was the last to arrive at the place of execution, he departed from this life before his earthly master (Pamphilus); for those who were to execute the first group delayed in doing so. Thus, one saw Porphyry—for that was the youth’s name—as a noble <term>champion</term> <note>The original "Streiter" refers to the concept of a "soldier of Christ" or an athlete in a spiritual contest</note> who obtained the victory in the holy struggle like a good wrestler. He was seen with his body indeed badly mangled by blood and dust, but with a face joyful and comforted, going to his death after all his martyrdom, full of the Holy Spirit. In a <term>philosophical manner</term> <note>This refers to the "pallium" or philosopher's cloak, which early Christians often adopted to show they practiced the "true philosophy" of Christ</note>, he had wrapped his cloak—the only thing he had left—around himself like a tunic. With a quiet and composed spirit, he entrusted everything he wished to his good acquaintances and nodded kindly with his head to those standing further away; indeed, even as he already stood bound to the stake, he maintained a bright countenance. When the pyre was laid quite far around him and set ablaze, he drew the flame into himself as if with his breath, and as

## Chapter 39.
->The Story of Seleucus’s Martyrdom.<-

Such was the nature of **Porphyry’s** final struggle. After its completion, a certain confessor <note>In the early church, a "confessor" was someone who had suffered for their faith and "confessed" Christ publicly, but had not yet been killed.</note> named **Seleucus**, who had previously served in the field as a man of war, hurriedly informed **Pamphilus** of the execution before his own death. For this report, he was immediately joined to the group of martyrs. Scarcely had he reported the death of **Porphyry** and greeted one of the martyrs with a kiss than the soldiers seized him at once and led him to the President <note>This refers to the Roman provincial governor, Firmilianus.</note>. The President immediately sentenced him to death by beheading, as if he intended for **Seleucus** to be **Porphyry’s** traveling companion to heaven. This **Seleucus** was a native of **Cappadocia** and had achieved no small rank of honor among the Roman Bodyguard. He far surpassed his comrades both in courageous spirit and in physical size and strength, so much so that his appearance was praised by all people, and his tall and beautiful stature struck everyone with wonder. At the beginning of the persecution, he had endured scourging and earned the title of a Confessor of Christ. After he had been discharged and left military service, he followed those who had given themselves entirely to godliness and a holy life. He took upon himself the oversight and care of helpless orphans and widows, the poor and the weak, acting as a father and guardian. For this reason, he was called to the glorious crown of martyrdom by Him who takes more delight in such works than in sacrifices and the shedding of blood. Thus, this tenth martyr was killed on that same day, following all those mentioned before. It is right to believe that the gate of honor to heaven was opened by means of **Pamphilus’s** martyr-death, and thus access to the Kingdom of Heaven stood open for **Pamphilus** himself, as well as for his companions.

->The Story of Theodulus’s Martyrdom.<-

After this, the turn came to **Theodulus**, a venerable and devout old man who was a member of the President’s household and was favored by **Firmilianus** above all his other servants...

...was pleasing to him, partly because of his age and because he already had children unto the fourth generation <note>This refers to having great-grandchildren.</note>; partly also for his sincerity and loyalty, which he had always shown him. ### Chapter 41.
->The Story of Julian’s Martyrdom.<-

Because one person was still lacking to complete the number of twelve among the aforementioned martyrs, **Julianus** finally appeared to fulfill this number. He had just been traveling and had not yet arrived at his destination when he heard of the execution of the martyrs. For this reason, just as he was in his traveling clothes, he came running from the road to see the spectacle. When he saw the bodies of the saints lying upon the earth, he approached them full of joy and embraced them. Because of this act, he was taken prisoner by the soldiers who had attended the execution and was brought to **Firmilianus**. The Governor did not abandon his usual cruelty but gave the order that he should be burned upon a large pyre. At this, **Julianus** began to leap and jump for joy, thanking the **Lord** with a clear voice for deeming him worthy of such honors; thus he obtained the crown of martyrdom. This **Julianus** was a **Cappadocian** <note>A native of Cappadocia, in modern-day Turkey.</note> by birth, very devout in his manners, and exceptional in his faithfulness and sincerity; furthermore, he was earnest and zealous in all things, and filled with the divine essence of the **Holy Spirit**.

### Chapter 42.
->The bodies of the martyrs are finally buried after lying there for four days.<-

This is the small group of those who obtained the crown of martyrdom along with **Pamphilus**. Their holy corpses lay out in public for four whole days and nights by order of the godless President, and were guarded by soldiers to the end that they should be consumed by flesh-eating beasts and birds. However, contrary to all expectations, neither wild animals, nor birds, nor dogs approached them; finally, by divine providence, they were carried away unharmed and properly buried.

## The 43rd Chapter.
->The Martyrdom Story of Adrianus and Eubulus.<-

But while the Governor's <note>original: "Präsidenten" – referring here to the Roman provincial governor, Firmilianus.</note> zeal and madness against the aforementioned martyr was still being spoken of everywhere, Adrianus and Eubulus came from the Manganaean region <note>A district in Palestine.</note> to <term>Caesarea</term> <note>Caesarea Maritima, the Roman capital of Judea.</note> to visit the other confessors of the faith. However, at the gates of the city, they were questioned just as others had been as to what their business was. When they confessed the truth, they were brought before Firmilianus, who, according to his custom, did not hesitate for long, but after torturing them with hooks, condemned them to the wild beasts. Thus, after two days—namely, on the fifth day of the month of Dystrus <note>The Macedonian name for the month of March.</note>, or on the 5th of March, a day on which the birthday of the guardian angel <note>The "Genius" or tutelary deity of the city, celebrated by the pagans.</note> of the city of Caesarea is celebrated by the heathens—the martyr Adrianus was thrown to a lion and afterwards finished off with a sword. Eubulus, however, followed three days later, namely on the 7th of March or the seventh day of the month of Dystrus. This occurred after the judge had pleaded with him extensively to comply and sacrifice to the gods so that he might obtain his freedom, according to their opinion. But he chose a glorious death for the sake of godliness and preferred it to this transitory life; he was thus stabbed after being bitten by the beasts, just as the previous man had been, and was the last of the martyrs in Caesarea.

## The 44th Chapter.
->The Downfall of the Judge Firmilianus.<-

It will be well worth the effort to make mention in this place of how Divine Providence took its revenge upon both the godless Governor and the tyrannical Emperors themselves. For Firmilianus, who had raged so shamefully against the martyrs of Christ, finally fell into the hands of the executioner <note>original: "Büttel" – a beadle or officer of the law.</note> himself along with others, and was beheaded by Imperial command. And so much for the martyrs who were killed in Caesarea during the time of the persecution.

## The 46th Chapter.

->*The confessors banished to the mines are scattered after a brief respite.*<-

The seventh year of the persecution came to an end, and our circumstances began imperceptibly to become more tolerable, with the blasphemies decreasing, until the eighth year of the tribulation. Now, when a great multitude of the confessors was gathered at the Palestinian mines <note>Likely the copper mines of Phaeno, a notoriously harsh site for forced labor.</note> and lived in unbelievable freedom—even to the point of establishing assemblies <note>Church gatherings or meetings for worship.</note>—the governor of that land arrived. He was an evil, godless man, as is evident from what he undertook against the martyrs. When he heard of their way of life, he immediately brought the matter to the Emperor's attention and wrote everything against them in a slanderous manner, whatever seemed good to him. Afterward, the Mine Captain <note>original: "Berg-Hauptmann" — The official in charge of the mining operations.</note> also arrived and, as if acting on Imperial command, divided the confessors into various groups. He sent one part to the island of Cyprus, others to the Lebanon mountains; the rest he scattered throughout all of Palestine.
