## The 47th Chapter.

->The Martyr-History of Peleus, Nilus, Elias, Patermuthius, and Silvanus.<-

Two of these were bishops from Egypt, named Peleus and Nilus; the third, Elias, was an elder <note>original: "Aeltester" — likely translating the Greek 'presbyter' or priest.</note>, and the fourth was named Patermuthius, a man known to everyone for his great kindness. When the governor demanded that they renounce their faith and received a refusal, he ordered that they be burned. Others were also there who had been assigned to live in a very specific area—namely, all those among the confessors <note>original: "Bekennern" — Christians who had publicly maintained their faith under torture but had not yet been executed.</note> who, due to age or infirmity, or various bodily weaknesses, had been excused from labor. Their leader and bishop was Silvanus, a native of Gaza; a man who was a perfect and venerable model of the Christian religion. This man, who had been famous for his manifold public confessions almost from the first day of the persecution and throughout its entire duration, was preserved until this time so that he might be, as it were, the seal of the persecution in Palestine.

## The 48th Chapter.

->The Martyr-History and Wondrous Memory of the Blind John.<-

There were many Egyptians with him, among whom was one named John, who was gifted with a better memory than any other man of our time. Although he had previously been deprived of his sight, his eyes—despite the fact that he could not see with them—were burned out with a branding iron <note>original: "Brenn-Eisen" — During this period, it was a common punishment to cauterize the right eye and ham-string the left leg of Christians sentenced to the mines.</note> after he had offered a confession in which he shone gloriously. This happened while one of his feet was maimed like the others; for the cruelty and inhumanity of the executioners had reached such a state of wildness and harshness. Furthermore, concerning this man, I need not praise him further for his character and philosophical life <note>original: "Philosophischen Lebens" — Early Christian writers often used 'philosophy' to describe a life of ascetic devotion and study of the scriptures.</note>, especially as he became less famous for those than for his excellent memory; for he [held] all the books of Divine Scripture not on stone tablets, as the Divine Apostle says, nor on the skins of animals (or parchment), nor on

## The 49th Chapter.

->History of the Martyrdom of Thirty-Nine Confessors<-

Furthermore, GOD wished to prepare the aforementioned men—who, due to age and physical weakness, lived alone and were accustomed to devoting themselves to prayer, fasting, and similar exercises—for a blessed and salutary end, and reached out His helping hand to them. But because the enemy and adversary of all that is good <note>A common reference to the Devil or Satan.</note> could not tolerate their constant watchfulness in prayer, and that they were always ready for the struggle and stood in arms, he sought to kill them and remove them from the path as burdensome; which GOD also permitted him to do; partly so that he might fulfill his voluntary malice, and partly and primarily so that those men might obtain the reward of so many glorious struggles. Thus, **thirty-nine people** were beheaded on a single day by the order of the wicked tyrant.

## Chapter 50.
### How this persecution lasted eight years in the East and the first two years in the West.

And these are the accounts of martyrdom <note>original: "Marter-Geschichten"</note> which occurred in Palestine over a period of eight years. This is the state of the persecution in our time, which began with the destruction of the meeting houses <note>referring to the church buildings destroyed during the Great Persecution under Diocletian</note>; afterwards, however, it progressed much further through the plots of the various governors <note>original: "Präsidenten" — the Roman provincial officials</note> of different times. Thus, countless martyrs arose everywhere, those who fought various battles for the sake of godliness, both in Libya and throughout all of Egypt and Syria, as well as in all provinces from the Roman borders in the East <note>original: "Morgen-Lande"</note> to Illyria or Dalmatia by the Venice Sea <note>The Adriatic Sea</note>. 

Regarding the lands situated further toward the West <note>original: "Abend"</note>, namely all of Italy, Sicily, Gaul or France, and everything that lies further toward the setting of the sun—Spain, Mauritania, and Africa—these regions experienced the swift help of a merciful GOD after suffering barely two whole years of persecution, and thus regained peace early; for Divine Providence wished to come to the aid of the simplicity and weak faith of those people (*). 

Furthermore, something occurred then against all expectations that had never before happened in the Roman Empire; for in this persecution, which raged in our time, the Roman Empire was divided into two parts. In one part, which we have just named toward the West <note>the Occident</note>, the brothers enjoyed peace; but those who lived in the other part of the Roman world toward the East <note>the Orient</note> had to take countless struggles upon themselves. But as soon as Divine Goodness became favorable to us and deigned to look upon us with mercy, the Emperors <note>likely Galerius or Constantine/Licinius</note> who had recently stirred up war against us immediately changed their sentence against all hope and sang a different tune; by extinguishing the fire of the persecution they had raised against us through gracious edicts <note>term: edicts — official public decrees</note> and kind regulations. Such an edict however...

## Chapter 51.

->Regarding the brief respite in the eighth year of the persecution, and the Divine Judgments upon the tyrant Galerius Maximianus.<-

Now, after eight years of persecution, Divine Grace looked upon us once again with kind eyes, as previously mentioned. Then the Emperors—the very ones who had started the war against us—recanted in a wondrous manner and, through benevolent, gracious edicts and decrees, extinguished the fire they had ignited against us everywhere. The true cause of such benevolence and mercy, however, was not the goodness of the Emperors, as one might think (for that would be far from the truth); since, until their final hour, they daily devised various evils against us and constantly invented new types of martyrdoms and punishments. Rather, it was visible Divine Providence <note>The concept that God actively intervenes in human history</note>, which was once again gracious to His people and put a stop to evil, while also taming the author of the persecution. Upon us, indeed, such Divine Judgments had to fall, yet woe to those through whom offense was given, as the Lord says in Luke 17, v. 1. 

Accordingly, the tyrant (Galerius Maximianus) <note>Gaius Galerius Valerius Maximianus, the Roman Emperor from 305 to 311, known as a fierce persecutor of Christians</note> was first struck in his own flesh by the Divinely-ordained punishment, which then also attacked his soul. For suddenly, a rotting <note>original: "Fäulniß"</note> overcame him in the secret parts of his body, followed by a deep fistulous wound which attacked the internal parts of the rectum and produced an unspeakable multitude of worms, causing a deadly stench. This was especially so because his entire body had already become swollen and excessively fat from excessive food, which, upon the onset of decay, presented an unbearable and repulsive spectacle to those who approached. For this reason, several doctors <note>original: "Medici"</note> who could not endure the unbelievable smell were put to death; others, who saw no hope of recovery in the swollen and universally unhealthy body, were likewise executed.

### Chapter 52.

->The ailing Emperor Galerius Maximianus commands the cessation of the persecution of Christians.<-

Finally, finding himself in such great distress, he began to recognize how wickedly he had mistreated the godly worshippers of the true God. After he had reflected on this, he confessed his sins before the Almighty God; thereafter, he summoned those who were around him and commanded them to act without delay to ensure that the persecution against the Christians was ceased, and that by means of an Imperial Edict and law, their meeting places <note>Likely referring to both church buildings and cemeteries where Christians gathered</note> would be restored to them, where they should diligently assemble, observe their devotions, and pray for the Emperor. Scarcely had he said this than it was put into effect; the Imperial Edicts were proclaimed in the cities and publicly posted, and they read as follows:

### Chapter 53.

->Imperial Edict regarding the lifting of the Persecution.<-

We, Sovereign and Emperor Galerius Maximianus, the Invincible, Multiplier of the Empire, High Priest <note>original: "Pabst" (Pope); here used as a German translation for the Roman title *Pontifex Maximus*</note>, supreme conqueror of Thebaid, Sarmatia, and five-time victor over Persia, vanquisher of the Germans, the Egyptians, twice over the Medes, six times over the Armenians, also victor over the Marsi <note>original: "Meyder," likely referring to the Marsi or a similar tribal group</note> and the Adiabenians, Tribune <note>original: "Zunftmeister" (Guild-master); a contemporary German translation for the Roman *Tribunicia Potestate*</note> for the twentieth time, in the nineteenth year of our reign, Consul <note>original: "Bürgermeister" (Mayor); here translating the Roman office of *Consul*</note> for the eighth time, a Father of the Fatherland, and Ruling Lord! Likewise:

We, Sovereign and Emperor Flavius Valerius Constantinus <note>Constantine the Great, at this time a junior Emperor or Caesar</note>, the pious, fortunate, invincible Multiplier of the Empire, High Priest <note>original: "Pabst"</note>, Tribune <note>original: "Zunftmeister"</note>, Consul <note>original: "Bürgermeister"</note> in the fifth year of our reign, a Father of the Fatherland, and Ruling Lord!

Among our other ordinances which we have made for the common good and benefit, we were indeed previously minded to reorganize everything according to the ancient laws and public customs of the Romans; and to see to it that even the Christians, who had abandoned the sect <note>The Roman authorities often viewed Christianity as a "sect" or "superstition" rather than a legitimate religion</note> of their ancestors, should be brought back to a right mind; since these same Christians had become so willful in their opinions and possessed by such folly that they in no way observed the ordinances of the ancients, which perhaps their own first parents had established.

## Chapter 54.
->The Death of Maximian. The Continued Tyranny of Maximinus.<-

This Edict was proclaimed by order of the Emperors throughout the provinces of Asia, specifically at Nicomedia <note>A major Roman city in modern-day Turkey</note> on the last day of April in the year 311. Thereupon the prisons were opened and the confessors of Christ <note>Christians who had maintained their faith despite imprisonment and torture</note> were set at liberty. Nevertheless, the tyrant Galerius Maximianus was unable to reconcile his wickedness with God by this act, but died a few days later in the month of May of a terrible plague, after his flesh had completely rotted away. When the other tyrant in the East, Maximinus, heard of this, he hurried there with great speed to seize all the provinces and made peace with Licinius. However, because he was no less a cruel tyrant and a very great enemy of the faith in the one God, he took no great pleasure in the aforementioned Edict. Instead of having it proclaimed everywhere in writing, he commanded the governors <term>Präsidenten: the Roman provincial administrators or praesides</term> orally that they should cease [persecuting] us; this was because it was not yet his time to contradict the more powerful co-Emperors and abolish the law they had given. He therefore only saw to it that it was not made known everywhere in his territory. With such a resolution made,

### Das 55. Capitel.
->The High Prefect's Command to the Sub-Presidents by Imperial Order.<-

**Our** Lords and Most Serene Imperial Majesties have indeed, with the highest diligence and devotion, wished to lead the hearts of all mortal men onto the holy and right path of life, so that even those who hold foreign customs instead of Roman ones might be found in the service of the immortal gods. ### 47. Palestinian [History]

...the third hand; for the actual instigator was Theotecnus, the most prominent man in Antioch, a powerful man and moreover a sorcerous idol-worshiper and a villain, entirely unworthy of his name (*), who at that time was the city's treasurer <term>Renmeister: a high-ranking financial official or curator of the city's treasury</term>. This Theotecnus—who had previously persecuted us fiercely and diligently sought out and captured our people as if they were the worst robbers from every hiding place, and also devised every means by which we might be denounced and accused, consequently causing countless executions—finally erected a certain image of Jupiter <note>original: "Jovis"</note> as an idol of Brotherly Friendship, using certain enchantments and incantations. He devised impure ceremonies, cursed initiations, and shameful atonement rites, and reported to the Emperor the lying miracles that this idol-image appeared to perform. Since the Emperor gave his approval to such things, he [Theotecnus] stirred up the impure spirit against the Christians according to the Emperor's pleasure, and claimed that God had commanded that the Christians, as his enemies, should retreat into exile outside the city of Antioch and its borders. After he first accomplished this according to his wish, all the authorities in the cities subject to him issued similar judgments. But when the provincial governors saw that this pleased the Emperor, they induced the lesser authorities to do the same; which the tyrant gladly approved through his decrees and confirmed in writing, until finally the persecution against us burned in full flame. Maximinus appointed idol-priests in all the cities, and over these he appointed High Priests and Chief Priests <note>The original German uses "Päbste" (Popes), here referring to the high-ranking pagan pontiffs</note> who had the greatest say in the commonwealth and were elevated above everyone, and who also applied great diligence to the religion they honored. Thus, the service of the Devil was renewed through the Emperor's superstition so that, to put it briefly, all subjects high and low were incited against us; to please him, they did us every conceivable evil, and they believed they were performing the greatest service for him when they sought favor by raging against us with murder and practicing new wickednesses.

## Chapter 62.
->War, Famine, and Plague among the Heathens.<-

Thus the messengers of death crept in one after another. For he himself, *Emperor Maximinus*, went into the field with the army against the *Armenians*; meanwhile, his other subjects in the cities and villages were plagued by hunger and pestilence, to such an extent that a measure of wheat was worth two thousand five hundred *Athenian groschen* <term>Athenian groschen: A reference to the drachma; the price indicates extreme hyperinflation where basic food became unaffordable</term>. Thus, countless people died in the cities, but most of all in the hamlets and villages, so that the great multitude of peasants was almost entirely wiped out, all of them suddenly seized by the lack of food and the pestilential disease. Some took their dearest possessions and sold them to the rich for bread; others had to sell their landed estates one after another until they finally became destitute. Some gathered herbs in the fields without distinction, eating the poisonous ones along with the healthy, whereby they lost the health of their bodies. Many noblewomen in the cities, having fallen into the outermost poverty, went about the countryside begging; one could recognize by their respectable appearance and clothing that they were accustomed to a better way of life. Others, emaciated by hunger, wandered about like staggering ghosts <note>original: "todte Bilder"—literally "dead images" or statues</note> and finally collapsed in the middle of the streets, and then, lying on their backs, held out their flat hands and begged—

Moreover, the Tyrant <note>Emperor Maximinus Daza</note> became embroiled in a war with the Armenians, who from the beginning until the time of the Romans had been friends and allies. Because they were Christians and God-fearing people, the God-hated Tyrant tried to force them into idolatry and the service of devils, thereby turning friends into enemies and allies into adversaries. All of this, which broke out suddenly and all at once, struck down the Tyrant’s boast against God—for he had gloried that in his time neither hunger, plague, nor war occurred because he honored the idols and persecuted us.

## Chapter 62.
->War, Hunger, and Plague among the Pagans.<-

Thus the messengers of death crept in gradually, one after another. For the Emperor Maximinus himself took the field with the army against the Armenians; meanwhile, his other subjects in the cities and villages were plagued by hunger and pestilence, to such an extent that a measure of wheat was worth two thousand five hundred Athenian groschen <note>original: "Atheniensische Groschen"—referring to the drachma; this highlights the extreme hyperinflation of the era</note>. Consequently, countless people died in the cities, but most of all in the market towns and villages; indeed, the vast multitude of peasants was almost entirely wiped out, all of them suddenly seized by the lack of food and the pestilential disease. Some took their most beloved <note>their children</note> and sold them to the rich for bread; others were forced to sell off their estates one by one until they finally became / became beggars. Some gathered herbs in the fields without distinction and ate the poisonous along with the healthy, whereby they lost their bodily health. Many noble persons in the cities, having fallen into the most extreme poverty, went about the countryside begging; one could recognize by their distinguished appearance and clothing that they had been accustomed to a better way of life. Others, wasted by hunger, wandered about like staggering ghosts and finally collapsed in the middle of the streets, where, lying on their backs, they held out their flat hands and begged—

**Constantine Augustus** and We, **Licinius Augustus**, having happily <note>original: "g-lich," likely "glücklich"</note> met together at **Milan** <note>original: "Meyland"</note>, and having carefully considered all things pertaining to the benefit and advantage of the common wealth, we have judged, among all other things most beneficial for the people, that we must first provide for that which concerns **Divine Worship**; namely, that both the Christians and all others should have free choice to follow whatever religion they deem best, so that the full power of the Divine Heavenly Being may be gracious and favorable to us and to all who live under our rule. 

Therefore, it is our will and law, which we have decided with understanding and counsel, that freedom shall in no way be taken from anyone to embrace and follow the Christian teaching and faith; and it shall be free for every individual, according to his conscience, to follow a religion that best suits his mind, so that the Divine Being may grant His blessing and kindness to all our undertakings. 

We have deemed it right to write our opinion plainly to Your Excellence <note>The German "Eurer Liebden" was a formal honorific title used for high-ranking officials</note>, so that the conflicting interpretations of our previous edicts regarding the Christians, which we sent to Your Excellence, may be entirely set aside, and hereafter every one of those who have a desire for the Christian religion may do so freely, without deception, and without hindrance or annoyance. All of which we wished to report to Your Excellence, so that Your Excellence may know that we have given the Christians absolute and complete freedom to diligently observe their religion; and Your Excellence should likewise make it known that we grant freedom of religion and conscience to everyone. 

For it is highly necessary for the promotion of peace in these current times that every person has the freedom to serve his God as he wishes, by which we also make it known that we do not wish to infringe upon any person's religion. Our duty, however, is to see to it that no one may be hindered in his faith. Moreover, we have also permitted this to the Christians above all others: that those houses in which they were accustomed to gather according to their habit (concerning which we had previously informed Your Excellence in a former letter, arranged differently according to the circumstances of that time), if our tax collectors or anyone else has purchased them, they shall restore them to them immediately and without payment. ## Chapter 65.

->The Letter of Maximinus to the Governor Sabinus regarding the Christians.<-

**J**ovius Maximinus Augustus sends greetings to Sabinus! Let your Loyalty then diligently take heed of what is unbidden, so that none of our subjects are oppressed with violence and insults; for it is proper, as has been mentioned several times, that our subjects be drawn to the service of the gods with a friendly manner. So that this our command may be known and manifest to all, draw it up formally and publish it.

# Chapter 66.

->**Maximinus’s** command finds no belief; he wages and loses a battle, kills his idol-priests, shows some repentance, and dies.<-

Because **Maximinus** <note>Maximinus Daza, a Roman Emperor known for his fierce persecution of Christians in the East.</note> issued such an order out of compulsion rather than from the heart, people were unwilling to place any trust in him; this was because he had previously issued a similar letter of grace and had kept it in a deceitful and shameful manner. Accordingly, none of our people dared to hold an assembly or appear in public; for such things were not permitted in the letter, but rather it was only commanded therein that no one should do us violence or despise us. However, holding assemblies or building public houses for that purpose <note>Referring to the construction of early churches.</note>, or doing other customary things, was not explicitly allowed; even though the princes of peace and piety, **Constantine** and **Licinius**, had written to **Maximinus** that he should permit it, and had indeed granted it to all their subjects through edicts and laws. But even then, that most ungodly man would not have desisted from his tyranny, had he not been forced to it by Divine Judgment in the following manner. For because he had neither the understanding nor the skill for governing, and was moreover proud, puffed up, and insolent, he began an irreconcilable war against **Licinius** <note>Referring to the Battle of Tzirallum in 313 AD.</note> and met him with a numerous army, upon which he relied, as well as upon the assistance of his gods or evil spirits. He was, however, put to flight, and could barely save himself through escape among the common soldiers after he had cast off his imperial robes. When he thus arrived back in his own territory in misery, he first raged against the priests and prophets of his gods, upon whose advice and word he had started the war, and killed them as sorcerers and deceivers who had robbed him of his prosperity. Thereupon he praised the God of the Christians and gave a complete and absolute command regarding their total liberty of conscience, fell then into a sudden illness, and died in a short time. The command, however, read as follows:

# 47. Palestinian [Martyrs]

...our subjects’ benefit incessantly and in every way to promote, and to seek to show them that which may be most useful and serviceable to them—both what is most healing and beneficial for the common good and most pleasant for each individual—is, we believe, unknown to no one. When we previously took careful note how, because of the command of our Divine Fathers <term>Diocletian</term> <note>original: Diocletiani; the Roman Emperor who began the "Great Persecution" in 303 AD</note> and <term>Maximian</term> <note>original: Maximiani; Diocletian's co-emperor</note>, of blessed memory, by which the **Christians** were forbidden to hold assemblies, the court officials caused many disruptions and robberies, and such things are still being practiced against our subjects—for which we nonetheless strive to take proper care, primarily for those who have been robbed of their goods—we have therefore sent letters to all governors and issued an ordinance a year ago, that if anyone wished to follow these (the **Christians'**) customs or their religion, he should be free to carry out his intention undisturbed, and be hindered by no one. 

Likewise, it should be permitted to every person, without any fear or worry, to do what he wishes in this regard. However, it is also not unknown to us here that some judges have observed our commands negligently, and have left our subjects in doubt regarding our will, causing them to be dilatory <note>slow or hesitant to act</note> in restoring their divine service, which they most desire. 

But so that after this, all suspicion, doubt, and fear may be removed, we have decided to make this command known, thereby making it clear to all: it is permitted to every person, as many as wish to follow this <term>sect</term> <note>At this time, "sect" was a common legal term for a religious group, not necessarily derogatory.</note> and religion, by virtue of this our pardon, just as it pleases and seems good to each one, to make use of the same as he wishes to practice it in his own way. 

Furthermore, it is also permitted to them that they may build houses of prayer. Further, so that our grace may shine forth all the more clearly, we have also most graciously deigned to ordain this: that all houses or estates which formerly belonged to the **Christians** and were confiscated by the command of our ancestors, or seized by the cities, or otherwise sold or given away, all such things shall be restored to the **Christians**, so that everyone may recognize our goodness and diligence in this matter.

## Chapter 2.
### Theodotus’s Holy Conduct.

Before he went to his final struggle of martyrdom, however, he tested his virtuous strengths on many occasions, just like a fighter who intends to battle against his enemy. At the beginning, he resolved to practice in the war against lusts, in which he conducted himself so virtuously that he could have been a master to all. For he did not surrender himself to the service of worldly pleasures or any other <term>unclean affect</term> <note>In the 17th-century context, "affects" or "passions" were seen as powerful emotional forces—like anger, lust, or greed—that a person had to master through faith and discipline</note>, but from his earliest youth, he brought forth the glorious fruits of beautiful spiritual exercises, as his subsequent life also proved. In particular, he held <term>temperance</term> <note>The virtue of moderation and self-control, particularly regarding food, drink, and physical desires</note>—as the beginning of other virtues—to be his shield in battle; he maintained that the <term>chastening</term> <note>original: "Casteyung"; the practice of self-denial or "mortification" of the body to strengthen the spirit</note> of the body was a fitting pleasure for a Christian, whose wealth and honor consist in bearing poverty with a free spirit. 

On the other hand, I have often seen that a high-minded man was overcome not only by the desire for wealth but also for honors; likewise, that beauty defeats wisdom, and that a gentle and quiet man is weakened by <term>tenderness</term> <note>In this context, "Verzärtelung" or tenderness refers to an excessive softness or indulgence toward physical comfort and luxury</note>. To the righteous man alone, however, are all lusts subject, as to a master. Accordingly, regular fasting served him against worldly pleasures, temperance against the pampering of the body, and against excessive wealth, his regular distribution of the same to the poor. All of this, however, we wish to explain one after another in what follows, and demonstrate that he acquired heaven for himself through shame instead of honor, through great poverty instead of wealth and abundance, and through temptations and tribulation.

# History of Martyrdom / Year 303.

## Chapter 3.
->He leads many away from the evil path.<-

He led many away from dissolute living <note>The original German "Liederlichkeit" implies a life of negligence, vice, or lack of moral discipline</note>, and through good instruction, he healed them as if from a pestilential disease. Many who appeared healthy in body, but lay burdened in spirit by unclean thoughts, he made well with his words; indeed, through his admirable teaching and exhortations, he brought a great multitude of Pagans and Jews into the fellowship of the faithful. For his business <note>Referring to the inn he managed, which he used as a cover for his ministry</note> served him, though in common clothing, as an episcopal office, where he came to the aid of those who suffered injustice according to his ability, offered his hand to the weak, had compassion for the sorrowful, and—being full of love—made himself a partaker in the sufferings of others. What is most to be admired, however, is that he also laid hands on all who were afflicted with incurable diseases, adding his prayer in place of medicine. He advised voluptuous people toward abstinence, and those too devoted to wine he led away from drunkenness; some, however, who seemed incurable in the sickness of greed, he brought through his exhortations to take an interest in the needy and to distribute their own possessions to the poor. From this man’s school, not a few are counted who, for Christ's sake, endured not only flogging but every kind of death. Concerning such exceptional struggles, this concise and pious warrior—who himself held the greatest struggle of them all—provides many and admirable histories, which I intend to relate in an orderly fashion, for which he himself assists me with his prayer and points the way (*). I will therefore make the beginning of my intended narrative.

Scarcely had the first ones wiped the dust from their feet before the second followed on their heels, testifying to the unrelenting earnestness of his cruelty and inhumanity. Then came the third, bearing Imperial commands which confirmed his attained absolute power and dictated that all houses where Christians gathered should be razed and leveled to the ground; that the priests should be dragged by force to the altars of the idols and compelled through torture to renounce their teachings. The property and goods of all those who resisted the command were to be forfeited to the public treasury <note>Original: "Schatz-Kasten," the fiscus or imperial exchequer</note>; and they themselves, along with their children, were to be thrown into the dungeon and held until the governor’s punishment <note>Refers to the formal judicial sentencing or execution carried out by the Roman praeses</note>, so that they might be tamed through bonds and beatings and brought to the judicial interrogation with a softened spirit.

They wandered about the entire wilderness and hid in caves and holes, each as best they could; but because they could no longer endure the hunger, many allowed themselves to be captured voluntarily, hoping they might yet obtain mercy. Thus, flight was a great misery for those who fled—especially for the prominent and those raised in luxury, who previously had suffered no lack of anything and now were forced to eat roots and herbs.

# 48. St. Theodotus and the 7 Virgins

Therefore, following the exhortation of the blessed Paul, he became all things to all who suffered persecution: a physician to the sick, a provider for the needy, a steward for the hungry, a baker and innkeeper for the destitute, and a teacher to those who practiced a holy life on earth in pursuit of godliness. He encouraged those being led away as captives to have enduring patience in their martyrdom <term>martyrdom: from the German "Marter," referring specifically to the torture and ultimate death suffered for one's faith.</term>, and even those who already stood before the altars of sacrifice: he exhorted them (with gestures) to endure death for Christ's sake. Thus, he could rightfully be considered the teacher of all those who received the crown of martyrdom at that time. Yet, a particular deed of this martyr has not yet occurred to me, which I almost passed over through forgetfulness, though it shall not escape me as I continue writing.

## Chapter 7.

->Since all food is defiled with idolatry, Theodotus provides clean supplies; and hallows his house for the service of the brothers.<-

For Theotecnus, that servant of the devil, had commanded that all types of human food—specifically bread and wine—be defiled with idol sacrifices, so that one could not even bring a pure offering to the true God, the Lord of all (in the Love-Feasts <term>Love-Feasts: From the Greek "Agape," these were communal meals where early Christians gathered for fellowship and to provide for the poor.</term>); and he had publicly appointed priests of error to carry this out (*). # History of the Martyrs / Year 303.

...persecution of the martyrs, Theodotus once [recovered] the body of the holy and famous martyr Valens(*)—specifically him who was first tortured at Medicon and finally scorched to death, and then thrown into the currents of the river Halys—whom he had fished out and buried. He did not go directly to the village of Malos, however, but a little lower to a certain cave that faced the east, from whence the river Halys flows, which place is a quarter-hour’s distance from the village. There it happened, through Divine providence, that he met several brothers who greeted him and thanked him greatly as a common benefactor of all those in distress; and they proceeded to recount their obligations to him one after another. They shared how, not long ago, they had been detained by their own blood-relatives who wanted to bring them before the judges because they had overturned the altars of Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt; in this period, Christians often faced execution for refusing to sacrifice at her altars or for destroying them.</note>; the holy man had finally, with great effort and no small expense, barely rescued them from their bonds. When he met them now, he considered it a great gain and asked that they dine with him and then continue their journey further.

## Chapter 13.
->The Martyrdom of the Seven Virgins.<-

There were seven virgins who had been raised in virtue from their youth, and specifically taught to hold chastity in high regard and to keep the fear of GOD before their eyes. When the tyrant <note>This refers to the Roman Governor or official overseeing the persecutions.</note> took them captive and could not move them to renounce their faith despite much torture, he finally handed them over to lustful fellows to be shamed, as he was raging with anger and wished to insult the holy religion. When they were sent to certain strong servants to suffer shameful violence, they sighed deeply and lifted their hands and eyes toward heaven, saying:

> O Lord Jesus Christ, as long as it has been in our power to keep our virginity undefiled, you yourself know how diligently we have done so until this very day; but now these unchaste fellows have gained power over our bodies.

<margin>(*) Tecusa, a mother. <note>In the early church, "Mother" was an honorary title for an elder or leader among the women.</note></margin>
As the supplicants said these and similar things, and wept besides, one of those men who seemed the most shameless seized the eldest, named Tecusa (*), and pulled her toward him. But she wept and fell at his feet, embracing them, and said: "What profit, my son, will you have from me, or what pleasure can it be to mingle with our bodies, which are consumed—as you see—by age, fasting, sickness, and torture?" (For she was already over her seventieth year, and the others were not much younger.) "It will be a shame to you if you love this flesh, which is properly speaking already dead, and which you shall soon see torn apart by birds and wild beasts; for the Governor <note>original: "Präsident"</note> has decreed that he will not even grant us a burial; rather, accept for us the Lord Jesus Christ,

...who will reward you with His great grace. When she had said this with tears to the companion, she tore the veil from her head and showed him her grey hair, and said: "Have some respect for these, my son! ### Chapter 14.

->The seven virgins are publicly led about to their shame as priestesses of Minerva and Diana.<-

But when Theotecnus <note>The Roman governor of Galatia during the Diocletianic Persecution.</note> heard that they had not been shamed, he did not wish to trouble them further with lewd desire; instead, he commanded that they should become priestesses of Diana and Minerva (*) and annually, according to the custom, wash their images in the nearby lake. It happened just then that the annual festival for the washing of the idols <note>Likely referring to the 'Plynteria' or a similar ritual cleaning of cult statues.</note> took place. Because each of them was required to ride upon a special wagon, he also commanded that they should be led to the lake and be washed just like the idols. Thus they were led there with exposed bodies, standing upon the wagons, amid mockery and laughter; behind them, however, the idols were driven. At the same time, the entire city went out to watch the spectacle. There one heard and saw the sound of pipes and cymbals, and the dancing ranks of women with flying hair, like the frenzied dancers of Bacchus; meanwhile, the rabble stamped their feet against the earth and made a great noise, beneath which the trumpets resounded; thus the images were driven forth. For this reason, a great multitude of people ran toward them—mostly, however, for the sake of the suffering virgins; some pitied their age, others admired their steadfastness, and some praised their modesty; many, however, wept because they saw them so severely battered by the scourging. The retinue of henchmen also rode out with them, along with Theotecnus, the governor.

(*) Diana and Minerva were, among the heathens, goddesses of virgins and the sciences. <note>In Roman mythology, Diana was the goddess of the hunt and chastity, while Minerva was the goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note>

History of the Martyrdom / Year of Our Lord 303.

->### Chapter 15.<-

->Theodotus prays for the virgins and receives news of their execution.<-

Meanwhile, the martyr of God, Theodotus, lived in great anxiety for each of those holy virgins; he feared that one of them might lose heart in the struggle, as might be expected of weak women <note>The text reflects the historical perspective of the time, which viewed women as the "weaker vessel" in spiritual combat.</note>. He therefore begged God with much pleading that He would help them in their final hour! For this purpose, he had shut himself away in a small house that stood near the chapel of the holy Patriarchs and belonged to a certain poor man named Theocharis (*). With him were Polychronius (**), who was a grandson of the martyr Tecusa; Theodotus the Younger, born of his female relative; and several other Christians who were gathered with him in that same house. 

They all lay together in prayer from early morning until the sixth hour <note>Roughly noon.</note>, when the wife of Theocharis announced that the virgins had been drowned in the lake. After receiving this report, the righteous man raised himself slightly from the ground, and while still kneeling, he spread his hands toward heaven and prayed through many tears in the following manner, saying: "I thank you, my Lord, that you have not despised my sighs!" Thereupon he asked the woman in what manner the virgins had been submerged, and at what place in the lake—whether in the middle or near the shore. 

She, however, who had gone out and watched along with others, said: "Although Theotecnus <note>The Roman governor.</note> used much persuasion and many promises, it was all in vain; for Tecusa drove him back with words of rebuke. Likewise, the priests of Diana and Minerva, who offered them a wreath and white robes so that they might serve the demons <note>A common early Christian term for pagan idols.</note> alongside them, were also rejected with shame. Accordingly, the governor commanded that stones should be tied around their necks, and that they should be taken by means of a small boat to where the lake is deepest! Thus they were thrown into the water about two *yokes of land* <term>Joch Landes: traditionally a unit of area, used here to estimate a distance of roughly 100 to 150 yards.</term> away from the shore."

### Chapter 16.

->Theodotus prepares himself with prayer to recover the holy virgins;<-
->Tecusa appears to him.<-

When the martyr heard this news, he remained quiet until evening, together with Polychronius and Theocharis <note>The right margin of the original manuscript is truncated; missing letters have been restored based on the historical "Acts of St. Theodotus."</note>, and consulted with them as to how their bodies might be brought out of the lake. At sunset, a youth came to them and brought the message that Theotecnus <note>The Roman governor of Ancyra.</note> had ordered sentries to be posted at the lake to prevent the bodies from being stolen. Upon hearing this, the holy man became very distressed; for he saw that recovering the holy bodies would now be very difficult, both because of the soldiers' watch and the heavy stones, each of which a boat could hardly carry. 

When evening had come, the companions of Theodotus remained there, but he himself went out to the Chapel of the Patriarchs. Finding it locked by the godless <note>The original German word "Gottlosen" refers here to the pagan authorities who had closed the Christian sites.</note> so that no Christian could enter, he cast himself down outside the door in prayer and remained there for a time. Afterward, he went further to the Chapel of the Fathers, and finding this one also locked, he cast himself down before it in prayer as well (*). Finally, as he heard a great noise coming from behind him and believed that some were about to attack him, he returned to the dwelling of Theocharis. 

When he had rested there a little and fallen asleep, the blessed Tecusa <note>The eldest of the seven martyred virgins and Theodotus' aunt.</note> appeared to him and said: "Are you sleeping, my son Theodotus, and do you not care for us? Do you not remember the admonitions with which I instructed you in your youth, and how, beyond the expectations of your parents, I led you toward virtue? Indeed, while I still lived, you did not forget me but honored me as a mother; but now that I am gone, have you forgotten that you are bound to serve me until your end? Do not allow us, I beg you, to become food for the fish in the waters of the lake; for in two days, a great struggle for victory awaits you. So stand up and go to the lake; but beware of the traitor." After she had said this, she vanished.

## Chapter 17.

->After gathering information, they go to the lake in the pitch-black night.<-

Then he arose from sleep and told the brothers the dream he had had; they all felt great compassion for him and prayed to GOD with tears that He might assist him in finding the sunken bodies. When day had broken, they sent the youth who had first reported that a guard of soldiers had been ordered to the lake to watch over the bodies (for he was also a Christian), alongside Theocharis, to inquire precisely into all the circumstances regarding the soldier-guard—whether they might perhaps have been withdrawn because of the Festival of Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt; her festivals were often occasions for public holidays that might distract local guards.</note>, which the godless were celebrating on that day. So Theocharis and Glycerius <gloss>(*) Glycerius: a little one / a young beginner.</gloss>—for such was the youth's name—went there, and upon their return, they announced that the guard was still present. Therefore, they remained quiet for the rest of that day. 

But when evening had come, they went soberly on their way to the lake, taking sharp sickles with them, with which they intended to cut the ropes around the necks of the sunken bodies in the water. It was a pitch-black night, as neither moon nor stars were shining. When they reached the place where criminals were usually executed <note>original: "abgetahn," meaning put to death or executed.</note>—which was a terrifying place that no one dared to visit after sunset because severed heads sat upon stakes there, or limbs left over from the fires lay scattered about—no small horror overcame them. However, they heard a voice that said: "Go forth with courage, Theodore!" <note>The text here uses "Theodore," though the protagonist is identified as "Theodotus" on the previous page; these names were occasionally conflated in early martyrologies.</note> At this, they were even more terrified, and each made the sign of the cross upon his forehead. Soon, a bright, shining cross appeared to them, which shot forth fiery rays from the east; at this sight, joy and fear were mingled, and they prayed with bended knees toward the place from which the cross appeared.

# History of Martyrdom / Year 303.

...[Alexandra, meaning] Male Helper), Phaine (the Clear and Bright one); the <term>Apotactics</term> <note>A group of early Christian ascetics who lived in renunciation and seclusion from the world.</note> say these three belong to them, which is indeed the truth; furthermore, the others are named Claudia (the Enclosed, Chaste one), Euphrasia (Holy Joy), Matrona (the Honorable one), and Julitta (the Modest one).

## Chapter 20.
->The city becomes rebellious upon the rumor of what occurred.<-
->Polychronius betrays the matter.<-

When day broke, the entire city began to stir because of the stolen holy bodies, for the rumor of it quickly spread among everyone; therefore, as soon as any Christian was spotted, they were dragged to a judicial hearing. When many had been seized in this manner, to be torn apart as if by the teeth of wild animals, the matter became known to the holy man [Theodotus], who wished to surrender himself but was prevented from doing so by the brothers. Polychronius, meanwhile, changed his clothes and disguised himself as a peasant, going to the market to investigate the truth of the matter more closely. However, he was soon recognized by several people and taken prisoner, whereupon they led him to the Governor. When the Governor had him scourged and further threatened him with death, showing him a bared sword, he allowed himself to be overcome by terror; he confessed how and in what manner the bodies of the virgins had been taken—that Theodotus had retrieved them from the lake—and pointed out the place where he had hidden them. Thus, they took the holy bodies from the graves and burned them. Through this, we realized that Polychronius was the traitor, and that those who had appeared [to us] had meant him when they said: "Beware of the traitor." Some, however, announced these events regarding Polychronius to the martyr, and informed him that the remains of the virgins had been burned.

As he thus prayed with tears, a great weeping arose among the brothers, who embraced him and said: "Farewell, Theodotus <note>original: "Theodore"</note>, you lovely light of the churches! When you depart from this tribulation, we will receive the heavenly lights, and the manifold glory of the angels and archangels, and the unchangeable purity of the Holy Spirit, and our Lord Jesus Christ sitting at the right hand of his Father; all this good will be brought to you by the forthcoming glorious and great struggle; but for us, who remain behind only in misery, your departure from this life brings nothing else but mourning, weeping, and sighing." Amidst such lamentation, the Saint embraced each one, and reminded them: if the blessed Father Fronto should come to the village of Malo and bring his ring with him, they should give him his bones, if they were able to bring them away secretly. <note>This refers to a prior arrangement Theodotus made with Fronto, a priest, to ensure his remains would be buried properly in a specific location.</note> After he had said this, and armed his body with the sign of the Cross, he went with undaunted courage to the place of battle.

## Chapter 22.

->On his way, good friends advise him to turn back, but he presents himself to the judge.<-

As he was going, however, two citizens came running toward him, who urged him to turn back most urgently, saying: "Save your life!" For they were good acquaintances and friends of the martyr, and intended to do him a service of love; for, they continued, "the priests of Minerva and Diana, along with the entire mob, accuse you before the Governor <note>original: "Präsidenten"</note> that you advise all Christians against worshipping the lifeless images, and they testify many other things against you; moreover, Polychronius has blamed you for having secretly carried away those bodies; since it is now high time, save yourself, Theodotus <note>original: "Theodore"</note>, for it would be the greatest folly to give yourself up voluntarily to martyrdom <note>original: "Marter"</note>." Upon this the Martyr spoke: "If you wish to be my friends and do me a favor, then cause me no distress and do not blame my undertaking; but rather go to the authorities and say: Theodotus, whom the priests and the whole city accuse, stands before the door." Having said this, he went before them and presented himself

## Chapter 24.

->Theodotus's Defense and the Exposure of the Pagan Gods.<-

The martyr, however, gave Theotecnus the following answer, saying: "First, I ask this grace of my Lord Jesus Christ—whom you just now contemptuously called a common man—that I might refute the error of your gods and briefly set before your eyes the wonder-works and mysteries of my Lord Jesus Christ's incarnation <note>The Christian doctrine of God becoming human in the person of Jesus</note>. It is necessary, Theotecnus, that I prove my faith through deeds, words, and many witnesses. As for the affairs of your gods, one cannot speak of them without shame; yet I will say something to your disgrace. The one you call Jupiter and consider the highest among all the gods has instigated such things, to the disgrace of all women and boys, that one must consider him the beginning and end of all evil. For Orpheus <note>An ancient Greek legendary figure and poet</note> promises you that Jupiter killed Saturn, his own father, and took his own mother, Rhea, as his wife, by whom he fathered Persephone, whom he also loved in an impure way. Furthermore, he slept with his sister Juno; just as Apollo violated his sister Diana before the altar on the island of Delos. Likewise, Mars with Venus, and Vulcan with Minerva—their own biological sisters—played the unchaste lecher. Look there, oh Governor <term>Landpfleger</term> <note>A historical German term for a regional administrator or governor</note>, what shameful beasts <note>original: "Schand-Böcke," literally 'shame-goats' or lechers</note> your supposed gods are! Would not the laws heavily punish anyone who did such things? Yet you still boast of your gods' indecency and are not ashamed to worship such corrupters of boys, adulterers, and sorcerers. Your own poets have boastfully sung such things of them."

## Chapter 26.

Indeed, he himself jumped down from his throne in a frenzy and wanted to lay hands on the saint himself to torture him. # Chapter 27.

->Further continuation of the most cruel martyrdom.<-

By now, not a single cruel instrument of torture was left untried: no fire, no iron, no hooks. Men rushed at him from all sides and stripped the clothes from his body, then hoisted the man up on a gallows-block. They divided themselves into groups and tore at his flesh with hooks on both sides as much as each was able, sparing no effort. But the martyr looked at his tormentors with a joyful and laughing face and endured the most agonizing torture completely undisturbed; in this, he neither contorted his face nor sought to ward off the cruelty of the tyrant <note>original: (*). The original text notes that while other prisoners might beg for mercy, Theodotus remained defiant</note>. For he had our **Lord Jesus Christ** as his helper until the tormentors grew weary. Indeed, when one group became exhausted, others relieved them; but the invincible champion presented his body to the tormentors as if it belonged to someone else, and fixed his spirit firmly upon the Lord of all mankind. 

Then Theotecnus <note>The Roman governor of Galatia, known for his cruelty toward Christians</note> ordered the strongest vinegar to be poured into the torn sides and burning torches to be held beneath them. When the saint shuddered slightly because of the vinegar and wrinkled his nose a little at the foul smell of his burning flesh, Theotecnus leaped down from his throne in haste and said: "Where now, O Theodotus, is the pride of your words? For I see that the torture has overcome you and you lie defeated. Had you not blasphemed the gods, but chosen to worship the strength of their power, these torments would not have befallen you. I would advise you—since you are an innkeeper <note>Theodotus was a prominent innkeeper in Ancyra who used his business to provide a secret sanctuary and burial services for persecuted Christians</note> and of low station—that you should no longer speak such words against the Emperor, who holds power over your life!" 

The martyr answered him, saying: "Do not let it move you, O Governor <term>Landpfleger: a high-ranking Roman administrative official or prefect</term>, that I wrinkled my nose at the smell of my burning flesh. Rather, command your servants to continue carrying out your will; for I notice they are becoming somewhat sluggish in their work. As for you, devise new tortures!"

## Chapter 28.
### He is brought into the dungeon and teaches the people along the way.

Finally, the Governor ordered the exhausted henchmen to take him down from the **torture block** and bring him into the dungeon until another hearing. But as he himself was led across the middle of the marketplace, his body entirely flayed and showing the victory in his wounds, he invited the citizens who came running to recognize the omnipotence of Christ in what he had suffered. "See," he said, "everyone, how wonderful the power of Christ is; and in what manner He grants <term>insensibility</term> <note>original: "Unempfindlichkeit" — a common theme in martyr literature where the saint is supernaturally shielded from the sensation of pain</note> to those who let themselves be tortured for His sake, and makes bodily weakness stronger than fire; also that the lowliest of men hold the Emperors with all their power in low regard, as well as the Imperial commands which are issued against godliness. And indeed, the Lord over all grants such grace to everyone, without respect of person, to the ignoble and the noble, to slaves and the free, likewise even to the barbarians!" Thus he spoke, and showed the wounds and welts he had received, saying further: it is fitting for those who believe in Christ to bring such sacrifices to Him as I have brought; since He Himself first suffered thus for every one of us.

# Chapter 31.
## He is sentenced to death and beheaded.

Finally, when Theotecnus saw that he was no longer capable of devising enough new tortures, and that the utterly exhausted torturers were unable to accomplish anything further; while on the other hand, the martyr was only further strengthened in his resolve, he then passed the death sentence upon him and spoke: 

> We command by our authority that Theodotus—the defender of the <term>Galileans</term> <note>A derogatory term used by Roman authorities for Christians to imply they were merely a localized, provincial sect.</note> and enemy of the gods, who would not obey the commands of the invincible Emperors and furthermore despised me—be brought from life to death by the sword; then his beheaded body shall be burned with fire, so that the Christians may not take it and bury it. 

After the sentence was passed, the martyr went out with the whole multitude of men and women who wished to witness the end. When they arrived at the place, the martyr prayed in the following manner:

> O **Lord Jesus Christ**, you Creator of Heaven and Earth, who does not forsake those who hope in you; I thank you that you have deemed me worthy to be a citizen of your heavenly city, and a companion of your kingdom! I thank you that you have granted me your grace to overcome the dragon <note>A symbolic reference to the Devil or the pagan Roman state, drawing on imagery from the Book of Revelation.</note> and to crush his head. Give your servants rest, and still the violence of the enemies through me! Give your congregation peace, and rescue her from the tyranny of the devil!

When he had spoken the "Amen" at the end of the prayer, he turned around and saw the brothers weeping, to whom he spoke:

> Do not mourn, dear brothers, but rather glorify our **Lord Jesus Christ**, who helped me finish my course and overcome the enemy; henceforth I will joyfully pray to **God** for you in heaven!

When he had said this, he received the stroke of the sword with joy.

Upon this the priest spoke: "I have truly made a mistake in not bringing an interpreter with me to explain your speech; for I understand nothing of all that you have said thus far; what sort of women those are who were stolen from the lake, and who the man of bronze might be whom you say you must guard? Or do you speak in riddles to mock my peasant simplicity?" **Metrodorus** intended to answer him, but another, who was named **Glaucentius** <margin>Glaucentius, the sharp-sighted one.</margin> anticipated him and spoke: "O guest, let nothing strange that my companions have told you surprise you: For in speaking of a man of bronze, they have not spared the truth; whether they call him bronze or iron, we know that he was better and more durable than ore and iron and than all nature: Seeing that ore and iron yield to fire and are shaped by art, indeed even the diamond is overcome by art and understanding...

Seven virgins who were drowned <note>original: "ersticket," literally suffocated or smothered; here referring to the drowning in the lake mentioned previously.</note> in this [place], and by command were to remain underwater, he secretly took away and buried. After he had been beaten and had endured every kind of martyrdom, one could not see that he had suffered anything, just as he himself assured us with his own words; he mocked his tormentors and laughed at them as if they were fallen ones, and addressed the President as a wretched man. 

When his tormentors grew weary, he seemed to be strengthened by the plagues and sang songs until he was finally beheaded and burned by command. We unfortunates now must be afraid once again on his account. ### Chapter 35.
->As the guards became drunk and fell asleep, Fronto carries away the holy body.<-

When Fronto realized that this was the holy **Theodotus**, he thanked God and prayed that His goodness would be with him in taking the body away. Out of joy, however, he gave them more and more wine and urged them to drink quite merrily <note>original: "(*)". See the explanatory note at the bottom regarding the spiritual interpretation of this intoxication.</note> until they were drunk and overcome by sleep. Then the priest stood up and took away the venerable body, placed it upon his she-ass, and said: "Well then, dear martyr, fulfill now what you promised me!" <note>Theodotus had previously promised Fronto that he would provide him with relics for a church in Malum.</note> At the same time, he placed the ring on his finger; afterward, he rearranged the brushwood and hay, just as it had previously lain upon the Saint, so that the guards would not suspect anything had been taken from beneath it. 

When morning had come, the priest stood up and searched for the she-ass as if he had lost her; he also made a great deal of noise, clapping his hands, weeping, and saying: "I have lost my she-ass!" Thus the guards believed he was truly in earnest and did not know what had happened; for they believed the holy body still lay under the hay. The she-ass, however, was led away by an angel and reached Malum <note>A village near Ancyra (modern Ankara) where Fronto served as priest.</note> by backroads, lying down with her burden at the very spot where the prayer chapel of the glorious martyr **Theodotus** now stands. 

Then some people came from the village and announced to the priest that the she-ass had brought the holy remains all by herself and had stopped at the aforementioned place. So the priest, who was lamenting the loss of the she-ass, returned to Malum; the guards, however, remained at their post, believing the body still lay under the hay. In this way, the relics of the glorious martyr came to Malum through God’s wondrous providence, which glorified the martyr’s struggle.

# 49. St. Procopius. <note>This Procopius was already briefly mentioned as a martyr among the Palestinian martyrs on page 332, chapter 1; here the account is presumably expanded by Eusebius himself.</note>
## at Caesarea / In the Year 303.
### Chapter 1.
->The Chaste Conduct of Procopius from his Youth.<-

The first of the martyrs who suffered in Palestine (during the Diocletian persecution <note>The Diocletian Persecution (303–313 AD) was the Roman Empire's last and most severe persecution of Christians.</note>) was **Procopius**, a man of heavenly grace. Even before his death as a martyr, he led his life in such a way that from his youth upward, he always applied himself to chastity and a virtuous walk. He wasted away his body to such an extent that he almost resembled a corpse; but he strengthened his soul with Divine words so thoroughly that even the body was refreshed and strengthened by them. His food and drink were bread and water; he used this nourishment alone, and even then only every second or third day; indeed, sometimes he did not eat before the end of an entire week. The contemplation of holy discourses had so completely taken possession of his mind that he persisted in them untiringly night and day. His example of kindness and gentleness was such as if he were the

## Chapter 2.
->Procopius's Confession and Execution.<-

Now, as he and his companions traveled from Scythopolis toward Caesarea for the sake of business, he was stopped at the gate and led straight to the governor. But he testified with a clear voice: There are not many gods, but only one Creator and Master-Builder of all. The judge, however, found himself moved by the weight of such words and wounded in his conscience, and gave his answer a secret approval; thus he began to speak of something else and requested that he should then sacrifice in honor of the Emperors. But the holy martyr of God dismissed him also with this, and spoke a verse from the pagan poet Homer—who was naturally blind to spiritual truth—saying:

> Many lords must not be in the government;
> One ruler is enough; let one King reign alone!

->Or:<-

> To serve many lords is too difficult;
> Better is one King and one Lord!

After the judge heard this word, he interpreted it as if he wanted to overthrow the reign of the four simultaneously elected Emperors <note>This refers to the Tetrarchy, the Roman system where power was divided among four rulers: two senior emperors (Augusti) and two juniors (Caesars).</note>, and condemned him to death. Thus the blessed man was beheaded, and attained in a short time the entrance into the Heavenly Life; this occurred on the eighth of June, in the first year of the persecution raised against us, in the year 303. This was the first martyrdom history in Caesarea at that time—

# 50. St. Felix / Bishop of Tubiza in Africa / Martyred at Venosa in Apulia / Year 303.

## Chapter 1.

->An imperial command is issued that the books of the Christians should be burned; subsequently, Aper, Cyrus, and Vitalis are taken prisoner.<-

When the Emperors Diocletian for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh time were consuls <note>The German text uses "Bürgermester" (burgomasters), but in the context of the Roman Empire, this refers to the office of Consul</note>, an imperial command went forth across the entire (Roman) world, and it was made known to all governors and authorities in the provinces and cities in every place that they should demand the Divine books <note>meaning the Holy Scriptures</note> from the hands of the bishops and priests. At that time, a copy of this command was posted in the city of Tubiza <note>Thibiuca, located in modern-day Tunisia</note> on the 5th of June (Year 303). Then the official Magnilianus commanded that the elders of the Christian people should be brought before him! But on that very same day, Bishop Felix had traveled to Carthage; therefore, Aper the priest, and Cyrus and Vitalis the readers <term>Reader: a minor clerical office in the early church responsible for reading the scriptures during liturgy</term>, had to appear; to whom Magnilianus the official spoke: "Do you have Divine books?" Aper answered: "Yes, we have some!" The official Magnilianus spoke: "Hand them over to be burned." Then Aper gave as an answer: "Our bishop has them with him." The official Magnilianus spoke: "Where is he?" Aper answered: "I do not know!" Magnilianus the official spoke: "You must then remain in custody until you have given an account to the governor Anullinus <note>original: "Anulio"</note>."

## Chapter 2.

->Bishop Felix refuses to hand over the books.<-

On the following day, however, Bishop Felix came back to Tubiza from Carthage. Then the official <meta>catchword: official (Amt)</meta>

History of Martyrdom / In the Year 303.

# 51. St. Romanus. (*)
## at Antioch / In the Year 303.
### Chapter 1.

->Romanus comes to Antioch and, out of Divine zeal, appears before the judge, who tortures him in vain.<-

In the city of Antioch, Romanus became a martyr. He had come there from another place (namely Caesarea). When he saw that the city was full of unrest and that many warriors of the church <note>a metaphorical term for faithful Christians standing firm in their belief</note> had already fallen away, he would not grant the Devil the victory. Instead, he stepped before the judge, who was rejoicing over those he had defeated, and like a hero who had laid hold of the kingdom of heaven with force <note>original: "Gewalt angetahn hatte," a reference to Matthew 11:12, suggesting a vigorous and determined faith</note>, he called out to him boldly and said: "You shall not go from here so joyfully; for God still has His warriors who cannot be overcome." The judge Asclepiades (drunk on the victory over those he had defeated, and who judged the steadfastness of this saint based on the weakness of the others) ordered that he be brought forward! For it was not fitting that the Lord Jesus should be without a victor at this time as well. Once he was brought forward, the judge tried all kinds of torture on him, inflicting as much on this single conqueror as he had on all those who had been defeated. For he did not want to be robbed of all his victories by this one man's triumph, considering that on the fields of battle, victory is judged by the end; and if this man should keep the victory, then the previous ones were not yet truly defeated. Therefore, he ordered all types of torment to be tried on him. For he wanted to bend this young man by force, threatening him with his eyes, gnashing his teeth, and even lending his own hands to the executioners; he even leaped down from his judge’s seat in rage. But the executioners grew weary before the martyr yielded, and the iron tools grew blunt; nevertheless, he preferred to be torn apart rather than fall away from the faith.

51. St. Romanus.

## Chapter 2.
### The Remarkable Account of a Child's Martyrdom.

**I**n the meantime, the martyr **Romanus** confessed the one **GOD** and Creator of heaven and earth, and testified that He had revealed Himself in the person of **JESUS** Christ for the destruction of all idolatry, the abominations of which he exposed before the judge **Asclepiades** and all the people. Finally, he appealed to the judgment of simple children, who as yet knew neither left nor right <note>a biblical idiom for innocence or lack of moral discernment, see Jonah 4:11</note>, testifying that by nature they recognized one **GOD**, but not many gods. "Give me as a judge," he said, "a boy of about seven years of age, who is still impartial and hates no one; see what he will say to this." The judge **Asclepiades** accepted this and had a mother’s child taken from her arms from among the crowd of spectators, who had barely been weaned from milk; he placed the child on the torture scaffold before the martyr and said: "Ask this child now; whatever he answers, that we shall follow." 

**Romanus** immediately spoke with joy to the little boy: "Tell me, my little son, what is true and right: to worship one Christ, and in Him the Father as the true **GOD**, or to honor a thousand idol-images as gods?" The child smiled and replied without delay: "Men must have but one single **GOD**, and since Christ is that very one, then Christ is also the true, only **GOD**; we children do not even believe in many gods." At this, the tyrant was horrified and utterly shamed; nevertheless, for the sake of avoiding further disgrace, he suppressed his anger against the child and asked who had taught him such things. The child answered: "My mother taught me, and the **GOD** of my mother; she has it from the Holy Spirit, and I have sucked Christ in from her <note>This refers to the common hagiographic motif of "nursing" faith from a mother's milk</note>." 

The judge **Asclepiades** cried out that the mother herself should come forward and witness the end of her ill-instructed child. "It would be a shame," he said, "that a woman should defeat us; but we will not kill her; rather, she shall have more heartache if she is forced to watch her child’s painful death." Thereupon he ordered the little one to be stretched on the rack <term>Peinige-Block: a torture device used for binding and stretching victims</term> and to be struck sharply on the loins with hands; when this was done, his clothes were stripped off, and he was scourged with rods until the blood ran down, so that even the executioners' assistants and the spectators wept over it. But the mother stood and watched cheerfully with a bright countenance, until the child began to call out and o-

It might have been that some Jews or other people said: "Where is their **God** now?" <note>A common taunt in martyrologies, echoing the mockery of Christ on the cross.</note> referencing those three men in the fiery furnace, and boastfully testifying and saying: "Among us, those were wonderfully rescued from the flame of the burning furnace, but these must burn." <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the biblical Book of Daniel.</note> For which reason the **Lord** of Heaven commanded this time that the clouds should crown and glorify the sky; for a mighty hail and torrential rain fell down from the clouds under a powerful wind, through which the fire was extinguished, and a greater miracle occurred than formerly in **Babylon**; because those three companions were indeed rescued out of the flame, but here the flame would not even burn. ->The martyr’s tongue is cut out.<-

The judge **Asclepiades**, however, flattered the tyrannical Emperor, because his will and purpose were ungodly—an atheist who did not wish to flatter in vain; thus he devised heaven knows what against the holy man, and added one wonder to another. <note>In this context, "adding wonder to wonder" refers to the judge forcing a new trial to see if God would perform another miracle, or perhaps a cynical attempt to overcome the previous miracle.</note> What did he do then? # 51. St. Romanus

...a new trial befell him. For when the judge’s order was issued that the martyr’s tongue should be cut out, and it was found that a certain surgeon happened to have his knives with him, the man was forced against his own will to cut out the martyr’s tongue. This he did, and he tucked the severed piece away and took it home with him, according to the superstitious custom of the weak; the faithful, however, hold the remains of the martyrs in honor alone. Now, the **Doctors** <note>original: *Medici*</note> admit, and nature teaches us, that the tongue is paralyzed from that moment on if even a small part of it is cut, bringing with it the danger of death. Yet the martyr of Christ had to be delivered from death a second time. If, therefore, the Jews present three men to us <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel.</note>, we present in contrast three miracles in this one man. Two we have already: first, that the flame could not even become a flame; and second, the preservation of life after the tongue was cut out, which is indeed against nature, but not against grace. But where is the third miracle of this martyr of Christ? **Romanus** was led into the dungeon; such "mercy" did the tyrannical judge show to one who no longer possessed a physical tongue. We read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit divided the tongues of the Apostles as if they were fiery; this we have not seen, but we have heard it and believe it. But of what I am about to say now, there are many eyewitnesses present.

### Chapter 6.

->Romanus still speaks without a physical tongue.<-

It is said that when this blessed **Romanus** still possessed his fleshly tongue, he spoke like **Moses**, namely stammering and with difficulty. Therefore, while he still had his whole tongue and could not speak well, he was called a stammerer. But now, as he was about to enter the dungeon and the jailer asked him what his name was—which is already difficult to pronounce for those who do not lisp because of the initial letter R—he gave a pure answer with the tongue of the Spirit: **"I am called Romanus; call me Romanus"** <note>original Latin: *Romanus dicor; Romanus sprich zu mir*</note> (*). This was reported once again to the judge in the presence of the tyrant **Galerius Maximianus**. At this, the surgeon, who

### Chapter 7.

->The surgeon cuts the tongue from another wrongdoer, who dies from the act.<-

When the surgeon was now hard-pressed, something occurred by which one may recognize how salutary even a small stirring of the heart toward devotion may be. For the little piece of the tongue, which he had simply taken with him as a treasure, now had to bear fruit for his faith. Namely, when the judge raged against him and threatened him with death, the surgeon spoke to him: "I still have the little piece of the tongue; let another man be brought forward to whom God does not grant aid, and let me cut just as much of the tongue from him. If he remains alive, then I have deceived you, and this is not God's work." Accordingly, a wrongdoer who had been sentenced to death was brought forward, and after a diligent measurement of the size of the piece, his tongue was also cut just as far. As soon as that cut was performed, his life was at an end, for he died immediately; but God’s light shone all the more brightly from this dark comparison. But if someone is weak and unbelieving, we can nevertheless place this miracle before the eyes of the unbelievers; for certainly the Church is not yet so poor in God's grace (*). <note>original: *Euseb. Caes. L. 2. de Resurrect. Ruin. p. 358.* — This refers to the writings of Eusebius of Caesarea, "On the Resurrection," found in Ruinart's collection of martyr acts.</note>

# 52. St. Afra / Hilaria / Digna / Eunomia and Eutropia / at Augsburg. Year 303

## Chapter 1.

->Afra, a repentant sinner, is brought to trial for the sake of the Christian name.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter A at the start of the first paragraph, featuring stylized floral and leaf flourishes within a rectangular border.</image-desc>When a heavy persecution of Christians arose in the land of Raetia <note>A Roman province that included parts of modern-day Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.</note> or Bavaria, and all were afflicted with various tortures for the sake of the name of Christ and forced to offer sacrifices; it happened at Augsburg that Afra—who was notorious for having been a common public prostitute <note>original: "l. v. Hure"; likely an abbreviation for *landverrufene* (notorious) or *leichtfertige* (loose/frivolous).</note> before her repentance—was taken captive by the persecutors. When she now stood before the judge, and the judge asked for her name and learned who she was, he spoke to her: "Sacrifice to the gods, for it is better for you to live longer than to perish under torture." Afra answered him: "I have enough sins upon my neck <note>A German idiom meaning she is already heavily burdened with past misdeeds.</note>, which I committed in ignorance against God; therefore, I will never consider doing what you command me." The judge Gaius spoke: "Step forward to the high altar and sacrifice." Afra replied: "My high altar is Christ, whom I have before my eyes; to Him I daily confess my committed vices and my sins; and because I am unworthy to bring Him an offering, I wish to become an offering myself for the sake of His name, so that the body in which I have sinned may be washed after enduring punishment." The judge Gaius spoke: "As I hear, you have been a prostitute; just sacrifice, for you are far removed from the God of the Christians." Afra replied: "My Lord Jesus Christ said that He came down from heaven for the sake of sinners; and His Gospels testify that a prostitute wet His feet with her tears and obtained forgiveness; so too He did not despise the prostitutes and tax collectors <note>Refers to the biblical accounts of the woman in Luke 7 and the calling of Matthew.</note>, with whom He even ate."
