## Chapter 2.

->Her further penitent confession and martyrdom.<-

The judge spoke: "Offer sacrifice, so that you may be loved again by your paramours <note>The German word 'Buhler' refers to illicit lovers or suitors, reminding the reader of Afra's former life as a public prostitute.</note>, just as you have always been loved by them; then they will bring you much money." *Afra* answered: "I will never again accept such cursed money; for whatever I once had, I have thrown away as filth <note>original: 'Koht'; literally dung or excrement, signifying her total revulsion toward her past earnings.</note>, because it was not earned with a good conscience. Therefore, even my poor fellow-brothers <note>Likely referring to the Christian community or the poor of the city.</note> did not want to accept it from me, though I pleaded with them and begged that they might deign to take something from me and pray for my sins. Since I have thrown away that which I had, how could it be possible for me to seek to regain it, since I have cast it off as filth?" The judge *Gaius* spoke: "*Christ* no longer cares for you; you call him your God in vain, for he does not recognize you as one of his own; for a harlot may not call herself a Christian." *Afra* answered: "I am indeed not worthy to be called a Christian, but the mercy of God—who judges not according to our worthiness but according to his goodness—has granted me this name." The judge *Gaius* spoke: "How do you know that he gave you this name?" *Afra* answered: "I know it by this: that I am not cast out from the face of God, because it is granted to me now to gloriously confess his holy name, through which I hope to obtain the forgiveness of all my sins." The judge spoke: "Those are fables; rather, sacrifice to the gods, so that you may be saved." *Afra* answered: "My salvation is *Christ*, who, as he hung on the cross, promised the treasures of paradise to the penitent thief." The judge *Gaius* spoke: "Sacrifice, so that I do not have you beaten with leather scourges in the sight of your paramours, who lived shamefully with you." *Afra* answered: "I am ashamed of nothing, except for my sins (*)." The judge spoke: "Sacrifice now to the gods, for it is a shame to me to argue with you for so many hours; if you will not, then you must die." *Afra* gave as her answer: "This is what I desire, if only I were worthy that I [should die for Him]..."

# Chapter 3.

->Her Death Sentence and Burning Alive.<-

Then the most godless judge passed the death sentence, and spoke: "Afra, the public harlot, who has confessed herself to be a Christian, and would take no part in the sacrifices, shall be burned alive!" So the bailiffs dragged her away and led her to an island in the Lech river <note>The Lech is a major river in Bavaria; the island mentioned is traditionally located near Augsburg.</note>, where she was stripped and bound to a stake. But she raised her eyes toward heaven, prayed with tears, and spoke: "O Lord almighty God Jesus Christ, you who did not come to call the righteous to repentance, but sinners; whose promise is true and certain, since you have graciously said that in whatever hour the sinner would turn from his sins, you would no longer remember his sins; receive at this hour of my suffering my repentance, and deliver me through this temporal fire which is prepared for my body, from the eternal fire that burns through soul and body alike!" When she had finished this prayer and was surrounded with firewood and brushwood, she was heard to pray thus even in the midst of the fire: "I thank you, my Lord Jesus Christ, that you have deemed me worthy to become a sacrifice for your name, you who alone became a sacrifice on the cross for the whole world, the righteous for the unrighteous, the good for the evil, the blessed for the cursed, the one pure from sin for all sinners; to you I bring my sacrifice, you who live and reign with the Father and Holy Spirit, true God, forever and ever! Amen." Having said this, she gave up the ghost.

# Chapter 4.

->Her Mother and Maids are Suffocated in her Tomb.<-

But when the blessed martyr of Christ, Afra, had entered into heavenly joy through the palms of martyrdom <note>The palm branch is a traditional symbol of victory over death in Christian art.</note>, there stood on the riverbank Digna, Eunomia, and Eutropia, who had been her maids and had likewise lived in sin with her...

The soldiers went there to them and began first to persuade them with flattering words, followed thereafter by hard threats. But when they saw that they all together despised the sacrifices, they filled the monument with brushwood and dry thorns, and closed the cave with them, set it on fire, and went away. 

In such a manner it happened, after Afra had been buried, that also her mother Hilaria, as well as her maids according to the flesh <note>The term 'Dirnen' here refers to young maidservants, though it carries a double meaning referring to their former life with Afra before their shared conversion.</note> but sisters in Christ—Digna, Eutropia, and Eunomia—attained the martyr's crown at the same time. For they had believed in Jesus Christ with one mind, and therefore also reached Him with equal martyr's palms; He who reigns together with the Father and Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

# 53. St. Anysia.
## of Thessaloniki. Year 303.
### The 1st Chapter.

->Saint Anysia is murdered on her way to church.<-

---

At that time, while the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian raged fiercely, it happened that Saint Anysia wished to go to the congregation for the service of the Lord (*); however, the Angel of the Lord called her to the state of martyrdom. As she was now passing through the Cassandrian Gate <note>A major gate in the city walls of ancient Thessaloniki.</note>, a commotion arose among the people. Thereupon, one of the Emperor's guards saw her; he was inflamed by her beauty, or rather incited by the Devil himself, so that he stood before her and said: "Stop, and tell me where you are going." 

When she saw his insolence and lack of restraint, and considered the temptation, she made the sign of the cross on her forehead with her finger. But he, who was quite beastly—indeed, more like a beast than a man—showed no respect for her serious and modest silence. Instead, he felt insulted and despised by it; for that reason, he seized her roughly and asked with a harsh voice who she was and where she was going. 

The little lamb of Christ, who wished to hide her face from him, thought to dismiss him with a short, good answer, and said: "I am a servant of Christ and am going to the congregation." At this he became even bolder and, driven by the evil spirit dwelling within him, said to her: "I will not let you go there, but will take you with me to sacrifice to the gods; for today we celebrate the Festival of the Sun <note original: "Sonnen-Fest">Refers to the Roman festival of Sol Invictus.</note>." 

As he said this, he tore the common veil from her head, wanting to see her face. But she resisted him bravely, rebuking him to his face, and said: "May the Lord Jesus Christ rebuke you, you devil!" At these words and the mention of the name of Christ, he was moved to a rage that he could not hide, but instead pierced her through with his drawn sword.

---

<note>(*) <note>original: "Ad Dominicum sc. corpus"</note> To the Lord's [body], that is, the body of the Lord; this is what the entire congregation was called when they held the Love Feast <note>The *Agape* feast, a communal meal shared by early Christians.</note>, according to 1 Corinthians 12:27.</note>

# 54. St. Saturninus, Dativus, and others.
## at Carthage. Year 304.

### The 1st Chapter.
-> Many martyrs resist the Imperial command to hand over the holy <-
-> scriptures and to cease their assemblies. <-

In the times of Diocletian and Maximian, the devil declared war against the Christians in the following manner: he demanded the most holy testimonies of the Lord and the Divine Scriptures to be burned; he wanted the meeting houses to be destroyed; and he forbade the holy church customs and the most sacred assemblies of the Lord. However, the army of the Lord God set itself against such a cruel command and loathed this predatory decree. They quickly seized the weapons of faith and went down to the conflict, fighting not so much against men as against the devil himself. Now, although some gave up the scriptures of the Lord and the Divine testimonies to the heathens to be burned, thus deviating from the foundation of faith <note>These individuals were historically known as "traditores," from which we get the word "traitor."</note>, very many others behaved with brave courage to preserve them, willingly shedding their blood for that cause. Since they, being filled with God, conquered and overcame the devil, they held the palms of victory in martyrdom in their hands. They also sealed the judgment against those who had surrendered the holy scriptures and against their associates—by banishing them from the fellowship of the saints—with their own blood, as martyrs. For it was not fitting that martyrs and traitors should exist together in the fellowship of God.

### The 2nd Chapter.
-> Concerning the holy martyrs at Abitina in Africa. <-

An innumerable multitude of the confessors of Christ <note>A "confessor" was someone who suffered for their faith but did not necessarily die, though many in this group eventually became martyrs.</note> then gathered from all corners to the place of conflict, and wherever each one found the enemy, there they struck camp...

### Chapter 4.
->They are led to Carthage to the governor.<-

In this city, the martyrs of Christ thus received their first welcome bonds; and as they were led from there toward Carthage, they were joyful and merry, singing songs and hymns of praise to the Lord the entire way. After they had arrived before the judgment seat of the governor of that time, Anulinus, and stood ready for the slaughter, they steadfastly and courageously repelled the attacks of the raging devil through the constancy provided by the Lord. But because the diabolical frenzy saw that it could not prevail against all the warriors of Christ at once, it challenged each one individually to the combat. I do not wish to relate the singular events of these battles in my own words so much as in the martyrs' own words; thus, the boldness of the raging enemy may be recognized in the torture and the malicious assault, and the almighty power of our Lord Christ may be praised in the enduring patience of the martyrs and in their own confession.

(*) *Dominicum* <note>original: "Dominicum"</note>—meaning the Lord’s service or work—was the name used at that time for everything belonging to the holy fellowship of Christ: the congregation itself, the church ceremonies, the Lord’s Day (Sunday), the Holy Supper <term>the Eucharist or Communion</term>, the assembly, the Bible, and the sacred scriptures. Everything concerning the Lord was called *Dominicus*. This history clearly testifies to this throughout, which is noted here to avoid any misunderstanding.

## Chapter 6.
### Thelica's further torture and testimony.

As he was praying thus, the governor said to him: “Who is the leader of your assembly along with you?” To which, while the executioner proceeded cruelly against him, he replied with a loud voice: “Saturninus the priest and all of us!” Oh, what a martyr, who gave the preference to all! For he did not place the priest above the people, but rather united the brothers with the priestly confession. Now, when the governor sought Saturninus, Thelica pointed him out; not because he wished to betray him—whom he already saw standing present and fighting alongside him against the Devil—but so that he might help him testify that he had kept the assembly fully and rightly, because he had been a priest among them. Thus, along with his voice, his blood also flowed, pleading to the Lord; and mindful of the **Gospel command** <note>A reference to Matthew 5:44, "Pray for those who persecute you"</note>, the martyr prayed even for his enemies in the midst of the most cruel torture. For under such grievous wounding, he addressed the torturers and the governor, saying: “You act unjustly, you miserable men; you act against God! O Most High God, strength...”

# Chapter 9.
## The Account of the Martyrdom of *Saturninus* along with *Dativus*.

As the harsh and savage tormentors wounded his breast in such a manner with sharp hooks according to the instructions of cruelty, *Saturninus* the priest was also summoned to the struggle; who, in consideration of the Heavenly Kingdom, recognized that his fellow martyrs had suffered only something slight and easy, and therefore he himself longed for it. For when the Governor said: "You have acted against the command of the Emperors when you gathered all these people!" He answered: "Because the work of the Lord must not be neglected!" As soon as he had said this, it was hastily commanded that he should be stretched upon the rack <term>the German 'Peinige-Block' refers to the equuleus, a wooden frame used to stretch the victim's limbs</term> along with *Dativus*. In the meantime, *Dativus* looked upon his mangled body rather than lamenting it; and as his spirit and mind hung upon the Lord, he thought nothing of the pains of the body, but only prayed to the Lord and said:

> Help me, *Christ*, I pray that you have mercy on me; preserve my soul, guard my spirit, that I may not be put to shame! I beseech you, *Christ*, give me enduring patience!

## Chapter 10.

->The Confession and Martyrdom of Saturninus and Emeritus.<-

But the priest Saturninus was splattered with the fresh blood of the martyrs and hung upon the torture rack <term>German: *Pein-Block*, a wooden frame or rack used for stretching the body and scraping the flesh with iron hooks</term>; there he was reminded to persist in the faith of those in whose blood he was already washed. When he was asked if he were the instigator and had united them all, he gave this answer: "Yes, I was present at the assembly." Then Emeritus the Reader <note>A 'Reader' (Lector) was a minor clerical rank in the early church responsible for the public reading of scripture</note> stepped forward into the struggle while the priest was still fighting, and said: "I am the instigator, in whose house the assemblies were held." The Governor, however, who had already been defeated so many times <note>Refers to the Governor's failure to break the spiritual resolve of the previous martyrs</note>, avoided the outbursts of Emeritus and turned to the priest, saying to him: "Saturninus, why have you acted against the command?" Saturninus answered: "The Lord's work <note>Original: *Des HErrn Werk*. This refers to the *Dominicum*, the forbidden celebration of the Eucharist or Lord’s Supper</note> cannot be neglected; the law demands it." The Governor spoke again: "You should not have despised the ban but rather observed it, and undertaken nothing against the Emperor's command." After waiting a long time for the martyr's answer, he urged the executioner to rage, who was not lazy in his obedience; for the henchmen fell upon the aged, priestly body and tore it in their madness in such a way that the nerves lay bare; and they devised deplorable new tortures against the priest of God. One should have seen how the hungry fury of the henchmen sated itself on his wounds, to the horror of those who watched, as the pale bones protruded through the red blood. Since the soul did not seem to have departed from the body hanging on the rack even while the executioners rested, the priest called upon the Lord, saying: "I beseech you, Christ, hear me! I thank you, O God, command that I be beheaded! I beseech you, Christ, have mercy on me! Son of God, come to my aid!" The Governor replied to this and said: "Why have you acted against the ban?" The priest gave as his answer: "The law commands it so."

## Chapter 12.
### The Martyrdom of Felix I and Felix II.

The animalistic rage of the bloody <term>Anulius</term> <note>Anulius was the Roman Proconsul of Africa who oversaw these trials during the Diocletianic Persecution in 304 AD.</note> was almost satiated and weary from the torture of the martyrs. Yet, when Felix—who by name and by his suffering could be called "blessed"—stepped forward for the struggle, and the armed army of the Lord still stood undivided and unconquered upon the truth, the tyrant lost heart. He spoke with a weak voice, slack in spirit and body: "I hope you will choose that which allows you to live, and keep the Imperial commands!" 

Thereupon the servants of the Lord and the unconquerable martyrs of Christ said, as if with one voice: "We are Christians; we can do nothing else but keep our Lord’s holy law, even unto the shedding of our blood." At these words, the tyrant was terrified and said to Felix: "I do not ask whether you are a Christian, but whether you have held an assembly, or possess holy scriptures?"

<margin>Oh, foolish and laughable question of the judge!</margin> 

"Whether you are a Christian," he says, "keep silent on that." But he adds: "Answer whether you have been in the assembly?" As if a Christian could exist without the Lord’s service, or the Lord’s service could be performed by anyone but a Christian! "Do you not know," Felix said, "that the Christian consists in the service of the Lord, and the service of the Lord in the Christian, so that one cannot exist without the other? When you hear the name 'Christian,' envision the Lord’s presence; and when you hear the 'assembly' mentioned, recognize the name." 

"Yet you shall hear it from my own mouth and be laughed at, put to shame by the following answer: We certainly hold the assembly, and we read the holy scriptures during our Lord’s service." At this answer, <term>Anulius</term> was greatly agitated and commanded that he be beaten with clubs, until he ordered him, half-dead, to be taken to the back-gathering of the martyrs in the dungeon, in order to prove his sufferings before the highest judgment seat. This Felix I was followed by another, Felix II, of the same name and confession, who also partook in the same sufferings. For he fought with equal bravery, and was—

## Chapter 13.
->The Martyrdom of Ampelius, Rogatianus, Quintus, and Felix III.<-

After these, Ampelius stepped into the fray—the sexton and faithful keeper of the Holy Scriptures. When the Governor <note>The Roman Proconsul Anulius, who presided over the trials in Carthage.</note> asked him if he had been at the assembly, he gave his answer cheerfully and confidently with a joyful voice: "I have held the assembly with the brothers, celebrated the Lord’s work, and I have the Holy Scriptures with me, but written in my heart; Christ, I praise You; hear me, Christ!" When he had said this, his back was beaten, and he was led joyfully to the brothers in the dungeon as if into the Lord’s tent. He was followed by Rogatianus, who confessed the Name of the Lord and was added to the aforementioned brothers unharmed. When Quintus came forward, he confessed the Name of the Lord excellently and gloriously; after being beaten with clubs, he was likewise thrown into the dungeon, reserved for the worthy state of martyrdom. He was followed by Maximianus, who was equal to the others in confession, similar in the struggle, and identical in the triumph of victory. After him came Felix III, the youngest, who cried out that the hope and salvation of Christians lay in performing the Lord’s work; when he too was beaten with clubs, he said: "I have performed the Lord’s service with a devout heart and gathered with the brothers because I am a Christian!" By this confession, he was found worthy to be joined with the brothers mentioned above.

"I am not asking you that," said the other, "but whether you performed your Lord’s service?" Saturninus answered: "I have performed my Lord’s service, for Christ is the Savior!" ## Chapter 16.

->The Life and History of Victoria.<-

So that the most devout female sex and the blossoming choir of holy virgins would not be deprived of the honor of such a victorious struggle, all women have been crowned through the struggle and victory of Victoria (*). For this Victoria—the holiest among women, the flower of virgins, the ornament and honor of the confessors; who was of noble descent, holy in religion, of modest character, in whom the natural virtue of clear chastity shone, and with whose physical beauty the even more beautiful faith of the spirit and holy integrity harmonized—rejoiced that she had attained these second palms of victory <note>This refers to her winning both the "palm" of virginity and the "palm" of martyrdom.</note> in the Lord’s martyrdom. Indeed, from childhood, the signs of noble chastity shone in her, and in her tender years, her chaste earnestness of spirit and worthiness for future martyrdom were already evident. Later, when her virginity reached full maturity and she was forced into marriage against her will by her parents, who gave her a bridegroom; she, to escape the "robber," <note>original: "Räuber." Early Christian hagiographies often framed unwanted suitors or husbands as "thieves" of a virgin's promised devotion to Christ.</note> let herself down secretly from above and reached the earth unhurt through the help of the wind; for she could not have suffered further for the Lord Christ had she died then for the sake of simple chastity. When she was thus delivered from the wedding torches and her parents and bridegroom were taught a lesson, she took refuge from the midst of the wedding preparations in the house of chastity and haven of modesty—namely, the Church of Christ—as a still untouched virgin, and there she preserved her God-consecra-

When Anulius heard this, he himself was driven nearly to madness, and commanded that the maiden, the holy martyr of Christ, be taken to the dungeon along with the others, where he had them all kept for the suffering of the Lord.

### Chapter 19.
#### The Miserable State of the Martyrs in the Dungeon.

After the aforementioned martyrs reached the longed-for dungeon, the confessors <term>Confessors (Bekenner): Christians who maintained their faith under interrogation and suffered for it, but were not yet put to death.</term> who had arrived there earlier united their victory-palms with them. Many other confessors from various provinces also arrived there, among whom were bishops, priests, deacons, and other ecclesiastical persons who kept the Law of the Lord and held the assembly together with the Lord’s service <note>referring to the celebration of the Eucharist or liturgy, which was illegal under the edicts of Diocletian.</note> constantly and boldly. They also preserved the Lord’s writings and the Divine Testaments from the flames and burning, and would rather offer themselves to the cruelest fire and manifold tortures in the Maccabean manner <note>A reference to the Jewish martyrs in the Books of Maccabees who famously chose death over violating their religious laws.</note> for the Divine laws. During that same somber time, while the terrible dungeon and thick darkness held the most faithful witnesses of God captive, and the God-devoted limbs were shackled with monstrously heavy chains; while hunger exhausted them, thirst tormented them, cold made them tremble, the crowd pressed against one another, and even their sides burned painfully from the recent tearing of the hooks <note>referring to the *ungulae*, iron claws used by Roman executioners to scrape the flesh of the martyrs.</note> beneath the chains and irons and other instruments of torture; there they held a council or holy assembly according to the command of the Law of God, which they had preserved for themselves and the subsequent martyrs, and they prepared heavenly decrees. For truly, the living Holy Spirit ruled the minds of the confessors through His inspiration of eternal truths and through Divine conversations.

# History of the Martyrs / Year 304.

...opposed the true religion, perverted the faith, and threw the Divine Laws into confusion; especially as Mensurius, the former Bishop of Carthage—who had stained himself with the recent surrender of the holy scriptures <note>original: "Uebergebung der heiligen Schriften." This refers to the act of being a *traditor*, one who handed over Bibles to be burned to escape Roman execution.</note>—revealed the folly of his mistake with even greater madness. For instead of asking the martyrs for forgiveness because of the burned books, he increased his crimes with even greater vices, raging against the martyrs themselves just as he had done against the Divine laws. For this man, who was more fierce than the tyrant and more cruel than the executioner, chose a fitting servant for his malice, namely his Deacon Caecilian. He stationed soldiers with scourges and whips before the door of the dungeon to prevent anyone from entering who wished to bring food and drink to the martyrs in the prison, driving them back with blows. Caecilian himself frequently beat those who came there to feed the martyrs. And for the poor, captive confessors <term>Confessors: Christians who had "confessed" their faith before a Roman judge and were imprisoned, but not yet executed.</term> sitting inside, the drinking cups intended for them were smashed before the prison door; the food was thrown to the dogs. Before the door of the martyrs' dungeon lay their holy fathers and mothers, keeping a weary watch day and night, yet they were denied a final farewell. There was a terrible wailing and a bitter lamenting of all who were there, who were prevented from devoutly embracing the martyrs and were kept back from acts of Christian love by the raging tyrant and cruel henchman Caecilian (*).

Enemies that one can see with physical eyes are now overcome by those enemies who cannot be seen with outward eyes; since even the devils themselves, who are invisible by nature, are overcome by the purest and most honorable women—full of the Holy Spirit—and delivered to the fire. Of such a kind were those three holy women who were natives of the city of *Thessalonica* <note>Thessalonica, modern-day Thessaloniki in Greece, was a major center of early Christianity and the recipient of two of Saint Paul’s epistles.</note>, a city made famous by the most holy *Paul* when he praised their faith and love, saying: In every place your faith toward God is spread abroad; *1 Thessalonians 1, v. 8.* And elsewhere: Concerning brotherly love, there is no need to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. *Chapter 4, v. 9.*

## Chapter 2.

### Saint *Agape*, *Chionia*, and *Irene* flee the persecution to the mountains and are captured.

Accordingly, when the persecution against the Christians was incited by the Emperor *Galerius Maximianus* <note>Galerius was the junior emperor (Caesar) under Diocletian and a fierce proponent of the Great Persecution against Christians starting in 303 AD.</note>, those women—who adorned themselves with virtues and were obedient to the Gospel commandments—left their fatherland, friendships, and entire fortune because of their great love for God and hope for heavenly goods. In following the deed of Father *Abraham*, and to flee the persecutors according to the command of *Christ* in *Matthew 10, v. 23*, they went up into a high mountain range where they devoted themselves to divine prayer. They brought only their bodies to the height of the mountain, but their spirit wandered in heaven. When they were seized in this place, they were led to the instigators of their persecution—the authorities—so that they might fulfill the remaining divine commandments, prove their love for *Christ* even unto death, and obtain the crown of immortality. 

One of these three, who possessed the perfection of the commandments and loved God with all her heart and her neighbor as herself—as the *Apostle* says: Love is the fulfillment of the law, *1 Timothy 1, v. 5*—was rightly called <term>Agape</term> <note>original: "Agape"; Greek for "charity" or "divine love."</note>, for that is what the Greeks call love. The second woman preserved the pure and shining radiance of her baptism, so that one could say of her that prophetic word: "Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow," *Psalm 51, v. 9*. She took her name from the snow and was called <term>Chionia</term> <note>original: "Chionia"; derived from the Greek word *chion*, meaning "snow."</note>. The third had the gift of our Savior and God within her, namely peace, and she preserved it toward everyone, as the Lord said: "My peace I give to you," *John 14, v. 27*. <insert>She was named Irene.</insert> <note>The name Irene is derived from the Greek *eirene*, meaning "peace."</note>

### Chapter 3.

->The Martyrs are brought before the President and interrogated.<-

When Dulcetius <note>Dulcetius was the Roman Governor (President) of Macedonia. The President Dulcetius said: "I command you to read it!" Then the court clerk spoke: "I will read everything to my lord in order, as it was received in writing; Cassander the War Commissioner writes thus: 'Know, my lord, that Agatho, Agape, Chionia, Irene, Casia, Philippa, and Eutychia refuse to eat what has been sacrificed to the gods; for which reason I have sent them to your Excellency!'"

Then Dulcetius the President spoke to them: "What is this madness in you, that you will not obey the devout commands of our Emperors?" To Agatho in particular, he further said: "Why, during the holy service of the gods, did you refuse to perform the sanctuary duties, as those priests do who are consecrated to the gods?" Agatho gave his answer: "Because I am a Christian!" Dulcetius replied: "Do you then still remain of this opinion today?" "Certainly!" Agatho answered. The official then spoke: "And what do you say, Agape?" She answered: "I believe in the living God, and I will not lose my good conscience." The President spoke: "And what do you say to this, Chionia?" She gave him her answer: "Because I believe in the living God, I cannot do what you say." Furthermore, the President turned to Irene and spoke: "What is your opinion? Why have you not wanted to obey the command of our most pious Emperors?" Irene answered: "For the sake of the fear of God <note>In this context, "fear" implies deep, holy reverence rather than terror.</note>." Thereupon the President spoke: "But what do you say, Casia?"

->After Irene was brought unviolated from the brothel,<-

After she had been brought by them to the public brothel according to the President’s command, not a single person—owing to the grace of the Holy Spirit which protected her—dared to approach her or attempted to do anything shameful against her. Dulcetius then summoned the holy woman <note>original: "Weibes-Bilder." Irene answered: "It is by no means audacity, but the fear of God <note>original: "GOttes-Furcht." In this context, it refers to her religious piety and loyalty to the Christian God over the Roman state.</note> in which I persevere." Dulcetius the President then spoke to her: "By your previous answer you clearly showed that you would not be obedient to the Emperor's commands; and now I see that you still persist in the same pride of your spirit; for which reason you shall receive the worthy punishment." Thus he called for paper and wrote the following judgment against her: "Inasmuch as Irene has not willed to obey the Emperor's commands, nor to offer sacrifice to the gods, and moreover still persists in the Christian state and religion, I therefore command that she, just like her two sisters before her, shall likewise be burned alive!"

### Chapter 7.
->The Burning of Saint Irene.<-

As soon as this judgment had been read aloud by the President, the soldiers seized Irene and led her to a high place where her sisters had previously suffered their martyr’s death. When they had lit a great pyre, they commanded her to climb up onto it. Thus the holy Irene sang psalms and glorified God; and therewith she threw herself upon the funeral pyre...

The judge spoke: "The Emperors have commanded that you virgins shall either sacrifice to the gods or be led into the public brothel." <note>original: "Hur-Haus." In the Roman persecution of Christians, virgins were often threatened with being sent to state-run brothels to humiliate them and break their vows of chastity.</note> Theodora answered: "I believe you are unaware that the Lord looks upon the will; for God looks upon the chaste will. The judge spoke: "Do not bring shame upon your gender, and do not put yourself into eternal disgrace; the City Provost <note>original: "Stadt-Vogt." Theodora answered: "I confess before all things the Lord Christ, who has granted me freedom and honor. He knows best how He will preserve His dove." <note>In early Christian art and writing, the "dove" was a frequent symbol for the pure soul or the Church.</note> The judge spoke: "How do you come to this error, that you believe in a crucified man? Do not imagine, once you are placed in the brothel, that He will keep you unstained; you will only be mocked by everyone for it." Theodora answered: "I believe in Christ, who suffered under Pontius Pilate; He will deliver me from the hands of my enemies and keep me unstained, I who persevere in His faith and do not deny Him."

## Chapter 2.

->After a further interrogation, during which she was beaten, she is granted three days to reconsider.<-

The judge spoke: "I have had great patience with you, you chatterbox, <note>original: "Schwätzerin." A dismissive term used by the judge to belittle Theodora’s theological arguments.</note> and have not yet had you tortured; but if you persist in your defiance, I will have you mistreated like a common slave-girl. It is my will that you carry out the command of my lords and Emperors, just as other women have done." Upon this, Theodora spoke: "I am ready to surrender my body, over which you have power; but over the soul, only God has power." The judge spoke: "Give her a hard slap across the mouth, and say to her: 'Do not be so foolish, but step forward and sacrifice to the gods.'" Theodora answered: "By the Lord, I will not sacrifice, and I do not worship evil spirits, for I have the Lord as my helper." The judge spoke: "You fool, you have forced me to cause you pain, even though you are a woman of noble appearance, and to shame you before such a great multitude of people who await your sentencing with sorrow." Theodora answered: "I am no fool in confessing the Lord; and what you call a shameful insult is to me an eternal honor and glory." The judge spoke: "I shall have patience with you no longer, but shall carry out the command of my lords and Emperors; for I have been patient only because I hoped to persuade you. Should I spare you any longer, it might appear as though I wished to oppose the Imperial command." Theodora answered: "Just as you fear and hasten to accomplish what is commanded of you, so do I also hasten not to deny my Lord, for I fear to despise the true King." The judge spoke: "Do you resist and despise the command of the eternal Emperors, and take me for a fool? See to it that you do not begin to feel the consequences! To that end, I give you three more days of grace; and I swear by the gods, if you will not consent, I will have you taken to the brothel, <note>original: "Hur-Haus." See note on page 454 regarding the Roman practice of sentencing Christian virgins to prostitution as a form of state punishment.</note> so that all women may see it and scold you for your shame." Theodora answered: "God is still the same God He has always been, who will not permit me to forsake Him; therefore, I am ready to surrender my body to you, for the three days have already passed for me. <note>Theodora implies her mind is already made up, making the waiting period redundant.</note> Do, then, what you will; yet I beg you, command that I be guarded unspotted <note>Theodora asks to be protected from sexual assault by the guards while awaiting her final sentencing.</note> until you pass the judgment!" Theodora answered: "God, who knows what is hidden, who knows all things before they happen, who has kept me unspotted until this day for the sake of His promise, He will also preserve me from the impure, evil men who are ready to disgrace the handmaid of God."

After the sentence was passed, he was beheaded, and his body was burned with fire. Thus he completed his martyrdom on the fifth of April through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and power and glory from eternity to eternity. Amen (*). # 57. St. Irenaeus / Bishop of Sirmium.
->In the Year 304.<-

### The 1st Chapter.
->The peacefulness of Irenaeus, Bishop of Sirmium.<-

During the time of the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian <note>Diocletian and Maximian were co-emperors of Rome who launched the most severe persecution of Christians in the early 4th century.</note>, when the Christians endured various struggles—in which they suffered the tortures inflicted upon them by tyrants with spirits devoted to God, thereby becoming partakers of the eternal reward—a similar thing occurred with the servant of God, Irenaeus, Bishop of the city of Sirmium (on the Save River in Hungary) <note>Sirmium was an important Roman city in the province of Pannonia; today it is Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia.</note>; whose struggle I will now tell you of, and show his victory. For indeed, according to his innate modesty and fear of God, which he proved with a righteous way of life, he worthily bore his name Irenaeus (meaning "a peaceful man"). <note>The name Irenaeus is derived from the Greek word "eirēnē," meaning peace.</note>

# 57. St. Irenaeus.

The Emperor commands, and sacrifice to the gods. The Bishop **Irenaeus** answered: Whoever sacrifices to the gods, and not to the living **GOD**, shall be rooted out. <note>This refers to the commandment in Exodus 22:20.</note> The President **Probus** <note>The "President" (Latin: Praeses) was the Roman provincial governor of Pannonia Secunda.</note> spoke: The most gracious Emperors have commanded that whoever will not sacrifice shall be tortured. **Irenaeus** answered: I am commanded to rather endure martyrdom than to sacrifice to the gods by denying the true **God**. The President **Probus** spoke: Either sacrifice, or I will have you tortured. **Irenaeus** answered: I am glad if you do so, so that I may share in my **Lord’s** suffering. The President **Probus** then ordered him to be tortured. While he was being severely martyred, the President spoke to him: What do you say now, Irenaeus? Sacrifice! **Irenaeus** answered: I sacrifice through a good confession to my **God**, to whom I have always sacrificed.

## The 3rd Chapter.
->How he was tempted by his parents and relatives.<-

<margin>Luke 12, v. 9. 2 Timothy 2, v. 12.</margin>
**A**s his parents arrived and saw him being tortured, they fell at his feet and begged him to comply and obey the Emperor’s commands; likewise, his young sons fell at his feet and embraced them, saying: Have mercy on yourself and on us, dear father! Furthermore, his mother and his wife came wailing and begged him to consider his youth! The mourning and weeping of all his relatives was upon him, the sighing of his household, the wailing of the neighbors, and the grief of good friends, who all spoke to him with a great cry: Have mercy on your young years! But as it is said, he was held by a better desire, and had the **Lord's** saying before his eyes: Whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father, who is in heaven. Accordingly, he put them all out of his sight and gave no one an answer; for he hurried to reach the hope of the high calling. **Probus** the President spoke: What do you say? Let their tears move you from your madness; have regard for your youth, and sacrifice! **Irenaeus** answered: I advise myself for eternity if I do not sacrifice. **Probus** then ordered him to be brought back to the dungeon; in which he lay for many days and suffered various torments.

# Chapter 4.

->His second interrogation and total renunciation of earthly things.<-

Once, at the hour of midnight, the President **Probus** <note>Probus was the Roman governor (Praeses) of the province of Pannonia Secunda.</note> took his seat upon the judge’s bench, and the most blessed martyr **Irenaeus** was brought forth for a second time. By saying "I have none," Irenaeus is not lying, but rather demonstrating that his spiritual commitment to Christ has superseded all earthly biological ties.</note> Thus he looked toward **God** in heaven and fixed his mind on His promises, despising all else; he thereby made it understood that he knew no one among those present except **God** alone, whom he held in his heart. **Probus** said: "At least sacrifice for their sake." **Irenaeus** answered: "My sons have **God** as their Father, whom I also have, and He can preserve them; but you, do what you are commanded." **Probus** said: "I advise you, for you are still a young man; sacrifice, so that I do not have to have you tormented!" **Irenaeus** answered: "Do what you will; you shall see how much patience the **Lord Jesus Christ** will grant me against your persecution." **Probus** said: "I must pass the death sentence upon you." **Irenaeus** said: "I will count myself happy if you do so." **Probus** then pronounced the sentence, saying: "**Irenaeus**, who would not obey the Imperial commands, shall be drowned in the river." **Irenaeus** answered: "I thought you would [inflict] many kinds <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "Quaal" indicates the next page begins with "of torment."</note>

### Chapter 5.
->**Irenaeus** is stabbed / and thrown into the water.<-

**T**hen **Probus**, enraged by the **boldness** <note>original: "Freymühtigkeit"</note> of this most blessed man, ordered that he should be executed with the sword! History of Martyrdoms / Year 304.

# 58. St. Pollio / First Reader at Cibalis.

## Year 304.

### Chapter 1.

->Montanus, Irenaeus, and Eusebius become martyrs.<-

**D**iocletian and Maximian <note>Joint Roman Emperors who initiated the "Great Persecution" against Christians in 303–304 AD.</note> had decided during their reign that they would right from the beginning either wipe out all Christians through persecution or turn them away from the faith. When this command reached Sirmium <note>An important Roman capital, now Sremska Mitrovica in modern Serbia.</note>, Governor Probus began the persecution he had been commanded to carry out by targeting the clergy. He seized the holy Elder <note>original: "Aelteſten"</note> of the congregation at Singidunum <note>Modern-day Belgrade.</note>, Montanus, who had long shone with the virtues of the Christian faith, and had him put to death. Likewise, Irenaeus, the Bishop of Sirmium—who had fought steadfastly and courageously for the faith and his entrusted flock—was also forced to seize the heavenly palms <note>The palm branch is a traditional symbol of victory and martyrdom.</note>. When he refused to acknowledge the idols and defied the godless commands, the Governor had him tortured in various ways and finally put to death in this life so that he might live eternally. But since his cruelty was not yet satisfied, he then prepared to rage through the surrounding cities.

When he came to Cibalis <note>Modern-day Vinkovci in Croatia.</note> under the pretext of public business—the city where Valentinian (*) the most Christian Emperor was born, and where in a previous persecution Eusebius, the venerable leader of that same congregation, had been killed for the sake of Christ’s name and had famously triumphed over death and the devil—it happened through the mercy of the Lord that on that very same day, Pollio, the First Reader <note>A "Reader" (Lector) was a specific clerical rank responsible for reading the Scriptures during the liturgy.</note>, whose fervor for the faith was widely known, was taken prisoner. He was brought before the Governor for interrogation by the agents of cruelty with these words: "This man is so puffed up with pride that he will not cease to blaspheme both the gods and our princes."

<note>(*) Who died around the year 373; the author of this description appears to have lived during his time.</note>

### Chapter 3.

->Pollio is finally sentenced to the fire.<-

**The** Governor **Probus** said: "What benefit does a man have if he allows himself to be killed, is deprived of this light, and loses all his bodily goods?" **Pollio** answered: "Because that eternal light is much better than this one, and the enduring goods are more lovely than the transitory ones; therefore, it is not acted wisely to prefer the fleeting things over the eternal ones." I must follow, to the best of my ability, in the footsteps of the Bishops, Elders, and all the Fathers whose teachings I have absorbed; therefore, I receive everything you wish to inflict upon me with great joy." Upon this, **Probus** pronounced the death sentence and commanded that he should be burned! So the servants of the devil dragged him away and led him a quarter-mile far from the city, where the martyr undauntedly completed his final struggle amidst praise, thanksgiving, and the glorification of **GOD**. He [God] knew beforehand of his [Pollio’s] devout suffering, as well as that of the holy Bishop of the same city, **Eusebius**, <note>Eusebius of Cibalae, a bishop who had been martyred during a previous persecution (likely under Valerian), reportedly on the same calendar day.</note> who had died many years before but on the same day, and He raised them to Heavenly Glory. As we now joyfully celebrate such a day of remembrance today, we pray to the Divine Power that He may grant us a share in their merits. This happened on the 27th of April by the command of the Emperors **Diocletian** and **Maximian**, while our **Lord Jesus Christ** reigns into the eternities of eternities. Amen. **Ruinart.** <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709) was a Benedictine scholar whose famous collection, *Acta primorum martyrum sincera*, is the likely source for this German translation.</note>

# 59. St. Euplius.
## in Catania, Sicily / Anno 304.
### Chapter 1.

->Euplius takes up the Divine Scriptures full of faith.<-

When Diocletian was Consul for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth time <note>The text uses "Bürgermeister" (Mayor/Burgomaster) to translate the Roman office of Consul, the highest elected office in the Empire.</note>, it happened on the 12th of August in the city of Catania, that Euplius the Deacon <note>original: "Diaconus"</note> was found by his pursuers reading the Gospel and teaching Christians. He was thus taken prisoner by them and led to the judge along with his book. As a crowd stood before the courtroom, he cried out: "I am a Christian, and I desire to die for the sake of the name of Christ!" ## Chapter 2.
->*Euplius* is interrogated under torture.<-

When *Diocletian* was mayor <note>original: "Bürgermeister," a term used here to translate the Roman office of Consul, the highest elected position in the Empire</note> for the ninth time and *Maximian* for the eighth time, on the 12th of *August*, *Calvisianus* the judge spoke to *Euplius*, who was lying upon the rack <note>original: "Peinige-Block," likely the "equuleus" or wooden horse used in Roman torture</note>: "What you confessed today of your own free will, what do you say of it now?" *Euplius* made the sign of the cross <note>original: "zeichnete sich," literally "marked himself"</note> on his forehead with his free hand and said: "What I said then, I say still: I am a *Christian*, and I read the Divine Scriptures." *Calvisianus* spoke: "Why did you have them with you, and why did you not surrender these writings, which the Emperors have forbidden?" *Euplius* answered: "Because I am a *Christian*, and it is not permitted for me to surrender them; it is better that I die than surrender them, for eternal life is within them. He diligently exhorted and strengthened his disciples, Severus the elder <note>original: "Aeltesten," referring to a presbyter or priest</note> and Hermes the deacon, in the doctrine, so that they might become like him not only in spirit but also in suffering; for just as they were his companions in the glorious mystery <note>the Eucharist or the ministry of the Gospel</note>, so too were they his colleagues in the confession of faith. He loved the divine commandments, and so this most venerable old man spent his life and offered himself to God as a sacrifice, to suffer in the city of Adrianople <note>Modern-day Edirne, Turkey</note>. Like an experienced and good helmsman, he had often steered the ship through the waves, sometimes resisting them and sometimes giving way, thus meeting every storm-wind like a wise master; or like an experienced charioteer, now slackening the reins, then pulling them tight, so that the horses might not stray improperly nor go too sluggishly.

## Chapter 2.
->He prepares his congregation for the upcoming persecution.<-

In like manner, the blessed Philip ruled his people with heavenly command and served them with episcopal love. But when a harsh persecution broke out, his spirit was not disturbed. When many advised him to leave the city to escape the cruel danger, he refused to retreat, teaching that one should rather desire such a fate than flee from it. He said: "Let the heavenly command be done!" Thus, he did not abandon the congregation, but strengthened all the brothers with a skillful speech to endure patiently, using among others the following words: "The prophesied time, if you can believe it, dear brothers, is approaching. The world hastens to its end. The hardened Devil is present and, with the small power given to him, will not destroy the servants of God, but only test them. The holy Feast of the Wise Men <note>original: "Weisen-Fest," referring to Epiphany</note> draws near, which gives us a reminder of glorification. Let no threats of the godless nor any martyrdom terrify you, for the Lord Christ grants His warriors the patience to endure pain and an eternal reward. I trust their entire purpose shall be frustrated."

He spoke of things to come and weighed the circumstances of their suffering very precisely: just as skilled surgeons <term>Wund-Aerzte: literally 'wound-doctors'</term> cut away rotten flesh from the sick, yet prefer to heal the healthy part with a plaster rather than iron <note>meaning they prefer gentle remedies over the "iron" of surgical knives or cauterization</note>; they remove the remaining evil so that it does not infect the healthy flesh by contact and corrupt all the limbs of the body; so that the healthy part is not harmed, the evil is cut away. Thus the holy Philip also made a distinction between the wicked and the good; the former he urged with earnestness to become better, while the latter he exhorted with friendly words not to change; thus he gave medicine to the sick and good counsel to the healthy.

# 60. St. Philip

...destroyed <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the list of idols destroyed by fire.</note> what the Ephesians had called a god, and attacked the Senate House and the temples of the city of Rome. This fire likewise burned Heliogabalus <note>Heliogabalus was a Roman Emperor (reigned 218–222) known for his controversial religious reforms; Philip likely refers here to the destruction of his idols or his own ignominious end.</note> and did not spare the Temple of Serapis <note>Serapis was a Greco-Egyptian deity; his massive temple in Alexandria, the Serapeum, was a wonder of the ancient world.</note> in Alexandria, where Serapis—along with the temple—was consumed by the flames. Who would now call upon these for help, when they could neither save themselves nor do anything at all? They are made by the very person who afterwards worships them; and if the image should burn in the morning, a cunning artist crafts another one during the night. Thus, a deity can never be lacking, so long as the artist does not run out of wood and stone. 

So it has been seen, to our mockery, that the Temple of Bacchus in Athens was burned under the pretext that Jupiter had destroyed it with his lightning. Likewise, the temple of the armed Minerva <note>original: "Minerven". Minerva was the goddess of wisdom and strategic war.</note> burned; her armored breast did her no good, and the painted appearance of her weapons could not protect her; the unfortunate goddess would have been better off at the spinning wheel <note>original: "Spinn-Rocken". A distaff used for spinning wool, used here to mock the goddess of war by suggesting she should have stuck to domestic "women's work."</note>. The oracle and the house of idols of the Delphic Apollo were first destroyed by a storm-wind and afterwards by fire; even these the fire did not wish to leave alone, despite the "aid of grace" <note>This likely sarcastically refers to the perceived divine protection the pagans expected.</note>. Thus, the righteous man is indeed tested, but the unrighteous man is punished; and the fire of wrath is not a consuming flame for the righteous, but a light.

### History of the Martyrs / Year 304.

...our sacrificial offerings to the deity! Philip answered: How can I, as a Christian, worship stones? Bassus said: It is only right and fitting to offer sacrifices to our lords. Philip answered: We are taught to obey the authorities and to yield obedience to the Emperor, but not worship. Bassus said: Then at least sacrifice to the Goddess of Fortune <note>original: "Glücks-Göttin", referring to Fortuna, the personification of luck and the fate of the city</note> of this city! See how beautiful and friendly she appears, and how gladly she admits all the people to her service! Philip answered: She may please you who honor her, but the artificial work of a man cannot draw me away from heavenly work. Bassus said: Then let yourself be moved by that beautiful and fearsome image of Hercules standing there. 

Philip answered: Oh, you miserable and pitiable people, who do not know the holy essence of the Godhead! Oh, you unfortunate ones, who transform the heavenly into earthly things, and for lack of the truth, invent and make what you worship! What are gold, silver, bronze <note>original: "Erz"</note>, iron, and lead? Do they not grow from the earth and consist of it? You do not know the divinity of Christ (*) <note>original: "Christi Numen", the divine essence of Christ</note>, which can neither be appraised, nor can the human mind grasp how great it is. 

But you ascribe power to that which a hungry or drunken artist has made; when he has diligently and hastily modeled an image, immediately a power is attributed to such a likeness, and divinity is granted to it. Your dwellings and pleasure houses are thus full of sin every day; for when wood is burned therein for domestic use, the body of your god is being burned. But how will you excuse yourself from such vice? If you say: "Such wood is not yet a god!" then I answer: "But it could have been one, had it pleased the artist." 

Nevertheless, you do not recognize the darkness in which you are stuck; a good white marble stone, once it is carved, must become a good Neptune; a beautiful piece of ivory <note>original: "Helfenbein"</note>, artistically carved, yields a Jupiter. Money-hungry artists invented this, so that a well-formed metal is worth more—not because it has more power, but because the art upon it is more highly esteemed. But everything is of the earth, which we must tread with our feet, not worship; God has given us the earth to possess, but for you, as I see, the earth gives birth to gods.

<summary>Saint Philip of Heraclea engages in a theological debate with the governor Bassus, arguing that Roman idols are merely man-made objects of wood, stone, and metal rather than true deities. He contrasts the material nature of pagan statues with the incomprehensible divinity of Christ.</summary>

[...whi]ch the Devil saw, it pained him that all should be snatched away from him through their teaching and exhortations; he therefore caused them to be brought back into the dungeon. This dungeon was near the theater <note>original: "Schau-Platz," referring to the public arena or amphitheater where games and executions were held</note> and built against its walls, so that one could come secretly from the dungeon into the enclosed theater. In this building of the theater they sat and received the multitude of those who came to them; everyone ran there with such eagerness that they did not let even the night pass without a visit. They sat daily upon the earth and kissed Philip’s feet, recognizing how much Divine Grace was within him.

# Chapter 8.

->Justinus, the successor of Bassus in office, interrogates Philip / and has him dragged.<-

While this was occurring, the President Bassus was succeeded by his annual successor, Justinus (a "Justifier" <note>The author plays on the name Justinus, derived from the Latin "justus," meaning just or righteous</note> by name, but a man of perverse spirit), who neither recognized nor feared God. This event greatly troubled the brothers; for Bassus had been more gentle and accepted reasoned arguments, because his wife had for some time been learning to serve God. But Zoilus, the city provost <term>Stadt-Vogt: a high-ranking municipal official or magistrate</term>, surrounded by a crowd of people and a guard of soldiers, commanded Philip to go with him to the new President. When he came before him, Justinus spoke: "Are you a Bishop of the Christians?" Philip answered: "I am, and I cannot deny it!" Justinus spoke: "Our lords have most graciously commanded that all Christians shall be forced to sacrifice if they will not do so willingly; but those who will not comply at all shall be tortured! Therefore, spare your old age, so that you do not find it necessary to suffer the unbearable martyrdom of these young men." Philip answered: "You observe the laws which you have received from your own kind of men out of fear of brief punishment; how much more must we obey God's command, who punishes the guilty without delay." Justinus spoke: "We must obey the Emperors." Philip answered: "I am a Christian; therefore, I cannot do what you say; you have the command to punish, not to force." Justinus spoke: "You do not yet know the torture that awaits you." Philip answered: "You may well torture, but you cannot overcome; for no one shall bring me to sacrifice." Justinus spoke: "I will have you dragged by your feet through the middle of the city; and if you remain alive, you shall [be...]"

### Chapter 9.

->The priest Severus is sought / he surrenders himself / and is judicially heard; as is Hermes once again.<-

**S**hortly thereafter, however, they ran about like raging animals and conducted a sharp house-search and kept diligent watch, so that they might find the priest **Severus**, who had hidden himself from this persecution in the most secret corners. Since they could not find him, he came forth himself by the impulse of the Holy Spirit; for he could no longer remain hidden, as the sufferings of Christ themselves summoned him. When he was led before the court, **Justinus** spoke: "Now I admonish you, do not let yourself be seduced by the senselessness <note>original: "Unsinnigkeit," referring to Philip's refusal to obey</note> that drove your teacher **Philip**, bringing the punishment for his madness upon his head; rather, obey the Emperor’s commands; spare your body; love your life, and embrace the goods of this world with joy." **Severus** answered: "I must of necessity preserve what I have learned, and eternally serve Him whom I worship." **Justinus** spoke: "Consider well in your mind all punishment and all well-being, and you will understand that sacrificing <note>Sacrificing to the Roman gods or the Emperor was the standard test used by officials to determine if a Christian would renounce their faith.</note> will be the best counsel." But when he merely heard the word 'sacrificing', he was indignant and was thus also brought into the dungeon by command of the President <term>Präsident: the Roman provincial governor or magistrate</term>. After that, they presented **Hermes** once more, to whom **Justinus** spoke: "These who have notoriously disregarded the Imperial commands, you shall soon see how I will punish them; so that you may not share in their torture, consider your own well-being, consider your children, and rescue yourself from all misfortune by sacrificing to the gods." **Hermes** answered: "You will never obtain what you desire; I have grown up in this faith; my holy teacher impressed it upon me from the cradle, and from it I cannot turn away nor deviate in any manner. Therefore, O President, tear me apart as you please, I confess Christ!" **Justinus** spoke:

### Chapter 10.

->The martyrs are brought to Adrianople / and there subjected to a<-
->painful interrogation / Philip is scourged.<-

When **Justinus** recognized his steadfast faith, he ordered him to be returned to the dungeon. For two days he commanded that they stay in a lodging within the city under guard, and he seemed to soften his ferocity slightly; however, the Devil soon fanned it into a flame once more. For he ordered that they should again be led into the dungeon, to spend seven consecutive months in the misery <note>original: "Unlust," referring here to the foul and depressing conditions of the prison</note> of the jail. After this, he had them led toward **Adrianople**. As they left the city (**Heraclea**), the brothers <note>The local Christian community</note> became very distressed, as they were to be deprived of the teaching and the presence of such a teacher. Just as small children, taken from their cradles while clinging to their dear mother's breasts, cannot be torn away without tears, so it was for these disciples. They felt they were being robbed of their spiritual nourishment and found comfort only in weeping, as they could find no better recourse. When they arrived at **Adrianople**, they were lodged with **Semporus** in the outskirts until the governor arrived. Finally, the governor arrived; on the very next day, he took his seat at the public place of judgment, called "near the baths," and ordered **Philip** to be brought before him, saying: "What have you decided by now? This delay was granted to you so that you might change your mind; therefore, offer a sacrifice if you wish to go free." **Philip** answered: "If we had gone into the dungeon where we have been until now voluntarily and not by force, you would be right to say this time was a gift to us. But since it was intended by you as punishment rather than by our own will, why do you count the time of punishment as a mercy? I stand by what I have said before: I am a Christian! I shall answer thus no matter how often you ask me. I will never surrender myself to these idols <note>original: "Götzen-Bildern," meaning the statues of Roman deities</note>; rather, I serve the eternal **God**, as I have begun to do." Then the governor commanded that he should be stripped of his clothes.

# 60. St. Philip

[...brought out]. When he was stripped down to his shirt, the Governor said: "Will you now do what we have commanded, or not?" Philip answered: "I have already testified before that I never intend to offer sacrifice." When **Justinus** heard this, he ordered him to be whipped with rods. While he endured all this with a calm spirit, and was firmly and well-grounded upon the rock of **Christ**, he even frightened those who had been ordered to carry out the punishment. It was an unbelievable miracle; for the part of the shirt which covered the modest part of his chest remained unharmed, but the part that went over his back was torn into small pieces. All his limbs were violently wounded by the hard strikes, and the blows went deep into the flesh, even to the internal organs. Nevertheless, the blessed servant of **Christ** remained of good cheer; at whose spirit and courage the judge was terrified, <margin><</margin> and he ordered him to be brought back to the dungeon. Then he summoned **Hermes**, who allowed himself to be neither frightened nor moved by the judge’s threats, nor by the exhortations of the attendants. For both the judge’s servants and other men loved him; because he had previously held an official administrative office himself, and through his kindness <note>original: "Leutseligkeit," a term implying a warm, approachable, and gracious manner toward those of lower rank</note> he had made friends of the Governor’s attendants, who on this occasion gladly wished to repay him and, as mentioned, cared for his well-being. When he had overcome and silenced them all <note>Hermes rejected their pleas to save his life by conforming to the Roman decree</note>, he had to return to the dungeon as if to his safe harbor. They thanked **Christ**, however, and told one another of their glorious victories over the Devil; they also became courageous through such a magnificent sight of suffering and received more strength for future trials. The blessed **Philip**, however, who previously had been sensitive even to a touch, felt no pain this time, being protected by the angels.

I show the Emperors my due obedience annually, and when they command just things, I submit to them; for Holy Scripture has commanded that one should give to **GOD** what is **God’s**, and to the Emperor what is the Emperor’s. Matthew 22, v. 21. In such a manner have I lived blamelessly until now; but as for the present, I must forsake worldly flatteries and prefer the heavenly to the earthly. Therefore, hear what I have said so often: **I am a Christian!** and I refuse to sacrifice to your gods. Then **Justinus** left him and addressed **Hermes** thus: "Even if old age and approaching death drive this man to despise the goodness of this light, you should sacrifice, and do not throw away your happiness." **Hermes** answered: "I will show you, O President <note>original: "Präsident," referring here to the presiding Roman governor</note>, and those present, briefly and clearly, that wretched vanity has made godliness hateful to you; for from whence does it come that falsehood persecutes truth, malice persecutes innocence, and finally one man persecutes another? What has **GOD** ever created that is equal to man? But the Devil has presumed to desecrate this Heavenly work; therefore he devised what you worship, and has made you his own bondservants through these sacrifices. For just as horses that have become unruly heed neither the bit nor the driver, but, being unrestrained and ignorant of the danger of death, often plunge down from the heights; so you have plunged yourselves into ruin through madness, neglecting the Word of **GOD**, and following the Devil’s evil schemes. This is therefore the Heavenly and true judgment: that He glorifies the good and the pious, but puts the wicked to shame; and that He grants the former a reward, and the latter a punishment. 

Thus the prophet **Zechariah** testifies and says: *The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan! Even the Lord that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee!* Zechariah 3, v. 2. We gladly let go of our short lives so that we may attain the eternal goods of the light; but you, who visit your tombs, temples, and dungeons with a monstrous clutter of clothing and bodies, and with filthy hair flying about your ears (*), seem to me not so much to [worship] your gods—

(*) In ancient times, it was a work of love to take something into safe custody in good faith, because among the Greeks and Romans there were many bond-servants <note>German: "Leib-eigene," referring to slaves or indentured servants</note> who, for the sake of safety, placed their earned wages or received gifts with others whom they could trust.

# Chapter 14.

->External Circumstances After the Burning.<-

Thus the blessed martyrs finished their lives with a glorious testimony—the happy disciples of Christ who followed in His footsteps, who granted them victory, as well as the teaching of the Apostles and martyrs who followed those Apostles, whose souls, freed from the earthly, entered into the heavenly kingdoms. The hands of the blessed Philip were found still spread out in prayer, and his body itself was transformed from an old man into a young man, and was crowned in death as well as in life, as if he were still challenging his adversary to look upon him. Likewise, the blessed Hermes still bloomed in his countenance with a pleasant redness, somewhat bluish at the ears, like a wrestler <term>Ringer: a reference to the classical metaphor of the martyr as an athlete of Christ</term> who has come from the match; as was shown to everyone after the burning <note>They were killed slowly by the heat, not burned to ashes.</note>. Then everyone thanked Divine Omnipotence, who glorifies and crowns those who hope in Him.

# Chapter 15.

->The Bodies of the Holy Martyrs are Cast into the River,<-
->Yet Fished Out Again and Interred.<-

However, the devil was not satisfied with this; instead, he drove the President Justinus into such a frenzy that he gave the order that they should sink the bodies of the saints in the river Hebrus <note>original: "Hebro", the ancient name for the Maritsa River</note> (today called Maritza); so that he might now also begrudge the burial of those whose lives he had taken through unjust persecution. After this had been done, several citizens of the city of Adrianople <note>Modern-day Edirne, Turkey</note> who feared God and saw this cruelty, took nets in hand and climbed into small boats or skiffs to see if they could be successful in fishing out the holy bodies. Their prayer was not denied them; for the corpses were pulled out with the net, unharmed. Thereupon, they hid the pleasant catch, which was dearer to them than gold and gemstones, half a mile away from the city for three days on a country estate, which in the

# 61. St. Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus.
## at Anazarbus in Cilicia / Year 304

->Introduction<-

->From the Brothers in Cilicia to the Brothers in Pisidia and Pamphylia<-

Amphilus, Marcianus, Lysias, Agathoc-
parmenon, Diodorus, Felix, Gemellus, At-
nion, Tarachus, and Orosius <note>These seem to have been the elders at Tarsus or Anazarbus.</note>; send to
Aquilo, Basso, Berullo, Timothy, and all the brothers
at Iconium, who are believers in the Truth, holy
and like-minded in Christ Jesus our Lord, our
greetings. We have undertaken to tell the history
of the martyrs in Cilicia, as we wish to be partakers 
of their bonds; and we have set out to reveal 
their deeds. Because it was then necessary that we gather 
all the writings of their confession, we have fully 
transcribed them from a man named Sebastus, 
who was a court official, for two hundred 
groschen <note>A significant sum of money, indicating the high value early Christians placed on obtaining official Roman court transcripts (acta) of the trials.</note>; therein their [deeds] are contained 
from the beginning to the end, and everything which 
God has seen fit to grant us through His most 
courageous martyrs. All of this we have sought to 
transcribe with manifold investigation for the 
glorification of our Lord Jesus Christ. We charge 
you, however, dear brothers, that you would share 
all of this with the brothers in the Lord who are 
in Pisidia and Pamphylia, so that they too may 
know what the courageous martyrs of God have done, 
so that they might praise and glorify our Lord Jesus 
Christ.

### Chapter 1.

->Tarachus is Judicially Interrogated by the Governor Maximus.<-

When Emperor Diocletian was Consul <note>original: "Bürger-meister" (Burgomaster/Mayor), here referring to the Roman political office of Consul</note> for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth time, on the 25th of March, it happened in Tarsus—the capital city of Cilicia—that the centurion <note>original: "Hauptmann" (Captain)</note> Demetrius appeared before the judgment seat of the Governor <note>original: "Präsidenten"</note> Flavianus Caius Numerianus Maximus and said: "Gracious Lord, there have been presented before your Highness at Pompeiopolis by Eurolmius and Palladius, the fiscal agents <note>original: "Fiscalen", officials managing state interests or legal prosecutions</note>, the most wicked and shameful Christians who refuse to obey the Emperors; these men stand here once again before your Illustrious judgment seat." Maximus the Governor then spoke to Tarachus: "What is your name? I must ask you first as you are the eldest and most prominent." Tarachus answered: "I am a Christian!" Maximus spoke: "Silence with this harmful confession; tell me, what is your name?" Tarachus gave as his answer: "I am a Christian!" Maximus the Governor spoke: "Strike him on the mouth, and say: Do not answer otherwise than you are asked!" Tarachus answered: "I am telling you what my name is! But if you wish to know my common name, which I received from my parents, I am called Tarachus; however, when I was still a soldier, I was called Victor." Maximus spoke: "What is your rank and status?" Tarachus answered: "I have been a soldier and am a Roman citizen by birth, born in Claudiopolis in Isauria; but since I became a Christian, I have resigned <note>original: "abgedanket" (discharged or retired from service)</note>." Maximus the Governor spoke: "You villain, you were not worthy to be a soldier; but tell me, how did you receive your discharge?" Tarachus answered: "I asked General Publio <note>original: "General Publionem"</note>, and he released me." Maximus spoke: "I pity your age; I wish to bestow gifts upon you and show you great honor, and even make you a friend of the Emperors. Come forward and sacrifice to the gods; for even the kings of the whole world do so."

### Chapter 4.

->Tarachus is painfully interrogated for the second time at Mopsuestia in Cilicia.<-

They were interrogated for the second time in the capital city of Mopsuestia <note>original: "Mopsuest"; an ancient city in Cilicia, modern-day Turkey</note>. **Flavius Cajuriannus Maximus**, the **Governor**, spoke to the herald **Demetrius**: "Call the godless, dissolute scoundrels—the **Christians**." **Demetrius**, the captain, spoke: "Lord, here they are before your face!"

**Maximus** the **Governor** spoke: "Well now, **Tarachus**! I know that you are held in honor by most people and possess the greatest wisdom; if you conduct yourself well now, do not fall back into your old mindset today, but sacrifice to the gods for the welfare of the **Emperors** <note>This likely refers to the Roman Emperors Diocletian and Maximian</note>, and you shall attain great honor."

**Tarachus** answered: "I am a **Christian**! If the **Emperors** had obtained such honor, and all those who agree with them, they would have received better understanding and been established as those made alive by the true **GOD**."

**Maximus** spoke: "Strike him on the mouth with stones, and say to him: 'Cease your folly.'"

**Tarachus** spoke: "Were I not wise, I would be just as senseless a fool as you are."

**Maximus** the **Governor** spoke: "See, your teeth are knocked out; have mercy on yourself, you wretch!"

**Tarachus** spoke: "You shall not persuade me with any piece of your argument, and even if you crushed all my limbs, I still remain constant in **Christ** who strengthens me."

**Maximus** the judge spoke: "Obey me, **Tarachus**; which is better for you? Offer the sacrifice."

**Tarachus** answered: "If I had recognized that such a thing were better for me, I would not have suffered all this."

**Maximus** spoke: "Stretch him out and scourge him with raw ox-sinews <note>A common Roman instrument of torture made from the dried tendons of cattle</note>."

But **Tarachus** answered nothing (under such torture).

**Maximus** spoke: "Strike him on the mouth and say: 'Answer!'"

**Tarachus** spoke: "My teeth are knocked out, and my jawbones as well; how then can I answer clearly?"

...arena, and there arose no small murmur on their account from the people, part of whom disparaged such unjust <margin>Text cut off: likely "conduct" or "judgment"</margin> by the judge, while others even left the arena, and all the people reviled Maximus. He, in turn, gave orders to the soldiers to watch closely who left the arena, so that he might later summon them for a judicial hearing. When the bear was released and approached them, it did them no harm; instead, it made its way to the holy Andronicus and licked his wounds, just as it is written in Scripture, Job 5:23: *The beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.* <note>The text cites Job 5:23 to show that God’s protection extends to making wild nature peaceful toward the righteous.</note> Holy Andronicus, however, placed his hand upon the bear to provoke it, hoping it might devour him and take his life; but the bear remained entirely tame toward the Saint. Then Maximus, filled with fury, ordered that they should kill the bear, so they stabbed it to death at Andronicus's feet. The High Official of Cilicia, out of precaution that the enraged Maximus might also turn on him, ordered a lioness to be brought out, which had recently been gifted to him by the High Official of Syria in Antioch. When she was released, a great fear arose among all the spectators because she roared most terribly; but as soon as she caught sight of the bodies of the Saints, she approached the blessed Tarachus and lay flat at his feet, as if she wished to humble herself before him. Tarachus, however, pulled her toward him by the hair and ears with his hand, so that she might devour him; but the lioness was like a sheep at the hand of the blessed martyr, and finally went over to holy Probus by the door (*). The cruel Maximus ordered that they should not open it for her; but the lioness seized the bars with her claws and, with a great roaring, tried to break them, whereupon the people cried out in great terror: "Open up for the lioness!"
