Then the wrathful Maximus commanded Terentianus <note>Terentianus was the official in charge of the games or the prison.</note> that he should call the masters of the games or executioners, who had to go in and stab the saints. Immediately the murder was carried out in the sight of Maximus, who gave orders to ten soldiers to mix the bodies of the holy martyrs with the bodies of the ungodly, slain gladiators, so that they might not be recognized, and to stand guard over them. But the dark evening set in (*). When this command had been executed, and the bodies—mixed together—were being watched by the soldiers, we lay near the mountain, bowed our knees, and offered our prayer to the Most High God, that it might please His kind love for mankind <note>original: "Menschen-Liebe," a translation of the Greek *philanthropia*</note> to grant us the grace to rescue the corpses of the holy martyrs from that place. We were then encouraged and went a little further down from the mountain, and saw that the guards were eating together and had built a fire to warm themselves. Thereupon we went a little further again, bowed our knees, and prayed very softly to God and His Anointed <note>original: "Gesalbten," referring to Christ</note> in the Holy Spirit, that He would show us from His high throne how we should distinguish and rescue the holy bodies from the unholy, shameful bodies! Immediately there arose a great earthquake, thunder, and lightning, and quickly a thick darkness came, which brought with it a terrifying downpour of rain. Now, after the storm subsided after a while, we prayed again and approached the bodies of the slain, finding the fire extinguished by the rain; the guards, however, had fled from it. So that we might search more closely, we boldly stepped quite near; but since we could not recognize the bodies of the saints, we spread our hands toward heaven and begged God that He would show us which were the corpses of His holy martyrs! Immediately the merciful God, according to His unfathomable mercy, let a bright star shine from heaven, and it settled upon each corpse and showed us which were the bodies of His servants. Then we joyfully carried away those corpses and reached—

# 62. Saint Crispina /
## at Thebeste in Numidia / <note>Thebeste, modern-day Tébessa in Algeria, was a significant city in the Roman province of Numidia.</note>
### Anno 304.

#### The 1st Chapter.

->Saint Crispina is judicially examined in Thebeste by the Proconsul Anulinus.<-

When **Diocletian** was Consul for the ninth time and **Maximian** for the eighth time <note>Consuls were the highest-ranking magistrates in Rome; their names were used to date the year. This refers to the year 304 AD.</note>, on the 5th of December, it occurred in the city of **Thebeste** that, in the private judicial chambers of the Proconsul **Anulinus**, the court clerk spoke in an official capacity: If you so command, **Crispina** of **Thagura** <note>Thagura was her home city, also in Numidia.</note>, who has shown contempt for the command of our Lords and Emperors, may now be heard. **Anulinus** the Governor <term>Landpfleger: a high-ranking official or Proconsul representing the Emperor's authority</term> said: Let her be brought in!

When the blessed **Crispina** had been brought forward, **Anulinus** the Governor said: Have you well understood the contents of the sacred decree? The blessed **Crispina** said: I do not know what decree that is. **Anulinus** the Governor said: That you are to sacrifice to all our gods for the welfare of the Emperors, according to the command of the pious Emperors **Diocletian**, **Maximian**, and **Constantius**. The blessed **Crispina** said: I worship my **GOD** daily; besides him, I know of no other.

**Anulinus** the Governor said: If you are stubborn and a despiser, you shall be made to taste the power of the laws. The blessed **Crispina** answered: Whatever comes upon me, I suffer gladly for the sake of the faith which I hold. **Anulinus** the Governor said: Is the foolishness of your mind so great that you cannot now let go of your superstition and worship the sacred gods? The blessed **Crispina** answered: I worship daily, but I worship my **Lord**, besides whom I know no other.

**Anulinus** the Governor said: I will place the sacred decree before you; take heed of it. The blessed **Crispina** answered: I take heed of the command, namely that of my **Lord Jesus Christ**. **Anulinus** the Governor said: You shall lose your head if you are disobedient to the commands of the Emperors, our Lords, whom you shall be forced to serve; just as all of **Africa** does so, therefore you should also not

The blessed **Crispina** answered: I have never done that since the day I was born, nor do I know how to go about it; nor shall I do it as long as I have life. **Anulinus** the Governor said: But do it nonetheless, if you wish to remain free from the severity of the laws. The blessed **Crispina** answered: What you speak of, I do not fear; it is nothing. But if I despise **GOD**, who is in heaven, then I would be a godless woman, and He would condemn me so that I could not lift up my eyes on that future day. **Anulinus** the Governor said: You are not a godless woman if you are obedient to the holy commands <note>Anulinus refers to the imperial decrees as "holy," whereas Crispina reserves that holiness for God.</note>. The blessed **Crispina** answered: What do you want? Should I perhaps be godless toward **GOD**, and not toward the Emperors? Far be it from me! **GOD** is great and almighty; He created the sea and the green plants upon the dry earth; but as for the men whom He also created, how can they help me? **Anulinus** the Governor said: Adopt the Roman religion, to which our lords the most invincible Emperors, as well as we ourselves, are devoted. The blessed **Crispina** answered: I know only of **GOD** alone; for your idols are but stones and the fabricated handiwork of men. **Anulinus** the Governor said: You speak too much blasphemy and do not take heed of your own welfare. Furthermore, the Governor **Anulinus** said to the jailer: Let her be disfigured, and shave her hair off smooth with a razor, so that her face, first and foremost, may serve as a public spectacle <note>Shaving the head of a free woman was a profound social disgrace in Roman culture, intended to strip the victim of her dignity before the public.</note>. The blessed **Crispina** answered: Let the gods themselves speak, then I will believe it. If I were not seeking my own welfare, I would not have come before your judgment seat for questioning. **Anulinus** the Governor said: Do you desire to live longer,

Just like your other companions, **Maxima**, **Donatilla**, and **Secunda** <note>These were three other famous African female martyrs from the same era, often grouped together in martyrologies.</note>. The blessed **Crispina** answered: I thank my **GOD** if I shall attain such a thing! I would only truly lose my head if I were to light incense for those gods. **Anulinus** the Governor said: Do you then persist entirely in your foolish mind? The blessed **Crispina** answered: My **GOD**, who is and has been eternally, allowed me to be born and gave me salvation through the water of holy baptism; He is with me, so that my soul shall not become godless according to your will.

## Chapter 2.
->Crispina is sentenced to death and beheaded.<-

**Anulinus** the Governor spoke: Why do we delay any longer with this godless **Crispina**? Read the acts from the court record <term>Gerichts-Protocol: the official transcript of the legal proceedings</term> once again. When these had been read, **Anulinus** the Governor gave the verdict from the writing tablet and read: **Crispina**, who persists in shameful superstition and refuses to sacrifice to our gods, shall be executed by the sword according to the heavenly decrees of the Emperors! The blessed **Crispina** answered: I thank my **GOD** Christ, and praise the Lord, who has willed to graciously deliver me from your hands. The blessed **Crispina** suffered death in Theveste <note>original: "Thebesten" – a city in Roman North Africa, modern-day Tébessa, Algeria.</note> on the 5th of December, while **Anulinus** was Governor there; there reigned our Lord **JESUS** Christ, to whom be praise, power, honor, and dominion, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for endless eternities. Amen. *Ruinart. page 449.* <note>Thierry Ruinart was a 17th-century scholar who collected authentic records of the early Christian martyrs.</note>

# 63. Saint Eulalia /
# at Merida in Spain. Year 304 <note>The original text abbreviates the year as "Aō. 30", but historical context and the previous page confirm the year 304 AD during the Diocletian persecution.</note>

## Chapter 1.

->The noble descent of Saint Eulalia, her home city, and the disposition of her youth.<-

<image-desc>Decorative floral drop cap 'D' at the start of the paragraph.</image-desc>
This holy virgin, Eulalia, was indeed of noble rank in the world, yet through her first martyr's death <note>original: "ersten Marter-Tod"</note>, she attained a much higher nobility. She was born in Merida, at that time the capital of Lusitania <term>Lusitania: a Roman province covering much of modern-day Portugal and western Spain</term> in the province of Estremadura in Spain, situated on the river Anas <note>Anas is the ancient Latin name for the Guadiana River</note> or Guadiana. There she was raised from the breast, there her bones rest, and her love is not yet extinguished. This city, where this firm virtue blossomed, lies not far from the setting of the sun, or from the great World-Sea <note>The Atlantic Ocean</note>. Although this place was already famous and very populous, it became far more renowned through the blood of this virginal martyr. She had scarcely reached her twelfth year when the President <term>Präſidente: the Roman provincial governor acting as judge</term> sentenced her to the pyre, and her gentleness terrified even the bailiffs. From her youth, she had already shown a desire to gaze toward heaven and had dedicated her chaste limbs to the Lord. While she was still young, she rejected all loud toys and took no pleasure in playing; instead, she incensed her little bed, strewed it with roses, and set aside her golden neck-jewelry. Her speech was serious, her gait honorable, and in all her manners, she conducted herself like a mature matron <note>original: "Matrone"</note>, however tender her age was.

## Chapter 2.

->She is taken to the country by her parents but escapes out of a burning desire for martyrdom.<-

<image-desc>Decorative ornate drop cap 'A' at the start of the second chapter text.</image-desc>
But when the frenzy against the servants of the Lord began, and the Christians were commanded to burn incense and to sacrifice the livers of slaughtered animals to the deadly gods, then the spirit of Saint Eulalia was ignited. Her heated mind prepared itself for the bitter struggle; the young heart, which longed for God, challenged masculine fury within her virginal breast. A

the faithful care of her parents kept this courageous daughter at home, and they retreated with her into the countryside, far removed from the city, so that the spirited maiden, out of her love for dying <note>referring to her desire for martyrdom</note>, would not put her life in danger. After she had sat in peace for a while in this manner, she became weary of these idle days and stole away at night, without anyone's knowledge, secretly through the gates. She then went through untrodden paths, over thorns and thistles—her feet indeed wounded, but continuing on in the company of angels. And although the dread-filled night was terrifying, she nonetheless had the light in her heart as a guide; just as those redeemed Israelites were illuminated by the bright pillar of fire and the way was prepared for them at night after the darkness was driven away; even so did the godly virgin walk by night as if in the bright day, and the darkness was no darkness to her, as she fled the Egyptian world <term>Egyptian world: a common Baroque metaphor for the sinful or pagan world, referencing the Israelites' flight from Egypt</term> with those others and hastened toward heaven. She hurried on with nimble feet and put many miles of road behind her before the sun showed itself at its rising.

### Chapter 3.

->She voluntarily presents herself before the judgment seat and testifies against idolatry.<-

As she reached the city of Merida at early daybreak, and the judge had seated himself upon his public judgment seat, she approached full of courage, called out loudly, and spoke to the people: "I beg you, tell me, what is this madness that plunges souls into such ruin, causing them to fall down with unrepentant hearts before carved stones of idol-images, while denying the universal God, our heavenly Father? Do you wretches seek the Christians? See, I am one such woman, and an enemy of the service of devils; I trample their idol-images under my feet and confess with heart and mouth the one God. Your gods and goddesses—*Isis*, *Apollo*, and *Venus*—are nothing; your Emperor *Maximilianus* <note>Maximian, the Roman co-emperor alongside Diocletian</note> is nothing. The former are nothing because they are the handiwork of men; the latter is nothing because he honors such human handiwork as divine. Both are vain, and on both sides, they are nothing. *Maximilianus* is indeed a lord of many goods, but he is a poor wretch who desires something from stones and debases himself before idol-images when he bows his crowned head before them and beats his otherwise brave breast. A fine prince, an excellent ruler, who feasts upon the blood of the innocent and hunts after holy bodies, their [bodies] accustomed to moderation..."

# 63. St. Eulalia

...tears out the entrails, and rejoices to root out faith and loyalty. Very well then, tormentor, burn, cut, and hack to pieces the limbs made of clay; it is no art <note>original: "Kunst"; here meaning a great feat or skill</note> to destroy a fragile thing; but know that through-piercing pains can neither ruin nor kill the soul.

### Chapter 4.

->The judge seeks to persuade her with both harsh and gentle words.<-

At this, the judge fell into a raging fury, jumped up and spoke: "Bailiff, seize her quickly, and torture her most severely; let her feel that the ancestral gods are something, and the Emperor’s command is not in vain. Yet I would gladly, maiden, if it were possible, lead you away from your malice before your execution! Behold, what joy you still have before you, when you shall be married according to your station; the tears of your grieving lineage follow you, and your noble kinsmen already sigh over you, that you should perish in the tender bloom of youth, when they stood in the near hope of wishing you joy as a bride on your wedding day. Does the golden splendor of the marriage-bed not move you, nor the devout veneration of the elders? What kind of reckless weakness is this? Do you not see the tormentors standing ready there for your miserable destruction, either to strike off your head with the sword, or to deliver you to the wild animals to tear your limbs; or to burn you with smoking torches, where you will become ash amidst piteous howling. Consider, I pray you, kind virgin, with how little effort you can escape all this? If you would only deign to touch a little salt and incense with the tips of your fingers, and scatter it upon the fire as a smoke-offering <term>smoke-offering: a ritual sacrifice (incense) to Roman gods, which functioned as a loyalty test to the Roman state</term>, then you would be freed from this heavy punishment."

### Chapter 5.

->She grows fierce in spirit and zealously opposes the idols / for which she is tortured to death.<-

The martyr answered not a word to this, but first restrained her zeal, then finally spat in the tyrant's face, overthrew the idols standing there, and kicked over the incense-censer with her foot. But the executioners’ servants did not delay; they seized her immediately and tore both her tender breasts with iron claws even to the bone; while Eulalia herself looked on...

...and said: "O Lord, your memorial is being written upon me; how healing it is to read such letters, which, my Lord Christ, are your signs of victory, bearing your holy name in the blood flowing out!" She said this without sighing or weeping, joyful and undaunted; her mind knew nothing of the cruel pain, even as the fresh blood washed her limbs as if from a newly-opened fountain spring. But the torture did not end with the bloody wounding, where her skin was torn crosswise like a grate <note>original: "Gegitter"; referring to the patterns of the iron claws used to rake the flesh</note>; instead, her breast and belly were further destroyed with burning torches. Her fragrant hair, which she had let fall down in front and behind to cover her virginal modesty, was caught by the flickering flames, which rose up to her head; but the blessed virgin sucked the fire into herself with her breath to hasten her end. Then, one saw something like a snow-white dove fly out of the virgin's mouth and toward heaven; this was the pure, innocent, and swift spirit of Saint Eulalia. After the spirit had departed, her head sank down, and the living funeral pyre of her body died out; the soulless limbs found rest, and the spiritual bird flew joyfully into the upper air. Even the executioner's assistant saw this miraculous bird fly publicly out of the virginal mouth, at which he jumped back full of terror and horror, abandoning his agonizing business; the bailiff also fled with him. Additionally, a heavy snow suddenly fell and covered the entire marketplace, along with the corpse of Saint Eulalia, in place of a linen shroud. Here the love of weeping people, who are accustomed to performing the final service for the deceased, must give way; the weeping mourning women must also stand back here, as the elements themselves, by divine command, perform the funeral rites for you, holy virgin! Her body still rests in the Vettonian <note>The Vettones were an ancient pre-Roman people of the Iberian Peninsula</note> city of Merida, where both strangers and locals still honor her ashes. <header>518 64. Saint Agnes</header>

# 64. Saint Agnes
## at Rome. Year 304.
### Chapter 1.

->The chaste Agnes rejects a noble suitor and chooses Christ as her bridegroom.<-

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut decorative initial letter 'D' featuring elaborate floral scrollwork and vine patterns.</image-desc>

The most blessed Agnes, born of a noble lineage, already in the thirteenth year of her age had conquered death and carried away life as her prize. She was indeed beautiful of countenance, but even more beautiful in her faith. When she had now left school, the son of the Prefect <note>The Roman "Urban Prefect," the highest city official</note> of the city of Rome fell in love with her. After he inquired who her parents were and found them, he began to offer great gifts and to promise many things; but the blessed Agnes regarded it all as dung <note>original: "Koht"; a common hagiographical term used to describe worldly wealth as worthless filth compared to spiritual rewards</note>, so that she might win Christ. "Depart from me," she said, "you fuel of sin, you supporter of misdeeds, you food of death! Depart from me, for I am already pledged to another lover who is far nobler than you are; he has already made a betrothal with me with the ring of faithfulness, whom the angels serve, and whose beauty the sun and moon admire. When I love him, I remain chaste; when I touch him, I remain pure; when I take him as a husband, I shall remain a virgin; and after the wedding, there shall be no lack of children, for the birth happens without pain, and daily fruitfulness increases."

When the foolish youth heard such things, he was carried away by blind love and tormented himself in his sick mind. The matter was made known to his father after the physicians <term>Medici</term> had investigated the cause of his illness; then the father repeated with a fatherly voice what the son had already attempted to do to obtain the maiden. The most blessed Agnes gave a negative answer and testified that she could never break the covenant with her bridegroom. When the Prefect said that he was nevertheless the Chief Prefect and therefore no one should be preferred before him in honor, he diligently searched to find out who her bridegroom might be, whose power Agnes so highly praised.

<summary>Thirteen-year-old Agnes of Rome rejects the marriage proposal of the Prefect's son, declaring her mystical betrothal to Christ. The Prefect, frustrated by her refusal and her claims of a superior "bridegroom," begins an investigation into her faith.</summary>

Then one of his sycophants <note>The German word "Schmarutzern" implies a parasite or a flatterer who hangs around a powerful person for personal gain.</note> stepped forward and said that she had been a Christian from her youth and was so possessed by sorcery that she claimed Christ was her bridegroom. When the President <note>In this context, the title "President" refers to Symphronius, the Urban Prefect and chief magistrate of Rome.</note> heard this, he was glad and immediately sent the guard to have her brought before his judgment seat. At first, he drew her aside and spoke to her with friendly words; but when this would not help, he threatened her with terrifying words. The virgin of Christ, however, was neither led astray by flattery nor softened by fear; instead, she remained with the same calm face and spirit, laughing in her heart at both the fear-monger and the flatterer.

When the President Symphronius saw such constancy in the young girl, he addressed her parents; but because they were of noble birth, he could not overcome them with force. Therefore, he reproached the virgin for her Christian name <note>Being a Christian was a crime against the Roman state at this time.</note> and commanded that she be presented to him again the following day. After he had several times mentioned the young man’s love for her and saw that all his persuasions were in vain, he said to her: "Choose one of two things: either sacrifice with the other virgins to the goddess Vesta <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth; her priestesses were required to remain virgins.</note> for the honor of your lineage, or become a public whore in a brothel, to the shame of your parents."

Then the blessed Agnes spoke with great steadfastness: "If you knew what kind of God mine is, you would not let such words pass from your mouth; for I have the Angel of the Lord with me as the guardian of my body." Then the senseless judge ordered her to be stripped completely naked and thus exposed to be led to the brothel; meanwhile, a crier had to walk before her and loudly announce the sentence with the words: "Agnes, the atheistic <note>Christians were often called "atheists" by Romans because they refused to acknowledge the traditional gods of the state.</note> virgin who has blasphemed the gods, is condemned to the brothel as a whore!" But as soon as she was stripped, her unbound hair, through divine grace, formed such a thick cloak around her that it seemed she was better covered by her hair than she had been before by her clothes.

<header>64. Saint Agnes</header>

### Chapter 3.

->Her chastity is preserved through a divine miracle; a violent suitor is killed because of it, whom she then restores to life.<-

When she had entered the place of shame <note>The "place of shame" refers to the Roman brothel where she was sent as punishment.</note>, she found the Angel of the Lord waiting in prayer, who provided such a very bright light and a shining garment that the house of ill-repute became a house of prayer, wherein all who entered were compelled to worship, show reverence, and honor the light. While this was happening, the aforementioned son of the President <note>The "President" refers to the Urban Prefect, Symphronius.</note> stood watching outside, seeing how the impure men entered boldly but soon came out again in great consternation; he began to mock and ridicule them as being powerless, and boldly went himself into the place where the holy virgin lay and prayed. When he saw such a light around her, he did not give honor to God but lunged at her despite the light; however, before his hand could even touch her, he fell upon his face and was strangled by the devil (*). When the President heard this, and everyone considered the virgin a sorceress, Agnes prayed for the young man, who soon after returned to life and publicly confessed that there is only one God in heaven and on earth, which is the God of the Christians. At these words, the soothsayers and temple priests were greatly horrified and incited a riot among the people even larger than before. The President, seeing such wonders himself, was terrified; but because he feared falling into Imperial disgrace if he opposed the temple priests, he handed over his authority to a Vice-President in his stead and withdrew from there in sorrow, because he could not set her free even after the rescue of his son.

### Chapter 4.

->Aspasius the Vice-President condemns her to the fire, which does not<-
->harm her; thus she is stabbed to death.<-

Then the Vice-President, named Aspasius, commanded a great fire to be lit before everyone's eyes and had her thrown into the middle of the flames; which flames, however—

This Constantia, the Emperor’s daughter, remained in virginity, and very many other virgins, of both middle-class and noble or princely standing, took up the holy virginal veil.

# 65. Saint Ferreolus
# of Vienne in France. A.

## Chapter 1.

->Ferreolus, a former military servant, <unclear>w.</unclear><-
->Judicially interrogated.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial A at the start of the paragraph.</image-desc>

As the God-pleasing race of Christians—who were, however, hated by the devil—was being [persecuted] through all lands to be torn away from [what the heathens called] shameful superstition, a man named Crispinus, acting as a Governor in the city of Vienne <note>An ancient city in southeastern France, then a major center of Roman Gaul.</note>, began upon imperial command to force the Christians to offer sacrifices. Accordingly, he had seated himself upon his judgment seat to announce the decree, along with his terrible counsel: to show honor to those who would be obedient, but to punish those who were contradictory. 

As he then raged most sharply through his mad fury against all servants of God, it happened that he also [ordered] among others the most blessed martyr Ferreolus. Although he still wore his soldier's clothing, he was no longer in active military service, because he had been betrayed as a Christian. [Crispinus] urged him to sacrifice and said to him: "It is fitting for you, Ferreolus, before all others, to obey the imperial commands, since you are bound to them with loyalty because of your military service, and owe respect to their Majesty; you are also obligated to humble obedience for further honor and promotion. Therefore, you should obey this counsel, so that in the event of your audacity, a hard punishment does not follow; you are thus commanded to sacrifice to the [gods]—why do you hesitate any longer?" 

The holy Ferreolus spoke: "I am a Christian, and I have no freedom to sacrifice to false gods. I have served the Emperors in war so long as my conscience allowed. What I [earned], so long as I obeyed you, I served for according to the fair laws; I never sought improper plunder; against the harmful, not against the Christians, have I [fought]."

New rewards of grace, of which you speak, I do not desire; let the predatory Emperor feed his predatory soldiers. <note>original: "Räuberische Kayser" — Ferreolus uses strong language here, likely referring to the Emperor Maximian, suggesting that the Roman military expansion and the seizure of Christian property was akin to robbery.</note> I do not seek the profit of this temporal life; it is enough for me if I may live as a Christian in religious freedom; but if such is not granted to me, I am ready to die.

## Chapter 2.
->His Confession against the Governor's Persuasion.<-

<margin>Year 304.</margin>
The Governor <note>original: "Präsidente" — referring to the Roman provincial governor or presiding judge.</note> said: From where, Ferreolus, do you get such a desire to die? Perhaps you have been wronged, or have been offended by the Emperors, so that you desire to end your life in full despair; but there is still a remedy for our human ills, both in what you have sinned against the gods, or how you have misbehaved in a stubborn manner against the Emperors. Only repent of your words and satisfy the laws by rejecting the sect of the Christians and by sacrificing to the gods.

Ferreolus answered: Your kindness and the forgiveness you promise may be accepted by those who wish to serve under you and your Emperors from now on; but no one harms their laws who prefers the Law of God over them. Rather, he is punishable who takes something away from the Divinity and worships unfeeling, perishable things. I worship the Creator, not the creature. <note>A common early Christian argument based on Romans 1:25, contrasting the eternal God with the physical idols made by human hands.</note> One should not seek God in the works of hands, as He Himself testifies who made everything, to which heaven and earth and all that is below and above are witnesses. Acts 7, verses 48, 49. <note>Ferreolus quotes the speech of Saint Stephen from the New Testament: "the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands."</note> All of this serves Him, and God created it for our benefit, not so that it should rule over us. You rather confuse what is right and well-ordered, by preferring the temporal to the eternal, the dead to the living, the irrational animals to reason, and lies to the truth; therefore you have also fallen into pride and are eternally damned with the malicious spirits. But God, who is Lord of all and an eternal King, has given his servants the courage to die through Jesus Christ His Son; through whom He also grants us the hope of the resurrection, so that we may firmly believe in a future eternal life instead of this perishable life.

# 66. St. Julitta and Cyricus / at Tarsus in Cilicia. Year 305.

## The Epistle of Bishop Theodore (*) of Iconium regarding the Martyrdom of Saint Julitta and her three-year-old son Cyricus.

### Chapter 1.

->*Bishop Theodore endeavors to find the true history of these martyrs in place of the falsified account.*<-

Since Your Honorable Devotion, by means of your esteemed letters, has requested of my lowly poverty to be informed of the actual circumstances of the notable and famous martyrdom of Cyricus and his mother Julitta; specifically, whether the account found in Iconium <note>Modern-day Konya, Turkey.</note>—from whence, according to rumor, the chosen Julitta and her glorious son Cyricus were born—contains the same content, seeing as it was their fatherland. This is because in the common records <term>Acten</term> <note>Official legal or ecclesiastical records of a trial or martyrdom.</note> of their martyrdom, some inflated, nonsensical words and weaknesses are found, which contain absurd things regarding Christian hope; thus, I was to write to Your Perfection whether their true history of martyrdom might be available. After I had [sought] this anointed...

(*) This author, Theodore, lived around the year 560 and, at the request of another bishop whom some call Zosimus, investigated this history of martyrdom—which was already falsified at that time—and distinguished the true circumstances from the fables, perhaps of the Manichaeans <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion that the early Church considered heretical; they often produced apocryphal texts.</note>, and thus shared a purer version.

[I have] taken up and reviewed the Acts of the martyrdom of the holy **Cyricus** and his mother **Julitta**, and after diligent reading, I found [that] you, most holy Father and proven priest, report the truth; for that addition of frogs and dragon-chatter <note>The Bishop is dismissing fantastical, legendary elements often added to martyr stories as "nonsense."</note> is rightly called idle talk, certainly invented by the **Manichaeans** <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion that the early Church viewed as a dangerous heresy.</note>, if I am not mistaken, or other perverse-minded **heretics**, who only play with and mock the great mystery of our salvation (*). After we have searched manifoldly and performed diligent investigation and could find nothing further, we inquired among the native men and most noble families of the **land** to see if one might learn something through news of **old** family documents, whereby the struggle of these holy martyrs might become more clearly revealed.

### Chapter 2.

->**Julitta**, of noble old lineage, flees with her three-year-<-
->old from **Iconium** <note>Modern Konya, Turkey.</note> to **Seleucia** as far as **Tarsus**.<-

**Marcianus** then, a devout man and Emperor **Justinian's** **Chancellor and Chief Secretary**, [who] was present there in the camps along with other official persons, as well as **Zeno**—his assessor and war counselor, a very wise man—have recounted the **following** of the holy martyrs: namely, how they heard from the noble **people** or families that the blessed **mother** **Julitta** was of the most noble blood of **Lycaonia**; whose eternal monument was honored among them not only because of her perfect life, but was also still **diligently** blessed among them because they recognized her as their **close** blood relative. This woman, because she was of princely blood, escaped by flight with two maids at the time when the persecution against the Christians broke out fiercely and **Domitian** was Governor of **Lycaonia**—a very desolate and **cruel** man who took a singular pleasure in shedding **their** blood.

But the boy looked at the President <note>The German text uses "sidenten," shorthand for "Präsidenten" (President), a title for a Roman provincial governor.</note> with staring eyes and pushed him away with his small hands; he also turned his face away from him, resisted with his hands, and scratched the President's face with his nails. And finally, like a young fledgling of the turtle-doves, the little **Cyricus** followed his mother's words and cried out: "I am a Christian!" He also kicked the judge in the ribs with his feet, as is typical of such young children when they are provoked beyond their capacity. Because of this, the wild beast <note>A common rhetorical device in martyr stories to describe cruel Roman officials.</note> flew into a rage (I cannot call someone a man who does not spare such an innocent child, nor forgives their weakness) and took the boy by the foot and hurled him down from the high seat against the ground. The little martyr’s brain and skull shattered in his confession <note>original: "Bekentniß"—in this context, it refers to a "confession of faith" made even unto death.</note> so that they flew as far as the stairs, and from the blow, everything around the judge’s chair was covered in blood. The divine child, however, surrendered his spirit into the hands of God; for the souls of the righteous are in God's hand. But when Saint **Julitta** saw this, she was overcome with joy and said: "I thank you, my God, that you have brought my son to completion before me, and have deigned to give him the unfading crown <note>The "unfading crown" is a traditional Christian symbol for the reward of martyrdom.</note> worthily!"

### Chapter 4.

->The further martyrdom and execution of Saint Julitta.<-

The deed pained even the judge himself, and he sighed over his action; yet he turned all his fury against the martyr, whom he ordered to be hoisted onto the rack <term>rack: a torture device (Peinige-Block) used to stretch the body</term> and commanded her sides to be torn with hooks; he also had her feet dripped with glowing pitch from a crucible. The court herald, however, had to say to her: "**Julitta**, have mercy on yourself and sacrifice to the gods, so that you may be freed from the torture, lest you die an evil death just like your son!" But she bravely endured the torture, cried out, and said: "I do not sacrifice to the evil spirits and your deaf and dumb idols, but to **Christ**, the only-begotten Son of God, through whom the Father created all things; and I hasten to come to my son, whose companion I wish to be in the kingdom of heaven!" Now when the cruel judge saw that the steadfast martyr’s spirit triumphed over all his devilry, he passed judgment upon her and ordered [her execution].

[The governor] ordered that the woman be struck on the head with a sword and thrown, together with the corpse of her young boy, at the place of skulls <note>original: "Schedelstätte" — a term mirroring "Golgotha," the site of Christ's crucifixion.</note>. Upon this, the beadles <term>beadles</term> <note>low-ranking court officials or guards</note> gagged her mouth and bound it shut, and led her to the usual place of execution to carry out what they had been commanded. Julitta, however, begged them to grant her a short delay until she could pray on her knees to God, who alone is good. The beadle’s heart was softened, and they gave her a small reprieve for prayer; as she prayed on bended knees, she said: "I thank you, O Lord, who called my son before me and, in place of this vain, transitory life, willed to give him the Eternal Life with the Saints for the sake of your holy and worshipful Name. Receive also me, your unworthy handmaid, and let me attain that good, so that I may be counted among the wise virgins <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25:1–13.</note> who have entered into the heavenly and immaculate wedding chamber; then shall my spirit praise your Father, the true God and preserver of all, and the creator of all things, together with the Holy Spirit throughout eternity. Amen." After she had spoken the "Amen," the executioner severed her brave neck with his flashing sword and then threw her corpse outside the city, at the spot where the body of her son, the victorious martyr, lay.

### Chapter 5.
->The Burial of Both.<-

Through the grace of Christ, both the victorious martyr Julitta and her glorious son Cyricus finished their course <note>A biblical idiom for completing one's life's work or journey, often used in hagiography (lives of the saints).</note> on July 15th. On the following night, their two maids came and took the bodies away, burying them in a field not far from there, outside of Tarsus. During the time of the most devout Emperor Constantine, one of these maids was still alive and brought the truth to light; after she had obtained her freedom through the generosity of the Church of God, she revealed the place of burial. Thus, many of the faithful wished to share in this holy pledge <note>original: "Unterpfande"—referring to the relics of the saints as a "pledge" or "guarantee" of divine favor.</note> and went there to the honor of our God, visiting the site with great devotion.

### Chapter 6.
->Concluding Address of Bishop Theodore.<-

This is the true account which I have wished to record for the service of your most devout soul. You, however, should share it again with faithful men,

# 67. St. Apollonius and Philemon.
## At Antinoöpolis in the Thebaid and Alexandria.
### Around the year 306.
#### Chapter 1.

->Apollonius, a hermit and deacon, is taken prisoner and converts Philemon, a jester.<- <note>original: "Schalks-Narren" — a professional fool or comic actor.</note>

The oldest Desert Fathers <term>Desert Fathers</term> <note>Early Christian hermits and ascetics who lived in the Egyptian desert during the 3rd and 4th centuries.</note> recount (from Rufinus, Palladius, and others) <note>Rufinus of Aquileia and Palladius of Galatia were early Christian historians who chronicled the lives of Egyptian monks.</note> that at the time of the persecution, there was a hermit named Apollonius, who, because of his holy way of life, was chosen by the brothers to be a deacon. During the time of the persecution, his work was to diligently visit the brothers and prepare them for martyrdom. When he himself was captured for this and thrown into the dungeon, many heathens came to him and mocked him, striving to overcome him with godless, wicked words. Among these was a certain famous harlequin or comic actor named Philemon, who was very pleasing to all the people; as this man troubled him with many abusive words, calling the martyr a godless person, a villain, and a deceiver—indeed, a deceitful trickster <note>original: "Sinnlichen Betrüger"</note> who deserved to be hated by all men. As he spoke this and much more such evil against him, Apollonius answered him and said: "May the Lord have mercy on you, my son, and not count against you anything of all that you have spoken." When Philemon heard this, his heart was struck, and he felt the power of such words in his soul in a way that surpassed human nature, so much so that he immediately confessed himself a Christian.

[Philemon] also immediately ran to the judgment seat, and cried out in the presence of all the people, saying: “You act unjustly, wicked judge, you who kill the devout and God-beloved men; for the Christians neither teach nor do anything evil.” However, when the judge heard this, he initially assumed that Philemon was offering jesting words <note>original: "Scherz-Reden" — reflecting Philemon's previous profession as a comic actor or jester.</note> according to his well-known manner; but when he saw that he persisted in earnest and testified with all steadfastness, he said to him: “You are insane, Philemon, and have suddenly lost your mind.” He, however, answered: “I am not insane, but you are; for you are a completely unjust and perverse judge, who unfairly kills so many righteous men; but I am a Christian, and such people are the very best among men.” Then the judge began to flatter him before the people with many smooth words to bring him back to his former way of thinking; but when he saw him unmovable, he attempted all kinds of martyrdom <note>In this context, "martyrdom" refers to various methods of torture used to produce a martyr.</note> upon him.

## Chapter 2.

->Apollonius and Philemon are sentenced to the fire and miraculously preserved through prayer.<-

After [the judge] realized that Philemon had been so changed by the words of Apollonius, he also had cruel torture inflicted upon Apollonius, accusing him of deceit. Apollonius, however, said to him: “Would to God that you and all who stand with you would follow this error and deceit of mine!” When the judge heard this, he commanded that he be thrown into the fire along with Philemon in the sight of the people. As they stood in the flames, the blessed Apollonius cried out to the Lord so that everyone heard it, saying: “Do not deliver the souls of those who confess you to the wild beasts, O Lord, but let us see your great mercy.” <note>original: "Ps. 74, v. 19. At this, both the judge and the people were terrified, and all began to cry out with one voice: “Great and unique is the God of the Christians; He alone is immortal!”

### Chapter 2.

<margin>The memory of Saint Euphemia still flourished in the year 400 at Chalcedon.</margin>
A certain virgin, consecrated to God and stainless, dedicated her chastity to God; her name was Euphemia. Now, when the tyrant once persecuted the pious people and Christians, she confidently placed her life in the balance. Her fellow citizens and companions in faith at Chalcedon, for whom she suffered death, admired her courageous spirit and holiness; they built a monument for her not far from the temple and placed her coffin within it, where they still publicly honor her memory and, on her annual day of remembrance, they all show themselves joyful at the assembly of the whole people and celebrate that day. The holy interpreters of the mysteries of God <note>A poetic term for the clergy or theologians</note> truly honor her memory in their sermons and instruct the people with all diligence as to how she completed her struggle of patience; but the painter also, who similarly lends his hands to godliness...

...wished to offer, has by his art designed this entire history upon the canvas with the most lifelike representation possible, and has hung the picture there next to the tomb for holy contemplation. This excellent piece of art presents the history in the following manner:

# Chapter 3.
->Depiction of how Saint Euphemia stands before the court.<-

The judge (who was named Priscus <note>Priscus was the Roman proconsul of Asia under Emperor Diocletian, around 303 AD</note>) sits upon an exalted throne and looks at the virgin with a bitter, grim face; for art also knows how to make lifelike things appear angry, when it pleases. Furthermore, the other magisterial persons are present, as well as guards and no small number of soldiers. The court scribes hold wax tablets and styluses in their hands, among whom one holds his hand ready to write and looks sharply at the virgin standing before the judge, so that he might not mishear and write falsely, and consequently become deserving of punishment. The virgin, however, stands there in a dark-brown dress and cloak, like a philosophical matron <note>The artist depicts her in the "pallium," a cloak associated with ancient philosophers, suggesting her wisdom and gravity</note>, as the painter imagined her, with a very joyful countenance; yet as I consider it, with an exceptionally virtuous and adorned spirit. Two soldiers lead her before the judge; one pulls her forward, the other holds her from behind. The virgin’s bearing is a mixture of modesty and steadfastness; she does indeed bow her head and casts her eyes downward, as if she were ashamed of the men’s gaze; yet she stands undaunted and allows nothing fearful to be seen in the struggle. For which reason, though I have hitherto praised those painters who depicted that fable of the Colchian woman (*) in such a way that, at the murder of her sons, mercy and wrath contend in her face—where one eye indicates wrath, but the other motherly mercy and terror—now my admiration has shifted from that and fallen upon this image. I admire the artist of this piece to the highest degree, for he has mixed characters rather than colors, and knew how to magnificently temper modesty and undaunted courage, which are otherwise two contrary qualities of nature.

---

<margin>(*) Medea, the daughter of the King of the Colchians, who married Jason and murdered the two sons she bore him before his eyes out of resentment; as the fables of the poets tell.</margin> <note>This refers to a famous ancient painting of Medea by Timomachus of Byzantium, often cited in antiquity for its emotional complexity</note>

## Chapter 4.

->How she was martyred and her teeth were broken out / and finally<-
->burnt.<-

The artistic imitation further presented in another place several <term>henchmen</term> <note>original: "Büttel"; these were low-level officials or executioner's assistants tasked with the physical labor of torture</note> in light clothing, almost naked, who were already at their work. One indeed seized her by the head and pulled it backwards; another held the virgin's mouth open for a more effective torture; a third stood by and broke out her teeth. Further, one sees the tools of torture, such as the hammer and iron scrapers <note>original: "Kratz-Eisen"; likely referring to the iron claws or combs used to flay the skin of martyrs</note>. Truly, I can hardly contain my tears, and compassion interrupts my speech, for the brush has so clearly formed the drops of blood that one would truly think they were falling from her lips, and one might walk away out of sheer distress.

Once again, the prison is to be seen; therein the chaste virgin sits alone in dark clothes, lifting both her hands toward heaven and calling upon GOD for help in her distress. However, where she sits and prays, there appears above her head that sign which Christians are accustomed to revere and usually to paint; I mean the monument of suffering, namely the Cross.

In another place, the painter has also lit a fire, from which the flickering reddish flame rises upward. He has placed the virgin in the midst of it, yet she allows no sadness to show in her face, but rather looks joyful, as one who journeys toward the blessed spiritual life. The painter has expressed it so far that he had to let his hand rest, just as I must let my speech and tongue rest. For the rest, it will be your part to complete the image in your heart, so that you may recognize in an unclouded way whether we have hit the mark.

<note>Asterius of Amasea, Volume 1, Supplement of Combefis. Ruinart, Acts of the Martyrs, page 490.</note>

# 69. St. Serenus
## at Sirmium in Slavonia <note>Sirmium, modern-day Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia, was a major capital of the Roman Empire; Slavonia refers to the historical region in the Pannonian Basin.</note>.
### Year 307.

---

### Chapter 1.

->Serenus, a gardener, drives an unchaste woman out of his garden.<-

When Serenus, a foreign hermit and Greek by birth, had come to Sirmium from foreign lands, he began to cultivate a garden to sustain himself, as he knew no other craft. During the time of persecution <note>This refers to the Diocletianic Persecution, the last and most severe persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire.</note>, however, he hid himself for a short time—for several months—out of fear of martyrdom. Afterward, he began once again to tend his garden without fear. While he was occupied with this, a certain woman came into the garden one day with her two daughters and began to walk about inside. When the aforementioned old man saw her, he said to her: "What do you seek, poor woman?" But she said: "I take pleasure in walking in this garden!" But he said: "What kind of honorable matron <note>original: "Matron"; a term used for a woman of high social standing and moral character.</note> is this, who still goes walking here so late, when it is already evening? I perceive well that you have not come here for the sake of walking, but out of wantonness and unchastity; therefore, go out and live modestly, as befits honorable women."

---

### Chapter 2.

->The woman complains to her husband, who receives permission from the Emperor to seek legal revenge.<-

She, however, went away with shame and bitterness, not so much because the expulsion pained her, but because she could not achieve the goal of her lewdness. Therefore, she wrote of it to her husband, who was a servant at the court of the Emperor Maximian <note>Maximian was the Roman Emperor (Augustus) of the West from 286 to 305, and again briefly until 310.</note>, and complained to him of the disgrace she had suffered. When her husband had read the letter, he immediately complained of the matter to the Emperor, saying: "While we are around and before Your Majesty, our wives are insulted in their honor far away!" Upon this, the Emperor gave him authority to avenge himself through the Governor of that land as he pleased. After he had received such power—

## Chapter 3.

->Serenus defends himself against the accusation brought against him.<-

When he arrived at the aforementioned city of Sirmium, he went immediately to the President <note>The "Präsidente" refers to the Roman provincial governor or high-ranking magistrate.</note> and initiated a legal suit for defamation <note>original: "Injurien-Proceß"; a formal legal proceeding regarding personal insult or injury to one’s honor.</note>, presenting the Imperial letters and saying: "Avenge the offense and shame that my wife suffered during my absence!" When the President heard this, he was filled with wonder and said to him: "Who then has dared to insult a married matron whose husband stands at the side of the Emperor?" He replied: "Serenus, that common fellow and gardener, did this!" As soon as the President heard the name, he ordered him to be brought forward at once. After he had been fetched, he stood before the face of the President, who said to him: "What is your name?" He answered: "Serenus." The President said: "What is your trade?" He answered: "I am a gardener." The President said: "Why did you insult the wife of such a man?" He answered: "I have never insulted a matron." The President said quite furiously: "Convict him, so that he may confess which matron he offended when she wished to take a stroll in the garden." But he answered without any fear: "I remember that a few days ago, a distinguished lady was walking in my garden at an unseemly hour; I rebuked her and told her that she did not live as befits an honorable woman, in that she left her husband's house at such a late hour." When her husband heard this account of his unclean and ill-behaved wife, he blushed and fell silent; he did not pursue the matter further with the President to avenge the shame he had suffered and for which he had come, for he was now ashamed of the business himself.

He then said to him: "What is your religion?" He immediately gave the answer: "I am a Christian!" The President said: "Where have you been hidden so..."

When Phileas stood upon the scaffold <note>original: "Schau-Gerüste"; a public platform used for trials and the pronouncement of sentences.</note>, the President Culcianus <note>Culcianus was the Prefect of Egypt known for his rigorous enforcement of the anti-Christian edicts.</note> said to him: "You still have time to become sober <note>The judge implies that Phileas's Christian faith is a form of intoxication or madness from which he should recover.</note>." (*) The martyr Phileas here not improperly cites the example of the pagan and Athenian philosopher Socrates, who lived in Athens at the time of Ezra, about 480 years before the Lord’s manifestation; to whom God did not leave Himself without witness, according to pagan circumstances. Because he strove for a virtuous life according to the law of nature, he was reported to the authorities [stating] he had spoken ill of the gods; and when the council at Athens interrogated him judicially because of this and asked what punishment he might have deserved for it, Socrates gave as an answer: "That I be well cared for in the best room of the Town Hall <note>original: "Rath-Hause"; Socrates specifically referred to being fed in the Prytaneum, an honor reserved for Olympic victors and heroes.</note> at the city's expense!" The council was outraged at this and sentenced him to death by a poisoned drink, which he drank down with peace of mind in the 70th year of his age, setting aside his wife and children. See Cicero's *Tusculan Disputations*, Books 1 and 5. What this Socrates and his student Plato recognized regarding the state of the world of light and of hell is thoughtfully noted by Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: "Præpar. [Philoromus], seeing **Phileas** surrounded by the tears of his kin and tormented by the President's <note>The "President" refers to Culcianus, the Prefect of Egypt.</note> deceptions—yet remaining in no way led astray or turned aside—cried out: "Why do you try this man’s constancy so long in vain and to no purpose? As they were being led out and went toward the customary place of execution, the brother of **Phileas**—who was one of the advocates <note>A legal counsel or lawyer.</note>—cried out and said: "**Phileas** asks for the annulment of the sentence!" **Culcianus** then had him called back and said to him: "What? Have you appealed?" **Phileas** answered: "I have not appealed; far be it from me! Do not heed the words of this most unfortunate man. Rather, I give thanks to the Emperors and the President that I have become a co-heir with **Jesus Christ**!"

So **Phileas** was finally led out; and when they had come to the place of execution, **Phileas** spread his hands toward the rising sun, called out, and said: "My dearest children, all you who seek **God**, take heed of your hearts; for our adversary prowls about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour <note>A reference to the New Testament, 1 Peter 5:8.</note>. We have yet endured nothing; now we are only beginning to suffer; now we begin to become true disciples of our **Lord Jesus Christ**. My beloved, mark well the commandments of our **Lord Jesus Christ**! Let us call upon the Spotless, Incomprehensible Creator of all things, who sits above the Cherubim, who is the beginning and the end; and to Him be the glory unto ages of ages. Amen." 

When he had said this, the executioners carried out the President’s command and drove both of their untiring spirits from their bodies with the stroke of the sword, through the aid of our **Lord Jesus Christ**, who with the Father and Holy Spirit lives and reigns, true God, unto ages of ages. Amen.

<header>71. Saint Quirinus</header>

# 71. Saint Quirinus <note>original: "S. Quirini"</note> / at Savaria <note>Sabara (modern-day Szombathely, Hungary), the capital of the province of Pannonia Prima.</note> in Lower Hungary.
## Year 309.

### Chapter 1.
->The Persecution of the Christians in Illyria and Hungary.<-

When the Devil had stirred up the princes of this world to torment the souls of the Saints, and everywhere troubled the congregations of the Lord with many kinds of storms of persecution, he also incited the favorites of the Emperors, through whom he continued the war against the people of **God** even further, and thus daily increased his cruelty. **Diocletian**, however, through his godless decrees, raged hostiley against the people of **Christ** throughout Illyria <note>A Roman province encompassing much of the modern-day Balkans.</note>; and he added **Maximian** to his tyranny as a co-regent, who likewise made his own madness and that of **Diocletian** known throughout all of Illyria. Malicious letters from these godless princes were sent to almost all the judges of the provinces, ordering them to force the Christians to sacrifice in the temples of unclean spirits <note>A common early Christian term for pagan deities.</note>; the meeting houses of the Christians were to be closed, and the priests and servants of **Christ** were to submit themselves to the public laws and acknowledge the gods; if they would not light incense to them, they were to suffer various punishments and modes of death.

### Chapter 2.
->Saint Quirinus, Bishop of Siscia, is captured while fleeing / delivers a glorious confession / and is beaten.<-

Among the many who were victorious in the army of **Christ**, the blessed **Quirinus**, Bishop of Siscia <note>modern-day Sisak in Croatia</note>, was also taken prisoner by order of the Governor **Maximus**. As they were diligently searching for him and the blessed Bishop noticed this, he withdrew from the city, but was captured while fleeing and dragged away into imprisonment. When the Governor **Maximus** asked him where he had intended to flee, Bishop **Quirinus** gave this answer: "I was not fleeing, but was doing the will of my **Lord**, who commanded us in writing: 'When they persecute you in one city, flee into another.'" <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 10:23.</note>

It describes the state-mandated suppression of Christianity in Illyria and the initial capture of Quirinus as he attempted to escape the city.</summary>

## Chapter 3.

-> Marcellus the jailer is converted by a miracle <-

After he had been bound and locked in the dungeon, he gave himself over to prayer and said: "I thank you, my **Lord**, that these bonds have been put upon me for your sake; and I pray you, let all who are in this distress learn that I am a worshiper of the true **GOD**, and let them believe that there is no other **GOD** but you." At midnight, however, a great light appeared in the dungeon. When the jailer Marcellus saw this, he opened the dungeon and threw himself at the feet of the blessed Bishop Quirinus, saying with tears: "Pray to the **Lord** for me, for I believe there is no other **GOD** but the one you honor." The blessed Bishop then exhorted him with many words and blessed him in the name of our **Lord** Jesus Christ. After three days, Maximus commanded that they should take the blessed Quirinus to the Governor Amantius in Lower Hungary, so that he might be sentenced to death for his stubbornness, as he had proven himself to be against the laws of the Emperors.

As he was being led, they dragged him bound with chains all around through all the cities to the tribunal of the Governor Amantius; for they led him through all the cities situated on the banks of the Danube River. Amantius returned that very day from the city of Scrabantia <note>Modern-day Sopron, Hungary.</note> when the blessed Bishop Quirinus was presented to him; the Governor ordered him to be led to the city of Sabaria <note>Modern-day Szombathely, Hungary.</note>, where he intended to interrogate him further. In the meantime, several Christian women visited the holy Bishop Quirinus in the dungeon and brought him food and drink. The blessed Bishop saw their faith, and as he blessed their gift, the chains with which his feet and hands were bound fell off. After he had taken the food and the women had departed, his guards led him toward Sabaria. There, the Governor Amantius ordered his servants to bring him publicly before him. 

After he had been presented, Governor Amantius said: "I ask you, is that which you answered to the judge Maximus in such a haughty manner, according to the submitted protocol, the truth?" Quirinus the Bishop answered: "At Siscia <note>Modern-day Sisak, Croatia.</note> I confessed the true **GOD**; Him have I served at all times, Him I keep in my heart, and no man shall turn me away from Him, the only true **GOD**." 

Governor Amantius said: "Out of compassion for your great age, we have reservations about shaming you with beatings; therefore, we attempt to change your mind with words and to improve your situation through the promised reward of life, so that you may spend the remaining time of your old age in peace in the service of the gods, according to the ordinance of the **Imperial laws**." 

The blessed Bishop Quirinus said: "Why do you have reservations regarding my age, which an uncorrupted faith can make stronger than all martyrdom? My confession shall not be broken by torture, nor changed by the favor of this life, nor shall the steadfastness of my mind be destroyed by fear of death, however heavy it may be." 

Governor Amantius said: "Why do you desire death so greatly, and refuse to be subject to the gods and the Roman Empire, choosing instead—contrary to human custom—that your life should be taken from you? On the contrary, those who seek to escape death would rather laugh at the torture than confess their misdeeds; but you call the sweetness of this life a vanity, and you rush headlong to de—" <note>The original German "To-" and the catchword "de," form "Tode," meaning death.</note>

### Chapter 5.

->He is drowned with a millstone around his neck / but<-
->miraculously floats on the surface for a time.<-

After all the other tortures the Bishop had endured, the President then ordered that a millstone be hung around the neck of this holy priest and servant of **GOD**, and that he be drowned in the river Sibarim <note>The river Gyöngyös in modern-day Hungary.</note>. When he had been thrown from the bridge into the current, he floated on the surface for a long time and spoke with the Christian onlookers, telling them they should not be deterred by the example of his suffering; finally, through prayer, he obtained the grace to sink to the bottom. His body was found again not far from the place where he had been submerged; there on the riverbank, the faithful are also accustomed to pray. The holy corpse, however, is buried in the church before the gate at Scarabantia <note>Modern-day Sopron, Hungary.</note>, where there is a great gathering of people due to his merits. The blessed Quirinus, Bishop of Siscia <note>Modern-day Sisak, Croatia.</note> and martyr of Christ, suffered on the 4th of June and was crowned <note>A common metaphor in hagiography for receiving the crown of martyrdom.</note> by our Lord **JESUS** Christ, to whom be honor and glory and power for ages of ages <note>original: "in die Ewigkeiten der Ewigkeiten"</note>. Amen!

# 72. St. Peter Balsamus (*) / at Aulana in Samaria. Anno 311.

## Chapter 1.

### St. Peter Balsamus is captured at Aulana and judicially examined.

At that same time, Peter, who was otherwise called Balsamus, was also taken prisoner in the city of Aulana <note>Likely the town of Aneivah or a similar location in Samaria.</note> during the time of the persecution. He was originally from the territory of the city of Eleutheropolis <note>A significant Roman city in Roman Palestine, known today as Beit Guvrin.</note> and was presented to the President Severus. 

Severus spoke then to him: "What is your name?" 

Peter answered: "By my father's name I am called Balsamus; my spiritual name, which I received at baptism, is Peter." 

The President spoke: "Of what lineage are you?" 

Peter answered: "I am a Christian!" 

The President spoke: "Of what rank and office are you?" 

Peter answered: "I cannot have a greater office than this, and what indeed can be better than that I am a Christian?" 

The President spoke: "Do you still have parents?" 

Peter answered: "I have them no longer." 

The President spoke: "You lie, for I have heard that you still have parents." 

Peter answered: "In the Gospel <note>Referencing the biblical command in Matthew 10:37 or Luke 14:26 to prioritize Christ over family.</note> I am commanded to deny everything when I come to the confession of the Christian name." 

The President spoke: "Do you know the Imperial command?" 

Peter answered: "I know the command of my **GOD**, who is the true and eternal King." 

The President spoke: "It is commanded by the most gracious Princes <note>Referring to the Roman Emperors, likely Galerius and Maximinus Daza.</note> that all Christians must either sacrifice, or be executed by various tortures!" 

Peter answered: "And the command of the true and eternal King is this: If anyone shall sacrifice to the evil spirits, and not to **GOD** alone, he shall be rooted out! What is better now—to die by your hand, or to be eternally rooted out by the true **GOD**? Judge this yourself, if you indeed know anything of true justice—"

> This I would dearly have:

While he was singing this, the President became even more furious and commanded that fresh bailiffs' assistants <term>Büttel-Knechte: low-ranking officials or henchmen who carried out punishments</term> should step forward and torment him even more. But as the surrounding crowd of spectators saw that much blood was dripping down from the scaffold <term>Schau-Gerüste: literally a "show-frame," referring to the elevated platform used for public torture or execution</term> onto the earth, they felt compassion for him and spoke: "Have mercy on yourself, O man, and sacrifice, so that you may free yourself from these cruel plagues!" The holy man of **GOD**, *Peter*, however, answered: "These plagues are nothing and cause me no pain at all; but if I were to deny the name of my **GOD**, then I know that I would come into the true pain and into much greater, eternal martyrdom." The President spoke: "Now, what do you say, *Peter*? Sacrifice; you will eventually regret it." *Peter* answered: "I will never regret it, and I will not sacrifice." The President spoke: "Then I must pass the death sentence upon you." *Peter* answered: "That is what I await with total longing." Then the President gave the verdict against him and spoke: "I command that *Peter*, who has greatly despised the commands of the invincible Emperors for the sake of the commands of his crucified **GOD**, shall be crucified!" Thus did the honorable warrior of *Christ* finish his course and was deemed worthy to share in the suffering and death-penalty of his **LORD**. This witness of *Christ, Balsamus*, who is also called *Peter*, was martyred in the city of *Aulana* <note>Likely Aulane in Palestine, near Eleutheropolis.</note> on the 3rd of *January* under the Emperor *Maximian*; while our **LORD** JESUS *Christ* reigned, to whom be the glory for ages of ages. *Amen.* *Ruinart. page* 501. <note>original: "in die Ewigkeiten der Ewigkeiten." <header>73. St. Arcadius</header>

# 73. St. Arcadius (*) / at Mazaca or *Caesarea* in *Cappadocia*. Year 312.

## Chapter 1.

-> The wretched state of the persecution at Mazaca or *Caesarea*. <-

When fierce wrath raged at Mazaca <note>Ancient city in central Turkey, later renamed Caesarea</note>, and the devil armed his servants against the people of **GOD**, the entire household of Christ was scattered by the various raids of the raging wolf, and the most grievous war was stirred up against **GOD** and His worshipers. Public malice crept into every corner where worshipers of Christ, or of the true **GOD**, were suspected or believed to be; and there was no place where an act of violence was not committed on account of religion. The people of Christ were forced to adhere to vain superstition, and either to slaughter all kinds of idolatrous sacrifices for shameful idol-worship, or to pull the sacrificial livestock—decorated with wreaths and flowers—through the streets, or to light the fragrant incense, or to sing songs of *Bacchus* <note>The Roman god of wine and ritual madness</note> amidst the smoking fire and the stench of burnt fat, so that through such unlawful performance of sacrifices, **GOD** might be driven out of the minds of the Christians.

## Chapter 2.

-> The martyr Arcadius hides himself; His kinsman is captured in his stead / whereupon he presents himself. <-

While such a hard, warrior-like struggle was being waged, and the family of the **LORD** was being challenged before the face of heaven, *Arcadius*, the soldier of Christ, seeing that the city was in a state of gruesome confusion, resolved—

<note>(*) It appears as though this martyr *Arcadius* might be the same person as the following *Gordius*; it is therefore suspected that in this description, the name of the place *Achaia*, as some know it, or *Caesarea in Mauritania*, as others have it, has been transposed by the scribes instead of *Mazaca* or *Caesarea Mazaca* in *Cappadocia*, where the history of *Gordius’s* martyrdom took place according to the testimony of *Basil the Great* <note>original: "Basilii Magni"</note>, whose writings have been much mixed with those of *Zeno of Verona* <note>original: "Zenonis Veronensis"</note>, to whom this description is attributed.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the martyrdom of St. Arcadius in 312 AD, describing the brutal atmosphere of Christian persecution in Caesarea and the pressure to participate in pagan rituals. A scholarly note discusses the potential confusion between Arcadius and another martyr named Gordius due to conflicting historical sources.</summary>

in the midst of confusion and ruin, where every person was being dragged into a savage spectacle, to forsake his possessions and escape this evil by a hasty flight from the city. Having found some hidden dens outside, he concealed himself for a time, serving Christ as he desired in secret, with vigils, prayers, and a most temperate life. ### Chapter 3.

->The Naming of Various Kinds of Torture and the Cruel<-
->Dismemberment of Arcadius.<-

Immediately now, as the most cruel President's <note>The Latin title *praeses*, referring to the Roman provincial governor.</note> snake-venomous bile was stirred, he pondered with what unheard-of revenge he might rage against the limbs of the Martyr, rather than following what the laws for punishing the guilty prescribe. The hooks seemed much too mild to him; the scourge with leaden balls he considered useless; the torture-block was displeasing to him; he forgot the standard rules of the arena while contemplating a greater and more cruel mindset, devising a new and horrifying method, whereby he foolishly thought he could overcome **GOD** in Arcadius. Finally, he commanded the executioners <note>original: *Büttel-Knechte*</note> to take the Martyr as partners in his madness; he commanded nothing less than that they should use all possible force to hasten the desired end of his life, yet force the spirit of the Martyr to depart slowly. "Do not let him," he said, "wait long for his death, but cut him limb-by-limb, so that he may himself behold the mangling of his body like a living carcass <term>living carcass: *lebendig Aas*, a derogatory term for a body that is technically alive but treated as carrion</term> or a block of wood. Cut one limb of the body after another from him, and loosen the joints; begin from the first joint of the fingers, then the hand to the wrist, further the arm to the elbow, and then to the shoulders. Do exactly the same with the limbs of the feet one after another; first the toes from the feet, then the feet from the ankles, thereafter the legs from the knees, and then loosen them up to the hips. But proceed with your skill slowly, so that through the length of the torture he may see his misfortune, because he abhorred sacrificing to the ancestral gods and honors a foreign **GOD**."

Once Arcadius had been led there, he stood and called upon **GOD** with eyes directed toward heaven and a most steadfast spirit; he then stretched out his neck to the executioner and offered it to receive the blow; for he supposed...

The judge’s rage would soon be satiated by a swift death; however, the martyr was commanded to hold out his hands. He stretched out his hand at that very hour, and as they took it from him joint by joint, he prayed and said: "Thy hands, O Lord, have made me and fashioned me; give me understanding!" <note>original: Psalm 119, v. 73. Arcadius quotes this to signify that even as his physical body is unmade by men, his spiritual form is authored by God.</note> The executioners <note>original: *Büttel*—low-ranking officials or henchmen tasked with carrying out corporal punishment.</note> grew weary of completing their cruelty sooner than he ceased from the praise of **GOD**. In his frenzy, the judge had forgotten to first have his tongue cut out, which, in the midst of the torture, unceasingly confessed the Lord and proved that the tyrant was overcome, and that the gods were nothing, but Christ alone was the true victor and overcomer, he cried. Now that he was completely mutilated in his upper parts, they laid him on his back. As he lay thus upon his back, he glorified **GOD** even more, for now he could truly look upon heaven during his martyrdom, from whence he entreated help; he then joyfully reached out his feet and his legs along with his hips to have them taken off in the same cruel manner, which followed immediately thereafter. The toes were severed from the feet, the feet from the legs, the legs from the loins, and these from the body itself through the cruel art of the executioners. Yet the martyr’s steadfastness, patience, and thanksgiving toward **GOD** were so great that even the cruel eyes of the spectators could not refrain from tears, and they fully recognized the heavenly power which caused such patience; they even began to repent that they had inflicted such an excessive burden <note>original: *Ueberlast*—referring here to the extreme, disproportionate nature of the torture.</note> upon him.

### Chapter 5.
#### The Martyr's Great Patience and Last Speeches.

After all such torture, as many as there were severed limbs, one saw the mutilated body of the martyr swimming in blood, and amidst all this, the martyr’s spirit remained invincible, and despite the slow lingering of death, he remained alive; thus he sent, as it were, the obstacles of his body and his remains ahead of him as signs of victory. And as he saw the mutilated members of his body lying upon the earth, he spoke: O you blessed limbs, you who have been found worthy to serve **GOD**! I never loved you so much while you were still attached to my body as I now rejoice to see you separated. Thus must we be parted for a short time, so that we may finally find one another again before our King, and instead of mortal members, you shall [return] to me in immortal quality...

will be given back to me again; you are now members <note>The word *Glieder* refers both to physical limbs and to "members" of the Church.</note>, and I feel that I am a member of Christ, which I have desired above all things. Furthermore, he spoke: "Let this not dismay you, O you men standing about and observers of this unusual spectacle! This can be easily endured by one who knows how to think of the coming eternity. Forsake the worthless gods who cannot help you; but recognize my **GOD**, who loves me, for whom to die is life, and to suffer for him is a pleasure; whose love does not grow cold, whose honor is always upheld; to whom I come eternally for this small pain, and from whom I shall never be separated again." When he had said this, he passed away peacefully on the 12th of January and surrendered his glorious soul to the Lord Christ. Those who beheld the end of the glorious martyr marveled at it, even though they were idol-worshippers: The Christians, however, were encouraged all the more to suffer every martyrdom; they also buried the martyr’s corpse with honor and placed his scattered limbs into the coffin with the body, and praised the Lord Christ in the martyr, who gives His fighters strength to overcome all torment, to whom be honor and glory eternally.
<note>original: Zeno Veron. Ruinart. pag. 529. refers to the works of Zeno of Verona and Thierry Ruinart, a Benedictine monk and scholar who compiled acts of the martyrs.</note>
