...of **GOD**, since you now wish to set out to the martyrs as if toward heavenly flowers, and I find you gathered here in such great numbers; under whose leadership do you wish to do this? Who has caused this great movement? Who has transformed the current sorrowful winter-time into a pleasant, bright spring? So that the people venture out joyfully from the houses of the city—as if from the bees' waxen huts—into the lovely field and the excellent martyr’s **place of combat** (*). Because we also, despite our weakness, have been awakened by the martyr’s solemn memorial; well then, let us likewise—as much as we are able with words—sound forth his glorious deeds like the humming bees that fly around the spring flowers, and perform a work that is both blessed by **God** and pleasing to those present; for when the righteous are praised, the people rejoice. *Proverbs 29, verse 2 etc.* Therefore, let it suffice for us this time to celebrate their memory; for they do not need our praise, but we need to remember their life and conduct for our own imitation. For just as a brilliance naturally shines forth from fire, and a lovely scent from precious oil, so all receive a benefit through the remembrance of the works of the saints. And it is to be esteemed as no small thing if we can truly know the former histories of the saints; however, the reports of our martyr today (**Gordius**) have come to us very obscurely <note>original: "dunkel," meaning the historical record was vague or poorly preserved even by the 4th century.</note>. For this reason, we are rightly compared to painters; for when they copy one painting from another, they always move a bit further away from the original likeness. So too we, since we were not present at the events themselves, it is to be feared that we obscure the truth even more. Nevertheless, on today’s feast day, we wish to tell of him who fought for the sake of the name of Christ, as much as we can surmise from historical reports.

...inclination of the spirit falls so entirely upon him, because he truly serves as a genuine and unique adornment. Just as trees that bear good fruit serve as praise for the earth in which they stand; so too does this man, who has sprung from our city and has reached the highest state of honor, and thus offers to his fatherland—which bore and nourished him—the native fruits of godliness. To be sure, foreign fruits are good when they have a pleasant taste and provide nourishment; but far more pleasant than foreign ones are these domestic fruits, which, besides their sweetness, bring us praise. 

He stood in military service and held a distinguished position therein, so that he had a hundred men to command <note>This refers to the rank of a Centurion, a professional officer in the Roman army.</note>; he was famous for the bravery of his spirit and the strength of his body. At that same time, the godless tyrant <note>A reference to the Roman Emperor Licinius or perhaps Maximinus Daia, under whom the Great Persecution continued in the East.</note> who ruled then poured out his wild poison against the Christian name and reached with his God-forsaken hand against the Church; the herald's trumpet resounded throughout the entire city; everywhere in the market and at the crossroads, death was proclaimed: that no one should worship Christ, and whoever should fulfill such a command <note>that is, continue to follow Christ's command in defiance of the edict</note> would be killed! The graven images were carried about so that everyone should worship them, and the stone and wooden likenesses of men were to be held as gods; if anyone refused this, he stood in danger of his life. 

Over this, the city was thrown into confusion, standing in a total tumult over this new state of affairs; all the houses of the Christians were plundered, the goods of the innocent were stolen, and the bodies of the faithful and those of distinguished rank were torn apart by the hands of the <term>bailiffs</term> <note>original: "Büttel," refers to the low-ranking officers or executioners who carried out the arrests and tortures.</note>. The honorable matrons were dragged through the streets; there was no compassion for the young, no respect given to the old; the innocent suffered as if they were the guilty evildoers. The prisons were filled beyond measure, and the large, distinguished, wealthy houses were turned into a wasteland; the forests and wildernesses were full of fugitives, because of the single accusation that they worshipped Christ. The son betrayed the father, the father cursed the son; and one brother raged against the other; the servant persecuted his master; the minds of men were so thoroughly confused by devilish arts that they walked as if in darkness and could not recognize one another. Moreover, even the houses of prayer...

# Chapter 3.
->Gordius flees from the city into the wild mountains.<-

When the high-minded captain <note>Gordius, who held the rank of Centurion.</note> saw such cruel examples, he wished to forestall the legal troubles; he therefore threw off his military belt <note>The *cingulum militare*, a belt that served as the primary symbol of a Roman soldier's status and office.</note> and voluntarily chose exile or departure from the land. Thus, he left his honorable status, all his wealth, his servants, close relatives, friends, pleasures, and everything that others most desire and strive for with the greatest effort; he withdrew into great wildernesses and onto untrodden paths where no humans usually come, and he considered life among the cattle more peaceful than the company and food of idol-worshippers. 

In this, he followed the example of Elijah, who, upon seeing the increasing idolatry of the Sidonian Jezebel, went to Mount Horeb, where he stayed in a cave and prayed to God until he was permitted to see Him as much as is fitting for a mortal man (1 Kings 19:1–14). In the same way, our Gordius also fled—setting all things aside—the tumult of the city, the frenzy of the marketplace, the pride of the great, the arrogance of the officials, the reviling of the orators, the buyers and sellers, the perjurers and liars, the idle chatter, foolish talk, and the like; which, just like small boats tied to the back of large ships, so too those vices [attach themselves] to populous cities

---

<note>original: "Die Christen dazumal hiessen das Abendmahl ihre Opfer..." 
At that time, Christians called the Lord’s Supper their "sacrifice," in which they offered themselves to God—both to die to their carnal will and to not fear physical death for Christ's sake. They also burned incense in their gatherings and homes as a sweet fragrance without superstition; all of this—the terminology of "sacrifice" and "altars," etc.—has fallen more and more into misunderstanding over time. Furthermore, everything St. Basil testifies here is to be understood more from the custom of his own time than from the era preceding it.</note>

### Chapter 4.

->He returns and presents himself in the public arena.<-

<margin>(*) St. Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), whose homily on St. Gordius is the primary source for this account.</note> rebukes his own listeners here even more, noting that the Christians did such things <note>i.e., attending pagan games.</note> even during the time of the great persecution; this was not to be expected, as no one’s life was safe then.</margin>

Proverbs 28, v. 1. <note>original: "Prov. 28, v. 1." The verse says: "The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a lion."</note> What more is needed? He was of such an undaunted and joyful spirit that he placed himself upon a high point in the arena and cried out with a loud voice—which several of those still present here have heard personally (*)—: *I was found by those who did not seek me; and to those who did not ask for me, I have revealed myself.* Romans 10, v. 20. With these words, he truly demonstrated that he had not come to that place by force, but that he had presented himself voluntarily for the struggle; following the example of the Savior, who, when He was not recognized by the Jews in the dark of night, revealed Himself to them. Accordingly, he drew all eyes upon himself, for his appearance was formidable <note>original: "entsetzlich." In this context, it suggests an awe-inspiring or startling wildness rather than something purely "horrible."</note>; and because he had lived for a long time in the mountains, his hair was unkempt, his beard long, and his clothes ragged. His whole body was emaciated, and he carried a knapsack and a staff to support himself. Yet from all of this, a grace shone forth from his hidden inner character, which illuminated him. But when it was recognized who he was, a loud cry arose from both heathens and Christians; the latter shouted for joy because he was their fellow brother, while the former, who resist the truth, incited the judge’s mind toward his execution and already condemned him to death. Thus, the whole place was filled with shouting and noise; the horses, chariots, and drivers were ignored, and the swift wheels turned in vain. No one wished to see anything but Gordius; no one desired to hear anything but the words of Gordius. A murmur went through the entire arena like a roaring wind, surpassing the tumult of the horses. But after silence was commanded by the herald, and the usual trumpets <note>original: "Drometen," an archaic form of "Trompeten" (trumpets).</note> grew still, the pipes were hushed, and all other musical instruments ceased to play, then one heard only Gordius, and one looked only at him.

After he had recounted his return, he spoke:

> "I have returned for this purpose: to prove publicly that I care nothing at all for your commands; instead, I confess Jesus Christ, my hope and my protector. And because I have heard that you surpass all other men in cruelty, I have deemed this time most fitting for the fulfillment of my wish!"

With these words, he ignited the Governor’s <note>original: "Präsidenten"; referring to the Roman provincial official presiding over the games.</note> anger like a funeral pyre, and all the madness within the official was turned upon him. "Quickly," he said, "let the <term>Büttel|low-ranking officers or executioners</term> come, along with whips and scourges with leaden balls. Yet what an advantage this villain has, that he can only die once!" Gordius, however, replied:

> "Truly, I see it as a notable loss that I cannot suffer the death penalty more often and in many different ways for Christ's sake."

But the Governor was even more inflamed with anger beyond his natural malice when he considered the man’s dignity and saw that he regarded his own shame as greatness of soul. The more he beheld Gordius's undaunted heart, the more furious he became, striving all the more to defeat his constancy with every kind of cunning torture. This the Governor did. But the martyr lifted his eyes toward heaven and sang holy Psalms, saying:

> "The Lord is my helper, I will not fear; what can a mortal man do to me!" <note>A quotation of Psalm 118:6, also found in Hebrews 13:6.</note>

And again:

> "I fear no evil, for you are with me!" <note>Psalm 23:4.</note>

And other such Psalms, with which he refreshed his spirit as if with a song of joy, which he had learned from Holy Scripture. Yet he was so far from fearing the threatened agony that he instead challenged it and showed himself indignant at its delay. "Why do you linger?" he said, "Why do you stand there?"

> "Tear this body, torture the limbs, and inflict upon me every torment you wish! Do not begrudge me my blessed hope; for the more you increase the torture, the more reward you bring to me. Such is the deal and agreement we have with the Lord. In place of the stripes that appear on our bodies, we shall be clothed in shining garments at the Resurrection; for insults and shame, we obtain palms and crowns; in place of bonds and dungeons, Paradise. That we are [condemned] along with the evildoers...

## Chapter 6.

->*The judge tries all kinds of gentle and harsh means.*<-

When at last the blessed man could not be turned from his stubborn faith through such severity, the Governor <note>original: "Präsident"; here referring to the Roman provincial official presiding over the trial.</note> took another path. He attempted to defile him with flattery and every form of gentleness; for the Devil is especially accustomed to using this art: he terrifies the fearful with fear, but catches the brave-hearted with gentleness and flattery. The Governor followed this example; when he could not frighten him away with terrifying things, he sought to deceive him with cunning and reconciliatory gestures. Therefore, he promised to give him great things—some of which he had at hand, while others were still to be expected from the Emperor—namely, a distinguished military post <note>original: "Krieges-Bedienung"; likely a promotion back into the centurionate or higher.</note>, many estates and wealth, and everything his heart desired. 

But Gordius was not overcome by this either; for he laughed at the Governor's senselessness, who imagined he possessed gifts as worthy as those of Heaven. The ungodly man then let his anger loose again and, in a rage, drew his sword from its scabbard, commanding the executioner <note>original: "Scharfrichter"</note> to stand ready, and prepared himself with hand and tongue for the man's condemnation. 

The entire crowd of spectators at the arena <note>original: "Schau-Platze"</note> approached the judgment seat; the rest of the people, who had remained in the city, also came out and hurried to this new spectacle, which was a wonder to the angels and all creation, but a bitter struggle for the Devil and a bath of anguish for the unclean spirits. To put it briefly: as everyone ran there, the city became almost empty, and the entire multitude poured out of the city like a stream toward the place of martyrdom; respectable matrons as well as common women hurried there together. The houses stood without guards, the shops were also abandoned, and whatever was for sale in the market lay scattered. In this alone was the city safe: that since everyone had gone outside the walls, no one remained inside who could have committed a crime. The servants neglected their duties and watched eagerly; likewise, all strangers and foreigners were at this place to see the man of wonders. Indeed, even the maidens dared to <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the word "entblödeten," suggesting the women cast off their usual modesty to witness the event.</note>

## Chapter 7.
### Cunning Temptation by the False Brothers / and Gordius’s <note>The text here is cut off by the binding; it likely read "Gordius’s Resolution" or "Firmness."</note>

Under such a great gathering of the entire city around the blessed Gordius / who looked upon that [eternal] life through the [death of] his body, a crowd of his relatives and <unclear>friends</unclear> who embraced and kissed him, finally begged him with <unclear>tears</unclear> that he should not throw himself into the burning <unclear>flames</unclear>; he should not cast away the bloom of his years, this earthly life, and the pleasant light of the sun. Some, when they saw that they could not turn him away from his faith, or perhaps even approved of it, attacked him cunningly with specious arguments <note>original: "Schein-Gründen"; deceptive reasons that appear logical but are intended to mislead.</note> and said that he could just keep Christ in his heart if he so pleased, but with his mouth he could certainly deny Him. God does not look at the words, they said, but at the heart of the <unclear>speaker</unclear>; in this way, the anger of the embittered judge would be softened, and one could nonetheless keep God in one’s heart (*). However, he stood like an immovable rock in the waves of the sea, and could be moved by neither <unclear>threats</unclear> nor words, but remained relentless in his firm resolve. For just as the house of a wise man built upon a rock cannot be moved by any violence, nor by heavy downpours from heaven, nor by the rushing of waters; so too could no prayers or threats shake his steadfastness in Christ. And as the sharpness of his <unclear>spirit</unclear> perceived the devil running here and there—through whose art some wept while others tried to persuade him with specious arguments—he spoke to those who were weeping a word of the Lord: "Do not weep for me, but weep for the enemies of God who rage against the Christians. These, I say, you should bewail, for they light the fire for us but kindle Hell for themselves, and gather the fire of <unclear>God's</unclear> wrath as a treasure for themselves. Cease from <unclear>this</unclear> and from troubling my heart; for I am not only..."

## Chapter 8.

->Gordius’s further defense against the hypocrites.<-

To the others, however, who had exhorted him to deny Christ with his mouth, he gave this answer: The tongue was created by Christ; how dare it deny its Creator? For with the heart we believe unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Romans 10, verse 10. Does the military profession perhaps have no hope for repentance and salvation? Has no captain <note>original: "Hauptmann"; referring here to the rank of Centurion, which Gordius himself held.</note> ever been converted? I remember that captain who stood by the cross of Christ and recognized His omnipotence from the miracles; even while the malice of the Jews was still smoking <note>A metaphor suggesting their anger was fresh and burning like a fire.</note>, he nevertheless did not fear their wrath, nor did he withdraw from the public confession of the truth, but confessed and did not deny that the Lord was truly the Son of God. Matthew 27, verse 54. I also know of another captain who recognized Him while He was still in the flesh—that He was God and a King of powers, and that He was powerful enough to help those in need through His serving spirits by His command alone; whose faith the Lord also held to be greater than that of all Israel. Matthew 8, verses 5–10. Cornelius—was he not a captain, and was he not made worthy of an angelic appearance? Since he finally attained salvation through Peter; for his alms and prayers were heard by God. Acts 10. I wish to be their disciple; how then can I deny my God, whom I have worshiped from my youth? Should not the heavens above turn black? Should not the stars darken on my account? And the earth would swallow me up! Do not be deceived; God cannot be led around by the nose <note>original: "bey der Nasen herum führen"; a German idiom meaning to be fooled or mocked.</note>; He judges us according to our words, He justifies us according to our speech, and condemns us according to the same. Have you not read the Lord’s terrifying words of warning? Namely: Whoever denies me before men, him I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 10, verse 33. But why do you advise me that I should pretend? Do I gain anything by it? Perhaps that I might live for a few days, and be damned for eternity? That I might escape the tribulation of the flesh, and not see the good of the righteous? It is indeed an obvious insanity to perish through cunning, and to bring eternal punishment upon one's own neck through deception. But I will advise you, you who [think] poorly...

### Chapter 9.
->Gordius goes to his death with comfort.<-

When the warrior of Christ had said this, he armed himself with the sign of the cross and went happily to his death with great steadfastness of mind, an undaunted face, and in a wondrous appearance. He displayed such joy of heart that it seemed as if he were not in the hands of the beadles <note>original: "Büttel"; the low-ranking officers or executioners' assistants.</note> but in the hands of the angels, who would swiftly bring him to the exalted heaven after death, like Lazarus <note>Referring to the biblical parable where angels carry the beggar Lazarus to paradise.</note>. Thereupon arose such a tumult and shouting of the people that no ordinary storm had ever been heard like it. Such was the nature of this man's death. etc. (\*) Basil the Great <note>original: "Basilius Magnus"; one of the "Great Cappadocians" and an influential 4th-century bishop.</note>, Homily 19 on Gordius. ### Anno 312.(*)
### Chapter 1.

->The Governor of Spain, Eugenius, interrogates Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis under torture, and has them burned.<-

When the wicked and ungodly Governor <term>Eugenius</term> <note>Historical records identify Eugenius as a Roman official who enforced the edicts of the Great Persecution in the Iberian Peninsula.</note> came to <term>Cordoba</term> <note>original: "Cordua"</note>, and rather distressed and tormented the servants of God than terrified them, and commanded them to worship his gods; Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis appeared before him and spoke: "What is your desire, O Eugenius? You who envy the servants of God more than you believe them—that one must serve God alone, name God alone, and give thanks to His infinite eternity!" Then Eugenius the Governor spoke full of anger: "O wretched men! For what do you present yourselves?" Faustus answered: "We are Christians, and confess Christ the only Lord, through whom all things—and we through Him—are created." Eugenius spoke: "For what reasons have you made such a desperate alliance?" Faustus answered: "In us there is no desperation, but only in you alone, you who needlessly compel us to deny God." When Faustus had said this, the Governor spoke even more enraged: "Fasten Faustus to the torture block, he who answers me so irreverently." ## Chapter 2.

->Genesius, a legal clerk or notary at Arles, refuses to transcribe the cruel<-
->commands and escapes.<-

Holy Genesius, then, in his blooming years, became a court official, having practiced with such diligence and art that he could record the judgments of his superiors by means of rapid characters and the swiftness of his right hand (**); which, in a spiritual manner, foreshadowed his future glorification, signifying that he would quickly hear the Divine commandments and faithfully note them in his heart. It happened, however, while he was performing the office of court clerk before the judge's bench, that the most cruel and malicious orders of the persecution were read out; which he, out of fear of God, did not wish to hear, and he refused to transcribe them with his holy hand onto the tablet prepared for that purpose. Accordingly, he threw the same <note>The writing tablet or wax board used for taking notes.</note> at the judge's feet, and his God-devoted soul withdrew from performing such a distressing service. But so that he would not stray in any part from the Evangelical commandments regarding the <term>state of martyrdom</term> <note>original: "Marter-Stand," referring to the specific trials and spiritual status of a martyr.</note>, whereby we Christians are permitted or even commanded to avoid the disaster of persecution, he stepped out of the path of the raging judge's anger for a while, hiding from one place to another and from one city to another; for thus it is written: *The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak!* Matthew 26, v. 41. Now, when the judge ordered that he be sought out and captured everywhere, and they could not easily find him, he commanded the cruel servants of torture to kill him with the sword wherever they might find him.

# 77. St. Leo and Paregorius /
# Patara in Lycia. In the year 312.

## Chapter 1.

->Paregorius was the first to complete his holy struggle.<-

<margin>77. Saint</margin>

There are indeed many cunning schemes with which the devil stalks the servants of God, but the protection of the only-begotten God over His servants is even greater and more significant; for the former does not oppose those who are Christians by nature with flesh and blood, but with spiritual wickedness <note>A reference to Ephesians 6:12, describing spiritual warfare.</note>; yet the help of Christ makes the members of the household of faith even stronger against the devil. This can be sufficiently proven by the enduring patience of the brave-hearted martyrs Leo and Paregorius. For after the blessed Paregorius was first patiently perfected <note>original: "volendet"; in this context, it refers to "finishing the race" or completing the act of martyrdom through death.</note> in the Lord, and after much labor had found the rest of the Heavenly Kingdom, the blessed martyr of Christ, Leo, regarded the struggle which the former had completed as blessed. He grieved greatly that he had not maintained the same struggle alongside him, since they had both walked the same path.

## Chapter 2.

->The blessed martyr Leo shows zeal against idol-worship / leads a secluded life / has a remarkable vision and rebukes the idolaters.<-

In those same days, it happened that the Governor Lollianus, whom the Emperors had appointed, arrived there because the seat of the Governor was at that time still in Patara <note>Patara was a major maritime city in Lycia, known for its temple and oracle of Apollo.</note>. The wicked President or Governor then celebrated the feast day of Serapis <note>Serapis was a Greco-Egyptian deity whose cult was widely promoted by Roman authorities.</note> and gathered the mob of the ungodly, with whom he took counsel against the Christians, wishing to force everyone into the senseless service of idols. As many people ran there and allowed themselves to be led astray out of human fear, the blessed Leo took this very poorly and could not even bear to hear the audacity of the ungodly mentioned. He went, however, with such thoughts to the place where the body of the blessed martyr Paregorius was buried. But in that place, where the ungodly—who were worthy of it—were observing their damnable and godless festival, everyone who saw him recognized that he was a Christian and an honorable man

For in him, everything was <note>original: "wol geartet"; meaning well-disposed or of good character.</note> virtuous. After he had then gone to the aforementioned place <note>likely the burial site of Paregorius mentioned on the previous page</note> and had offered his prayers there in the customary manner, he returned home. Having arrived there and prayed once again according to his habit, he took his rest and remained withdrawn in constant meditation on the excellent conduct of the blessed Paregorius. While he was thus weighing these things in his mind, he fell into a light sleep, so that he might behold his own future glory. For just as the Patriarch Joseph saw what God intended for him <note>See Genesis 37.</note>, so too did the blessed Leo see, through the Holy Spirit, the outcome of his own future events.

It seemed to him, then, that a great storm arose, as if a heavy cloudburst were falling down with great force, and Paregorius stood in the midst of it. Although the rainwater rushed very strongly against him, he nonetheless ran toward the blessed martyr Paregorius, appearing to take his way toward the place of his martyrdom, where he was buried. 

When he awoke from such a vision and considered its meaning within himself, he surmised that which actually came to pass <note>Leo interprets the storm and his journey to Paregorius as a sign that he will soon follow him in martyrdom.</note>. Yet he considered himself no less fortunate for having walked for a time with the blessed Paregorius. Thereupon, he went to the tomb, as if to a faithful fellow-soldier and companion of the struggle; and he did this not in secret, but went there right through the middle of the market and the Tychaeon square <note>The area surrounding the Temple of Tyche, the goddess of fortune.</note>. 

And when he came to the place where the idolatrous rites were being performed, he saw lamps and wax candles burning around the temple of the idol. He truly pitied those who had lit them (*), as deceived souls, and regarded their godlessness as an absurd confidence. # Chapter 3.

->Holy Leo is captured on his return and interrogated by the court.<-

The servants of secret malice gathered a mob of the ungodly and cried out against the holy Leo, saying that he would drive the favor of the Goddess of Fortune away from the city. As the tumult grew and the report of his undertaking ran through the entire city until it reached the ears of the Governor <term>Stadthalter; a Roman provincial official acting as a judge</term> who reigned at that time, he made use of his own wickedness and commanded the soldiers to keep watch until Leo returned and then to take the man captive. 

Leo did indeed return, having already envisioned what would come of it, and raised the eyes of his mind toward God. When the soldiers approached and laid hands on him, he did not resist them, nor did he make any movement; thus they led him away to the President <note>The text uses "Präsidenten" and "Stadthalter" interchangeably to refer to the Roman official.</note>. This man, like a wild and bloodthirsty beast, was full of rage against the martyr and thought to himself that such a deed must by no means be tolerated—that Christians should be so bold as to dare destroy the idols of the heathens. 

When he saw that the blessed Leo was near, he immediately reproached him for the boldness he had shown against the lamps, saying: "It appears, old man, that you either do not know the power of the heavenly gods, since you destroy their religion; or you are senseless, because you defy the commands of our Divine Emperors, who are called our second preservers and gods, and whose deeds are most praiseworthy!" 

The holy Leo replied to this: "You speak, O President, of many heavenly gods who, in truth, do not exist; for there is only one single God in heaven and on earth, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who does not require that men serve Him in such a manner. For a contrite spirit and a soul accustomed to holding itself in humility are held in great esteem by God. But the lamps and wax lights that burn around your images are vain and worthless, because stones, bronze, and wood—from which men have fashioned an image—know nothing of them. If you, O Governor, knew Him who is the true God..."

## Chapter 4.

->After a long defense, he is sentenced to death by being dragged.<-

As the holy Leo testified to this and more besides, and earnestly set forth the foundations of Christianity, the wicked crowd of Jews and heathens <note>original: "Juden und Heyden"</note> cried out and pleaded with the President <note>The "President" refers to the Roman Provincial Governor or *Praeses*</note> that he should not allow him to say whatever he wished. Thereupon the President spoke again to the rabble: "I grant him the power to speak freely, and I promise him general friendship <note>A promise of legal immunity or Imperial favor</note> if he obeys the gods!" 

But the holy Leo said: "If you have perhaps forgotten my words, O President, then you do right to ask such a question again; but if you remember them, then you surely know that it shall never happen that I should consent to worship those as gods who are not so by nature!" At such words, the Governor was moved to anger and commanded that the venerable body of the martyr be scourged with leather straps. 

Even when the number of lashes and wounds was beyond counting, and greater than the human body could endure, the brave warrior of Christ, Leo, did not allow this to trouble him, nor did he let out even the slightest sigh; for he directed his longing toward the Lord. Then the President spoke: "These are but small sufferings, O Leo, which are being inflicted upon you, if I compare them with those yet to follow; therefore obey me, and offer the sacrifices to the gods which are ordained by the law!" 

The holy Leo said: "O judge, what I have already said many times, I do not hesitate to say once more: I do not know these gods, and I will never allow the thought that I should sacrifice to them, for I know the saving laws of the Scripture." Thereupon the President spoke: "Say only this one thing: 'Great are the gods!' and you shall be set free; for I would spare you in respect for your gray hair and your otherwise dignified physical stature!" 

The holy Leo replied: "I say this too: that they are truly great and powerful—at destroying the souls that believe in them." The enraged judge spoke: "I will give the order that you shall be dragged to death over sharp stones!" <note>The punishment of "dragging" (German: *schleifen*) involved being tied to a horse or chariot and pulled across rough terrain until dead.</note> The blessed Leo answered: "Every kind of death is dear to me for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven; for I call it life and [Blessedness—]"

<margin>St. Leo is dragged away and cast down from a rock.</margin>
There, the servants of malice dragged the body of the saint onto a high rock and threw him from above into a deep pit <note>original: "Gruft," here meaning a rocky cleft or hollow</note>; however, the body that fell down was not shattered, but lay there as if it had been laid down with care; and one saw only that he had received small marks of the fall from the roughness of the rock. In such a manner did the brave-hearted Leo, after he had overcome the devil, attain the glorious crown. # 78. St. Julius / at Dorostorum in Moesia or Bulgaria. Anno 312.
<note>Dorostorum is modern-day Silistra, Bulgaria. Moesia was a Roman province in the Balkans.</note>

## Chapter 1.

->Julius, an old soldier <note>original: "Kriegs-Mann"</note>, is judicially interrogated and confesses Christ.<-

At the time of the persecution, when the believers hoped for the blessed reward by means of glorious struggles, Julius was seized by the court officials and presented to the President <note>The Roman Governor</note> Maximus. Maximus spoke: "What do you say, Julius? Is that true of which you are accused?" Julius answered: "Yes, it is so; I am a Christian! I say nothing else of myself than what I am." Maximus spoke: "What will follow from that? Are you not aware of the Imperial command..."

<page-num>580</page-num>

known, which commands that one should offer sacrifices to the gods. <note>The text continues from the previous page's catchword "kant," completing the word "bekant" (known).</note> Julius answered: This is not unknown to me, but I am a Christian, and I cannot do what you have commanded, seeing as I cannot deny my living and true God. Maximus said: What is it for such a great matter, to just offer incense and then go home? Julius answered: I cannot transgress the commandments of God and obey the unfaithful; for while I was still in the lower ranks of military service, in which I wandered <note>The original German "geirret" implies serving or traveling through his terms of duty</note> for twenty-six years, I was never once brought before a military court as a wrongdoer or a brawler. Maximus said: Julius, I see that you are a wise and steady man; therefore, sacrifice to the gods upon my advice. Julius answered: I will not do what you desire, and I will not let myself be plunged into sin and eternal punishment. Maximus said: If you consider this a sin, let the sin be credited to me; I will use force against you so that it does not appear as if you gave your will to it; then you can go home in peace, and you shall receive ten **denarii** (**) or two **Imperial Thalers** every day; moreover, no one shall trouble you further. Julius answered: Neither such money nor your deceptive persuasion can rob me of the eternal light, for I cannot deny the eternal God; therefore, simply pronounce the death sentence against me.

---

(*) *Veteranorum Vexillum* <note>original: "Veteranorum Vexillum"</note> is not better understood than by comparing it to the **Elite Guard**. It was a special banner of 500 old, brave soldiers who had already served 16 years in other legions; they were also called **Veterans** and **Emeriti** <note>original: "Veterani und Emeriti." These terms refer to retired soldiers who had completed their service with honor.</note>. *See Lipsius on Tacitus, Book I of the Annals.* <note>Referencing the scholar Justus Lipsius’s commentary on the Roman historian Tacitus.</note>
(**) The **Veterans** usually received only one **denarius** (a groschen) daily; instead of that, the martyr was to receive [ten times as much] if he would choose to be a hypocrite.

I beseech you, pious President <note>The German "Präsidente" refers to the Roman provincial governor or presiding official.</note>, by the welfare of your Emperors (*), that you carry out your thoughts and pass the death sentence upon me, so that my wish may be fulfilled! **Maximus** said: If you will show no repentance and refuse to sacrifice, then your desire shall be fulfilled. **Julius** answered: I thank you if you do it. **Maximus** said: You hasten toward death; do you surely believe you will gain honor by such a death? **Julius** answered: If I am found worthy to suffer now, then I shall attain eternal glory. **Maximus** said: One should advise you to suffer death for the Fatherland and the laws, so you would have everlasting praise for it. **Julius** said: I am indeed suffering for the laws, but for the Divine ones. **Maximus** said: Surely you mean those which the Crucified and Deceased also gave; see how foolish you are, holding more of a dead man than of the Emperors who live! **Julius** answered: He died for our sins, that He might give us eternal life. But He has remained God for eternity; whoever confesses Him has eternal life, but whoever denies Him shall receive eternal punishment. **Maximus** said: I have compassion for you and give you the advice that you should rather sacrifice and live with us. **Julius** answered: If I live with you, I die; but if I die now, then I live. **Maximus** said: Obey me and sacrifice, so that I need not have you killed according to my promise! **Julius** answered: For that very reason have I prayed so many times—if I am worthy of it—that you would do it. **Maximus** said: Have you then decided that you would rather die than live? **Julius** answered: I have chosen to die for a short time so that I may live eternally! Therefore, **Maximus** the President gave the following sentence: **Julius**, who would not submit to the commands of the Emperors, shall be beheaded!

## at Venafrum in Campania.
### Year 312.
### Chapter 1.

->Marcianus and Nicander are interrogated by the Governor Maximus. The bold confession of Saint Daria.<-

abandoning [all vanity], they proceeded by the grace of Christ toward the heavenly struggle <note>A common metaphor in early Christian texts where martyrdom is viewed as a spiritual "battle" or "contest" (Greek: agon).</note>. Thereupon they were immediately brought before the court, as if they had committed some great crime; where the Governor <note>original: "Präsidente."</note> Maximus, to whom this office had been entrusted, addressed them in the following manner: "Since you are not unaware," he said, "Nicander and Marcianus, of the Emperor's commands which bid you to sacrifice to the gods, step forward and fulfill such a command!" To this Nicander replied: "Such things are commanded of those who find pleasure in sacrificing; but we are Christians, and we do not allow ourselves to be bound by such commands." Maximus said: "Why do you not remain in your service?" <note>Referring to their military service in the Roman army.</note> Nicander said: "Because the money of the ungodly is an abomination to those who wish to serve God." Maximus said: "Only honor the gods with incense, O Nicander!" Nicander replied: "How is it possible that a Christian should be able to worship stone and wood, and forsake the immortal God who created everything from nothing? It is Him we serve, and He is able to preserve me and all who hope in Him." 

However, the wife of the holy Nicander, named Daria, was present there, and she exhorted her own husband with these words, saying: "Guard yourself, my lord, that you do not do this; guard yourself, my lord, that you do not deny our Lord Jesus Christ! Look up into heaven, and there you shall behold the one to whom you keep your loyalty and a good conscience; for He Himself is your helper!" 

But the Governor Maximus said to her: "You wicked vixen <note>original: "böse Haut vom Weibe." A derogatory idiom roughly meaning "evil hide of a woman."</note>, why do you desire that your husband should die?" She gave him this answer: "So that he may live with God and never die again!" Maximus said: "It is not so; rather, it is because you desire a stronger husband that you wish for this one to lose his life quickly." But she gave answer to this again and said: "If you think that I have this in my heart and will do such a thing, then kill me first for Christ’s sake, if you have any such command regarding women." Maximus said: "I have indeed received no such command concerning women, and I do not intend to fulfill your desire; nevertheless, you shall be taken to the dungeon."

...ordered [this] to be done, and as a great multitude of people filled the place, he raised his voice in the following manner and spoke: "Fire and water have the same Author as the human race; the almighty and eternal God created all these things out of nothing through his only-begotten Son. From fire, indeed, he commanded that the light, the sun, and the remaining shining stars should come forth, and he ordered them to shine partly by day and partly by night; for his power to act extends as far as his will. From water, however, he made the firmament <term>Veste des Himmels</term> <note>The "firmament" refers to the ancient cosmological view of the sky as a solid dome or "fortress" that separated the waters of the heavens from the earth.</note> of heaven, and upon the waters he made the earth solid. In both of these, with his diligent and provident power, he wrought everything which he knew that the humans he was soon to form could not do without. 

Because he also knew beforehand that humans would offend their Creator and Lord, and after rejecting the true Divine Being would serve fashioned images <note>Referring to idols or statues of pagan gods.</note>, he moreover prepared two dwelling-places. One of these shines full of eternal light, which he has filled with all the most excellent goods; the other, however, is filled with everlasting darkness and a never-ending fire of discipline for everlasting punishment. This was done so that those who please him and are obedient to his word might, after the resurrection, obtain the dwelling of the good and live in eternal light; but those who deserve his wrath through an arrogant life would be cast into the darkness for all punishment and everlasting torment. 

In dividing the fire from the water and the light from the darkness, just as he created each one specially, he also assigned to them special containers and places. The firmament of heaven is above the earth, while fire and water are beneath it. The water that is gathered together upon the earth is called the sea; but that which is inside the earth is called the abyss <note>Original: *Abgrund*.</note>, from which it wells up for the use of the human race upon the earth as if from certain spigots <note>Original: *Zapfen*.</note> or pipes. From this also arise the healing springs <term>Gesund-Brunnen</term> and baths. Those which are far removed from the subterranean fire are cold through Divine favorable providence; but those which have flowed closer past that fire well up boiling hot. In some places, lukewarm waters are also found, according as they are further separated from the fire. The subterranean fire is destined for the torment of godless souls; and—

## Chapter 2.

After further testimony, St. Patricius is sentenced to death and thrown into the hot water without harm; finally, he is beheaded.

Thereupon the President <note>The Roman provincial governor.</note> spoke: "Is Christ then the author of these things?" Patricius answered: "Yes, Christ; for it is written that all things were made through him. <note>John 1:3</note> And that the gods of the heathens are unclean spirits; but the Lord has made the heavens. <note>Psalm 96:5</note>" The President spoke again: "Do you say that Christ made the heavens?" Patricius answered: "I certainly say so, according to what is written: I shall see the heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you have prepared. <note>Psalm 8:3-4</note>" The President spoke hereupon: "If I then have you plunged into these hot baths, because you despise the gods and hold Christ to be their author, will he not surely prevent you from being killed by the heat?" Patricius spoke: "I do not despise the gods, who are not even in existence; for no one can despise that which is nothing. But concerning Christ, know that he can certainly preserve me if he wills; yet he also has the power, if he wills, to dissolve the bond of my mortal life through these baths. For know, as far as I am concerned and what shall happen to me, he knows it beforehand and it is not hidden from him; indeed, he is present in all things in such a way that without his will and decree <note>original: "Raht-Schluß" (counsel or divine decree)</note>, not a single hair can fall from a single person's head, nor does a bird fall into a snare. And of this which I say, all are assured that it is the pronouncement of Truth itself; those, however, who together with you worship stones, are reserved for the Abyss,

and dedicated therein to eternal punishment. When the President <note>The Roman provincial governor.</note> heard this, he was greatly enraged and commanded that he should be thrown naked into the boiling-hot spring water! As he was being plunged into it, he cried out and prayed:

> O Lord Jesus Christ, stand by your servant!

By profession he was a gardener, and he possessed this garden outside the gate of the city, not far from the sea; there he worked diligently to provide for his own needs and for the comfort of others. But he also hosted strangers in his poor and small little house with a joyful and willing heart. And because he lived on the public highway, he offered to those arriving whatever they required; thus he was a Lot—not indeed in Sodom, but among the heathens in Sinope. <note>A reference to the biblical figure Lot, who was known for his righteous hospitality toward strangers in the wicked city of Sodom.</note> In time, this did not remain unrewarded, for through his hospitality he found the opportunity for a blessed and living death. How this came to pass, I will relate in greater detail.

### Chapter 2.

->He is sought during the time of persecution / and the soldiers who seek him / lodge with him.<-

When the word of Christian godliness rang in every ear, making Christ and His mysteries known, the heathens raged (as the Psalmist speaks) and the kings and princes gathered together; <note>original: "Ps. 2, v. 1." Referring to Psalm 2:1: "Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?"</note> the peoples wandering in error were angered that Christ reigned. All Christians were sought out as if they were wicked men; whomever they found was punished, and whoever remained hidden was scouted out. For this reason, Phocas could not remain hidden despite his humble profession and gardener’s life, but was denounced as a true disciple of Christ. Accordingly, those men came to him who had orders to tear him away from this transitory and miserable life, without any legal order or defense. For his "crime" was of such a nature <margin>n.</margin> that this brave-hearted man confessed it with a clear voice, and even without being questioned, he carried it out through his way of life; yet upon being questioned, he testified to it with great joy. Thus his catchpolls <note>original: "Büttel," meaning bailiffs or low-ranking officers sent to make an arrest.</note> arrived—the very ones who would cause our festival today—and they lodged with him, unaware of who he was; for they did not know him, nor did he know them. However, they concealed the reason for their arrival so that once they had heard from those living outside the <margin>Sino-</margin> city who Phocas was and where he lived, they might then suddenly fall upon him, just as the Jews formerly seized the Lord in the garden upon the instruction of Judas. But they did not know that they already had the prey in their net, the sheep among the dogs, the lamb among the wolves, and the dove in the talons of the birds of prey;

## Chapter 2.
### The Sacristan’s Tale of the Schoolmaster Cassian and His Sentencing.

This martyr was a teacher of the youth who instructed many children in reading and writing, showing them how to compose whole words quickly with certain signs <note>This refers to an early form of shorthand or stenography used in the Roman world, known as Tironian notes.</note>, so that they could write as fast as a person spoke. His often strict commands and perceived offenses seemed a terrifying thing to the uneducated youth, for which they secretly fumed; for a teacher is usually a source of annoyance to a student, because discipline is displeasing to the young. 

Look! At that time, when a heavy persecution oppressed the faith and Christians were being extremely persecuted, this schoolman was dragged out from the midst of his company and placed before the court. Because he then refused to sacrifice to the gods, the judge consulted with his assessors as to what kind of punishment they should inflict upon this rebellious spirit. The decision was reached as follows: "Because he has led the tender youth astray, take him captive and hand this disciplinarian over to the boys, so that they may mock and tear him apart as they please, and stain their hands with the blood of their seductive teacher." "It pleases us," the judge further spoke, "that the strict teacher should now become a mockery to those whom he previously held in check with harsh words of threat!" Consequently, his hands were bound behind his back after he had been stripped naked, and he was handed over to the ill-will of the godless pagan youth.

## Chapter 3.
### The Wicked Boys Stab Their Teacher Cassian with Sharp Styli.

These boys were then ready with their sharp <term>writing-styli</term> (**) <note>original: "Solche Schreibe-Griffeln waren von Eisen..." These styli were made of iron, about a span (nine inches) long, pointed and sharp at one end for writing in wax; with the other end, which featured a flat knob, they smoothed the wax to erase errors.</note>, and as much secret poison as each had harbored in his heart...

harbored, he now poured out freely with a bitter spirit. Some took their boxwood writing tablets and threw them at his face, so that they broke against his forehead and were soaked with his blood; others took the pointed ends of their styluses <note>A stylus was a metal or bone tool used for writing on wax-covered tablets; one end was sharp for carving letters, and the other was flat for erasing.</note>, with which they usually wrote in wax, and wounded the Confessor of Christ <note>A "Confessor" is one who maintains their faith under torture without denying it.</note> with them—some stabbing deep into his intestines, others only through the skin. Yet their evil will lacked enough force, and the more they grew weary, the more his martyrdom was prolonged.

## Chapter 4.

->They mock and torture him until he finally gives up his spirit.<-

One villain, however, began to mock him and cried: "Why do you sigh? Are you not our master, who taught us how to use the stylus and placed it in our hands himself? We now give back to you as many letters and signs as we learned from you while standing and weeping <note>It was common in Roman schools for students to stand while the teacher sat, often under the threat of the rod.</note>. You must not be angry while we are writing, for you yourself previously commanded us that we should never be idle; we demand no holidays or break-hours now, which you so often denied us; it pleases us to write in this way; if we do not make the lines straight, then you correct what the hand misses. Prove your authority now; you have the power to punish us if anyone happens to write too slowly!" In this way, these boys mocked their schoolmaster and tormented the poor man with slow agony; until finally the Lord Christ took pity on him and commanded the bonds of his life to be loosed, so that he gradually began to give up his spirit in his final throes; the blood, which flowed copiously from the many wounds, left his heart, and his pulse ceased to beat, until he finally passed away. This, dear guest, is the meaning of this image and the glorification of Cassian, according to Prudentius' *On the Crowns*, Hymn 9, also known as 12 <note>original: "Prudent. de Coronis Hymn. 9. al. 12." Prudentius was a 4th-century Christian poet.</note>.

83. Of the holy Martyrs

# 83. Of the holy Martyrs in the East / under the tyrant Licinius
### Anno 318–323.

## Chapter 1.

->On the peace of the Churches under Constantine / and the unrest<-
->of Licinius in the East.<-

In the tenth year of the reign of Emperor *Constantine* the Great, festivals and days of joy were celebrated by the Church because of the general state of peace. Praise and thanks were offered to the King of all <note>Referring to God as the "universal King."</note>, which were not ignited by any outward fire or incense <note>A contrast to pagan sacrifices; the author suggests Christian worship is spiritual rather than physical.</note>. While the pious Emperor took his highest pleasure in this, no small sorrow was brought to him by the news of the great disruption and unrest in the East. For it was announced to him how a certain fierce, wild beast <note>original: "wüste Bestie"; a metaphorical reference to the Emperor Licinius.</note> was cunningly stalking both the Church of God and his other subjects. At that time, the Devil was exerting all his evil powers to undo the good that Emperor *Constantine* had begun.

Thus, one could clearly see how the Roman Empire, divided under a twofold government (*Licinius* and *Constantine*), stood in dark night under the former, but in the bright light of day under the latter. Those in the East sat, as it were, in darkness, while the bright sun shone upon the subjects of this [Western] part. Such enjoyment of infinite goodness, which Divine providence had granted them, could neither be endured with patience by the envious enemy of all good, the Devil, nor by the tyrant who possessed and oppressed that part of the empire. Although he [Licinius] had enjoyed a prosperous reign and a marriage with the virtuous sister of the excellent Emperor *Constantine*, and followed her conduct, he instead pursued the wicked customs and way of life of the previous ungodly Emperors. He had seen their miserable ends with his own eyes; nevertheless, he preferred to imitate their malicious spirit rather than remain in the steadfast friendship of an excellent man.

<meta>The catchword "harren" (to wait/remain) indicates the text continues Licinius's failure to remain faithful to his alliance.</meta>

under Licinius / Year 318–323.

## Chapter 2.

->*Licinius forbids the Christians all types of assembly and councils.*<-

For after much deception and trickery, he finally began an open war against God himself and Emperor Constantine, his faithful friend and brother-in-law <note>Licinius was married to Constantine's half-sister, Constantia.</note>. At the very first, he sought out malicious and falsely fabricated causes against the servants of God, who were subject to his rule and had never undertaken anything against his government. But because he could find no guilt, and did not know what to accuse them of, he had a law proclaimed to the effect that the bishops of his territory should not take counsel in spiritual matters with the other bishops under Constantine, nor should anyone be allowed to travel to neighboring communities to hold meetings (<term>councils</term> <note>original: "Concilia"</note> and <term>synods</term> <note>original: "Synodus"</note>), consultations, or deliberations on things that served their best interests. This was intended to serve as an opportunity for him to treat us insolently and shamefully; for we were forced either to disregard the given law and submit to punishment, or to obey such a command and subvert the customs and order of the Church; since great and important matters in disputed cases can only be resolved through just counsel and wise deliberations. However, the enemy of God, Licinius, had specifically resolved to act in direct opposition to the decrees of the pious Emperor Constantine, and for that reason had issued such a command against us; for while the latter [Constantine] wished to provide guidance toward peace and harmony through the establishment of <term>councils</term> (*) among the priests of God—whose honor they holily sought and whom he wished to help glorify—the former [Licinius] sought to hinder such a good purpose, and to interrupt and tear apart the unity of the churches.

## Chapter 3.

->*Licinius removes all Christians from the court; forbids the assembly of both sexes in the churches.*<-

Since, therefore, this favorite of God [Constantine] kindly received the servants of God into his palace, that enemy of God, with a contrary mind, drove all the pious who obeyed his other commands out of his palace; he also banished into misery his most faithful servants and those who wished him well; likewise those...

83. Of the Holy Martyrs

[Those] who, because of their magnificent deeds, were placed in great [offices] and dignities by him, now had to [stand among] others and perform menial tasks. At [first], he took their goods for the sake of his own gain; [afterward], he threatened them with death if they would confess the saving [name] of Christ. Furthermore, because his mind was deranged and abandoned to all unchastity, committing countless adulteries and shameful deeds, he [denied] that any human being could possess the exceptional virtue of chastity, and he judged the nature of other people according to his own vice-ridden mind. For this reason, [he issued] a law for the second time, stating that men should not assemble with women in the churches for prayer (*); and the female sex should not go to the honorable school of virtue, nor should the bishops explain the holy words of God to the female sex, but women should choose some from among themselves to instruct them. But because such things were laughed at by all, he devised something else for the destruction of the churches: he wanted the people to hold their usual assemblies outside the city gates in an open field, for he claimed the air outside was much healthier and more beneficial than in the temples within the city.

# Chapter 4.

-> Furthermore, Emperor Licinius dismisses all Christian soldiers and officers <-
-> from service / and forbids works of love. <-

Since no one wanted to follow him in this, he [commanded] that the military servants in the city, if they would in no way sacrifice to the devils <note>original: "Teufeln"; a common term used by early Christian writers to refer to pagan gods or idols</note>, should be dismissed from their office. In such a way, whole troops of armed men were deprived of their honors, and the tyrant who commanded such things, through his own actions, completely deprived [himself] of the prayers of holy men. What more shall I say? He gave an order that no one should refresh those who were miserably plagued in prison with a generous hand of necessity <note>meaning basic provisions like food, water, or clothing</note>, nor take pity on those who were languishing in bonds; indeed, he held that if one were by nature compassionate toward their neighbor, they must not be counted among the good, nor that such a person [should be esteemed...]

One sees here the [crafty] snake <note>A reference to the Devil or a deceitful person</note> under the cover of chastity.

## Chapter 5.
### His Tyranny at Amasia in Pontus.

What was undertaken by him at Amasia in Pontus <note>Amasia was a city in the Roman province of Pontus, now part of modern-day Turkey.</note> surpassed all other cruelty. There, he had those churches which had already been torn down once before razed to the ground a second time; others were locked by the governors so that no one could hold an assembly there or serve God as they wished. But he who issued such a command did not believe that people prayed for him there—which his evil conscience convinced him of—but rather he thought that God was being called upon solely for the welfare of Constantine. <note>Constantine and Licinius were rivals; Licinius became paranoid that the Christians in his territory were a "fifth column" supporting his political enemy in the West.</note> His flatterers, and those who had decided to hypocritically praise him, had the most excellent leaders of the congregations executed, because they knew they were doing the tyrant a pleasing service. Consequently, these innocent people, like blood-stained murderers, were led without cause to the place of judgment and cruelly killed; some of whom suffered a new kind of death, being chopped into small pieces and, after such cruel torture, thrown into the depths of the sea as food for the fish. The pious servants of God thus fled, as had happened shortly before, into the countryside and hid themselves in the wilderness. When the tyrant saw that everything was succeeding according to his wish, he resolved to let the persecution fall upon everyone. <term>Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book 1, chapter 44, etc.; Book 2, chapter 2.</term>

## Chapter 6.
### The History of Bishop Paul.

Before others, Paul, Bishop of Neo-Caesarea <note>A fortress city located on the Euphrates river.</note>, had to feel the wrath of Licinius, because he had not ceased to instruct all believers, both women and men. The tyrant had him captured and, as a mockery, had his genitals burned with a glowing iron, and likewise...

## Chapter 7.
->The History of the War-Secretary Auxentius.<-

Among those whom Emperor Licinius dismissed and banished from the court was also the War-Secretary Auxentius. The occasion was as follows: In a courtyard of the palace, there was a fountain, and upon it was placed an image of Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine and revelry.</note>; likewise, a large grapevine spread out wide and shaded the place. When Licinius once went there for his pleasure, and Auxentius followed him along with many other courtiers, the Emperor looked at the grapevine and saw a large and ripe cluster of grapes hanging from the vine; he ordered Auxentius to cut it off. He immediately drew the dagger which he carried at his side and cut the cluster, suspecting no ill. But Licinius said to him: "Lay the cluster at the feet of Bacchus." Auxentius [shuddered] at this and gave the answer: "Far be it from me, Emperor, for I am a Christian!" Then Licinius replied and said: "Then be gone, and lay down your office; for you must necessarily do one of these two." He [lost] not a moment, untied his sash <note>original: *Scherve*. This refers to the *cingulum militia*, a belt or sash that symbolized official Roman military or civil rank; removing it was a formal act of resignation.</note>, and went immediately out of the palace; but the elders chose him not long afterward to be the Bishop of Mopsuestia. This man's younger brother was Theodore, who learned worldly wisdom <note>original: *Welt-Weisheit*, meaning philosophy and the liberal arts.</note> in Athens, and afterward became the bishop of Tarsus. Suidas under the entry "Auxentius." <note>original: *Svidas in verbo Auxentius*. Referring to the *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note>

## Chapter 8.
### The History of the Lion-Keeper Arsacius.

Arsacius, a Persian and a soldier who had oversight of the Emperor's lions, became at that time a glorious confessor <note>In the early church, a "confessor" was someone who remained steadfast in their faith despite persecution and suffering, though they did not die a martyr's death.</note> and was forced to leave the court and his service. Thereupon, he retired to the castle at Nicomedia <note>The city of Nicomedia (modern-day İzmit, Turkey) served as a temporary capital of the Roman Empire.</note> and led a secluded, holy life there. Here, it was revealed to him through a divine vision that he should depart from that place so that he might escape the misfortune that was imminent for the location. After this warning, he went early to the church and warned the clergy that they should pray earnestly and diligently to God to quench His wrath, so that the destruction facing the city might be turned away from it. However, when he could not persuade them and they laughed at him, he indicated to them once more that the misfortune would strike them when they least expected it, and he returned again to the castle. There, he lay on his face upon the earth, pleading with God to avert the evil!

In the meantime, a powerful earthquake arose, causing the houses in the city to collapse and killing many people; those who remained, however, fled to the countryside and the wilderness. Because the city was large and wealthy, fires had been lit in all the houses before the earthquake—in the kitchens, ovens, and baths, and by all those whose profession required a fire. When the houses collapsed, the flames caught the dry woodwork as well as the abundant oil and fat, which burn easily, and continued to grow until the entire city stood in full flame like a single funeral pyre. And because no one dared to venture near in such misery, some of those who had escaped the earthquake ran to the castle, which lay outside the city.

Arsacius, however, lay in the tower—which still stood undamaged in the middle of the fortress—on his face, just as he had thrown himself down in prayer, and was found dead. The story goes that he had previously asked God that He would rather kill him than let him witness the misfortune of the city in which he had first come to know Christ and had grasped the foundation of Christian doctrine. By means of the great love of God that was in him, he could drive out evil spirits and free those possessed by them; for when a man tormented by the devil ran about the market with a drawn sword, and everyone fled from the man, and a great tumult arose in the city, Arsacius went toward him and named Chri-

This was recounted by those who heard it from people who had seen Arsacius with their own eyes. *Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, Book 4, Chapter 15.*

## Chapter 9.
->The History of General Theodore, as well as<-
->Archäus, Narcissus, and Marcellinus.<-

Theodore, the Emperor's General over the Mariandyni <note>An ancient tribe in Bithynia, Asia Minor</note>, was a brave man who resided at Heraclea in Pontus and was summoned to the court by Licinius. When he arrived and was entertained in the Emperor’s palace, Theodore took the silver idols which he found there, broke them into pieces, and distributed the silver to the poor. Although Licinius held this man in high esteem, he nevertheless had him cruelly tortured for this deed. He had him crucified and ordered long, sharp awls <note>A small pointed tool used for piercing holes</note> to be thrust into the secret passages of his body, and finally had him beheaded. His body was afterwards carried with great pomp to Euchaita, his fatherland, where a chapel was built in his honor. *Nicephorus, Book 7, Chapter 44.*

At Tomis in Pontus <note>Modern-day Constanța, Romania</note> is the memorial of the three brothers Archäus, Narcissus, and Marcellinus; the latter was still a youth and, under the Emperor Licinius, was forced to take up military service. Since he did not wish to go to war, they beat him until he bled and tormented him for a long time in prison, until they finally drowned him in the sea and thus put an end to his martyrdom. His brothers, however, were beheaded with the sword. *Martyrology.*

## Chapter 10.
->Of the Forty Martyrs at Sebaste.<-

At that time, when the Emperor Licinius's command was issued that his military men should sacrifice to the gods, he did not trust the Christians who were among them, fearing they might take the side of his adversary Constantine and go over to him during battle;

Forty men stepped forward boldly and fearlessly and confessed that they were Christians. Each was then asked specifically for his name and religion, but they would know of no other name or faith than that of Christ. The President <note>likely the provincial governor or magistrate</note> was in doubt whether he should bring them to obedience with sharp or gentle words. Initially, he indeed tried with gentleness, to see if he might break their supposed stubbornness:

-> “You brave, vigorous men,” he spoke, “do not destroy your own welfare, and do not exchange this sweet and pleasant life for an untimely death; for it would surely be shameful that those who are accustomed to performing heroic deeds in war should die like the common rabble!” <-

Furthermore, he promised them money and offices of honor under the Emperor, and he tempted them with a thousand other kinds of cunning. As they were not moved by any of this, he began to threaten them with plagues, manifold tortures, and death. But the martyrs cared as little for one as for the other, and testified that all he promised was but a small thing of the world, which they had entirely renounced; heaven was much greater and more glorious than he could perceive with his eyes, for therein lay the eternal and imperishable good; and for the sake of love and faith in God, they were ready to endure all torture. At this, the pompous judge became highly enraged and began to deliberate how he might execute them in the most cruel manner; and because it was winter and the nights were longest, he sentenced them to stand entirely naked in a frozen lake outside the city up to their necks, and when they had frozen stiff, they were then to be burned. The martyrs were then led there; when they saw the place, they became joyful, took off their clothes, and said to one another:

-> “Now we strip off our clothes along with the old man <note>A reference to the “old self” or sinful nature mentioned in the New Testament, specifically Ephesians 4:22</note>; thanks be to You, O Lord, that we are rid of the burden of sin, which we put on because of the serpent <note>Referring to the Fall of Man in the Garden of Eden</note> and now lay aside again for Christ's sake; let our sacrifice be acceptable to You, O Lord, for the sake of Your own suffering and nakedness!” <-

With these and similar words, they went briskly into the frozen water, stood therein the whole night, and laughed at the enemy. There were, as mentioned, forty of them in number; but one of them abandoned his post, and thereby caused the others the most unbearable pain. Nearby was a warm bath-house, to which the appointed guards...

to bring those who were commanded to be there, namely those who wished to fall away <note>original: "abfallen," meaning to renounce their Christian faith</note>; Now, when this unfortunate man arrived there and entered the [warm] water to refresh himself, he suddenly died a wretched death. But the martyrs were burned to ashes, and then the ashes were thrown into the water; their spirits, however, shine with crowns of honor in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be honor and dominion for all eternity. # 84. St. Glaphyra and Basileus
# at Amasea and Nicomedia.
### In the Year 321.

### Chapter 1.

-> Licinius’s wicked life is reported by his wife to her brother, Constantine the Great. <-

In addition to his shameful idolatry, Licinius <note>Valerius Licinianus Licinius, Roman Emperor from 308 to 324 AD</note> was also devoted to carnal impurity and fornication; he dishonored the most noble matrons before everyone's eyes, and spared neither mothers nor daughters in his unrestrained lust

History of Martyrs / Year 321.

Moreover, he did not cease to impose infinite hardships upon all his subjects. When his wife Constantia, the biological sister of the Emperor Constantine, saw and heard this and could no longer bear it, she secretly sent letters to her brother Constantine—the pious man and friend of God—wherein she made known to him what Licinius had dared to undertake against both the Christians and all his subjects; how he had abandoned the previously accepted Christian faith, surrendered himself again to pagan superstition, and, as an enemy of God, had banished all Christians from his palace, thereby visibly stripping himself of Christ’s divine protection (*).

## Chapter 2.
->Glaphyra, the Empress's Lady-in-Waiting, saves her honor through flight<-

While Licinius continued such things daily, it happened that a lady-in-waiting—one of those who attended and served the Queen—who was of Christian descent, well-bred, and of a chaste mind, named Glaphyra, learned of the aforementioned impure matters. Licinius desired to violate her <note>original: "zur Schändung verlanget," referring to sexual assault or dishonoring</note>, at which she was greatly terrified. However, so that she would not be dismissed by her mistress due to jealousy or suspicion, she revealed this secret to the Queen, saying: "The Emperor intends to do such-and-such to me; for Benignus, His Majesty's chamberlain, revealed it to me, thinking he was bringing me pleasant news worthy of a reward. Therefore, I implore Your Majesty by God, the Lord of Heaven and Earth—whom Your Majesty yourself fears, just as the Emperor Constantine does—that Your Majesty would not permit me to be defiled and robbed of my virginity!" When the Queen heard this and received the maiden’s upright mind very graciously, she hid her, first under the pretext that she had fallen into a melancholy <note>original: "Melancholey," a historical term for a state of deep sadness or depression</note>; and finally,

---

(*) The Co-Emperors <note>original: "Neben-Kayser"</note>—such as Licinius was—were subordinate to the rightful Emperor, who chose them as co-regents due to the vast size of the Roman Empire at that time. They were called "Kings" <note>original: "Reges"</note> by the writers, while the true Emperors were called "Commanders" <note>original: "Imperatores"</note> and "the Greatest" <note>original: "Maximi"</note>—that is, the highest Emperors—such as Constantine. Consequently, Constantine had to watch as Licinius overthrew everything good concerning his subjects. Constantine, however, was a pious and God-fearing lord, in keeping with the opportunities provided by the teachers of that time; he only lacked upright leaders.

## Chapter 3.

->They arrive at Amasea and are received by Quintius.<-

Through Divine Providence, they reached the city of Amasea, the capital city in the province of Pontus <note>A historical region on the southern coast of the Black Sea, in modern-day Turkey</note>. This place pleased Glaphyra so much that she commanded her servants to inquire whether there were Christians in the place, as she would be inclined to remain there. A certain servant of Quintius—a prominent man of that place—happened to hear that this company were Christians, as they were asking if there were also Christians in the city. He reported this to his master, Quintius, who immediately went to them and requested that they might be pleased to come into his house and stay there; for he too was a Christian, and there was a Christian Bishop in the city who was an extraordinary man, worthy of being compared to the Apostles. Thus, they obeyed his words and moved into a part of his house; they remained thereafter with the aforementioned nobleman Quintius.

### Chapter 5.

->She supports the Bishop’s church construction with her fortune and writes to Queen Constantia.<-

At that very time, the Bishop was occupied with building a temple <note>The author uses "Tempel" to refer to a church building</note> for the assembly of the churches; for until then, the Christians in Amasea had possessed no such temple (*); the chaste virgin Glaphyra, however, gave much gold and silver for this temple construction—indeed, she spent almost her entire fortune on that which the blessed Bishop commanded. She also wrote to her mistress, the Queen, stating where she was at present and with whom she was staying; she also reported the circumstances of the holy building, with the request that she might send more money for the complete finishing of the temple construction. This the sister of the great Constantine <note>Queen Constantia, wife of Licinius and sister of Constantine the Great</note> did gladly, and sent more money and gifts; she also wrote a letter in her own hand to the Bishop, in which she faithfully commended the virgin to him (**).

### Chapter 6.

->Glaphyra’s situation is revealed to Licinius; while the command for her and the Bishop’s imprisonment is issued, she dies.<-

After some time had passed, it happened through the cunning of the evil spirit that Glaphyra’s letter to the Queen fell into the hands of Benignus—of whom we spoke before. When he had read it and understood that Glaphyra was still alive and was staying with a certain man in Amasea, he revealed this to King Licinius. The King became almost maddened with rage at this and immediately sent a command to the Governor <note>original: "Präsidenten," likely the Roman "Praeses" or provincial governor</note> in the province of Pontus, in which he ordered that the Bishop Basileus, together with Glaphyra, should be bound with iron chains and sent to him. Through Divine Providence, however, it happened that before the King’s letter reached the hands of the Governor, Glaphyra departed from this earthly life <note>original: "dieses Zeitliche gesegnete," a common German idiom for dying</note>.

# Chapter 7.

->Bishop Basileus is led as a prisoner to Nicomedia.<-

When the corrupt and heartless governor <note>original: "Präsident," referring here to the provincial governor or local Roman official</note> received the King's command, he took the holy Bishop Basileus prisoner and sent him, bound in iron chains, to the King. ### The 1st Chapter.

->*The Persian Magi and Jews instigate a persecution / and accuse Archbishop Simeon.*<-

<margin>(*) Eusebius and Jerome testify that there had already been Christians in Persia since the time of the Apostles; and Bardesanes, who lived around the year 170, mentions the Christians of his time in Persia, who had spread to such an extent that in this persecution alone sixteen thousand names of the martyrs were known, but of the unnamed there was an innumerable multitude. <note>original: vid.
