After the number of Christians in Persia grew from time to time(*), and they gathered congregations everywhere that were provided with priests and deacons, this business weighed heavily on the hearts of the Persian <term>Magi|The Magi were a hereditary caste of Zoroastrian priests in ancient Persia who served as advisors to the kings and guardians of the state religion.</term> or priests of idols; these were as it were a priestly nation who, from generation to generation, had administered the Persian religion from the beginning. It also provoked the Jews, who, out of an implanted envy, are by nature enemies of the Christian religion. These two parties then accused **Simeon**, the Archbishop of **Seleucia** and **Ctesiphon**—which are very prominent cities of Persia—before the then-King of Persia, **Sapor II**, claiming that he was a secret friend of the Roman Emperor and betrayed Persian affairs to him. When he had said this, the King commanded him to worship the sun (*), promising to give him great gifts and to hold him in high honor, while also threatening to exterminate the entire race of Christians. But when he could neither frighten him with threats nor bend him with promises, but Simeon testified with a steadfast mind that he would neither worship the sun nor abandon his religion, the King commanded that he be kept in prison, with the intention, as it seems, that he might yet change his mind.

## The 3rd Chapter.

### Saint Simeon is beheaded along with a hundred other bishops and priests.

On the following day, which was a **Saturday** <note>original: "Sonabend." In older German, this specifically refers to the day before Sunday.</note>, the day before the Feast of the Resurrection on which the annual memorial of the salutary suffering is celebrated <note>This refers to Great Saturday or Holy Saturday during Holy Week.</note>, the King also had Simeon beheaded. For after he had been led again from the prison into the Royal palace, he constantly defended the religion before the King *in person* <note>original Latin: "corpore"</note>, and would bow idolatrously neither before him nor before the sun. On that same day, another hundred prisoners were killed in the same way; among all of whom Simeon was the last to be beheaded—after he had watched their murder—of whom some were bishops, others priests, and clergy of various ranks.

As they were all now led to the place of judgment, the High Priest of the Idols and Prince of the Persian Sages <note>original: "Persischen Weisen." This refers to the Magi, the Zoroastrian priestly class who held significant political power in the Sassanid Empire.</note> stepped into their midst and asked them whether they had a desire to live, and would accept the King’s religion and worship the sun?

But as none among them wished to live under such a condition, they were led to the appointed place of execution; there the executioners did indeed what they were commanded, and labored through the killing of the martyrs <note>original: "in dem Todten der Märtyrer sichs saur werden liessen"—literally "let it become sour for them," a German idiom meaning they found the mass execution to be grueling or arduous work.</note>. **Simeon**, however, stood near those who were being killed and exhorted them to remain steadfast; he spoke therein of death and resurrection, and of godliness. He also showed from the testimony of Holy Scripture that to die in such a manner was the true life, but to deny **God** out of despair was certain death. They must, he argued, even if no one did them violence, die naturally not long after; for this life comes to an end for all people. What follows after this life, however, is not the same for all, but each will be exactly repaid according to their works: where those who walked well have an immortal reward to expect, but those who lived poorly must suffer eternal punishment. Furthermore, among good works, the highest and most blessed is to suffer death voluntarily for **God**. 

As **Simeon** said this, all listened to him diligently, as to a practiced exhorter in the spiritual combat, and went joyfully to their deaths. After the executioner had killed the hundred, he also finally beheaded **Simeon**, and with him **Abdechalaam** and **Annian**, who had both been old priests in the congregation of **Simeon**, and had both been captured and thrown into prison along with him.

As he said this, he was seized at that very hour and led to the King. And because he confessed himself a Christian, and delivered a bold testimony before the King regarding Christian doctrine and the martyrs, this was interpreted as an outrage <note>original: "Frevel"</note>, and he was therefore [treated] in a new and cruel...

### Chapter 5.

->Among many others, Azades, a eunuch, is also executed.<-

In the following year, on the very same day when the memory of Christ’s suffering is celebrated <note>original: "Gedächtniß des Leidens Christi." This refers to Good Friday.</note> and the festival of the Resurrection is at the door, the most cruel edict of Shapur <note>original: "Saporis." This is Shapur II, the Sasanian King of Kings who ruled for 70 years and oversaw a major persecution of Christians as a "fifth column" aligned with the newly Christianized Roman Empire.</note> was proclaimed throughout all of Persia, which announced the death penalty for all who confessed to being Christians. At such a time, as the report goes, an innumerable multitude of Christians were executed with the sword. For the Magi <note>original: "Magi." These were the Zoroastrian priestly class who served as judges and advisors in the Persian Empire.</note> also diligently sought out through all cities and villages those who kept themselves hidden; although many Christians voluntarily gave themselves up without a guide, so that it might not seem they wished to deny **Christ** through their silence. As all Christians were being killed without any mercy, many in the royal palace were also executed, among whom was **Azades**, a eunuch <note>original: "Verschnittener." In the Persian court, eunuchs often held high-ranking and trusted administrative positions.</note>, who had been very dear to the King. Therefore the King, when he heard of his death, felt such unbelievable pain that he even had the general persecution of the Christians lifted, and commanded only the teachers of the Christian law to be killed.

The Queen then, in the manner of the sick, who give approval to the most disgusting cures, held this accusation to be true, especially because the Jews said it, as she was a born Jewess. # 86. St. Tarbula or Pherbuthe, in Persia. Year 345.

## The 1st Chapter.

*Tarbula or Pherbuthe is captured along with her sister and maidservant, and accused of being sorceresses.*

During the time of the persecution, the Queen of Persia suddenly fell ill; she was particularly well-disposed toward the Jews, who are enemies of the cross of Christ, and she gladly obeyed everything they said. When the Jews came to the Queen, they convinced her of this: because Bishop Simeon—surnamed Gnapheus <note>original: "Gnapheus"; a Greek-derived name meaning "The Fuller" or cloth-cleaner</note>—had been killed, his sisters had supposedly bewitched the Queen in order to kill her. When such talk reached the King's ears, the holy Pherbuthe, along with her sister and maidservant, was immediately taken prisoner. This Pherbuthe was a model of virtuous female warriors <note>meaning spiritual "athletes" or champions of the faith</note>; likewise, her sister had attained an excellent way of life in Christ Jesus. Thus, they were led to the royal palace so they might be questioned about the matter. Then, by the King's command, there came forth the <term>Mauptes</term> <note>a title for a high-ranking Zoroastrian priest, likely a corruption of the word "Mobad"</note>, a word which signifies a "Pope of the sorcerers" or idol-priests (High Priest of the Magi <note>original Latin: "Pontifex Magorum"</note>), together with two officials, so that they might judicially interrogate these women. 

When the holy Pherbuthe stood before them with the other two who were with her, they saw her beauty; for the holy virgin was truly of an exceptionally beautiful form. Immediately, each of them burned with lust for her in their shameful minds, yet they secretly hid their impure thoughts within themselves. They then said to them: "Why have you bewitched the Queen and Mistress of the whole world? You must die for this!" The holy Pherbuthe replied: "Why has Satan put such thoughts into your hearts, which wander so far from the truth? And why do you slander us so unjustly? If you wish to drink our blood, who prevents you from doing so? If you seek our death, do you not already stain your hands with it every day? But we die for our God, as befits Christians, and..."

[We] do not deny him; for He is our life, as it is written, that we shall worship one God and serve Him alone! This we do. So it is also written elsewhere: A sorcerer shall die by the hands of his people; Leviticus 20, verse 27. How then should we practice sorcery, since such is just as great an evil as if we were to deny God? For both these sins, and those who commit them, are subject to the penalty of death. When the virgin Pherbuthe said this, both <note>The High Priest Mauptes and the other officials.</note> listened to her with pleasure; and because they admired her eloquence and beauty, they could not speak, but each thought to himself: I will ask the King that they remain alive, and then I will take her as my wife! Finally, Mauptes spoke to her: "Even if, as you yourself say, you are not permitted to practice sorcery so that you do not dishonor your law, you have nevertheless done it out of resentment because of your murdered brother." Pherbuthe spoke: "What evil would our brother have suffered that we would want to lose this life, which comes from God, on his account? For although you have killed him out of malice and envy, he nevertheless lives and is joyful in the Heavenly Kingdom; which kingdom is so much more excellent than your dominion and power, that compared to it, yours is a hollow nothing!" When she had said this, he commanded that they should be led to the dungeon and kept under guard.

## Chapter 3.

->They are sentenced to a cruel death.<-

When all three of them <note>The High Priest Mauptes and the two other judges.</note> saw themselves defeated, and their lust did not achieve what they had vainly sought, they consulted with one another and bore false witness against the virgins, claiming that they were sorceresses. When the Emperor <note>This refers to the Sassanid King Shapur II of Persia.</note> heard this, he commanded that if they would worship the sun, they should be spared from death. When it was announced to them that the Emperor had commanded they should worship the sun, these holy virgins answered: "We worship the Creator of Heaven and Earth, and cannot show such honor to the sun; since it is itself a creature of our God, whom we worship; but your threats will never be able to separate us from the love of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ." As they spoke this with one spirit, the <term>Magi</term> <note>Magi: Zoroastrian priests and advisors to the Persian King.</note> cried out with a loud voice: "These must be rooted out from the earth, who have bewitched the Queen so that she has become sick and must perish!" Immediately such a judgment was passed, that these women should die such a death as the Magi saw fit; for these evil and impure men said that unless their bodies were sawn into two pieces and the Queen walked between the two parts, she could not be made well. <note>This reflects a contemporary superstitious belief that passing between the parts of a sacrificed or executed "sorcerer" could heal a victim of a spell.</note> After they were sentenced, Mauptes sent once more to the holy virgin Pherbuthe as they were being led to their death, and had her told: "If you will obey me, neither you nor your companions shall die." But the holy Pherbuthe answered with a loud and bitter voice: "Why do you, unclean dog, say such things to me that I do not wish to hear? For I will gladly die so that I may attain eternal life. I will never be moved for the sake of this temporal life, lest I die the eternal death."

# 87. St. Sadoth along with 128 others,
## in Persia. Anno 346.
### The First Chapter.

->Sadoth has a vision, which he relates to his spiritual brothers, exhorting them to suffering.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' within a square frame, featuring intricate floral and foliage scrollwork in the background.</image-desc>
After the holy Bishop Simeon had completed his martyrdom, the holy Sadoth followed in his place in the city called Salec or Ctesiphon, which are royal cities in Persia situated very close to one another. One day, he had a miraculous vision, which filled his heart with wonder. He summoned his clergy, priests, and deacons—all of whom were keeping themselves hidden for fear of the King—and related the matter to them thus: "I saw," he said, "this night in my sleep, a ladder of great brightness, the top of which reached into heaven; but at the top stood the holy Bishop Simeon in infinite radiance, while I stood below on the earth. Then he spoke to me with great joy, saying: 'Climb up to me, Sadoth; climb up, and do not be afraid; for I climbed up yesterday, and you must climb up today!'" From that hour, I believed that I should be called to the glorious confession of Christ <note>A "confession of Christ" refers to the public declaration of faith, often leading to martyrdom.</note>. That he said: "I climbed up yesterday, but you must climb up today," signifies that he suffered the martyr's death last year, but I should suffer and die this year. Thereupon, he began to exhort them from the Holy Scriptures, saying: "My brothers, let us love God with all our souls, and our Lord Jesus Christ with all our hearts; and being clad in the breastplate of faith, let us fear no evil. If death and execution should fall upon us and overcome us, let us not lose heart; rather, let each among us fight as a brave and strong man, and as a perfect warrior, so that if we die, we may die righteously; for we die for the sake of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. As long as our life lasts, well then, as long as it lasts, let us avenge ourselves against the evil enemy; and while the sword of persecution still gleams, let us strive to become eternally rich. ## The Second Chapter.

->Bishop Sadoth is martyred along with 128 other clergy members.<-

In the second year of the persecution, King Shapur <note>original: "Sapores"; Shapur II, the Sasanian King of Persia</note> came to the aforementioned city of Seleucia <note>original: "Selec"</note> and Ctesiphon. Before him was presented the victorious warrior, namely Bishop Sadoth, whose name, when translated, means "a lover of the King"; for he truly loved the Heavenly King with all his soul and all his strength. For he was holy and of perfect temperance, full of faith and righteousness, a true successor of Saint Simeon, whom he had followed in office. When the King sent his court officials, they took him captive along with his <term>clerisey: the body of ordained clergy</term>, as well as other neighboring clergymen, and likewise several solitary-living men and women <note>likely referring to monks, nuns, or consecrated virgins</note>, totaling one hundred and twenty-eight in number. All of these were bound with iron chains and shut up for five months in a dark and oppressive part of the dungeon, where they endured much tribulation and many kinds of hardship. For the wicked and ungodly tied their legs so tightly together with ropes and forced their loins and shoulders apart in wooden blocks <note>a reference to a torture rack or stocks</note> so that their bones rubbed together like bundles of wood. While under such torment, they stood over them and said: "Worship the sun and fulfill the King’s will, and you shall stay alive!" # 88. St. Cyril / Aemilianus / Marcus of Arethusa / and Theodore / etc.
## Under Julian the Apostate / at Heliopolis etc. Year 362.

### The 1st Chapter.

->Concerning the persecution during the time of the evil Emperor Julian; the martyrdom of Cyril and Aemilianus.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D' decorated with swirling vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>
The troubles which the erring idolaters instigated during the time of the ungodly Emperor Julian the Apostate <note>Julian was the last pagan Roman emperor, who attempted to revive traditional Roman religion after decades of Christian rule.</note> are indeed almost countless and require a work of their own; nevertheless, I wish to recount a few stories out of many. For at Ascalon and Gaza—which are cities in Palestine—they sliced open the bellies of priestly men and spiritually-minded women who had dedicated themselves to eternal virginity, and scattered barley inside, then gave them to the swine to eat. In Sebaste, however, which is also a city of that same land, they opened the coffin of John the Baptist and burned his bones, scattering the ashes here and there. But who can recount without tears the horrors they committed in Phoenicia? In Heliopolis, a city situated by the Lebanon Mountains, there was a certain deacon named Cyril. This same man had previously, during Constantine’s <note>original: "Constantini"; referring to the reign of Constantine the Great.</note>

## Chapter 2.
->The Cruel Martyrdom of Marcus of Arethusa.<-

The tragic story of Marcus of Arethusa <note>Arethusa was a city in Roman Syria.</note> would surely require the eloquence of Aeschylus or Sophocles <note>Famous Greek tragic playwrights.</note> to represent his affliction worthily. For during the time of Emperor Constantine, he had torn down a certain pagan temple and rebuilt a church in its place; the people of Arethusa now made him pay for this with hostility, sensing the favor of Julian. He first thought to flee in accordance with the command of the Gospel; but when he noticed that several others had been captured in his stead, he returned and presented himself to the bloodthirsty crowd. When they had captured him, they showed themselves neither merciful toward his old age nor ashamed by his love for virtue; instead, they stripped the man—who was adorned with good conduct and teaching—naked and scourged his body so that he was bloody all over from the blows. After that, they threw him into a stinking manure pit; when they had pulled him out again, they handed him over to the wicked boys, who were made to stab him with writing styluses <note>term: "Schreib-Griffeln" (styluses); sharp pointed tools used for writing on wax tablets, here used as instruments of torture.</note>. Finally, they placed him in a basket and smeared him with honey, hanging him thus in the open air in the greatest <note>The text cuts off mid-word here; "grössesten" means "greatest."</note>

### Chapter 3.
->Julian forbids the Christians from school-philosophy.<-

**B**ut countless other bold undertakings did the ungodly carry out by land and water; for the enemy of God, **Julian**, had already publicly proclaimed laws against godliness. Afterward, he gave yet another law, that the Galileans should be unworthy of any military service.

## Chapter 6.
### The History of the Martyrdom of the Youth Theodore.

Julian, however, who did not wish to let the shame shown to him stand, had the most prominent leaders of such a procession seized the following day. Salustius <note>Salustius (or Sallustius) was the Praetorian Prefect of the East and a close advisor to Julian, though often depicted as more moderate.</note>, who at that time was the chief commander and a pagan man, sought to persuade the tyrant that he should not even perform such a service for the honor-seeking Christians, which they themselves desired; but when he saw that he could not break Julian's anger, he commanded that a young man, burning with divine love, who happened to be walking in the market, be seized. He was hung naked by his hands from a gallows, then his back was lashed with leather straps, and his chest was wounded with sharp shards <note>term: "Scherben" (shards); likely referring to the use of jagged pottery or stones to scrape the flesh.</note>. The next morning, Salustius reported all of this to Julian and recounted the youth's bravery; he mentioned that through such dealings they were only being put to shame, while the honor of the Christians was spread further. ### Chapter 9.

->The Deceitfulness of Emperor Julian. The History of the Martyrdom of Juventinus and Maximinus.<-

Emperor Julian, however, contested godliness in a bold manner, or rather with even greater impudence; outwardly he indeed gave off an appearance of affability, but in deed he set snares and nets which drew those who allowed themselves to be deceived into godless ruin. For first, he polluted all the wells in the city and near the city as far as Daphne <note>A suburb of Antioch famous for its grove dedicated to Apollo.</note> a few miles distant, with his abominable sacrifices; so that in his opinion, everyone who drank or enjoyed the water would be, as it were, defiled. Furthermore, he had all bread and meat, garden produce and apples—indeed, all sustenance—sprinkled with lustral water. <note>original: *Weih-Wasser*; here referring to pagan sacrificial water used to "purify" food according to Roman rites.</note> When the Christians saw this, they indeed sighed and lamented, as they held it in loathing; yet they ate in obedience to the Apostolic command:

> Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. <note>original: *1 Cor. 10, v. 25*</note>

It then happened that two noble military officers, who were the Emperor’s squires <note>shield-bearers or bodyguards</note> and were required to be constantly around him, very sensitively lamented these abominations at a certain banquet, and made use of the words of the three youths in Babylon: <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3), specifically a verse from the "Prayer of Azariah" found in the Apocrypha.</note>

One of the guests reported this to the Emperor, who immediately had the faithful men appear before him and asked them what they had said about him. They, having received the opportunity to speak boldly at the Emperor's questioning, said with magnificent zeal the following: "We were, most mighty Emperor, raised in true godliness, and we obey the excellent laws given by Constantine and his sons; but we are now grieved that you fill everything with abominations, and with the shameful..."

# Chapter 14.
## A School Official in Antioch prophesies Julian's death.

In **Antioch** there was also a certain excellent man who had kept a school for a long time. This man, as a scholar, lived on familiar terms with the most prominent pagan philosopher of that time, the famous sophist **Libanius** <note>Libanius (314–392 AD) was a celebrated Greek teacher of rhetoric and a close friend of Emperor Julian.</note>. As a pagan, **Libanius** counted on **Julian's** victory and his threats against the Christians; he therefore asked that Christian schoolmaster, in order to mock the Christians, "What was the carpenter's son doing?" <note>A derogatory reference to Jesus Christ, common among pagans who mocked his humble origins.</note> But the other, filled with divine grace, prophesied what was soon to follow and gave this answer: "The Master Builder of all things is building a coffin!" After a few days, news arrived of the Emperor's death, who was indeed brought to **Carrhae** <note>An ancient city in Mesopotamia where Julian's body was taken after he was mortally wounded in battle against the Persians.</note> in a coffin, and his haughty threats were exchanged for the greatest glorification of **God**.

->Of both apostate Julians: the Emperor and the Governor:<-
->[How they] caused Theodoritus to be tormented.<-

(**) Julian was unexpectedly mortally wounded by an arrow or a javelin throw when he intended to attack the Persians.

But after Constantius had departed this temporal life, Julianus fell away from the Christian faith and became an unbeliever who worshipped idols and obtained the Imperial throne. Thus, he sought to persuade all Christians to join the unbelieving party—not through force or threats, but with gifts and honorary offices. When, in such a manner, his cousin Julianus also fell away and offered sacrifices <note>referring to pagan ritual sacrifices</note>, the same received a high magisterial office and became the Count of the East <note>original: "Land-Grafe in Orient"; historically, this was Julian’s uncle, Julianus, who served as the *Comes Orientis*.</note>, where he everywhere restored the idols (which had been destroyed in former times under Constantine and Constantius). 

However, when he heard that the church at Antioch possessed a great quantity of silver and gold, he brought a charge against the clergy, drove them out, and had the church locked up. Those who were scattered continued to serve **GOD**, each as best they could. Only the holy **Theodoritus**, who was a priest or elder of the aforementioned church, did not flee the city but gathered several brothers and held daily meetings with them, during which they offered prayer-sacrifices pleasing to God. 

Now, when Julian the Count heard that he was holding meetings, he wished to do the Emperor a favor; and having seated himself in the courtroom, he had him brought before him. When **Theodoritus** had entered with his hands bound behind his back, this Julian said to him: "Are you the Theodoritus who, in the time of Emperor Constantius, prevented the worship of the gods, and destroyed the altars and temples, and erected churches and burial chapels?" 

**Theodoritus** answered: "I have, according to all my ability, established churches and chapels over the graves of the martyrs, but I destroyed the idols and altars of unclean spirits to set free the souls of those who were erring." 

Julian said: "Then humble yourself before the gods, since you have freely confessed to having done such things." 

**Theodoritus** answered: "Know that I did such things openly and freely in the time of the Emperor, and he never hindered me in it; but I marvel now at you, apostate, that you have so suddenly become a champion of the devils." 

Julian said: "Beat him upon the soles of his feet, because he does not recognize the idols as gods!" **Theodoritus**

After they had completely torn the martyrs apart and smashed their heads in such a way that their brains lay along the ground, they dragged their corpses out of the city to the carrion pit <note>original: "Schind-Anger." ## Chapter 2.

->The martyrs are burned; a woman gathers their bones and brings them to Zeno. Also, concerning Nestero.<-

Now, after they had completely torn the martyrs apart and shattered their heads in such a way that their brains lay along the ground, they dragged their corpses out of the city to the execution grounds <note>original: "Schind-Anger." ## Chapter 4.
### Concerning the Desert Father *Hilarion*.

At that same time, **Hilarion** (*) the Hermit was also sought out by the mob in **Gaza**, and for that reason, he fled from there to **Sicily**. There, he gathered wood on the desolate mountains and carried it on his shoulders to the market of a certain city to sell it, from which he obtained his daily sustenance. However, when he eventually delivered a certain prominent man from a demon, and it thereby became known who he was, he escaped to **Dalmatia**. There he again performed many miraculous works, so much so that through his prayer, the sea receded when it had flooded the dry land; as the people showed him too much honor for this, he also departed from there; for it was burdensome for him to live amidst constant speeches of praise. Thus, he sought to escape his reputation by frequently changing lands and locations. Finally, he traveled to **Cyprus** and landed at **Paphos**; there, at the request of the then-Bishop of Cyprus, he agreed to stay and led a solitary life at the place called **Charbyris**. That he did not become a martyr was due to his flight. For he fled according to the Gospel <note>A reference to Matthew 10:23: "When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next."</note>

> [which had] lain there, and was led about the entire day to be mocked, and finally burned in the evening. Regarding this, **Julian** gave the **Alexandrians** a written rebuke for appearance's sake. <note>original Latin: "vid. Sozom. Lib. 5. c. 7." — This marginal note likely refers to the martyrdom of George of Cappadocia in Alexandria.</note>

It also happened at that time in Meros <note>original: "Myro"; historically identifying the city of Meros in Phrygia, modern-day Turkey.</note> in Phrygia, that the governor <term>Präsidente</term> of that same province, Amachius, ordered the closed pagan temple to be opened. ## Chapter 2.

### Busiris’s Great Steadfastness during Torture.

It is also recounted that Busiris, in Ancyra <note>Modern-day Ankara, Turkey.</note> in Galatia, maintained a magnificent and courageous struggle for the sake of his confession of faith. At that time, he belonged to the party of the Encratites <term>Encratiten</term> <note>A sect of early Christians who practiced extreme asceticism, often rejecting marriage and certain foods.</note> and was taken prisoner by the governor in Galatia because he had mocked the pagan religious customs. He was scourged, and the governor had him publicly hung upon a torture block <term>Peinige-Block</term>; Busiris, however, held his arms high above his head, bared his chest, and said to the governor: "It is not necessary for the bailiffs to trouble themselves so much with lifting me up and down on the torture block; for even without their help, I will present both my sides to the torturers as you command." 

At first, the governor admired this promise, but upon seeing it in practice, he was even more terrified; for while his sides were being torn apart by the iron claws <note>Comb-like instruments used to rake the flesh of the victim.</note> as much as the governor saw fit, he held his free hands high in the air and bore everything patiently. He accepted the torture with a willing spirit, after which he was returned to the dungeon. Not long after, however, when the news arrived that Julian <note>The Emperor Julian the Apostate, who died in 363 AD.</note> had been killed, he was set free and lived until the reign of Emperor Theodosius the Great. Having left his former party, he joined the general Church of God (**).

### Chapter 3.

->The Martyrdom of Eupychius and Others at Caesarea.<-

Similarly, it is reported that Basilius, a priest of the congregation at Ancyra, and Eupychius, the son of a patrician from Caesarea in Cappadocia <note>A historic region in modern-day central Turkey.</note>—who had only recently married and was, so to speak, still a new bridegroom—attained the crown of martyrdom at the same time. Regarding Eupychius, as far as I can surmise, he was put to death because of the Temple of Fortune <note>original: "Glücks-Göttin" or Tyche, the patron goddess of the city.</note>, which he, along with other Christian inhabitants, had torn down in Caesarea; indeed, all of Caesarea fell into the Emperor's disgrace on account of that temple. All those who had lent a hand in the destruction of the idol-temple were either punished with death or driven into exile and misery. <note>original citation: Sozomen, Book 5, Chapter 11.</note>

### Chapter 1.

->Basilius opposes idolatry through his teachings; he is hindered by the Arians <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of Arius, who held the belief that Jesus was a created being and not of the same substance as God the Father; this was a major theological conflict in the 4th century.</note>, yet is confirmed by the orthodox believers.<-

This Basilius had entirely devoted himself to teaching the people the Christian truth, and warning them away from the path of the Devil and all his works. He did not cease to proclaim that a sorrowful time was at hand, and various hellish princes of war; for the Devil also has servants clothed in sheep’s clothing who are inwardly ravening wolves. So that no one might live in peace, they went about seeking to trap souls, whose end shall become manifest to all in the coming time. He spoke undaunted: "I proclaim to you the way of salvation in God and Christ, and reveal the error of the godless. ...preserve the [heavenly] treasure <note>The sentence fragment "liche Kleinod" likely refers to the *göttliche* (divine) or *himmlische* (heavenly) treasure of faith.</note>, trample the great schemes of the deceitful evil spirits underfoot, and flee the cursed folly of their charms, trusting in Christ our Helper, our eternal rewarder! So he did daily, and went about in the whole city, strengthening everyone to hold fast to the perfect faith and to escape the coming evil. 

However, during the time of Eudoxius, Macarius, and Eugenius, and several others (Arians <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of a theological belief that denied the full divinity of Christ, a major source of conflict in the early Church.</note>) who had gathered at Constantinople, this Basilius was forbidden from holding holy gatherings with the brothers because he was devoted to godliness and strictly preserved the faith. Yet, by two hundred and thirty orthodox bishops who had gathered in Palestine, he was commanded to proceed with courage, as one who had holy men and friends of the Lord as teachers, and as one who had himself been among the nobles in the Imperial Palace. 

Accordingly, he continued in his righteous walk before God and proclaimed the blameless word of faith, whereby he led many away from error. At that time, when the souls of all Christians were in turmoil, he was denounced as a rebel to the Emperors (Constantius and Constans <note>Constantius II and Constans were sons of Constantine the Great; the text refers to their joint and subsequent rules.</note>). Thereupon, each of them questioned him to search for the truth, through which many became orthodox believers, because he was steadfast in the faith and the teachings of the holy fathers, and could not be swayed from the confession of the true faith.

## Chapter 3.
->Basilius is captured, dragged before the court, and tortured.<-

This vexed the ungodly men, and they dragged him to the Governor <term>Landpfleger</term> <note>original: "Landpfleger." Saturninus said: "If you are a Christian, why then do you not do what befits a Christian?" Saturninus replied: "But why do you make our city rebellious and blaspheme the King <note>Referring to Emperor Julian.</note> by everywhere calling him an apostate <note>original: "Abgefallenen." Basilius answered: "I blaspheme neither the Emperor nor the religion he has made; for God is the Emperor who dwells in heaven, whom His worthy worshipers—our fathers—everywhere adore in purity of heart. He can, in a short time, frustrate the ungodliness that you have vainly renewed!" 

"So you think then," said Saturninus, "that the religion which our Emperor has ordained is false?" "How indeed," Basilius replied, "can that religion be true..."

# 92. St. Basil of Ancyra
658
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

...be, O President, <note>Saturninus holds the rank of "Praeses" or provincial governor, here addressed as President.</note> which teaches how mad dogs drag about sacrificial meat and eat it, and bark before the altars of the devils, sacrificing their own flesh to them and shedding their blood before them? How can such a religion, I say, be healthy and right? Saturninus replied: 
"Put an end to your empty chatter and obey the Emperor!" 
Basilius answered: "I have obeyed the Heavenly King <note>Referring to Jesus Christ as the supreme authority over the Roman Emperor.</note> until now, and I will never allow myself to be led away from His faith." Saturninus spoke then: "Of what Heavenly King do you speak, whom you obey?" 
"Of the one," answered Basilius, "who dwells in heaven and beholds all things; for the one whom you praise is earthly, and since he is but a man, he will soon fall into the hands of the Great King!" When Saturninus heard this, he became angry and ordered the holy man to be hung upon the torture block and tormented. But as soon as he was hoisted up, he began to pray in the following manner:

> I thank you, Lord and God of the Ages, that you have deemed me worthy to find the way of life through this martyrdom, upon which I behold the heirs of your promise!

While he was being torn with hooks, the President said to him: "What do you think now, Basilius? Can the Emperor immediately punish those who resist his commands according to their deserts? Come now, learn to be obedient through such experience of evil!" 
"I have said it," spoke Basilius, "O despondent man, who has no part in the Christian hope; yes, I have said it, that I believe in the true King and cannot be turned from such a mind." 
Saturninus spoke again to Basilius, after he had commanded the weary bailiffs to rest a little: "Believe us, and sacrifice!" To this the Saint gave the answer: "I have never sacrificed to such empty godheads, nor taken part in their sacrifices, which kill the soul." 
Then the President ordered the Saint to be led back into the dungeon. As he was going there, he met an unclean fellow named Felix, <note>In this context, "unclean" suggests Felix was a pagan or perhaps a Christian who had renounced his faith to please the authorities.</note> who said to him: "What is this, Basilius, that you plunge yourself into ruin? Rather become a friend of the gods, so that you may enjoy the Imperial promises; for if you will not, you shall be severely punished, and indeed in a most deserving manner." 
Basilius said: "Be gone, you perverse and unclean man, who are a stranger to the word of truth and unworthy of it."

## Chapter 4.
->Three apostates continue to persecute Basilius.<-

The Governor, however, reported to the Emperor **Julian** what had occurred with **Basilius**. When the Emperor heard this, he sent a servant of destruction named **Elpidius**, along with **Pegasius**, who had also been disinherited of his heavenly treasures <note>Pegasius was historically a Christian bishop who renounced his faith to join Julian the Apostate's pagan revival.</note>. When these two arrived in **Nicomedia**, they found there **Asclepius**, a priest of **Aesculapius** <note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine and healing.</note>, whom they took with them; and all three, as leaders of the devilish struggle, continued their journey until they reached **Ancyra** <note>Modern-day Ankara, Turkey.</note>. There they immediately asked about **Basilius** and how things stood with him; they learned he was in the dungeon, where he did not cease to praise and glorify God day and night. On the following day, **Pegasius**, who had shamefully abandoned the truth, went to the dungeon, greeted **Basilius**, and said: "Good fortune to you, **Basil**!" But the latter answered him: "You have no fortune, you transgressor and despiser of the truth; you, I say, who formerly drank from the fountain of **Christ**, but now fill yourself from the manure-puddles of the idols; formerly a partaker of the Divine mysteries, now of the table of devils; formerly a servant of the truth, now a leader of destruction; you who formerly celebrated the feasts with the saints, now lead the dance with the hordes of **Satan**; you who formerly led the wandering out of the darkness into the light by the hand, now sit in the dark yourself. Oh, how you have lost your hope and become a loser of your soul's treasure! What will you do when the **Lord** visits you?" When he had said this, he prayed to the **Lord** and said:

> Praise be to you, O **God**, that you make yourself known to your servants, and lead to the light those who desire to see your Divinity; you who glorify those who hope in you, and put to shame those who hate your commandments; you who have promised salvation to those who were far from you, and are glorified in heaven and worshipped on earth. May you, O most high **God**, turn away all the bonds of the devil from the soul of your servant; so that I may escape those who hate your righteousness, and overcome the power of those who threaten me!

# Chapter 6.
### St. Basil is tortured further.

The commander <note>This refers to Frumentinus, the captain of the guards mentioned on the previous page.</note>, however, was filled with shame and hurried to leave; for he realized that the Emperor was incensed with him because of the insult Basil had inflicted upon him. For this reason, he became even more embittered against the saint and considered with what torture he might best execute him. Therefore, he sat upon the judgment seat and gave the order that his skin should be cut daily even more cruelly than before, so that one could even see his entrails.

As the holy man was being tortured in this way, he prayed to the Lord, saying: "Praised be You, my Lord and God, the hope of Christians, who strengthens the fallen and raises up those who are cast down; who delivers from destruction those who hope in You; who heals our ruin and is gracious, merciful, compassionate, and long-suffering. Look down from the exalted throne of Your glory and grant that I may faithfully finish my course and persevere in the faith of the fathers, so that I may be worthy to attain Your eternal and imperishable kingdom!" 

When evening had fallen, the commander ordered him to be returned to the prison. Julian, however, departed the next morning for Antioch and would not let the commander come before his sight. This official became very enraged because of the Emperor’s attitude and gave the order for the jailer to bring the holy man forth, to whom he said: "What have you resolved to do? Will you obey us, or would you rather die?"

Bonosus and Maximilianus spoke: "We are ready to suffer martyrdom for the sake of Christ’s name." **Julianus** the Count <note>Julius Julianus, the maternal uncle of Emperor Julian the Apostate, served as the governor or "Count of the East."</note> spoke: "Bring **Bonosus** forward alone!" When he stood there, **Julianus** said to him: "Worship the gods whom the Emperor and we revere." **Bonosus** answered: "We hold and preserve the commandment which we have received from our Christian parents, but of those gods, we know nothing." **Julianus** the Count spoke: "I have received full power to torment and burn you." **Bonosus** answered: "We do not fear your threats." **Julianus** said: "Prepare him so that he may be scourged with leaden balls." As he was then beaten with the scourge from which leaden balls hung, and had received over three hundred strokes, **Julianus** spoke to **Bonosus**: "Save yourself from these punishments, and do what you are commanded." But **Bonosus** smiled under the scourging and gave no answer. **Julianus** spoke: "What do you say, **Bonosus**?" **Bonosus** answered: "We honor the living God and serve him alone; but these gods, we do not know who they are." **Julianus** spoke: "Bring **Maximilianus** forward." When he was presented, **Julianus** spoke: "Honor the gods whom we honor, and change the emblem on your standard <note>original: "Wapen in eurer Fahne"; this refers to the *labarum*, the military standard which, since Constantine, featured the Christian Chi-Rho symbol.</note>." **Maximilianus** gave **Julianus** an answer and spoke: "First, let these gods of yours hear you and speak with you; when they have spoken with you, then we also can worship them. But how can you honor and worship your gods, who can neither speak nor feel? Our God, however, has great power, in whom we hope, and we hasten toward martyrdom, obtaining our hope as we trust; for you yourself know well, and it is not unknown to you, that it is commanded of us that we shall worship no deaf and dumb images."

### Chapter 3.

->*Julian seeks to force them into idolatry through hunger / and to burn them with unslaked lime; however, they are miraculously preserved. Hormisda is converted.*<-

When those [materials of torture] were consumed, **Julian** the <term>Count</term><note>The German "Land-Grafe" here refers to Julianus, the maternal uncle of Emperor Julian the Apostate, who held the Roman office of *Comes Orientis* (Count of the East).</note> stood ashamed, and commanded that **Bonosus** and **Maximilianus** be taken back to the dungeon until the Governor should also interrogate them. When they had lain in the dungeon for seven days, the chains fell off all the prisoners who believed in Christ. The Count, however, had the image of his idol pressed onto the bread of the prisoners and then sent it into the dungeon, so that they might at least be deceived by the bread <note>By eating bread stamped with an image of a pagan god, the prisoners would technically be participating in a pagan sacrifice, a common trap set for Christians.</note>. But on the day that **Bonosus** and **Maximilianus** were interrogated again, they spoke to **Julian**: "See the loaves of bread which you sent us; we have not eaten them; for He in whom we believe has satisfied us, therefore we do not fear your temptations. Our God, Jesus Christ, will demand [an account of] our martyrdom from you!" Then the Governor **Secundus** became angry and spoke to **Julian**: "Let us interrogate them judicially today!" Once they had seated themselves and heard them out, but were unable to achieve anything against them with all their malice, **Julian** spoke: "Bring <term>quicklime</term><note>Original: "lebendigen Kalk." This is unslaked lime, which produces intense heat and caustic burns when it comes into contact with moisture.</note> here; I will bury them in it and then ignite the lime; then we shall see where their God is, and whether He will be able to deliver them!" And when they were thrown into the quicklime and it was ignited, they cried out with a great voice, saying: "Praised be You, O Lord, You God of our fathers, You God of Abraham, You God of Isaac, and You God of Jacob; You who graciously deliver us from the hand of our enemies, be praised and glorified unto eternity!" When the lime was completely <term>slaked</term><note>Meaning the chemical reaction had finished and the heat subsided.</note> and had not harmed them, the enraged **Julian** put them into the dungeon once more and commanded that the dungeon be sealed, but he had the keys brought to his palace. When the dungeon was opened again twelve days later, it was seen that they had lights with them that shone very brightly and could not be extinguished. Then **Julian** commanded—as he presumed they would now be starving—that they be given sacrificial bread to eat, so that they might be forced by hunger to defile themselves with their sacrifices. However, they, being fed and nourished by the Holy Spirit of our Lord Jesus Christ, remained undefiled and unpolluted by their sacrifices. Thereupon

-> They are further heard judicially, the court officials are convinced, and President Secundus warns Julian. <-

When **Julian** the <term>Count</term><note>German: *Land-Graf*. Weighing this with inner rage, he sighed and said: "Bring them before me in the **old bathhouse**; there I will hear them." When **Bonosus** and **Maximilianus** were brought there before the court, Julian the Count spoke to **Bonosus**: "What power of God do you show me, by which you have escaped my hands as a Christian?" **Bonosus** answered: "Our God is mighty, in whom we believe, to bring us to the completion of the <term>state of martyrdom</term><note>German: *Marter-Stand*. This refers to the final testimony of a Christian through suffering and death.</note> for which we long, so that as Christians we may be snatched from your hands." **Julian** spoke: "You shall be thrown to the wild beasts." **Bonosus** answered: "The God of the Christians can certainly rescue us and place upon us the **crown** for which we hope; but we do not dread the beasts, nor do we fear your threats, for we have with us God the Father and Jesus Christ His Son, together with the Holy Spirit, through whom we overcome all of this." Julian the Count spoke: "I will throw you into the **fiery furnace** once more, then you will fulfill the command of the consecrated ones." When all the select heathens present heard this, they opposed such a command and spoke with one mind: "As we see the struggle of our brothers, who are ready for martyrdom, we also wish to see to it that we worship the one God, who shows us all His power through His servants, our brothers **Bonosus** and **Maximilianus**." **Secundus** the <term>President</term><note>Likely the provincial governor acting as a magistrate.</note> spoke hereupon: "I can no longer interrogate them under torture; you shall experience it, **Julian**, when the worms crawl out of your mouth!" <note>This is a prophetic warning regarding the historical death of Julian the Count, who reportedly died of a gruesome intestinal disease where his body putrefied while he was still alive.</note>

For when a rumor arose that the **Persians** were preparing for war, he hurried to **Antioch** in **Syria** to be at hand for the necessary counter-preparations. However, after the **Persians** made no movements, the idle Emperor took the opportunity to involve himself in church affairs. Now, in the great city of **Antioch**, there were three bishops at once: **Euzojus** stood over the **Arian** congregation, while **Paulinus** and **Meletius** were the bishops of the divided **Orthodox**; the Emperor did no harm to **Paulinus** because of his exceptional holiness, but **Meletius** he drove into exile. From **Constantinople**, he likewise expelled all who did not agree with the **Arian** doctrine; even the **Novatians** (*), who were orthodox in their confession of Christ, had their churches closed. Their bishop, **Agelius**—a man who had governed the congregation since the time of **Constantine** and led a completely apostolic life—was driven into exile. Throughout his entire life, he had gone barefoot and, following the Gospel command, owned only a single coat. ### Chapter 6.

#### Persecution of the Church at Edessa, and a remarkable story concerning a faithful woman.

At **Edessa** there was a famous church named after the holy **Apostle Thomas**; the Emperor traveled there from **Antioch** to visit it. But when he saw that the **True-Believers** <note>The Nicene Christians who remained loyal to the doctrine of the Trinity, as opposed to the Emperor’s Arianism.</note>—from whom all churches and houses of prayer had been taken—were nevertheless still gathering outside the city in a garden, he harshly rebuked the Governor, **Modestus**, and gave him a slap on the face because he had permitted such gatherings against his prohibition. **Modestus** then, though he was an **Arian**, nevertheless secretly had the others warned to be on their guard and to hold no assembly at the usual place on the following day; for the Emperor had strictly commanded him that if he should find any, he should punish them severely. With such a warning, the Governor sought to prevent them from all falling into danger at once, and at the same time to escape the Emperor's wrath. But the people of **Edessa** despised such threats and came together at the usual place much more eagerly than had happened before. ### Chapter 7.

->The ministers of the congregation at Edessa are banished into exile<-

The leaders of the congregation, namely the **Elders** and **Ministers**, were brought forth so that they might reap one of two things: either to unite themselves with the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius who believed Christ was a created being, rather than co-equal with God the Father.</note>, or to be banished from the city into exile. When they were all brought together, the Governor sought to entice them with a gentle-minded speech, so that they might obey the Imperial commands. "For," he spoke, "it is indeed a kind of foolishness to resist the Emperor, who is a master of all men, especially for such a large crowd." But as they all stood around him and kept silent, he turned to the most prominent among them, who was named **Eulogius** and was a praiseworthy man, and spoke: "Why do you answer nothing to what I say?" But he replied: "I thought it was not fitting for me to answer, since I was not specifically asked." "Well then," spoke the Governor, "I have exhorted you for your own good with a lengthy speech; what do you say to it?"

"this," **Eulogius** replied, "was spoken to everyone, and in my opinion, it would be improper to hinder others with my answer; but if you ask me alone, I will not hide my view." Thus he commanded that they should be separated from one another in pairs, and some scattered in **Thrace**, some in **Arabia**, and some even in the **Thebaid** <note>The Thebaid was a region in ancient Egypt, often used as a place of exile due to its remote desert environment.</note> villages. It is said they were then separated from each other with the utmost cruelty, so that each was torn away from his closest friend and brother. **Eulogius**, indeed, the most prominent among them, and with him **Protogenes**, were led toward **Antinoopolis** <note>original: "Antinoo"</note> in the **Thebaid**; I (**Theodoret**) <note>Theodoret of Cyrus was a 5th-century bishop and historian whose writings are the source for this account.</note> cannot help but mention the virtuous conduct of these two.

## Chapter 9.
->Valens, misled by meddlesome magic arts, causes many to be killed whose names began with "Theod."<-

At the same time that **Valens** had persecuted the congregation at **Edessa**, a cruel and evil spirit used the Emperor’s rage for his own wantonness. He led astray the minds of several meddlesome people so that they sought to discover, through **necromantic arts** <term>divination through the summoning of the spirits of the dead</term>, which person would become Emperor after **Valens**. Now, the Devil gladly makes use of such lovers of magical trickery, and he gave them an answer that was not clear, but rather ambiguous—namely, the four letters **TH.E.O.D.**, with which the successor's name would begin. When this reached the Emperor's ears, he did not leave the matter to **GOD**, who rules over all and wisely arranges future things; instead, he abandoned the commandments of the Christian religion—for which he had previously seemed to have such great zeal—and killed a great many people whose names began with **Theod.** Thus, he had all those executed who were named **Theodorus**, or **Theodotus**, or **Theodosius**, or **Theodulus**, and so forth. Among their number was also **Theodosiolus**, a noble man of an ancient family, who was brought from **Spain** to **Valens** and put to death. Because of this, many people changed the names their parents had given them at birth out of fear (*). **Socrates, Book 4, Chapter 15.**

## 94. The Orthodox

...to let go of their faith, they would be pleasing to Emperor Valens <note>The text says "Valent-", referring to Emperor Valens (reigned 364–378), who was a staunch supporter of Arianism and oversaw the persecution of those who held to the Nicene Creed.</note>. Upon this, they were kept imprisoned for many days to see if they might reconsider; but they conducted themselves as brave warriors and regarded the place of torture as a school of virtues. As they now, in the words of the Apostle, became a **spectacle before angels and men** <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 4:9, comparing the suffering of the faithful to a public arena or theater.</note>, the whole city ran there to see the warriors fight, seeing with what courageous spirit they defeated the judge's torments and lashings, and through patience raised the signs of victory. 

Finally, as the inhuman judge despaired of his methods of torture, and all the people felt compassion for the oppressed, he sentenced them to deportation and banishment into the misery of **Heliopolis** <note>Likely Heliopolis in Phoenicia (modern-day Baalbek), famous in antiquity for its massive pagan temples and resistance to Christianity.</note>, a city whose inhabitants are all idol-worshippers and cannot bear even to hear the name of Christ.

Thus he gave the order that they should set sail without provisions or other necessary things. ## Chapter 12.

### Continuation of the letter of Peter regarding the Alexandrian Martyrs. <note>Referring to Peter II, the Bishop of Alexandria who succeeded Athanasius and was forced into exile in Rome, from where he wrote an encyclical letter about these events.</note>

->On the Goths' Origin, Conversion, and Persecution.<-
->I.<-

The Goths—also called **Getes** or **Dacians**—were a Germanic nation living on this side of the **Danube** in **Hungary**, **Transylvania**, **Moldavia**, and **Wallachia**; namely, during the time of the Emperors **Valens** and **Valentinian** in the **4th century** <note>original: *4ten Seculo*</note>. These people already had bishops, priests, **deacons** <note>original: *diaconos*</note>, hermits, virginal souls, and common Christians among them as early as the time of **Cyril of Jerusalem** in the year **347 AD** (*Catechesis 16*), and indeed even martyrs (*Catechesis 10*). Initially, they were adherents of the true-believing <note>Referring to the Nicene or Orthodox faith</note> Church. However, after their bishop **Ulphila** joined the **Arian** <note>Arians followed the teachings of Arius, who claimed Jesus was not co-eternal with God the Father; this was the primary theological conflict of the 4th century.</note> faction during the time of Emperor **Constantius**, he drew his entire nation away from the universal Church; For because

<margin>(*) The manner in which Bishop **Lucius** persecuted the holy fathers in the desert at that time is cited in the first part, **No. 82**, in the life of **Macarius of Alexandria**, chapter 20, page 304, from the pen of **Ruffinus**, an eyewitness; this is also testified to by **Socrates**, Book 4, Chapter 18, and **Sozomen**, Book 6, Chapter 20. How shortly thereafter the Emperor **Valens** lost his life in the war against the Goths—a shameful end <note>Valens was famously defeated and killed at the Battle of Adrianople.</note>, in the year **378 AD**—and was burned together with the house into which he had fled, is reported in greater detail by all contemporary writers.</margin>

<margin>(†) **Gothia** was the capital city of the Goths, which consisted of three parts, and was where the King resided...</margin>

History of Martyrs / Year 372. 685

Those who had previously been instructed by him <note>Referring to Bishop Ulphila</note> in godliness and the true religion, and who through his guidance had attained milder customs, easily obeyed his counsel during this transition; they held the firm confidence that he would teach them nothing improper, but would seek their highest salvation. He was also the first to invent the alphabet for them and translated the Holy Scriptures into their native language. At that same time (under the Emperor Valens), a great multitude of the subjects of King Fritigern <note>original: "Phritigerniß (Friedegern)"</note> were martyred and killed for Christ's sake. Likewise, Athanaric <note>original: "Asthalaricus (Otto Oehlrich)"</note>, the king of the other group (for they had divided into two kingdoms), took it badly after Bishop Ulphila also led his subjects to the Christian religion. He wished to know nothing of innovation in the old religion of the fathers and therefore executed many people with various death penalties. Some of these he brought before a court, where they confessed the Christian faith freely and with courageous spirits; others did not even receive a hearing and were nonetheless killed along with the rest. It is said that some who were commanded to do so placed an idol on a wagon and drove it before the tents of all those who had been identified as Christians. They were commanded to worship this image and offer incense before it; when they refused, the persecutors set fire to their tents and burned them along with everything inside. Furthermore, I <note>The historian Sozomen</note> have heard of another far more cruel event: for many had weighed the value of their lives against the violence of those commanded to force the believers to sacrifice; and both men and women—some carrying their nursing children at their breasts, others leading older ones by the hand—had fled into the church located there. The pagans set it on fire, so that all were consumed by the flames. *Sozomen, Book 6, Chapter 37. Socrates [Scholasticus], Book 4, Chapter 27. Eutropius, Book 12, Roman History.*

Therefore, according to the testimony of Theodoret <note>original: "Theodoriti"</note>, *Book 5, Chapter 37*, they said they found no difference between the doctrines of the two parties, and that it was merely an ambitious bickering. # 95. Saint Saba / the Goth / etc.

...Constantinople remained in peace and friendship, and clearly taught the faithful Goths: The Son of God is not a created being; as Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458), an influential theologian and church historian</note> testifies in the cited passage. For although a fire of resentment and ill-will had naturally arisen through the dispute, little by little, here and there, a small light of understanding began to shine forth. Through this, those Arians <note>Followers of Arianism, which taught that Jesus was a created being rather than co-eternal with God the Father</note> who feared God drew ever closer to the Divine mystery in Christ. The other party, following the example of the holy fathers in the deserts, improved their conduct as long as the fathers lived, until finally the name of the Arians was extinguished. Isidore of Seville <note>original: "Isidorus Hispanensis"</note> further reports of these Gothic martyrs that Athanaric <note>original: "Athalaricus," the King of the Thervingian Goths</note> made martyrs of many of his Christian subjects who refused to sacrifice to the pagan gods. To the rest, however, after many tribulations he inflicted upon them—because he felt a loathing for killing such a great multitude—he gave freedom, or rather forced them to leave his kingdom and go into the territory of the Romans. When the Goths later overcame Valens <note>The Roman Emperor Valens, who died at the Battle of Adrianople in 378 AD</note> and took spoils, they also encountered the banished confessors of Christ again, to whom they wished to give a share of the booty. These, however, took no part in it, and thus some were killed, others fled into the mountains, and remained true-believing Christians. Isidore of Seville, Eras 407, 415, 416 <note>These dates refer to the "Spanish Era" calendar; Era 407 corresponds to approximately 369 AD</note>.

...walked, he nevertheless followed the lives of the saints in such a way, and served Christ with them in all kinds of exercises of virtue, that he shone like a star in the world. From his youth, he was incorporated into the religion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and considered it the most perfect virtue to become a complete man through the knowledge of the Son of God. But since all things must work for the best for those who love God <note>A reference to the biblical verse Romans 8:28</note>, he also, in the earnest struggle against the enemy, not only overcame all the tribulations of this life but also preserved peace with everyone and obtained the prize of the heavenly calling <note>A reference to Philippians 3:14; the "prize" or "gem" refers to eternal life</note>. Therefore, we cannot remain silent or idle in his memory and for the edification of the devout, now that he rests in the Lord, but are driven to describe his glorious deeds. He was not proud, but submissive as befits the lowly; not bold in words, but quiet; ready for all good works. He sang diligently in the assembly <note>Referring to the liturgical singing within the Christian congregation</note> and took great care for the congregation. He despised money and property, possessing no more than his daily needs; he lived soberly and was continent in all things, especially concerning the female sex. Day by day he devoted himself to prayer and fasting, disregarded vain honor, enticed everyone to an upright life, performed his own affairs uprightly, and fled from vice.

<margin>*)/</margin> Finally, he fully preserved the faith that becomes active through love, and never neglected to speak boldly in the Lord; for not only once, but often, before he obtained the crown of martyrdom <note>The "crown of martyrdom" is a traditional Christian concept where the martyr receives a spiritual reward and recognition in heaven for dying for their faith</note>, he truly showed himself to be an upright defender of true godliness.

When thereupon the persecutor and investigator arrived, the foremost heathens swore, while concealing their Christian friends, that in the same village there was no one else but only a single Christian. When the wicked king heard this, he had the only one, who was the blessed Sabas, brought forward. When he was brought forth, the king asked the bystanders what the prisoner possessed in terms of property, and how wealthy he was. Since they gave the answer that he possessed nothing more than the clothes he stood in, the unjust man despised him and said: "Such a man can neither help nor harm." After this was said, he commanded that they should send him out and let him go.

...he had just returned; therefore Sabas, who did not know this, answered thus and continued his way to the priest Gutthica <note>A Gothic priest of the Christian faith</note>. But because he did not follow the command of the great man <note>A supernatural or angelic apparition that had appeared to Sabas in a vision</note> whom he had seen, a heavy snow fell quickly, even though the sky had been bright and clear, so that the way could no longer be recognized, and Sabas could not proceed. Then he recognized that he was prevented from the journey by God's will, who had commanded him to go to the priest Sansala. He then turned back and thanked God, and when he arrived with joy at Sansala's, he told him and many others what had happened to him on the way. Together they celebrated the Easter Day. 

But on the third night of the festival, Atharidus—the son (or brother) of the sub-king Rothesteus—fell upon the village with a great marauding force. When he found the priest Sansala at home, he commanded him to be bound along with Sabas, whom he ordered to be torn naked from his bed. The priest they placed upon a wagon, but Sabas they dragged stark naked, just as he was born, through the thorns which they had set on fire shortly before; meanwhile, they pushed him and struck him with clubs and whips. In such an unkind and cruel manner did they treat the servants of God. Yet the cruelty of the enemies only tested the patience and the faith of the righteous man. 

When day broke, however, he rejoiced in the Lord and addressed his persecutors in this manner: "Have you not," he said, "dragged me naked and barefoot through stony and thorny paths? Look now whether my feet are injured, and whether any marks of the blows you gave me can be found on my body." When they found absolutely no wounds or welts from their cruelty upon him, they took a wheel from the wagon and laid it on his back, bound his hands and feet tightly to it, and left him lying thus on his back throughout the night. They did not cease to torment him in this way until it was nearly day. 

But while the servants were still sleeping, a woman came by and released him, for she had woken early to prepare the meal for the household servants. He, however, remained there with the woman without changing his demeanor <note>He did not flee despite being freed</note> and offered her his help. When day broke and the matter became known, the cruel Atharidus commanded that both his hands should be bound together and that he should be hung from the beam of the house.

## Chapter 4
->Sansala and Sabas refuse to eat meat sacrificed to idols; Sabas feels no pain<-

Not long thereafter, several men sent by Atharidus arrived, bringing food that had already been sacrificed to idols. They addressed the priest Sansala and Sabas, saying: "The great Atharidus sends you this, so that you may eat and save your lives from death." But the priest answered them: "We will not eat this, for it is not permitted for us; therefore, we ask Atharidus to much rather have us crucified or put to death in another way!" The blessed Sabas also spoke up and said, "Who sends this?" They replied, "Our Lord Atharidus." Sabas said, "There is only one Lord, namely GOD who is in Heaven; such damnable food, however, is unclean and worthless <note>original: "nichtig"</note>, just as Atharidus is, who has sent it." When Sabas spoke thus, one of Atharidus's servants flew into a rage and struck the holy man in the chest with the point of his javelin <note>A throwing spear or pike</note> with such force that all those present believed he would die instantly from the powerful blow. But he, whose godliness overcame the pain, spoke to the perpetrator: "Now you certainly think I shall die from your blow? But know that it pained me so little that it seems to me as if you had thrown a bit of wool at me." Of this, he gave clear testimony, for he neither cried out nor behaved piteously, as usually happens in pain, nor was any other mark of the blow to be seen upon him.

But the blessed man, mindful of the commandment of his Lord, and who loved his neighbor as himself, said: "What sin has the priest committed, that he should not die with me?" The henchmen <term>Büttel-Knechte: low-ranking officials or executioners who carried out the orders of a magistrate</term> answered: "You have no business giving orders regarding that." But he cried out in the joy of the Holy Spirit and said: "Praised be You, O Lord, and praised be the name of Your Son for all eternity, Amen; for although Atharidus has condemned himself to death and eternal destruction, he sends me into eternal life." Thus this wretched man, in seeking to have both, lost both; for he lost the Divine life because he fled from martyrdom, and he could not enjoy the pleasures of this world with a quiet conscience, as he still craved heavenly glory. Since he valued the honor of the earthly and transitory king more than that of the eternal and heavenly God, he confessed that he wished to fall away from God and do everything that would please the King. When the King heard that Nersan was so minded, he rejoiced greatly and immediately thought of the holy Bademus, whom he ordered to be brought from the dungeon and led onto the castle courtyard through the side gate. 

When Bademus had entered the place where Nersan stood bound, the King spoke to two of his officials: "If Nersan will kill Bademus, he shall be released from his bonds and receive back his goods (*);" for the King had ordered all his former possessions to be confiscated. They then hurriedly placed the holy Bademus in the center. But the wretched Nersan, hearing what the King had said, went forward with a drawn sword out of love for the perishable goods of this world to kill the martyr of Christ. 

Yet, as he wished to strike the holy martyr, he remained standing motionless, paralyzed by fear. But the servant of Christ looked at him and said: "To what lengths, O Nersan, has your wickedness come, that you have not only denied your God but now wish to kill His servant? Woe to you, unfortunate man! What will you do on that day, and where will you flee from the terrible judgment, when you must stand before the fearful throne <note>original: "Stul", meaning the judgment seat of God.</note> and give an account to the great and eternal God? I, indeed, O most wretched man, am ready to complete my <term>martyrdom</term> <note>From "Marter-Stand," referring to the state of suffering or testimony for the faith.</note> for Christ; yet I would not gladly die by your hands, but would rather endure death by another!" 

Nersan, however, turned red with shame at these words, yet he could not resist what was commanded of him. He hardened his face like a stone and, with an iron-hard heart, struck the holy man several times with the sword. Yet he could not strike him properly nor kill him at once, for his hands trembled greatly. Under such painful suffering, the holy Bademus gave up [his spirit]...

### Chapter 3.

->His Burial and the Liberation of the Seven Disciples.<-

The holy Bademus completed his <term>martyrdom</term> <note>original: "Marter-Stand," referring to his status or testimony as a martyr.</note> on the 8th of April, in Christ Jesus our Lord. # Chapter 2.
->Dreadful Kinds of Torment.<-

After the death of Isdegerdis <note>King Yazdegerd I.</note>, his son Gororanes <note>King Bahram V, often called "Gororanes" in Western ecclesiastical histories.</note> followed his father in the government, who simultaneously with his reign continued the war against godliness, just as his dying father had left instructions for his son. ## Chapter 3.

### Hormisda, a Noble Persian, Becomes a Camel Driver for Christ’s Sake.

There was a noble Persian named Hormisda, of the Achaemenid lineage <note>The Achaemenids were the first ruling dynasty of the Persian Empire; mentioning this highlights Hormisda's extremely high social status and royal connections.</note>, whose father had held the most distinguished offices. When the King learned that he was a Christian, he had him summoned and commanded him to deny God his Savior. But he replied that the King's command was neither just nor useful; for if one first despises and denies God, the Lord of all things, he would then very easily despise the King, who is but a man and mortal. "If now, O King," he said, "one is worthy of punishment who rebels against your kingdom, how much greater punishment does he deserve who denies the Creator of all things?" 

But the King, who ought to have admired these wise sayings, stripped him of his goods and honors, and ordered him to lead the camels that were in the camp, wearing only a smock <note>original: "Kittel," a simple, coarse tunic worn by laborers.</note>. After many days, the King looked down from the vault of his palace and beheld the excellent man, how he was scorched by the heat of the sun and soiled by dust. Then he thought of his father’s glory <note>The high standing and prestige Hormisda's family had previously enjoyed.</note> and had him come before him in a white linen garment, thinking that he would be more soft-hearted, partly because of the suffering he had endured and partly because of the mercy now shown. He said to him: "Set aside your stubbornness now, and deny the Carpenter's Son <note>original: "Zimmermanns Sohn," a derogatory term used by the King to mock the humble earthly origins of Jesus Christ.</note>." But Hormisda, filled with divine zeal, tore his robe and threw it from him with the words: "If you think I will abandon my fear of God for this reason, then keep your gift along with your godlessness." When the King saw such bravery of spirit, he cast him out of the palace naked.

97. St. Hormisda / Suenes / Benjamin.

## Chapter 4.

*Suenes Forsakes Wife, Possessions, and Property for Christ’s Sake.*

Regarding Suenes, who owned one hundred bondservants and dared to defy the King by refusing to deny the Creator of all things: the King asked him which of all his servants was the worst. He then gave this servant authority over the others and over his former master, even giving him the master’s wife in marriage. The King hoped by this means to lead the champion of truth away from his faith; however, his hope utterly failed him, for Suenes had built his house upon a rock <note>A reference to Matthew 7:24–25; Suenes's faith was unshakable because it was founded on Christ.</note>.

## Chapter 5.

*Benjamin, a Deacon, is Cast into Dungeon for the Testimony of Christ, Released, Continues to Confess Christ, and is Cruelly Martyred.*

The King also threw the Deacon Benjamin into the dungeon. After two years, a Roman ambassador, who was there on other business, petitioned for the Deacon’s freedom and obtained it. However, the King had forbidden him from speaking of Christian doctrine to the <term>Magi</term> <note>The Magi were the priestly caste of the Zoroastrian religion, which was the state religion of the Sasanian Persian Empire.</note>, a promise which the ambassador made to the King on Benjamin’s behalf. Benjamin, however, refused to keep this condition, for he could not withhold the light he had received from others; he noted that the Gospel teaches how great a punishment he deserves who buries his talent <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25:14–30, where a servant is punished for hiding the money entrusted to him rather than using it.</note>. 

These words were not reported to the King at the time, who ordered the Deacon’s chains to be removed. But Benjamin sought, as was his custom, to save as many as he could from destruction and to kindle the light of understanding within them. After a year’s time, this was again reported to the King, who once more ordered him to be brought forward and commanded him to deny the true God whom he worshipped. Benjamin then asked the King what punishment a traitor to the realm deserved who fled to another master. When the King answered "death and the most grievous punishment," this most wise man replied: "What punishment then do you think a traitor to his Maker and Creator deserves, who attributes divinity and the worship due to Him to a fellow servant?"

# 98. St. Peter, Stephen, John, George, Theodore, Felix, Laurus, etc.

## In the Arabian Desert, Year 410.

### Chapter 1.

->Seven fathers in the desert live in holy communion.<-

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'E' featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

Seven proven men lived in that desert which is closest to the <term>Saracens</term> <note>At this time, "Saracen" was a term used by late Roman and Byzantine writers to describe the nomadic tribes of the Arabian desert.</note>; their huts were built not very far from one another, but they were joined together by the bond of love. Their names were: 1. Peter, 2. Stephen, 3. John, 4. George, 5. Theodore, 6. Felix, 7. Laurus. These men, who stayed in the vast and barren desert where almost no human was to be found, visited each other only once a week. For on the <term>Sabbath day</term> <note>original: "Sabbath-Tage als am Sonabend." In this context, it refers to Saturday, following the traditional liturgical calendar.</note>, at three o'clock in the afternoon, everyone came from his own place to the spot they had agreed upon. Each brought with him nuts, dates, figs, all sorts of herbs, parsnip roots, beans, and parsley roots; for all of this was their usual fare. But they had no bread, oil, or wine; they were thus sustained solely by the aforementioned herbs and tree-fruits. They obtained their clothing only from the palm tree. No water was to be found in that place at all, and they drank nothing except what they gathered early in the morning, when they went and collected the dew from the herbs, which falls very heavily there; from that alone they drank.
