# 98. St. Peter / Stephen / etc.

## Chapter 2.

->They come together on the Sabbath and Sunday.<-

When they then came together in an agreed place in the manner previously mentioned, they gave thanks to God and ate with one another. After such refreshment, they sat until the evening and spoke of spiritual matters from the Holy Scripture; among them, no worldly gossip occurred, nor miserable worry, nor earthly business, but only spiritual conversation and a longing remembrance of the heavenly kingdom, of future salvation, of the glory of the righteous, of the punishment of sinners, and of the holy eternal rest. They spoke of these things with deep, heartfelt sighs and frequent tears. And when they had remained awake through the night and praised the Lord, they departed from one another again on the Day of the Lord—which is Sunday—at three o'clock in the afternoon; for each one returned again to his hut, wherein he alone served the one God day and night.

## Chapter 3.

->They are martyred by the Saracens.<-

During such spiritual labors, they were encountered by the <term>Saracens</term> <note>A term used by late antique and medieval writers for the nomadic Arab tribes of the desert.</note>, who roamed the deserts far and wide. They dragged the men out of their solitary huts, bound their hands and feet together, and hung them up by them. After they had inflicted many kinds of evil upon them, they even lit a fire of poisonous herbs beneath them, by which they were incredibly tormented and lost the sight of their eyes from the bitter smoke. After they had performed many kinds of martyrdom upon them, they left them lying half dead. We <note>referring to the chronicler</note> later knew one such man (either Rufinus or perhaps Palladius) who lived somewhere for a long time afterward, but where the others remained, we do not know. <note>original: "Ruffin. in Vit. PP. lib. 5. num. 200." This refers to Rufinus of Aquileia's *Lives of the Desert Fathers*, Book 5, entry 200.</note>

## Chapter 4.

->Several fathers are killed by the Saracens, and the various parties quarrel over their bodies.<-

In Palestine, in the region of the small town of <term>Tekoa</term> <note>original: "Thecue"; the birthplace of the prophet Amos, located south of Bethlehem.</note>, where the prophet Amos himself was born, a great desert begins, which stretches as far as Arabia and the Dead Sea, into which the Jordan River pours and where the ashes of Sodom are. In this desert, several highly holy and solitary brothers, who had lived there for a long time, were suddenly attacked and killed by the Saracens.

## The History of Nilus (*) and his son Theodulus.

### Chapter 1.

->Father Nilus recounts his flight and the tribulations he suffered.<-

## Chapter 2.
->How Nilus came from the world to the solitary life.<-

I, wretched man, dearest friends, had two children, a son and a daughter; the former is the cause of my tears, the latter remained with her mother in Constantinople. A violent desire, however, drew me to these places, and I was entirely inclined toward <term>peace and stillness</term> <note>The original German "Ruhe und Stille" translates the Greek "hesychia," the central goal of Eastern Orthodox monasticism involving inner silence and prayer.</note>, of which I thought alone. For as she saw my best and constant resolution, and at the same time considered within herself the painful separation, she nonetheless let her own intention go, and looked only upon what was pleasing to me. ## Chapter 4.
->Description of the Wild Arabs.<-

Regarding the barbarians, they dwell in the desert of Arabia / from the Red Sea and Egypt as far as the Jordan; they practice no arts, nor commerce, nor agriculture, but possess only the sword with which they obtain their sustenance; for they either hunt the wild animals that are in the desert, whose meat they eat, or they rob those whom they encounter, and obtain their necessities from the loot. They do not acknowledge God—neither the true God, who is recognized through the intellect, nor even the false idols made by human hands; instead, they worship the Morning Star <note>The planet Venus, often associated with the pre-Islamic goddess al-Uzza</note>. When it rises, they sacrifice to it the best of the plunder they have gathered on their raids. In particular, they take pleasure in sacrificing young boys who are handsome, beautiful, and in the bloom of youth (*); these they sacrifice upon several stones piled one on top of the other, in the morning when the Morning Star has risen. This, O dear friends, fills me with great anxiety once again, because I must fear for my own son—that he might have been suitable for their sacrifice, since he was of a beautiful physical form, and evil spirits delight in the shedding of blood. For this reason, those who perform such sacrifices have no mercy for the boys they intend to kill. However, if they lack such a boy for sacrifice, they take a white camel without blemish; they make it kneel, and the entire swarm circles around it. One of them—either one of their leaders, a priest, or some other distinguished elder—goes before the circle and sings a song composed for the star of Venus. Once the people have circled three times and the song is nearly at its end, one of them cuts the camel's tendon with a naked sword, and the one who led the procession drinks the warm blood with great greed. Thereupon the rest run forward with naked swords in hand; some cut off a piece of skin and hair; others take what flesh they can get; the last consume the entrails and leave nothing of this sacrifice remaining by the time the sun rises, which must see nothing of it. Indeed, even the bones and marrow must be consumed, for they cannot withstand the barbarians' ferocity, and they eat them with persistence. Such is the way of life, custom, and religion of the barbarians, whereby they constantly change their dwelling place in the desert, pitching their camp wherever the livestock finds pasture and there is water.

## Chapter 7.
->Outrageous murder committed against a boy.<-

One of the barbarians commanded this boy to gather up the spilled fruit. Then, so that he might please the one who had commanded him, he bent down busily to the earth; he was active in showing that he was still fit to serve, hoping that he might thus preserve his life. However, he was already dead before the blow fell, out of fear of the sudden death; the cruel blow took away all his thoughts, suddenly releasing the soul from the body and freeing it quickly from the bonds which it otherwise does not let go of so easily, having been firmly united with them by the Creator's hand.

I could neither retreat nor remain, as the bond of nature had fettered me, until the boy signaled with his eyes and said to me, "Away, away!" by which he barely moved me to retreat. My feet indeed went forward, and my body followed, I know not how; but my heart did not want to go along, and I turned my face often back toward the boy. With sorrowful glances, my eyes paid more heed to him behind me than to the path ahead. When I had reached the height of the mountain—though I know not how, for my spirit had not traveled with my body—I wished to see my son once more from a high vantage point, but I could no longer catch sight of him, as he was hidden from my eyes by the distance. After the barbarians <note>A term used in this period for nomadic tribes outside the Roman/Byzantine world, likely Saracens in this context</note> had killed many others and devastated everything in the wilderness, they quickly retreated a great distance.

### Chapter 10.

-> A fugitive tells how the Arabs intended to <-

While we were still speaking of this, it was announced that a man had escaped unharmed from the hands of the barbarians <note>A term for the nomadic tribes, likely Saracens, mentioned in the previous chapter</note>; he arrived among us shortly thereafter, still bearing the marks of fear in his eyes, nor could he hide the disturbance of his soul. I then told your son of the barbarians' plan and signaled to him that unless we saved our lives by flight, the sun would not see us alive again. But he feared they might overtake him again; so he remained and said: 'What God pleases, one cannot escape, wherever one may be, even if one hid in the most secret corners.' When I saw thereafter in the darkness that they all lay in deep sleep, overcome by great drunkenness, I first crawled along the earth for a while, so that if any were awake, the shadow of my upright body might not betray me. When I was then a little distance from the camp, I ran with a swift pace toward this place, where fear led me as if on wings, because I wished to escape the decreed murder. For even if they should catch me again, I thought, I could suffer nothing worse than the death they already intended, and I held uncertain hope to be better than certain death. See now, my intuition <term>Muhtmassung: an old term for a conjecture or gut feeling</term> did not deceive me, and I am here with you as you see, without any injury."

As they went forth together, their guides—who were supposed to protect them—unexpectedly became their attackers. They first killed the little son before the father’s eyes, so that by witnessing his son’s death and the anticipation of his own, his pain might be doubled. As soon as they had killed the child, they murdered the father with many wounds, while he cried out against their treachery and deceit with a loud voice. In such a manner was this man betrayed by great promises and miserably executed."

They traveled through the desert, not in a straight line, but by detours through rough and pathless places, turning now here, now there. They bypassed the high, steep mountains and went on foot through uncertain, broken paths and over uneven hills, until they spotted a green place in the distance. Beside it, there was plenty of grass to pasture the horses and camels. After they had unloaded the camels, they let them roam free on the pasture; they themselves, however, hurried to the water, drank, washed, and bathed, and hardly knew how to make full use of such abundance.

## Chapter 13.
->The Execution of Two Hermits.<-

While they were jumping and dancing nearby and praising the spring, they noticed a small sign of an inhabited cave on the side of the mountain. They all raced there, each trying to outdo the other. When they drew near, they surrounded the cave, the entrance of which was blocked with stones—except for a small hole—to keep out wild animals. After they had cleared the stones away and several of them had entered (as many could not fit inside), they led out a dignified and venerable old man. As they dragged him away, he appeared neither distraught nor pale, nor did he show or speak any sign of dejection or sorrow. They led him to a rock, and because the villains had no swords with them, they killed him with stones, laughing and shouting "Hurrah!" as they did so. They then searched a little further and seized a pale, thin young man, whose face bore the marks of his self-denial <note>The German 'Enthaltung' refers to the ascetic practice of fasting and physical discipline common among desert monks</note>. They killed him in the same manner with stones, while he spoke many words of thanks to God, testifying that he was deeply indebted to them for shortening his path of virtue and helping him toward [eternal] life.

99. St. Paul and the Fathers on Sinai

## Chapter 14.
->A joyful youth is killed in his hut.<-

They had not come far from there when, behold, a green place appeared, surrounded by many trees; the barbarians <note>In this 5th-century context, "barbarians" refers to the nomadic non-Romanized tribes of the desert, likely Saracens or Blemmyes.</note> ran there as fast as they could. When they drew near, they came upon a small hut in which a youth was practicing his devotions, whose great and noble spirit even the barbarians themselves admired. For he would not show them the hidden huts of the solitary ones <note>The German *Einsame* refers to anchorites or hermits living in total isolation.</note> to escape the death that the barbarians had promised him, nor would he come out of his hut or explain himself. To betray another, he said, was treachery; and to be obedient to them was a sign of a weak mind. For those, he further spoke, who exercise themselves in the spirit must have a great and fresh courage; and it would be a shame for them if, out of fear and threats, they gave way to folly, even if it meant the danger of death. Therefore, he continued, since your desire is completely refused, do not delay in carrying out your intention; for I will not show you the places where the holy men reside, nor will I step out before the door, nor take off my tunic <note>The original German *Kittel* refers to the simple, rough garment worn by monks.</note>, so that anyone might see me naked while I am still alive and free, and gaze upon my body, which I myself have not looked upon to this very day. But after my death, when I no longer have any feeling, anyone may do as he pleases; for those who commit the cruelty, not those who must suffer it, are punishable. In this I wish to die, in my tunic as I have resolved, and I will do nothing against such a resolution, nor betray myself like a slave; I would rather die in this hut where I have struggled, and this little house shall be my grave, where I have endured many a battle for the sake of virtue and have sweated; there may my blood now flow. When the villains heard him speak so boldly and could no longer bear it, they gave the youth as many blows with embittered spirits as his body had room to receive; and after many of them had mortally wounded him, they went away, dissatisfied that they could not inflict greater torture upon him.

They, however, jumped up in confusion toward me, and as they seized me, they mistreated me in an inhuman manner. But those who had gone with me to seek the water, when they saw that they had not yet been discovered, they turned back stealthily and crept away like snakes on the earth, thus saving themselves by flight. As for me, although they bound, dragged, and tore at me (indeed, what did I not have to suffer?), I paid no heed to it and hardly felt it, but my whole heart was directed toward my son, and I looked closely about to see if I might catch sight of him.

When this happened, it did not take long; behold, fighting men of our own arrived. # 100. African Martyr-History / or Persecution of the Orthodox by the Arian Vandals /

## From the Year 427 to 475.

### Chapter 1.

->*The Vandals arrive in Africa / and are there a heavy rod of discipline for the Church.*<-

It is now, by common knowledge, sixty years (writes Victor of Vita <note>Victor of Vita (c. 430–490) was a bishop and the primary contemporary historian of the Vandal persecutions. His work "History of the Vandal Persecution" is the main source for these events.</note> in the year 487) since the cruel and fierce people of the Vandals first miserably set foot upon the African borders; they crossed with little effort over the strait between Spain and Africa, where the great and wide sea narrows to a width of three miles. After the entire swarm had crossed over, their cunning king Gaiseric <note>original: "Genserichus." He was the King of the Vandals and Alans who established the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa.</note>—so that reports of him might spread all the more terrifyingly—ordered the entire multitude to be counted, namely, all the souls who had been born into the world under his rule up to that day; eighty thousand were then counted, including old and young, masters and servants. This number has remained spread among the nations to this day, as if there had been so many fighting men, though they are now found to be weak and few. 

As they then found a peaceful and quiet land, which stood everywhere in full glory, they overran the country in raiding parties and laid it waste, burning and killing everything they encountered; they did not even spare the fruit-bearing trees, so that those who might be hiding in mountain caves or earthen pits, or anywhere else, could not use them for food after their march. While their cruelty raged in such a manner, no place remained undamaged by them; they raged most maliciously against the congregations of God, the churches of the saints, chapels and churchyards, and the huts of the solitary brothers <note>The "solitary brothers" refers to monks or hermits living in ascetic communities in the North African desert.</note>; so that they attacked the [houses of] pray-

Houses of prayer burned, as did the cities and towns themselves. Where they perhaps found the doors of the holy houses locked, they chopped them down with their combined might; so that one could truly say of that time: One sees the axes gleaming, as one hews in a forest, and they break down all your paneling with axes and hammers; they burn your sanctuary and desecrate the dwelling of your name to the ground. **Psalm 74, v. 5, 6, 7.** How many excellent bishops and noble priests were executed with manifold martydom, so that they might surrender what gold, silver, or church vessels they held in safekeeping? And even though they, moved by the pain, gladly gave what they had, the Vandals nevertheless repeated the most cruel tortures, believing that only a portion and not everything had been declared; for the more a person gave, the more they believed he still possessed. They forced open the mouths of some with a large stick and put foul filth <note>The German "stinkenden Unflaht" refers to excrement or rotting refuse used as a form of sensory torture and humiliation.</note> inside to extort money through this; others they tormented with ropes, which they wound around their foreheads and legs, twisting them about; into the mouths of many they poured salty seawater, into others vinegar, and into still others the dregs of oil <note>original: "Grund-Suppe vom Oehl." This refers to the bitter, rancid sediment found at the bottom of olive oil vats.</note> and more such cruel things, as if into a wineskin, without any mercy. Neither the female sex, nor noble status, nor priestly dignity could soften their cruel minds; rather, their madness grew greater when they had honorable people in their hands. I do not wish to recount how many priests and how many nobles they burdened with monstrous loads, like camels and other beasts of burden; whom they drove along with iron goads, some of whom had to leave their lives miserably under the weight. They had absolutely no mercy for old age and venerable gray hairs, which adorned the head like white wool; and their barbaric madness even tore nursing children from their mother's breasts and dashed the innocent infants <note>original: "unmündige Alter," literally "the age of those who cannot yet speak."</note> against the earth; others they held aloft by their feet and then chopped them in half, so that in those days, it was sung in the captured gates of Zion:

## Chapter 9.

->God’s wrath strikes the house of the Vandal. The witnesses of Christ are given to the King of the Moors and converted many heathens.<-

But when the **Vandal** master refused to take heed of their virtuous power, divine vengeance began to rage in his house; for he himself died, and at the same time his son, and furthermore his best livestock perished. Thereupon the remaining widow, who was robbed of her husband, sons, and property, gave the servants of GOD to **Sersaoni** <note>original: "Sersaoni," a relative of the Vandal King</note>, a relative of the King, as a gift. He received and accepted them with gratitude as his bondservants, but because of this, his sons and household members were plagued by evil spirits in many ways. The King’s relatives complained of this to the King himself, who decided that they should be sent away to a King of the **Moors** <note>original: "Maurer," referring to the Mauri or Moorish tribes of North Africa</note> named **Capsus**. However, for the sake of decency, he voluntarily released the handmaid of Christ, **Maxima**, who is still alive today and is a spiritual mother to many virgins, and is by no means unknown to us (*) in person. The others reached the King of the **Moors** and were delivered to him; he dwelt, however, in the desert called **Prapicta**. When the servants of Christ saw the abominable types of heathenish idol sacrifices, they began through their word and conduct to invite the barbarians to the grace of our GOD; and in such a manner they won for the LORD a countless multitude of heathen people in a place where previously even the Christian name had never been heard.

## Chapter 10.

->The Holy Scriptures are burned / the churches plundered / Bishop **Valerianus** is exiled; Church-murder is committed.<-

After this, **Genseric** was ignited with new fury against the congregation of GOD’s orthodox believers <note>The Vandals were Arian Christians, who often persecuted the "Orthodox" or Nicene Christians they found in Africa</note>, and he sent **Proclus** into the **Zeugitana** province <note>original: "Eugitanische Landschaft," referring to the Roman province of Zeugitana in modern-day Tunisia</note> to demand the Divine Mysteries—that is, all the books—so that the priests of the LORD would first be made defenseless, and the cunning enemy might then more easily capture the unarmed. Who would not have compassion here for the wailing priests, as this gang of Proclus's robbed everything from the churches? From the coverings of the altar, they, alas, made camisoles <note>waistcoats or undershirts</note> and trousers; for which act, however, **Proclus** the ringleader later bit off and devoured his own tongue.

After they entered the church, they unsheathed their swords and began to slaughter; others climbed onto the roof and shot through the windows with arrows. Even as the people of **God** were singing and chanting psalms in turn, a cantor stood before the lectern and began the **Hallelujah**; at that very moment, he was struck by an arrow, causing him to drop the book from his hand and fall dead to the ground. Many others were shot with arrows and javelins in the middle of the choir before the altar. Those who did not perish by the sword at that time were later miserably punished and all executed by the King’s command, especially those who were of full age.

# History of Martyrdom / AD 427–475.

When the straps snapped, they took stronger ones, specifically made of horse-hide, which nonetheless had no power over him; instead, he called upon the name of **Christ**. Even though he hung upside down by only one foot, it seemed to everyone as if he were resting gently upon a soft feather-bed. When **Theodoricus**, the royal prince who was his master, saw that the aforementioned torture had no power over him, he ordered him to be beheaded. However, he was discouraged from this by his priest **Jocundo** <note>Likely Jucundus, an Arian priest</note>, who said to him: "You would do better to inflict various other tribulations upon him; for if you kill him with the sword, the Romans <note>In this context, "Romans" refers to the local Nicene/Catholic population who remained loyal to the theology of the Roman Empire</note> will make a martyr out of him!" 

Thereupon, **Theodoricus** condemned him to the mines of the **Byzacena** <note>A Roman province in North Africa, in what is now Tunisia</note> landscape. Later, for his intended greater humiliation, it was ordered that the martyr should herd cows at a place near **Carthage** where he could be seen by everyone. 

In the meantime, through a revelation from the **Lord**, he foresaw the approaching day of his death. He called for a worthy Christian named **Felix**, who was the prince's Court Marshal and who respected **Armogastes** as an honorable apostle. He spoke to him: "The time of my departure is come. I adjure you by the faith which we both share, that you bury me under this oak tree; if you do not do this, you shall give an account for it to **God**!" He said this not because he was worried about how or where he should be buried, but to prove that the **Lord Christ** had revealed the end to His servant. 

**Felix**, however, answered him and said: "Far be that from us, venerable confessor; rather, I will have you buried as you deserve, with joy and songs of praise, in one of the main churches." To this, the blessed **Armogastes** replied: "No, you shall do what I have said!" Fearing to grieve the man of **God**, **Felix** promised to truly fulfill his command. 

Immediately after, in just a few days, the witness of a good confession departed from this life. **Felix** hurried to prepare the designated grave under the oak. When the workers were hindered in their digging by the roots of the tree, they cut them away so that the holy limbs of the body might soon be laid in the earth; until finally, they dug very deep and came upon a coffin of gleaming marble, such as no king might have ever possessed.

His wife came to the place where her husband was alone and praying, with torn clothes and disheveled hair, accompanied by her two sons and a nursing infant whom she carried in her arms. ### Chapter 14.

-> Huneric comes to power in Africa, persecutes the erring, <-
-> and, at the intercession of Emperor Zeno, grants the <-
-> orthodox religious freedom. <-

After the death of *Genseric* <note>original: "Genserici"</note>, *Huneric* <note>original: "Hunericus"</note>, the eldest and crown prince, succeeded his father in the government. At the beginning of his reign, he acted with mildness and kindness—though with Arian craftiness—especially regarding our religion. He went so far as to allow the spiritual assemblies, which had been forbidden in *Genseric’s* time, to be held by all people. However, to prove his zeal for his own religion <note>The Vandals followed Arianism, which taught that Jesus was not equal to God the Father, a view considered heretical by the Roman "orthodox" or Trinitarian church.</note>, he ordered a search for several heretical Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement from Persia that was heavily persecuted by both Arian and Trinitarian Christians.</note>. Some of these he burned, and many others he sent across the sea in ships. He found that almost all these Manichaeans shared Arian views; specifically, their priests and deacons were adherents of the Arian heresy. He was ashamed of this and grew even more incensed with anger. Among them was one named *Clementianus*, a hermit <note>original: "Einsamer"</note>, who had written upon his body: *Manichaeus, a disciple of Jesus Christ* <note>original: "Manichäus ein Jünger Jesu Christi"</note>. Because of this, the aforementioned tyrant subjected them to even more mockery.

In one matter, however, he displeased even his own people: he possessed an insatiable hunger for greed and burdened the subjects of his kingdom with various taxes; so that it could chiefly be said of him: "A prince without income is a great misery!" Yet, at the written request of Emperor *Zeno* <note>The Eastern Roman Emperor in Constantinople.</note> and his wife *Placidia*, he granted freedom for the orthodox in *Carthage* to open their church and to elect a bishop as they pleased, after they had been deprived of such joy for twenty-four years. He then sent a nobleman named *Alexander* to the congregation, who brought the following message: that the orthodox people should elect a worthy bishop in his presence. He also had his notary <note>term: Notarium (a legal official or secretary)</note>, named *Jutarit*, announce a decree and read it publicly, with this content:

> Our Lord has commanded us to announce that Emperor *Zeno* and the most noble *Placidia* have sent a letter through *Alexander*, a great lord, in which they request that the congregation of our city of *Carthage* may have its own bishop. Our king has now granted this and has sent word of his answer through...

## Chapter 17.

### The Tyranny of the Vandal King Huneric against his own relatives and Arian coreligionists.

He himself, however—who had long been well-known to everyone—sought after his passing to leave the kingdom to his sons, which nevertheless did not come to pass. He cruelly persecuted his brothers, Theodoric <note>original: "Theodorichum"</note> and his sons, and Genton <note>original: "Gentonium"</note> along with his sons; he let none of them escape before death fulfilled his desire. First, because he knew that Theodoric’s wife was a clever woman and feared she might incite her husband or eldest son with heated schemes against him, he accused her of a committed vice and had her executed by the sword. Afterward, their eldest prince was also killed; he was a well-educated man to whom the kingdom should have belonged by the decree of King Geiseric <note>original: "Genserici"</note>, as he was the eldest of the grandsons <note>Geiseric had established a law of "agnatic seniority," where the throne passed to the oldest living male in the royal family rather than from father to son.</note>. After such a deed, he was inflamed to even more cruel acts. He had Jocundus—the bishop of his own Arian sect <term>Arianism</term> <note>Arianism was a Christian belief that held that Jesus was created by God the Father and was not co-eternal with Him. This was the faith of the Vandal kings, which put them at odds with the Roman population.</note>, whom they called a patriarch—burned in his presence in the middle of the New Street. This was because the bishop was very popular in the palace of his biological brother Theodoric, and Huneric feared that Theodoric might one day obtain the kingdom through the bishop's help. From this murderous deed, we could measure our own impending, even greater tribulations, as we said to one another: "Since he acts so cruelly toward his own priest, how should he spare our religion or ourselves?" Thereupon, he also banished the eldest prince of his brother Genton, named Godagis, along with his wife, into a merciless exile without any comfort from servants or maids. He likewise disposed of his brother Theodoric—after executing the man's wife and children—sending him away naked and destitute; who after his death [yet...]

## Chapter 18.
### Visions and Signs that Preceded the Persecution.

For almost two years before the tribulation truly began, a certain man saw the Church of Faustus <note>A famous basilica in Carthage dedicated to Saint Faustus.</note> shining in its usual splendor. But while he was rejoicing that the wax candles burned so brightly, and the altar and pulpit cloths along with the candlesticks gleamed so brilliantly, behold, in a single moment the lovely glow vanished, and a foul odor arose in the darkness. At the same time, all the venerable clergymen were thrust out by **black Moors** <note>original: "schwarzen Mohren." In the context of 5th-century African visions, "Moors" often symbolized demonic forces or the impending Vandal/Arian threat.</note>; the most lamentable part was that he did not see them restored to their former radiance. This vision was recounted by the one who had the dream to Eugenius <note>Saint Eugenius, the Bishop of Carthage (d. 505), who led the church during the Vandal persecution.</note> in our presence. Also, a certain priest saw the main church of Faustus filled with a great multitude of **pigs and goats**. Another saw a threshing floor prepared with wheat, in which the chaff and grain still lay mixed together. As he marveled at this great heap, a sudden storm wind arose, announcing its arrival with thick dust; by its assault, all the chaff was blown away, and only the grain remained. Then came a distinguished man, whose face and clothing shone, and he began to purge the empty, withered, and useless bits from it, until after a long examination only a very small pile of pure wheat remained. Another related: A very tall man stood on the Mountain of the Lord, which is called the **Siquensian** <note>Refers to the region of Sicca Veneria in modern-day Tunisia.</note>, who cried out to the right and to the left: "Depart from here! Depart from here!" Another saw in the red sky sulfurous, dark clouds, from which monstrous stones were shot forth; when these stones fell to the earth, they burned even more and gave off even larger flames, and whenever they entered a house, they ignited everything they encountered. He who saw this said he hid himself in a chamber, and through divine mercy the flame was not permitted to approach him; so that, in my opinion, that prophetic word was fulfilled:

> Close your door, and hide yourself a little while until the wrath of God passes. Isaiah 26, v. 20.

## Chapter 20.

### All Right-Believing Officials are Dismissed and Episcopal Properties are Confiscated.

What happened then after this? First, the tyrant <note>King Huneric (reigned 477–484), depicted here as a "tyrant" due to his fierce promotion of Arianism over the Nicene faith.</note> issued a sharp command that no one should remain in service at his court, nor hold a public office, unless they were or would become an <term>Arian</term> <note>Arianism: A theological movement that held that Jesus Christ was created by God the Father and was not co-eternal or of the same substance; it was considered a heresy by the Nicene "Right-believing" Christians.</note>. At this, a great multitude, with invincible courage, chose to leave their temporal service rather than their faith; these he later drove from their houses, hearths, and homes, and banished them into misery on the islands of Sicily and Sardinia. Furthermore, he issued a decree throughout all Africa that whenever one of our bishops departed this temporal life, his income and property should fall to the royal treasury; and whoever wished to succeed the deceased in office could not be installed until they had paid five hundred <term>Reichs-Thaler</term> <note>original: "Reichs-Thaler." The German translator uses the currency of his own time (17th/18th century) to represent the original Roman-era fine, likely measured in gold solidi.</note> to him. However, this structure which the devil had built with great pretense was soon torn down again by the Lord Christ in His mercy; for King Huneric’s advisors dissuaded him from this, saying: "If we were to establish this firmly, it would go even worse for our Arian fellow-believers in Thrace and other lands under Roman rule" <note>This reveals the political tension between the Vandal Kingdom in Africa and the Eastern Roman Empire; the Vandals feared that if they were too harsh, the Roman Emperor would retaliate against Arians living in Byzantium.</note>.

### Chapter 22.

->Nearly five thousand clergy are banished into misery.<-

With what torrents of tears should I further report how he banished the bishops, priests, deacons, and other members of the congregation—numbering four thousand, nine hundred, and seventy-six—into misery in the deserts? Among these were many who had <term>Podagra</term> <note>original: "Podagra"; an old medical term for gout, particularly in the feet.</note>, and others who were deprived of their physical sight due to old age; among which number was included the blessed Felix, the forty-year bishop of Abbirita, who was paralyzed by a stroke and was entirely insensitive and speechless. For this reason, we were most concerned for him because he could not ride, and we had it brought before the King through his people, begging him that he might graciously allow him to die nearby Carthage, as there was no way or means to lead him so far into exile. To this, the King is said to have answered in full rage: "If he cannot ride, then couple a pair of wild oxen together and let them drag him by a rope to where we have commanded!" Thus, we carried him laid crosswise over a stretcher, like a log, the entire way. However, all the banished gathered in the city of Sicca and Laris, from where the Moors <note>The indigenous North African tribes who were often used by the Vandals to escort prisoners into the deep desert.</note> were to lead them further into the wilderness. There, two counts came to them, who sought to deceive the confessors of God with damnable cunning and flattering words. "What do you think," they said, "that you are so stubborn and will in no way obey our Lord's command, you who could live in honor before the King, if you would only submit to his will..."

### Chapter 23.
### A Christian old widow’s voluntary misery for Christ's sake.

What a certain old mother did at that time, I must tell you briefly. As we traveled on, accompanying God’s army <note>The "army" refers to the massive group of nearly 5,000 exiled Christians being marched into the desert.</note> and, because of the great heat, covering most of the distance by night, we saw an old woman carrying a bundle of old clothes and such things, leading by the hand a little boy. She called out: "Run, my lord! Do you not see how all the saints are moving forward and hastening toward the crown?" When we saw her and scolded her for her audacity—that she had mingled with the crowd and joined herself to Christ’s army—she gave for an answer: "God’s will be done! God’s will be done! Also for me and for this my little grandson; for I, a poor sinner, am a daughter of the late Bishop of Surinana!" <note>Likely referring to a bishop from a North African diocese, possibly Sures or a similarly named region in the Roman province.</note> Thereupon we asked her and said: "Why then do you walk so miserably, and for what reason do you come this long way?" (*) She answered: "I go into misery <note>In this context, "misery" (Elend) refers to exile or banishment into the desert wilderness.</note> with this my little servant, so that the enemy <note>Referring to the Arian persecutors or the Devil.</note> does not find him alone and lead him astray from the way of truth!" At such words, we were moved to tears and were able to say nothing, except that God’s will may be done.

# Chapter 25.
->The continued journey of the exiles, to whom Bishop Cyprian shows great love.<-

Suddenly the Moors caused an uproar and ordered them to get ready for the journey, so as to reach the designated place quickly. Thus they went out on the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>, with filthy clothes and faces; though the Moors threatened them cruelly, they nevertheless sang a song of praise to the Lord and said: *This honor have all his saints; we must joyfully embrace and kiss it.* <note>original: "Diß Recht der Heiligen müssen wir fröhlich umarmen und küssen." — Psalm 149:9.</note>
For at that time, Bishop Cyprian of Unzibilis <note>A bishop of a town in Roman North Africa who was eventually exiled himself.</note> was present—an exceptional preacher of comfort who refreshed everyone with godly, fatherly love, not without frequent flowing tears. He was ready to give his life for his brothers and would have voluntarily entered into the same suffering if it had been permitted. He distributed all his wealth to the needy brothers in this distress, for he sought only the opportunity to be united with these confessors. He was already a confessor in spirit and power, and later, through various struggles and the misery of the dungeon, he joyfully entered the longed-for exile.

Afterward, the Vandals commanded the Moors to drag those who could no longer walk by their bound feet like dead horses over the rough path. There, first their clothes, and then their skin and flesh were torn as they struck their heads here and their sides there against the sharp, rocky places, giving up the ghost in the hands of those dragging them. We could not learn their number because of the haste of the march. Yet, along the entire public road, the simple burial mounds of the saints can still be counted, which bear witness to these events.

->The miserable state of the confessors in the desert. New movements<-
->in Carthage.<-

The others, who were stronger, finally reached the designated place in the desert, where they were given only raw, unground barley to eat, just like cattle. It is said, however, that there is such a multitude of venomous animals and scorpions there that it seems unbelievable to those who do not know it; these creatures are said to emit a deadly poison even from a distance with their mere breath. ### Chapter 28.

->Huneric’s Command to the Orthodox.<-

Huneric, King of the Vandals and Alans, sends word to all bishops who teach that the Son and the Father are of one essence <term>Homoousios: the Nicene belief that God the Father and Jesus are of the exact same divine substance</term> (*): It is well known that your priests have been forbidden, not once but often, from holding any assembly within the territory of the Vandals, or from subverting Christian souls with their unrest; many of them have despised this command and have nonetheless held assemblies in the Vandal territory, testifying that they held fast to the perfect rule of the true Christian faith. Because we will tolerate no division or offense in the provinces that God has entrusted to us, know then that by Divine providence, and with the consent of our holy bishops <note>These "holy bishops" refer to the Arian clergy favored by the Vandal king.</note>, we have decreed that on the coming first of January, you shall all assemble at Carthage without any excuse of fear, so that you may enter into a debate regarding the foundation of the faith with our venerable bishops and demonstrate from the Scriptures the faith of the Homoousians <note>The "Same-Substance" believers.</note> which you defend; from this, we may test whether you hold the correct faith. We have sent the contents of this command to all your fellow bishops throughout all Africa. Given the 19th of June in the seventh year of Huneric (**).

# Chapter 29.
->Bishop Eugenius’ Response.<-

When we who were present saw and read these things, our hearts were immediately crushed, and our eyes were troubled and darkened. Our feast days were—so to speak—truly turned into days of mourning (Amos 8:10), because the content of this edict clearly revealed the severe persecution to come; especially where it states that they will no longer tolerate any division or offense in their lands. Thus, we deliberated on what should be done and found no remedy for the impending distress. Whenever matters concerning the soul, eternal life, and the Christian faith are discussed, it is necessary that we properly present ourselves at the court without fear, according to the Royal promise. Since His Royal Majesty recently deigned to command something through the Sub-Chancellor, which was publicly read in the congregation in the presence of the clergy and the people of our faith and religion; we understood from this that this Royal command was issued to all fellow bishops at once: namely, that we should gather on a set day to dispute concerning the faith, which we accept with all reverence. 

However, after the Chancellor read this, I <note>original: "meine Wenigkeit," literally "my littleness"—a common humble self-reference in formal letters of this period.</note> reminded him that it would be proper for all the bishops across the sea <note>Referring to the wider Christian world across the Mediterranean, including Rome and Constantinople.</note> who share one faith, religion, and communion with us to also be informed of this, because we all obey one Lord; especially since this concerns the affairs of all Christendom, not just these *African* churches. And because I have sacredly vowed to present myself, I ask your Excellency that you might deign to report to the Lord and most gracious King that His Goodness should please take to heart how we do not at all refuse the said disputation regarding the Law and the Faith, but cannot begin such a thing without the consent of all Christendom. Therefore, we pray that His Majesty, according to his goodness, justice, and wisdom, would find this acceptable.

### Chapter 30.

But when this answer was sent in by the blessed *Eugenius*, the birth pangs of persecution immediately stirred, so that wickedness might be brought into the world. Therefore, the King commanded through *Cubadus*, his court councilor, that the holy Bishop *Eugenius* be told: "Bring the whole world under my power, so that the entire globe is subject to me, and then I will deliver the message of which you spoke." Thereupon *Cubadus* replied: "So, are you and my lord both kings at the same time?" Bishop *Eugenius* said: "I do not compare myself to the King; rather, I say: If he desires to know the true faith, he should send to his friends, the Emperors, so that they may grant permission to our orthodox <note>original: "recht-gläubigen," meaning those adhering to the Nicene Creed as opposed to the King's Arianism.</note> bishops of the Roman Empire to travel here. But he <note>King Huneric.</note>, who went to work deceitfully, would not accept our reasons, but instead made twisted conclusions and began to persecute all the bishops who were skillful and learned.

## Chapter 32.

->A remarkable occurrence involving a blind man who regained his sight.<-

There was in that same city, namely **Carthage**, a certain well-known blind man named **Felix**. The Lord visited him, and in that same night it was revealed and told to him through a vision: "Arise, and go to my servant, Bishop **Eugenius**, and tell him that I have sent you to him; and in the same hour that I shall bless the font <note>original: "Brunnen (des Tauf-Steins)," meaning the water of the baptismal font</note> and therein baptize the faithful, your eyes shall be opened and you shall see the light!" When he was awakened by such a vision, he thought to himself that it might only be a fleeting dream, and the blind man did not wish to get up; until it came to him again, and he was once more driven to go to Bishop **Eugenius**. He neglected it yet again, until for the third time he was even more severely rebuked and exhorted to hurry. Thus, he woke his boy, who used to lead him, and went with a quick pace to the Church of **Faustus**, and came before God with many tears; he then asked a certain deacon named **Peregrinus** to announce him to the Bishop, for he had a secret to reveal to him. When the Bishop heard this, he ordered the man to be let in; for because of the coming festival, the nightly hymns resounded throughout the whole church. The blind man then described the vision he had with all the circumstances he had gathered, and added: "I will not leave you, unless you, according to the command of my Lord..."

The man who had been blind went with **Eugenius** to the altar, as is the custom, to thank the Lord for his well-being and to present an offering, which Bishop **Eugenius** accepted and placed upon the altar. The commotion grew, and the joy of the people was unspeakable. 

Word of this soon reached the tyrant <note>referring to the Vandal King Huneric, who was an Arian</note>. **Felix** was forced to appear before him and was asked how it had happened that he regained his sight. He recounted everything in order. To this, the Arian bishops <note>The Arians were a sect that denied the full divinity of Christ; they were the favored group of the Vandal kings</note> claimed that **Eugenius** had accomplished this through sorcery. And because they were troubled and could not obscure the light—since **Felix** was well-known throughout the city—they nevertheless desired to kill him if possible, just as the Jews once wished to kill the resurrected **Lazarus**.

This decree stipulated that no party, except for their own superstitious teachers, should be granted religious freedom; otherwise, no one should be permitted to dine together, or hold assemblies and build churches, neither publicly in the city nor in the most remote places, but such property should instead fall to the **public treasury**. This law, which flows from the fountainhead of justice, we have made known to all, so that no one may excuse themselves with ignorance. We wish that you may fare well! ### Chapter 38.

->Severity of the Edict against all the Orthodox.<-

It then happened that, according to the merit of their confession <note>Meaning their refusal to renounce the Nicene Creed</note>, they were made into slaves and were completely deprived of all their honors and privileges, as they were recognized as being without honor, and such persons were declared subject to public punishment. They imposed a fine of thirty pounds of silver on the (orthodox) officials in various courts; if they had paid this five times while persisting in their error, they were to be declared completely dishonored, flogged, and banished into exile. Furthermore, they commanded that all books and writings of the priests whom they persecuted be burned with fire; however, those books which they still approved of in their malice were sold. As stated, every person had to pay a fine for themselves: every person of the nobility forty pounds of gold, other dignitaries twenty pounds of gold, the priests thirty pounds of gold, the captains and elders fifteen pounds of gold, every common man five pounds of gold, and the unmarried who as yet had no trade ten pounds of silver. If anyone should persist in his ruin <note>That is, stay faithful to his religious "error"</note>, the command stated that all his goods were to be confiscated and he was ultimately to be banished into exile. The city councils, officials, and owners of landed estates were warned under penalty that if they were inclined to hide the others, and did not discover them and place them under arrest before the court, they themselves should suffer the punishment. The (orthodox) tenants of the Royal Table-Estates <note>Lands designated for the personal maintenance and expenses of the King's household</note> were to pay as much in fines as they paid in rent to the King; this was observed for all who persisted in the (supposed) superstition. Regarding the judges who would remain constant in such an opinion, they were to be outlawed and punished with death. Three of their most prominent officials were thus to be executed, while others were to pay twenty pounds of gold. Under such conditions (the Edict further stated), we must bind all the <term>Homoousians: those who believe that God the Son is "of the same substance" as God the Father, the central doctrine of the Nicene Creed</term>, as those who have secretly harbored the fuel of this fire; we therefore resolve to persecute such people, not only in all ranks within the cities, but even those judges who behave sluggishly in carrying out the punishment. We furthermore command all those who are devoted to the aforementioned Homoousian error, and [who have been] by the previously mentioned Councils so...

### Chapter 39.

Since the local judges were slow to carry out these [orders], they were punished by the Superior Court, and others, whom the King had appointed for that purpose, hurried to force the oath upon the Bishops. ### Chapter 42.
#### The History of the Martyrdom of Saint Victoria.

But as for what occurred in the city of <term>Culusitana</term> <note>An ancient city in the Roman province of Africa, located in modern-day Tunisia.</note>, I am unable to recount it all, for it is impossible for a person even to calculate the sheer number of <term>martyrs</term> <note>those killed for their faith</note> and <term>confessors</term> <note>those who suffered for their faith but survived or died later from their wounds</note>. There was a certain matron there who bore the name **Victoria**—meaning "a victress"—and she truly lived up to it through her deeds. In the sight of the people, she was repeatedly hoisted up and scorched with smoke; meanwhile, her corrupt husband, in the presence of their sons, pleaded with her as follows: "Why do you suffer this, dear wife? If you have no regard for me, then at least have mercy on these small children you have borne! Why do you forget the fruit of your womb, and think nothing of those you brought into the world with such pain? Where are the covenants of married love? Where are the bonds of our partnership? Where are our marriage contracts, which we drew up long ago for the sake of our social standing? Look upon your children and your husband, I pray, and do not delay in obeying the King’s command, so that you may escape the torture yet to come and be restored to me and our children!" But she heard neither the children’s weeping nor the snake’s flattering words, but instead looked with her eyes from the earth toward heaven, and despised the world with its desires. When they saw her in a deathly faint after hanging for a long time, which had dislocated her shoulder blades, the executioners took her down, leaving her for dead. However, after she recovered from her faint, she recounted that a virgin had stood by her and touched all her limbs, through which she was made whole again.

## Chapter 43.
->Victorianus's Confession and Martyrdom.<-

I know not how I should extol **Victorianus**—a citizen of <term>Adrumitum</term> <note>Modern Sousse, Tunisia; a major Roman city in North Africa.</note> and at that time the <term>Mayor</term> <note>original: "Bürgemeister"; likely referring to the office of Proconsul or a high administrative rank under the Vandals.</note> of Carthage—for I find myself lacking the words to do him justice. In all of Africa, no one was wealthier than he, and he was held as the most faithful in confidential matters by the most godless King <note>Referring to the Vandal King Huneric (reigned 477–484 AD), who was an Arian Christian and persecuted the Nicene "Catholic" Christians.</note>. The King sent a joint message to him, saying that he would hold Victorianus more beloved and esteemed than all others if he would only obey his command <note>i.e., to convert to Arianism</note>. But this man of God, with a courageous heart, gave this answer to those who had been sent: "I rely upon Christ, my God and Lord; tell this to the King: He may torment me with fire, or wild beasts, or with every kind of torture; if I yield, then I have been baptized in the <term>Universal Church</term> <note>original: "allgemeinen Kirchen"; here meaning the Nicene Catholic Church as opposed to the Arian sect favored by the Vandals.</note> in vain. For even if this temporal life were all there was, and we did not hope for another true life, and I nonetheless did not suffer patiently for Christ's sake just to enjoy a little temporal glory, I would surely be an ungrateful man toward the Creator who bestowed His faith upon me." At this, the tyrant grew incensed and had him tortured so severely and inflicted so much agony upon him that no man can find the words to describe it. He, however, exulted and happily completed the struggle, where he received the martyr's crown.

## Chapter 44.
->The Martyrdom Story of Two Brothers at Tambada.<-

Who can also recount all the struggles of the martyrs in the city of **Tambada**? There, two biological brothers from the city of **Aquaregia** <note>Both Tambada and Aquaregia were towns in Roman North Africa (modern Tunisia/Algeria).</note> courageously bound themselves together by an oath in the Lord, stating that they would ask the tormentors to ensure they were martyred in the same manner. When they were first hung up by their hands, with heavy millstones tied to their feet, and left hanging there the entire day, one of them begged to be let down and given time to reconsider. The other brother, fearing that he might renounce his faith, called out from above where he hung: "Do not do it, do not do it, dear brother! You know what we promised to Christ. I shall accuse you when we appear before His <term>dreadful throne</term> <note>original: "entsetzlichen Trohn"; refers to the Bema or Judgment Seat of Christ.</note>, because we bound ourselves by His Body and Blood <note>A reference to the brothers having taken the Eucharist (Holy Communion) together before their arrest.</note> that we would both suffer for Him at the same time." After he had said this and more of the like, he strengthened his brother for new sufferings.

## Chapter 45.
->The Flight of the Orthodox to Tipasa.<-

What also occurred in the Mauritanian city of <term>Tipasa</term> <note>An ancient Roman colony in modern-day Algeria, now a UNESCO World Heritage site.</note>, we wish to relate to the glory of God. When the <term>Orthodox</term> <note>original: "Recht-Gläubigen"; referring to the Nicene Christians who held to the Trinity, as opposed to the Arians.</note> there were forced to receive an Arian Bishop—who had been a <term>notary</term> <note>original: "Notarius"; a high-ranking secretary or administrative official.</note> at the court—to the destruction of their souls, nearly the entire city fled across the straits to Spain; except for a few who were unable to find passage across the narrow sea and remained behind. At first, the Arian Bishop sought to move these people to the Arian faith with flatteries, and afterward with threats. But they, being strengthened in the Lord, not only laughed at the advisor's <note>Likely a typo for "Rahtgebers" (advisors), though the first letter resembles the "N" in "Nachfolge".</note> insanity, but also began to publicly observe the <term>Mysteries of God</term> <note>Meaning the Divine Liturgy or the Eucharist.</note> with solemnity in a house where they had gathered. When the King heard this, he sent a certain Count there in anger, with orders to gather all the <term>Homousians</term> <note>From the Greek "homoousios," meaning "of the same substance"; those who believed Christ was of the same essence as God the Father.</note> of that entire province in the local marketplace and to cut off their tongues and right hands. Yet, through the power of the Holy Spirit, they nevertheless spoke, and they speak still as well as they did before. Should anyone be unable to believe this, let him go to Constantinople; there he will still find one of them who is a <term>subdeacon</term> and can speak very skillfully without any impediment; for which reason he is held in great honor in the palace of the Emperor **Zeno**, and the Empress especially holds him very dear.

## Chapter 48.
### The Story of Deacon Mirita and the Apostate Epidiphorus.

But later, when he became an <term>Apostate</term> <note>Someone who renounces their religious faith, in this case, likely converting to the Arian Christianity favored by the Vandal rulers.</note>, he became so enraged against the Church of God that he was the worst among all the previous persecutors. 

Recently, when the priests were first summoned to be tortured, the aforementioned Mirita had to go to the torture block immediately after the <term>Archdeacon</term> <note>The most senior deacon, often the bishop's right-hand man.</note> Salutaris. For one of the servants was there who—while Epidiphorus sat and gnashed his teeth and before the honorable old man was tortured (though he was already being prepared)—secretly and without anyone's knowledge brought the white shirt <note>The baptismal robe, traditionally worn for eight days after baptism as a symbol of spiritual purity.</note> which Epidiphorus had worn after his baptism to the old man. Mirita brought it out and showed it before everyone, and with the following words, he moved the entire city to tears and weeping:

> "This is the shirt," he spoke, "O Epidiphorus, you servant of error, which will accuse you at the coming of the Majestic Judge. It has been diligently preserved by me as a witness to your ruin, you who plunge yourself into the abyss of the lake of sulfur. This shirt surrounded you when you emerged unstained from the water of baptism; now it will pursue you as you possess the flames of hell, because you have put on the curse like a garment when you tore and lost the covenant of the holy true baptism and the faith. What will you do, you miserable man, when the Master’s servants lead the invited guests to the Royal Banquet? Then the King will be mightily wroth with you, because as one who was called, you have cast away the wedding garment you once wore, and he will say to you: *Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?* <note>A reference to the Parable of the Wedding Feast in Matthew 22:12.</note> I no longer see in you what I shared with you; I do not recognize what I gave to you. You have lost the breastplate which you wore for the protection of your virginal limbs. For ten months <note>Likely referring to the period of instruction or 'carrying' the candidate as a catechumen before baptism.</note> I carried you, and I purified you through the water with the Cross, and with the purple of my blood I [cleansed] you..."

## Chapter 49.

->Twelve boys, who are able to sing, are snatched away from the holy confessors,<-
->yet they remain steadfast.<-

From the multitude of departing Confessors and the Carthaginian clergy, twelve boys were chosen upon the advice of the lost **Lector** <note>original: "Vorleser"; a church official responsible for reading the scriptures.</note> **Theucorius**, because he knew they were very skilled in singing; for when he was still an Orthodox believer, he had them as his pupils. Immediately, upon his advice, men were sent after them, and with barbarian severity, the twelve boys were pulled back from the journey; thus they were torn from the flock of the saints in body, but not in spirit. Fearing their destruction, they clung with their arms to the knees of their companions and begged with tears that they might not be separated; but the **heretical** <note>Referencing the Arian Vandal authorities.</note> violence tore them away with threats of the sword and led them toward **Carthage** <note>The capital city of the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa.</note>.

At the same time, there arose an incredible <unclear>drought</unclear> that devastated all of Africa. The land stood mourning, and all Africa was shaken by this divine plague; neither humans nor the earth [provided] the strength of green herbs; the [fields] dried up and the veins of the springs failed. ...even if it was to be seen in a damp valley, the grass appeared more withered than green, because a burning hot wind ruined everything completely, as the dust in the dry air burnt everything up like a mist. At that time, there was no trade or agriculture at all, because neither livestock nor plow were available. The villages had died out from hunger and plague, and if anyone still lived, he was already preparing his own grave. For because of the famine, neither trade nor commerce, as mentioned, nor agriculture could be carried out, one saw instead young and old, youths and maidens, boys and girls, swarming about in crowds as best they could through cities, market towns, and villages. For because they had walked perversely and provoked **GOD** at the Waters of Strife <note>original: "Hader-Wasser." This is a biblical reference to Meribah (Exodus 17), where the Israelites quarreled with Moses and God. Here, the author uses it as a metaphor for the theological disputes of the time.</note> (*), they now suffered hunger like dogs—not because they had no bread to eat, but rather because they felt the wrath of the Holy Trinity, whom they had denied <note>The Vandals were Arians, meaning they did not believe in the co-equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which the author considers a denial of the Trinity.</note>. Some ran about through the fields, some searched in the forests for the withered roots of herbs or anything else to satisfy their hunger. Some, when they tried to enter a house, collapsed together in the doorway, wasted away by hunger. The roads and footpaths lay full of dead corpses, by whose stench the passers-by were also killed. There was no daily lack of the dead, but certainly a lack of mercy to bury them; because there were not enough living people, who, consumed by hunger themselves, awaited their own imminent death. Everyone wanted to sell their freedom and place their children into eternal servitude <note>a reference to people attempting to sell themselves or their children into slavery just to be fed</note>, but no one could find a buyer. Mountains and hills, the alleys in the city, roads and footpaths were all one graveyard, where the starved lay. Even the Vandals themselves, who had previously become rich through the frequent looting and conquest of Africa, had to feel the hunger all the more now. The more they had boasted of their multitude of serfs and servants, the greater the lack they suffered now during the famine. No one looked after his son, wife, or servant any longer, but each went where he wanted and could, or died immediately without returning. The unfortunate multitude thought they would find help in the city of Carthage; but as they gathered there in heaps, half dead, and the King saw the deadly devastation, he commanded them to be driven out of the city—

# 100. African [History]

... [forbid]den, so that the infectious plague would not also prepare their graves. Therefore he commanded that everyone return to his own place and home, but there were few who were able to turn back, because everyone already bore the sign of death upon their faces. Those who had allowed themselves to be rebaptized <note>The Arian Vandals required Nicene/Orthodox Christians to be rebaptized into the Arian faith, a practice the author views as a spiritual death.</note>, and had received the promise of eternal life from the Arians, could now no longer enjoy it; rather, the first death followed the second death. Meanwhile, hunger raged so cruelly that in places where people were previously seen, there was now only a great silence and bare walls. But why do I undertake to count that which I cannot count? For even if the most skillful orators were present, the flow of Tullian eloquence <note>Refers to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator.</note> would dry up, and the tongue of Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian.</note> would fall silent. So that I might pass by such unworthy things: even if Eusebius of Caesarea <note>The "father of church history" (c. 260–339 AD).</note> were to rise again, he would not be sufficient for this work, nor would his translator Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, who translated Eusebius’s Greek "Church History" into Latin.</note>, though adorned with his Greek and Latin eloquence. Truly, neither Ambrose, nor Jerome, nor our own Augustine are adequate for this task (*).

# The 57th Chapter.

## Repetition of the beginning of the persecution / and the Arian Bishop Cyril’s evil counsel and end.

As I finally wish to report something of the victories of the martyrs, I pray for the [Divine] help, that He who gave them the victory of overcoming may also make me, unworthy and undeserving as I am, fit for this task. Then I shall explain everything according to my desire, if they themselves intercede with the **LORD** for me, a miserable man. In the seventh year of the reign of the cruel and [unju]st King Huneric <note>Huneric (reigned 477–484 AD) was the King of the Vandals and Alans in North Africa, known for his fierce persecution of Nicene Christians.</note>, the old cunning [serpent] <note>A common metaphor for the Devil.</note> made use of her sharp tongue through an Arian bishop, who perverted the King's mind even further with the persuasion that he would not rule peacefully or for long unless he completely rooted out the innocent [Orthodox Christians]. However, by Divine judgment, this counselor was consumed by worms shortly thereafter and died a shameful death. The King, however, began with a bloody throat to [devour] the whole...

# Martyr History / Year 427–475
(Ccc) 4
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

...to persecute the orthodox believers, who throughout all of Africa—following the pattern of Abraham’s blessing—had multiplied like the sand of the sand-sea (*); so that he might execute them with the murderous sword of re-baptism <note>The Arian Vandals considered orthodox baptism invalid and forced believers to be rebaptized into the Arian faith; the author views this as a spiritual execution.</note>, and so that he might defile and stain the white garment of simple, pure baptism, which Christ had cleansed and made bright through his suffering.

## Chapter 58.
->The banishment of the priests into misery; their poor bread; and<-
->The closing of the churches.<-

The tyrant then, who was prone to anger and wild, allowed the promptings of the serpent <note>A reference to the devil or the Arian bishop Cyril, who influenced King Huneric.</note> to take hold, and suddenly stirred up all of Africa by means of his harsh edicts. In the beginning, he banished a great multitude of priests and ministers of the congregation to misery in the most remote places; to whom, out of "mercy," pure, unground, prickly barley was given as food, just like for cattle, with the chaff and all. But later, as the godless madness grew, even this was taken from them; and shortly thereafter, the cruel tyrant had all the churches and their venerable gates closed up with large quarry stones. All the solitary huts <note>Small monastic dwellings or hermitages.</note> of both the men and the holy virgins <note>Nuns.</note> he gave over to the heathens—namely the Moors—along with their inhabitants. Then one heard the cries of lamentation united; all were completely of one mind to die for Christ; all shed the same rivers of tears because the Lord now fed them with the bread of tears and gave them measured—even immeasurable—tears to drink. But although some ravens from this Christian ark were lost—those who followed after carrion <note>A metaphor for those who abandoned the faith for worldly survival or Arianism.</note>—the number of blessed doves in the name of the Trinity was much greater. How many noble and excellent men had to exchange their vast estates for the blue sky <note>A poetic way of saying they were made homeless and destitute.</note>, surrendering their bodies and possessions at once? Meanwhile, tender noblewomen were whipped with rods before all the common people, contrary to natural decency, and martyred in many ways, through which they carried away the signs of victory. How many children laughed at the cruel commands rather than choosing to walk upon alluring, deviant paths?

---

(*) The sandy deserts in Egypt and Arabia are called sand-seas because one must travel through them by the compass, and the tracks are constantly blown over again; also, the sand is seen therein moving in waves.

# 100. African [History]. Chapter 59.
<meta>catchword: Kin-</meta>

->Regarding Seven Solitary Brotherly Martyrs.<-

At that time, seven brothers were seized who lived together as solitaries <note>The text refers to monks or cenobites living in a monastic community.</note> in the harmonious service of the Lord, for it is good and pleasant when brothers dwell together in unity. These were: Liberatus, the Father Abbot; Boniface, the Deacon; Rusticus and Serus, the Sub-deacons; Rogatianus, a solitary brother; along with Septimus and one other. These seven—resembling the number of the Maccabees <note>A reference to the seven Maccabean brothers martyred for their faith in 2 Maccabees 7.</note>—had one mother: the faithful Church. She had conceived them and brought them forth through the womb of the eternal fountain <note>The baptismal font.</note>, having been born again. They were natives of the city of Capsa <note>Modern-day Gafsa, Tunisia.</note>, where the holy Vindemialis was then the reigning priest and a faithful overseer of Christ. 

When they were led toward Carthage, the "cunning serpent" <note>A metaphor for the devil or the Vandal persecutors.</note> first attempted to entice them with charming flatteries, promising them fleeting honors and great wealth in their hour of need, as well as the King’s favor and other things. These are the means by which the minds of the foolish are often snared, using the "birdlime" <note>A sticky substance used by hunters to trap birds; here, a metaphor for worldly temptation.</note> of the diabolical stalker. But the knights of Christ rejected all such things as filth and cried out with one voice: "We acknowledge only one God, one faith, and one baptism <note>original: "Einen GOtt, Einen Glauben, und Eine Taufe." A reference to Ephesians 4:5.</note>, which has been confirmed in us through the assistance of the Holy Spirit. For it is written in the holy Gospel: *He who has bathed once does not need to wash again, but is entirely clean.* <note>original: "Wer einmal gewaschen ist, der bedarfs nicht mehr, ſondern er ist ganz rein." John 13:10.</note> Do what you will with our bodies; it is better for us to suffer temporal shame and torment. Keep the things you promise us, for you and your riches shall shortly perish. No one will lead us away from the baptism we have received, for we have been graced through the Holy Trinity in a single baptism." 

In short, as they maintained the divine truth with such constancy, the command was given that they should be cast into the dungeon. Thus, they were cruelly locked in heavy irons and placed in such a dark place that no mercy could refresh them. However, the faithful people of the city of Carthage bribed the guards with money and visited the prisoners of Christ day and night. By these visits, the people were so strengthened in doctrine and the power of life that they themselves became full of desire to endure the same for the sake of Christ’s name and to stretch out their necks for the sword. But this came to the Kin- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page; the "Kin-" refers to King Huneric.</note>

# History of Martyrs / Year 427–475.

[The news] reached [the King's] ears; who, full of wrath, gave the command to punish them without a hearing and to bind them with even heavier chains. He commanded that a ship be filled with dry wood, and that they all be placed and bound within it and led out into the middle of the sea, and then the ship set on fire and burned. Thus they were brought forth from the dungeon, and the opponents of the Trinity <note>original: "Bestreiter der Dreyeinigkeit"; this refers to the Arians, who held the heterodox belief that Jesus was a created being rather than co-equal and co-eternal with God the Father.</note> led the people of God like innocent sheep to the slaughter-bench; the clanking heavy chains were to be seen as pleasant necklaces, because they regarded them not as bonds but as ornaments. They therefore went as confidently to death as to a banquet, and sang with one accord along the streets to the praise of the Lord:

> Glory be to God in the highest, and peace on earth to those people pleasing to God! <note>Luke 2:14.</note> This is the desired day, and the most solemn of all! This is the acceptable time! This is the day of salvation, when we shall suffer the prepared martyr-death for the sake of the faith of our God and Lord, so that we may not lose the hard-won long robe of faith.

But the people also cried out loudly: "Do not fear, you witnesses of God, and do not be terrified by the threats of the present tribulation, but rather die for Christ, just as He died for us and has redeemed us with His precious blood!"

## Chapter 60.

### The courageous spirit of the youth Maximus. The martyrs are slain after the fire fails.

The authors of all this misery vehemently pursued one among them, whom the Arians regarded as a youth, named Maximus. They sought to draw him away from the holy company, saying to him: "Youth, why do you hasten to your death? Let them go, they are insane; but obey our counsel, so that you may live further and be received into our great King's palace!" To this he, who was only a boy in age but of a mature age of spirit, gave the answer: "No one shall separate me from my holy Father Liberatus and my brothers, who have raised me in their lonely huts. With them I have walked in the fear of God, with them I also wish to suffer and die, with whom I await the future glory in faith. Do not think that you will lead my childhood astray. The Lord has willed to gather us seven together; He also deems us worthy to be crowned together now in one martyrdom. Just as none of the seven Mac- <note>The text cuts off here, referring to the "Maccabees," seven brothers in the biblical Apocrypha who were martyred together for their faith.</note>

(Ccc) 5
<meta>catchword: chabäi- [Maccabees]</meta>

Here, the narrative details their miraculous resistance to fire and their eventual brutal execution.</meta>

<page-num>778</page-num>
<header>100. African History of Martyrs. Years 427–475.</header>

[seen] brothers <note>This refers to the other six monks who were Maximus's mentors.</note> were lost, so too shall our blessed number not be broken; for if I deny Him, He will also deny me, because He Himself says: *Whoever denies me before men, him will I also deny before my Heavenly Father; and whoever confesses me before men, him will I also confess before my Heavenly Father!* Matthew 10, v. 33. Thus they were hastily brought to death and to the ship, according to the will of the wicked King <note>King Huneric, the Vandal ruler who persecuted the Nicene Christians.</note> and his cruel servants, where they were dragged along and bound tightly with their hands and feet spread out. Now, when the wood had been lit, it happened—so that all could see it—that it was immediately extinguished; and though it was repeated several times by means of ignited stubble and brushwood, the fiery flame nevertheless went out every time. 

Now, as the tyrant became very angry and ashamed because of this, he gave the order that they should be beaten almost to death with oars; thus they smashed in the brains of each one as if they had been dogs. In this manner, they blessedly surrendered their spirits to the Lord, and did not fear being killed by the striking wood, for they had always placed their hope in the wood of the Cross. 

When their honorable corpses were thrown into the sea, the water—contrary to the nature of the sea—gave the bodies back unharmed that very same day and cast them onto the shore. It did not dare to keep them for three days in the depths, as is otherwise customary, so that it would not be disobedient to the command of the Lord. It is said that the tyrant was so terrified by this miracle. The joyful multitude of believers who were present buried the bodies of the holy martyrs with all diligence, led by the Carthaginian clergy. There, the remains of the praiseworthy Deacon (a confessor) and of Mirita <note>Likely a reference to a specific saint or location associated with the Celerine church.</note> rest. The bodies of the blessed saints were interred with public hymns in the monastery near the Celerine Church. In this manner, the most blessed martyrs and confessors of the Holy Trinity suffered and completed their glorious race, and were crowned by the Lord; to whom belongs the honor and glorification into the eternity of eternities. Amen!

# Manuscript Cover

**Exterior Binding Description**

This page illustrates the decorative **marbled paper** used for the book's cover. The design features a **"peacock"** or **"feather"** pattern, a classic style in bookbinding characterized by repeating, overlapping fan-like or scalloped shapes that resemble bird plumage.

The color palette of the marbling includes:
* **Maroon-red**
* **Light blue**
* **Pale yellow**
* **Cream**

The marbled paper is mounted onto a stiff board. The edge shows a worn, **dark brown leather binding** <note>This style of binding, using leather for the spine/corners and paper for the sides, is known as a "half-binding" or "quarter-binding."</note>. There is visible scuffing and loss of the leather's finish at the corners and edges, consistent with historical handling and age.

->**Technical Terms**<-

<term>Marbled paper</term> <note>A decorative paper created by floating pigments on a liquid surface, manipulate them with combs or brushes, and then lifting the pattern onto a sheet of paper.</note>
<term>Peacock pattern</term> <note>A specific marbling design achieved by using a specialized comb to create feathered, arched shapes.</note>
<term>Bookbinding</term> <note>The craft of physically assembling a book from a stack of paper sheets, encompassing the sewing of pages and the application of protective covers.</note>
<term>Decorative arts</term> <note>The design and manufacture of functional objects that are also aesthetically pleasing, such as these ornamental papers.</note>

<summary>This page presents the physical exterior of the manuscript, which is bound in a traditional peacock-patterned marbled paper with a weathered dark brown leather spine.</summary>
<keywords>marbled paper, peacock pattern, bookbinding, decorative arts, leather binding</keywords>
